title: Any / Unit / Nothing hierarchy
text: Walk me through Kotlin's type hierarchy. Where do Any , Any? , Unit , Nothing and Nothing? sit, and what does each map to on the JVM? " Any? is the top type: every value, null included, is an Any? . Any is the top of non-null types and maps to java.lang.Object . Every non-null type T is a subtype of its nullable twin T? . At the bottom is Nothing , which has no values and is a subtype of every type, so an expression that never completes, such as throw , fits anywhere. Nothing? has exactly one value, null , which is why null can go into any nullable type. Unit is just an ordinary singleton object that means 'no useful result'. It is not the bottom type."

title: Safe call / elvis / `!!`
text: Explain ?. , ?: and !! . What type does each expression have, and when is each one the right tool? " a?.b evaluates a . If a is null the whole expression is null and b is never touched. Otherwise it accesses b . The result is always nullable. a ?: b returns a if it is not null, otherwise it evaluates b , lazily. The result type is the common supertype of non-null A and B . Because throw and return have type Nothing , ?: return and ?: throw narrow the value to non-null. a!! turns A? into A and throws a NullPointerException if it is null. I use !! only where null would be a programmer error and I want a crash right at that line. Anything that comes from I/O, Java or the user gets a safe call or elvis."

title: Unit vs Void
text: What is Unit and how is it different from Java's void and Void ? " Unit is a real type with exactly one value, the Unit object. A Kotlin function returning Unit compiles to JVM void , so normal calls cost nothing. Because it is a real type, it works as a type argument: - Unit is Function0<Unit , and Deferred<Unit is fine. Java void is not a type, so you can't write List<void . Java's Void is a type, but its only legal value is null , so it is closer to Kotlin's Nothing? . The practical pain is Java code implementing a Kotlin lambda: it has to return Unit.INSTANCE; ."

title: Platform types
text: What is a platform type, what does String! mean, and why didn't Kotlin just treat every Java type as nullable? "When Kotlin sees a Java type with no nullability information, it gives it a platform type, written T! in IDE hints and error messages. You can't write it in source. It means 'the nullability is unknown'. The compiler lets you use it as either T or T? , and it does not check. If you treat it as non-null and it is null, you get an NPE. That's either at the dereference, or earlier, at an inserted check, if you assign it to a declared non-null type. Kotlin chose this over 'everything is nullable' because that would force !! or ?. on every Java call, including generics like ArrayList<String? , and the language would be unusable with Java."

title: Nothing in expressions
text: Show me how Nothing works in everyday code: throw , TODO , ?: return , functions that never return. What does the compiler do with it? " throw , return , break and continue are expressions of type Nothing . Because Nothing is a subtype of everything, they can sit in any expression slot, such as an elvis right-hand side, an if branch or a when branch, without changing the result type. The compiler also does flow analysis: after an expression of type Nothing , the code is unreachable. So after val x = y ?: return , x is non-null, and after a call to a function returning Nothing you get an 'unreachable code' warning. TODO and error are just stdlib functions returning Nothing ."

title: How null safety compiles (Intrinsics)
text: Kotlin types are erased to plain JVM references. So how is null safety enforced at runtime? What does the compiler actually insert? "Null safety is mostly compile-time. At the boundaries where Java can sneak in a null, the compiler inserts calls to kotlin.jvm.internal.Intrinsics . Every non-private function gets checkNotNullParameter for each non-null reference parameter, because Java or reflection could call it with null. When a platform-typed Java result is stored in, or passed as, a non-null Kotlin type, the compiler inserts checkNotNullExpressionValue , which gives the 'getX ... must not be null' message. !! compiles to a plain null check that throws. Since Kotlin 1.4 these all throw NullPointerException . Private functions skip the parameter check, because only Kotlin code that has already been type-checked can call them."

title: Smart-cast rules
text: When does Kotlin smart cast a value after an is or null check, and when does it refuse? Explain the reasoning behind each rule. "The compiler only smart casts when it can prove the value can't change between the check and the use. It calls such a value 'stable'. Local val s are always stable, except for local delegated properties, because a delegate's getValue can return anything. Local var s are stable if nothing modifies them between check and use, and no lambda that modifies them has captured them. A val property is stable only if it is private or internal , or is declared in the same module, and has no custom getter and isn't open . Each of those could make two reads return different values. A var property is never smart cast, since another thread or method can write to it. The fix is almost always to copy it into a local val first."

title: Smart cast vs `!!` on mutable properties
text: What's wrong, why did the compiler "allow" it, and how do you fix it properly? A news app 1.5M DAU, 60% Android 12+ shipped release 8.4. Crash-free sessions dropped from 99.82% to 99.61%. The top new crash: java.lang.NullPointerException at com.app.feed.FeedPresenter.renderHeader FeedPresenter.kt:88 at com.app.feed.FeedPresenter.onFeedLoaded FeedPresenter.kt:61 at com.app.feed.FeedRepository$load$1.onResponse FeedRepository.kt:44 at okhttp3.internal.connection.RealCall$AsyncCall.run RealCall.kt:519 Line 88 is if session != null header.bind session!!.displayName . session is var session: Session? = null on the presenter. The 8.4 diff added "logout on 401", which sets session = null from an auth callback. 70% of crashes come from users on flaky networks. The same release bumped OkHttp, and that is what the team is looking at.

title: Elvis precedence & safe-call evaluation
text: Find the bugs and explain the exact evaluation rules behind each one. A checkout screen cart sizes 1 to 40 items . QA reports: "Total shows ₹49 for a ₹1,200 cart" and "audit log missing for guest users". The code: data class Cart val subtotal: Int?, val items: List<Item fun total cart: Cart?, shipping: Int : Int = cart?.subtotal ?: 0 + shipping fun applyCoupon order: Order?, code: String { order?.coupon = couponService.redeem code // redeem also writes an audit record } fun isBigCart cart: Cart? = cart?.items?.size ?: 0 10 The ₹49 is the shipping fee. The team thinks the backend is sending a wrong subtotal .

title: Platform types & Java-interop NPEs
text: Where exactly do NPEs come from when Kotlin calls Java? Walk through the different failure points and how you'd design the boundary. "There are four ways it goes wrong. First, I dereference a platform value: a plain JVM NPE at that line. Second, I assign or pass a platform value into a declared non-null Kotlin type: a Kotlin-generated check throws 'X must not be null' at that line. Third, I override a Java method with non-null params and Java passes null: a checkNotNullParameter NPE at method entry. Fourth, a Java collection has null elements but I typed it List<String : nothing checks, and it crashes wherever I use the element. My boundary rule: at every Java seam, declare explicit Kotlin types, nullable unless the Java side is annotated or documented non-null, and convert in one adapter layer."

title: Nullability annotations Kotlin honors
text: Which nullability annotations does the Kotlin compiler understand, and how strictly does it enforce them? How do you control that? "Kotlin reads a fixed set of annotation families from Java and turns annotated types into real T or T? instead of platform types. The families are JetBrains org.jetbrains.annotations , AndroidX and the old Android support annotations, JSR-305 javax.annotation , FindBugs, Eclipse, Lombok @NonNull , RxJava 3, Vert.x, and JSpecify org.jspecify.annotations . How hard a violation hits depends on the family. JSpecify mismatches are errors by default in current Kotlin. Most others can be set per package with -Xnullability-annotations=@pkg:ignore warn strict . JSR-305 has its own -Xjsr305 flag. For new Java code I'd use JSpecify with @NullMarked ."

title: Platform types from a Java SDK
text: Diagnose this and fix it, both now and structurally. A fintech app 2M DAU bumped a Java-only payments SDK from 4.2 to 4.3 in release 11.0. 36 hours after a 20% rollout, the crash rate went from 0.15% to 1.2% of sessions on the checkout screen: java.lang.NullPointerException: getSessionToken ... must not be null at com.app.pay.PaymentRepository.startCheckout PaymentRepository.kt:41 at com.app.pay.CheckoutViewModel$pay$1.invokeSuspend CheckoutViewModel.kt:77 Line 41 is val token: String = sdk.getSession .getSessionToken . 62% of crashes are on Samsung Android 14 devices. The same release also changed R8 keep rules. The SDK changelog says: "Session initialization is now lazy and asynchronous."

title: Holes in null safety
text: Can a value declared as a non-null Kotlin type ever be null at runtime? List the ways, and say which ones the compiler-inserted checks catch. "Yes. Null safety is a compile-time guarantee about Kotlin code, plus runtime checks only at function entry and at platform-type assignments. Nulls get in through Java callers writing fields directly, Java subclasses overriding a Kotlin method and returning null, reflection-based deserializers that skip constructors, generic containers filled by Java, unchecked casts on erased generics, and reading a property before it's initialized during construction. The inserted checks catch Java calling non-private functions with null and platform values assigned to non-null types. They don't catch fields, reflection, generic contents, or override return values."

title: Annotating a legacy Java module
text: Plan the migration. How do you get the safety without a big-bang PR or breaking the weekly train? A ride-hailing app has a 180k-LOC Java module :legacy-core pricing, trips, user . 70% of feature work is now Kotlin, calling into it. Over the last 90 days, 41% of all NPE crashes about 0.09% of sessions out of 3M DAU originate at Kotlin/Java seams in this module. A spike PR adding JSpecify @NullMarked to every package and building with default strict JSpecify handling produced 1,140 Kotlin compile errors across 9 feature modules. Releases go out weekly. The team can't freeze features.

title: `TODO()` / Nothing-returning helpers in production
text: Run the review. What's the real root cause, and what changes do you drive? You're leading the post-incident review. A food-delivery app 800k DAU had a 3-hour window where crash-free sessions dropped from 99.7% to 98.9%. Timeline: the backend shipped a new order status "REASSIGNED" at 18:05. The app crashed when opening order tracking: kotlin.NotImplementedError: An operation is not implemented: map REASSIGNED later at com.app.orders.StatusMapper.map StatusMapper.kt:23 at com.app.orders.OrderRepository.track OrderRepository.kt:58 The code: fun map raw: String : OrderStatus = when raw { "PLACED" - OrderStatus.Placed "PICKED" - OrderStatus.Picked "DELIVERED" - OrderStatus.Delivered else - TODO "map $raw later" } // OrderRepository.track try { emitStatus mapper.map dto.status } catch e: Exception { emitStatus OrderStatus.Unknown } Someone says, "But we have a try/catch, so this can't crash." The backend team is being blamed for the deploy.

title: Smart casts across modules & custom getters
text: What do you recommend and why? Explain what the compiler is protecting against. A team is splitting a monolith app into 48 Gradle modules. After moving Config , UserSession and the model classes into :core:model , the feature modules show 640 errors like: Smart cast to 'String' is impossible, because 'config.cdnHost' is a public API property declared in different module. A senior dev proposes a codemod that adds !! at all 640 sites "since the code worked before". Another proposes making the models internal with @PublishedApi tricks. Meanwhile, Config.cdnHost is declared as val cdnHost: String? get = remoteConfig.getString "cdn" .takeIf { it.isNotBlank } . Remote config refreshes in the background every 12 hours.

title: Designing null-safe APIs
text: When you design a Kotlin API, how do you decide between returning T? , throwing a Nothing -typed path , or returning a richer result type? What conventions does the stdlib follow? "I return T? when absence is a normal, single-meaning outcome. A lookup miss is the classic case, and the caller can handle it in one ?: . I throw when the caller broke a precondition or the state is impossible, using require , check or error , whose Nothing paths smart-cast cleanly. When there's more than one way to fail, or the caller needs the reason, I return a sealed result instead of null. The stdlib convention is pairs: first throws and firstOrNull returns null. getOrNull , getOrElse and getOrThrow work the same way. Name the nullable variant with OrNull , so the call site says what happens."

title: Cost of null-safety checks
text: Do you approve? How would you evaluate it? A performance squad on a large super-app 140 modules, 95k Kotlin methods in release dex, cold start p50 1.9s on a Snapdragon 6-series reference device proposes for release builds: kotlin { compilerOptions { freeCompilerArgs.addAll "-Xno-param-assertions", "-Xno-call-assertions" } } plus an R8 rule: -assumenosideeffects class kotlin.jvm.internal.Intrinsics { public static void checkNotNullParameter java.lang.Object, java.lang.String ; public static void checkNotNullExpressionValue java.lang.Object, java.lang.String ; } Their claim, from a blog post: "1 to 2% smaller dex and measurably faster startup." There's no benchmark yet. Crash-free users are 99.6%, and 18% of NPE crash groups today show checkNotNullParameter or must not be null in the top frame.

title: lateinit vs lazy vs nullable
text: You have a property that can't be given a value in the constructor. When do you pick lateinit var , by lazy , or a nullable var x: T? = null ? I start by asking who supplies the value. If something outside the class supplies it later, through an injector, a lifecycle callback or a test setup, I use lateinit var . I'm promising it gets set before first read, and if I break that promise I get a loud UninitializedPropertyAccessException . If the class can compute the value itself but it's costly or not always needed, I use val by lazy : it computes once on first read and caches. If "no value" is a real, valid state, such as no logged-in user or a view that was destroyed, I use a nullable type, so the compiler makes every caller handle it.

title: lateinit compilation & runtime
text: What does a lateinit var compile to on the JVM, and what exactly happens when you read one that hasn't been set? A lateinit var compiles to a normal nullable JVM reference field, with null meaning "not set yet". The getter checks that field. If it's null, the getter calls Intrinsics.throwUninitializedPropertyAccessException with the property name, which throws kotlin.UninitializedPropertyAccessException: lateinit property x has not been initialized . The setter has no check. One unusual detail: the backing field is exposed to Java with the same visibility as the property's setter. That is what lets Dagger/Hilt write @Inject lateinit var fields directly.

title: lateinit restrictions
text: Why can't lateinit be used with Int , with nullable types, with val , or with custom getters? What do you use instead? Every restriction comes from one design choice: lateinit uses null in the backing field to mean "not set". A primitive int field can't hold null, so Int , Long , Boolean and the other primitives are out. A nullable type would make null mean both "not set" and "set to null", so that is banned too. val is banned because the whole point is to assign the value after construction. Custom accessors are banned because the compiler generates the getter that does the check. For primitives I use Delegates.notNull<Int , or I rethink the design and use a nullable or a default value.

title: ::x.isInitialized
text: How does ::x.isInitialized work, where can you call it, and why do some reviewers treat it as a code smell? this::x.isInitialized available since Kotlin 1.2 returns whether the lateinit backing field is non-null. The compiler doesn't use reflection for it. It compiles straight to a null check on the field. That's why you can only call it where the backing field is lexically accessible: inside the declaring class, an outer class, or the same file for top-level properties. I treat frequent use as a smell, because a lateinit that needs checking is usually a nullable value in disguise.

title: lateinit & lifecycle order
text: What's going on, and how do you fix it? A shopping app has 2M DAU. A week after release 7.4, Crashlytics shows a new top crash at 0.35% of sessions: Fatal Exception: kotlin.UninitializedPropertyAccessException: lateinit property cartPresenter has not been initialized at com.shop.MainActivity.getCartPresenter MainActivity.kt:41 at com.shop.cart.CartBadgeFragment.onCreate CartBadgeFragment.kt:28 at androidx.fragment.app.Fragment.performCreate Fragment.java:3094 ... at androidx.fragment.app.FragmentActivity.onCreate FragmentActivity.java:... at com.shop.MainActivity.onCreate MainActivity.kt:55 MainActivity.onCreate calls super.onCreate savedInstanceState on line 55 and assigns cartPresenter = CartPresenter ... on line 58. CartBadgeFragment.onCreate does requireActivity as MainActivity .cartPresenter.attach this . QA can't reproduce it on fresh launches. 80% of crashes come from devices with 3 GB of RAM or less. The release also bumped the Firebase SDK.

title: is / as / as?
text: Explain is , as , and as? in Kotlin. What does each do at runtime, and when would you use each? is is a runtime type check that returns a Boolean. After it succeeds on a stable value, the compiler smart-casts the value, so I don't need an explicit cast. as is an unsafe cast: if the value isn't that type it throws ClassCastException , and casting null to a non-null type throws NullPointerException since Kotlin 1.4. as? is the safe cast: it returns null on mismatch. I usually pair it with ?: to supply a default or return early. I use when x { is A - ... } for branching on types, as? at trust boundaries, and as only when a mismatch really is a programmer error and I want it to crash.

title: Unsafe & unchecked casts
text: What is an unchecked cast in Kotlin? Why can a bad cast throw ClassCastException somewhere other than where you wrote as ? When you cast to a generic type such as as List<String , or as T inside a generic function, the JVM can only check the raw class, or nothing at all for T . So the compiler warns "Unchecked cast" and emits little or no check. The wrong value passes through, and the ClassCastException appears later. It appears wherever the compiler inserted a concrete checkcast , which is usually where you first read an element as String . I treat every @Suppress "UNCHECKED CAST" as a debt that needs a justification comment. I prefer reified type parameters or explicit element checks.

title: Unsafe casts on Android Context
text: Find the bugs, explain why they only showed up now, and fix them. The profile screen used to be an Activity. It was migrated into a @AndroidEntryPoint Fragment inside MainActivity . The custom view below hasn't changed in 2 years. The day after release, the ClassCastException rate jumps from 0 to 1.2% of profile-screen opens, on all OS versions. Pixel and Samsung devices are equally affected. The Compose-based settings screen, which uses a similar helper, shows a smaller but non-zero number of the same crash. class AvatarView context: Context, attrs: AttributeSet? : FrameLayout context, attrs { private val host = context as AppCompatActivity init { setOnClickListener { host.supportFragmentManager.beginTransaction .add AvatarPickerDialog , "picker" .commit } } } @Composable fun ShareButton { val activity = LocalContext.current as Activity Button onClick = { activity.startActivity shareIntent } { Text "Share" } } java.lang.ClassCastException: dagger.hilt.android.internal.managers.ViewComponentManager$FragmentContextWrapper cannot be cast to androidx.appcompat.app.AppCompatActivity at com.app.profile.AvatarView.<init AvatarView.kt:3

title: Int vs Int? and boxing
text: Kotlin has no separate int and Integer . So how does Kotlin decide whether an Int is a JVM primitive or a boxed object, and why should you care? Kotlin's Int becomes a JVM int wherever it can. It gets boxed into java.lang.Integer when it has to be an object: when it's nullable Int? , when it's used as a generic type argument List<Int , Map<String, Int , T , when it's passed as Any , or when it goes into a non-reified generic. Boxing costs an allocation, except for cached small values, and an unboxing read. It also makes identity comparison === unreliable. For hot paths and large arrays I use non-null Int and IntArray .

title: Integer cache and === trap
text: Why does val a: Int? = 127; val b: Int? = 127; a === b print true , while the same code with 128 prints false ? Int? values are boxed through Integer.valueOf , and the JDK keeps a cache of Integer objects for -128 to 127. So two boxings of 127 return the same object and === reference identity is true. 128 is outside the cache, so each boxing allocates a new object and === is false, even though == is true. == in Kotlin calls equals , which is what you want for values. === on numbers is almost always a bug.

title: Boxed identity comparison
text: Walk me through how you'd diagnose and fix this, and what you'd put in place so it can't recur. A notes app has 600k DAU and a RecyclerView with a ListAdapter. After release 3.8, users report "the whole list flashes on every edit", "scroll jumps to top", and "the swipe animation is gone". Play Console shows slow frames rising from 4% to 19% on the notes list, but only for long-time users. New users and QA, who use seeded DBs with about 30 notes, see nothing. The release also updated RecyclerView 1.3.1 → 1.3.2 and enabled R8 full mode. The diff in the adapter: @Entity data class NoteEntity @PrimaryKey autoGenerate = true val id: Long? = null, val title: String, val updatedAt: Long object NoteDiff : DiffUtil.ItemCallback<NoteEntity { override fun areItemsTheSame old: NoteEntity, new: NoteEntity = old.id === new.id // changed from == in 3.8 "for speed" override fun areContentsTheSame old: NoteEntity, new: NoteEntity = old == new } Perfetto on an affected device shows RV OnBindView for every visible row on each submitList , instead of one row.

title: Number conversions
text: Kotlin won't let you assign an Int to a Long variable. Why not, and what are the rules for numeric conversions, literals, and mixed arithmetic? In Kotlin, numeric types aren't subtypes of each other. Int isn't a Long , so there's no implicit widening on assignment or argument passing. You convert explicitly with toLong , toInt , toDouble and so on. Literals are the exception: an integer literal takes the expected type if it fits val l: Long = 5 , and it defaults to Int , or to Long if it's too big for Int . Arithmetic between mixed types is allowed through operator overloads and returns the wider type Int + Long → Long . Narrowing conversions silently truncate or wrap, and Double.toInt truncates toward zero and saturates.

title: Integer overflow in time math
text: Lead the review. What happened mechanically, why didn't tests catch it, and what changes do you commit to? You're running the post-incident review. A news app 1.5M DAU caches article lists, and the TTL is driven by remote config cache ttl days default 7 . On Tuesday at 10:00 product changed it to 30 to "reduce backend load". By 10:20 the article API's QPS had gone from 2.1k to 17k 8x . The backend started returning 429s, and app-side p95 feed load went from 380 ms to 4.2 s. Rolling the config back to 7 at 11:05 restored everything. Relevant code: fun ttlMillis days: Int : Long = days 24 60 60 1000 .toLong fun isFresh savedAt: Long, now: Long, days: Int = now - savedAt < ttlMillis days A unit test isFresh savedAt = 0, now = 1000, days = 7 passes. There's also a Slack thread blaming a CDN change that went out Tuesday at 09:30.

title: Char/String internals, templates, raw strings
text: What is a Char in Kotlin, how are String s represented, and what do string templates and raw strings compile to? Where do they bite you? On the JVM a Char is a 16-bit UTF-16 code unit. It is not a number: you get its code with .code and a digit's value with digitToInt . A String is an immutable java.lang.String , and its API is in UTF-16 units, so length counts code units, not user-visible characters. String templates "$a ${b.c}" compile to concatenation, either a StringBuilder chain or invokedynamic string concat when the JVM target is 9+, which D8 desugars on Android. They call toString on each value, so a null prints as "null" . Raw strings """...""" have no escape sequences and keep newlines. $ still interpolates, so you write ${'$'} for a literal dollar sign, and you normally finish with trimIndent or trimMargin .

title: Unicode length and truncation
text: What does "20 characters" mean, and how would you implement validation and truncation correctly across clients and backend? A chat app 900k DAU, 40% of users in markets where emoji-heavy names are common has the product spec "Display name: max 20 characters. Notification preview: first 40 characters + ellipsis." The current code: fun isValidName name: String = name.isNotBlank && name.length <= 20 fun preview body: String = if body.length 40 body.take 40 + "…" else body Support tickets: a "App says my name is too long but it's only 6 flags" each flag is 2 code points = 4 UTF-16 units, so 6 flags = 24 units . b The iOS app accepts the same name. c Notification previews sometimes end with a box or a ? before the ellipsis. d The backend rejected about 0.2% of profile updates with 400 invalid UTF-8 after the client started doing name.toByteArray for a signature. The backend column is VARCHAR 20 with utf8mb4 counts code points . A red herring in the Slack thread: "it's the font on Samsung devices".

title: Type inference limits
text: Where does Kotlin's type inference fail, or infer a type you didn't want? When do you choose to write explicit types even though inference would work? Inference fails outright in a few places: recursive functions with expression bodies, lambdas without an expected type { x - x 2 } , and empty generic factories emptyList with nothing to infer from . The more dangerous cases are when it succeeds with the wrong type. var state = UiState.Loading infers the Loading subtype, so you can never assign Success . val state = MutableStateFlow UiState.Loading infers MutableStateFlow<UiState.Loading . if c 1 else "x" infers an intersection type. Public members with inferred types leak implementation types MutableStateFlow , ArrayList , RepoImpl into your API. So I write explicit types on public or protected API, on sealed-state holders, and wherever the declared type should be wider than the initializer.

title: Reflection parsers vs null-safety
text: Explain how a non-null Kotlin property ended up null, why the crash is far from the parse, and how you'd fix it for good. An e-commerce app 3M DAU, Retrofit + Gson shipped 9.2. Two days later, a new crash group at 0.6% of sessions, all in the product-list screen, mostly from one region: java.lang.NullPointerException: Parameter specified as non-null is null: method com.shop.ui.PriceFormatter.format, parameter currency at com.shop.ui.PriceFormatter.format PriceFormatter.kt:12 at com.shop.ui.ProductViewHolder.bind ProductViewHolder.kt:57 at androidx.recyclerview.widget.RecyclerView$Adapter.onBindViewHolder ... The model: data class ProductDto val id: String, val title: String, val price: Long, val currency: String, // non-null in Kotlin val badges: List<String = emptyList Other facts: 9.2 also turned on R8 full mode AGP 8 upgrade . The backend team says "no API changes". But the regional pricing service was migrated on the same day, and for products in a promo it omits currency . A second, rarer crash elsewhere: NullPointerException ... List.size on a null object reference from badges , even though it has a default value.

title: Data class generated members
text: What does the compiler generate for a data class , and which properties take part in it? For a data class the compiler generates equals , hashCode , toString , copy and component1 ..componentN . All of them use only the properties declared in the primary constructor. A property declared in the class body is invisible to every generated member. If I write equals , hashCode or toString myself, or a supertype has a final version, the compiler doesn't generate that member. copy and componentN can't be hand-written.

title: == vs ===
text: What's the difference between == and === in Kotlin, and what does a == b compile to? == is structural equality. It compiles to a?.equals b ?: b === null , so it's null-safe and calls equals . === is referential equality: same object or not, and it never calls equals . One trap: for Float / Double statically typed as such, == follows IEEE 754 NaN != NaN , 0.0 == -0.0 . When the static type is Any or generic, == falls back to equals , which has the opposite results.

title: equals/hashCode contract
text: State the equals/hashCode contract. What goes wrong in a HashMap if I override equals but not hashCode , and how does inheritance break equals ? equals must be reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent and return false for null. Equal objects must have equal hash codes, though unequal objects may collide. If I override equals without hashCode , two equal objects land in different buckets, so map key misses and a Set holds duplicates. With inheritance, an is -based equals in a base class plus an extra field in a subclass breaks symmetry. That's why data classes are final and compare with other !is Type .

title: copy() semantics
text: Is a data class copy deep or shallow? What are the consequences, and what changed about copy visibility in Kotlin 2.x? copy is shallow. It calls the primary constructor with the same references for every property I don't override, so a MutableList or nested mutable object is shared between the original and the copy. That's fine and fast if everything nested is immutable, and dangerous if anything is mutable. On visibility: before Kotlin 2.0.20, copy was always public, even with a private constructor, which let callers bypass validation. 2.0.20 started a deprecation cycle so that copy matches the constructor's visibility. You opt in now with @ConsistentCopyVisibility or -Xconsistent-data-class-copy-visibility .

title: Destructuring & componentN
text: How does destructuring like val id, name = user work, and what's the risk of using it on data classes? Destructuring compiles to calls to component1 , component2 and so on. Those are operator functions that a data class generates in primary-constructor order. Any class can opt in by declaring operator fun componentN . The risk is that it's positional, not by name. If someone reorders two same-typed properties in the constructor, every destructuring site silently swaps values and still compiles.

title: Data class inheritance limits
text: Why can't a data class be open ? What can a data class inherit from, and what happens to the generated members when it does? A data class is implicitly final and can't be open , abstract , sealed or inner . A subclass adding fields would break equals symmetry and make copy return the wrong type. A data class can extend an open or abstract class and implement interfaces. That's the standard sealed interface UiState + data class Success ... : UiState pattern. If the parent has final equals / hashCode / toString , the data class uses the parent's versions. If the parent declares open properties, the data class can override them in its constructor.

title: Enum classes
text: What can a Kotlin enum class contain? Show constructor properties, per-constant bodies and interface implementation. What does each compile to? An enum is a class with a fixed set of instances created once in its static initializer. It can have constructor properties, methods, abstract members that each constant implements in its own body, and it can implement interfaces. Every constant gets name and ordinal . The class gets valueOf String , values and, since Kotlin 1.9, entries . A constant with a body compiles to an anonymous subclass. That affects javaClass , so use declaringJavaClass instead.

title: Enum entries, values(), EnumMap/EnumSet
text: Why did Kotlin add Enum.entries to replace values ? And when would you use EnumMap / EnumSet instead of HashMap / HashSet keyed by an enum? values returns a fresh clone of the internal array on every call, because arrays are mutable and the JVM can't hand out the shared one. Calling it in a loop or in onBind allocates every time. entries , stable since Kotlin 1.9.0, returns a pre-built immutable EnumEntries<E , a List<E , so it costs nothing per call and works with collection APIs. Kotlin 2.0.0 added the generic enumEntries<T to replace enumValues<T for the same reason. EnumMap and EnumSet index by ordinal into an array or bit vector, which is faster and smaller than hashing. I use them for any enum-keyed lookup.

title: when exhaustiveness with enums
text: When does the compiler force a when on an enum to be exhaustive, and why do senior engineers avoid else branches on enums? A when used as an expression must be exhaustive. Since Kotlin 1.7, a when statement whose subject is an enum, sealed type or Boolean must also be exhaustive it was a warning in 1.6 . I list every constant and skip else . Then adding a constant breaks the build at every place that needs a decision, instead of silently falling into a default branch. The exception is enums owned by another module or the server, where new values can arrive at runtime without a recompile.

title: object declarations internals
text: How does a Kotlin object compile? Is it thread-safe, when exactly is it initialized, and what happens if its initialization throws? An object compiles to a final class with a private constructor and a public static final INSTANCE field assigned in its static initializer <clinit . It's lazy because the JVM and ART initialize a class on first active use, such as accessing INSTANCE or a static member. It's thread-safe because class initialization runs under a per-class init lock JLS 12.4.2 . Other threads block until it finishes, with no double-checked locking needed. If <clinit throws, the first caller gets ExceptionInInitializerError and the class is marked erroneous. Every later access then throws NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class X for the life of the process.

title: companion objects
text: What is a companion object at the bytecode level, when is it initialized, and how is it different from a top-level declaration or a plain object ? A companion compiles to a nested class Outer$Companion plus a public static final Companion field on Outer . Backing fields of companion properties are actually private static fields on Outer , accessed through instance getters on Companion . It's initialized in Outer 's static initializer, so it initializes when Outer is first used, including the first Outer construction. That's Java static-init semantics. Unlike a top-level function, it can implement interfaces, be passed as a value and receive extension functions. A top-level declaration is cheaper and simpler when you don't need any of that.

title: data object (Kotlin 1.9+)
text: What is a data object , what exactly does it generate, and why should sealed-state singletons like Loading be data object s rather than plain object s? A data object is a singleton that generates toString , which returns just the name Loading instead of Loading@1b6d3586 , plus equals and hashCode that treat any instance of that type as equal. It doesn't generate copy or componentN , since there are no properties, and you can't override its equals / hashCode . It went from preview in 1.8.20 to stable in 1.9.0. For sealed hierarchies it gives readable logs and test diffs, and stays correct even if reflection or serialization creates a second instance. The docs say to compare data objects with == , never === .

title: Mutable data class as hash key
text: Find the bug, explain it mechanically, and fix it. A download manager in a 1.2M-DAU podcast app shows a "N downloads active" badge. After the last release, about 6% of users report the badge stuck at "1" or "2" with nothing downloading, and heap dumps from internal testers show DownloadTask objects accumulating 4k per long session . The team suspects a threading issue because progress comes from Dispatchers.IO . The code simplified, assume single-threaded access for now : data class DownloadTask val episodeId: String, var progress: Int = 0, var state: State = State.QUEUED enum class State { QUEUED, RUNNING, DONE } class DownloadTracker { private val active = mutableSetOf<DownloadTask // LinkedHashSet val activeCount: Int get = active.size fun start task: DownloadTask { task.state = State.RUNNING; active += task } fun onProgress task: DownloadTask, p: Int { task.progress = p } fun finish task: DownloadTask { task.state = State.DONE val removed = active.remove task Log.d "DL", "finish ${task.episodeId} removed=$removed" // logs removed=false } }

title: copy() bypassing invariants & copy visibility
text: What's the root cause, how do you fix it, and how do you roll out the copy visibility change without breaking partner apps? A wallet app 2.5M MAU models money as a validated value, and also ships the type in a small public SDK used by 3 partner apps: data class Amount private constructor val cents: Long, val currency: String { companion object { fun of cents: Long, currency: String : Amount? = if cents = 0 && currency.length == 3 Amount cents, currency else null } } // somewhere in refunds: val net = original.copy cents = original.cents - fee.cents The backend reports 0.3% of refund requests arriving with negative amounts about 900/day , which it rejects. title: Persisting enums (ordinal vs name)
text: Walk me through mitigation, data repair under live traffic, and the long-term design. A food-delivery app 4M DAU, about 3.4M locally cached order rows across devices stores order status in Room through a custom converter, and the user's theme in SharedPreferences: enum class OrderStatus { PENDING, PREPARING, OUT FOR DELIVERY, DELIVERED, CANCELLED } class Converters { @TypeConverter fun toInt s: OrderStatus = s.ordinal @TypeConverter fun toStatus i: Int = OrderStatus.entries i } prefs.edit .putInt "theme", theme.ordinal .apply In v8.4, a developer adds SCHEDULED after PENDING , "to keep the lifecycle in order", and adds SEPIA at the top of the Theme enum. title: Cost of generated hashCode/equals
text: Diagnose and fix. Quantify the problem. A shopping app's product grid has a filter memo cache: data class FilterQuery val category: String, val brandIds: Set<Long , val priceRange: IntRange, val hiddenIds: Set<Long // products the user hid; power users have 15k–20k private val memo = HashMap<FilterQuery, List<Product fun visibleProducts q: FilterQuery : List<Product = memo.getOrPut q { compute q } // called from onBindViewHolder for "badge" logic, 6x per frame while scrolling On a Galaxy A-series device, scroll jank is 22% janky frames for users with large hiddenIds , versus 3% for others. A Perfetto trace on RenderThread /main shows FilterQuery.hashCode → AbstractSet.hashCode taking about 1.8 ms per call, and the occasional FilterQuery.equals → AbstractSet.equals → containsAll taking about 2.5 ms. GC is noticeable too, but the team's first idea is "switch to Sequences" or "it's GC, increase the heap".

title: object singleton vs DI singleton
text: What's ambiguous in the requirement, and how would you design this? A tech lead asks for a cart that's "the same everywhere, just make it a singleton". The app has 25 feature modules and about 1,400 JVM unit tests. A developer ships: object CartStore { private val items = mutableMapOf<String, Int lateinit var api: CartApi // set in Application.onCreate fun add sku: String { items sku = items sku ?: 0 + 1 } fun count = items.values.sum } Within two weeks: - CI flakiness rises from 1% to 7% of runs: tests pass alone and fail in the full suite. - A QA bug: after logout and login as another user, the previous user's cart shows. - A crash: UninitializedPropertyAccessException: lateinit property api has not been initialized , 0.05% of sessions, from a BroadcastReceiver cold start.

title: Singleton identity across serialization
text: Write the root cause and corrective actions for the review. Why did the else "fix" produce an infinite spinner? You're running the post-incident review for a 0.08% session crash that lasted three releases on a 6M-MAU news app: kotlin.NoWhenBranchMatchedException at com.app.article.ArticleFragment.render ArticleFragment.kt:88 It reproduces only after process death "Don't keep activities" plus backgrounding, or low-RAM devices like 2 GB Android Go . The ViewModel stores the current state in SavedStateHandle : sealed class ArticleState : java.io.Serializable { object Loading : ArticleState object Offline : ArticleState data class Loaded val id: String, val title: String : ArticleState } // ViewModel savedStateHandle "state" = state // Serializable into Bundle val state = savedStateHandle.get<ArticleState "state" ?: ArticleState.Loading // Fragment fun render s: ArticleState = when s { ArticleState.Loading - showSpinner ArticleState.Offline - showOffline is ArticleState.Loaded - showArticle s } Earlier "fixes" in the timeline: someone added else - showSpinner , which stopped the crash, but then users reported "infinite spinner after returning to the app". That was reverted. Red herring in the timeline: a Fragment library upgrade in the same period.

title: Sealed class vs sealed interface vs enum
text: When would you use an enum, a sealed class, or a sealed interface? Give me a concrete example of each. I use an enum when every case has the same shape and exactly one instance, like SortOrder.ASC/DESC . I use a sealed type when the cases carry different data, like Loading , Success items and Error throwable , because each subtype can be a data class, an object or a regular class with its own properties. Between the two sealed kinds, I default to a sealed interface. A sealed class only earns its place when the cases share constructor state or a common implementation. A sealed interface also lets one type belong to several hierarchies, and an enum can implement one.

title: final by default, open, abstract, override
text: Why are Kotlin classes and members final by default? How do open, abstract and override interact? Kotlin follows the "design for inheritance or prohibit it" rule. Every class and member is final unless you mark it open , so a subclass can't depend on internals you never promised to keep stable. abstract implies open and has no implementation. An override is itself open unless you write final override . The cost shows up with tools that need subclassing, like mocking libraries and some frameworks. In practice that's solved with Mockito's inline mock maker or MockK, or with the all-open compiler plugin. I don't solve it by sprinkling open everywhere.

title: Visibility modifiers
text: Explain Kotlin's visibility modifiers. How do they differ from Java's, especially protected and the default? Kotlin has four modifiers: public the default , internal visible inside the same compilation module , protected visible in the class and its subclasses only, with no package access unlike Java , and private . private on a class member means that class only. private on a top-level declaration means that file only. Kotlin has no package-private. internal replaces that idea at the module level, which in Android means a Gradle module.

title: Nested vs inner classes
text: What's the difference between a nested class and an inner class in Kotlin? Why does it matter on Android? In Kotlin, a class declared inside another class is nested by default. That's like a Java static nested class: it holds no reference to the outer instance. Marking it inner gives it a hidden reference to the outer instance, so it can use outer members. That reference is exactly what leaks an Activity or Fragment when an inner-class instance is held by something longer-lived, like a singleton listener list, a Handler message or a background task.

title: Exhaustive when and adding a subclass
text: How does exhaustive when work with sealed types? What happens when someone adds a new subclass? Because the compiler knows every direct subtype of a sealed type, a when that covers them all needs no else . If someone adds a subtype, every exhaustive when without an else becomes a compile error, which is exactly what I want. Since Kotlin 1.7, that applies to when statements over sealed, enum and Boolean subjects as well as to when expressions. The guarantee disappears the moment someone writes else - , so I avoid else on sealed subjects in domain code.

title: Sealed hierarchy package and module rules
text: Where can subclasses of a sealed class or interface be declared? What about indirect subclasses, Java, and multiplatform? Since Kotlin 1.5, direct subclasses must be in the same module and the same package as the sealed type, in any file. Before 1.5 they had to be in the same file. They can be top-level or nested in named classes or objects, but not local classes or anonymous objects. The restriction applies only to direct subtypes. If a direct subtype is open , anyone who can see it can extend it, and exhaustiveness then treats that whole branch as a single case. In multiplatform, direct subclasses must be in the same source set, and an expect sealed type needs else in common code.

title: Value classes basics
text: What is a value class? How is it different from a typealias and from a data class wrapping one field? A value class, @JvmInline value class UserId val raw: String , wraps exactly one value and gives it a distinct compile-time type. At runtime the compiler usually passes the underlying String directly, with no wrapper object. A typealias is just another name for the same type, so a String still passes where a UserIdAlias is expected. A data class gives type safety but always allocates. A value class gives type safety plus, in most call sites, no allocation. The catch is that it gets boxed whenever it's used as another type: generic, nullable for primitives, or through an interface.

title: When value classes box
text: When does a value class actually get boxed? What does that cost? The rule of thumb is that a value class is boxed whenever it's used as some type other than itself. That means passing it as a generic T , storing it in a collection or Array<V , using it through an interface it implements, treating it as Any , and making it nullable when the underlying type is a primitive or is itself nullable . Used as its own non-null type in parameters, locals, fields and return values, it stays unboxed. Each box is a small heap allocation. One box is nothing, but millions per second in a scroll or render loop show up as GC churn and jank.

title: Value class name mangling and Java interop
text: What is name mangling for value classes? What breaks when Java, reflection or serialization meets a value class? A value class erases to its underlying type, so fun find id: UserId and fun find raw: String would both become find String on the JVM. To avoid that clash, Kotlin appends a hash to the name of functions that take value-class parameters, giving something like find-a1b2c3 String . Getters of value-class-typed properties are mangled too. Java can't call those names normally, and Java also can't call constructors that take value-class parameters. The fixes are @JvmName on functions, or @JvmExposeBoxed , which is experimental in Kotlin 2.2 and generates Java-callable boxed variants. Reflection-based libraries see only the underlying type, so I prefer codegen serializers like kotlinx.serialization, which support value classes.

title: Interfaces, default methods, abstract classes
text: How do Kotlin interfaces with method bodies compile to JVM bytecode, and what changed with Kotlin 2.2? When would you use an abstract class instead? Before Kotlin 2.2, a method body in a Kotlin interface wasn't a Java 8 default method by default. Kotlin put the body in a static nested DefaultImpls class, and every Kotlin implementing class got a bridge method calling it. Java implementors had to implement every method themselves. You could opt into real JVM default methods with -Xjvm-default=all or all-compatibility . Since Kotlin 2.2 there's a stable -jvm-default option whose default is enable : real default methods plus DefaultImpls and bridges kept for compatibility. no-compatibility drops the compatibility layer, and disable is the old behavior. I use an abstract class when I need constructor state or protected members. Otherwise I use an interface, because a class can implement many of them.

title: Constructors and initialization order
text: Walk me through the exact order in which Kotlin runs constructors, property initializers and init blocks, including with inheritance and secondary constructors. For class D ... : B args , the arguments to B are evaluated first. Then B fully initializes: its property initializers and init blocks run top to bottom in source order. Then D 's property initializers and init blocks run top to bottom in source order, interleaved exactly as written. Only after that does the body of whatever secondary constructor was called run. Every secondary constructor must delegate to the primary, directly or through another secondary, so the primary path and all initializers run before any secondary body.

title: Anonymous objects (object expressions)
text: What exactly is an object expression? What does it capture, and what's its type when you return it from a function? object : Foo , Bar { ... } creates a new instance of an unnamed class each time the expression runs. It can extend at most one class and any number of interfaces. Unlike Java, it can capture and mutate local var s Kotlin wraps them in Ref holders , and it captures the outer this if it uses outer members. The anonymous type is visible only from local or private, non-inline declarations. If you return it from a public function, the type becomes the declared supertype, or Any if there's none, and the extra members disappear.

title: internal visibility under the hood
text: How is internal implemented on the JVM? What are its practical limits in a multi-module Android app or a published library? internal exists only in Kotlin's type system. In bytecode, internal classes and members are public . To discourage Java callers, internal member names are mangled with the module name, like refresh$feature feed release , but internal classes keep their names. A module is one compilation unit: a Gradle source set, with test and androidTest compilations treated as friends that can see main's internals. So Java and reflection can still reach internal code, and R8 may rename it anyway. I use internal plus Gradle module boundaries as an architecture fence, and explicitApi and an ABI check for libraries.

title: Nested vs inner classes
text: Find the bug, explain the mechanism, and fix it properly. A photo app 1.2M DAU shows an upload-progress banner on GalleryActivity . Since release 7.4, Crashlytics shows an OutOfMemoryError cluster 0.3% of sessions, mostly 3 GB RAM devices after users rotate or reopen the gallery a few times. A teammate blames Glide's bitmap cache, and that's a red herring: the cache size didn't change. title: Sealed hierarchies across modules
text: How would you restructure this? What do you give up? A super-app has 34 Gradle feature modules and 45 Android engineers. Analytics is modeled as one sealed interface AnalyticsEvent in :core:analytics , with 310 subtypes data classes in a 2,800-line file, so the tracker's when is exhaustive. Every feature that adds an event edits :core:analytics . Since that module is depended on by everything, each event change invalidates about 30 modules. Incremental CI builds went from about 6 min to about 19 min p50. The core file is the top source of merge conflicts about 25 per week . A tech lead proposes "move each feature's events into its feature module but keep them in the sealed interface", which won't compile. Product insists that "no event may be silently dropped by the tracker".

title: Evolving sealed types with external data
text: How do you ship the new block safely to all versions, and how do you make the next one painless? A shopping app renders its home screen from server-driven UI: a JSON list of blocks , each with a "type" discriminator. The client models it as a @Serializable sealed interface HomeBlock with 9 subtypes banner , carousel , grid , … decoded by kotlinx.serialization. The server team wants to launch a new "countdown" block for a sale in 10 days. Install base: 3.1M users, of which 22% are on app versions 2+ releases old, and older versions keep traffic for months. In staging, an old build fed a payload containing "countdown" shows a blank home screen, and logs: kotlinx.serialization.json.internal.JsonDecodingException: Serializer for subclass 'countdown' is not found in the polymorphic scope of 'HomeBlock'. The whole response fails to parse, not just one block. A PM asks, "can't we just add Countdown to the sealed interface?"

title: Value class boxing in hot paths
text: Explain where the allocations come from, and how you'd keep the type safety without the cost. A maps/fitness app renders GPS tracks on a custom Canvas view. An engineer introduced type-safety value classes across the rendering code: @JvmInline value class Meters val v: Double , value class Px val v: Float , value class PointIndex val i: Int . Within a week, the Android vitals slow-frame rate on the track screen rose from 4% to 11% on mid- and low-end devices Snapdragon 6xx-class . p95 frame time while panning went from 14 ms to 27 ms. Track sizes are 5k–40k points. A teammate suspects the Kotlin 2.1 upgrade in the same release. That's a red herring: a build with the old compiler but the new code is equally slow. Hot code excerpt: data class TrackPoint val x: Px, val y: Px, val distance: Meters class TrackRenderer { var highlight: PointIndex? = null private val points: MutableList<TrackPoint = mutableListOf private val visible: MutableList<Px = mutableListOf fun onDraw canvas: Canvas, project: Meters - Px { visible.clear points.forEachIndexed { i, p - val px = project p.distance if px.v in 0f..canvas.width.toFloat visible += px if highlight == PointIndex i drawHighlight canvas, p } // ... draw using visible } } A Memory Profiler allocation recording during a 5-second pan shows about 2.4M allocations, with the top classes being Px , Meters , PointIndex and TrackPoint .

title: Interface default methods and binary compatibility
text: Run the post-incident review. What happened mechanically, what's the remediation, and what process changes do you make? Your team owns a payments SDK, published as an AAR to about 40 internal and partner apps. In SDK 4.3.0 you upgraded to Kotlin 2.2 and, "to clean up bytecode", set jvmDefault = JvmDefaultMode.NO COMPATIBILITY . You also added fun onRetry attempt: Int {} with a default body to the public PaymentListener interface. Release notes said "minor, no API changes". Two days later: - Partner app A Kotlin, but it bundles a prebuilt analytics plugin AAR that implements PaymentListener and was compiled against SDK 4.2 with Kotlin 1.9 : java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: Failed resolution of: Lcom/pay/PaymentListener$DefaultImpls; on every payment, 1.1% of sessions. - Partner app B Java : no crashes. That's a red herring: it implements every method itself. - Your own sample app: fine, because it's rebuilt from source. Crashlytics excerpt: Fatal Exception: java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: Failed resolution of: Lcom/pay/PaymentListener$DefaultImpls; at com.vendor.analytics.PayTracker.onCancelled PayTracker.kt at com.pay.internal.CheckoutController.cancel CheckoutController.kt:88

title: Function types & higher-order functions
text: What is a higher-order function in Kotlin, and how do function types like Int - String or - Unit ? work? A higher-order function takes a function as a parameter or returns one. Kotlin has real function types: Int - String means "takes an Int, returns a String". You can store them in variables, pass them around and call them with f x or f.invoke x . A function type can be nullable, written - Unit ? , and then you call it with f?.invoke . Parameter names inside the type, like userId: String - Unit , are documentation only.

title: Lambda syntax & return rules
text: Walk me through Kotlin lambda syntax: trailing lambdas, it , what the lambda returns, and what return means inside one. A lambda is { params - body } . If it has exactly one parameter, I can skip the name and use it . If the last parameter of a function is a function, I can move the lambda outside the parentheses, and drop the parentheses if it is the only argument. The value of the last expression is what the lambda returns; there is no return needed. A bare return inside a lambda is only allowed if the lambda is passed to an inline function, and then it returns from the enclosing function, not the lambda. To return from just the lambda I use a label, return@map .

title: Function types on the JVM
text: What does a Kotlin function type like Int - Int become in JVM bytecode, and what does that cost at runtime? On the JVM, Int - Int is the interface kotlin.jvm.functions.Function1<Integer, Integer with a single invoke method. Because it is generic and JVM generics are erased, the parameters and result are passed as objects, so primitives get boxed when you call through the interface. There are Function0 to Function22 ; bigger arities use FunctionN with a vararg invoke since Kotlin 1.3 . So each call through a function type is an interface call, often with boxing, plus whatever allocation created the lambda object.

title: Lambda compilation (classes vs invokedynamic)
text: How do Kotlin lambdas compile to bytecode, and what changed in Kotlin 2.0? Before Kotlin 2.0, each non-inline lambda became its own anonymous class extending kotlin.jvm.internal.Lambda and implementing FunctionN . Non-capturing ones were cached in a static INSTANCE field; capturing ones were allocated with the captured values as constructor fields. Since Kotlin 2.0, lambdas are compiled by default with invokedynamic and LambdaMetafactory , the way Java compiles its lambdas: the body becomes a synthetic method on the enclosing class and the function object is created at runtime. That gives smaller binaries. The trade-offs listed in the 2.0 release notes: indy lambdas are not serializable, the experimental reflect API does not work on them, and toString is less readable. You can opt out per lambda with @JvmSerializableLambda or per module with -Xlambdas=class .

title: Closure capture of var (Ref wrappers)
text: Java lambdas can only capture effectively final variables. Kotlin lambdas can modify a captured var . How does that work, and what are the consequences? When a non-inline lambda captures a local var and the variable is modified, the compiler moves it to the heap: it wraps it in kotlin.jvm.internal.Ref.IntRef , ObjectRef and similar, with a single mutable field element . Both the function and the lambda share that box, so a write in one is seen by the other. Consequences: an extra allocation, the lambda sees the latest value and not the value at capture time, and the field is a plain non-volatile field, so sharing it across threads is a data race. For inline lambdas there is no box, because the body is in the same frame.

title: inline functions basics
text: What does the inline modifier do, and why does the standard library use it for functions like let , forEach and repeat ? When a function is inline , the compiler copies its body into every call site, and also copies the bodies of the lambdas passed to it. So no function object is created for those lambdas, nothing is boxed, and there is no extra call. Inlining also enables things normal lambdas cannot do: non-local return from the caller, reified type parameters, and calling suspend functions inside the lambda when the caller is suspend. The cost is bigger bytecode at each call site, so it pays off mainly for small functions that take function-type parameters.

title: Non-local returns, labels & anonymous functions
text: Explain non-local returns. What do return , return@label and return inside an anonymous function each do in Kotlin? A bare return always returns from the nearest enclosing fun . Inside a lambda passed to an inline function, that fun is the outer function, so the return leaves the whole function: that is a non-local return. return@label returns only from the lambda labeled label ; the implicit label is the name of the function the lambda was passed to, like return@forEach . An anonymous function, fun x: Int { ... } , is a real function, so a bare return inside it returns only from itself. In forEach , return@forEach acts like continue , not break .

title: noinline
text: What is noinline , when are you forced to use it, and what do you lose when you add it? In an inline function, every function-type parameter is inlined by default, which means it is not a real object: I cannot store it in a field, put it in a list, or pass it to a non-inline function. If I need to do any of that with one parameter, I mark that parameter noinline . That parameter then becomes a normal lambda object with allocation and possibly boxing, and it loses non-local return, while the other parameters stay inlined. If every lambda parameter ends up noinline , the function should not be inline at all.

title: crossinline
text: Why does crossinline exist? Show the compile error it solves and explain what it guarantees. Sometimes an inline function does not call its lambda directly but inside another lambda or an object, like a Runnable , a listener, or a flow {} block. That inner context runs later, possibly after the outer function has returned. If the caller's lambda contained a non-local return , there would be no frame to return to. So the compiler refuses unless I mark the parameter crossinline . crossinline keeps the lambda inlined into that inner body, so I still avoid a separate lambda object for it, but forbids non-local returns from the caller's lambda.

title: reified type parameters
text: What does reified do, why does it only work on inline functions, and what are its limits? On the JVM, generic type arguments are erased, so inside a normal fun <T I cannot do T::class , is T or as T safely. A reified type parameter fixes that at compile time: because the function is inline, the compiler copies its body into each call site and substitutes the actual type there, so T::class becomes String::class at one call and User::class at another. That is why it only works with inline . Limits: the caller must know a concrete type or itself have a reified T , Java cannot call such functions, and nested generics are still erased below the top level, for example List<User becomes just List .

title: When NOT to inline (code size, public API & ABI)
text: When should you not make a function inline ? Talk about code size and about publishing public inline functions in a library. I skip inline when the function has no function-type parameters and no reified type, when its body is large and it is called from many places, when I need recursion, or when the lambda must be stored anyway. For public library APIs I am careful because the body of a public inline function gets copied into the consumer's compiled code. Changing that body does not reach consumers until they recompile, everything it calls has to be public or @PublishedApi internal , and renaming or removing those helpers breaks already-compiled consumers with NoSuchMethodError . So a public inline function is part of my binary ABI, not just my source API.

title: Non-local return
text: Find the bug, explain why it only hits some orders, and fix it. An e-commerce app 1.2M DAU shows "Out of stock" errors only after payment, about 0.4 percent of orders, rising since a refactor two weeks ago. Backend logs show those orders were sent without a stock check token. QA cannot reproduce with normal carts. Crashlytics is clean. title: Designing APIs with inline & lambdas
text: Which do you choose and why? Show the implementation and explain how each requirement is met or consciously dropped. Your team has 60 ViewModels with copy-pasted loading/error logic. The tech lead asks for one shared helper, with these requirements gathered in a meeting partly contradictory : - "Works from suspend code repository calls and from plain code validation ." - "Callers should be able to bail out early, like return when input is invalid." - "Must show a loading spinner during the work and always hide it, even on errors." - "Should not swallow coroutine cancellation." - "Keep APK size impact small" the app is at 48 MB, budget 50 MB . Three proposals are on the table: // A: inline, generic block inline fun <T withLoading state: MutableStateFlow<Boolean , block: - T : T { ... } // B: suspend, non-inline suspend fun <T withLoading state: MutableStateFlow<Boolean , block: suspend - T : T { ... } // C: launches for the caller fun ViewModel.launchWithLoading state: MutableStateFlow<Boolean , block: suspend CoroutineScope. - Unit : Job

title: SAM conversion & fun interface
text: What is a SAM conversion, and why does a plain Kotlin interface with one method not accept a lambda unless you mark it fun interface ? SAM means Single Abstract Method. A SAM conversion lets me pass a lambda where an interface with exactly one abstract method is expected. The compiler builds an instance of that interface whose method runs the lambda body. Java interfaces always get this, because Java has no function types. Kotlin interfaces only get it if I declare them fun interface , which arrived in Kotlin 1.4. Kotlin makes it opt-in because it already has function types, and turning every one-method interface into a lambda target would quietly lock that interface into a public contract: adding a second abstract method later would break every lambda call site.

title: Function references
text: Walk me through the kinds of callable references in Kotlin ::foo , Type::member , ::Constructor , property references . What type does each have? A callable reference turns a named function, constructor or property into a function value without writing a lambda. ::topLevel has type A - R . String::length is an unbound member reference: the receiver becomes the first parameter, so its type is String - Int . ::User references a constructor and has type String, Int - User . User::name is a KProperty1<User, String , which is also usable as User - String . All of them implement KFunction / KProperty , but invoking them is a plain call. Only introspection, such as reading parameters or annotations, needs kotlin-reflect .

title: Default & named arguments
text: How do default and named arguments work, and what does the compiler actually generate for a function with default parameters? A default argument is an expression evaluated at the call site only when the caller omits that argument . The compiler emits the real method with all parameters, plus a static synthetic method foo$default that takes the same parameters, an int bitmask saying which ones were omitted, and a marker object. The caller passes placeholder values zeros or nulls and the mask. The $default method fills in the defaults and calls the real method. Named arguments are purely a compile-time feature: the compiler reorders them into positional order. Java sees only the full-arity method, which is why @JvmOverloads exists.

title: vararg & spread
text: How does vararg work in Kotlin, what is the spread operator, and what does it cost? A vararg parameter collects zero or more arguments into an array. For primitives it is a primitive array, so vararg xs: Int is an IntArray . Otherwise it is Array<out T . If I already have an array, I pass it with the spread operator arr . Spreading copies the array, so the callee can never mutate mine. Combining a, x, b builds a new array. There can be only one vararg per function. If it isn't last, the parameters after it must be named or be a trailing lambda.

title: Bound references
text: What's the difference between viewModel::onClick and { viewModel.onClick } ? When is the receiver evaluated, and why does it matter? A bound reference expr::member evaluates expr once, when the reference is created , and stores that object inside the function value. A lambda { expr.member } captures the enclosing scope and re-evaluates expr every time it is invoked. So if the receiver is a lateinit not yet initialized, the reference throws immediately. If the receiver is later replaced, the reference still points at the old object. The reference also holds a strong reference to that receiver for as long as the function value lives.

title: Java SAM interop
text: How does SAM interop work in both directions: Kotlin calling Java SAM APIs, and Java calling Kotlin APIs that take function types? Kotlin calling Java is easy. Any Java interface with one abstract method accepts a Kotlin lambda, and I can use a SAM constructor such as Runnable { } when the compiler needs the type spelled out, for example for a variable or to break overload ambiguity. Java calling Kotlin is the awkward direction. A Kotlin String - Unit parameter appears in Java as Function1<? super String, Unit , so a Java lambda must return Unit.INSTANCE; . If an API will be called from Java, I expose a fun interface with a void -returning method instead of a function type.

title: Lambdas with receiver
text: What is a function type with receiver like StringBuilder. - Unit , how does it differ from StringBuilder - Unit , and how does it compile? A. - R is a function type whose first parameter is an implicit receiver. Inside the lambda, this is the A , so I can call its members unqualified. On the JVM it is exactly the same as A - R : a Function1<A, R where the receiver is just the first argument. The difference is only in the lambda body's scope and in how you call it: sb.block or block sb . Non-literal values of the two types are even assignable to each other.

title: Local functions
text: When would you use a local function instead of a private function or a lambda, and what do local functions compile to? A local function is a fun declared inside another function. It can read and write the enclosing function's locals and parameters, so I use it for a helper that only makes sense inside one function, like validation steps that share the same inputs, without widening the class API or passing six parameters around. Unlike a lambda it can be recursive, have default arguments and be generic, and a plain call allocates nothing. With the current JVM IR backend it is lifted to a private static method on the enclosing class, with captured values passed as extra parameters and captured var s wrapped in Ref objects.

title: SAM conversion identity
text: What is wrong, why doesn't the teammate's fix work, and what's the correct fix? A video player screen integrates a Java SDK. After QA navigates in and out of the player 10 times, CPU usage on a Pixel 6a sits at 35% while idle, render logs fire 10 times per state change, and LeakCanary reports 9 retained PlayerScreen instances. Crash-free rate is unaffected. Someone points at the new ExoPlayer version upgraded in the same release red herring . title: @JvmOverloads
text: What happened, how do you confirm it, and how should the constructor be written? A team migrates its design-system module from Java to Kotlin, 40 custom views, using the IDE converter plus cleanup. One of them: class PrimaryChip @JvmOverloads constructor context: Context, attrs: AttributeSet? = null, defStyleAttr: Int = 0 : com.google.android.material.button.MaterialButton context, attrs, defStyleAttr The Java original had three constructors, and the 2-arg one called super context, attrs . After a 10% staged rollout about 120k DAU , screenshot tests are green they use programmatic construction with an explicit style , but users report chips "look like plain text": no background tint, no ripple, wrong padding, on every inflated chip. A dark-mode theme change in the same release is suspected red herring .

title: operator invoke
text: What does operator fun invoke give you, where is it a good idea use cases, function-like classes, factory-style companions , and where does it hurt? Declaring operator fun invoke ... lets an instance be called like a function: getUser id instead of getUser.execute id . It's what function types use under the hood, since a lambda's f x is f.invoke x . Good uses are single-responsibility use cases, classes that implement a function type like Event - Unit , and a companion invoke as a pseudo-constructor that validates or returns a different implementation. It hurts when it hides that an object is being called, when there are several overloaded invoke s, or when nullable function properties need ?.invoke .

title: fun interface vs function type vs typealias
text: You're designing a public callback API for a library used by Kotlin and Java apps. Function type, typealias , or fun interface , and why? For an internal Kotlin-only callback I use a function type, optionally named with a typealias , because it's the lightest option and any lambda or reference fits. For a public, multi-language or long-lived API I use a fun interface . It gives Java a natural void method and no Unit.INSTANCE , it avoids boxing primitive parameters, it gives me a nominal type I can document and extend, and I can evolve it by adding default methods. A typealias is only a name: zero type safety, and Java sees the raw Function1 .

title: tailrec
text: What does tailrec do, what exactly qualifies as a tail call, and what do you do for recursion that isn't tail-recursive but is too deep for the stack? tailrec tells the compiler to rewrite self-recursion into a loop when the recursive call is the very last operation, meaning nothing remains to be done with its result. The function then uses constant stack and can't StackOverflowError . It must call itself directly in tail position, can't be open , and the tail call can't sit inside try/catch/finally . If no call qualifies, I get a warning, not an error, and the function stays recursive. For non-tail recursion, like a tree walk with two recursive calls, I use DeepRecursiveFunction stable since Kotlin 1.7 , which keeps the frames on the heap, or an explicit ArrayDeque stack.
