Per-device heap limit largeHeap off is typically 192–256 MB, and 128 MB on the oldest devices. class Recorder { val hr = mutableListOf<Float val speed = mutableListOf<Float val cadence = mutableListOf<Float fun onSample h: Float, s: Float, c: Float { hr += h; speed += s; cadence += c } fun averageHr = hr.average // runs every second for the UI fun smoothedHr = hr.windowed 25 { it.average } // for the chart, every second }

title: windowed vs chunked
text: Lead the review: explain the mechanism and the numbers, why it wasn't caught, and what changes you'd make to code and process. Postmortem for last week's incident. An analytics SDK wrapper batches events and uploads in groups of 100. After release 12.3: the analytics backend ingested 100x the normal event volume for 3 hours 200M events instead of 2M , dashboards showed a fake "engagement spike", the ingestion bill for the day tripled, and the on-call spent two hours looking at retry logic and a reported OkHttp upgrade. Client CPU and battery were also slightly up. The change in 12.3 was a "refactor for readability" of the uploader. suspend fun flush events: List<Event { events.windowed 100, partialWindows = true .forEach { batch - api.upload batch } } // Before the refactor: // for i in events.indices step 100 api.upload events.subList i, minOf i + 100, events.size Typical events.size at flush is 3,000.

title: Top-level declarations from Java
text: I have fun formatPrice ... and val DEFAULT CURRENCY at the top level of PriceUtils.kt . How does a Java class call them, and how do I control the name Java sees? The JVM only has classes, so the compiler puts every top-level declaration of PriceUtils.kt into a synthetic final class PriceUtilsKt as static members. Java calls PriceUtilsKt.formatPrice ... and PriceUtilsKt.getDEFAULT CURRENCY . I rename the facade with @file:JvmName "PriceUtils" , and if several files should share one facade I add @file:JvmMultifileClass with the same name. Private top-level declarations are still emitted but private to that class.

title: @JvmStatic and companion/object from Java
text: Why does Java have to write Analytics.Companion.track ... or Logger.INSTANCE.log ... , and what does @JvmStatic actually change in the bytecode? An object is a class with a static INSTANCE field, and a companion object is a nested class Companion with a static Companion field on the outer class. Their members are instance methods, so Java must go through INSTANCE or Companion . @JvmStatic makes the compiler also emit a real static method: on the outer class for a companion, on the object class itself for an object . The instance method stays, and the static one delegates to it or the reverse for objects . Kotlin callers do not change at all.

title: @JvmField vs const vs accessors
text: From Java, what is the difference between a Kotlin val , a const val , a @JvmField val , and a lateinit var ? A normal Kotlin property is a private field plus getX / setX , so Java calls the getter. const val is only for primitives and String known at compile time; it becomes a public static final field and Java inlines the value. @JvmField removes the accessors and makes the field itself public, which is what frameworks like JUnit rules or some serializers need. lateinit var already exposes its field publicly with the setter's visibility, plus a getter that throws UninitializedPropertyAccessException if unset.

title: @JvmOverloads
text: What does @JvmOverloads generate, what are its limits, and when should a library not use it? Kotlin compiles a function with defaults into the full-parameter method plus a synthetic foo$default ..., int mask, Object marker that fills in defaults based on a bitmask. Java can't call the synthetic one, so it must pass everything. @JvmOverloads generates additional overloads by dropping defaulted parameters from the end, one at a time. It does not generate every combination, only trailing prefixes. For libraries it locks in parameter order, and adding a new default parameter later changes the overload set, so I decide deliberately.

title: Checked exceptions and @Throws
text: Kotlin has no checked exceptions. What problems does that cause when Java calls Kotlin, and what does @Throws do? Kotlin lets any function throw any exception without declaring it, and the compiled method has no throws clause. Java's compiler then refuses catch IOException e around that call, because from its point of view the try block can't throw IOException, so Java devs catch Exception broadly or not at all. @Throws IOException::class adds the throws clause to the JVM signature so Java can and must handle it. It matters also for dynamic proxies and for overriding Java interfaces.

title: @JvmName and platform declaration clash
text: Why does this fail to compile: fun List<String .joinIds : String and fun List<Int .joinIds : String in the same file, and how do you fix it? Both compile to static String joinIds List because generics are erased, so the JVM would see two identical methods. Kotlin reports "Platform declaration clash: the following declarations have the same JVM signature". I give one or both a different JVM name with @JvmName "joinStringIds" . Kotlin callers still call joinIds because Kotlin resolves on the full generic type; only the bytecode name differs. The same tool fixes property getter clashes like a val x with a fun getX .

title: @JvmSuppressWildcards / @JvmWildcard
text: Dagger fails with "cannot be provided without an @Provides-annotated method" for a Map<Class<out ViewModel , Provider<ViewModel that clearly is bound. Why, and what do @JvmSuppressWildcards and @JvmWildcard do? Kotlin's List<out E and Map<K, out V are covariant at the declaration site. When Kotlin emits a Java signature for a parameter of such a type, it adds wildcards so Java callers get the same flexibility: Map<Class<? extends ViewModel , ? extends Provider<ViewModel . Dagger matches types exactly, and the bound type has no wildcard, so the lookup fails. @JvmSuppressWildcards tells the compiler not to emit those wildcards; @JvmWildcard forces them where they would normally be omitted, like return types.

title: Reading decompiled bytecode
text: How do you find out what a piece of Kotlin actually compiles to, and what do you look for when you read it? In Android Studio I use Tools Kotlin Show Kotlin Bytecode, then Decompile to get Java-like source. For exact detail I run javap -c -p on the class in build/tmp/kotlin-classes , and for release behavior I look at the dexed, R8-processed output with the APK Analyzer or r8 's mapping. I look for hidden allocations boxing, lambda objects, iterators , synthetic methods $default , accessors , null-check intrinsics, where annotations landed, and generated classes from plugins.

title: Kotlin metadata and kotlin-reflect cost
text: What is the @kotlin.Metadata annotation, why does it matter for reflection and R8, and what does using kotlin-reflect cost on Android? The JVM class format can't express Kotlin-only facts: nullability, val vs var , default arguments, data/sealed/value classes, extension receivers, suspend, internal. Kotlin stores these in a @Metadata annotation with protobuf-encoded strings on every class. kotlin-reflect full KClass reflection like memberProperties , primaryConstructor , isData parses that metadata at runtime. On Android that means a large library, slow first calls class loading plus parsing , and dependence on R8 keeping both the metadata and the names. Foo::class.java and Foo::class.simpleName -style light reflection don't need kotlin-reflect.

title: K2 compiler basics
text: What is K2, what changed with Kotlin 2.0, and where are we now? K2 is the rewritten Kotlin compiler frontend, the part that parses, resolves names and types, and reports errors. Its internal representation is called FIR Frontend Intermediate Representation . It became the default and stable in Kotlin 2.0.0 May 2024 . One frontend now serves JVM, Native, JS and Wasm, feeding the existing IR backends. It's faster at analysis, has more consistent rules notably better smart casts , and is the base for new language features. K1 was kept as an opt-out via language version 1.9 for a while; Kotlin 2.4 July 2026 removed language version 1.9, so K1 is gone.

title: K2 smart-cast improvements
text: Give concrete examples of code that K2 smart-casts but K1 didn't. Kotlin 2.0 smart-casts in more places: when the type check is stored in a local val and used later; after between type checks, it casts to the closest common supertype; inside lambdas of inline functions, because the compiler assumes they run in place; for function-type properties when calling them; after try/catch/finally with better flow tracking; and with increment/decrement on vars. Smart-cast stability rules themselves no casts on open or custom-getter properties, mutable vars captured by concurrently running lambdas didn't change.

title: Kotlin 2.1-2.4 language features
text: Which language features arrived after Kotlin 2.0, what do they do, and which are stable? Three previews landed in 2.1 and became Stable in 2.2: guard conditions in when is X if cond - , non-local break / continue inside inline lambdas, and multi-dollar string interpolation for text full of $ . Context parameters were a preview in 2.2 and are Stable in 2.4 except explicit context arguments and callable references. Kotlin 2.3 added experimental explicit backing fields and an experimental unused-return-value checker; explicit backing fields are Stable in 2.4. Nested type aliases were Beta in 2.2 and Stable in 2.3. In production I use Stable features freely and treat Preview/Experimental as opt-in behind a compiler flag, with no use in published library APIs.

title: Context parameters
text: What are context parameters, how are they different from context receivers and extension receivers, and would you use them in an Android codebase? A context parameter is a named or anonymous parameter declared with context logger: Logger that callers don't pass explicitly; the compiler resolves it from contexts available at the call site, like an enclosing with logger { } or the caller's own context parameters. They replace the earlier experimental context receivers, which put the context into this scope and caused ambiguity. Context parameters are named, so they're explicit at the use site, and anonymous ones just forward. Preview in 2.2, Stable in 2.4 except explicit context arguments and callable references. I'd use them for cross-cutting capabilities logging, transaction scope, a DSL scope , not to hide ordinary dependencies that DI should inject.

title: Compiler plugins on Android
text: What is a Kotlin compiler plugin, how is it different from an annotation processor, and what do Compose, kotlinx.serialization, Parcelize and all-open/no-arg do? A compiler plugin runs inside kotlinc and can change the program: add members, rewrite IR, add checks. An annotation processor KAPT/KSP can only read declarations and generate new source files; it can't modify existing classes. Compose's plugin rewrites @Composable functions to add a Composer parameter and change groups, skipping and remembering; since Kotlin 2.0 it lives in the Kotlin repo and ships with the same version as Kotlin. kotlinx.serialization generates serializer and $serializer classes. Parcelize generates writeToParcel / CREATOR . all-open and no-arg make classes open or add a no-arg constructor for frameworks like Spring or JPA.

title: kotlinx.serialization plugin vs reflection-based JSON
text: Why does kotlinx.serialization respect Kotlin default values and non-null types when Gson doesn't, and what does the compiler plugin actually generate? Gson creates objects with Unsafe.allocateInstance when there is no no-arg constructor, then writes fields reflectively. No Kotlin constructor runs, so defaults and null checks are skipped. kotlinx.serialization's compiler plugin generates, at compile time, a $serializer object with a descriptor and serialize / deserialize methods, plus a synthetic constructor that takes a bitmask of which fields were present. Missing fields get their Kotlin default; missing fields without a default throw MissingFieldException ; JSON null for a non-null type throws instead of sneaking in. No runtime reflection, so R8 needs very few rules.

title: KAPT vs KSP
text: Briefly, how do KAPT and KSP differ, and what should a team on Kotlin 2.x do about KAPT? KAPT runs Java annotation processors on Kotlin code by first generating Java stub files for every Kotlin class, then running javac's processing, which is slow and loses Kotlin-only information. KSP is a Kotlin-native API: processors read Kotlin symbols directly, no stubs, typically around twice as fast for the processing step, and it understands nullability, default args and so on. KAPT is in maintenance mode; its K2 implementation became default in Kotlin 2.1.20 kapt.use.k2=false to temporarily revert . Room, Hilt/Dagger, Moshi and Glide support KSP. A 2.x team should move every processor to KSP and remove the kapt plugin from each module once its last processor is gone.

title: Java caller passes null into Kotlin
text: What happened, how do you stop the crash today, and how do you make this class of bug unlikely? A payments app 1.2M DAU, 35% legacy Java code moved PaymentFormatter from Java to Kotlin in release 8.14. Crash-free users dropped from 99.6% to 99.1% within a day. Crashlytics top issue 11k events : java.lang.NullPointerException: Parameter specified as non-null is null: method com.pay.ui.PaymentFormatter.formatAmount, parameter currencyCode at com.pay.ui.PaymentFormatter.formatAmount PaymentFormatter.kt at com.pay.legacy.ReceiptActivity.bindHeader ReceiptActivity.java:212 at com.pay.legacy.ReceiptActivity.onCreate ReceiptActivity.java:98 Kotlin signature: fun formatAmount amountMinor: Long, currencyCode: String : String . The Java side reads currencyCode from getIntent .getStringExtra "currency" . Crashes cluster on receipts opened from push notifications deep links built by a server template . The previous Java version of formatAmount "handled null" by printing an empty currency. Also noticed: a spike of ANR reports on the same release red herring: from an unrelated image-loading change .

title: @JvmOverloads on custom View constructors
text: Find the bugs, explain why they only show on some themes/devices, and fix them. A design-system team converted PrimaryButton from Java to Kotlin. After the release, buttons in dark mode and on two OEM skins lost their ripple, padding and text appearance; on most Pixels they looked fine in light mode. No crashes. The Kotlin code: class PrimaryButton @JvmOverloads constructor context: Context, attrs: AttributeSet? = null, defStyleAttr: Int = 0 : AppCompatButton context, attrs, defStyleAttr { init { context.obtainStyledAttributes attrs, R.styleable.PrimaryButton, defStyleAttr, 0 .use { a - cornerRadius = a.getDimension R.styleable.PrimaryButton cornerRadius, 0f } } var cornerRadius = 0f } The old Java class had three constructors, the 2-arg one calling super context, attrs . Red herring: the release also bumped Material Components by a patch version.

title: K2 migration breaks the build
text: Plan and execute this migration without freezing development. A 140-module app Kotlin 1.9.24, Compose compiler 1.5.14, KAPT for Room/Hilt/Glide/data binding, KSP1 for Moshi must move to Kotlin 2.x this quarter because a new library needs it. Weekly releases cannot pause; 60 engineers merge 150 PRs/day. First attempt on a branch kotlin = 2.0.21 fails: e: This version 1.5.14 of the Compose Compiler requires Kotlin version 1.9.24 but you appear to be using Kotlin version 2.0.21 w: Kapt currently doesn't support language version 2.0+. Falling back to 1.9. e: file:///.../CheckoutReducer.kt:88:21 Smart cast to 'Loaded' is impossible, because 'state' is a mutable property that could have been changed by this time e: Unresolved reference: JvmDefault legacy module detekt: Unsupported Kotlin version, crashes on parsing Red herring: Gradle configuration cache warnings that also appeared on the branch they existed on main too .

title: kotlin-reflect in startup
text: What's happening and how do you get the startup time back? A food delivery app 8M MAU, 60% of users on devices with <= 4 GB RAM sees cold-start p95 regress from 1.9 s to 2.25 s over three releases. A Perfetto trace of Application.onCreate on a low-end device shows a 210 ms block in RemoteConfigRepository.init with frames in kotlin.reflect.jvm.internal.KClassImpl , ReflectionFactoryImpl , com.squareup.moshi.kotlin.reflect.KotlinJsonAdapterFactory . The repository parses a 40-model config JSON with Moshi.Builder .add KotlinJsonAdapterFactory . APK size also grew 1.1 MB when moshi-kotlin was added. Red herrings: a new analytics SDK initialized in onCreate trace shows 18 ms , and GC events that track overall allocation.

title: Checked exceptions across a Java proxy
text: Walk through the review: root cause, fix, and what you'd change process-wise. Post-incident review. A banking app's Java "resilience" layer wraps Kotlin repository interfaces in java.lang.reflect.Proxy to add logging and retries. Kotlin interface: interface StatementRepository { fun download month: YearMonth : File } The Kotlin implementation throws IOException on network failure. The Java retry handler only retries IOException : } catch InvocationTargetException e { throw e.getCause ; } // inside InvocationHandler ... try { repo.download m ; } catch UndeclaredThrowableException RuntimeException e { showGenericError ; } During a 40-minute backend degradation, retries never fired: 92k users saw "Something went wrong" instead of a transparent retry; support tickets up 6x. Logs: java.lang.reflect.UndeclaredThrowableException ... Caused by: java.io.IOException: unexpected end of stream . Red herring: OkHttp connection pool warnings in the same window.

title: Parcelize
text: Why are those values lost, and how do you fix it and prevent it? A ride-hailing app 3M DAU passes a Trip between screens in a Bundle. Crashlytics shows 0.4% of sessions with IllegalStateException: Trip.driverName not set after returning from the background process death restore and a few users seeing a blank fare after rotating the screen on the payment page. Code: @Parcelize class Trip val id: String, val pickup: String : Parcelable { var driverName: String? = null var fareMinor: Long = 0L @IgnoredOnParcel var cachedMap: Bitmap? = null } // Warning in build output, ignored by the team: // w: Trip.kt: Property would not be serialized into a Parcel. Add '@IgnoredOnParcel' annotation to remove this warning driverName and fareMinor are set after the trip is assigned. Red herring: a recent Navigation library upgrade.

title: KAPT to KSP build-time
text: What do you do, in what order, and how do you show it worked? A 90-module Android app has clean builds at 14 minutes and incremental one-line change in a leaf Kotlin file at 3 min 40 s on CI-class laptops. A build scan shows the top tasks: :feature: :kaptGenerateStubsDebugKotlin and :feature: :kaptDebugKotlin totalling about 41% of CPU time. Processors in use: Hilt Dagger , Room, Glide, Moshi codegen already KSP , and data binding in 6 legacy modules. Kotlin 2.2.x, AGP 8.x. Management asks for a plan to cut incremental builds by 40%. Red herring: the team wants to enable the Gradle remote cache first.

title: Designing a Kotlin library API for Java consumers
text: Redesign the public API surface and the release process so it works for Java partners without wrecking the Kotlin API. Your team owns sdk-core , a Kotlin SDK distributed as an AAR to 14 partner apps; roughly half are still Java, and three partners are on Java 8 with no Kotlin stdlib of their own. The v1 API: class SdkClient val config: Config { companion object { fun create ctx: Context, apiKey: String, env: Env = Env.PROD, timeoutMs: Int = 30 000 : SdkClient } suspend fun fetchProfile id: String : Profile fun events : Flow<SdkEvent fun <T run block: Session. - T : T } data class Profile val id: String, val name: String, val tier: Tier = Tier.FREE enum class Env { PROD, STAGING } Partner tickets: "cannot call fetchProfile from Java", "SdkClient.Companion.create everywhere", "adding a field to Profile broke our build", "NoSuchMethodError after your 1.3 release". Binary compatibility is a stated promise semver .

title: kotlinx.serialization defaults and rollout
text: Explain both failures and the safest rollout from here. A fintech app 900k DAU finished migrating from Gson to kotlinx.serialization Kotlin 2.2, plugin applied . Next morning: support reports that "Save payee" silently saves with country = null for 3% of users, and crash rate rises 0.3% with: kotlinx.serialization.MissingFieldException: Fields ledgerId are required for type with serial name 'com.fin.api.AccountDto', but they were missing at path: $.accounts 2 Models: @Serializable data class PayeeRequest val name: String, val iban: String, val country: String = "IN", val isFavorite: Boolean = false @Serializable data class AccountDto val id: String, val ledgerId: String, val balanceMinor: Long val json = Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true } The backend treats an absent country as "use user's profile country" null , but the app previously Gson always sent country: null when unset. Some accounts from a legacy backend shard never include ledgerId . Red herring: a CDN certificate rotation that morning.

title: Operator conventions
text: What does the operator keyword do in Kotlin, and which operators can you overload? In Kotlin an operator is syntax sugar for a call to a function with a fixed name. a + b compiles to a.plus b , a i to a.get i , x in c to c.contains x . You mark that function operator to say you meant it to be used that way. The set of operators is closed: you can't create new symbols, change precedence, or overload === , && or . The function can be a member or an extension, so you can add operators to types you don't own.

title: Infix functions
text: What is an infix function, what rules does it have to follow, and where does its precedence sit? An infix function is a member or extension function with exactly one parameter, marked infix , so you can call it without the dot and parentheses: a to b instead of a.to b . The parameter can't be vararg or have a default value. Infix calls bind more loosely than arithmetic, range and type casts, but more tightly than elvis, in / is , comparison and equality. So 1 shl 2 + 3 is 1 shl 5 . The best-known one is to , and it allocates a Pair on every call.

title: Indexed access, contains, ranges, iterator conventions
text: How do get / set , contains , rangeTo / rangeUntil and the iterator convention work? Show how you'd make a custom type usable with , in and for . a i, j calls operator fun get i, j , which can take any number of parameters of any types. a i = v calls set i, v , with the value as the last parameter. x in c calls c.contains x . a..b and a..<b call rangeTo and rangeUntil . A for loop only needs an operator fun iterator whose return type has operator fun hasNext : Boolean and operator fun next . You don't need to implement Iterable , and an extension works too. For integer ranges the compiler optimises for i in 0 until n and x in 0..10 into plain comparisons with no range object.

title: plus vs plusAssign, compareTo, equality
text: What does a += b compile to? Why can var list = mutableListOf<Int ; list += 1 fail to compile, and how do compareTo and == work as operators? For a += b the compiler looks for plusAssign and for plus . If only plusAssign applies, it mutates in place. If only plus applies and a is a var , it becomes a = a + b , which creates a new object and reassigns. If both apply and a is a var , the compiler reports an "assignment operators ambiguity" error, because it can't know whether you meant to mutate or reassign. MutableList has both plus returns a new list and plusAssign adds in place , so var plus MutableList is ambiguous. Use val with a mutable list, or var with a read-only List . < and the other comparisons go through compareTo ... < 0 . == goes through equals with a built-in null check, and === can't be overloaded.

title: Type-safe builders & lambdas with receiver
text: How do type-safe builders work in Kotlin? Explain lambdas with receiver, how they compile, and walk me through building a small DSL. A lambda with receiver has the type T. - R . Inside it, this is a T , so you can call T 's members without a qualifier. A builder function creates a T , runs the lambda on it, and returns the result. That's the whole pattern: fun html block: HTML. - Unit = HTML .apply block . Nesting comes from member functions that take their own receiver lambdas. On the JVM, T. - R is just a Function1<T, R with the receiver passed as the first argument. If the builder is inline , the lambda is inlined and costs nothing.

title: @DslMarker
text: What problem does @DslMarker solve and how does it work? What can still go wrong with it in place? In nested lambdas with receiver, every outer receiver stays implicitly in scope. So inside tr { } I can accidentally call table.tr or html.head without a qualifier, and it compiles. @DslMarker is a meta-annotation. I create my own annotation, mark it @DslMarker , and put it on my builder classes. When more than one implicit receiver carries the same marker, only the innermost one can be used implicitly. Calling an outer one becomes a compile error unless I write this@outer.foo on purpose. It only restricts implicit receivers. Explicit qualification, top-level functions and other markers still work.

title: Gradle Kotlin DSL & Compose as DSLs
text: Gradle Kotlin DSL and Jetpack Compose are both described as Kotlin DSLs. Which language features actually make them work, and where do those features cause pain? Gradle Kotlin DSL is mostly lambdas with receiver. android { ... } is a generated extension function on Project that configures the android extension. Gradle's Java Action<T interfaces behave as if they had a receiver because the kotlin-dsl setup applies the SAM-with-receiver compiler plugin. The type-safe accessors android , implementation ... , libs.xyz are generated, and only for plugins applied in the plugins {} block. Compose is different. Composables are plain functions transformed by the Compose compiler plugin. The DSL feel comes from trailing lambdas, and layout scopes RowScope , ColumnScope , BoxScope are lambdas with receiver carrying a @DslMarker @LayoutScopeMarker . That's why Modifier.weight only resolves inside a Row or Column .

title: Contracts (callsInPlace, returns implies)
text: What are Kotlin contracts? Explain callsInPlace and returns ... implies ... , what they let the compiler do, their stability and opt-in status, and the risk of writing your own. A contract is a statement a function makes to the compiler's data-flow analysis about its behaviour, declared in a contract { } block as the first statement of the body. callsInPlace block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY ONCE says the lambda runs during the call, a known number of times, and doesn't escape. That's why you can initialise a val inside run { } . returns implies x != null or returns true implies x is Foo tell the compiler what's true after the call returns, so callers get smart casts, as with require , check and isNullOrEmpty . Declaring contracts needs @OptIn ExperimentalContracts::class and is still experimental. Callers don't need to opt in. The critical part: the compiler mostly trusts contracts without proving them, so a wrong contract gives you an NPE or ClassCastException with no !! anywhere in sight.

title: @DslMarker / builder scoping
text: Find the bug, explain why it compiled, and fix it so this whole class of bug can't happen again. Your app 3.1M MAU has an internal deep-link DSL in :core:navigation . After release 8.4, analytics show that 11% of /product/{id}/reviews links land on the home fallback instead of the reviews screen. Product-detail links work. The release also bumped AGP and changed an <intent-filter in the manifest. QA says links work "most of the time". Here's the DSL and its usage: class DeepLinkConfig { val patterns = mutableListOf<String } class HostBuilder private val host: String, private val config: DeepLinkConfig { fun path pattern: String, block: PathBuilder. - Unit = {} { val builder = PathBuilder "https://$host$pattern", config config.patterns += builder.base builder.block } } class PathBuilder val base: String, private val config: DeepLinkConfig { fun child segment: String { config.patterns += "$base$segment" } } fun deepLinks block: DeepLinkConfig. - Unit = DeepLinkConfig .apply block fun DeepLinkConfig.host name: String, block: HostBuilder. - Unit = HostBuilder name, this .block val links = deepLinks { host "shop.example.com" { path "/product/{id}" { path "/reviews" // added in 8.4 child "/questions" } } } The "most of the time" comes from the fact that some users open review links through a web fallback that has its own matcher.

title: DSL API design
text: Which API do you ship and why? Cover required-field safety, Java interop, binary compatibility and performance. You own the analytics SDK used by 3 apps and about 60 engineers. There are 420 event types today, and roughly 25 new events land each sprint. 30% of call sites are in legacy Java modules. Data science reports that 6% of events arrive missing required fields screen , userTier , and 2% have keys with typos. A staff engineer proposes a Kotlin DSL: track "checkout started" { screen = "cart" prop "items", 3 prop "value inr", 1299 } Another engineer wants generated data classes per event from a schema CheckoutStarted screen, items, valueInr .track . The SDK is published as a binary artifact, and the apps update it on different schedules.

title: Contracts
text: Walk me through the investigation, the root cause, the fix, and how you'd stop it happening again. Release 7.3 goes to 1.2M DAU. Crash-free users drop from 99.92% to 99.41% within 24 hours. The top Crashlytics issue is new: java.lang.NullPointerException: Attempt to invoke virtual method 'int java.lang.String.length ' on a null object reference at com.example.auth.SessionHeaderInterceptor.intercept SessionHeaderInterceptor.kt:31 at okhttp3.internal.http.RealInterceptorChain.proceed RealInterceptorChain.kt:109 Line 31 is if !token.isMissing builder.header "X-Len", token.length.toString . There's no !! anywhere in the file. The release also upgraded OkHttp 4.12 to 5.x a red herring and the crashes skew towards Android 14 devices also a red herring: those users simply updated first . git blame shows a "cleanup" PR in :core:common that renamed and reimplemented a helper: @OptIn ExperimentalContracts::class fun String?.isMissing : Boolean { contract { returns false implies this@isMissing != null } return this?.isBlank ?: false // was: this == null this.isBlank }

title: Operator overloading cost
text: Diagnose this and optimise it while keeping the code readable. What do operators cost, and what would you change? A trading-style chart a custom View , not Compose draws 4,000 points per series, 3 series, at 60 fps during pan and zoom. Code review loved the operator-based geometry: data class Vec val x: Float, val y: Float { operator fun plus o: Vec = Vec x + o.x, y + o.y operator fun minus o: Vec = Vec x - o.x, y - o.y operator fun times s: Float = Vec x s, y s } override fun onDraw canvas: Canvas { for series in seriesList { val screen = series.points.map { it - viewport.origin scale + padding } // List<Vec for a, b in screen.zipWithNext canvas.drawLine a.x, a.y, b.x, b.y, paint } } On a mid-range device Snapdragon 6-series, 4 GB RAM , the macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric shows a p50 frame time of 11 ms, a p95 of 27 ms and a p99 of 41 ms while panning. The Perfetto trace shows frequent HeapTaskDaemon concurrent GC slices overlapping frames. Someone suggests switching to SurfaceView and hardware layers a red herring for this symptom .

title: What suspend means
text: What does the suspend keyword actually do? Does it make a function run in the background? suspend doesn't create a thread and doesn't move work off the main thread. It marks a function that is allowed to pause at suspension points calls to other suspend functions without blocking its thread, and resume later, possibly on a different thread. The compiler adds a hidden Continuation parameter so the function can be stopped and restarted. Which thread the code runs on depends on the dispatcher in the coroutine's context, not on the keyword.

title: Suspend vs blocking
text: What is the difference between suspending and blocking? Compare delay 1000 with Thread.sleep 1000 inside a coroutine. Blocking holds the thread hostage. Thread.sleep 1000 keeps the OS thread parked for a second, and nothing else can use it. Suspending releases the thread. delay 1000 schedules a resume one second from now and returns COROUTINE SUSPENDED , so the thread goes back to the dispatcher and runs other coroutines. On Main, the first freezes the UI. The second doesn't.

title: Suspend call restrictions
text: Why can a suspend function only be called from another suspend function or a coroutine? Why does it work inside forEach {} but not inside setOnClickListener {} ? Every suspend function takes a hidden Continuation parameter: the "rest of the computation" to call when it resumes. Only a suspend function or suspend lambda has one to pass. A regular function has no continuation, so the compiler rejects the call. forEach is an inline function, so its lambda body is pasted into the enclosing suspend function and uses that function's continuation. A click listener lambda is a real object invoked later by Android, outside any coroutine, so it can't suspend.

title: Coroutine vs thread
text: Coroutines are called "lightweight threads". Quantify that. What does a thread cost vs a coroutine, and what happens if you start 100,000 of each on Android? A thread is an OS object with its own native stack. On ART a default java.lang.Thread reserves about 1 MB of virtual stack, plus kernel structures, and creating and context-switching threads costs microseconds of kernel work. A suspended coroutine is just a few heap objects a Job, its continuation chain and the spilled locals , typically hundreds of bytes. 100k threads on a phone fails with OutOfMemoryError: pthread create ... failed . 100k coroutines that delay fit in a few tens of MB and run on a handful of threads. But coroutines are multiplexed onto threads, so 100k coroutines doing blocking work are still limited by the thread pool.

title: CPS transformation
text: Explain the CPS transformation the Kotlin compiler applies to suspend functions. What does suspend fun getUser id: String : User look like at the bytecode level? CPS means Continuation-Passing Style. The compiler rewrites every suspend function to take an extra last parameter, Continuation<T , which represents "what to do with the result", and changes its return type to Any? . So getUser id: String : User becomes getUser id: String, $completion: Continuation<User : Any? . The return value is either the real User it finished without suspending or the special marker COROUTINE SUSPENDED , meaning "I've paused, and I'll deliver the result later by calling resumeWith on the continuation you gave me".

title: Generated state machine
text: Walk me through the state machine the compiler generates for a suspend function with two suspension points. What are label , the L$0 fields and invokeSuspend ? For each suspend function with non-tail suspension points, the compiler generates a continuation class a subclass of ContinuationImpl . It has an int label saying which suspension point we're at, a result field for the value we resumed with, and fields like L$0 , I$0 holding locals that are still needed after the suspension: "spilled" locals. The function body becomes a switch label . Before each suspension, it saves the live locals into fields, sets the next label and calls the callee. On resume, invokeSuspend result calls back into the function, which jumps to the saved label, restores the locals and continues.

title: Continuation & resumeWith
text: What is the Continuation interface? Explain resumeWith Result<T , its context , and the contract a resumer must follow. Continuation<in T has exactly two members: val context: CoroutineContext and fun resumeWith result: Result<T . It's the "rest of the program" after a suspension point. You resume it once, with Result.success value or Result.failure exception , and resume / resumeWithException are extension shortcuts for those. The context carries the Job, dispatcher, name and so on. That's how the runtime knows which thread to resume on and whether the coroutine is cancelled. The contract: if a function returned COROUTINE SUSPENDED , its continuation must be resumed exactly once. Never zero times hang , never twice IllegalStateException .

title: Stackless coroutines
text: Kotlin coroutines are "stackless". What does that mean, and what are its practical consequences compared to stackful coroutines or virtual threads? Stackless means a suspended coroutine doesn't keep a native call stack. When it suspends, every frame returns propagating COROUTINE SUSPENDED , and only the locals each frame needs are saved into heap continuation objects. A stackful design such as Go goroutines or Java virtual threads saves or switches the whole stack, so any function at any depth can suspend. Kotlin's choice has three consequences. It's cheap and needs no runtime/VM support works on ART, JS, Native . Only functions the compiler transformed, the suspend ones, can suspend: that's function colouring. And a suspend call can't hide inside a non-inline callback or a Java library frame.

title: Suspension fast path & function colouring
text: Does calling a suspend function always suspend? What does a suspend modifier cost if nothing suspends, and when should a function not be suspend? No. A suspend function only suspends if, along its path, some primitive actually returns COROUTINE SUSPENDED . A cache hit, an already-completed Deferred , withContext to the dispatcher you're already on it skips the re-dispatch , or a Mutex that's free all return straight away, synchronously. The modifier still has a cost: the hidden parameter, possibly a state-machine allocation per call, and it forces every caller to be suspend. So I make a function suspend only if it actually suspends or will need to IO, waiting, switching context . Pure computation and getters stay regular functions.

title: Coroutine vs thread cost
text: Diagnose this, evaluate the proposal, and give the fix. A social app 4M DAU, 35% of users on devices with 3 GB of RAM or less has an image prefetcher for its feed. It was written years ago as one Thread per image: thread { download url ; decode url } . A new "infinite carousel" feature prefetches up to 300 images per scroll burst. Crash-free users drop from 99.6% to 98.9% within two days of rollout. Top crash: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: pthread create 1040KB stack failed: Try again at java.lang.Thread.nativeCreate Native Method at java.lang.Thread.start Thread.java:... at com.app.feed.Prefetcher.prefetch Prefetcher.kt:41 It's concentrated on two OEM brands. A teammate notes Java heap usage at crash time is only 120 MB of a 512 MB largeHeap . Another teammate proposes "just switch to GlobalScope.launch , coroutines are lightweight".

title: Suspend call restrictions
text: What's wrong with the fix, why did the original fail to compile, and how would you rewrite it? A PR migrating a sync engine from callbacks to coroutines fails to compile. The author "fixed" it and requests review. The original attempt: suspend fun syncAll ids: List<String : List<Item = ids.asSequence .filter { it.isNotBlank } .map { api.fetch it } // error: suspension functions can be called .toList // only within coroutine body class ItemComparator : Comparator<Item { override fun compare a: Item, b: Item : Int = priorityOf a - priorityOf b // priorityOf is suspend reads DataStore } The "fixed" version in the PR: suspend fun syncAll ids: List<String : List<Item = ids.asSequence .filter { it.isNotBlank } .map { runBlocking { api.fetch it } }.toList class ItemComparator : Comparator<Item { override fun compare a: Item, b: Item : Int = runBlocking { priorityOf a - priorityOf b } } syncAll is called from viewModelScope.launch {} Main.immediate . The sync list is 400 items. Sorting 400 items does 3,500 comparisons.

title: Spilled locals & memory retention
text: Explain what the heap dump is telling you, and fix the memory profile. A document-scanning app uploads multi-page scans. On 2 GB RAM devices 22% of 1.1M MAU , the OS kills the process in the background during uploads: low-memory kills rise 3x after a release. The upload code: suspend fun uploadScan scanId: String { val pages: List<ByteArray = store.loadPages scanId // 12 pages × 3 MB = 36 MB val pdf: ByteArray = pdfEncoder.encode pages // 25 MB val receipt = api.upload scanId, pdf // p95 = 40 s on 3G analytics.track "uploaded", pages.size, receipt.id // uses pages after the wait notifyUser receipt } A heap dump taken during api.upload shows ScanRepo$uploadScan$1 retaining 61 MB through fields L$0 , L$1 , L$2 . A teammate says "the GC will collect pages once encoding is done, so the dump must be from a debug build". Another suggests adding System.gc after encoding. The build that produced the dump is a release build R8 on .

title: Continuation context & completion
text: Lead the post-incident review. Explain each finding mechanically and propose the design. A game-engine SDK team embedded in 30+ partner apps exposes a Kotlin scripting hook. Partners write suspend scripts, and the SDK runs them from its frame loop using only stdlib APIs, to avoid a kotlinx.coroutines dependency: fun runScript script: suspend - Unit { script.startCoroutine Continuation EmptyCoroutineContext { result - if result.isSuccess log "script ok" } } Partner scripts use kotlinx.coroutines internally delay , withContext Dispatchers.IO , ensureActive . Post-incident findings after a partner escalation: - Scripts kept running after the user left the level. CPU and battery use stayed up for minutes one partner reported 9% extra battery per hour . - ensureActive calls in scripts "never fire". - A crash in a script IOException never appeared in Crashlytics. The level just silently didn't load. - Code after delay ran on a kotlinx.coroutines.DefaultExecutor thread and touched engine state that isn't thread-safe. A rare native crash appeared SIGSEGV in engine::Scene::update .

title: Stackless implications & recursion
text: Explain why a "stackless" coroutine overflowed, and fix it for arbitrary depth. A notes app renders nested comment threads. A recursive suspend loader worked fine for 2 years with threads at most 200 replies deep: suspend fun loadThread id: String : Node { val c = dao.comment id // Room suspend; usually a cache hit val kids = c.childIds.map { loadThread it } // recursion return Node c, kids } A B2B customer imports a ticket-system export with one reply chain 12,000 deep a 10x+ jump in depth . Crashlytics: java.lang.StackOverflowError: stack size 1039KB at com.app.ThreadRepo.loadThread ThreadRepo.kt:12 at com.app.ThreadRepo.loadThread ThreadRepo.kt:13 ... repeats It only occurs on Dispatchers.Default worker threads, never on Main. A teammate argues: "Coroutines are stackless. They can't stack-overflow. This must be a Room bug." Another proposes running the loader on a custom Thread with a 64 MB stack.

title: Stackless vs stackful design
text: Evaluate the proposal and give a recommendation for each platform. Your company is building a Kotlin Multiplatform "core" module shared by the Android app minSdk 26, 6M MAU , the iOS app, and a JVM backend service on JDK 21. The backend lead proposes: "Let's drop coroutines from the shared module. JDK 21 virtual threads let us write plain blocking code that scales to millions of tasks, with no suspend colouring, and stack traces are normal. Android can just use a thread pool." The shared module has about 140 repository/use-case functions. 90 are currently suspend , and 40 expose Flow .

title: Resumption
text: After a coroutine suspends, which thread does it resume on? Is it guaranteed to come back to the same thread? A coroutine does not own a thread. When it suspends, its state is saved in a continuation object and the thread is released. When something later calls resume , the continuation goes through the ContinuationInterceptor in the coroutine's context, which is normally a CoroutineDispatcher , and that dispatcher decides where the rest of the code runs. On Dispatchers.Main that means the main thread. On Dispatchers.Default or IO it means any thread in the pool, which may differ from the one before the suspension. Only a single-threaded dispatcher guarantees the same thread. With Dispatchers.Unconfined , or with no interceptor at all, the code continues on whatever thread called resume .

title: Suspend function types & lambdas
text: What is a suspend function type like suspend - Unit , and why can you call delay inside list.forEach { } but not inside Thread { } or a Runnable ? suspend - T is its own function type. A value of that type can only be invoked from a coroutine or another suspend function, because the compiler passes it a hidden Continuation . A regular - T lambda body is not a suspend context, so suspend calls inside it don't compile. The exception is lambdas passed to inline functions such as forEach , map , and let . Their bodies are inlined into the enclosing suspend function, so a suspend call inside them is really a suspend call in your function. Thread { } and Runnable take non-inline lambdas that run later on another stack, so suspension is impossible there.

title: Blocking inside suspend
text: What's wrong, how do you fix it, and how do you stop it from happening again? A photo-gallery app has 1.2M DAU and 60% of its users are on low-end devices 2-4 GB RAM . Release 5.3 moved thumbnail loading from AsyncTask to coroutines. The user-perceived ANR rate went from 0.21% to 0.68%, above Play's 0.47% bad-behavior threshold. The new code: class ThumbRepository private val resolver: ContentResolver { suspend fun loadThumb uri: Uri, size: Int : Bitmap { val opts = BitmapFactory.Options .apply { inSampleSize = 4 } return resolver.openInputStream uri !!.use { BitmapFactory.decodeStream it, null, opts !! } } } class GalleryViewModel private val repo: ThumbRepository : ViewModel { fun onBind uri: Uri = viewModelScope.launch { thumbs.update { it + uri to repo.loadThumb uri, 256 } } } ANR traces show main in BitmapFactory.nativeDecodeStream under ThumbRepository.loadThumb , which is under DispatchedTask.run and Handler.handleCallback . The same release also upgraded the image library and enabled a new GC config, and the Crashlytics breadcrumbs mention GC pauses. The author says "it's a suspend function, so it's async".

title: ContinuationInterceptor
text: What is ContinuationInterceptor , and how does CoroutineDispatcher use it to control where a coroutine runs? ContinuationInterceptor is a CoroutineContext.Element from the Kotlin standard library with one main job: wrap a continuation before it's resumed. Its interceptContinuation c method returns a new continuation that can redirect the resume. CoroutineDispatcher implements it by returning a DispatchedContinuation . When that is resumed, it asks isDispatchNeeded context . If the answer is yes, it calls dispatch context, runnable to run the rest of the coroutine on its threads. If the answer is no, it runs inline. There can be only one interceptor per context, because it's keyed by ContinuationInterceptor.Key , so adding a dispatcher replaces the previous one.

title: suspendCoroutine primitive
text: Every suspending API eventually bottoms out in something like suspendCoroutine . How does it actually work? What happens if resume is called before the block returns, or called twice? suspendCoroutine { cont - ... } hands my lambda a continuation for "the rest of this function" and suspends until someone resumes it. It is built on the compiler intrinsic suspendCoroutineUninterceptedOrReturn . It wraps the intercepted continuation in a SafeContinuation , runs my block on the current thread, then calls getOrThrow . If my block already called resume synchronously, getOrThrow returns the value and nothing suspends. If not, it returns COROUTINE SUSPENDED and the thread is released. Resuming a second time throws IllegalStateException "Already resumed" . Plain suspendCoroutine does not react to cancellation. In production code I use suspendCancellableCoroutine compared in chunk 23 .

title: Suspend lambdas compilation & starting coroutines
text: How is a suspend lambda like the block in launch { } compiled, and how does the library actually start running it? A suspend lambda compiles to a class that extends the stdlib's internal SuspendLambda . That class is both the lambda object and its own continuation/state machine. Its invokeSuspend method holds the body as a label-based state machine, and create makes a fresh instance bound to a completion continuation. The stdlib provides createCoroutine and startCoroutine on suspend function types. launch uses the unintercepted variant: it creates the coroutine with the StandaloneCoroutine /Job as completion, intercepts it with the context's dispatcher, and resumes it with Unit . That first resume either dispatches to a thread or, with UNDISPATCHED , runs immediately.

title: Calling suspend from Java
text: What does a Kotlin suspend fun look like from Java, and what are the realistic ways for Java code to call it? From Java, suspend fun user id: String : User becomes Object user String id, Continuation<? super User $completion . It takes an extra Continuation parameter, returns Object , and returns either the result or the COROUTINE SUSPENDED marker. Java can technically implement Continuation by hand, but that's fragile. In practice I add a Kotlin-side adapter: one that returns a CompletableFuture via scope.future { } in kotlinx-coroutines-core since 1.7, needs API 24+ on Android , a Guava ListenableFuture via kotlinx-coroutines-guava, an Rx type via the rx3 bridge, or a plain callback plus a cancel handle. runBlocking works but blocks the calling thread, so it's acceptable only off the main thread, in tests or tooling.

title: ThreadLocal across suspension
text: Why do ThreadLocals break with coroutines, and how does ThreadLocal.asContextElement fix it? What can still go wrong? A ThreadLocal is bound to a thread, but a coroutine can resume on a different thread after each suspension, and other coroutines run on "its" thread in between. So reading a ThreadLocal after a suspension gives you some other coroutine's value, or none. tl.asContextElement value creates a ThreadContextElement . It sets the ThreadLocal to value every time the coroutine starts or resumes on any thread, and restores the thread's previous value when the coroutine suspends or completes. The catch: calling tl.set inside the coroutine is not persisted across suspensions. To change the value you need withContext tl.asContextElement newValue . And code that isn't running inside such a coroutine sees whatever the thread had, so use ensurePresent to fail fast.

title: Stack traces & stack-trace recovery
text: Why are exception stack traces from coroutines often useless, and what does kotlinx.coroutines' stack-trace recovery do about it? Coroutines are stackless. When a coroutine suspends, the call stack unwinds completely, and on resume the thread stack starts from the dispatcher's run loop: DispatchedTask.run → resumeWith → invokeSuspend . So an exception's trace shows only the frames since the last resume, not who called the function in the first place. Stack-trace recovery is a debug-mode feature on the JVM. When an exception crosses a coroutine boundary, for example via await or withContext , the library copies it and appends the receiving coroutine's frames, keeping the original as the cause. It is on by default only in debug mode: -Dkotlinx.coroutines.debug , or JVM assertions enabled. On Android, assertions are effectively off, so you must set the property yourself, typically only in debug builds.

title: Calling suspend from Java
text: How would you design the Java-facing API, and what do you reject? Your team owns a Kotlin-first analytics/feature-flag SDK used by 120 partner apps. Telemetry shows 35% of integrations are Java-only and 40% have minSdk 21-23. The core API is suspend fun fetchFlags userId: String : Flags . Partners complain they "can't call it". One engineer proposes fun fetchFlagsBlocking userId: String = runBlocking { fetchFlags userId } . Another proposes exposing only CompletableFuture . A third suggests a third-party compiler plugin that auto-generates blocking bridges. Partner crash reports already show 3 ANRs per 10k sessions traced to an older blocking SDK method being called on main.

title: Inline vs dispatched resumption
text: When does resume run the coroutine's continuation synchronously inside the resumer's call stack, instead of dispatching it, and why does that matter for correctness? resume goes to the DispatchedContinuation , which asks dispatcher.isDispatchNeeded context . If the answer is false, the continuation runs right there, on the resumer's thread and inside the resumer's stack, before resume returns. That happens with Dispatchers.Unconfined always, and with Dispatchers.Main.immediate when the resumer is already on the main thread. That second case covers viewModelScope , lifecycleScope and Compose's main-thread work. So code like deferred.complete x , stateFlow.value = x , or a callback calling cont.resume x can run the resumed coroutine's code in the middle of the caller's function, including while the caller holds a lock. With ordinary dispatchers, the resume is just an enqueue.

title: Allocation cost per suspension
text: What does a suspension cost in allocations and CPU? When does it actually matter, and what can you do about it? A suspend function that has real suspension points allocates one continuation object its state machine per invocation, holding the label, spilled locals and the completion reference. That object is reused across all of that call's suspensions. A suspension that actually parks adds more: library primitives such as suspendCancellableCoroutine allocate a CancellableContinuationImpl , the dispatcher path uses a DispatchedContinuation cached on the continuation , and delay also allocates a timer task. A suspend call that returns immediately still paid the continuation allocation. The compiler skips the state machine for functions whose only suspend call is in tail position. The cost is tens of bytes and tens of nanoseconds per call, so it is irrelevant for network or disk work, and it matters in tight loops with millions of calls, such as per-element withContext , per-item launch , or tiny suspend functions called in a hot path.

title: Lock held across suspension
text: Find the bugs, explain why they only appear in production, and fix it properly. A ride-hailing app 4M DAU has a FareEstimator that caches estimates per route. A recent PR "made it thread-safe" with a ReentrantLock . Crashlytics shows IllegalMonitorStateException: attempt to unlock lock, not locked by current thread at 0.4% of sessions, plus a rarer pattern of the estimate screen freezing forever about 30 reports per week with all DefaultDispatcher-worker threads parked. The red herring: the crash started the same week as an OkHttp upgrade. class FareEstimator private val api: FareApi { private val lock = ReentrantLock private val cache = HashMap<String, Fare suspend fun estimate route: String : Fare { lock.lock try { cache route ?.let { return it } val fare = withContext Dispatchers.IO { api.fetch route } // suspension point cache route = fare return fare } finally { lock.unlock } } } Callers: viewModelScope.launch { fare.value = estimator.estimate route } from several screens, on Dispatchers.Main.immediate .

title: ThreadLocal across suspension
text: Diagnose the wrong session IDs and design a fix that does not require rewriting every call site at once. A fintech app 900k DAU has a legacy analytics tracker with Tracker.setSession id backed by a ThreadLocal<String . Every event reads Tracker.currentSession . Last sprint the networking and repository layers moved to coroutines running on Dispatchers.IO . Data team reports that 2.1% of events carry another user-session's ID mostly in the first minute after login on shared tablets in a retail partner's stores , and funnel numbers are inconsistent. Unit tests pass. A teammate says the red herring: "the backend must be mixing up sessions", because the same bug did not show in iOS. Code: class CheckoutRepo private val api: Api, private val tracker: Tracker { suspend fun submit cart: Cart = withContext Dispatchers.IO { tracker.track "checkout started" // reads ThreadLocal val r = api.submit cart // suspends tracker.track "checkout done" // reads ThreadLocal again r } } // somewhere at login Tracker.setSession session.id // called on Main

title: Resume under lock
text: Why does it freeze, why only sometimes, and how do you fix it without risking BLE ordering? A BLE medical-device app 150k devices, p95 session 25 minutes wraps a GATT client in a coroutine API. Since release 8.2, about 0.9% of sessions freeze: the UI stops responding for 5+ seconds, then Play reports an ANR rate moved from 0.12% to 0.55% . It happens mostly when users tap "sync" immediately after connecting. Main-thread ANR trace: "main" prio=5 tid=1 Blocked - waiting to lock <0x0a1b2c3d a java.lang.Object held by thread 1 main // shown on API 30 as self-owned monitor re-entrance attempt via wrapper at com.app.ble.GattBridge.writeNext GattBridge.kt:58 at com.app.ble.SyncUseCase$run$1.invokeSuspend SyncUseCase.kt:34 at kotlinx.coroutines.DispatchedTask.run DispatchedTask.kt:... at com.app.ble.GattBridge$callback$1.onCharacteristicWrite GattBridge.kt:41 Some devices show a frozen non-reentrant custom lock instead of a Java monitor. Another team suspects the BLE stack firmware red herring, since devices on firmware 2.1 and 2.3 both fail . Code: class GattBridge private val gatt: BluetoothGatt { private val lock = Any private var pending: CancellableContinuation<Unit ? = null suspend fun writeNext chunk: ByteArray { suspendCancellableCoroutine<Unit { cont - synchronized lock { pending = cont } gatt.writeCharacteristic chunk // simplified } } val callback = object : BluetoothGattCallback { override fun onCharacteristicWrite g: BluetoothGatt, c: BluetoothGattCharacteristic, status: Int { synchronized lock { pending?.resume Unit // runs the coroutine's next step inline on Main.immediate pending = null } } } } The sync use case loops for chunk in chunks bridge.writeNext chunk in viewModelScope Main.immediate , and the GATT callback is delivered on the main thread on this app's target setup.

title: launch vs async
text: What is the difference between launch and async ? When do you pick one over the other? Both are extension functions on CoroutineScope that start a child coroutine and return right away. launch returns a Job , which is a handle with no result, so I use it for fire-and-forget work like "save this, then update state". async returns a Deferred<T , which is a Job that also carries a result. I call await to suspend until the value is ready. I use async only when I need a value back and want to run several of those at the same time. For a single value on another thread I use withContext , not async { }.await .

title: await semantics
text: What exactly does Deferred.await do? What happens if the deferred already finished, failed, or was cancelled? await suspends the calling coroutine until the Deferred completes. It never blocks the thread. If the deferred already succeeded, it returns the value at once. If it failed, await rethrows that exception. If it was cancelled, await throws CancellationException . The outcome is stored, so every caller gets the same result. If the coroutine that is waiting gets cancelled, its await throws, but the deferred keeps running. Only the waiter stops.

title: withContext
text: What does withContext do? Is it a new coroutine? What does it cost when the dispatcher does not change? withContext ctx { } is a suspend function. It runs the block with the current context merged with ctx , suspends the caller until the block and all of its children finish, then returns the block's result on the original context. With a different dispatcher it dispatches into that dispatcher and dispatches back afterwards. With the same dispatcher it skips the dispatch and just runs the block, so it is cheap. Its main job is to make a function main-safe: suspend fun load = withContext io { ... } .

title: runBlocking
text: What does runBlocking do, and where is it actually acceptable to use it? runBlocking starts a coroutine and blocks the current thread until that coroutine and all of its children finish, then returns the result. It is the bridge from blocking code into coroutines. It is fine in a main function, in some framework callbacks that must be synchronous and already run on a background thread, and in older tests today I use runTest . In Android app code on the main thread it is wrong: it freezes the UI and can deadlock. Inside another coroutine it is also wrong, because it blocks a pool thread.

title: awaitAll vs sequential awaits
text: listOf a, b, c .awaitAll versus a.await ; b.await ; c.await . Is there any difference if all three are already running? If all three are children of a regular coroutineScope , the end result is almost the same. Any failure cancels the scope and the siblings anyway. The difference shows when the deferreds are not tied together by a cancelling parent, for example in supervisorScope or when they come from another scope. Then sequential awaits wait for a even if c has already failed, so I only learn about the failure after the slowest earlier item finishes. awaitAll resumes with the first exception as soon as any deferred fails. awaitAll also starts lazy deferreds together, while sequential awaits start them one at a time.

title: coroutineScope vs supervisorScope vs withContext
text: Compare coroutineScope , supervisorScope and withContext . When do you reach for each? All three are suspend functions that create a child scope, run a block, wait for every child launched inside, and return the block's value. coroutineScope keeps the current context, and if any child fails it cancels all the other children and rethrows. supervisorScope has a SupervisorJob -like job, so a failing child does not cancel its siblings or the scope, and each child has to handle its own failure. withContext is coroutineScope plus a context change, usually a dispatcher. I use coroutineScope for all-or-nothing parallel decomposition, supervisorScope for independent tasks with partial results, and withContext to change thread or context for a sequential block.

title: async whose result is never awaited
text: What happens to an async whose Deferred nobody ever awaits? The work still runs. DEFAULT start means it is scheduled at once, whether or not anyone awaits. On success the value just sits in the Deferred until it is collected. On failure it depends on the parent. Under a regular Job or coroutineScope , the failure still cancels the parent and its siblings, so it is not silent. Under a SupervisorJob , supervisorScope or GlobalScope , the exception is held inside the Deferred and is never reported anywhere. Nothing crashes, no handler runs, no log. So an un-awaited async is either a side effect in disguise, which should be a launch , or a silent failure.

title: CoroutineStart DEFAULT vs LAZY
text: What does start = CoroutineStart.LAZY change compared with DEFAULT ? What traps come with lazy coroutines? With DEFAULT , the coroutine is scheduled on its dispatcher right away. With LAZY , it is created in the "New" state and does nothing until someone calls start , join or await . The traps: if I await lazy deferreds one by one, each one starts only when awaited, so parallel work becomes sequential. A lazy child that is never started keeps its parent scope from completing, so coroutineScope hangs forever. If a lazy job is cancelled before it starts, its body never runs.

title: CoroutineStart ATOMIC and UNDISPATCHED
text: Explain CoroutineStart.ATOMIC and CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED . When are they the right tool, and what can go wrong? Both guarantee that the body starts even if the job is already cancelled. With DEFAULT it wouldn't. ATOMIC still dispatches normally, so the body is guaranteed to run eventually on the target dispatcher. Its classic use is a try/finally that must release something acquired before the launch. UNDISPATCHED runs the body right away on the caller's thread until the first real suspension point, then resumes on the coroutine's own dispatcher. I use it when code must run synchronously before launch returns, for example subscribing to a hot source before emitting into it. Its traps: that first segment ignores the dispatcher you passed, and deep nesting of undispatched coroutines can overflow the stack.

title: Parallel decomposition
text: How do you structure "fetch A and B in parallel, then combine" correctly? Why is the structured version better than starting work in an outside scope? I write a suspend function that opens coroutineScope , starts async for each independent piece, and awaits them. The function only returns when both are done. If one fails, the other is cancelled and the error is rethrown to the caller. If the caller is cancelled, both are cancelled. Starting the async s in GlobalScope or in an injected scope instead means a failure or cancellation does not propagate. Work leaks past the caller, and the other request keeps burning network after the screen is gone.

title: async vs withContext for a single result
text: A teammate writes val x = async Dispatchers.IO { load }.await . What is wrong with it, and what about val d = async { a }; val x = b ; d.await ? The first line starts a coroutine and waits for it at once. That is sequential, just slower and noisier than withContext Dispatchers.IO { load } . It costs an extra Deferred , an extra child job, and a failure path that cancels the parent before await even rethrows. The second shape is legitimate: a runs while b runs, and we only wait when we need a 's result. The rule: use async only when something useful happens between starting it and awaiting it.

title: withContext cancellation on return
text: If the block inside withContext finishes but the caller was cancelled at the same moment, what does withContext return? Why does that matter for resources? It returns nothing. withContext checks cancellation when it hands the result back. If the calling job was cancelled while the block ran, it throws CancellationException and the result is discarded, even though the block completed successfully. That is the prompt-cancellation guarantee, so a cancelled caller never continues. The consequence: if the block opens or creates something closeable and returns it, and cancellation races with the return, nobody owns that resource and it leaks. So I close resources inside the block, or use them inside it, and never pass them out across a withContext boundary.

title: runBlocking deadlock mechanics
text: Explain exactly how runBlocking on the Android main thread can deadlock rather than just "be slow". runBlocking parks the main thread until its coroutine finishes. If any code inside needs to resume on Dispatchers.Main , that resume is posted as a message to the main Looper. The Looper can't process messages because its thread is parked inside runBlocking . The coroutine waits for Main and Main waits for the coroutine, so it is a deadlock, and the ANR dialog appears after the input-dispatch timeout. Typical triggers: a repository that does withContext Dispatchers.Main , a Flow with flowOn that collects on Main, or a library callback that posts to the main Handler.

title: runBlocking inside coroutines
text: Why is calling runBlocking from inside a coroutine, or from a thread of Dispatchers.Default / IO , dangerous even when it's not on the main thread? runBlocking parks the current worker thread, so that thread does nothing until the inner coroutine finishes. On Dispatchers.Default there are only as many threads as CPU cores, for example 8. If 8 coroutines each call runBlocking and the inner work needs a Default thread to make progress, nothing can run, and the app is in a pool-starvation deadlock. On IO the limit is 64 threads by default, so it hides longer and then fails under load. The library docs say plainly that runBlocking should not be used from a coroutine. Inside suspend code I call the suspend function directly or use withContext .

title: Builder API conventions
text: When should a function be suspend fun and when should it be an extension on CoroutineScope ? Why is suspend fun CoroutineScope.foo a smell? A suspend fun does its work and returns when the work is done. It may use coroutineScope for internal parallelism, but nothing outlives the call. A function with a CoroutineScope receiver, like launch and async , starts work and returns right away, and the work continues in the caller's scope. Those are two different contracts. Combining them, suspend fun CoroutineScope.foo , is ambiguous. Inside it, launch resolves to the receiver scope rather than to the suspend call's own context, so work can escape the "this function finishes before returning" promise. Pick one: suspend and wait, or scope extension and fire.

title: Sharing a Deferred for in-flight deduplication
text: Three screens request the same config at once. How would you use async / Deferred to make one network call and share the result, and what are the pitfalls? I keep a map from key to Deferred . The first caller creates the deferred with async in a long-lived scope I own an app scope , not in its own scope, then everyone await s the same instance. Because the deferred's owner is the app scope, one caller cancelling only stops that caller's wait, not the request. When the deferred completes I remove it from the map, so a failure isn't cached forever and later calls refresh. Map access is guarded, and nothing suspends while holding the guard.

title: Parallel decomposition
text: What is the bug, and how do you fix it? A product page should load in roughly the time of its slowest call. Each of the 4 calls takes 300–500 ms on p50. QA measures about 1.6 s for the page on Wi-Fi and asks why "the async version" is not faster than the old sequential code. suspend fun loadProduct id: String : Product = coroutineScope { val parts = listOf "info", "price", "stock", "reviews" .map { part - async { api.part id, part }.await } Product.from parts } A teammate suggests the dispatcher is the problem and wants to add Dispatchers.IO .

title: Parallel decomposition
text: How would you restructure the loading with coroutine builders, and what numbers do you expect? A banking dashboard 1.2M DAU, 60% of devices are mid- or low-end Android 10–13 shows 5 widgets on open: balance p50 250 ms / p95 900 ms , transactions 400 / 1,400 , offers 600 / 2,500 , credit score 300 / 1,100 , notifications 150 / 500 . The current ViewModel calls them one after another and shows a full-screen spinner until all are done. The product team wants "dashboard visible under 1 s at p95". Today the p95 time-to-content is about 5.8 s. The offers service is owned by another team and has a known 2–3% error rate.

title: async in GlobalScope
text: Explain every symptom, and fix it. After a release, a news app 800k DAU sees: no crash increase, but backend traffic to /article/related up 2.4x, battery complaints in reviews, and LeakCanary reports in internal builds about ArticleFragment retained via a lambda. The relevant new code: class ArticleViewModel private val api: Api : ViewModel { private var related: Deferred<List<Article ? = null fun open id: String { related = GlobalScope.async Dispatchers.IO { api.related id } } suspend fun relatedArticles = related?.await .orEmpty } // Fragment viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch { adapter.submit vm.relatedArticles ; binding.relatedHeader.isVisible = true } Users swipe between articles quickly, about 7 articles a minute.

title: CoroutineStart LAZY
text: Why does it hang, and how do you fix it? A checkout screen's "Place order" button stays in loading state forever for about 30% of users those without a coupon . No crash, no error log. The spinner is cleared in the line after coroutineScope returns. suspend fun prepareCheckout cart: Cart : Summary = coroutineScope { val coupon = async start = CoroutineStart.LAZY { api.validateCoupon cart.couponCode!! } val totals = async { api.totals cart } val discount = if cart.couponCode != null coupon.await .amount else 0 Summary totals.await , discount } A teammate suspects the !! causes a hidden NPE and wants to add logging around api.totals .

title: supervisorScope partial results
text: What is wrong with this code, and how do you fix it? A travel app's search results page fetches flights, hotels and cars in parallel. Product wants "show whatever succeeded". After release, the following is observed. When the cars API returns 503 about 4% of requests , the page shows flights and hotels correctly, which is good. But when users leave the page mid-load, Crashlytics shows no crash, yet the leaving users' next screen sometimes freezes on a spinner. Also, a coroutine-timeout bug report: "pressing back during search doesn't stop the network calls". suspend fun search q: Query : SearchResult = supervisorScope { val flights = async { api.flights q } val hotels = async { api.hotels q } val cars = async { api.cars q } SearchResult flights = runCatching { flights.await }.getOrNull , hotels = runCatching { hotels.await }.getOrNull , cars = runCatching { cars.await }.getOrNull , }

title: CoroutineStart UNDISPATCHED
text: Why are messages lost, and what is the right fix? Discuss at least three options. A chat app 2M DAU has a SharedFlow<Message replay = 0 in a repository, fed by a WebSocket. In ChatViewModel.init the team launches a collector and then immediately asks the repository to request "history sync", which makes the server push the last messages through the same socket. About 1 in 150 opens loses the first few messages: the list is missing the newest message until the next one arrives. It only happens on fast devices and fast networks. A teammate proposes delay 50 between the collect and the sync request. Another proposes replay = 1 . init { viewModelScope.launch { repo.messages.collect { append it } } repo.requestHistorySync // server pushes messages immediately }

title: Parallel decomposition at scale
text: What is wrong at 15,000 items, and how do you redesign it? A photo-backup feature calls api.checkExists hash for every local photo before upload. In beta users with about 300 photos it was fine. The launch cohort has users with 15,000 photos on 3 GB RAM devices. The code: suspend fun missing photos: List<Photo : List<Photo = coroutineScope { photos.map { p - async { p to api.checkExists p.hash } } .awaitAll .filter { !it.second } .map { it.first } } Symptoms: the server returns many 429s; OkHttp logs show IOException: Canceled /timeouts; Crashlytics shows OutOfMemoryError in 0.8% of sessions; the whole feature fails when one call returns 500 about 1 in 3,000 calls fails, so with 15,000 calls nearly every run fails .

title: coroutineScope waits for children
text: Why is it slow, and what do you do? The product owner says "analytics must not delay the user, but we still want it to be sent". A "Place order" function should respond to the user as soon as the order is confirmed. Analytics and a push-registration refresh are "nice to have". The developer wrote: suspend fun placeOrder cart: Cart : Order = coroutineScope { val order = api.placeOrder cart // p50 400 ms launch { analytics.track order } // p50 150 ms, p95 6 s third-party SDK launch { push.refreshRegistration } // p50 300 ms order } Users on slow networks complain the confirmation screen appears "late", and the p95 of "tap to confirmation" is 6.6 s although the order endpoint's p95 is 900 ms. QA says "the function returns order on the last line, so it should return immediately".

title: runBlocking bridge during migration
text: Is the bridge acceptable? How do you make it safe, and how do you roll it out? A large app is migrating its data layer from callbacks and ExecutorService to coroutines. A legacy TokenProvider interface used by an OkHttp Authenticator called on an OkHttp dispatcher thread must stay synchronous: fun refreshToken : String . The new implementation is suspend fun refresh : String uses Retrofit suspend plus DataStore . The migration PR implements the bridge as = runBlocking { refresh } . During the staged rollout at 10%, the team observes: no ANR, no crash, but p99 API latency for the 10% group is 3x worse during token expiry waves, and some requests fail with java.net.SocketTimeoutException while the auth server shows few refresh calls. Thread dumps show many OkHttp Dispatcher threads parked in BlockingCoroutine.joinBlocking .

title: Dispatcher fundamentals
text: What is a CoroutineDispatcher, and which dispatchers ship with kotlinx.coroutines on Android? A dispatcher is the coroutine context element that decides which thread or thread pool runs a coroutine's code, both when it starts and every time it resumes after a suspension. On Android you get four: Dispatchers.Main the UI thread, with a Main.immediate variant , Dispatchers.Default a pool sized to the CPU core count, for CPU work , Dispatchers.IO an elastic pool capped at 64 parallel tasks by default, for blocking I/O , and Dispatchers.Unconfined no thread switching, mostly for special cases . You can also build your own from an Executor or with limitedParallelism .

title: Dispatchers.Main on Android
text: How does Dispatchers.Main actually work on Android, and what happens if it isn't available? On Android, Dispatchers.Main is a HandlerDispatcher backed by a Handler on the main Looper. dispatch posts a Runnable to the main message queue, so resumed code runs as an ordinary message on the UI thread, in turn with input events and frame callbacks. It ships in kotlinx-coroutines-android and is discovered at runtime. On a plain JVM local unit tests it can't initialize, and the first use throws an IllegalStateException telling you to add the Android module or use Dispatchers.setMain in tests.

title: Main vs Main.immediate
text: What is the difference between Dispatchers.Main and Dispatchers.Main.immediate , and why do viewModelScope and lifecycleScope use immediate ? Both run on the main thread. The difference is isDispatchNeeded . Plain Main always posts to the message queue, even if you are already on the main thread. Main.immediate checks whether the current thread is the main Looper's thread and, if so, runs the code inline, right now, with no post. AndroidX scopes use immediate because a coroutine launched from the main thread can then render its first state in the same frame, with no extra message hop. That avoids one-frame flicker and the risk of losing an update if the lifecycle changes in between.

title: Dispatchers.Default
text: How many threads does Dispatchers.Default have and what should run on it? Default is backed by a pool whose parallelism equals the number of CPU cores, with a minimum of 2.
