Code: class OrderRepo private val api: OrderApi { private var counter = 0 fun placeOrder cart: Cart : Flow<Receipt = flow { counter++ // local sequence for display val res = api.submit cart, clientSeq = counter emit Receipt res.id, seq = counter } } // ViewModel val receipt = repo.placeOrder cart fun onConfirm { viewModelScope.launch { receipt.collect { ui.value = it } } } fun onRetryTapped { viewModelScope.launch { receipt.collect { ui.value = it } } } Server logs show two POST /orders for these users 1-3 seconds apart with clientSeq 1 and 2 and the same cart. 100% of affected users tapped Retry after seeing a slow spinner p95 submit latency is 2.8 s . Red herring: the idempotency key is generated server-side.

title: Room Flow
text: Explain why it emits 3/sec and how you'd cut recomposition and DB load. A fitness app shows a live workout screen on mid-range devices 3 GB RAM, Android 11 . Perfetto shows 11-14 recompositions per second of the entire exercise list 180 items and Choreographer frame drops: jank rate 18% during workouts. Heart-rate samples 1 write/sec and rep counts 2 writes/sec are inserted into workout event and the UI observes: @Query "SELECT FROM exercise WHERE workoutId = :id ORDER BY pos" fun exercises id: Long : Flow<List<ExerciseWithSets // @Relation to set, and to workout event for latest HR A red herring: someone suspects Compose stability of ExerciseWithSets . Logging shows the DAO flow emits 3 times per second even though the visible list content changes only when a set is completed about once per 40 s .

title: Flow vs suspend vs List
text: Decide the API shape, justify it, and describe the migration plan. You are the tech lead for an app with 6 teams. A shared UserRepository currently exposes suspend fun getUser id : User , suspend fun getFollowers id : List<User and fun observeUser id : Flow<User backed by Room. A new engineer proposes making all methods return Flow "for consistency and future live updates", including updateProfile which would return Flow<Unit . Another proposes Flow<Result<T everywhere. Crash analytics show the main existing pain: 3% of crashes are CancellationException mishandled in runCatching , and unit tests are flaky around first on Room flows.

title: Testing cold flows
text: How do you unit test a cold Flow? What goes wrong with first , toList and runTest virtual time, and when do you use Turbine? For a finite cold flow I call toList inside runTest and assert the list; delays are skipped because runTest uses virtual time. For never-ending flows Room, DataStore, StateFlow toList hangs, so I use take n .toList , first , or Turbine's test {} with awaitItem and cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents . I inject dispatchers so flowOn uses the test scheduler, and I check call counts to prove cold re-execution behavior.

title: Flow vs Rx
text: How do you plan the migration and what semantic differences between Observable and cold Flow do you watch for? A fintech app 3.5M MAU, 70% of sessions on Android 9-12 has 140 RxJava 2 call sites in the data layer: Observable<T for streams, Single<T for requests, Completable for commands. You are asked to migrate to coroutines/Flow module by module, shipping weekly, with no regression in crash-free rate currently 99.62% . In a pilot module the first migrated code looked like: fun prices : Flow<Price = priceSocket.observe .asFlow // Observable - Flow via rxjava2 interop val disposable = prices .subscribe ... // does not exist: someone tried to port subscribe Pilot results: 2 crashes in beta, UndeliverableException disappeared, but a new 0.3% of sessions show a stuck loading spinner. A red herring: someone blames the interop library version.

title: DataStore Flow
text: What happened, what's the root cause, and what changes prevent it? Post-incident review for a release that raised the ANR rate from 0.35% to 1.4% Play Console threshold is 0.47% user-perceived ANR; you are in the bad-behavior zone . Affected: 60% on devices with 2-3 GB RAM and eMMC storage, concentrated at cold start. Trace from Play Console: "main" prio=5 tid=1 Waiting at java.lang.Object.wait at kotlinx.coroutines.BlockingCoroutine.joinBlocking Builders.kt:... at kotlinx.coroutines.BuildersKt BuildersKt.runBlocking Builders.kt:... at com.app.Prefs.getToken Prefs.kt:22 at com.app.AuthInterceptor.intercept AuthInterceptor.kt:14 // runs on OkHttp thread ... at com.app.App.onCreate App.kt:41 The commit: "Migrate SharedPreferences to DataStore". Code: fun getToken : String = runBlocking { ctx.store.data.map { it TOKEN ?: "" }.first } Also App.onCreate calls Prefs.getFlagsBlocking the same way. A red herring: Firebase init time grew by 30 ms in the same release.

title: Completion semantics
text: Which Flow sources complete and which never do? How does that affect toList , single , code after collect , and onCompletion ? A flow completes when its producer block returns. flow { } with a finite body, flowOf , asFlow , and a single network call wrapped in flow {} complete. Room queries, DataStore data , StateFlow , SharedFlow and callbackFlow with awaitClose do not complete on their own; they end only when the collector is cancelled or an operator like first / take n cancels upstream. Terminal operators that need completion toList , single , count , fold , reduce hang on those, and code after collect {} never runs.

title: Performance of Flow pipelines
text: What is the runtime cost of Flow, and when is Flow the wrong tool? Think of 1M elements or 60 events per second. A plain operator pipeline costs one lambda call per operator per element plus boxing for primitives; it is cheap per element tens of nanoseconds but not zero. Operators that introduce coroutines/channels flowOn , buffer , flatMapMerge , combine , debounce add a context switch and channel hand-off per element, which is microseconds. For 1M in-memory numbers, a Sequence or a plain loop is much faster, and for batch processing I process chunks chunked -style windowing instead of per-element flows. At UI event rates 60/s the cost is irrelevant; the problem is what the collector does with each value.

title: Terminal operators
text: Explain why the spinner never disappears and fix it. Also note two other defects. An e-commerce app's Orders screen shows a progress bar forever for 4% of sessions, primarily returning users with cached orders. Support tickets say "orders load, then spinner keeps spinning". No crash, no ANR. After a refactor from LiveData to Flow : fun load = viewModelScope.launch { state.value = State.Loading orderDao.observeOrders .collect { state.value = State.Content it } state.value = State.Idle // "hide spinner" } fun refresh = viewModelScope.launch { state.value = State.Loading val fresh = api.orders // may throw IOException orderDao.replaceAll fresh state.value = State.Idle } UI shows spinner when state is Loading refreshing ; a second bar is displayed during Content if refreshing . Logs: refresh threw UnknownHostException in 90% of affected sessions offline on metro , with no catch . The team also notes first-launch no cache users are fine. Red herring: Room version bump.

title: StateFlow basics
text: What is a StateFlow , how does it differ from a regular cold Flow , and what are the rules you must know before using MutableStateFlow ? "A StateFlow is a hot flow that always holds exactly one current value. It needs an initial value, .value reads it without suspending, every new collector immediately receives the current value, and it conflates: a slow collector only ever sees the latest value, and setting a value equal to the current one does nothing. It never completes, so collect never returns normally. A cold Flow has no state and re-runs its producer for each collector; a StateFlow has one shared state and no producer."

title: Read-only exposure
text: Why do we write private val state = MutableStateFlow ... and val state: StateFlow<... = state.asStateFlow ? What does asStateFlow actually do, and what's the difference between that and just declaring the type as StateFlow ? "The ViewModel must be the only writer. I keep the mutable one private and expose a read-only type. asStateFlow returns a wrapper that delegates to the original but is not a MutableStateFlow , so even a cast fails at runtime. Just declaring val state: StateFlow<X = state is only a compile-time restriction; anyone can do state as MutableStateFlow<X and write to it. The same applies to asSharedFlow ."

title: SharedFlow configuration
text: Explain the three parameters of MutableSharedFlow replay, extraBufferCapacity, onBufferOverflow : what each does, what the defaults are, and what the default MutableSharedFlow actually does. " replay is how many past values a new subscriber gets. extraBufferCapacity is extra buffer space beyond replay for slow subscribers. onBufferOverflow decides what happens when that buffer is full: SUSPEND default , DROP OLDEST, or DROP LATEST. Defaults are 0, 0, SUSPEND. So MutableSharedFlow has no buffer: with no subscribers an emitted value is simply dropped, and with subscribers emit suspends until every one of them has received it."

title: StateFlow conflation & equality
text: StateFlow is described as "conflated" and "distinct-until-changed". What exactly does that mean, when can a collector miss a value, and what breaks if your state class has a weird equals ? "Writing to MutableStateFlow.value compares the new value to the current one using equals . If equal, nothing happens, no emission, no version bump. Separately, each collector only sees the latest value at the time it resumes, so if you set A, B, C quickly, a slow collector may see only C. Also A then back to A before the collector wakes up means it sees nothing. So correctness depends on your state having a correct equals ; data classes are fine; mutating an object in place and re-assigning the same reference does nothing."

title: Atomic updates
text: Why is state.value = state.value.copy x = ... considered unsafe, and how do update {} , getAndUpdate , updateAndGet and compareAndSet fix it? What rules must the lambda follow? " value is thread-safe for a single read or write, but read-then-write is two operations. Two coroutines can both read count=5 and both write 6, losing an update. update {} runs a compare-and-set loop: read current, compute next from your lambda, compareAndSet current, next , retry if someone else changed it in the meantime. The lambda must be pure and fast because it can run several times."

title: emit vs tryEmit
text: What's the difference between emit and tryEmit on MutableSharedFlow , when does tryEmit return false, and why does tryEmit on a default MutableSharedFlow seem to "not work"? " emit is suspending: it waits if the buffer is full. tryEmit never suspends and returns a Boolean: true if the value was accepted, false if it would have needed to suspend. On a default SharedFlow with no buffer and SUSPEND overflow, there's never room, so with subscribers present tryEmit returns false and the value is dropped; with no subscribers it returns true but the value is lost anyway because nobody is listening and replay is 0. Add extraBufferCapacity or a DROP overflow policy, and tryEmit works from callbacks."

title: emit vs tryEmit
text: Find the bug s , explain exactly why it fails on some devices, and fix it. A fitness app 1.2M DAU wraps a vendor BLE heart-rate SDK. The SDK calls onSample bpm: Int on its own binder thread about 1 Hz. A new ViewModel was written like this, and QA reports "the BPM tile stays at -- on Pixel 7 and Galaxy S23; it works on one old test phone". No crash, no logs. class HrViewModel private val sdk: HrSdk : ViewModel { private val samples = MutableSharedFlow<Int val samples: SharedFlow<Int = samples init { sdk.setListener { bpm - samples.tryEmit bpm } sdk.start } } // Fragment viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch { repeatOnLifecycle Lifecycle.State.STARTED { vm.samples.collect { tile.text = it.toString } } }

title: Subscription timing & subscriptionCount
text: I call emit on a MutableSharedFlow right after launching a collector, and the collector sometimes misses the first value. Why, and what are subscriptionCount and onSubscription for? "A SharedFlow without replay delivers a value only to subscribers that exist at the moment of emission. launch { flow.collect {} } returns immediately; the coroutine hasn't necessarily started collecting yet, so an emit right after can happen before the subscription exists, and it's dropped. To coordinate, subscriptionCount is a StateFlow of the number of active collectors you can first { it 0 } before emitting , and onSubscription { } runs an action after the collector is registered, guaranteeing it won't miss what follows. Or give the flow replay ."

title: Conflation
text: Is the analytics SDK dropping events? What's going on and what do you change? A checkout ViewModel exposes StateFlow<PaymentState with states Idle - Authorizing - Verifying3DS - Capturing - Success . The repository's local mock path updates these synchronously; the real path updates them with 50-400 ms between. Product analytics shows funnel steps Verifying3DS and Capturing logged for only 62% of successful payments, while server logs show every payment went through all steps. A PM says "analytics is dropping events, fix the SDK". The analytics call is inside viewModel.state.collect { analytics.track it } on Main. About 380k payments/day.

title: StateFlow vs SharedFlow(replay=1)
text: MutableSharedFlow replay = 1, onBufferOverflow = DROP OLDEST looks like a StateFlow. What are the actual differences, and when would you pick each? "They look similar but differ in four ways: StateFlow requires an initial value and has .value ; StateFlow ignores writes equal to the current value, SharedFlow delivers every emission including duplicates; StateFlow's replayCache can't be reset, SharedFlow's can; and StateFlow always has a value to hand to new collectors, while the SharedFlow variant has none until the first emit. I use StateFlow for state, SharedFlow for events or when I need duplicates, no initial value, or resetReplayCache ."

title: Equality dedupe
text: Evaluate the proposal and design the state so users get correct feedback. A stock-watch screen 900k DAU shows a quote list. A QuoteRepository polls every 5 s and the ViewModel does ui.value = UiState quotes = repo.fetch . During market closure, quotes are identical, so the UI shows no change; support is flooded with "app is frozen, data is not refreshing". Design adds a "Last updated 12:03:15" label and pull-to-refresh which must show the spinner for the duration of a manual fetch. A junior proposes: "StateFlow ignores equal values. Let's make UiState non-data class identity equals so every fetch re-emits."

title: Internals
text: How do StateFlowImpl and SharedFlowImpl work internally? What explains conflation in one and per-subscriber delivery and backpressure in the other? "StateFlow keeps one atomic value plus a version and one tiny slot per collector; a write bumps the version and wakes each slot, and each collector re-reads the value, so intermediates are naturally skipped. SharedFlow keeps a circular buffer with indices: replay window, the position of the slowest subscriber, and a queue of suspended emitters; each subscriber has a slot with its own read index. The buffer entries can be freed only after the slowest subscriber has passed them, which is why one slow subscriber blocks the emitter under SUSPEND."

title: Replay cache
text: Explain the leak mechanically, mitigate it, and fix it durably. Be specific about what you would and wouldn't do in the flow layer. A banking-lite app 2.4M MAU has a @Singleton ProfileRepository exposing val profile: SharedFlow<Profile backed by MutableSharedFlow<Profile replay = 1 . Screens collect it. After a rollout, security gets a report: after logging out and logging in as a different user shared family tablet , the Home screen briefly 300-900 ms shows the previous user's name and balance badge. Crash-free rate is unaffected; it shows up in about 0.02% of sessions roughly 480 users/day have multiple accounts on one device . Logout clears the DB, tokens, and navigates to Login. The first login's network call is slow p95 700 ms .

title: Operators on shared flows
text: What happens when you apply distinctUntilChanged , conflate , flowOn , map {} or catch {} to a StateFlow or SharedFlow? What does each return, and which are meaningless? "Operators like map or filter on a StateFlow return a plain Flow , not a StateFlow, so you lose .value and the hot-state type; the result is cold in the sense that each collector re-runs the operator chain on top of the shared source. Some operators are redundant on shared flows and are deprecated error level for that reason: distinctUntilChanged on StateFlow already distinct , conflate / flowOn / cancellable on SharedFlow no effect on the shared upstream . catch is meaningless on them in practice because a shared flow never completes with an exception from its own emission. If I need a StateFlow again after transforming, I use stateIn ."

title: SharedFlow buffering
text: Why does a 10x increase cause disconnects and ANRs, and how do you redesign the bus? A trading app's price ticker uses a PriceBus singleton: MutableSharedFlow<Tick extraBufferCapacity = 8 default SUSPEND . A WebSocket reader coroutine on Dispatchers.IO calls bus.emit tick for each message. Three collectors: a Compose list cheap, 0.3 ms/tick , a mini-chart on Main 8 ms/tick drawing , and a Room writer 3 ms/tick, batched off-main . With 40 symbols the feed is about 150 ticks/s and is fine. The company adds 400 symbols for premium: about 1,500 ticks/s. After rollout: socket disconnects with "ping timeout" every 40 s, ANR rate rises from 0.2% to 0.9%, battery drain complaints. Server says the client stops reading from the socket.

title: replayCache & resetReplayCache
text: Walk me through replayCache and resetReplayCache : what exactly do new and existing subscribers see, how does it differ for StateFlow, and where does replay become a liability? " replayCache is a read-only snapshot of the last replay values that a new subscriber will receive first. resetReplayCache empties it: new subscribers get only values emitted afterwards, but subscribers already attached still receive values already buffered for them. On StateFlow the replay cache is always exactly the current value and resetReplayCache throws UnsupportedOperationException , so you reset state by writing a sentinel value. Replay is a liability when the value is an event it replays on every resubscribe, like after rotation or repeatOnLifecycle restarts , when it holds user-scoped data that outlives a session, and when it keeps large objects alive."

title: SharedFlow to StateFlow
text: What changes behaviorally between the two, which of those can bite you in prod, and how do you execute the migration safely? A 6-year-old codebase has a helper used in 40 ViewModels: fun <T stateLike = MutableSharedFlow<T replay = 1, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP OLDEST , because "StateFlow didn't allow no-initial-value". Compose screens read .replayCache.lastOrNull in places. Plan: migrate to MutableStateFlow across the board, 3.1M DAU, staged rollout 1% - 10% - 50% - 100% over two weeks. Known risks: unit tests, analytics, some screens call resetReplayCache on logout.

title: Multi-flow consistency
text: Write the post-incident review: cause, why the delay "worked" partially, the fix, and what you'd change in team practice. A marketplace search screen 1.8M DAU shows a spinner, results, or an empty-state "No results" . The ViewModel keeps two flows and combines them for the UI: private val loading = MutableStateFlow false private val results = MutableStateFlow<List<Item emptyList val ui: StateFlow<Ui = combine loading, results { loading, items - when { loading - Ui.Spinner items.isEmpty - Ui.Empty else - Ui.Content items } }.stateIn viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed 5 000 , Ui.Spinner fun search q: String = viewModelScope.launch { loading.value = true val r = repo.search q loading.value = false // A results.value = r // B } Post-incident: 4% of searches flash "No results" for 1-2 frames before the real list on mid-range devices; a screenshot-test flaked once; QA also saw the empty state flash with a spinner skipped under heavy load. The team first "fixed" it by adding delay 16 between A and B , which reduced but didn't remove it.

title: StateFlow vs LiveData
text: What are the main differences between LiveData and StateFlow, and why did Google move its guidance toward StateFlow for ViewModel state? "Both are observable state holders that replay the latest value to new observers. LiveData is lifecycle-aware by itself and Android-only, so it stops delivering when the UI is not started. StateFlow is a plain Kotlin coroutines type: it needs an initial value, has .value readable from any thread, de-duplicates equal values, works with all Flow operators, and runs in pure-Kotlin and multiplatform code. The price is that lifecycle awareness is no longer free: I must collect with repeatOnLifecycle or collectAsStateWithLifecycle ."

title: Initial value & reading state
text: LiveData can be empty but StateFlow must have an initial value. How does that change how you model "not loaded yet", and what does .value give you vs liveData.value ? "A MutableLiveData with no value does not notify observers until someone sets one, and getValue returns null, so 'no value yet' is implicit. StateFlow can never be empty, so I make loading an explicit state in a sealed UiState: Loading , Content , Error . stateFlow.value is non-null and thread-safe to read, but reading it is a snapshot, not a subscription."

title: Lifecycle awareness
text: LiveData is lifecycle-aware; StateFlow is not. What exactly does LiveData do at each lifecycle transition, and how do you get equivalent behavior with StateFlow? "LiveData wraps each observer in a LifecycleBoundObserver . It only delivers when the owner is at least STARTED, parks the latest value while stopped, redelivers it on restart if it changed, and removes the observer at DESTROYED. StateFlow has none of that: the collector runs until its coroutine is cancelled. To match it I collect inside repeatOnLifecycle STARTED , which cancels the collection at STOPPED and relaunches at STARTED. In Compose I use collectAsStateWithLifecycle ."

title: setValue / postValue / threading
text: Explain setValue vs postValue on MutableLiveData, the value-loss problem with postValue , and how StateFlow's threading model compares. " setValue must run on the main thread and dispatches synchronously to active observers. postValue can run on any thread: it stores the value in a field and posts one Runnable to the main thread; if you call postValue several times before that Runnable runs, only the last value is delivered. So postValue is lossy and also asynchronous: reading .value right after postValue returns the old value. StateFlow's .value = is safe from any thread, doesn't hop to main, and conflates by design; delivery thread is the collector's dispatcher."

title: Conflation & equality
text: Both LiveData and StateFlow are said to hold "the latest value". How do equality checks and conflation differ between them, and when does that change app behavior? "StateFlow compares new vs old with equals and doesn't emit if equal; it's also conflated, so a slow collector only sees the latest value. LiveData has no equality check: setValue x twice dispatches twice. postValue coalesces between main-thread runs. So if a feature relied on re-setting the same value to re-trigger the UI, it breaks with StateFlow. And with StateFlow, mutating an object in place and re-assigning the same reference never emits."

title: Java & View-system interop
text: Your app has Java screens, data binding layouts, and a ViewModel exposing StateFlow. How do you make that work, and what are the limits? "Java can't consume suspending or coroutine-scoped APIs cleanly, so for Java screens I expose LiveData via flow.asLiveData at the ViewModel edge, or keep LiveData for those screens. For Kotlin Fragments with ViewBinding I collect in repeatOnLifecycle . Data binding supports StateFlow directly when I set binding.lifecycleOwner = viewLifecycleOwner , with AGP 7+; otherwise I bridge with asLiveData ."

title: Migrating LiveData to Flow
text: How would you migrate a 200-screen app from LiveData to Flow without a big-bang rewrite? What are the semantic traps? "Bottom-up, in the layers that already speak coroutines: Room and repositories return Flow, domain/use-cases use Flow, and the ViewModel exposes StateFlow. At the ViewModel edge, asLiveData keeps unmigrated screens working. Then I migrate screens one at a time to repeatOnLifecycle / collectAsStateWithLifecycle . The traps: dedupe, no lifecycle awareness, MediatorLiveData and switchMap replacements, and events modelled as LiveData."

title: One-off events - stickiness
text: Why did the "SingleLiveEvent" pattern exist, why is it considered broken, and what is the underlying problem all event-modelling approaches must solve? "LiveData and StateFlow are both sticky: a new observer immediately gets the last value. That's right for state and wrong for events: after rotation the Fragment re-observes and replays 'navigate to details' or 'show error' again. SingleLiveEvent used an AtomicBoolean to hand the value to one observer once. It breaks with multiple observers only one gets it , loses events when no observer is active, and the pending-flag is not tied to the actual UI consuming it. The root problem is that an event has a producer lifetime ViewModel longer than the consumer lifetime view , so delivery must be decoupled from observation."

title: One-off events - options compared
text: Compare MutableSharedFlow, Channel, and events-as-state for one-off ViewModel-to-UI events. Which would you choose by default and why? "SharedFlow with replay 0 drops events when no collector exists, e.g. during rotation or while in background. SharedFlow with replay 1 re-delivers after rotation. A Channel buffers events until a collector arrives and delivers each to one consumer, which solves most loss, but it can still lose an event cancelled mid-handling and it's still a stream, which Google now discourages. Events-as-state keeps the event in UI state until the UI acknowledges it, which gives deterministic behavior across config change and process death with saved state. My default is events-as-state; I use a Channel only for fire-and-forget effects where a small loss is acceptable and there is exactly one collector."

title: Channel as event bus - where it loses events
text: You choose Channel.receiveAsFlow for events. Walk me through every scenario in which an event can still be lost or duplicated. "Loss: the collector is cancelled after receive took the element but before the UI handled it, because repeatOnLifecycle cancels at STOPPED; process death; buffer overflow with trySend or DROP overflow; consumeAsFlow closing the channel when a collector is cancelled; and ViewModel clear. Duplicate-or-misdirected: two collectors, e.g. two Fragments or a collector launched twice, each get a subset. It's more robust than replay-0 SharedFlow but it's not a guarantee."

title: One-off events - Google guidance
text: What is Google's current guidance on ViewModel-to-UI one-off events, and how would you implement it for a snackbar and for navigation? Where does the guidance hurt? "The Android architecture docs say ViewModel events should always result in a UI state update; they discourage Channels and other reactive streams for this because delivery is not guaranteed when the producer outlives the consumer. So a snackbar message becomes a nullable field in UiState; the UI shows it, then calls viewModel.messageShown to clear it. Navigation triggered by business logic works the same: a navigateTo field consumed after navigating. The costs: ack boilerplate, one-slot overwrites, risk of showing twice if the UI is torn down before the ack, and awkwardness when the navigation back stack keeps the screen alive."

title: StateFlow & mutable collections
text: Find the bug s , explain why it worked with LiveData, and fix it properly. A shopping cart screen was migrated from LiveData to StateFlow. QA reports: adding an item does nothing visually until the user rotates the device; then the item is there. Crash rate is flat 0.2% . Code: class CartViewModel : ViewModel { private val items = MutableStateFlow mutableListOf<CartItem val items: StateFlow<List<CartItem = items fun add item: CartItem { items.value.add item items.value = items.value } fun remove id: Long { items.value.removeAll { it.id == id } } } The RecyclerView adapter is a ListAdapter with DiffUtil. Product also says "it worked with LiveData postValue list ".

title: One-off events - navigation
text: Diagnose both symptoms, ship a fix, and say what you would standardize across the codebase. Login screen, 1.2M DAU, 60% on Android 12+. After release 8.4, support tickets: "after logging in the home screen opens twice - I have to press back twice" about 1.5% of logins and "login succeeds but nothing happens" about 0.4% . Crash rate unchanged. Code in 8.4 changed from SingleLiveEvent : class LoginViewModel : ViewModel { private val nav = MutableSharedFlow<NavEvent replay = 1 val nav = nav.asSharedFlow fun onLoginSuccess { viewModelScope.launch { nav.emit NavEvent.Home } } } // Fragment.onViewCreated: viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch { viewModel.nav.collect { findNavController .navigate R.id.action login to home } } Duplicates correlate with rotation or returning from background shortly after login. The "nothing happens" cases correlate with users who tapped login and then locked the screen.

title: One-off events - snackbar
text: Why is it shown twice and why are consecutive identical failures sometimes not shown at all? Fix it. A Compose screen shows an error snackbar using events-as-state per Google's guidance. Users on slow devices report the same "Could not sync" snackbar appearing a second time after rotating the phone while it was showing, and about 2% of sessions show it again after returning from a deep link screen. Code: @Composable fun SyncScreen vm: SyncViewModel, snackbar: SnackbarHostState { val state by vm.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle state.userMessage?.let { msg - LaunchedEffect msg { snackbar.showSnackbar msg vm.userMessageShown } } } fun userMessageShown { state.update { it.copy userMessage = null } } The user message is a plain String . Two sync failures in a row produce the identical text.

title: LiveData to Flow migration
text: Explain both symptoms, how you'd roll back/mitigate, and the permanent fix. Release 5.2 migrated the Orders screen from LiveData to StateFlow staged rollout 20% - 100% . Crashlytics now shows a new top crash on the migrated screen, 0.9% of sessions, 70% on Android 13+: java.lang.IllegalStateException: Can not perform this action after onSaveInstanceState at androidx.fragment.app.FragmentManager.checkStateLoss at androidx.fragment.app.DialogFragment.show at OrdersFragment$onViewCreated$1.invokeSuspend OrdersFragment.kt:58 Battery dashboard also shows 2x background network calls on that screen. Code: override fun onViewCreated v: View, s: Bundle? { lifecycleScope.launch { viewModel.state.collect { render it } // render may show a ConfirmDialog } } // ViewModel val state = repo.orders .stateIn viewModelScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, OrdersState.Loading Before the migration it was viewModel.state.observe viewLifecycleOwner { render it } .

title: Upstream lifetime & leaks
text: How do LiveData and StateFlow differ in when their upstream work starts and stops, and what leaks can each cause? "A MutableLiveData/MutableStateFlow itself has no upstream; the question is about derived ones. liveData {} / asLiveData start when the first observer is active onActive and cancel 5 seconds after the last one goes inactive. stateIn takes a SharingStarted policy: Eagerly / Lazily never stop, WhileSubscribed 5 000 mirrors the LiveData behavior. Leaks: observeForever that's never removed; a StateFlow collector in a scope that outlives the UI; a ViewModel holding a Fragment/Context reference in a lambda; a hot upstream kept alive by Eagerly ."

title: One-off events standardization
text: What standard do you propose, how do you roll it out, and how do you decide exceptions? You join a 25-engineer team, 60 screens. Event handling is inconsistent: 20 screens use SingleLiveEvent , 15 use MutableSharedFlow<Event , 10 use Channel , 15 are Compose with ad-hoc mutableStateOf flags. Last quarter produced 3 incidents: duplicate order submissions after rotation, a missing "session expired" dialog after a background-to-foreground transition, and a double snackbar. The tech lead wants a single standard and a migration plan with no feature freeze. Roadmap: Compose migration over the next 3 quarters.

title: Basic operators
text: What do map , filter , transform and onEach do on a Flow, and how do you choose between them? " map converts each item one-to-one, filter drops items by predicate, onEach runs a side effect and passes the same item downstream, and transform is the general one: it gets a collector receiver, so I can emit zero, one or many items per input, even before or after the item. map and filter are just thin wrappers over transform . All of them are lazy: nothing runs until a terminal operator collects."

title: Operator semantics (cold, lazy, per-collector state)
text: If I build a chain like flow.filter{}.map{}.distinctUntilChanged and collect it twice, what runs, how many times, and where does the operator state live? "Each operator just builds a new Flow object that wraps the previous one; nothing executes at build time. Every terminal call re-runs the whole chain from the source, so two collectors means the producer runs twice. Stateful operators like distinctUntilChanged , take , scan keep their state in local variables inside the collect call, so each collection gets fresh state. The danger is state I capture myself outside the lambda."

title: distinctUntilChanged
text: How do distinctUntilChanged and distinctUntilChangedBy work, and what are their limits? "It drops an item if it equals the previous emitted item == . It is only consecutive de-duplication, not a global set. distinctUntilChangedBy { it.id } compares a derived key, and there is an overload taking a custom old, new - Boolean . On a StateFlow it is pointless because StateFlow already de-duplicates by equality, and the stdlib marks it as having no effect."

title: take / takeWhile / drop
text: What do take , takeWhile , drop , dropWhile and first do, and what happens to the upstream producer when you stop early? " take n passes the first n items then completes the flow and cancels the upstream; takeWhile does the same when the predicate first fails the failing item is not emitted ; drop n skips the first n; dropWhile skips until the predicate first fails then passes everything. first is effectively take 1 plus a terminal. Early completion is implemented by cancelling the upstream collection, so cleanup in finally or onCompletion runs."

title: onStart / onEmpty / onCompletion
text: What are onStart , onEmpty and onCompletion for, and when does each fire? " onStart runs before the upstream is collected and can emit, so it is where I emit Loading . onEmpty runs only if the upstream completes without emitting anything, and can emit a fallback. onCompletion runs on normal completion, failure or cancellation, with a nullable cause ; it observes the failure but does not catch it, so catch is still needed."

title: flatMapConcat / flatMapMerge / flatMapLatest
text: Explain flatMapConcat , flatMapMerge and flatMapLatest . Give a use case for each and how their output differs for the same input. "All three map each upstream item to an inner flow and flatten. flatMapConcat runs inner flows one at a time, preserving order. flatMapMerge runs up to N inner flows concurrently and emits in whatever order results arrive. flatMapLatest cancels the previous inner flow when a new upstream item arrives, so only the latest inner flow produces output. Concat for ordered writes, merge for parallel independent work, latest for search-as-you-type."

title: combine vs zip vs merge
text: Compare combine , zip and merge . When does each emit and complete, and which would you use to build a screen state from three sources? " merge interleaves several flows of the same type into one and completes when all complete. combine emits whenever any source emits, using the latest value of every other source, but only after each source has emitted at least once. zip pairs the n-th item of each flow with the n-th of the others and completes when the shortest completes. For screen state from several sources I use combine ."

title: debounce vs sample
text: What is the difference between debounce and sample ? When would each be the wrong choice? " debounce t emits an item only if no newer item arrives within t; it restarts its timer on every item, so a continuous stream never emits. sample period emits the most recent item once per period, regardless of activity, so it guarantees a steady rate. I use debounce for user typing, sample for high-frequency telemetry like sensors or scroll."

title: scan / runningFold / runningReduce
text: What do scan , runningFold and runningReduce do, and how would you use them to build a state reducer? What is the trap with the initial value? " scan initial { acc, v - } emits the initial value first, then every intermediate accumulation. runningFold is the same operation under the collection-style name. runningReduce has no initial; its first output is the first element. For a state reducer I do events.scan initialState, ::reduce . The trap: the initial value object is created once at assembly time, so a mutable initial is shared across collections."

title: combine of many flows
text: combine has typed overloads only up to five flows. How do you combine seven flows, or a dynamic list of flows, and what are the pitfalls? "Typed overloads go up to 5. Beyond that I use the combine vararg flows or combine Iterable<Flow<T overload whose transform receives an Array<T , which means casting, or I nest: combine combine a,b,c {...}, combine d,e,f {...} {...} into small intermediate models. Pitfalls: an empty list completes immediately without emitting, the array overload needs a common supertype, and combine waits for every source to emit once."

title: Operator ordering
text: Does the order of operators in a Flow chain matter? Give concrete examples where swapping two operators changes behavior or cost. "Yes, constantly. Cheap, selective operators go first filter, take so expensive ones see fewer items. distinctUntilChanged goes after the projection it should compare. debounce goes before flatMapLatest so I don't start a request per keystroke. catch only handles errors from upstream of it, and onStart / flowOn apply to what is above them. Same operators, different order, different result."

title: combine
text: Find the cause, fix it for users now, and prevent the class of bug. A profile screen DAU 400k builds its state with combine userFlow, avatarFlow, badgesFlow { u, a, b - ProfileState u, a, b } collected via stateIn in the ViewModel. After a release, support reports "profile loading forever", about 6% of sessions, concentrated on new accounts. No crashes, no ANRs, Crashlytics clean. avatarFlow is a callbackFlow over an SDK listener that only invokes the callback when an avatar file exists. Backend latency p95 is normal. The release also bumped the Compose BOM and changed the image loader red herrings .

title: catch placement
text: Why does search die permanently after one error, and how do you fix it properly? Search-as-you-type for a marketplace app 1.2M DAU . After shipping, QA reports "search works until I type something that makes the server return a 500, then it never works again until I leave the screen". Crashlytics shows nothing. Here is the ViewModel code: class SearchVm private val repo: Repo : ViewModel { val query = MutableStateFlow "" val state: StateFlow<UiState = query .debounce 300 .distinctUntilChanged .flatMapLatest { q - repo.search q .map { UiState.Content it } } .catch { emit UiState.Error it.message } .stateIn viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed 5 000 , UiState.Idle } repo.search is a flow {} that throws HttpException on 500. Backend 5xx rate is about 0.3%. Red herring: someone suspects debounce is broken.

title: distinctUntilChanged
text: Why does the UI not update, and how do you fix it robustly? A to-do app 350k DAU migrated from LiveData to Flow. After the migration, users report "I add an item and the list does not update until I rotate the phone". The ViewModel: class TodoVm : ViewModel { private val items = mutableListOf<Todo private val list = MutableStateFlow<List<Todo items val list: StateFlow<List<Todo = list fun add t: Todo { items.add t list.value = items // "triggers update" } } // UI vm.list.map { it.sortedBy Todo::due }.distinctUntilChanged .collect adapter::submitList Unit tests with 1 item pass. Release notes mention RecyclerView 1.3 upgrade red herring . Crash-free rate is 99.9%.

title: zip vs combine
text: Diagnose, propose the right operator, and say what clarifying questions you would ask the PM before changing it. A trading-lite app 180k DAU must show "price in the user's currency". Prices tick about 10 times per second per symbol; FX rates arrive about once a minute. A developer wrote price.zip fxRate { p, r - p r } and QA says: "the displayed price updates only once a minute and is always behind". The product manager's spec says only: "combine the price with the FX rate". Memory is fine, no crashes; the websocket is healthy.

title: debounce vs sample
text: Fix the pipeline so UI and sync are both sensible, and justify your operator choices. A fitness app records accelerometer samples at 50 Hz and forwards a "current cadence" metric to a Compose UI and a cloud sync. A dev added .debounce 500 to reduce UI load; now the cadence widget is blank while the user runs and only updates when they stop. Before the change, the UI recomposed 50 times per second and p95 frame time on a Galaxy A13 was 31 ms jank , battery drain reported at 9%/hour for the feature. The cloud sync also sends one request per sample 50 req/s and was throttled by the backend.

title: flatMapMerge concurrency
text: How does flatMapMerge limit concurrency, what is the default, and how does it interact with backpressure, ordering and failure? How would you size it? " flatMapMerge concurrency collects the upstream and launches each inner flow in a child coroutine, using a semaphore to cap how many run at once. The default is 16 DEFAULT CONCURRENCY , tunable via the kotlinx.coroutines.flow.defaultConcurrency system property . When the cap is reached the upstream is suspended, which is natural backpressure. Output order is arrival order, and one inner failure cancels everything. I size it by the scarcest resource: memory per item, connection pool, or server rate limit, not by CPU count."

title: flatMapLatest / transformLatest internals
text: How does flatMapLatest actually cancel the previous inner flow? What does "cancellation is cooperative" imply for it, and what are the subtleties with buffering? " flatMapLatest is transformLatest { emitAll transform it } . It collects the upstream in one coroutine and runs each transform block in a child job. When a new upstream item arrives it cancels the previous child and waits for it to finish cancelling before starting the new one. Because cancellation is cooperative, an inner block that never reaches a suspension point or ignores cancellation delays the next one. The operator is channel based, so it has an internal buffer, and results of a cancelled block that were already sent can still reach the collector."

title: Custom operators (throttleFirst)
text: There is no built-in throttleFirst . Implement one, explain its semantics versus debounce and sample , and discuss testing. " throttleFirst window emits the first item, drops everything for the window duration, then accepts the next item. I implement it with flow { } , collecting the upstream and tracking a monotonic time mark; no extra coroutines needed. I use a monotonic clock, not wall-clock, and for tests I inject a TimeSource so virtual time works."

title: Writing custom operators correctly
text: What rules must a custom Flow operator follow, and what breaks if you violate them? Write a chunked size operator as an example. "A custom operator should be built with flow { collect { emit } } or transform , so that it emits only from the collector's own coroutine. Rules: preserve context never emit from another coroutine or dispatcher; use channelFlow if concurrency is needed , keep exception transparency never catch exceptions that come from emit , i.e. the downstream , be cancellation-friendly don't swallow CancellationException , and keep state local to the collection. I write chunked with a local buffer and a flush after the upstream completes."

title: flatMapLatest
text: What is the bug, why only on slow networks and long sessions, and how do you redesign the save pipeline? A notes app 900k DAU autosaves drafts. Since a refactor, support sees "my last paragraph disappeared" on about 3% of long editing sessions, with no crash. Server logs show the draft endpoint receiving requests whose body is truncated relative to the final text, and some requests with client-side cancellation 499 . Code: private val edits = MutableSharedFlow<Draft extraBufferCapacity = 64 init { edits .debounce 400 .flatMapLatest { draft - flow { api.saveDraft draft.id, draft.text // suspend POST emit SaveState.Saved draft.id }.onStart { emit SaveState.Saving } } .onEach { saveState.value = it } .launchIn viewModelScope } Typical typing bursts have pauses of 300-1200 ms; mobile p95 request latency is 900 ms on 3G-class networks. The team suspects the server red herring and debounce .

title: flatMapMerge
text: Explain the OOM from the code, fix it, and describe how you would choose the right parallelism. A social app 2.5M DAU lets users attach up to 40 photos from the gallery; many are 12 MP 4000 x 3000 . A new "faster uploads" release processes them as: photos.asFlow .flatMapMerge { uri - flow { emit upload compress decode uri } } .collect { progress.advance } After release, Crashlytics shows OutOfMemoryError at BitmapFactory.decodeStream , concentrated on devices with a 256 MB heap limit and 3 GB RAM; crash-free sessions dropped from 99.6% to 97.5% for the attach-photos flow. Logcat excerpt: Throwing OutOfMemoryError "Failed to allocate a 48000012 byte allocation with ... free bytes" . Upload bandwidth utilization stays about 20% on the same devices. Red herring: the team had also updated Coil.

title: flatMapMerge vs flatMapConcat
text: Lead the post-incident review: root cause, what went wrong in process, and what the design should be. Post-incident review for a messaging app 6M DAU . Outbound messages go through outbox.flatMapMerge concurrency = 4 { msg - flow { emit api.send msg } } . Over two weeks, 0.4% of conversations had messages shown out of order on the recipient's device e.g., "see you at 5" before "dinner tonight?" , and some edits arrived before the original. The backend assigns the server timestamp on receipt. The incident was detected only through support tickets about 1,100 . The dev who introduced it says "it was a perf fix, latency of send queue dropped 35%". Red herring: clock skew between servers was investigated for three days.

title: End-to-end pipeline
text: Design the pipeline end to end with Flow operators, explain each stage, and say how you would test it. You own search for a food-delivery app 3M DAU, peak 40k searches/min . Requirements: type-ahead results as the user types; no request for queries under 2 characters; no request per keystroke backend cost: each request costs about 0.4 vCPU-ms and p95 latency is 450 ms ; clearing the field must be instant; errors must not break typing; rotation must not re-fire the last search; results should survive for 5 s when the screen is backgrounded briefly; stale responses must never overwrite fresh ones. Current implementation is a TextWatcher + Handler.postDelayed + Retrofit callbacks with a race-condition bug about 1.5% of searches show stale results .

title: mapLatest / collectLatest / transformLatest
text: How do mapLatest , transformLatest , flatMapLatest and collectLatest relate? Where exactly does cancellation land in each, and when is "latest" the wrong semantic? "They are all the same idea: a new upstream value cancels the block still running for the previous value. transformLatest is the base block with an emitter , mapLatest is transformLatest { emit transform it } , flatMapLatest is transformLatest { emitAll transform it } , and collectLatest is a terminal: mapLatest action .buffer 0 .collect . Cancellation hits whichever block is suspended at that moment, and only at suspension points. 'Latest' is wrong whenever the block has non-idempotent side effects like writes."

title: Suspension-based backpressure
text: A plain flow { } has no buffer. If the collector is slower than the producer, what actually happens, and why is there no "MissingBackpressureException" in Flow like in RxJava? "A cold Flow runs the producer and the collector in the same coroutine. emit is a suspend function that directly calls the collector lambda and returns only when the lambda finishes. So a slow collector simply makes the producer wait; backpressure is implicit through suspension. Nothing is queued, nothing overflows, nothing is dropped. The cost is that total time is the sum of producer and collector work per item."

title: flowOn
text: What does flowOn Dispatchers.IO change and what does it not change? Where in a chain should it go? " flowOn changes the context of everything upstream of it, up to the previous flowOn or the source. Everything downstream, including collect , keeps running in the collector's context. So it is a boundary, not a global switch. Place it right after the operators that need the other dispatcher, usually at the end of the data-layer chain, before the ViewModel or UI consumes it."

title: flowOn internals
text: Does flowOn always create a channel? What exactly happens under the hood when the dispatcher does and doesn't change? " flowOn is implemented as a ChannelFlow operator. If the new context has a different dispatcher than the collector's, it launches the upstream in a producer coroutine on that dispatcher and passes items through a channel to the collector, default buffer size 64. If the dispatcher is the same, it skips the channel and collects directly in the same coroutine. So a dispatcher switch means a coroutine plus a buffered channel, and that means upstream can run ahead of downstream by up to the buffer size."

title: Multiple flowOn
text: What happens when a chain has two or three flowOn operators? Give an example and say which code runs where. "Each flowOn governs the segment between itself and the previous flowOn or the source . So with two flowOn s you get two segments on two dispatchers plus the collector's, connected by channels. They don't override each other; a later flowOn never changes what an earlier one set."

title: Context preservation
text: Why does this crash with "Flow invariant is violated", and how do you fix it properly? val f = flow { withContext Dispatchers.IO { emit loadFromDisk } } "Flow requires that emit be called from the same coroutine context the collector uses. withContext changes the context, so the emit happens in a different one and Flow throws IllegalStateException: Flow invariant is violated: Flow was collected in ... but emission happened in ... . The fix is to do the work in withContext and emit outside it, or move the dispatcher change to flowOn , or use channelFlow / callbackFlow if you truly must emit from another coroutine."

title: buffer
text: Explain buffer capacity, onBufferOverflow . What does each parameter do, and what is the default capacity? " buffer runs the upstream in a separate coroutine and puts a channel between it and the collector, so they overlap. capacity is the channel size: BUFFERED default, 64 unless the system property changes it , RENDEZVOUS 0 , CONFLATED , UNLIMITED or a number. onBufferOverflow says what to do when full: SUSPEND default, producer waits , DROP OLDEST , or DROP LATEST . Only SUSPEND preserves every item."

title: conflate
text: What does conflate do and when is it the right tool? Is it the same as StateFlow 's conflation? " conflate is buffer CONFLATED : a one-slot buffer where a new value overwrites the pending one. The collector is never behind by more than one item and always eventually sees the latest value, but intermediate values are skipped. It's right for state-like streams position, progress, sensor readings where only the freshest value matters. StateFlow conflates by design too, but it's a hot holder with equality check; conflate just applies the policy to any cold flow."

title: collectLatest vs conflate
text: conflate .collect { } and collectLatest { } both skip stale values. What is the actual difference, and when would you choose one over the other? " conflate never interrupts the collector: if it's busy with item 1, new items overwrite each other and the collector finishes item 1, then takes the newest. collectLatest cancels the running block for item 1 as soon as item 2 arrives, then starts on item 2. Choose collectLatest when old work is worthless and cancellable render a search result, load details , and conflate when the work must finish once started write to disk, commit a frame ."

title: Backpressure strategies
text: Compare the options for dealing with a producer faster than its consumer in Flow: suspend, buffer, drop, conflate, collectLatest . How do you choose, and how does this differ from RxJava? "Default is suspension: lossless, no memory growth, but producer throughput equals consumer. Buffer decouples but moves the problem into memory. Drop policies and conflate trade completeness for freshness and bounded memory. collectLatest trades work for freshness. I choose by asking: must every item be processed, may old items be skipped, may in-flight work be cancelled, how big can the backlog get. RxJava needs explicit onBackpressureXXX operators because its protocol is request n based and Observable has none; Flow's suspend gives lossless pacing by default."

title: produceIn / launchIn
text: What do launchIn , produceIn and onEach { }.launchIn scope do, and why would you ever use produceIn ? " launchIn scope is scope.launch { collect } : it starts collecting in that scope and returns the Job . produceIn scope collects the flow in a new coroutine in scope and exposes the items as a ReceiveChannel ; it's how you convert a cold flow into a channel for select , fan-out to multiple workers, or manual receive loops. In both, the lifetime is the scope's, so cancel the job/channel or the scope."

title: channelFlow
text: When do you use channelFlow instead of flow { } ? What does it let you do, what are its default buffering semantics, and how is it different from callbackFlow ? " flow { } must emit sequentially from one coroutine. channelFlow { } gives you a ProducerScope : you can launch several child coroutines, on any dispatcher, each calling send thread-safe , and the flow completes when the block and all its children finish. It is backed by a buffered channel default 64 . callbackFlow is the same builder specialised for callback APIs; it additionally requires awaitClose { } and fails with IllegalStateException if the block returns without it."

title: Operator fusion
text: You write flow.flowOn IO .buffer 10 .buffer 5 .conflate . How many channels exist and what is the effective capacity? What are the fusion rules? "Adjacent channel-based operators flowOn , buffer , conflate , channelFlow , produceIn are fused into one channel; the documented rules: explicit capacity beats the default BUFFERED request, several explicit capacities are summed, and a non-SUSPEND overflow policy overrides everything buffering before it. So here: one channel, the conflate last overrides the earlier buffers, effectively CONFLATED."

title: flowOn exceptions & cancellation
text: With flow { ... }.flowOn IO .collect { } , what happens when a the upstream throws, b the collector throws, c the collector's scope is cancelled? Which items does the collector see? "Across a flowOn boundary there are two coroutines linked by a channel. a An upstream exception closes the channel with that cause; the collector first drains items already buffered, then the exception is rethrown from collect . b A collector exception cancels the producer coroutine structured concurrency , and propagates to the caller. c Cancelling the collector's scope cancels the producer too; buffered unread items are discarded. So the collector can observe items followed by the exception, and in-flight upstream work is never orphaned."

title: Firehose sources
text: Why did it degrade, how do you make it safe at 400 Hz, and what do you decide about data loss? A fitness app streams accelerometer data via callbackFlow registered with SensorManager at SENSOR DELAY GAME 50 Hz on test devices; many mid-range devices deliver 100 Hz . The product wants a "high accuracy" mode at 400 Hz for 10-minute workouts, on 5.2M DAU, mid-range devices 4 GB RAM . Current code: fun accel : Flow<Reading = callbackFlow { val l = object : SensorEventListener { override fun onSensorChanged e: SensorEvent { trySend Reading e.timestamp, e.values 0 , e.values 1 , e.values 2 } override fun onAccuracyChanged s: Sensor?, a: Int {} } sm.registerListener l, sensor, 2 500 // 2.5 ms awaitClose { sm.unregisterListener l } } // ViewModel accel .map { filter.apply it }.onEach { db.insert it }.launchIn viewModelScope Beta: at 400 Hz, 8% of sessions report "freezing" after about 4 minutes, and some reports of OutOfMemoryError . Heap dump shows 70% Reading objects. At 50 Hz no issue.

title: Slow collector
text: Diagnose and fix without changing the server. A trading-watchlist screen shows live prices for 30 symbols. WebSocket pushes 120 messages/s through a callbackFlow . After a release adding sparkline calculation, Crashlytics shows ANR rate up from 0.15% to 0.9% on mid-range devices Android 11-13 , plus janky frames Perfetto: 40% of frames 16 ms . The ViewModel: repo.prices // callbackFlow, Dispatchers.Main.immediate collector .map { buildSparkline it } // 12 ms CPU per message .collect { state.update { s - s.with it } } Logs: Skipped 87 frames! The application may be doing too much work on its main thread. Backend team says "server is fine".

title: flowOn placement
text: What runs where, why does the screen freeze, and how do you fix it? A code review. The goal: parse a 3 MB JSON file off the main thread and show a list; QA says the screen freezes 900 ms on a Pixel 4a. fun items : Flow<List<Item = flow { val text = file.readText // 3 MB emit parser.parse text // 700 ms CPU }.flowOn Dispatchers.IO .map { list - list.sortedBy { it.name } } // 150 ms CPU for 40k items .onEach { cache.put it } // 50 ms .flowOn Dispatchers.Main viewModelScope.launch { items .collect { ui.value = it } } The author says "I put flowOn at the end so everything runs on the right thread".

title: channelFlow concurrency
text: Choose and implement an approach; discuss ordering, failure, memory, cancellation. A home screen needs enrichments for up to 60 product IDs: each api.detail id takes 250-900 ms p95 1.2 s , the backend allows at most 6 concurrent requests per client before returning 429. UX wants cards to appear as they arrive, not wait for all, and wants cancellation when the user leaves. Current sequential implementation: flow { ids.forEach { emit api.detail it } } // 60 x 500 ms = 30 s total A teammate proposes ids.map { async { api.detail it } }.awaitAll ; another proposes ids.asFlow .flatMapMerge { flow { emit api.detail it } } .

title: Location pipeline
text: The requirements conflict "smooth" vs "never lose" . How do you structure the flow pipeline, buffers and loss policies? A ride-hailing driver app: FusedLocationProvider delivers updates every 1 s drivers via callbackFlow . Three consumers: a map marker 60 fps, latest only , b trip-distance calculator needs every fix, in order , c uploader sending a batch to the server every 5 s over flaky 3G can stall for 30+ s . PM says: "make sure it's smooth and we never lose data". Current: one shared flow collected by all three in the same coroutine via merge -like code; when uploads stall the marker freezes.

title: Unbounded buffer
text: Walk through the review: root cause, timeline math, fix, and process changes. Post-incident review of an OOM crash spike: 2.1% of sessions on Android Go 2 GB RAM devices crashed within 10 minutes on the "Gallery sync" screen. Crashlytics: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Failed to allocate a 12582928 byte allocation ... free memory 7MB . Change in release 5.14: "speed up thumbnails pipeline". photos.asFlow // 4,000 local URIs .map { decodeThumb it } // 12 MB bitmap 4 MP ARGB 8888 , 40 ms each .buffer Channel.UNLIMITED // "so decoding never waits for the UI" .collect { uploadAndShow it } // 600 ms each on average Heap graph: thousands of Bitmap instances retained by BufferedChannel segments. Rollback restored stability.

title: flowOn cost
text: What would you change in the Flow pipeline, and what would you measure? An inbox screen observes Room: dao.observeThreads : Flow<List<ThreadEntity about 5,000 rows, 1.5 KB each . A new sync writes in bursts: 30 inserts within 1 s as messages arrive. Profile on a Redmi 9 Android 11 : each Room invalidation re-queries 5,000 rows 35 ms and the pipeline below runs per emission; battery team reports the screen at 11% CPU while idle-syncing, and p95 time-to-render after a sync is 480 ms. dao.observeThreads .flowOn Dispatchers.IO // added "to keep Room off main" .map { rows - rows.map { it.toUi clock, fmt } } // 5,000 mappings, 60 ms .flowOn Dispatchers.Default .collect { adapter.submitList it } Perf review asks to cut CPU and render latency without changing the DB schema.

title: stateIn/shareIn semantics
text: What do stateIn and shareIn do, and why would you use them instead of just exposing the cold flow from your repository? "A cold flow re-runs its producer for every collector. stateIn and shareIn start exactly one collection of the upstream inside a scope I give them, and multicast the results to any number of downstream collectors. stateIn gives me a StateFlow always has a value, conflated, equality-deduplicated , shareIn gives me a SharedFlow configurable replay and buffer . I use them so the screen has one upstream, a current value to read synchronously, and survives rotation without re-querying."

title: SharingStarted strategies
text: Explain SharingStarted.Eagerly , Lazily , and WhileSubscribed . When would you pick each? "Eagerly starts the upstream immediately and never stops until the scope dies. Lazily starts when the first subscriber appears and also never stops. WhileSubscribed starts on the first subscriber and stops when the subscriber count drops to zero, after an optional timeout. For UI state in a ViewModel I default to WhileSubscribed 5 000 . Eagerly/Lazily are for state that must keep updating regardless of UI, like an app-level session or cache, and I accept the cost."

title: WhileSubscribed parameters
text: What exactly do stopTimeoutMillis and replayExpirationMillis do in WhileSubscribed ? What are the defaults and how do they interact? " stopTimeoutMillis is how long after the last subscriber leaves before the upstream is cancelled; default 0. replayExpirationMillis is how long after that stop before the replay cache is reset; default Long.MAX VALUE , meaning never. For a StateFlow, reset means going back to the initial value. They are sequential: stop at T+stopTimeout, reset at T+stopTimeout+replayExpiration."

title: Why 5_000 ms
text: Why does every Android sample use WhileSubscribed 5 000 ? Where does 5 seconds come from and is it a rule? "During a configuration change the Activity is destroyed and recreated within a fraction of a second, so the collector disappears and reappears. With timeout 0 the upstream would be cancelled and restarted on every rotation. A 5-second grace period absorbs that. The 5 s matches the ANR threshold for input events, a conservative upper bound for recreation, and it is not a rule; I tune it per upstream cost."

title: stateIn overloads
text: What is the difference between stateIn scope, started, initialValue and the suspending stateIn scope ? When is each appropriate? "The three-arg version returns immediately with an initial value and follows a SharingStarted policy. The suspend version has no policy: it starts the upstream eagerly in my scope, suspends until the first value arrives, and returns a StateFlow that is already populated. It throws NoSuchElementException if the flow completes with no value. I use the first in ViewModels, and the suspend one where I need a non-null initial state, such as a DI initializer or a test."

title: stateIn vs shareIn
text: stateIn vs shareIn : how do they differ in behavior, and how do you choose? " stateIn produces a StateFlow: always has a value, conflates, drops equal consecutive values, .value readable. shareIn produces a SharedFlow: no required initial value, replay and buffer configurable, every emission is delivered equal values included subject to buffering. I choose stateIn for state the UI renders, shareIn for streams or events where each item matters or where there's no meaningful initial value."

title: .value and WhileSubscribed
text: With stateIn viewModelScope, WhileSubscribed 5000 , initial , I read viewModel.state.value from a click handler with no collector active. What do I get, and what are the implications? "I get the last cached value, or the initial value if the upstream has never run or the cache was reset. Reading .value doesn't subscribe, so it doesn't start the upstream. If the flow is only active while the UI is collecting, then any logic that reads .value from outside collection in tests, in a notification handler, in onCleared can see stale or placeholder data."

title: Why plain lifecycleScope collect is wrong
text: Why is lifecycleScope.launch { flow.collect { ... } } considered unsafe in an Activity? What are launchWhenStarted and repeatOnLifecycle and why was the former deprecated? " lifecycleScope is cancelled only at DESTROYED. So a plain launch { collect } keeps collecting while the app is stopped, wasting CPU/battery and updating views no one sees. launchWhenStarted suspends the coroutine below STARTED but does not cancel it, so the upstream producer stays active and keeps buffering; that's why it was deprecated in lifecycle 2.6. repeatOnLifecycle STARTED cancels the block on STOP and relaunches it on START, which cancels the upstream too."

title: repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) in an Activity
text: Show the correct way to collect a StateFlow and a one-time event stream in an Activity. What happens step by step through start, stop, rotation? "I call lifecycleScope.launch { repeatOnLifecycle STARTED { launch { collect state }; launch { collect events } } } . On every ON START the block starts fresh; on ON STOP it's cancelled, cancelling the collectors; the next ON START runs it again. On rotation the old Activity's scope is cancelled at DESTROYED, and the new Activity registers new collectors. The ViewModel's flows persist, so the StateFlow replays its latest value."

title: repeatOnLifecycle internals
text: How is repeatOnLifecycle implemented? What guarantees does it give around cancellation, ordering and thread? "It switches to Dispatchers.Main.immediate , adds a LifecycleEventObserver , and suspends the caller on a cancellable continuation. On the upTo state event it launches the block in a child coroutine; on the downFrom state event it cancels that child; on ON DESTROY it resumes the continuation so the function returns. A mutex ensures the previous block fully finishes cancelling before the next one starts."

title: Multiple collectors inside repeatOnLifecycle
text: I have three flows to collect in one screen. Why doesn't this work, and what are my options? lifecycleScope.launch { repeatOnLifecycle Lifecycle.State.STARTED { vm.state.collect { render it } vm.events.collect { handle it } vm.title.collect { setTitle it } } } " collect on a StateFlow never completes, so the first collect suspends the block forever and the later lines never execute. I launch each collector in its own child coroutine inside the block, or use flowWithLifecycle / merge / combine when the flows belong together."

title: flowWithLifecycle
text: What is flowWithLifecycle , how does it differ from repeatOnLifecycle , and what does the position of operators relative to it mean? " flow.flowWithLifecycle lifecycle, minActiveState returns a flow that only collects the upstream while the lifecycle is at least that state, cancelling and restarting it as the state changes. It's built on callbackFlow + repeatOnLifecycle . Operators placed before it are cancelled/restarted with the lifecycle; operators after it keep running downstream and only get what passes through. It's best for a single flow; for several, repeatOnLifecycle is clearer."

title: Lifecycle collection
text: Find all bugs, explain each mechanically, and fix. A Fragment-based "Orders" screen 1.2M DAU has two reported bugs: a Snackbar messages from the ViewModel never appear; b after navigating Orders - Details - back, the list sometimes crashes with NullPointerException: binding must not be null from adapter.submitList ... in a lambda; Crashlytics shows 0.4% of sessions affected. Code: class OrdersFragment : Fragment R.layout.fragment orders { private var binding: FragmentOrdersBinding? = null private val binding get = binding!! private val vm: OrdersViewModel by viewModels override fun onViewCreated view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle? { binding = FragmentOrdersBinding.bind view lifecycleScope.launch { repeatOnLifecycle Lifecycle.State.STARTED { vm.orders.collect { binding.list.adapter.submitList it } vm.snackbar.collect { Snackbar.make binding.root, it, 2000 .show } } } } override fun onDestroyView { binding = null; super.onDestroyView } }

title: Compose lifecycle-aware collection
text: In Jetpack Compose, what is the difference between collectAsState and collectAsStateWithLifecycle , and which do you use on Android? " collectAsState collects for as long as the composable is in composition, with no knowledge of the Activity lifecycle, so the flow is still collected after onStop . collectAsStateWithLifecycle lifecycle-runtime-compose, stable since 2.6.0 wraps repeatOnLifecycle , defaulting to STARTED, so collection stops in the background and WhileSubscribed upstreams can shut down. On Android I use it by default; collectAsState is right in multiplatform or non-Android-lifecycle code."

title: Choosing minActiveState
text: STARTED, RESUMED or CREATED: which state should I use for repeatOnLifecycle , and what goes wrong with the others? "STARTED is the default: the UI is visible, so I collect. RESUMED means focused and interactive; it pauses when a dialog-themed activity or a system overlay partially covers my screen, and in older multi-window modes the unfocused visible app is only STARTED. CREATED keeps collecting while invisible, effectively the same problem as plain lifecycleScope until destroy. I use STARTED for rendering, RESUMED only for things that require interactivity such as sensors tied to user focus."

title: Hot flow lifetime
text: Why is GPS still on, how would you confirm, and how would you fix it? A ride-hailing app 3.5M DAU ships a map screen. Play Console / support show "location icon stays on after leaving the app" and a battery-drain complaint cluster: users report 8-12% extra battery per hour when the app is backgrounded. Android vitals flags "excessive wakeups". Code: class MapViewModel locationRepo: LocationRepository : ViewModel { val location: StateFlow<LatLng? = locationRepo.updates // callbackFlow { requestLocationUpdates ... ; awaitClose { remove } } .stateIn viewModelScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, null } // Fragment viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch { repeatOnLifecycle Lifecycle.State.STARTED { vm.location.collect ::moveCamera } } Update interval is 1 s with PRIORITY HIGH ACCURACY . The fragment collector is correctly lifecycle-scoped.

title: Custom SharingStarted
text: How does SharingStarted work under the hood, and when would you write your own strategy? " SharingStarted is an interface with one method: command subscriptionCount: StateFlow<Int : Flow<SharingCommand . The sharing coroutine collects those commands: START begins collecting upstream, STOP cancels it, STOP AND RESET REPLAY CACHE cancels and resets the cache. I'd write a custom one when the stop condition isn't just subscriber count, like keeping the upstream alive while a foreground service is running, or while the app has network."

title: stateIn placement
text: What is wrong, and how would you fix it? A Compose chat-list screen 400k DAU shows rising ANR rate 0.9% - 2.3% and memory growth after scrolling. Profiler shows hundreds of Room InvalidationTracker observers. Code: class ChatViewModel private val repo: ChatRepository : ViewModel { fun unreadCount chatId: String : StateFlow<Int = repo.observeUnread chatId .stateIn viewModelScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, 0 } @Composable fun ChatRow chat: Chat, vm: ChatViewModel { val unread by vm.unreadCount chat.id .collectAsStateWithLifecycle Badge unread } A list of 250 chats; each recomposition of ChatRow calls unreadCount again.

title: stateIn upstream failure
text: What happens if the upstream of a stateIn throws? Which scope and handler receive the exception, and what do collectors see? "The upstream is collected by a coroutine launched in my scope. If it throws without catch , that coroutine fails like any child: with viewModelScope SupervisorJob + Main.immediate the exception goes to the thread's uncaught handler and crashes the app, unless I installed a CoroutineExceptionHandler . Collectors don't get the exception; the StateFlow just stops updating, and it doesn't restart even when new subscribers come, because the sharing coroutine is dead. So I put catch / retry upstream of stateIn and model errors as state."

title: WhileSubscribed timeout
text: Explain the extra traffic and the spinner, and fix it. A news app 2.5M DAU migrated its article screen from LiveData to StateFlow. After release 7.4: backend team reports /article/{id} request volume up 38% from 1,900 to 2,600 RPS at peak , and users on tablets complain the article "reloads and flashes a spinner" on rotation. Android vitals unchanged. Code: val article: StateFlow<UiState = flow { emit UiState.Loading emit UiState.Success repo.fetchArticle id // network call, 600 ms p50 } .stateIn viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed , UiState.Loading The Activity collects with repeatOnLifecycle STARTED . Tablet users rotate frequently; 11% of sessions have at least one rotation.

title: replayExpirationMillis
text: How do you resolve the ambiguity and what do you ship? A trading app's portfolio screen uses stateIn viewModelScope, WhileSubscribed 5 000 , PortfolioUi.Loading over a websocket-backed flow. QA files a bug: "when I come back to the app after lunch, I briefly see my old portfolio value from before lunch, then it jumps." Product replies: "That's expected, it's like a cached screen" while the risk team insists: "showing stale balances as live is a compliance problem." Another team wants no flicker on quick return < 1 minute . Activities get killed rarely ViewModel retained, process alive, 35% of returns .

title: Testing stateIn
text: Why does this fail, and how do you fix the tests and what would you NOT do ? A new engineer's ViewModel test passes locally with Eagerly but after the team standardizes on WhileSubscribed 5 000 it fails in CI with expected: Success ... but was: Loading . 140 tests in 22 ViewModels fail. Test: @Test fun showsItems = runTest { val vm = ItemsViewModel FakeRepo listOf Item 1 advanceUntilIdle assertEquals UiState.Success listOf Item 1 , vm.uiState.value } ViewModel: val uiState = repo.items .map { UiState.Success it }.stateIn viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed 5 000 , UiState.Loading . A MainDispatcherRule sets Dispatchers.Main to UnconfinedTestDispatcher .

title: Sharing at scale
text: Redesign the sharing layer. Where do shareIn / stateIn live, with which policy and scope, and what are the risks? A stock-quote app has a websocket feed one subscription per symbol, server limit 5 concurrent subscriptions/user, server cost $0.002 per 1,000 subscription-minutes . Five screens watchlist, detail, chart, alerts, widget host observe the same symbols. Today each ViewModel does quoteRepo.quotes symbol .stateIn viewModelScope, WhileSubscribed 5 000 , null . At 600k DAU, backend sees 4.1 subscriptions per active user and users with large watchlists get 429 s. Product wants 10x symbols watchlists up to 50 symbols next quarter.

title: shareIn buffering & slow subscribers
text: With shareIn , what happens when a subscriber is slow? How do replay , buffer operators and BufferOverflow interact, and what does it mean for a shared upstream like a sensor or a socket? "A SharedFlow with BufferOverflow.SUSPEND suspends the emitter when any subscriber's buffer is full, so one slow subscriber slows everyone, and the upstream producer. With no buffer operator, shareIn has no extra buffer; emission waits for slow subscribers. I put .buffer capacity, DROP OLDEST or .conflate before shareIn when freshness matters, which becomes the SharedFlow's buffer policy. With zero subscribers and replay=0 , values are dropped."

title: Migration under live traffic
text: How do you plan the migration safely? A large app 6M DAU, 40 ViewModels has stateIn viewModelScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, ... everywhere. The company wants to move to WhileSubscribed 5 000 to cut background battery and DB load Android vitals: background CPU wakeups above peer median . Past incidents: unit tests relying on .value , a few ViewModels read .value in click handlers, one screen has an analytics side effect inside a map . Release train is weekly, rollback is hard once released.

title: catch operator
text: What does the catch operator on a Flow actually catch? Does it catch an exception thrown inside collect { } ? catch only catches exceptions from the flow above it, meaning the producer and every operator placed before it. Anything thrown below it, including inside collect { } , onEach after the catch, or a downstream map , sails past it. So placement is the whole game: put catch as the last operator before collect if you want to guard the whole pipeline, and handle collector-side exceptions with a normal try/catch.

title: try/catch vs catch
text: When would you wrap collect in try/catch versus using the catch operator? Can both be used together? The catch operator covers upstream only and lets me recover by emitting. A try/catch around collect covers everything: upstream, operators, and my collector lambda, but it ends the collection and can't emit into the flow. I normally use .catch for expected upstream failures network, IO and a surrounding try/catch or a final .catch plus launchIn when the terminal block itself can throw.

title: onCompletion
