text: What does onCompletion do, and what is the cause parameter? How is it different from catch ? onCompletion { cause - } runs when the flow ends, like finally . cause is null on normal completion; non-null if the flow failed or was cancelled, and it also reports exceptions that came from downstream . Unlike catch it does not swallow the exception; it keeps propagating after your block. So I use it for cleanup, hiding a loading spinner, or logging, and catch for recovery.

title: retry
text: How does retry work on a Flow? What exactly is re-executed, and what does the predicate do? retry n { predicate } catches an upstream exception, and if the predicate returns true and attempts remain , it re-collects the entire upstream from the start . For a cold flow that means re-running the builder a new network call . Downstream never sees the failure unless retries are exhausted or the predicate returns false, in which case the exception is rethrown. Values emitted before the failure have already reached the collector, so retry can produce duplicates.

title: retryWhen & backoff
text: Implement exponential backoff with jitter for a Flow using retryWhen . What are cause and attempt , and how do you stop retrying? retryWhen { cause, attempt - } gives me the exception and a zero-based attempt counter. I return true to resubscribe, false to give up and rethrow cause . Inside I can delay , so exponential backoff is delay min base 2^attempt, cap + jitter , gated by a max attempt count and an "is transient?" check.

title: Exception transparency
text: What is "exception transparency" in Flow, and what happens if you wrap emit in a try/catch inside a flow { } builder? Exception transparency means a flow must not swallow exceptions thrown by its downstream collector. If I wrap emit in try/catch inside flow { } and swallow the exception, then keep emitting, the runtime throws IllegalStateException: Flow exception transparency is violated . The producer may only catch its own failures the code that produces values , and must rethrow collector failures. To handle upstream errors, use catch .

title: Errors as state
text: Why do we often model errors as part of the stream's data UiState / Result instead of letting the Flow throw? How do you do it for a ViewModel? A Flow that throws is finished. For a long-lived UI stream a screen's state that is wrong: the user hits a transient error and the screen can never update again. So I convert failures into values: either map the source to a Result /sealed UiState with .map { Success it }.catch { emit Error it } terminates after the error or, better, catch inside the per-request unit so the outer stream survives flatMapLatest { flow{...}.catch{...} } .

title: stateIn / shareIn failure
text: What happens to a stateIn / shareIn when the upstream flow throws? How do you make a shared flow survive upstream errors? The upstream is collected inside a coroutine that stateIn / shareIn launches in the scope I passed. An unhandled upstream exception fails that coroutine: it propagates to the scope in viewModelScope , with no handler it reaches the thread's uncaught-exception handler and crashes the app on Android , and the sharing is dead; the StateFlow just keeps its last value forever. Fix: catch/retry upstream of stateIn . Even then, with Eagerly / Lazily the upstream completed and never restarts; with WhileSubscribed it restarts when subscribers go to zero and come back.

title: Cancellation vs failure in operators
text: In catch , retry , and onCompletion , how are CancellationException s treated, and how do you avoid breaking cancellation in your own error handling? Cancellation of the collector is not an error these operators handle: catch and retry rethrow it instead of running my lambda or retrying, while onCompletion observes it as a non-null cause. The danger is hand-written code: catch e: Exception or runCatching around suspend calls swallows CancellationException , so the coroutine keeps running after being cancelled. I rethrow it explicitly or catch specific types.

title: catch placement
text: Find all the problems and fix the code. A news app 1.2M DAU crashes for 0.6% of sessions on the feed screen. Crashlytics shows kotlinx.serialization.SerializationException from a map in the ViewModel, and the team insists they "already catch errors". class FeedViewModel private val api: FeedApi : ViewModel { val state: StateFlow<FeedUi = api.feedFlow // may throw IOException .catch { emit emptyList } .map { dtos - dtos.map { it.toDomain } } // throws on a bad payload .map<List<Article , FeedUi { FeedUi.Content it } .stateIn viewModelScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, FeedUi.Loading }

title: retry
text: What went wrong on the client, and how do you fix it properly? Ride-hailing app, 400k concurrent users at peak. At 18:02 the pricing API starts returning 503 for 4 minutes. Backend dashboards show requests/s jump from 3k to 41k, the load balancer starts returning 429, and the outage extends to 19 minutes. Client code shipped last week: fun fareStream : Flow<Fare = api.fares // cold flow, one HTTP call .retry // "make it resilient" .catch { emit Fare.Unavailable } Logs: HttpException: HTTP 503 repeating roughly every 30 ms per device. Battery-drain complaints rise in the store reviews.

title: stateIn failure
text: Diagnose and fix; explain why the app does not crash anymore but is stuck. Trading-watchlist app, 250k DAU. Support reports: "prices freeze after I lose signal in the subway and never recover until I kill the app." No crash reports increase. A global CoroutineExceptionHandler was added last release to "stop the crashes". Code: class WatchlistViewModel repo: QuoteRepo : ViewModel { val quotes: StateFlow<List<Quote = repo.streamQuotes // websocket-backed callbackFlow .stateIn viewModelScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, emptyList } // viewModelScope created with the app's handler in a custom CoroutineScope factory Logs: java.net.SocketException: Connection reset once, then silence. UI collectors use repeatOnLifecycle STARTED .

title: Errors as state
text: Which do you pick and why? Walk through the trade-offs and the implementation shape. You are designing error handling for a banking app's transactions screen 800k DAU . Requirements from product: 1 show cached transactions instantly, then refresh; 2 if refresh fails, keep showing cached data with a dismissible banner; 3 a failed "export statement" action should show a one-time snackbar; 4 auth expiry 401 must navigate to login exactly once, even across rotation. Engineers propose three designs: A let the Flow throw and catch in the UI; B wrap everything in Result<T emitted by the repository; C sealed UiState with errors as data plus a separate event channel.

title: Cancellation vs failure
text: List every bug and fix it. A messaging app 600k DAU has a "sync messages" flow. QA reports: after leaving the chat screen, network sync continues for up to 30 s, and on slow networks the progress spinner sometimes never stops. A staff reviewer flags this snippet: fun syncFlow : Flow<SyncProgress = flow { emit SyncProgress.Started try { val msgs = api.fetchMessages // suspend, 2-30 s emit SyncProgress.Fetched msgs.size db.insertAll msgs // suspend emit SyncProgress.Done } catch e: Exception { emit SyncProgress.Failed e } finally { emit SyncProgress.Idle } } viewModelScope.launch { val result = runCatching { syncFlow .collect { progress.value = it } } if result.isFailure progress.value = SyncProgress.Failed result.exceptionOrNull !! } Crashlytics: occasional IllegalStateException: Flow exception transparency is violated and JobCancellationException: StandaloneCoroutine was cancelled logged as errors.

title: Fallback values
text: How do you clarify and implement "fallback values"? What are the pitfalls of each operator? Product writes: "If the network fails, show something useful instead of an error." The screen is a product-detail page 2M DAU, median 3G-ish users in some markets, p95 API latency 2.8 s, failure rate 4% . Existing code: fun product id: String : Flow<Product = flow { emit api.product id } The team debates: emit a default empty product? Emit cached copy? Emit nothing? One engineer proposes .catch { emit Product.EMPTY } , another .onEmpty { emit cached } .

title: runTest & virtual time
text: What does runTest do, and why does a test containing delay 10 000 finish in milliseconds? " runTest runs the test body in a TestScope whose dispatcher is backed by a TestCoroutineScheduler . That scheduler keeps a virtual clock and a priority queue of tasks ordered by virtual time. When the test body suspends and nothing is runnable at the current virtual time, the scheduler jumps the clock to the next scheduled task instead of sleeping. So delay 10 000 just schedules a task at t+10000 and the clock skips ahead. The test is deterministic and fast, and currentTime tells me how much virtual time passed."

title: runTest timeout
text: What is the default timeout of runTest , is it virtual or real time, and how do you change it? " runTest has a whole-test timeout, added in kotlinx.coroutines 1.7.0 with a 10 second default and raised to 60 seconds in 1.8.0. It is measured in real wall-clock time, not virtual time, because its purpose is to stop a genuinely stuck test. I can override it per test with runTest timeout = 5.seconds . On the JVM the default can also be changed globally with a system property, which I would check in the current docs for the exact name before relying on it."

title: Test dispatchers
text: What is the difference between StandardTestDispatcher and UnconfinedTestDispatcher , and which would you use by default? " StandardTestDispatcher queues every dispatched coroutine and runs it only when the scheduler is advanced or the test body suspends, so I control ordering exactly. UnconfinedTestDispatcher starts coroutines eagerly on the calling thread like Dispatchers.Unconfined , but its delay still uses virtual time. runTest defaults to Standard. I default to Standard for the code under test, and use Unconfined mostly to make collectors in backgroundScope subscribe immediately."

title: TestScope & scheduler sharing
text: How do TestScope , TestCoroutineScheduler , and the dispatchers relate? When two dispatchers in one test must see the same virtual time, how do you ensure it? "A TestCoroutineScheduler owns the virtual clock and the task queue. A TestDispatcher is just a front-end bound to one scheduler. TestScope holds a scheduler plus a dispatcher. All dispatchers in a test must use the same scheduler, otherwise each has its own clock and advancing one does nothing to the other. Inside runTest I pass testScheduler when creating extra dispatchers, and if I setMain with a test dispatcher, runTest automatically adopts its scheduler."

title: Controlling virtual time
text: Explain advanceUntilIdle , advanceTimeBy , and runCurrent . What exactly does advanceTimeBy 1000 run, and what does it not run? " runCurrent runs tasks scheduled at the current virtual time and stops. advanceTimeBy n moves the clock forward n ms, running tasks scheduled strictly before currentTime + n ; tasks exactly at the target time are not run, so I follow it with runCurrent . advanceUntilIdle keeps running everything, jumping through all pending delays until the queue is empty. It does not wait for real threads, and it never terminates on an endless periodic coroutine."

title: Dispatchers.setMain & MainDispatcherRule
text: Why do local unit tests of a ViewModel crash with "Module with the Main dispatcher had failed to initialize", and how do you fix it properly? " viewModelScope uses Dispatchers.Main.immediate . On the JVM there is no Android main Looper, so the Main dispatcher fails to initialize. kotlinx-coroutines-test provides Dispatchers.setMain testDispatcher to replace it, and resetMain to restore it. I wrap both in a JUnit TestWatcher rule, MainDispatcherRule , so each test sets Main before and resets it after."

title: Injecting dispatchers
text: Why should production classes receive a CoroutineDispatcher instead of referencing Dispatchers.IO directly, and how do you structure it? "Hard-coded dispatchers cannot be replaced in tests, so withContext Dispatchers.IO runs on real threads with real time, which is slow and non-deterministic. I inject dispatchers through the constructor with a production default, or use a small DispatcherProvider interface or Hilt qualifiers. In tests I pass StandardTestDispatcher testScheduler so everything runs on virtual time."

title: Testing ViewModels
text: Find every problem and fix the test. A teammate adds a unit test for SearchViewModel . It passes locally in the IDE but you see this on CI for the whole class, and a second problem on one test. class SearchViewModel private val repo: SearchRepo : ViewModel { private val state = MutableStateFlow<UiState UiState.Idle val state: StateFlow<UiState = state fun search q: String { viewModelScope.launch { state.value = UiState.Loading state.value = UiState.Done repo.search q } } } class SearchViewModelTest { @Test fun search updatesState { val vm = SearchViewModel FakeRepo delayMs = 500 vm.search "kotlin" assertEquals UiState.Done listOf "kotlin" , vm.state.value } } CI log: java.lang.IllegalStateException: Module with the Main dispatcher had failed to initialize. For tests Dispatchers.setMain from kotlinx-coroutines-test module can be used . After a fix by another engineer who added Dispatchers.setMain StandardTestDispatcher never reset , the test now fails with expected Done but was Idle . 1 in 40 CI runs of unrelated test classes also fails with weird Main behaviour.

title: Testing StateFlow with backgroundScope
text: A ViewModel exposes uiState built with stateIn viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed 5 000 , Loading . How do you test it, and why does vm.uiState.value always return Loading in your first attempt? "With WhileSubscribed , the upstream only runs while there is a collector, so reading .value without a subscriber just returns the initial value. In the test I start a collector in backgroundScope using an UnconfinedTestDispatcher testScheduler and gather emissions into a list. backgroundScope is cancelled automatically at test end and runTest does not wait for it, which matters because StateFlow.collect never completes."

title: Turbine
text: How does Turbine work, and what are the essential APIs? Why use it instead of toList in a background coroutine? " flow.test { ... } collects the flow in a coroutine into an internal channel and gives me a ReceiveTurbine where I pull events in order: awaitItem , awaitComplete , awaitError , expectNoEvents . It fails if an event was not consumed when the block ends, unless I call cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents . Compared to a manual list it gives me ordered, suspend-based assertions, a timeout so tests never hang, and the unconsumed-events check. The current stable release is 1.2.x."

title: Turbine pitfalls with StateFlow/SharedFlow
text: You test a StateFlow with Turbine and the test either misses states or fails with "Unconsumed events." Explain why, and how do you write assertions that are robust to conflation and ordering? "A StateFlow only guarantees the latest value, and it is equality-conflated, so setting the same value twice emits once, and rapid updates can skip intermediates. Turbine gets exactly what the StateFlow delivers, no more. Replay of the current value means the first awaitItem is the current state, not the first change. For robust tests I use a dispatcher where collection is eager Turbine collects undispatched , drive actions with explicit runCurrent , assert only the transitions the contract promises, and use expectMostRecentItem or skipItems where intermediate states are not part of the contract."

title: Testing debounce & delays
text: Why does this fail, how do you test debounce correctly, and how do you handle the ambiguous requirement? Search-as-you-type for a catalog app 1.2M DAU, p95 query latency 350 ms . Requirement from product: "search after the user pauses typing for 300 ms". The ViewModel: private val query = MutableStateFlow "" val results: StateFlow<List<Item = query .debounce 300 .distinctUntilChanged .flatMapLatest { repo.search it } .stateIn viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed 5 000 , emptyList An engineer wrote this test and it fails: expected 1 call to repo.search but was 0 . @Test fun debounces = runTest { backgroundScope.launch UnconfinedTestDispatcher testScheduler { vm.results.collect {} } vm.onQuery "k" ; advanceTimeBy 100 vm.onQuery "ko" ; advanceTimeBy 100 vm.onQuery "kot" ; advanceTimeBy 300 assertEquals 1, fakeRepo.callCount } Product also asks: "does it search for the empty string when the user clears the box?" Nobody knows.

title: Testing cancellation
text: How do you write a test that proves your suspend function cleans up when cancelled and does not swallow CancellationException ? "I launch the operation in the test scope, advance to the point it is suspended, call job.cancel , then runCurrent and assert on observable cleanup: a finally or invokeOnCompletion flag, a fake's closed state, and job.isCancelled . I also test that the code rethrows CancellationException , for example by catching Exception in the code under test and verifying that the job still ends cancelled, not completed."

title: Testing exceptions
text: How do exceptions behave inside runTest ? Cover exceptions thrown from the test body, from launch children, from async , and from backgroundScope , and how to assert them. "An exception thrown in the test body fails the test, and I assert expected ones with assertFailsWith . An exception in a launch child propagates through structured concurrency and the TestScope 's uncaught-exception handling, failing the test at the end of runTest . For async , it is held until await , but also cancels the parent unless in a supervisor. For backgroundScope , unhandled exceptions still fail the test. To test a failure path without failing the test, I either catch it where the production code catches it, supply my own CoroutineExceptionHandler , or use a SupervisorJob plus await / join and inspect the result."

title: Flaky tests
text: You are tech lead. How do you stop the bleeding and find the root cause? Android monorepo, 3,800 unit tests, CI on 8 parallel Gradle workers. Over two weeks the pipeline went from 2% to 14% red builds; re-run goes green 9 times out of 10. Merge queue is backing up median time-to-merge 25 min to 70 min . Failures are spread over about 60 different tests, mostly ViewModel and repository tests, with messages like: AssertionError: expected:<Loaded but was:<Loading kotlinx.coroutines.test.UncompletedCoroutinesError: After waiting for 60s, the test coroutine is not completing IllegalStateException: This job has not completed yet Changes in those two weeks: Kotlin and coroutines upgrade 1.7 to 1.9 , a new shared MainDispatcherRule , 25 new tests by a new team, and Gradle maxParallelForks raised from 2 to 4. Failures cluster on CI and almost never reproduce on laptops.

title: Sources of flaky coroutine tests
text: List the main causes of flaky coroutine tests and how you eliminate each. "Flakiness comes from letting anything nondeterministic into the test: real dispatchers and threads, real time Thread.sleep , wall-clock timeouts , shared state between tests unreset Main, singletons, leaked scopes , uncontrolled ordering Unconfined hiding races, or Standard without advancing , and unbounded waits. The cure is to put every coroutine on one test scheduler, inject dispatchers and clocks, reset global state, and make every wait explicit and bounded."

title: MockK coEvery vs fakes
text: How do you stub suspend functions and flows with MockK, and when would you prefer a hand-written fake over a mock? "With MockK I use coEvery { repo.get 1 } returns x to stub suspend functions and coVerify to check calls; for flows I return flowOf ... or a MutableSharedFlow I control. coAnswers { delay 100 ; x } lets a stub suspend in virtual time. I prefer fakes for repositories and data sources: they hold real state, behave consistently across tests, and test behavior rather than call sequences. I use mocks for interaction boundaries I only need to verify, such as an analytics logger or a one-way command."

title: Virtual time boundary
text: Explain what is happening and fix it. A test for a token-refresh component takes 3.2 seconds locally and passes; on CI, with shared CPUs, it sometimes fails with a Turbine timeout. The author insists "it uses runTest, so delays are virtual." class TokenRefresher private val api: AuthApi { suspend fun refreshWithBackoff : Token = withContext Dispatchers.IO { var wait = 500L repeat 3 { try { return@withContext api.refresh } catch e: IOException { delay wait ; wait = 2 } } api.refresh } } @Test fun retriesThenSucceeds = runTest { val api = FakeApi failures = 3 val t = TokenRefresher api .refreshWithBackoff assertEquals "tok", t.value assertEquals 3500, currentTime } Observed: the final assertion fails with expected:<3500 but was:<0 when the author removes a leftover Thread.sleep , and the test visibly takes 3.5 s of real time.

title: Migrating test infrastructure
text: Plan the migration so that CI stays green and no feature team is blocked. Monolith Android app, 14 feature modules, 2,300 coroutine tests. The suite uses runBlockingTest , TestCoroutineDispatcher , and TestCoroutineScope deprecated in kotlinx-coroutines-test 1.6 . Platform wants to upgrade to coroutines 1.9 and Kotlin 2.x this quarter, which requires removing those APIs they are removed in recent versions . Main branch merges about 120 PRs per week; feature teams cannot freeze. 15% of tests use TestCoroutineDispatcher directly through a shared CoroutineRule . Some tests rely on the old eager-by-default behaviour TestCoroutineDispatcher ran launches immediately .

title: runTest internals
text: Walk me through what runTest does internally from start to finish, including how it decides when the test is done, what it does with leaked coroutines, and how real asynchronous work interacts with the virtual clock. " runTest builds a TestScope , starts the body as a child coroutine on the test dispatcher, and then loops on the real thread: it runs the scheduler executing queued tasks and jumping virtual time until the body is done and no work remains, and if the scheduler is idle but the body is not complete, it waits in real time for external completion such as a real-thread coroutine finishing, up to the timeout. At the end it cancels backgroundScope , fails if non-background children are still running, and rethrows collected uncaught exceptions."

title: Hanging tests
text: What's going on, and what do you do? CI nightly shows 23 tests failing with: kotlinx.coroutines.test.UncompletedCoroutinesError: After waiting for 1m, the test coroutine is not completing, there were active child jobs: StandaloneCoroutine{Active}@3f2a, StateFlowImpl collect ... Each failing test blocks a runner for the full 60 s; the suite grew from 6 min to 31 min. All failing tests are ViewModel tests for screens that recently moved from LiveData to StateFlow with stateIn ..., WhileSubscribed 5 000 , ... . The same tests passed with LiveData. There are 340 other ViewModel tests that are fine. Reviewer comments suggest "just bump the timeout".

title: Testing SharedFlow events
text: Explain why these tests behave this way, fix the tests, and say whether the production code has a bug. A checkout ViewModel emits one-shot navigation events through a MutableSharedFlow replay = 0, no extra buffer . The test is green locally, but a second test for "payment failed" is red on every run and a third passes only on some machines. class CheckoutViewModel private val pay: PayUseCase : ViewModel { private val events = MutableSharedFlow<Event val events: SharedFlow<Event = events fun onPayClicked = viewModelScope.launch { events.emit if pay Event.GoToReceipt else Event.ShowError } } class CheckoutTest { @get:Rule val main = MainDispatcherRule UnconfinedTestDispatcher @Test fun success = runTest { val vm = CheckoutViewModel FakePay ok = true vm.onPayClicked assertEquals Event.GoToReceipt, vm.events.first // test 1 } @Test fun failure = runTest { val vm = CheckoutViewModel FakePay ok = false vm.onPayClicked assertEquals Event.ShowError, vm.events.first // test 2 } } Test 2 times out; 50k DAU feature, and QA reports the receipt screen sometimes opens twice on slow devices. The team asks whether the test or the code is wrong.

title: Dispatcher choice hides state
text: Why did the test not catch it, and how would you restructure the tests and dispatcher strategy? A team's tests all use UnconfinedTestDispatcher because "Standard needs advanceUntilIdle everywhere." A spinner bug shipped: on a 3G network the screen flashes Loaded empty for one frame before Loaded data . The ViewModel: val state: StateFlow<UiState = combine userFlow, ordersFlow { u, o - UiState.Loaded u, o } .stateIn viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed 5 000 , UiState.Loading userFlow emits at 40 ms, ordersFlow at 900 ms from a slow API; combine on a Room-backed ordersFlow first emits emptyList immediately. The existing test: @Test fun loads = runTest UnconfinedTestDispatcher { val vm = VM FakeUser user , FakeOrders orders // both fakes emit synchronously assertEquals UiState.Loaded user, orders , vm.state.value } It passes. Release candidate has 12k crash-free sessions and 4% of QA runs see the flash.

title: Testing time-dependent logic
text: How do you test logic that depends on time: withTimeout , exponential backoff retries, periodic polling, cache expiry TTL , and Clock reads? What do you inject and what do you assert on? "Anything driven by delay , withTimeout , debounce , sample , or timeout runs on the test scheduler and I assert on currentTime . Anything reading wall-clock time System.currentTimeMillis , Instant.now , TTL checks is a hidden dependency, so I inject a Clock or TimeSource , backed in tests by testScheduler.timeSource or a controllable fake. Then I assert exact timestamps: backoff sums, call times, expiry boundaries at TTL-1 and TTL."

title: Test strategy & hidden races
text: Run the post-incident review for the testing side: why did tests miss it, what do you change in the test strategy, and what is the code fix? Incident review. A release shipped with a race in a favorites-sync feature: tapping the heart quickly twice left the server in the wrong state for about 1.8% of toggles 12k affected users in 3 days . Unit coverage of the ViewModel and repository was 91%, all green. The repository: class FavRepo private val api: Api, private val scope: CoroutineScope { private var inFlight: Job? = null fun toggle id: String, on: Boolean { inFlight?.cancel inFlight = scope.launch { api.setFavorite id, on } } } Tests used UnconfinedTestDispatcher , a fake API that returns immediately, and one test toggle id, true ; toggle id, false ; assertEquals false, fakeApi.server id . The server state there is correct. In production, api.setFavorite is a Retrofit suspend call: cancelling the first request after it was already sent does not undo it, and the second request can reach the server before the first because of connection pooling and retries.

title: Debug mode (-Dkotlinx.coroutines.debug)
text: What does the -Dkotlinx.coroutines.debug flag do, and how would you use it on an Android project where you see log lines like Thread DefaultDispatcher-worker-3 and cannot tell which coroutine is running? "It turns on kotlinx.coroutines debug mode. Every coroutine gets a unique id, and while a thread runs a coroutine, the library renames the thread to something like DefaultDispatcher-worker-3 @fetchUser 42 . It also turns on stack-trace recovery. It is auto by default, which means on only when JVM assertions are enabled, so it is on in JVM unit tests but off in a normal Android app. On Android I flip it on in debug builds by setting the system property before any coroutine class loads."

title: CoroutineName and log correlation
text: How do you make logs from concurrent coroutines traceable? Where does CoroutineName actually show up and where does it not? " CoroutineName is a context element, so it is inherited by children and can be overridden with + . It is visible via coroutineContext CoroutineName , in Job.toString , in the diagnostic context attached to uncaught-exception reports, and in thread names only when debug mode is on. For logs I write a small helper that reads it from the context, or put a request id into MDC via asContextElement ."

title: IDE coroutine debugger
text: What does the IDE coroutine debugger give you that a regular breakpoint and stack view does not, and how does it work given that a suspended coroutine has no thread? "A suspended coroutine is not on any thread stack, so the normal Frames view cannot show it. The Kotlin debugger plugin reads the continuation objects on the heap, using @DebugMetadata the compiler adds to each state-machine class, and rebuilds a virtual stack of suspend frames. The Coroutines tab lists all coroutines with state running, suspended, created and their async stack. It can also show the creation stack if creation tracking is enabled."

title: Stack-trace recovery
text: Why are coroutine stack traces often missing your call site, and what is stack-trace recovery? What does it change about exceptions you catch? "When a coroutine resumes, the thread stack only has the dispatcher frames plus the current state-machine frame, not the original callers. Stack-trace recovery, enabled in debug mode, copies the exception when it crosses a suspension boundary, such as await , and stitches the receiving coroutine's frames onto it, with the original as cause . So the exception you catch can be a different instance of the same class."

title: Debugging a crash with an unhelpful trace
text: How do you find which caller produces the crash and what do you ship? A shopping app 1.2M DAU, Android 8-14, Pixel and Samsung mix shows a new top crash after release 5.14 at 0.6% of sessions: FATAL EXCEPTION: DefaultDispatcher-worker-2 java.lang.IllegalStateException: Cart item missing at com.shop.cart.CartMapper.map CartMapper.kt:58 at com.shop.cart.CartRepo$load$2.invokeSuspend CartRepo.kt:34 at kotlin.coroutines.jvm.internal.BaseContinuationImpl.resumeWith ContinuationImpl.kt:33 at kotlinx.coroutines.DispatchedTask.run DispatchedTask.kt:108 at kotlinx.coroutines.scheduling.CoroutineScheduler.runSafely ... Nothing shows which screen triggered it. The team has 40 launch calls in 12 view models. A background refresh and the checkout screen both call CartRepo.load .

title: DebugProbes dump
text: What is DebugProbes , what does dumpCoroutines print, and can you use it on Android? " DebugProbes is in the kotlinx-coroutines-debug module. It installs a Byte Buddy-based agent that tracks every coroutine's creation and state, so dumpCoroutines prints all live coroutines with their state and stack, and printScope / printJob show hierarchies. It is a JVM feature: the debug agent is not supported on Android runtime, so I use it in JVM unit tests and Robolectric, and in the IDE during debug sessions."

title: Finding leaked coroutines
text: What does a "leaked coroutine" mean in Android, how do you detect one, and what tools do you reach for? "A leaked coroutine is one that outlives the thing it works for: a collector or request still running after its screen or owner is gone, or a job parked forever on something that never completes. Because a running coroutine is reachable from its dispatcher and its Job, everything it captures Activity, view, big list stays reachable too. I detect them with LeakCanary for the captured objects, counting children of long-lived scopes, a coroutine dump in JVM tests, and by auditing for scopes without an owner like GlobalScope or an uncancelled CoroutineScope ... ."

title: Leaked coroutines
text: Diagnose and fix, and explain how you would prevent the class of bug. A messaging app 800k DAU shipped chat 7.2. Crashlytics shows OOM rate up from 0.15% to 0.9% of sessions on 3 GB RAM devices, mostly after 40+ minutes of use. Heap dump from QA shows 2,100 instances of ChatFragment$onViewCreated$1 continuations and 260 retained ChatFragment objects user opened and left chats . Code: class ChatRepo @Inject constructor private val socket: Socket { private val scope = CoroutineScope SupervisorJob + Dispatchers.IO fun observe chatId: String, onMsg: Msg - Unit { scope.launch { socket.messages chatId .collect { onMsg it } } } } // in ChatFragment.onViewCreated: repo.observe chatId { msg - adapter.add msg } The ChatRepo is @Singleton . The team suspects Glide image cache red herring , and a recent RecyclerView upgrade.

title: Testing for coroutine leaks
text: How do you write a test that fails when code leaves a coroutine running? What does runTest give you for free and what does it not? " runTest waits for its child coroutines and fails if they don't finish within the timeout, and it reports uncaught exceptions. Work launched in backgroundScope is cancelled at the end, so it never fails a test even if leaking, and anything launched in a scope outside the test is invisible to it. So for leak tests I inject the scope, run the action, cancel the owner, then assert on job.children or isActive , and for hangs I add DebugProbes with @CoroutinesTimeout ."

title: Coroutine overhead and performance
text: How expensive is a coroutine in memory and CPU compared with a thread, and where does the real overhead show up in an Android app? "A coroutine is a heap object graph, not an OS thread: a Job plus a compiler-generated state-machine continuation holding the live locals, on the order of low hundreds of bytes, so 100k of them is tens of MB at most, whereas 100k threads is impossible. Switching between them is a dispatch of a Runnable, not a kernel context switch. The real costs are allocation and GC from short-lived suspend calls, dispatcher hops, and over-parallelising work on a small thread pool."

title: Coroutines at scale
text: What is wrong and how do you restructure? A photo app uploads 50,000 queued images in a background sync on app start after a long offline period. Current code: suspend fun syncAll items: List<Photo = coroutineScope { items.map { async Dispatchers.IO { upload it } }.awaitAll } On mid-range devices 4 GB RAM, 8 cores Perfetto shows UI jank p95 frame time 38 ms , OkHttp reporting SocketTimeoutException s at 22 percent, the process sits at 480 MB, and battery-drain complaints are rising. upload does a 2 MB file read, compress, and OkHttp call. The backend rate-limits at 10 concurrent requests per user.

title: Coroutines vs threads
text: What is the difference between a coroutine and a thread? Isn't a coroutine just a lightweight thread? "A thread is an OS-scheduled unit with its own stack that blocks when it waits. A coroutine is a suspendable computation managed by a library: when it waits it suspends, saving its state in a heap object and freeing the thread to run something else. It is not a lightweight thread; it runs on threads chosen by a dispatcher, can hop between them, and is cancelled cooperatively with structured parent-child lifetimes."

title: Coroutines vs Executors / AsyncTask
text: How do coroutines compare with ExecutorService / AsyncTask / HandlerThread , and how do you bridge an existing Executor into coroutines? "Executors give you a thread pool and a Future , but no structured lifetime, no composition without callbacks, and cancellation via interrupt that blocking code may ignore. AsyncTask is deprecated since API 30 and had Activity-leak and serial-execution problems. Coroutines add structured scopes, cooperative cancellation, and sequential-looking code. I bridge with executor.asCoroutineDispatcher and own its shutdown."

title: Coroutines vs callbacks
text: What problems do coroutines solve compared with callbacks, and how do you correctly wrap a callback API as a suspend function or a Flow? "Callbacks give inversion of control: no return value, nesting, manual error plumbing, and no cancellation story. Coroutines restore sequential code, normal try/catch, and structured cancellation. To wrap a one-shot callback I use suspendCancellableCoroutine , resume exactly once, and unregister in invokeOnCancellation . For many-shot callbacks I use callbackFlow with trySend and awaitClose { unregister } ."

title: Coroutines vs RxJava
text: Compare Kotlin coroutines/Flow with RxJava on semantics, not just syntax. What differs in threading, error handling, cancellation, backpressure, and hot/cold behavior? "Rx is a push-based library with many types Observable, Flowable, Single, Completable, Maybe , explicit Schedulers, Disposable s and an onError terminal channel. Coroutines are a language feature plus library: one suspend for single values, Flow for streams, dispatchers via context, structured concurrency instead of CompositeDisposable , and cancellation is cooperative through exceptions. Backpressure in Flow is built in by suspension; Rx needs Flowable."

title: When RxJava still makes sense
text: Your team lead says "kill Rx, move everything to coroutines." When would you argue that RxJava should stay? "I'd migrate new code and touch-points, but keep Rx where the cost-benefit is negative: large stable Rx-heavy modules that rarely change, features using Rx's richer time-window operators, code shared with Java-only modules or libraries exposing Rx types, and teams with strong Rx expertise on a tight delivery schedule. A big-bang rewrite adds regression risk without user value, so I'd make Rx boundaries explicit and migrate by use."

title: Rx operator to Flow operator mapping
text: Map the common RxJava operators and types to their coroutine/Flow equivalents. Which ones have no direct equivalent or behave differently? "Single/Maybe/Completable become suspend functions; Observable/Flowable become Flow; Subjects become SharedFlow/StateFlow; Disposable becomes Job. switchMap is flatMapLatest , flatMap is flatMapMerge , concatMap is flatMapConcat , combineLatest is combine , observeOn / subscribeOn collapse into flowOn , which only moves upstream. throttleFirst , buffer count / window need custom code, and retry , onErrorReturn map to retry and catch { emit } ."

title: Migration strategy
text: Do you approve the rewrite? What do you propose instead, and how do you decide per module? A fintech Android app 4M MAU, 380k LOC, 14 modules is built on RxJava 2 with MVP. RxJava 2 has been end-of-life since 2021. The team of 18 wants coroutines. Leadership asks for a plan; roadmap has two feature-critical quarters ahead. Crash-free rate is 99.7%, and a payments module 35k LOC, heavy combineLatest , retryWhen , window -based rate limiting changes about twice a year. A proposal exists to freeze features for one quarter and rewrite everything.

title: Incremental Rx migration
text: Lay out the migration sequence, the interop seams, and how you protect production at each step. You are migrating the order-tracking feature of a food-delivery app 2.5M DAU, peak 18k orders/min from RxJava 3 to coroutines while it serves live traffic. The feature has OrderRepository Rx, 22 call sites across 9 ViewModels , a websocket Observable<OrderEvent shared via publish .refCount , and a BehaviorSubject<Order cache. Rules: no big-bang, each release must be shippable, rollback must be possible per release, crash-free must stay at or above 99.8%. The team has kotlinx-coroutines-rx3 available.

title: Rx and coroutine interop (rx3 bridges)
text: How do you interoperate between RxJava 3 and coroutines using kotlinx-coroutines-rx3 , and what happens to cancellation and disposal across the bridge? " kotlinx-coroutines-rx3 gives await , awaitSingle , awaitFirst for Single/Maybe/Completable/Observable, asFlow for Observable/Flowable, and Flow.asObservable /asFlowable plus builders rxSingle , rxObservable , rxFlowable , rxCompletable . Cancelling the coroutine disposes the Rx subscription, and disposing the Rx stream cancels the coroutine. The catches are error routing after disposal and thread/dispatcher differences."

title: Error semantics Rx vs coroutines
text: Why can an RxJava app crash with UndeliverableException while a coroutines app with the same bug usually does not? Compare how errors travel in each model. "In Rx, an error is a terminal signal delivered to onError . If the stream is already disposed or terminated, there is nobody to deliver it to, so RxJava 2/3 routes it to RxJavaPlugins.onError , which by default calls the thread's uncaught handler and crashes Android. In coroutines, an exception propagates up the Job hierarchy to the parent; if it reaches a root with no handler it goes to the thread's uncaught handler, but a cancelled coroutine's exceptions are mostly dropped or attached as suppressed, so late errors after cancellation don't crash."

title: Rx to Flow port bugs
text: Find the four bugs and fix them. After porting a ViewModel from Rx to Flow, QA reports: 1 the search results sometimes show the previous query's results; 2 the loading spinner never resets when the user retries the same query; 3 after a network error the screen stops reacting to any further queries; 4 UI updates sometimes happen off the main thread, crash rate 0.2% with CalledFromWrongThreadException . Original Rx used switchMap , BehaviorSubject , onErrorReturn , observeOn main . Ported code: class SearchVM private val api: Api : ViewModel { private val query = MutableStateFlow "" private val state = MutableStateFlow<UiState UiState.Idle val state: StateFlow<UiState = state init { viewModelScope.launch { query .debounce 300 .flatMapMerge { q - flow { emit api.search q } } .catch { state.value = UiState.Error it } .flowOn Dispatchers.IO .collect { state.value = UiState.Results it } } } fun onQuery q: String { query.value = q; state.value = UiState.Loading } }

title: Debugging a hung coroutine
text: How do you find out where it hangs, what's the root cause, and how do you fix it and detect it next time? A booking app 300k DAU gets reports: "the confirm button spins forever" on roughly 0.8% of confirmations, reproducible in QA about 1 in 30 times on Android 12 devices. No crash, no ANR, no error log. The code path: class BookingVM private val repo: BookingRepo : ViewModel { private val lock = Mutex fun confirm = viewModelScope.launch { loading.value = true lock.withLock { val token = repo.fetchPaymentToken // suspend, wraps SDK callback repo.book token } loading.value = false } } // SDK wrapper suspend fun fetchPaymentToken : String = suspendCoroutine { c - sdk.requestToken object : TokenListener { override fun onToken t: String = c.resume t override fun onFailure e: Exception = c.resumeWithException e } } Logs show nothing after "confirm start". The payments SDK is closed-source; its callbacks are documented as "may not fire if the app is backgrounded during init".

title: Post-incident review with coroutine tooling
text: Run the review: what happened mechanically, what tooling would have caught it earlier, and what are the action items? Post-incident review of an ANR spike: ANR rate on a news app 2M DAU jumped from 0.25% to 1.1% after release 9.3, concentrated on Android 10-12 low-end devices. Play Console ANR clusters show main thread in Object.wait inside kotlinx.coroutines.BlockingCoroutine.joinBlocking from runBlocking . Another thread dump shows all 64 DefaultDispatcher-worker-N threads in SocketInputStream.read . The release introduced a "prefetch next 30 articles" feature using Dispatchers.IO and a legacy synchronous ImageLoader.loadBlocking called inside runBlocking from an old ContentProvider . Timeline: rollout began Tuesday, ANR alerts Wednesday, rollback Thursday.

title: Search screen architecture
text: Design the search pipeline end to end, from the text field to the rendered list. Name every operator and scope choice and defend it. You own the search screen of a shopping app: 2M DAU, 9 searches per session, p95 backend latency 450 ms on 4G, 18% of users on low-end devices 2 GB RAM, API 26-28 . Product wants "search as you type", recent searches shown when the field is empty, results that survive rotation and process death of the query text, and no stale results ever shown for an older query. Crashlytics currently shows 0.4% of search sessions with "results flicker back to old query" and the backend team complains search QPS is 6x what it was before the type-ahead launch. The current code launches viewModelScope.launch { repo.search text } from a TextWatcher on every keystroke.

title: Token refresh with OkHttp + coroutines
text: Explain exactly why this fails, fix it so exactly one refresh happens per expiry, and discuss the failure modes of your fix. Fintech app, 800K DAU. Access tokens live 15 minutes. After a backend change that shortened them from 60 to 15 minutes, support tickets spike: users are randomly logged out. Logs on the auth server show bursts of 6-12 POST /oauth/refresh calls within 200 ms from the same device, with the same refresh token. The auth server uses rotating refresh tokens each refresh token is single-use , so only the first succeeds; the rest get 400 invalid grant , and the app treats that as "session expired" and logs the user out. Your app fires up to 8 parallel requests on the home screen. Client code in an OkHttp Authenticator : class TokenAuthenticator private val auth: AuthRepository : Authenticator { override fun authenticate route: Route?, response: Response : Request? { val newToken = runBlocking { auth.refresh } // suspend, hits network return response.request.newBuilder .header "Authorization", "Bearer $newToken" .build } }

title: Idempotency and double-tap
text: Run the post-incident review. What failed at each layer UI, ViewModel, coroutines, network, server , and what do you change? Payments screen, "Pay Now" button. Over a weekend, 312 customers 0.09% of 340K payments were charged twice. Timeline: the payment endpoint p95 jumped from 600 ms to 3.8 s after a gateway issue. Users double-tapped because nothing happened. Code: fun onPayClicked { viewModelScope.launch { state.value = Loading val result = runCatching { repo.pay orderId, amount } state.value = result.fold { Success }, { Error it } } } Backend log excerpt: two POST /pay with different X-Request-Id , 180 ms apart, same orderId, both processed.

title: runBlocking and ANR
text: Explain the failure mechanically, give a mitigation you can ship today, and the proper fix. Media app, 1.5M DAU. After release 7.12, Play Console shows ANR rate 0.31% - 1.1% bad-behavior threshold is 0.47% per the Android vitals docs . Top ANR trace main thread : "main" tid=1 Waiting at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park / java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.park at kotlinx.coroutines.BlockingCoroutine.joinBlocking Builders.kt at kotlinx.coroutines.BuildersKt BuildersKt.runBlocking Builders.kt at com.app.net.HeaderInterceptor.intercept HeaderInterceptor.kt:22 at okhttp3.internal.http.RealInterceptorChain.proceed at okhttp3.internal.connection.RealCall.execute at com.app.legacy.AdLoader.fetchSync AdLoader.java:88 HeaderInterceptor does val flags = runBlocking { featureFlags.snapshot } where snapshot does withContext Dispatchers.Main { ... } plain Main, not immediate . It is used by every OkHttp call.

title: Offline sync engine
text: Design the sync engine. Where do coroutines, Flow and Kotlin types fit, and what do you delegate to the platform? Field-service app: technicians log jobs offline up to 8 hours with no signal , 40K devices, 150 writes per device per day, 20% on flaky 2G. Today each write does api.post and shows a Toast on failure; 3% of writes are silently lost. Requirements: no data loss, order per entity preserved, retries with backoff, survive process death and reboot, show per-item "pending/failed" in the UI, battery-friendly, and conflicts resolved server-wins on version mismatch.

title: Chat stream merging socket + DB
text: Design the data flow so the UI is a pure function of the DB, duplicates are impossible, and reconnects are correct. Where do Flow and coroutines go? Chat screen. Messages come from three sources: Room history, source of truth , a WebSocket live , and a REST "catch-up since cursor" call run on reconnect. Users report duplicate messages after a flaky-network reconnect 0.7% of sessions , messages out of order, and the list jumping when the keyboard opens. Average conversation: 5K messages, 60 live messages/min in group chats. Message ids are server-assigned; locally sent messages have a client id until acked.

title: Download manager with progress and cancellation
text: List every defect and write the corrected version. A video app lets users download episodes 200 MB-1.2 GB . Bugs reported: cancelling a download leaves a partial file and a still-running network connection data usage keeps going ; the progress bar jumps and the UI janks progress emitted 12K times/second on Wi-Fi ; on low-memory devices OOM occurs; two quick taps start two downloads of the same file. Code: fun download url: String, dest: File : Flow<Progress = flow { val resp = client.newCall Request.Builder .url url .build .execute // blocking val body = resp.body!! val total = body.contentLength var read = 0L val buf = ByteArray 512 body.byteStream .use { input - dest.outputStream .use { out - while true { val n = input.read buf if n == -1 break out.write buf, 0, n read += n emit Progress read, total } } } emit Progress total, total } Collected with viewModelScope.launch { download ... .collect { progress.value = it } } .

title: Crash spike after dependency upgrade
text: Triage this. How do you stop the rollout safely, find the cause, and make upgrades like this safe in future? You bumped Kotlin 1.9 - 2.0 and kotlinx.coroutines 1.6.4 - 1.8.x in one PR also AGP and a few libs . Staged rollout at 10% of 2M DAU. Crashlytics 40 minutes later: new crash cluster, 1.9% of sessions, device-agnostic, OS 8-14: Fatal Exception: java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: No static method <someMethod Lkotlinx/coroutines/flow/Flow;... ... in class Lkotlinx/coroutines/flow/FlowKt; at com.vendor.analytics.EventPipeline$start$1.invokeSuspend Unknown Source at kotlin.coroutines.jvm.internal.BaseContinuationImpl.resume ContinuationImpl.kt Also a second, smaller cluster: IllegalStateException: Module with the Main dispatcher had failed to initialize on 0.1% of sessions mostly one OEM . Your own code compiles and unit tests pass.

title: Custom scope leak
text: Explain the leak, and fix it without breaking "export continues when user leaves the screen". Photo-editing app, OOM crash rate 0.9% up from 0.2% on 2-3 GB devices after adding a "background export" feature. LeakCanary debug reports: ┬─── │ GC Root: Thread kotlinx.coroutines.DefaultExecutor ├─ kotlinx.coroutines.StandaloneCoroutine │ Leaking: UNKNOWN ├─ com.app.export.ExportManager$export$1 │ ↓ ExportManager$export$1.$onDone captured lambda ├─ com.app.editor.EditorFragment$$ExternalSyntheticLambda3 │ ↓ EditorFragment.binding ╰→ android.widget.FrameLayout Leaking: YES View detached Code: object ExportManager { private val scope = CoroutineScope Dispatchers.Default fun export project: Project, onDone: File - Unit { scope.launch { val file = render project // 30-90 s, 120 MB bitmap working set withContext Dispatchers.Main { onDone file } } } } // Fragment ExportManager.export project { file - binding.progress.isVisible = false; share file }

title: ViewModel code review
text: Find at least six defects, rank them by production impact, and show the corrected class. You are reviewing a PR from a mid-level dev. The screen shows a list of orders with pull-to-refresh. QA reports: the spinner sometimes never stops, a crash IllegalStateException: Cannot invoke setValue on a background thread , errors toast "randomly" missing, and memory climbs after repeated navigation. Code: class OrdersViewModel private val repo: OrdersRepo, private val context: Context, // injected from Activity : ViewModel { val orders = MutableLiveData<List<Order val loading = MutableStateFlow false val events = MutableSharedFlow<UiEvent init { GlobalScope.launch { repo.observeOrders .collect { orders.postValue it } } } fun refresh { viewModelScope.launch Dispatchers.IO { try { loading.value = true orders.value = repo.fetchOrders loading.value = false } catch e: Exception { events.emit UiEvent.ShowError e.message ?: context.getString R.string.generic error } } } }

title: Hot flow lifecycle and battery
text: Find the problems, quantify the impact, and fix without breaking the "driver nearby" map when the user returns within a few seconds. Ride-sharing app, 1.2M DAU. Android vitals flags "excessive background GPS" and battery team measures +4.8% battery/hour for users who open the app then switch away the app is not in a trip . Perfetto/Battery Historian show the fused location provider requesting updates every 1 s for the entire session, including while backgrounded. Code: class LocationRepository @AppScope scope: CoroutineScope, client: FusedLocationProviderClient { val location: SharedFlow<Location = callbackFlow { val cb = object : LocationCallback { override fun onLocationResult r: LocationResult { r.lastLocation?.let ::trySend } } client.requestLocationUpdates LocationRequest.Builder Priority.PRIORITY HIGH ACCURACY, 1 000 .build , cb, Looper.getMainLooper }.shareIn scope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, replay = 1 }

title: RxJava to coroutines migration
text: Lay out the migration plan: ordering, interop mechanics, behavior differences that will bite you, and how you de-risk each step in production. App with 380K lines, 70% of data layer in RxJava 2/3 Single , Observable , BehaviorSubject , PublishSubject , flatMap , combineLatest , 40 engineers, 3.2M DAU, crash-free rate 99.7% that leadership will not let you drop. Mandate: move to coroutines/Flow over 12 months without a rewrite freeze. Known pain: RxJava UndeliverableException crashes 0.15% of sessions , thread-hopping bugs, test flakiness.

title: Polling repository with backoff and lifecycle
text: Design the polling repository, including backoff, jitter, lifecycle, and testability. Order-tracking screen must show status updates; the backend has no push channel yet push is 2 quarters away . 600K concurrent users at peak; backend capacity is 40K req/s for this endpoint, current clients poll every 2 s with a while true in lifecycleScope , which at peak is 300K req/s equivalent if everyone is on-screen, and during a partial outage retries are immediate, producing a retry storm. Requirements: fresh within 5 s while visible, minimal load, graceful under failures, nothing running in background, stop when status is terminal DELIVERED/CANCELLED .

title: Race between DB write and UI read
text: Explain the race s and fix them. What guarantees does Room's Flow give you, and what does it not? Shopping-list app. User taps a checkbox; 1.1% of taps visually revert checkbox flickers back, then sometimes corrects after a second . More frequent on slower devices and when the user taps multiple items quickly. Stack: Room Flow<List<Item query , Compose list. Code: // DAO @Query "SELECT FROM item ORDER BY position" fun observe : Flow<List<Item @Query "SELECT FROM item WHERE id = :id" suspend fun get id: Long : Item @Update suspend fun update item: Item // Repository suspend fun toggle id: Long { val item = dao.get id dao.update item.copy checked = !item.checked } // ViewModel fun onToggle id: Long { viewModelScope.launch { repo.toggle id } } // UI state val items = repo.observe .stateIn viewModelScope, WhileSubscribed 5 000 , emptyList Additionally a background sync WorkManager writes the whole list from the server every 60 s with dao.replaceAll list .

title: Paging + filters pipeline
text: Design the filter-to-list pipeline using Paging 3, Flow and coroutines. What combines with what, where does caching happen, and what survives rotation? Marketplace app, catalog of 2M listings, 700K DAU. The browse screen has: free-text search, category chips, price range slider, sort order, and "in stock only" toggle. Today each filter change calls loadFirstPage manually; users report a the list jumps back to the top when the screen rotates, b results from an old filter appear after a new filter is applied about 1 in 300 filter changes , c the slider fires 40 requests per drag. Server pages are 30 items; target p95 first-page latency 600 ms. Paging 3 is available androidx.paging 3.x .

title: Parallel fan-out and partial failure
text: Explain why one failing endpoint blanks the entire screen, and redesign for partial results, bounded latency, and correct error reporting. Home screen loads six independent sections banners, recommendations, orders, wallet, offers, notifications . Cold-start-to-content p95 is 3.9 s on mid-range devices; users on bad networks often see a blank screen for 10+ s. One flaky endpoint offers, 8% error rate and sometimes 20 s hangs is blamed. Code: suspend fun loadHome : HomeData = coroutineScope { val banners = async { api.banners } val recs = async { api.recommendations } val orders = async { api.orders } val wallet = async { api.wallet } val offers = async { api.offers } val notifs = async { api.notifications } HomeData banners.await , recs.await , orders.await , wallet.await , offers.await , notifs.await } Crashlytics also shows a rare crash: JobCancellationException: Parent job is Cancelling surfacing in the UI as an error toast.

title: Cache-then-network (stale-while-revalidate)
text: Turn this ambiguity into a concrete design: caching policy, Flow shape, refresh triggers, error states, and how you'd prove it's better. PM: "Make the feed feel instant, but never show wrong data." Feed has 20 items per page, data changes every few minutes server-side, average user opens the app 5x/day. Current behavior: always show a spinner until the network responds p50 700 ms, p95 2.6 s, offline = error screen . Engineering has Room, Retrofit, Flow. The PM cannot define "wrong" precisely; some items are price-sensitive cannot be stale 5 minutes , others are editorial.

title: Event batching pipeline at scale
text: Design the client pipeline for 10x the event rate. Cover buffering, flush policy, backpressure, persistence, and coroutines/Flow structure. Analytics SDK wrapper in a streaming app. Today: each event does scope.launch { api.send event } , 15 events/min/user. Product will add player telemetry: 4 events/second during playback peak 600K concurrent players . Backend asks for batches max 50 events or 5 s, whichever first , gzip, and no loss on app kill best-effort . Currently 2-3% of events are lost, and we've seen OutOfMemoryError in the SDK on low-end devices after long offline periods. Battery team complains about radio wakeups.

title: Startup parallelization
text: How do you approach this? What goes where, how do you use coroutines safely, and how do you prove improvement? Leadership: "Cold start is slow, fix it." Data: cold start p50 2.4 s, p95 5.8 s on low-end devices time to initial display, Play Console + Firebase Performance . Application.onCreate synchronously initializes 14 SDKs 1.9 s total on a Moto G-class device , Firebase, DI graph, Crashlytics, analytics, an ads SDK, feature flags blocking network read with 1 s timeout and a runBlocking { dataStore.data.first } . Someone proposes "just move everything into GlobalScope.launch ".

title: Parallel upload queue
text: Redesign for throughput, memory, partial failure, retries, and cancellation. State your concurrency number and justify it. A real-estate app uploads up to 30 photos 3-6 MB each per listing. Complaints: uploads take 8 minutes on LTE, the app crashes with OOM on 3 GB devices when the user selects 30 photos, one failed photo aborts the whole batch and discards the 17 already uploaded, and cancelling leaves orphaned server objects. Current code: suspend fun uploadAll uris: List<Uri = coroutineScope { uris.map { uri - async Dispatchers.IO { val bytes = contentResolver.openInputStream uri !!.readBytes // full file in memory api.upload bytes } }.awaitAll }

title: Dispatcher starvation
text: Why is unrelated work slowed? How do you diagnose and fix it with dispatcher design? Delivery app, evening peak. Crash-free is fine but "app feels frozen": taps ok, yet screens show spinners for 10-20 s, p95 API-to-render jumped from 900 ms to 14 s on 12% of sessions, mostly mid-range devices on Wi-Fi. No ANRs. A new "reconcile contacts" job was released that runs an 800-contact loop. Thread dump excerpt shows many threads: "DefaultDispatcher-worker-23" ... Blocked at java.io.FileInputStream.readBytes at com.app.contacts.PhoneBook.hashAll PhoneBook.kt:41 at com.app.contacts.Reconciler$run$2.invokeSuspend Reconciler.kt:19 "DefaultDispatcher-worker-64" ... Reconciler.run does contacts.map { async Dispatchers.IO { hashAll it } }.awaitAll and each hashAll does a blocking SQLite/file read and a 40 ms CPU hash. Also, other features use Dispatchers.IO for their own Room reads and SDK blocking calls.

title: Optimistic updates with ordering and rollback
text: Explain the bugs and design a correct approach. What are the options for ordering, and which do you choose? Grocery app cart, 900K DAU. Users tap "+" quickly 3-6 taps in 2 s . Each tap does an optimistic UI increment and fires PUT /cart/items/{id} with the new quantity. Support tickets: cart shows 4 but checkout has 2 about 0.6% of carts with edits . Server logs show requests arriving out of order qty=3 processed after qty=4 . A failed request 5xx currently reverts the UI to the quantity before that tap, producing flicker and wrong numbers. Code: fun increment itemId: String { val newQty = cart.value itemId ?: 0 + 1 cart.update { it + itemId to newQty } // optimistic viewModelScope.launch { try { api.setQty itemId, newQty } catch e: Exception { cart.update { it + itemId to newQty - 1 } } // rollback } }

title: Lost updates in StateFlow state reduction
text: Find the race, explain why it is rare, and fix it. Then explain what you would change if there were 12 such fields and 5 writers. A screen uses a single UiState data class in a MutableStateFlow . Several coroutines update parts of it: profile loaded, notifications count from a Flow , a "dismiss banner" action, and a refresh result. Users report that the banner sometimes reappears after dismissing, and occasionally the profile is "empty" until the next refresh 0.5% of sessions . Code: data class UiState val profile: Profile? = null, val unread: Int = 0, val bannerVisible: Boolean = true, val loading: Boolean = false, class HomeViewModel private val repo: Repo : ViewModel { private val state = MutableStateFlow UiState val state: StateFlow<UiState = state init { viewModelScope.launch { repo.unread .collect { state.value = state.value.copy unread = it } } refresh } fun refresh = viewModelScope.launch { state.value = state.value.copy loading = true val p = repo.profile // 300-1500 ms state.value = state.value.copy profile = p, loading = false } fun dismissBanner { state.value = state.value.copy bannerVisible = false } }

title: High-rate stream fan-out and backpressure
text: Explain the symptoms mechanically and fix the pipeline end to end. Live-trading-style screen in a fintech/sports app: a WebSocket pushes 3,000 price updates per second across 400 instruments. The watchlist 30 visible symbols is a Compose LazyColumn . On mid-range devices the UI drops to 11 fps, Choreographer logs "Skipped 87 frames", and memory climbs by 40 MB/min until GC thrashes. Three screens collect the same stream. Code: class PriceRepo socket: PriceSocket, scope: CoroutineScope { val prices: SharedFlow<Tick = socket.ticks // Flow<Tick .shareIn scope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, replay = 0 } // ViewModel val rows = prices.scan emptyMap<String, Tick { acc, t - acc + t.symbol to t } // copies the whole map per tick .map { it.values.sortedBy Tick::symbol } .stateIn viewModelScope, SharingStarted.Lazily, emptyList socket.ticks is a callbackFlow { ... trySend tick ... awaitClose{} } default buffer .

title: Resilience layer: timeouts, retries, circuit breaker
text: Design a shared Resilience API in Kotlin. Cover timeouts, retries, idempotency, circuit-breaking, and the cancellation pitfalls. Explain the API surface and the defaults you'd choose. Your org asks you to standardize network resilience across 15 feature teams. Today every team writes its own try/catch + retry. Incidents seen: 1 a retry-on-any-exception wrapper swallowed CancellationException , so screens kept loading after the user left leaked work, 6% extra backend load ; 2 a payment POST retried after a read timeout and double-charged; 3 during a backend brownout, 900K clients retried 3 times each, amplifying load 4x; 4 a withTimeout 5 000 around a Flow collector surfaced as a user-visible "Job was cancelled" error.

title: Callback order
text: Walk me through the Activity lifecycle callbacks in order, from launch to destruction, and tell me what the OS is actually telling you at each step. "onCreate runs once per instance and is where I build the UI and wire dependencies. onStart means the activity is becoming visible. onResume means it is in the foreground and has user focus. Going away is the mirror: onPause means focus is lost or about to be lost, onStop means it is no longer visible, onDestroy means this instance is being discarded, either because the user finished it or because of a configuration change. There are two nested loops: visible lifetime onStart to onStop and foreground lifetime onResume to onPause . onRestart sits between onStop and onStart when a stopped instance comes back."

title: Multi-activity transitions
text: Activity A starts Activity B. Give me the exact callback order across both, and then the order when the user presses Back from B. "A.onPause, then B.onCreate, B.onStart, B.onResume, and only then A.onStop, because A must stay alive until B's window is up. On Back: B.onPause, then A.onRestart, A.onStart, A.onResume, then B.onStop and B.onDestroy. If B is translucent or dialog-themed, A is still visible so A.onStop never runs."

title: Visible vs focused
text: What is the difference between an activity being visible and being in the foreground? Give me concrete cases where onPause is called but onStop is not, and cases where neither is called but the user loses input. "Visible means any part of the window is on screen, which is the onStart to onStop span. Foreground, or focused, means the user is interacting with it, onResume to onPause. onPause without onStop happens with a translucent activity on top, a system permission dialog, split-screen when you touch the other pane, or Picture-in-Picture. Neither is called for an AlertDialog in your own activity, the notification shade, or the power menu; you only get onWindowFocusChanged false ."

title: What belongs where
text: Where do you put view setup, listeners, sensor and location registration, data loading, and persistence in the Activity lifecycle, and why there? "Match acquire and release to the same pair. One-time setup like inflating layout and creating the ViewModel goes in onCreate. Things that only matter while visible, like observing data or registering a broadcast receiver, go in onStart and onStop. Things that need exclusive or focus-dependent behavior, like starting an animation or claiming the camera exclusively in older multi-window-less models, go in onResume and onPause. Persistence goes in onPause/onStop only as a safety net; real saving happens when the user acts."

title: onDestroy and isFinishing
text: Is onDestroy guaranteed to be called? What does isFinishing tell you, and what are the correct uses of both? "No. If the process is killed, for example by the low memory killer or the user swiping the app away, onDestroy never runs. When it does run, it is either because the instance is finishing, where isFinishing is true, or because of a configuration change where isChangingConfigurations is true and the system will create a replacement. So I use onDestroy only for releasing instance-scoped, in-memory resources, never for saving data."

title: Screen off and lock screen
text: What happens to your activity's lifecycle when the screen turns off or the device locks, and what do you do if you need to show over the lock screen or keep the screen on? "Screen off drives onPause then onStop for the foreground activity; unlocking brings back onRestart, onStart, onResume. If I need to show over the keyguard, I call setShowWhenLocked true and setTurnScreenOn true on API 27+, or the older window flags. To keep the screen on while visible, I set keepScreenOn on the view or FLAG KEEP SCREEN ON on the window, which needs no permission."

title: Activity Result API
text: Why was onActivityResult replaced by the Activity Result API, and how does registerForActivityResult actually work, including across process death? "onActivityResult relied on global integer request codes and a giant switch, and it breaks composition for libraries. registerForActivityResult takes a typed contract and a callback, returns a launcher, and the registry keys each registration, so results are routed to the right callback even after the activity is recreated or the process dies. The one rule: you must register before the owner reaches STARTED, so register in onCreate or as a property initializer, never inside a click handler."

title: onNewIntent
text: When is onNewIntent called, what is the exact callback order, and what are the classic bugs? "When an already existing instance is reused for a new start, due to singleTop at the top of the stack, singleTask, singleInstance, or flags like CLEAR TOP or SINGLE TOP. If the activity was resumed the order is onPause, onNewIntent, onResume. If it was stopped, onNewIntent comes first, then onRestart, onStart, onResume. The bug is forgetting setIntent: getIntent still returns the first intent."

title: Lifecycle states and events
text: Explain Lifecycle.State versus Lifecycle.Event, how they map to activity callbacks, and what isAtLeast means for lifecycle-aware code. "Events are transitions: ON CREATE, ON START, ON RESUME, ON PAUSE, ON STOP, ON DESTROY. States are stable positions: INITIALIZED, CREATED, STARTED, RESUMED, DESTROYED. ON START and ON PAUSE both land in STARTED; ON CREATE and ON STOP both land in CREATED. So 'STARTED' means visible, 'RESUMED' means focused. isAtLeast STARTED means visible or better."

title: Lifecycle-aware collection
text: How should you collect a Flow or observe LiveData from an Activity so it does not do work in the background? Why were launchWhenStarted and friends deprecated? "Use repeatOnLifecycle STARTED inside lifecycleScope.launch, or flowWithLifecycle, or collectAsStateWithLifecycle in Compose. launchWhenStarted only suspends the coroutine when the lifecycle falls below STARTED; the upstream producer, say a location flow or a callbackFlow, keeps running. repeatOnLifecycle cancels the block and restarts it, so upstream collection really stops. launchWhenX was deprecated in lifecycle-runtime 2.6 for that reason."

title: Resource release callbacks
text: What is going on and how do you fix it? A video-call feature 800k DAU, 40% Android 11-12 mid-range opens the camera in onCreate and releases it in onDestroy . After release, support tickets say: "Scanning a QR code from another app says camera in use", and battery stats show the app at 9% drain for users who left the call screen but stayed in the app. Logcat on the other app: CameraAccessException: CAMERA IN USE 4 ... and in your own app CameraDevice.StateCallback.onError ERROR CAMERA IN USE=1 shows up when returning from a share sheet. Crashlytics shows nothing. The release is two days old.

title: ActivityLifecycleCallbacks
text: What is Application.ActivityLifecycleCallbacks, what is it good for, and what are the limits when used to detect foreground or background? "It is a callback interface registered on Application that notifies you for every activity in the process: created, started, resumed, paused, stopped, saveInstanceState, destroyed. I use it for cross-cutting concerns like screen analytics, crash breadcrumbs, or leak detection. It is not a reliable foreground detector by itself because a rotation produces stop then start, and activity counting needs a debounce, which ProcessLifecycleOwner already implements."

title: ProcessLifecycleOwner
text: How does ProcessLifecycleOwner work, what delay does it add, and when would you not trust it? "It is a LifecycleOwner for the whole process from androidx.lifecycle:lifecycle-process. It emits ON CREATE once and never ON DESTROY. ON START and ON RESUME fire when the first activity starts or resumes. ON PAUSE and ON STOP are delayed by about 700 ms after the last activity pauses or stops, so a rotation, where one activity stops and a new one starts, does not look like a background transition. It is per process, not per app, and not accurate to the millisecond, so I don't use it for security timeouts."

title: Screen-view analytics
text: Why is this happening, and how do you fix and prevent it? Product notices that "screen view" counts on the Checkout screen are 1.9x higher than server-side order-start events DAU 2M, checkout visited by about 6% daily . Funnel conversion looks like it dropped 35% overnight, though revenue is flat. The release added logScreenView in onResume of CheckoutActivity . Sessions from Android 13 devices show 3 events within 4 seconds. Suspicions: an analytics SDK upgrade, backend dedupe, or bots.

title: LifecycleRegistry internals
text: How does a Lifecycle actually dispatch to observers? What happens if I add an observer late, remove one during dispatch, or call handleLifecycleEvent from a background thread? "LifecycleRegistry keeps an ordered map of observers with their own state. When the owner moves to a new state, it syncs each observer forward or backward one event at a time, so each observer sees every intermediate event. An observer added late is replayed events up to the current state. It enforces main-thread access, and it tolerates adds and removes during dispatch by tracking a parent-state and a re-entrancy flag. Observers added earlier are notified first when moving up and last when moving down."

title: Multi-window, PiP, multi-resume
text: How do multi-window, Picture-in-Picture, and the multi-resume model change lifecycle assumptions, and what should apps do about it? "Since Android 7 in split-screen, an activity that is visible but not focused is only paused, not stopped. Since Android 10 multi-resume lets every visible activity be RESUMED, and the system tells the focused one through onTopResumedActivityChanged. PiP keeps the activity paused but visible. So I put media and rendering in onStart/onStop, use onTopResumedActivityChanged for exclusive things like camera or mic priority, and handle PiP explicitly with onPictureInPictureModeChanged."

title: Listener registration
text: Find the bugs and fix them properly. Customers on a fitness app 3M MAU report heart-rate screen "counting up by 2x, then 3x" after dismissing permission or share dialogs; battery drain is 6% per hour in the foreground. The code: class HrActivity : AppCompatActivity { private lateinit var sm: SensorManager override fun onCreate savedInstanceState: Bundle? { super.onCreate savedInstanceState sm = getSystemService SensorManager::class.java } override fun onResume { super.onResume sm.registerListener object : SensorEventListener { override fun onSensorChanged e: SensorEvent { vm.onSample e.values 0 } override fun onAccuracyChanged s: Sensor?, a: Int {} }, sm.getDefaultSensor Sensor.TYPE HEART RATE , SensorManager.SENSOR DELAY NORMAL } override fun onStop { super.onStop sm.unregisterListener listener // 'listener' is a field set elsewhere, never the one registered above } } Crash rate is flat; Perfetto shows sensor batches at 3 Hz where 1 Hz is expected after two dialog cycles.

title: First frame vs onResume
text: Does onResume mean the user can see your UI? What happens between onResume and the first drawn frame, and how do you hook the right moment? "No. onResume means the activity is resumed in ATMS. The window is added and made visible just after onResume, and the first measure/layout/draw happens on the next Choreographer frame. So views have no size in the first onResume, and the screen may still be blank. For 'screen is visible' I use a pre-draw or first-draw listener, for 'user can interact' I use onWindowFocusChanged or reportFullyDrawn, and for measurement I use ViewTreeObserver or doOnLayout."

title: Media and multi-window
text: Decide where playback should start, pause and release, and justify it, including PiP. A video app 5M MAU pauses playback in onPause and releases the player in onStop , written for API 23. Tablets and foldables are now 22% of sessions; 31% of those use split-screen. Tickets: "video freezes when I type in the other app", plus a 1-star review wave. Another report: in Picture-in-Picture, video disappears after tapping the PiP "close" button but audio continues for about 3 seconds. A proposal on the table: move everything to onResume / onPause "because Google says so".

title: Foreground/background detection
text: Write the post-incident analysis: causes, fix, and how to prevent recurrence. A banking app 1.2M DAU shows a PIN prompt when returning from background after 30 s. After a release, users reported being asked for the PIN on every screen rotation, and security logged 4x more "session expired" events. The implementation counts onActivityStarted / onActivityStopped via ActivityLifecycleCallbacks and starts a 30 s Handler.postDelayed timer when the count hits zero. The timer works in testing screen off, wait 30 s . Rotation reproduces on 100% of Android 13 devices. A second report: on phones left idle for 10 minutes the PIN sometimes did not appear at all.

title: Work in onResume
text: What is generating the load, and how do you fix it at the client? A marketplace app loads the home feed from onResume vm.refresh . DAU is 5M, average 14 resumes per session. A push campaign targeted at 3M users led to API p95 latency rising from 180 ms to 2.4 s and 429s from the gateway, though request volume per user looked normal in earlier release tests. Crashlytics shows nothing. Backend logs show bursts of 3-4 identical requests per user within 2 seconds. Android Vitals shows normal ANR rates. A teammate suggests caching on the server.

title: Migrating onActivityResult
text: Explain both failures and describe the safe migration pattern and rollout. A team migrates 40 screens from startActivityForResult / onActivityResult to the Activity Result API in a staged rollout 10% then 50% . At 10%, a new crash appears at 0.4% of sessions on the migrated screens: java.lang.IllegalStateException: LifecycleOwner com.shop.CartActivity@3f2a1 is attempting to register while current state is RESUMED. LifecycleOwners must call register before they are STARTED. at androidx.activity.result.ActivityResultRegistry.register ActivityResultRegistry.java:... at androidx.activity.ComponentActivity.registerForActivityResult ... at com.shop.CartActivity.onPromoClicked CartActivity.kt:88 Also QA reports that after "Don't keep activities" or real process death, the chosen photo is sometimes delivered to the wrong screen's handler on the profile screen, which registers launchers conditionally.

title: Recreation triggers
text: What is a configuration change in Android, and which events cause the system to destroy and recreate an Activity? A configuration change is any change to the device Configuration object that could alter which resources the app should load.
