By default the system destroys the Activity and recreates it so it re-inflates with the new resources. Rotation is the famous one, but locale, dark mode uiMode , font scale, display density, window size in multi-window or on a foldable, keyboard attach and layout direction do it too. It is not triggered by the soft keyboard showing or by backgrounding.

title: Recreate flow
text: Walk me through exactly what happens, callback by callback, when the user rotates the device while an Activity is in the foreground. The old instance goes onPause, onStop, onSaveInstanceState, onDestroy. The system keeps the ViewModelStore and any non-configuration instance aside. Then a brand-new instance runs onCreate with the saved Bundle, onStart, onRestoreInstanceState, onResume. All views and fields of the old instance are gone, only the Bundle and ViewModels survive.

title: Alternate resources
text: On rotation, how does the app end up with a different layout, and how would you give tablets a two-pane layout without writing orientation checks in code? The recreated Activity calls setContentView R.layout.x , and the resource system matches the best folder against the current Configuration : layout-land , layout-sw600dp , layout-w840dp . So the platform picks the layout, not my code. I prefer sw600dp / w qualifiers or window size classes over -land / -large , because phones in landscape and tablets are different concerns.

title: Orientation locking
text: Is locking the orientation with android:screenOrientation="portrait" a valid way to avoid configuration change bugs? It removes the rotation trigger for that Activity, but not locale, dark mode, font scale, density, multi-window resize or process death, so the bug is still there, just rarer and harder to reproduce. It is fine as a product decision a camera screen , not as a bug fix. Also on large screens the system may ignore orientation locks, so my layout must still resize.

title: ViewModel across rotation
text: Why does a ViewModel survive rotation, and what exactly does it not survive? A ViewModel lives in a ViewModelStore owned by the Activity; during a config change the store is handed to the next instance via onRetainNonConfigurationInstance , so I get the same ViewModel back. It is cleared only when the owner is truly finishing. It does not survive process death, finish /back, or the user swiping the app away, so for restore I need SavedStateHandle or persistence.

title: android:configChanges
text: What does android:configChanges do, and why do most style guides say not to use it to "fix" rotation? It tells the system, "for these configuration fields, don't recreate me, call onConfigurationChanged instead". The Resources object is already updated, but I must re-apply layout, strings and drawables manually. It's valid for narrow cases video player, game, a camera preview, multi-window apps that handle resize but discouraged as a general fix: it doesn't prevent recreation for undeclared changes or process death, and it creates a second code path nobody tests.

title: onConfigurationChanged
text: Who receives onConfigurationChanged , when, and what are the pitfalls of using it? The Application, Services, ContentProviders and registered ComponentCallbacks get it for every configuration change, because they aren't recreated. An Activity gets it only for bits listed in configChanges ; otherwise it is relaunched without that call. In the callback Resources is already updated, so I re-apply resource dependent UI and call super .

title: Video restart on rotate
text: Diagnose the bug and tell me how you'd fix it for good, including whether you'd accept the configChanges proposal. A video-course app 1.2M DAU, 35% on 3-4 GB mid-range devices plays 20-40 minute lessons. After a release, support reports "video restarts from 0 when I rotate" and watch-time per session drops 11%. Crashlytics is clean. The player is created in PlayerActivity.onCreate and released in onDestroy ; last position is saved to the backend only every 30 s. The Activity has no configChanges . Logcat on rotation shows ExoPlayerImpl: Release ... then ExoPlayerImpl: Init ... within 150 ms. An engineer proposes configChanges="orientation screenSize" plus screenOrientation="sensor" .

title: Retained fragments
text: What was setRetainInstance true for, why was it deprecated, and what do you use instead? A retained Fragment survives a config change: its instance and fields are reused, only its view is destroyed and re-created onCreate / onDestroy are skipped . It was used to keep AsyncTasks, sockets and big objects across rotation. It was deprecated in AndroidX Fragment 1.3.0 because ViewModel does the same thing with a clearer lifecycle and without the sharp edges hidden lifecycle, retained fragments with no UI, leaks when they hold Activity references . Replacement: ViewModel, plus SavedStateHandle for process death.

title: View state restore
text: Explain every symptom, and fix it. A support-ticket form 800k MAU, 4% on API 26-28 shows a bug: after rotation the "Subject" field is empty, the "Priority" spinner is reset, but the "Description" field survives. Product says it's inconsistent. The layout and Activity are below. <LinearLayout ... <EditText android:id="@+id/subject" ... / <Spinner android:id="@+id/priority" ... / <com.acme.ui.NotesView android:id="@+id/notes" ... / <!-- custom view -- </LinearLayout class NotesView c: Context, a: AttributeSet : LinearLayout c, a { var text: String = "" // no onSaveInstanceState/onRestoreInstanceState } class FormActivity : AppCompatActivity { override fun onCreate b: Bundle? { super.onCreate b setContentView R.layout.form findViewById<EditText R.id.subject .setText viewModel.draft.subject // always findViewById<Spinner R.id.priority .adapter = adapter // new adapter every time } } The Description field is a plain EditText inside NotesView . Logs are clean; the issue reproduces in dark mode toggle too.

title: Dialog re-shown
text: Why two dialogs, and how do you fix it without introducing a new bug? A food-delivery app 5M MAU shows an "Enable notifications?" prompt on first launch. After release 8.4, 6% of users report seeing the dialog twice, one stacked on the other, after rotating or switching dark mode while it is open. Tapping "Not now" on the top one reveals another underneath. The code: class HomeActivity : AppCompatActivity { override fun onCreate savedInstanceState: Bundle? { super.onCreate savedInstanceState setContentView R.layout.home if !prefs.getBoolean "asked notif", false { NotifPromptDialog .show supportFragmentManager, "notif" } } } class NotifPromptDialog : DialogFragment { override fun onCreateDialog s: Bundle? = AlertDialog.Builder requireContext .setMessage "Enable notifications?" .setPositiveButton "Yes" { , - prefs.edit .putBoolean "asked notif", true .apply } .create } No crash logs. Rotation while the dialog is open is the repro.

title: Locale, dark mode, font scale, density
text: For locale, dark mode, font scale and display density changes, what actually happens inside the app, and how should each be handled? All four are configuration changes, so the Activity is recreated and resources are resolved again: values-fr , values-night , sp text scaled by fontScale , and dp converted by density . My job is to make recreation safe and not hardcode pixels or cache resolved resources. For dark mode I use AppCompatDelegate or DayNight themes with values-night ; for font scale I use sp for text only and test at 200%; for density I use dp and vector drawables; for locale I use resource folders and never concatenate strings.

title: Per-app language
text: How do per-app language preferences work on Android 13+, and how do you support them on older versions? On API 33+ the system exposes a per-app language picker in Settings, backed by LocaleManager . The app declares its supported languages in a localeConfig XML and can set it programmatically. Below 33, AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales AppCompat 1.6.0+ backports it, persisting the choice through a metadata-flagged service. Changing it triggers a locale configuration change, so Activities are recreated.

title: Font scale
text: Run the post-incident review: what happened, why was it missed, and how do you prevent a recurrence? After a release, a banking app 2.4M MAU, 14% aged 55+ sees a 9% drop in "Pay" completion among users with large-font settings. Crashlytics shows no crash. QA verified only fontScale 1.3. Support screenshots show the "Pay" button clipped to half height, and some users who change font size while the app is open see the previous screen layout kept while the text is bigger. The Pay screen declares android:configChanges="fontScale screenSize orientation" . The button is android:layout height="48dp" with textSize="18sp" ; one custom AmountView caches paint.textSize = 18 resources.displayMetrics.scaledDensity in its constructor.

title: Restore flow and recreation cost
text: Describe the full state save and restore pipeline during a configuration change, and explain what makes recreation expensive. The system tears down the old instance stop, save state, retain, destroy , then builds a new one: new Activity, window, inflation, fragments, view hierarchy restore, first measure/layout/draw. All of that is on the main thread, so cost is roughly inflation + fragment restore + binding + first frame. I reduce it by moving data into a ViewModel, keeping onCreate light, avoiding heavy init in views and using lazy or async work.

title: ViewModelStore internals
text: Mechanically, how does a ViewModelStore get from the destroyed Activity to the new one, and in which cases does it get cleared or lost? ComponentActivity implements onRetainNonConfigurationInstance and returns a holder containing its ViewModelStore . ActivityThread keeps that object on the ActivityClientRecord while the old Activity is destroyed and passes it to the new instance, which retrieves it with getLastNonConfigurationInstance in ComponentActivity.ensureViewModelStore . A lifecycle observer clears the store on ON DESTROY unless isChangingConfigurations is true. It is lost on process death.

title: Foldables and multi-window resize
text: How do foldables, split-screen and freeform windows change how you think about configuration changes? Resizing is now continuous and independent of rotation: a window can be resized by dragging, unfolding or entering split-screen, which delivers screenSize / smallestScreenSize / screenLayout config changes. By default that recreates the Activity every time, so state handling must be airtight. I build layouts from window size classes using Jetpack WindowManager, not orientation, avoid assuming display size equals window size, and I treat posture tabletop/book as separate information from WindowInfoTracker .

title: Recreation cost on low-end devices
text: Bring p95 under 300 ms. What do you change, in what order, and what would you refuse to do? A marketplace app 10M MAU, 40% on devices with 3 GB RAM or less, median device Snapdragon 4-series shows p95 rotation time of 900 ms from Firebase Performance custom trace "config change ttfd" and 2% of rotations produce ANR-adjacent frame drops Choreographer: "Skipped 54 frames!" . The product screen has a 6-level nested LinearLayout , a ViewPager2 with 3 fragments, a RecyclerView of 40 items, and Retrofit calls fired in onStart . Traces show: inflate 310 ms, fragment restore 140 ms, onStart network call dispatch and JSON parse on main for cached response 90 ms, bitmap decode 180 ms. Red herring: Hilt component creation takes 6 ms.

title: Leaks across config change
text: Explain why heaps grow only on rotation, why it's 22 instances and not 1, and how you fix and prevent it. A news app 3M DAU gets increasing OutOfMemoryError after 15-20 rotations in a session; heap grows 18 MB per rotation Android Studio heap dump: 22 instances of ArticleActivity , retained size 14 MB each . Crash rate for OOM is 0.4% of sessions, concentrated on 2 GB devices. Code excerpt: class ArticleViewModel : ViewModel { var listener: Article - Unit ? = null // set by Activity lateinit var headerView: ImageView // cached "to avoid re-finding" private val article = MutableLiveData<Article val article: LiveData<Article = article fun load id: String = viewModelScope.launch { article.value = repo.get id listener?.invoke article.value!! } } class ArticleActivity : AppCompatActivity { private val vm: ArticleViewModel by viewModels override fun onCreate b: Bundle? { super.onCreate b setContentView R.layout.article vm.headerView = findViewById R.id.header vm.listener = { a - title = a.title } // captures this vm.load intent.getStringExtra "id" !! } } LeakCanary reports: GC ROOT thread ... → ArticleViewModel.listener → ArticleActivity$onCreate$1 → ArticleActivity destroyed .

title: configChanges policy
text: What do you recommend? Include what you'd tell her and the team, and how you'd measure success. A new engineering manager at a 40-engineer fintech Android team wants to reduce "state loss" bugs 11 open tickets this quarter, all reproduced on rotation or dark mode . She proposes a policy: add android:configChanges="orientation screenSize screenLayout smallestScreenSize keyboardHidden uiMode locale layoutDirection fontScale density" to every Activity and lock portrait on phones. The app has 1 Activity per feature 14 , a few fragments with retained state, and a ViewModel layer used inconsistently. Target SDK 34, 25% of users on tablets and foldables, 6% use accessibility font scale = 1.5.

title: Fragment lifecycle
text: Walk me through the Fragment lifecycle. Why does a Fragment have both a lifecycle and a "view lifecycle", and in which callback would you do what? "A Fragment goes onAttach, onCreate, onCreateView, onViewCreated, onViewStateRestored, onStart, onResume, then back down through onPause, onStop, onDestroyView, onDestroy, onDetach. The key point is that the Fragment instance and its view have separate lifetimes. When a fragment goes on the back stack, onDestroyView runs but the instance survives in CREATED state, and onCreateView runs again on return. So anything that touches views belongs to the view lifecycle, available through viewLifecycleOwner, and anything that is instance-level, like arguments and non-view setup, belongs in onCreate."

title: FragmentManager hierarchy
text: What is the difference between supportFragmentManager , parentFragmentManager and childFragmentManager , and when would you use each? "Each FragmentActivity has one FragmentManager, supportFragmentManager . Each Fragment has two references: parentFragmentManager , the manager that holds this fragment the activity's or a parent fragment's , and childFragmentManager , its own manager for fragments nested inside it. Siblings talk through the parent manager; nesting uses the child one. getFragmentManager is deprecated in favour of parentFragmentManager ."

title: viewLifecycleOwner
text: In a Fragment, when do you pass viewLifecycleOwner instead of this to observe , collect and similar APIs? What goes wrong with this ? "Anything that updates views must be bound to viewLifecycleOwner . The Fragment's own lifecycle keeps running while the fragment sits on the back stack with no view. If I observe LiveData with this in onViewCreated, the observer is not removed when the view dies, and each return adds another one, so I get duplicate updates, work against a destroyed view, and leaked views. With viewLifecycleOwner the observer dies with the view."

title: View binding leak
text: Why does holding a ViewBinding reference in a Fragment leak, and what is the correct pattern? "A Fragment instance can outlive its view, for example on the back stack. If the Fragment holds a binding field, it keeps the whole view tree alive, which holds the Activity context, bitmaps and adapters, after onDestroyView. The fix is to null the binding in onDestroyView, usually with a nullable backing field binding and a non-null binding getter, and to clear things like RecyclerView adapters and ViewPager2 adapters too."

title: commit variants and state loss
text: What is the difference between commit , commitNow , commitAllowingStateLoss and commitNowAllowingStateLoss ? Why do we see "Can not perform this action after onSaveInstanceState" and how do you fix it properly? " commit schedules the transaction asynchronously on the main thread; commitNow runs it synchronously but cannot be added to the back stack. Both throw IllegalStateException if the FragmentManager has already saved its state, because a change after saving would be lost when the process is killed and the UI restored. AllowingStateLoss variants skip the check and accept that the change may be lost. The proper fix is not to suppress the exception but to avoid issuing transactions when state is saved, by tying the trigger to the lifecycle, or to accept loss only for transient UI."

title: add vs replace and back stack
text: What does replace vs add do to existing fragments, and what exactly does addToBackStack change in lifecycle terms? What happens to the replaced fragment's view and instance? " add puts a fragment next to existing ones in the container; replace removes every fragment currently in that container and adds the new one. Without addToBackStack , the removed fragment is destroyed completely onDestroyView, onDestroy, onDetach . With addToBackStack , the transaction is reversible: the removed fragment keeps its instance in CREATED state but its view is destroyed, so on pop it gets onCreateView again with restored view state. For add , the old fragment's view stays alive but gets covered, which means it still receives touches if the new view is not opaque or clickable."

title: Fragment Result API
text: How do two fragments or a DialogFragment and its host exchange results today? Why was setTargetFragment / onActivityResult replaced, and what are the delivery semantics of the Fragment Result API? "I use the Fragment Result API: the receiver calls setFragmentResultListener requestKey, viewLifecycleOwner on the FragmentManager both fragments share, and the sender calls setFragmentResult requestKey, bundle . Delivery is lifecycle-aware: if the receiver is not at least STARTED, the result is held and delivered when it is. Only the latest result per key is kept. It survives process death because the results are saved with the manager. It replaces setTargetFragment , which created hidden coupling and was deprecated."

title: ViewModel scoping
text: How do fragments share a ViewModel, and how do you choose the scope: fragment, parent fragment, Activity, or navigation graph? What are the lifetime and staleness consequences? "A ViewModel lives as long as its ViewModelStoreOwner. by viewModels scopes to the fragment, by viewModels { requireParentFragment } to the parent, by activityViewModels to the Activity, and by navGraphViewModels R.id.graph to a Navigation graph back stack entry. I pick the smallest scope that covers every consumer. Activity scope is easy but long-lived and global to the screen, which leads to stale data when a flow is re-entered and hidden coupling between unrelated screens. A nav-graph scope matches a flow like checkout and is cleared when the flow is popped."

title: FragmentFactory
text: Why do Fragments require a no-arg constructor, how does FragmentFactory change that, and what breaks if you pass dependencies through a custom constructor? "The system recreates fragments reflectively from the class name saved in the instance state, with no knowledge of your arguments. By default it needs a public no-arg constructor, and state comes from arguments and saved state. Since fragment 1.1 I can set a FragmentFactory on the FragmentManager to construct fragments with dependencies. It must be installed before restoration happens, that is before super.onCreate in the Activity, or restoration throws Fragment.InstantiationException ."

title: Fragment view leak
text: Find what is wrong, explain the memory growth mechanism, and fix it. A news app 900k DAU has a feed Fragment that opens article detail via replace + addToBackStack . After users open 4-5 articles and press back, memory climbs; Crashlytics shows 1.4% of sessions end in OOM on 2 GB devices. LeakCanary on a debug build reports: "FeedFragment received Fragment onDestroyView callback ... leaking: DestroyedView". Code: class FeedFragment : Fragment { private lateinit var binding: FragmentFeedBinding private val vm: FeedViewModel by viewModels private val adapter = FeedAdapter { id - openArticle id } override fun onCreateView i: LayoutInflater, c: ViewGroup?, s: Bundle? : View { binding = FragmentFeedBinding.inflate i, c, false return binding.root } override fun onViewCreated view: View, s: Bundle? { binding.list.adapter = adapter vm.items.observe this { adapter.submitList it } lifecycleScope.launch { vm.refreshing.collect { binding.swipe.isRefreshing = it } } } } Red herrings: the team suspects Glide caching and the feed's image sizes; heap dumps show the dominators are bitmaps.

title: DialogFragment
text: What are the common pitfalls with DialogFragment , and why prefer it over showing AlertDialog directly from an Activity or Fragment? "A DialogFragment is a Fragment whose view lives in a dialog window, so the FragmentManager recreates it on rotation and process restoration, while a raw AlertDialog.show is destroyed with the Activity and throws WindowLeaked if not dismissed. Pitfalls: show is a commit, so it throws IllegalStateException if state is saved; dismiss the same, so use dismissAllowingStateLoss when needed; keep listeners out of constructors and use the Fragment Result API; check for an existing instance before showing; use onCreateDialog or onCreateView , not both unintentionally; and use viewLifecycleOwner carefully, since it exists only when you supply a view."

title: Transactions in background
text: How do you triage, stop the bleeding, find the root cause, and prevent the class of bug? A food-delivery app 2.5M DAU shipped version 8.12 on Monday. By Wednesday Crashlytics shows a new top crash affecting 0.6% of sessions about 15k users/day , concentrated on Android 9-13, mostly on the order tracking screen: Fatal Exception: java.lang.IllegalStateException: Can not perform this action after onSaveInstanceState at androidx.fragment.app.FragmentManager.checkStateLoss FragmentManager.java:1856 at androidx.fragment.app.FragmentManager.enqueueAction FragmentManager.java:1894 at androidx.fragment.app.BackStackRecord.commitInternal BackStackRecord.java:329 at androidx.fragment.app.BackStackRecord.commit BackStackRecord.java:294 at com.app.tracking.TrackingActivity$onOrderUpdate$1.invokeSuspend TrackingActivity.kt:88 Release notes: migrated the order tracking from polling to a WebSocket; on ORDER DELIVERED the Activity replaces the map fragment with a "Rate your order" fragment. Red herring: the crash rate also moved on devices without the new feature flag, because a library bump Fragment 1.5 - 1.6 shipped in the same release.

title: Navigation-hosted fragments
text: The requirement says "still be filled in". How do you clarify it, and how do you design it so it works for rotation, back navigation, and the 20-minute background case? A fintech app uses Navigation component single Activity, NavHostFragment , Navigation 2.7 with a 3-step "Add beneficiary" form: Details - Verify - Review. Product says: "When the user goes back from Review to Details, the form must still be filled in." QA reports that on back, the name field is filled but the dropdown selection and a RecyclerView of suggested banks reset to the top, and sometimes the whole form is empty after the user took a call app in background 20 min . Typical device mix: 55% mid-range 4 GB, 30% 2-3 GB. Red herring: someone suggests using hide /show fragments instead of Navigation to "keep the views".

title: ViewPager2 with fragments
text: How does FragmentStateAdapter manage fragments in a ViewPager2? Which lifecycle state does each page's fragment reach, what is offscreenPageLimit , and what do you need to watch out for when the ViewPager2 lives inside a Fragment? "ViewPager2 is built on RecyclerView; FragmentStateAdapter creates a Fragment per page and attaches it to the pager item's container. Only the current page's fragment is RESUMED; neighbours are held at STARTED via setMaxLifecycle , so onResume is a reliable 'this tab is current' signal. By default, pages beyond the RecyclerView cache are destroyed and their fragment state is saved f <itemId keys , then restored when scrolled back. Inside a Fragment, I must pass childFragmentManager and viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycle , and clear the adapter in onDestroyView."

title: FragmentManager internals
text: What actually happens between calling commit and the fragment's onCreateView running? Explain how the FragmentManager schedules transactions, what setMaxLifecycle and setReorderingAllowed do, and why a fragment added in onCreate might not be created yet. " commit does not run the transaction. It adds a BackStackRecord to a pending list and posts an Runnable to the host's main-thread handler. When it runs, the manager executes the ops, and each fragment's state is moved toward the host's current state by a FragmentStateManager : attach, create, create view, activity-created, start, resume, never above what the host or the setMaxLifecycle cap allows. So right after commit , findFragmentByTag returns null. commitNow or executePendingTransactions run it synchronously."

title: Fragment state saving and restoration
text: What exactly is saved and restored for a Fragment across configuration change and across process death? Where do arguments , onSaveInstanceState , view state, ViewModel, and the FragmentManager's own state fit? "Three layers. The FragmentManager saves which fragments exist, their class names, ids, tags, arguments, back stack, and each fragment's onSaveInstanceState Bundle, as part of the Activity's saved state, and recreates the instances reflectively. View state for views with ids is saved separately and restored in onViewStateRestored . ViewModels survive configuration changes but not process death, so important data needs SavedStateHandle or persistent storage. Everything saved passes through a Binder transaction with about a 1 MB shared budget."

title: MenuProvider and setHasOptionsMenu
text: How should a Fragment contribute to the toolbar menu today? Why was setHasOptionsMenu / onCreateOptionsMenu deprecated, and what does MenuProvider change about lifecycle? " setHasOptionsMenu true and the Fragment onCreateOptionsMenu callbacks were deprecated in Fragment 1.5.0 in favour of MenuProvider . The Activity a MenuHost , from Activity 1.4.0 lets me add providers with addMenuProvider provider, viewLifecycleOwner, Lifecycle.State.RESUMED . The menu items are then active only while the lifecycle owner is at that state and removed automatically when it's destroyed, which avoids the stale items and double-inflation seen with fragment-owned callbacks."

title: Duplicate fragments on recreation
text: What is the bug, why only after recreation, and how do you fix it robustly? A messaging app 1.2M DAU has a ChatActivity that hosts a ChatFragment and a ComposerFragment . Support tickets: "after rotating, the message list is shown twice, overlapping, and sending a message inserts it into only one of them." Crash-free is fine; no stack trace. Reported 8x more on tablets and foldables which rotate and resize often . Code: class ChatActivity : AppCompatActivity { override fun onCreate savedInstanceState: Bundle? { super.onCreate savedInstanceState setContentView R.layout.activity chat // contains FrameLayout @+id/chat container, @+id/composer container supportFragmentManager.beginTransaction .add R.id.chat container, ChatFragment.newInstance intent.getStringExtra "chatId" !! .add R.id.composer container, ComposerFragment .commit } } Red herrings: someone suspects RecyclerView item animator duplication and the new Paging library bump.

title: Fragment detached in async work
text: Run the post-incident review: why did the first fix not work, what is the real root cause, and what systemic changes do you propose? Post-incident review for a ride-hailing app 4M DAU . Release 5.40 had 0.9% crash-affected sessions, 70% on one signature across Android 8-14: java.lang.IllegalStateException: Fragment RideSummaryFragment{...} not attached to a context. at androidx.fragment.app.Fragment.requireContext Fragment.java:... at androidx.fragment.app.Fragment.getResources Fragment.java:... at androidx.fragment.app.Fragment.getString Fragment.java:... at com.app.ride.RideSummaryFragment.showFare$lambda RideSummaryFragment.kt:142 and a second, 20% signature java.lang.IllegalStateException: Fragment RideSummaryFragment not associated with a fragment manager. from parentFragmentManager . The fare is fetched with a callback-based client; the screen is popped by users in 12% of cases before the fare returns p95 fare latency is 2.8 s on 3G . The fix attempted in 5.40.1 wrapped the calls in if isAdded ; crash rate fell by only 25%.

title: ViewPager2 tabs performance
text: How do you reduce startup time and memory without bringing back "flicker" when users switch tabs? A social app's home screen has a ViewPager2 with 5 tabs Feed, Reels, Explore, Notifications, Profile as Fragment s; offscreenPageLimit = 4 was set last year "to avoid reload flicker". After the Reels tab launched video thumbnails the numbers are: cold-start-to-first-content p95 2.9 s on mid-range phones target 2.0 s , 11.2% of sessions on 2-3 GB devices use more than 380 MB PSS, OOM crash rate 0.7% on those devices, and every tab fires its first network call in onViewCreated 5 parallel requests, 3 of which are not visible . A Perfetto trace shows 5 fragments inflating layouts in the first 700 ms on the main thread. Red herring: engineers suspect the image library.

title: Migrating to Navigation under live traffic
text: How would you plan and execute this migration safely? What are the risks and how do you measure them? A banking app 6M MAU, 40 screens has a multi-Activity-plus-fragment architecture with hand-written FragmentTransaction s about 140 call sites to replace / add / addToBackStack , several commitAllowingStateLoss calls, and a custom back stack helper. Leadership wants the Navigation component Navigation 2.7+ with a single-Activity per feature, with no downtime and no big-bang. Constraints: two release trains per month, crash-free target 99.7%, deep links from SMS and push must keep working, and 30% of users are on Android 9-11 with 3 GB RAM or less. The team has 6 engineers.

title: One-shot events and view recreation
text: Explain why each symptom occurs and recommend a design, with trade-offs among SingleLiveEvent , Channel , SharedFlow , and state-based UI. In an e-commerce app, CartFragment shows a Snackbar "Item added to cart" and navigates to Checkout on Event s from the ViewModel. The ViewModel exposes LiveData<CartEvent . Bugs from QA and production about 3% of sessions touching the cart : 1 after returning from Checkout via back, the Snackbar shows again; 2 after rotating, "Navigate to checkout" fires again and the user is thrown back to Checkout; 3 when the app is in the background and the event arrives, the Snackbar is lost. The team proposes a SingleLiveEvent hack and a Channel with receiveAsFlow . Red herring: some say it's a Fragment bug and want to avoid the ViewModel.

title: Why the OS kills processes
text: Why does Android kill app processes, and when does it happen? Does the user or the app get any warning? Android has finite RAM and no swap for app heaps, so it keeps apps as cached processes and kills the least important ones when memory is needed. The kill is by lmkd low memory killer daemon sending SIGKILL, so my code gets no callback, not even onDestroy. The user may also kill me swipe from recents, force stop , and the system kills me for permission changes, crashes, and ANRs. A backgrounded app can be killed at any time, and when the user returns the system recreates the process and the top activity from saved state.

title: What survives process death
text: After the OS kills your process while the app is in the background, what survives and what is lost when the user comes back? Everything in the process memory is lost: statics, singletons, ViewModels, in-memory caches, running threads and coroutines. What survives is the Activity back stack records held in system server, the saved-instance-state Bundle that I wrote in onSaveInstanceState for each activity, and anything on disk files, SharedPreferences/DataStore, Room, account tokens in secure storage . The system recreates the process, runs Application.onCreate , and recreates the top activity with its Bundle.

title: Simulating process death
text: How do you reproduce process death locally? Is "Don't keep activities" enough? "Don't keep activities" only destroys activities as I leave them; the process stays alive, so statics and singletons still hold their values and I miss the singleton bugs. For true process death I background the app Home , then run adb shell am kill <package , then reopen from Recents. am force-stop is not equivalent, because it also removes the saved state and the task.

title: onSaveInstanceState timing
text: When exactly is onSaveInstanceState called, and did that change across API levels? What are the cases where it is not called? It is called when the system might need to recreate the activity later: when the activity goes to the background, or before a configuration-change recreation. Before API 28 it could run before or after onPause , but always before onStop . For apps targeting API 28+, it is called after onStop . It is not called when the user explicitly finishes the activity back press, finish , and it's not a lifecycle callback I can rely on for persistence.

title: Bundle size limit & TransactionTooLargeException
text: What is the size limit on saved instance state, and what happens when you exceed it? The saved Bundle is sent to system server over Binder, and Binder has a 1 MB transaction buffer shared by all in-flight transactions of the process. Overshoot and you get TransactionTooLargeException , which since Android 7 API 24 crashes the app instead of being silently logged. In practice, I keep saved state to a few tens of KB, store ids and small state, and put big data on disk or in a repository.

title: Application re-creation & singletons
text: After process death, what exactly runs when the user returns, and what does it mean for singletons, DI graphs and initialization order? The system forks a new process, creates the Application , runs ContentProvider onCreate first and then Application.onCreate , then recreates the top activity with its saved Bundle. All singletons are rebuilt empty. So any state loaded by a splash or login flow is gone, and the restored activity is now the entry point; it must work without the earlier screens having run.

title: Swipe-away vs system kill vs finish
text: The user swiped the app away from Recents, versus the system killed the cached process. What is the difference for state, and what does the user expect? System kill preserves the task and the saved-state Bundle, so the user returns to the same screen and my restore code must rebuild it. Swiping away removes the task and discards saved state, so the next launch is a fresh start and savedInstanceState is null. Back-pressing out of the root activity finishes it: no state saved, ViewModel cleared. So restoration is for the "I did not leave" case; things the user explicitly dismissed should reset.

title: View state restoration
text: Which UI state does Android restore automatically after recreation, and which does it not? Why do some EditTexts lose text? On recreation, the framework saves and restores the state of Views that have a unique ID and implement state saving: EditText text, CheckBox, scroll positions of RecyclerView's layout manager, etc. It does not save state of Views without an ID, nor data held in my fields, ViewModel or adapter. Text is lost when the View has no ID, the same ID is used twice, or I overwrite it in onCreate with a default.

title: SavedStateRegistry
text: What is SavedStateRegistry and how does it relate to onSaveInstanceState ? How would you plug your own component into it? SavedStateRegistry is an AndroidX owner-scoped registry Activity, Fragment, NavBackStackEntry that lets components contribute to the saved Bundle without overriding onSaveInstanceState . Components register a SavedStateProvider under a key; when the owner is saved, each provider's saveState is collected into one Bundle. On recreation I call consumeRestoredStateForKey to get my part back. It is the base for SavedStateHandle and rememberSaveable .

title: SavedStateHandle
text: How does SavedStateHandle work, what can you store in it, and how does it combine with ViewModel scope? SavedStateHandle is a key-value map handed to the ViewModel that is backed by the owner's saved-state Bundle. The ViewModel itself dies with the process, but the handle's content is saved by the registry and handed to the recreated ViewModel. It stores Bundle-compatible types primitives, String, Parcelable, Serializable, arrays... , so I keep small UI state like selected ID, query text, filter. Large data goes to disk.

title: ViewModel vs saved state vs persistence
text: How do you decide where a piece of state lives: ViewModel, SavedStateHandle, or persistent storage? I ask what the user expects and what the cost to recompute is. UI-scoped, expensive-to-rebuild data that only needs to survive rotation loaded lists, in-flight request goes in the ViewModel. Small, user-input-driven UI state that must survive process death selected tab, query, scroll key, form text goes in SavedStateHandle. Anything the user would be upset to lose after a swipe-away, or that is the source of truth drafts, cart, auth , goes to disk/server.

title: rememberSaveable (link)
text: How does rememberSaveable relate to process death, and when does it fail? remember is lost on recreation; rememberSaveable stores its value in the same saved-state Bundle, so it survives configuration change and process death. It requires the value to be Bundle-saveable primitives, Parcelable, Serializable or provided with a custom Saver . It is subject to the same size limits as onSaveInstanceState .

title: Process death
text: Find the bug, explain why QA misses it, and fix it. Crashlytics: kotlin.UninitializedPropertyAccessException: lateinit property item has not been initialized at DetailViewModel.load . 0.7% of sessions, only on Android 11+ devices with 3 GB RAM, never in QA. The detail screen is opened from a list via startActivity . class DetailActivity : AppCompatActivity { private val vm: DetailViewModel by viewModels override fun onCreate savedInstanceState: Bundle? { super.onCreate savedInstanceState if savedInstanceState == null { vm.item = intent.getParcelableExtra "item" !! // set once } vm.load } } class DetailViewModel : ViewModel { lateinit var item: Item fun load { / uses item.id / } } Red herring: the team suspects a race with a background sync.

title: Navigation back stack restoration
text: After process death, how is the navigation back stack restored, and what is not restored? The NavController saves its back stack as part of the saved-state Bundle: for each entry, the destination ID, arguments, and the entry's saved state. On recreation it restores the graph and the back stack, then re-instantiates only the visible destination; entries below are recreated when popped to. ViewModels scoped to a back stack entry are new, but their SavedStateHandle is restored. Large arguments and in-memory objects are not restored beyond what is in the Bundle.

title: Fragment restoration after process death
text: What does the FragmentManager do on recreation after process death, and which Fragment mistakes only show up then? During super.onCreate savedInstanceState of the FragmentActivity, the FragmentManager restores its saved state and re-instantiates every fragment by class name, through the FragmentFactory default: the public no-arg constructor , and restores their arguments Bundle and their saved state. So fragments need a no-arg-constructible class, data passed through arguments , and the Activity must not add them again when savedInstanceState != null .

title: Process death
text: Walk me through diagnosis and fix. What do you tell the product manager? A news app with 400k DAU. Support receives "I open the app from the multitask view after lunch and see a blank white screen; sometimes it crashes." Crashlytics shows NullPointerException: Attempt to invoke virtual method 'java.util.List ... getArticles ' on a null object reference in ArticleListFragment.onViewCreated , 0.9% of sessions, bucketed mostly in "background duration 30 min." Release 6 weeks ago replaced an object ArticleCache with a DI singleton. Logcat from a repro device: I ActivityManager: Start proc 18231:com.news/u0a212 for top-resumed-activity D MainActivity: onCreate saved=Bundle {android:viewHierarchyState=..., androidx.lifecycle...} E AndroidRuntime: java.lang.NullPointerException ... ArticleListFragment.onViewCreated

title: Bundle size
text: Why is it crashing, how large is it, what do you change, and how do you stop it recurring? A photo-album app, 150k DAU. Crash cluster: RuntimeException: android.os.TransactionTooLargeException: data parcel size 1042136 bytes thrown from ActivityThread.performStopActivity , 1.8% of sessions on devices with 2-3 GB RAM, mostly after viewing big albums. The album screen code: override fun onSaveInstanceState outState: Bundle { super.onSaveInstanceState outState outState.putParcelableArrayList "photos", ArrayList photos // up to 2,000 Photo objects outState.putParcelable "selectedThumb", selectedBitmap // 600x600 Bitmap } Each Photo has id, uri, caption, exif map about 400 B . Red herring: a recent Glide upgrade.

title: Testing process death
text: Why did the tests pass, and what test strategy would have caught it without making CI unbearable? Post-incident review after the blank-screen outage see previous incident . The team claims: "We have a test suite with ActivityScenario.recreate for every screen and it all passed." The incident only reproduced after real process death. The suite runs on emulators in CI, 1,400 UI tests, 42 minutes.

title: How the system restores a task
text: Walk me through what the system does when the user taps the app in Recents after the process was killed. Who holds what, and why are only some activities recreated? The task and each ActivityRecord component, Intent, state flags, saved Bundle are kept in system server, in ActivityTaskManager's root task hierarchy. When I return, the system sees the record's process is dead, starts a new process via Zygote, and asks the new ActivityThread to launch the top activity with the stored Bundle. Activities below it are not recreated until the user navigates back, at which point the same mechanism runs for each.

title: Permission revocation & process death
text: What happens to your process if the user revokes a runtime permission in Settings while the app is in the background? How should your code handle the return? The system kills the app's process when a runtime permission is revoked from Settings so the app doesn't keep running with the old grant; this is documented behavior. When the user returns, the process is recreated and the restored activity runs with the permission now missing. So I check permissions at the point of use every time, never assume that a restored screen still has what it had, and degrade or re-request.

title: Detecting process death in production
text: How do you detect and measure process death in production, and tell it apart from a crash, an ANR, or the user's swipe? On API 30+ I call ActivityManager.getHistoricalProcessExitReasons at startup to read why previous processes ended: REASON LOW MEMORY , REASON USER REQUESTED , REASON CRASH , REASON ANR , REASON PERMISSION CHANGE , and so on, plus the importance when it died. I report it as telemetry. To detect a restored launch inside a process, I combine savedInstanceState != null with a "fresh process" flag set in Application.onCreate . Below API 30, I can only infer it.

title: Singletons after death
text: What happened, how do you fix it without weakening security, and how do you avoid logging users out? A fintech app, 1.2M DAU. Crashlytics: IllegalStateException: No auth token thrown from TransferRepository.send , plus a spike of HTTP 401 on /accounts for users who return after long backgrounds. 0.6% of sessions. Code: @Singleton class AuthManager @Inject constructor private val api: AuthApi { @Volatile var token: String? = null // set by LoginActivity after login fun requireToken = token ?: error "No auth token" } Splash/login sets the token; MainActivity restores into the "Transfers" tab. Security team insists tokens must never be stored in plain SharedPreferences. Red herring: server-side token TTL was shortened to 15 minutes the same week.

title: Migration under live traffic
text: How do you plan and execute the migration safely? A marketplace app currently saves screen state with a hand-rolled onSaveInstanceState JSON strings of the form model, about 30 KB per screen . Leadership plans to grow flows 10x: multi-step listing creation with up to 40 fields per step and 12 photos. Today: 2M DAU, 0.05% TransactionTooLarge. You must migrate to SavedStateHandle plus persistence while shipping weekly, with 70% of sessions in the old version at any time, and Android 8-15 support. Existing sessions in the middle of a listing must not lose drafts across the app update.

title: Android 14 restore bug
text: List every bug you can find and prioritize them. After targeting API 34, a ride-hailing app sees a crash in MapActivity only after the device has been idle for hours: IllegalStateException: Trip not loaded 0.3% of 800k DAU . Reviewing: class MapActivity : AppCompatActivity { private val vm: TripViewModel by viewModels private var receiver: BroadcastReceiver? = null override fun onCreate savedInstanceState: Bundle? { super.onCreate savedInstanceState TripSession.current = intent.getParcelableExtra "trip" // static holder setContentView R.layout.activity map } override fun onStart { super.onStart receiver = object : BroadcastReceiver { override fun onReceive c: Context, i: Intent { vm.onDriverUpdate i } } registerReceiver receiver, IntentFilter "com.ride.DRIVER UPDATE" } override fun onStop { unregisterReceiver receiver ; super.onStop } } object TripSession { var current: Trip? = null } // Logcat on affected devices: // W/ActivityTaskManager: Process com.ride has died: cch+0 CEM // E/AndroidRuntime: Caused by: SecurityException: ...: One of RECEIVER EXPORTED or RECEIVER NOT EXPORTED should be specified when a receiver isn't being registered exclusively for system broadcasts Red herring: the team blames the new Android 14 battery policy.

title: Checkout state design
text: Where does each piece of state live, and how do you handle the OTP round-trip? Design state handling for a 4-step checkout address - shipping - payment - review used by 600k DAU. Requirements: survive rotation and process death; user must not re-type an address; card number must never be stored on device by the app; the cart is server-owned; users often leave to a banking app for OTP the app stays backgrounded 1-5 minutes, on 2-3 GB devices the process is killed in about 8% of those trips . Single-activity with Navigation.

title: Resume where I left off
text: How do you turn this into something buildable, and what is explicitly out of scope? Product requirement from the PM: "The app should always resume exactly where the user left off." The app: a learning platform with video lessons HLS , quizzes, notes editor, and a feed. 900k DAU, 40% on devices with 3 GB RAM or less. No more detail given. You have two weeks.

title: Process importance classes
text: What are the process importance classes in Android, and how does the system decide which class your app's process is in? Android keeps one process per app by default and ranks it by the most important component running inside it. The classes, from most to least protected, are foreground, visible, service, and cached. A process with a resumed Activity or a running foreground service is foreground. One with a visible but not focused Activity is visible. One with only started or bound services is service. One with nothing user-relevant is cached and is the first to be killed when memory is short. The rank is recomputed continuously, and the highest-ranked component wins.

title: Cold, warm and hot start
text: Define cold, warm and hot app start. What work happens in each, and which one do you optimise for? Cold start means no process exists: the system forks one, creates the Application, then creates and shows the Activity. Warm start means the process is alive but the Activity must be recreated, so we skip process creation but still pay onCreate and first frame. Hot start means the Activity is in memory and the system just brings it to the front, running onRestart/onStart/onResume . I optimise cold start first because it is the worst case and what most new users and low-memory devices hit.

title: onTrimMemory
text: What is onTrimMemory , what do its levels mean, and what should an app do in response? onTrimMemory level is a ComponentCallbacks2 callback telling the app the system wants memory back. TRIM MEMORY UI HIDDEN fires when all UI becomes hidden, so drop UI-only caches like bitmaps. The RUNNING levels say we are still on screen while the device is low on memory. The BACKGROUND/MODERATE/COMPLETE levels say we are in the cached LRU list and how close to the kill end we are. On each I release caches I can rebuild. I never rely on it, since the process can be killed without any callback.

title: oom_adj and lmkd
text: How does Android decide which process to kill under memory pressure? Explain oom adj , lmkd , and how it relates to the importance classes. AMS assigns every process an oom score adj from its components' state: roughly 0 for foreground, 100 visible, 200 perceptible, 500 service, 900 and up for cached. It pushes the value to lmkd , a native daemon. When memory pressure hits, lmkd kills the process with the highest score first, and among equals prefers the larger one. So cached, big, old processes die first, the foreground app last. The kill is SIGKILL: no callback, no onDestroy .

title: What keeps a process alive
text: What actually keeps an Android process alive in the background, and what does not? The system keeps a process ranked by its components, not by what its threads are doing. A resumed Activity, a foreground service, a running receiver, a service bound by an important client or a provider in use make the process important. A bare Thread, a Handler, a static object, a WakeLock or a notification does not. START STICKY does not keep the process alive; it asks the system to restart the service after the process is killed.

title: Application.onCreate timing and cost
text: When exactly does Application.onCreate run relative to other components, how often, and what are the consequences for what you put there? Application.onCreate runs once per process, on the main thread, before any Activity, Service, or Receiver is created in that process. Declared ContentProviders in that process are installed before it runs, so provider-based SDK init fires even earlier. It does not run again on rotation or Activity recreation, but it does run on every cold start, including starts triggered by a broadcast or JobScheduler with no UI. So it should be tiny: no I/O, no heavy SDKs, nothing that assumes a UI.

title: Background kill during work
text: What is happening, how do you confirm it, and what do you change? A video-sharing app uploads 80 MB clips. The upload runs in a coroutine launched from viewModelScope through a plain UploadRepository . DAU is 600k; about 9 percent of uploads never finish. Failures cluster on 3 GB devices when the user presses Home or switches to the camera. QA on a Pixel 8 cannot reproduce. Logcat from a failing user via bug report : ActivityManager: Killing 14873:com.example.clips/u0a312 adj 920 : empty 17 lmkd: Kill 'com.example.clips' 14873 , uid 10312, oom score adj 920 to free 212MB rss The backend shows a partial multipart upload that is never completed. The server team blames mobile network flakiness.

title: Multi-process apps
text: What does android:process do? What changes for your app when components run in a second process? android:process runs a component in a different OS process. A name starting with a colon, like :remote , is private to the app; a lowercase dotted name is global and shareable between apps with the same UID. Each process gets its own VM, heap budget, static state, and its own Application instance whose onCreate runs separately. So singletons, caches, and in-memory flags are not shared; you need IPC Binder, ContentProvider, files, a Room multi-instance setup to communicate. People use it for crash isolation, memory isolation, or an independent lifecycle like a player or push process.

title: Per-process Application
text: Why is this happening and how do you fix it without breaking the sync? A fintech app has a bound SyncService declared with android:process=":remote" . After a release adding a periodic sync, dashboards show app open analytics events doubled for 38 percent of sessions about 210k extra events/day , and Crashlytics shows SQLiteDatabaseLockedException: database is locked at startup in 0.7 percent of sessions. Two log lines appear per start: I/App: Application.onCreate pid=5120 process=com.example.fin I/App: Application.onCreate pid=5188 process=com.example.fin:remote W/Firebase: FirebaseApp is not initialized in this process com.example.fin:remote class App : Application { override fun onCreate { super.onCreate Analytics.init this ; Analytics.track "app open" Db.migrateIfNeeded this // runs Room migrations eagerly FirebaseMessaging.getInstance .token // used by SyncService too } }

title: App standby buckets (brief)
text: What are app standby buckets, and how do they relate to process priority? Do they change oom adj ? Standby buckets API 28+ classify apps by how recently and how often the user engages with them: Active, Working set, Frequent, Rare, and later Restricted API 30 . The bucket does not change process rank or kill order. It limits what the app can do in the background: when jobs run, how many alarms fire, how many high-priority FCM messages count. So a "dead" background app may be alive but deferred, which is a different bug than lmkd.

title: WebView in a second process
text: Find the bug and explain the fix. A support-chat feature runs in android:process=":chat" to isolate a heavy third-party SDK. After release, Crashlytics shows a new crash at 0.4 percent of sessions, only on Android 9+ and only after opening the "Help" screen, which uses a WebView inside :chat . java.lang.RuntimeException: Using WebView from more than one process at once with the same data directory is not supported. https://crbug.com/558377 at android.webkit.WebViewFactory.createProviderImpl ... at android.webkit.WebView.<init WebView.java:... at com.example.chat.HelpActivity.onCreate HelpActivity.kt:31 class App : Application { override fun onCreate { super.onCreate WebView this .settings.javaScriptEnabled = true // warm up WebView } } The main process also uses a WebView for terms and conditions. QA only tested chat on its own.

title: Deaths that are not low-memory kills
text: Besides low-memory kills, what can end your app's process while the user is using it or just after, and how does each differ in what you can observe or handle? There are several. An uncaught exception or native signal kills our own process. An ANR makes the system kill it or the user taps Close . Revoking a runtime permission in Settings kills the process. Updating or reinstalling the app kills it. Force-stop kills it and also blocks background components until next launch. A dependency dying a provider we are a client of can kill us. Under heavy pressure lmkd can even kill the foreground app. OEM battery managers add their own kills. Each leaves different evidence, and only some give a callback.

title: ApplicationExitInfo
text: How can an app find out why its previous process died? Walk me through ApplicationExitInfo and how you would use it in production. Since API 30, ActivityManager.getHistoricalProcessExitReasons returns recent exit records for my package: reason low memory, ANR, crash, user requested, permission change... , the importance at death, PSS/RSS, a description, a timestamp, and for ANRs a trace stream. I read it on next launch and send a compact event to analytics. I can also attach my own state with setProcessStateSummary and get it back in the record, so I know what the user was doing when the process died.

title: Importance propagation through bindings
text: A service in a separate process is bound by your Activity. How does that affect each process's priority, and which flags change the behavior? A bound service process is ranked at least as high as its most important client, as long as the binding is a normal one. If my UI process is foreground, the service process is lifted to match. If my UI goes to cached, the service falls with it unless something else holds it. Content providers work the same way: a process hosting a provider with an active client is ranked with that client. Flags such as BIND WAIVE PRIORITY , BIND NOT FOREGROUND , BIND ABOVE CLIENT , and BIND IMPORTANT adjust this.

title: Cold start regression
text: How do you diagnose the regression and decide what to initialise when? A marketplace app with 800k DAU shipped version 7.4. Android vitals: cold start p90 rose from 1.9 s to 3.1 s; on 2 GB devices 40 percent of the base p90 is 4.6 s and 1-star reviews mention "slow open". The diff added six SDKs: analytics, attribution, crash, remote config, ads, and a feature-flag SDK, all initialised in Application.onCreate plus two via App Startup providers. Logcat: I/ActivityTaskManager: Displayed com.example/.MainActivity: +3s112ms I/Choreographer: Skipped 74 frames! The application may be doing too much work on its main thread. Product wants all SDKs ready before the first screen "for correct attribution". Push-notification wakes 40 percent of process starts also got slower.

title: Cached app freezer and phantom process limit
text: What are the cached app freezer and the Android 12 phantom process killer, and how can they change behavior of an app that "worked" in the background? The freezer, introduced in Android 11 as an optional feature and used on newer devices, freezes cached processes using the cgroup freezer, so their threads get no CPU while cached; they are not killed, just paused. Android 12 added a limit on phantom processes native child processes forked outside the normal app components ; beyond a device-wide cap 32 in AOSP, as I recall , the system kills the extras with SIGKILL. Both break code that assumed a cached process keeps running or that native children are free.

title: Process isolation trade-off
text: Do you adopt a separate process? Which kind, and how do you design the interface and failure handling? A document-scanning app 3M MAU, crash-free sessions 99.1 percent embeds a third-party PDF/OCR library. Crashlytics attributes 0.8 percent of sessions to native crashes SIGSEGV in libocr.so , mostly on malformed PDFs from email attachments, and 0.3 percent to OutOfMemoryError on 2 GB devices when decoding 40 MP pages. An engineer proposes running the library in android:process=":ocr" . Another proposes android:isolatedProcess="true" . The library needs the input file and returns a 200-page text result about 3 MB .

title: Staying alive in background
text: How do you respond to this requirement, and what do you build? A messaging app 2M DAU gets a product request: "The app must stay connected in the background so messages show up instantly. On our Pixel test phone it gets killed after about 5 minutes with the screen off." The current design keeps a WebSocket open in a plain Service started on app launch. Support tickets report delayed messages median 4 min, p95 27 min on Android 12+ devices, and battery complaints from the 15 percent of users whose OEM keeps the service alive. FCM is integrated but only used for marketing pushes. No further detail is given on what "instantly" means.

title: Looper/MessageQueue/Handler model
text: Explain how Looper, MessageQueue, Handler and Message work together. Why does the main thread never "finish"? Every thread that wants to receive work has one Looper, which owns one MessageQueue. The Looper runs an infinite loop: take the next due Message off the queue, hand it to the Handler it targets, repeat; when nothing is due, the thread sleeps in native code. A Handler is the front door: any thread calls handler.post or sendMessage to enqueue work, and the work later runs on the thread that owns the Looper. The main thread never finishes because ActivityThread.main ends by calling Looper.loop , and everything the framework does there lifecycle callbacks, input, traversals, broadcasts arrives as messages.

title: Handler.post vs sendMessage, dispatch order
text: What is the difference between handler.post Runnable and handler.sendMessage Message ? When both a Handler.Callback and handleMessage exist, who runs first? post Runnable wraps the Runnable into a Message via getPostMessage callback field set, what unused and enqueues it; sendMessage enqueues a message the Handler later decodes by what . They share one queue and one ordering rule. On dispatch: if msg.callback is set, run that Runnable and stop; otherwise if a Handler.Callback was passed to the constructor, call it; if it returns true the message is consumed, if false fall through to handleMessage .

title: Looper.prepare/loop
text: How do you create your own Looper on a plain Thread? What happens if you create a Handler on a thread without one? Call Looper.prepare creates the Looper and its queue, stores it in a ThreadLocal , create Handlers, then call Looper.loop , which blocks forever; to stop, call looper.quit from any thread. Creating a Handler on a thread with no Looper throws RuntimeException: Can't create handler inside thread ... that has not called Looper.prepare . In practice use HandlerThread rather than hand-rolling this.

title: HandlerThread
text: What is a HandlerThread, when would you still use it today, and how do you shut it down correctly? HandlerThread is a Thread that sets up a Looper in run and exposes it via getLooper , which blocks until the Looper is ready, so there is no startup race. Work posted through a Handler on it runs serially, in time order, on one background thread. I use it for ordered, long-lived single-thread work sensor/camera callbacks, a serialized disk writer, Bluetooth/GATT callbacks that need a Looper . Shutdown is quitSafely delivers already-due messages, drops future-delayed ones or quit drops everything pending ; and I must do it, or the thread leaks.

title: uptime vs elapsed time
text: What clock does postDelayed use? Compare uptimeMillis , elapsedRealtime and currentTimeMillis , and say when each is right. Handler delays are based on SystemClock.uptimeMillis , which counts time since boot excluding deep sleep when the CPU is suspended . elapsedRealtime counts since boot including deep sleep and is the right clock for measuring real elapsed time. currentTimeMillis is wall clock, which the user or network can change, so it is wrong for measuring intervals. So a postDelayed 10 min when the device deep-sleeps for 8 minutes still has most of its delay left when the device wakes.

title: View.post semantics
text: What exactly does view.post { } do? Why does view.post { view.width } give a real width in onCreate when view.width directly gives 0? If the view is attached to a window, View.post posts to the main Handler the AttachInfo 's handler . If it is not attached yet, the Runnable is parked in the view's own RunQueue and replayed when the view is attached, posted to that handler during the first traversal, after that traversal's measure and layout have run. So it runs after layout, which is why width is non-zero. It returns false and does nothing useful if the Looper is quitting.

title: CalledFromWrongThreadException
text: Why does this crash only sometimes, and what is the correct fix? A profile screen about 2M DAU loads a user over Retrofit via a plain Thread . QA on the debug build sees nothing; in production Crashlytics shows 0.4% of sessions crashing, only on some devices and mostly when the network is fast: android.view.ViewRootImpl$CalledFromWrongThreadException: Only the original thread that created a view hierarchy can touch its views. at android.view.ViewRootImpl.checkThread ViewRootImpl.java:9006 at android.view.ViewRootImpl.requestLayout ViewRootImpl.java:1900 at android.view.View.requestLayout View.java:25000 at android.widget.TextView.setText TextView.java:6000 at com.app.ProfileActivity$load$1.run ProfileActivity.kt:42 class ProfileActivity : AppCompatActivity { private lateinit var name: TextView override fun onCreate savedInstanceState: Bundle? { super.onCreate savedInstanceState setContentView R.layout.profile name = findViewById R.id.name Thread { val user = api.getUser .execute .body !! // sometimes served from OkHttp cache in 3 ms name.text = user.name }.start } } A teammate says: "it works in most runs, so it can't be a threading bug."

title: Handler leaks
text: Why does this leak, how bad is it, and how do you fix it properly? A weather app's DashboardActivity shows a refresh countdown. LeakCanary debug reports on every rotation: ┬─── │ GC Root: Thread main - MessageQueue ├─ android.os.MessageQueue │ ↓ MessageQueue.mMessages ├─ android.os.Message │ ↓ Message.target ├─ DashboardActivity$refreshHandler$1 anonymous Handler │ ↓ this$0 ╰→ DashboardActivity leaked, destroyed class DashboardActivity : AppCompatActivity { private val refreshHandler = object : Handler Looper.getMainLooper { override fun handleMessage msg: Message { tick sendEmptyMessageDelayed 0, 60 000 } } override fun onStart { super.onStart ; refreshHandler.sendEmptyMessageDelayed 0, 60 000 } override fun onStop { super.onStop / forgot to stop / } } Prod: Activity retains a 6 MB bitmap graph; 8% of low-RAM users 2 GB devices hit OOM after 12 rotations. Rotation is exactly the trigger the PM wants kept working.

title: removeCallbacks
text: How do you cancel a delayed postDelayed task? Why does handler.removeCallbacks { ... } with a fresh lambda not cancel anything? removeCallbacks Runnable removes pending messages whose callback is the same object reference equality for plain Runnables . A fresh lambda is a new object or for non-capturing lambdas a different instance than the one you posted via a SAM-converted lambda in a different call site , so nothing matches. Keep the Runnable in a field, or use a token / what , or removeCallbacksAndMessages null to clear everything for that Handler.

title: MessageQueue internals
text: How does MessageQueue.next actually work? How does the main thread sleep, wake up for a delayed message, and wake up for input? next loops: call nativePollOnce ptr, timeoutMs , which blocks in epoll wait on the native Looper ; after it returns, look at the head of the time-sorted list. If the head is due, unlink and return it; if it is in the future, compute the remaining time as the next timeout and if idle handlers exist run them; if the list is empty, timeout is -1 sleep until woken . enqueueMessage inserts into the sorted list and, if the new message is at the head or a barrier case , calls nativeWake to write to an eventfd that wakes the poll. Input and vsync reach the loop through file descriptors registered on the same native Looper, so epoll wakes for them without any Java message.

title: Sync barriers & async messages
text: What are sync barriers and asynchronous messages in MessageQueue? Who uses them and what breaks if a barrier is leaked? A sync barrier is a special message with target == null placed in the queue; while it is at the head, next skips all synchronous messages and delivers only messages marked asynchronous, until someone removes the barrier by its token. ViewRootImpl posts a barrier when it schedules a traversal so that vsync/Choreographer frame messages async run ahead of ordinary post s, and removes it when the traversal runs. A leaked barrier means every normal Handler.post , including lifecycle H messages, stops being delivered, while async frame messages and input still work, so the app looks half-alive and eventually ANRs.

title: IdleHandler
text: What is a MessageQueue.IdleHandler ? When is it called and what are the rules for using it safely? An IdleHandler runs when the queue has nothing due to run right now: the head message is in the future or the queue is empty. queueIdle returns true to stay registered for future idle moments, false to be removed after this call. It runs on the Looper's thread, so it blocks messages that arrive while it runs. It is good for small deferrable work warming a cache after first frame but not a place for heavy work, and it provides no deadline guarantee.

title: Handler delay & Doze
text: Why is the local reminder late, and how do you make it reliable? A medication-reminder app 600k DAU lets users start a "take pill in 20 minutes" countdown. The implementation: handler.postDelayed { showReminderNotification }, 20 60 000 from a foreground Activity, then the user locks the phone. Support tickets: "reminder came at 47 minutes", worst on Android 12-14 Pixels and Samsung; none on the QA phone that sits on a charger with the screen on. Telemetry shows fired at - scheduled at p50 = 21 min, p95 = 58 min, max = 6 h. There is a red herring: the app also has an FCM data message for server-side reminders that arrives on time.

title: Choreographer
text: How does Choreographer relate to the Looper and MessageQueue? Walk through what happens between invalidate and pixels, at the message level. Choreographer is a per-thread singleton created lazily for a thread with a Looper that sequences work to display vsync. invalidate or requestLayout leads to ViewRootImpl.scheduleTraversals , which posts a sync barrier and asks Choreographer for a TRAVERSAL callback. Choreographer requests the next vsync from the display event receiver; when vsync arrives as a file descriptor event on the Looper , it enqueues an asynchronous message that runs doFrame , which runs callbacks in order INPUT, ANIMATION, INSETS ANIMATION, TRAVERSAL, COMMIT. The traversal removes the barrier, measures, lays out and draws recording display lists; RenderThread does the GPU part .

title: Dispatchers.Main on Handler
text: How is Dispatchers.Main implemented on Android? What is the difference between Dispatchers.Main and Dispatchers.Main.immediate , and how does delay work there? The kotlinx-coroutines-android artifact provides a main dispatcher backed by a Handler on the main Looper a HandlerContext ; on API 28+ it uses an async Handler . dispatch simply posts the continuation as a Runnable. Dispatchers.Main.immediate skips the post if you are already on the main thread, running the block inline; Dispatchers.Main always posts. delay on that dispatcher is implemented with handler.postDelayed , and cancellation removes the callback. So all the Looper rules apply: uptime-based delays, one message at a time, ordering by posting time.

title: Slow message / main Looper stall
text: How do you find which message is stalling the main Looper when stack traces are inconclusive, and what do you do in the first 24 hours? A food-delivery app 3M DAU sees ANR rate rise from 0.3% to 1.1% after a release Play Console threshold for "bad behavior" is 0.47% user-perceived ANR . Android Vitals clusters show the main thread idle or inside generic framework frames: "main" tid=1 Native at android.os.MessageQueue.nativePollOnce Native method at android.os.Looper.loop Looper.java:299 at android.app.ActivityThread.main ActivityThread.java:8282 Reason: Input dispatching timed out ... Waiting to send non-key event because the touched window has not finished processing certain input events that were delivered to it over 500.0ms ago. Other traces only 20% show SharedPreferences.apply - QueuedWork.waitToFinish and a few show a JSON parse . The release added 14 PRs, three touching background sync.

title: Handler to coroutines migration
text: How do you migrate safely, and what behavior might silently change? A messaging app with 5M DAU has a 7-year-old MessageSyncer built on Handler plus callbacks. You are asked to migrate it to coroutines in two sprints without a feature freeze. The class's contract is undocumented, but tests show it relies on: 1 results delivered on the main thread in the order requests were made; 2 a postDelayed retry with backoff 2 s/4 s/8 s; 3 a cancel path on Activity destroy that calls removeCallbacksAndMessages null . A previous migration attempt caused duplicated messages for 0.3% of users.

title: HandlerThread lifecycle
text: Write the post-incident review: what happened, why it was invisible, and what changes. A document-scanner app 1.2M DAU crashed for 0.9% of sessions on 3 GB devices after a release, always after the user had scanned many pages. Crashlytics: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: pthread create 1040KB stack failed: Try again at java.lang.Thread.nativeCreate Native Method at java.lang.Thread.start Thread.java:1063 at android.os.HandlerThread.start ... at com.app.scan.PageProcessor.<init PageProcessor.kt:18 PageProcessor is created per scanned page; its init does HandlerThread "page-proc" .apply { start } . No quit anywhere. Thread count in adb shell ls /proc/<pid /task wc -l is 1,400 on a crashing device. The heap is fine red herring: the team first raised largeHeap . A previous postmortem blamed "Android memory".

title: Quitting Loopers, exceptions in the loop
text: What happens when you call quit on a Looper, when you post to a quit Looper, when you try to quit the main Looper, and when a Runnable throws inside the loop? quit marks the queue as quitting, drops all pending messages, and makes next return null so loop returns and the thread can end; quitSafely drops only future-dated messages and lets due ones run. Posting afterwards returns false, recycles the message, and logs "sending message to a Handler on a dead thread". The main Looper cannot be quit: it throws IllegalStateException "Main thread not allowed to quit." . An uncaught exception in a Runnable propagates out of Looper.loop , up the thread, and on the main thread the default handler terminates the process the stack shows Handler.dispatchMessage and Looper.loop .

title: Queue size & timers at scale
text: Why does this degrade at 10x, and how would you redesign it? A chat app supports disappearing messages. Each message item posts its own expiry: handler.postDelayed expiryRunnable id , ttl ; scrolling cancels with handler.removeCallbacks runnable when a row is unbound. Today a typical power user has 500 pending expiries. A new "Communities" feature will load up to 5,000 messages per screen and 30 rows get bound/unbound per scroll frame. Prototype numbers on a mid-range device: scroll p95 frame time 9 ms today, 31 ms in the prototype; Perfetto shows main-thread slices in MessageQueue.enqueueMessage and removeMessages growing; no GC pressure issues. A teammate says "postDelayed is cheap, it's a timer."

title: Message pool
text: Why do people say "use Message.obtain instead of new Message "? How does the Message pool work and what are its failure modes? Messages are recycled through a small global linked-list pool max 50 . Message.obtain takes one from the pool, or allocates if empty; after dispatch the Looper calls recycleUnchecked , clearing fields and returning it to the pool. This avoids allocation churn for the framework's constant message traffic. You must not touch a Message after sending it, and must not enqueue the same Message twice.

title: Handler vs alternatives
text: How would you design it and what would you reject? You are the tech lead for a photo-backup app 800k DAU . A new requirement: upload queue with sequential uploads, retry with backoff 5 s, 30 s, 2 min , cancel on user action, survive screen rotation, and keep working when the user leaves the app for up to 10 minutes. A mid-level engineer proposes: a HandlerThread , postDelayed for retries, and a Handler shared across screens. Another suggests a started Service. Product says "uploads must eventually finish even if the app is closed, but nobody expects exact timing". Upload sizes: 3-25 MB, typically 5-40 pending, on cellular 25% of the time.

title: What runs on the main thread
text: What exactly runs on an Android app's main UI thread, and what are you not allowed to do there? The main thread is the one thread that runs the app's Looper. Lifecycle callbacks of Activity, Service, BroadcastReceiver and Application, input event handling, measure/layout/draw of the view tree, and anything posted via Handler or Dispatchers.Main all run there serially. Views can only be touched from it. So anything slow, like disk, network or heavy computation, blocks input and frames and eventually causes an ANR.

title: Frame deadline
text: What is the frame deadline on Android, and how does it change on 90/120 Hz devices? What happens when you miss it? The deadline is 1000 ms divided by the display refresh rate: 16.67 ms at 60 Hz, 11.1 ms at 90 Hz, 8.33 ms at 120 Hz. In that window the main thread must run input, animation, measure/layout and record draw, and the RenderThread must finish GPU work. If it misses vsync, the previous frame is shown again, so the user sees a dropped frame as jank.

title: Choreographer and vsync
text: Explain how a vsync signal turns into a drawn frame in the View system. What is the order of Choreographer callbacks? SurfaceFlinger sends vsync to the app via DisplayEventReceiver. Choreographer, on the main thread, runs callbacks in a fixed order for that frame: input, animation, insets animation, traversal measure/layout/draw record , and commit. invalidate or requestLayout only schedules a traversal for the next vsync, so many calls in one frame coalesce into a single draw.

title: UI thread vs RenderThread
text: Since Android 5 there is a RenderThread. What does it do, and what does it change about where jank can come from? The UI thread records drawing commands into display lists, then hands them to the RenderThread, which replays them on the GPU. So main thread work and GPU work are pipelined. Jank can now come from either: slow measure/layout/record on main, or heavy GPU work like overdraw, blur or big bitmap uploads on RenderThread. Some operations, like RenderNode property animations, can run on RenderThread even when main is busy.

title: Touch event dispatch
text: Walk through how a touch event travels through the View hierarchy. What do dispatchTouchEvent , onInterceptTouchEvent and onTouchEvent each do, and what do their return values mean? The event goes Activity.dispatchTouchEvent, then the window and DecorView, then down ViewGroups via dispatchTouchEvent . Each ViewGroup may steal the gesture in onInterceptTouchEvent . The deepest view that returns true from onTouchEvent on ACTION DOWN becomes the touch target and receives the rest of the gesture. If a parent intercepts later, the child gets ACTION CANCEL.

title: AsyncTask removal
