text: AsyncTask is deprecated. What was wrong with it and what replaces it today? AsyncTask was deprecated in API 30 Android 11 . It leaked Activities via inner classes, did not survive configuration changes, had a serial executor by default that made tasks queue behind one another, and swallowed cancel semantics. Today I use Kotlin coroutines with structured concurrency tied to a lifecycle scope, or an Executor for Java, and WorkManager when the work must survive the process.

title: Threading options
text: Give an overview of threading options on Android and how you choose between them. I choose by lifetime and need. Coroutines with a lifecycle-bound scope for work tied to UI; Executors or dispatchers for pooled blocking work; HandlerThread when I need a single looper thread with ordered messages; WorkManager for guaranteed deferrable work; foreground service for user-visible long running work. Raw Thread I avoid except in libraries.

title: StrictMode
text: What is StrictMode, which policies does it have, and how do you use it responsibly in a team? StrictMode is a developer tool that detects accidental disk, network and resource misuse on the main thread ThreadPolicy and leaks or insecure patterns process-wide VmPolicy . I enable it in debug builds, with penaltyLog locally and penaltyDeath on CI/internal builds for new violations, and I never rely on it in production.

title: ANR watchdog mechanics
text: Where does the 5-second ANR limit come from, and what does the platform actually measure for input, broadcasts and services? An ANR is not a general "main thread busy for 5 s" check. The platform tracks specific pending work with timeouts: for input, InputDispatcher waits for the app to acknowledge an event; 5 s without a response triggers an ANR. For broadcasts it is 10 s foreground and 60 s background, for services 20 s foreground and 200 s background, and about 10 s for ContentProvider publish. Then system server collects stacks and shows the dialog.

title: Input pipeline and latency
text: Describe the path of a touch event from the screen to your onTouchEvent , and what contributes to touch latency. What is MotionEvent batching? The touch driver reports to the kernel, InputReader in system server converts raw events, InputDispatcher picks the target window and sends it over an InputChannel socket to my app. My main Looper wakes on that fd, ViewRootImpl's input stages process it, and views see it. For MOVE events the app batches multiple samples per frame and delivers them aligned to Choreographer, so onTouchEvent receives one MotionEvent with historical samples per frame.

title: SurfaceView vs TextureView
text: Compare SurfaceView and TextureView from a threading and composition standpoint. When would you pick each? A SurfaceView owns a separate Surface that SurfaceFlinger composes as its own layer, so any thread can render into it without involving the View hierarchy; it is the most efficient and supports secure/DRM output. A TextureView renders into a SurfaceTexture and is drawn as part of the hardware-accelerated View tree, so it can be transformed, faded and scrolled like a normal view, at the cost of an extra GPU copy and more memory. I pick SurfaceView for video and games by default and TextureView only when I need view-level transforms or alpha in a scrolling or animated container.

title: invalidate vs requestLayout cost
text: What is the difference between invalidate , postInvalidate and requestLayout , and how do they affect frame cost? What is layout thrashing? invalidate marks a region dirty and causes a redraw record display list on the next frame; requestLayout marks the view and its ancestors for remeasure and relayout and then redraw, which is far more expensive. postInvalidate is the thread-safe version of invalidate for non-UI threads. Layout thrashing is changing layout-affecting properties repeatedly, or reading and writing in a loop, so layouts run multiple times or every frame.

title: Measuring frames in the app
text: How can you measure frame performance from inside the app in production, and what do "slow" and "frozen" frames mean? I use the platform's FrameMetrics API API 24 or the Jetpack JankStats library, which hook per-frame timing and report janky frames with the UI state at the time. Play Console classifies frames over 16 ms as slow and over 700 ms as frozen. I sample in production, attach the screen name and scroll state, and track the janky-frame percentage per screen.

title: StrictMode / main-thread I/O
text: Find what is wrong, explain the impact and how you would prevent a recurrence. A junior's PR for a "recent searches" feature passes review and QA on a Pixel 8. After release, vitals show cold-start p90 up from 1.9 s to 2.7 s on devices with 2-3 GB RAM and slow eMMC storage; ANR rate rises from 0.2% to 0.5%. The code: class SearchActivity : AppCompatActivity { private val prefs by lazy { getSharedPreferences "search", MODE PRIVATE } override fun onCreate savedInstanceState: Bundle? { super.onCreate savedInstanceState setContentView R.layout.activity search val saved = prefs.getString "recent", " " !! // 1 recent.addAll Json.decodeFromString<List<String saved File cacheDir, "suggest.db" .copyTo File filesDir, "suggest.db" , overwrite = true // 2 } fun addRecent q: String { recent.add 0, q prefs.edit .putString "recent", Json.encodeToString recent .commit // 3 } }

title: Touch dispatch
text: What is wrong with both attempts and how should it be solved? An app shows a vertical NestedScrollView feed that contains a horizontal "stories" RecyclerView . QA reports that on some devices horizontal swipes feel "sticky": 1 in 3 swipes scroll the page vertically instead of the carousel, especially when the swipe is slightly diagonal. Analytics: carousel engagement dropped 18% since the redesign that moved the carousel inside the page. The developer's fix: class StoriesRecyclerView ctx: Context, attrs: AttributeSet : RecyclerView ctx, attrs { override fun onTouchEvent e: MotionEvent : Boolean { parent.requestDisallowInterceptTouchEvent true // always return super.onTouchEvent e } } After that fix, vertical scroll starting on the carousel is dead, and users complain they cannot scroll the feed when their finger starts on stories. Another dev proposes overriding onInterceptTouchEvent in the NestedScrollView to return true when dx dy .

title: Input ANR
text: Walk me through diagnosis, mitigation and the permanent fix. A ride-hailing app 4M DAU, 60% on Android 11-14, 35% on 3 GB RAM devices sees ANR rate jump from 0.25% to 1.1% overnight after release 8.41. Play Console clusters: Input dispatching timed out … Waiting because the focused window has not finished processing the input event . The main-thread stack in the traces: "main" prio=5 tid=1 Waiting at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park Native Method at java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.park at com.app.location.LocationCache.get LocationCache.kt:44 // synchronized lock at com.app.map.MapPresenter.onCameraIdle MapPresenter.kt:112 "DefaultDispatcher-worker-3" Blocked at com.app.location.LocationCache.refresh LocationCache.kt:88 // holding lock at android.os.BinderProxy.transactNative at android.location.ILocationManager$Stub$Proxy.getLastLocation Release 8.41 added a periodic location refresh every 5 s on a worker. Crash-free is unaffected. The release also upgraded OkHttp and moved image loading to a new library.

title: Refresh rate / animation timing
text: Explain what is happening and how you would re-implement it. A fintech app animates a "balance count-up" and a custom pull-to-refresh with this logic, tuned in 2020 on 60 Hz devices: private val handler = Handler Looper.getMainLooper private var step = 0 private val tick = object : Runnable { override fun run { step++ progress = step / 18f .coerceAtMost 1f // 18 steps 16 ms 300 ms invalidate if progress < 1f handler.postDelayed this, 16 } } After the new flagship phones 120 Hz, 18% of DAU arrived, support tickets say the animation "judders and runs slow". Perfetto shows the animation taking 510 ms on those devices and visibly uneven frames; on 60 Hz devices it takes 300-320 ms. Another report: on battery-saver reduced refresh 60 Hz it's fine. Product wants animations to be exactly 300 ms everywhere.

title: AsyncTask migration
text: How do you migrate without a big-bang rewrite and without regressions? A 9-year-old Java/Kotlin app 6M MAU, 70 screens still has 214 AsyncTask subclasses, many as non-static inner classes of Activities. Crashlytics: 0.4% of sessions crash with IllegalStateException / NullPointerException in onPostExecute after rotation or back press, and RejectedExecutionException: Task rejected from ThreadPoolExecutor ... queued tasks = 128 about 600/day in the image-grid screen. The team wants to target a newer SDK, drop AsyncTask, and has one quarter with 3 engineers; feature delivery must continue; there is no good test coverage. Leadership asks for a plan and a definition of "done".

title: SurfaceView vs TextureView
text: Which view type and structure do you choose, and what do you do about the animations and the black flashes? You are building a short-video feed like a vertical pager, 8M DAU, 55% devices with 3-4 GB RAM, p95 swipe-to-first-frame target 250 ms . A prototype uses TextureView per page inside ViewPager2 , with a single ExoPlayer instance per visible page. Complaints: heat and battery drain +11% battery per hour of use vs competitor , memory of 45 MB extra, and sometimes a black frame flash when swiping. A staff engineer proposes switching to SurfaceView everywhere; the designer wants a crossfade and rounded corners with a scale-down "peek" animation when opening comments.

title: ANR post-incident review
text: Run the post-incident review: what went wrong in the investigation, and what is the technical and process fix? Post-incident review for last week's incident: release 5.12 of a retail app 1.8M DAU saw ANR rate rise from 0.3% to 0.9% for 36 hours. The on-call engineer saw in logcat on their own device Choreographer: Skipped 47 frames! The application may be doing too much work on its main thread at startup, spent two days optimizing Application.onCreate saved 120 ms , but the ANR rate did not change. Play Console clusters showed Broadcast of Intent { act=android.intent.action.BOOT COMPLETED } and executing service com.app/.SyncService ANRs, mostly background, mostly on Android 13 devices from two OEMs. The real fix, found by someone else on day three, was a receiver doing a 14 s synchronous database migration inside onReceive . Management asks: why did it take three days, and how do we avoid it?

title: Started vs bound vs both
text: What is the difference between a started service, a bound service, and a service that is both? How does each one stop? A started service is created by startService and lives until someone calls stopSelf or stopService . A bound service is created by bindService and lives only while at least one client is bound. A service can be both: it stays alive until it has been explicitly stopped AND all clients have unbound. I think of it as two independent reasons to stay alive, and the system destroys the service only when both reasons are gone.

title: Service threading
text: On which thread do Service callbacks run? Is a Service a background thread? When do you still need your own thread or coroutine inside a Service? A Service is not a thread and not a separate process by default. Its callbacks onCreate , onStartCommand , onBind , onDestroy run on the main thread of the app process. If I do disk or network work there, I block the UI and can hit a Service ANR. So I dispatch work to a coroutine scope, executor, or HandlerThread owned by the service and cancel it in onDestroy .

title: onStartCommand return values
text: Explain START STICKY, START NOT STICKY, START REDELIVER INTENT and START STICKY COMPATIBILITY. What does each do when the process is killed, and what should I do with the flags argument? The return value tells the system what to do if it kills my service process while it is still "started". START NOT STICKY: do not recreate it. START STICKY: recreate it and call onStartCommand with a null Intent. START REDELIVER INTENT: recreate it and redeliver the last Intent retrying pending ones . My service must therefore treat a null Intent as a valid input under START STICKY.

title: stopSelf, stopService, destroy
text: What are the ways a started service can stop, and what is the difference between stopSelf , stopSelf startId , and stopService ? When does onDestroy run? The service can stop itself with stopSelf or stopSelf startId , or any component can call stopService intent . stopSelf startId stops only if no newer start request has arrived, which makes it safe when work is queued. The service is destroyed only when it is not started and has no bound clients; then onDestroy runs on the main thread, and I cancel my scope there.

title: Foreground service and notification
text: What is a foreground service, why does it require a notification, and what is the "5 second rule" for startForegroundService ? What happens if I violate it? A foreground service tells the OS "the user is aware of and benefits from this ongoing work", so the process gets higher priority and is far less likely to be killed. In exchange it must show an ongoing notification. Since API 26 I start it with startForegroundService from the allowed contexts, and I must call startForeground within about five seconds of the Service starting, otherwise the app crashes with ForegroundServiceDidNotStartInTimeException and on older releases an ANR-style RemoteServiceException .

title: Restart semantics
text: What is the bug, why does it only happen on low-RAM devices, and how do you fix it? A messaging app has ChatSyncService , started when the app backgrounds. In production Crashlytics shows a fatal NullPointerException at ChatSyncService.onStartCommand for 12k crashes/day, only on devices with <3 GB RAM, mostly right after the user returns from other apps. Code: class ChatSyncService : Service { private lateinit var userId: String override fun onStartCommand intent: Intent, flags: Int, startId: Int : Int { userId = intent.getStringExtra "uid" !! CoroutineScope Dispatchers.IO .launch { sync userId stopSelf } return START STICKY } override fun onBind i: Intent? : IBinder? = null } Stack: java.lang.NullPointerException: Parameter specified as non-null is null: ... parameter intent . Red herring: the team suspects a race in sync because crashes cluster near a recent sync refactor.

title: Local bound service via Binder
text: How do you implement a bound service for same-process clients using Binder? What are the lifecycle rules for binding and unbinding from an Activity, and what are the leak risks? The service returns a Binder subclass from onBind that exposes itself or an interface . The client calls bindService intent, conn, BIND AUTO CREATE and gets the IBinder in onServiceConnected . I bind in onStart , unbind in onStop , and never keep the service reference past unbind. Leaks come from forgetting unbindService or holding the service reference in a static or ViewModel.

title: Messenger vs AIDL vs local Binder
text: How do you choose between a local Binder, a Messenger, and AIDL for talking to a service? What threading and safety differences matter? If the client and service are in the same process, I use a local Binder or better, an interface . For cross-process one-way message passing I use a Messenger: it serialises calls on a Handler thread, so no thread-safety worries. For cross-process request/response with typed methods and concurrency I use AIDL, where calls arrive on Binder pool threads and I must make my service thread-safe.

title: Background start restrictions (API 26+)
text: What changed in Android 8.0 for starting services from the background, what counts as "background", and what are the legitimate ways to start work from there? From API 26, an app that is in the background cannot call startService and gets IllegalStateException "app is in background" . It can call startForegroundService and must call startForeground within about five seconds. An app counts as foreground if it has a visible activity, a foreground service, or is bound by a foreground app. After the app moves to the background, there is a short grace window a few minutes before restrictions apply. Legit alternatives: WorkManager/JobScheduler, high-priority FCM, alarms, bound services, or user-visible FGS.

title: IntentService deprecation
text: IntentService is deprecated. What did it do, why was it deprecated, and what do you use instead? IntentService was a Service that ran each Intent sequentially on a worker HandlerThread and stopped itself when the queue drained. It was deprecated in API 30 it still exists; it was not removed because it is a background service, which Android 8+ blocks, and WorkManager/coroutines supersede it. I use WorkManager for deferrable guaranteed work, a coroutine in a foreground service for ongoing user-visible work, or a plain coroutine in the app process for short in-process tasks.

title: Foreground service types (Android 14)
text: What changed for foreground service types in Android 14 API 34 ? How do you choose a type, and what breaks if you pick wrong? For apps targeting 34, every foreground service must declare at least one android:foregroundServiceType in the manifest and hold the matching FOREGROUND SERVICE <TYPE permission, and runtime-required permissions for the type location, camera, microphone must be granted before starting. Missing type throws MissingForegroundServiceTypeException ; wrong or missing permission throws SecurityException . Types are semantically chosen: mediaPlayback for playback, location for tracking, dataSync for transfers and that one gets timeouts on 15 , specialUse as an escape hatch requiring Play justification.

title: Background FGS start
text: Walk through diagnosis, fix, and prevention. A ride-hailing app has 3M DAU. After a release that moved a "driver location sharing" feature to a foreground service, Crashlytics shows a new top crash on Android 12+ devices only: 0.9% of sessions about 27k crashes/day . android.app.ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException: startForegroundService not allowed due to mAllowStartForeground false: service com.ride/.LocationShareService at android.app.ContextImpl.startForegroundServiceCommon at com.ride.push.RideFcmService.onMessageReceived RideFcmService.kt:41 The FCM payload is a data message with normal priority. The same code worked on API 26-30. Product says the feature is core. A red herring: the crash rate also correlates with Samsung devices, and the team suspects the OEM.

title: Android 15 FGS changes
text: What changed for foreground services in Android 15 API 35 ? Cover dataSync timeouts, BOOT COMPLETED restrictions, and what you must change in an app that targets 35. Android 15 adds a timeout to dataSync and the new mediaProcessing FGS types: roughly 6 hours in a rolling 24-hour window across the app. When the budget is hit the system calls Service.onTimeout startId, fgsType , and the service must stop quickly call stopSelf or the app gets an ANR-style failure. Also, BOOT COMPLETED receivers can no longer start certain FGS types dataSync, camera, mediaPlayback, mediaProjection, microphone, phoneCall . I would verify the exact lists on developer.android.com because they are per-targetSdk.

title: Process priority effect
text: How does a Service change the priority of its process? Compare a started service, a bound service, and a foreground service, and explain what actually gets killed under memory pressure. The OS ranks processes by importance and kills the least important when memory is low. A process with a started background service is above cached processes but below visible UI; a process bound by a foreground client inherits that client's importance; a foreground service raises the process to roughly perceptible/foreground level. Long-running started services also get demoted over time the old "service B" list after 30 min . Services therefore reduce, but do not eliminate, the chance of being killed.

title: Service vs WorkManager
text: Choose the mechanism for each feature and justify it. What are the failure modes of the engineer's proposal? You're designing three features for a note-taking app with 800k DAU: 1. Auto-backup of notes every night when charging and on Wi-Fi. 2. "Record voice memo" that must continue while the screen is off, with an on-screen timer. 3. Upload of a 500 MB attachment the user starts manually, taking up to 20 min on 4G. An engineer proposes one BackgroundService for all three. The target is API 34.

title: startForegroundService 5s timeout
text: Why does it crash, and how do you fix it? Crash dashboard after a release: 1.4% of sessions, concentrated on Android 11 and Android 13 low-end devices ≤3 GB RAM , spike during morning hours. android.app.ForegroundServiceDidNotStartInTimeException: Context.startForegroundService did not then call Service.startForeground : ServiceRecord{... com.fit/.WorkoutService} Code snippet: class WorkoutService : Service { override fun onCreate { super.onCreate Graph.init applicationContext // opens DB, loads 40 prefs } override fun onStartCommand i: Intent?, f: Int, id: Int : Int { if i?.action == "STOP" { stopSelf ; return START NOT STICKY } startForeground 1, buildNotification return START STICKY } } The widget "stop workout" button sends startForegroundService Intent "STOP" . Team suspicion: the notification channel is missing red herring; channel is created in Application .

title: Bound service leak
text: Find all leaks and fix the code. A navigation app shows steadily growing memory: LeakCanary reports MapActivity leaked after rotation 5 instances after 5 rotations , and logcat shows Activity com.nav.MapActivity has leaked ServiceConnection ... that was originally bound here . After 20 rotations on a 2 GB device the app OOMs. Code: class MapActivity : AppCompatActivity { private var svc: NavService? = null override fun onCreate b: Bundle? { super.onCreate b bindService Intent this, NavService::class.java , object : ServiceConnection { override fun onServiceConnected n: ComponentName, s: IBinder { svc = s as NavService.LocalBinder .service NavService.listener = { eta - findViewById<TextView R.id.eta .text = eta } } override fun onServiceDisconnected n: ComponentName { svc = null } }, Context.BIND AUTO CREATE } } class NavService : Service { companion object { var listener: String - Unit ? = null } // ... } Red herring: the team suspects the MapView native memory.

title: Swipe-from-recents, stopWithTask, restart backoff
text: What happens to your services when the user swipes the app away from Recents? Explain android:stopWithTask , onTaskRemoved , force stop, and the restart/backoff behavior for sticky services. Swiping the task from Recents removes the task; by default stopWithTask="true" the system stops services started by that task's app, but the process may still stay alive in a cached state on stock Android. With stopWithTask="false" the service keeps running and gets onTaskRemoved Intent . "Force stop" in Settings is different: it kills the process, clears started services, alarms, jobs, and blocks all broadcasts until the user opens the app again; no sticky restart. Some OEMs treat swipe as force stop.

title: Media playback FGS killed
text: How do you approach this, and what would you change as the app grows 10x in users? A music streaming app 5M DAU has a PlaybackService foreground service of type mediaPlayback . Support tickets: "music stops after 20-40 minutes with the screen off" 2.3% of sessions, 70% from one OEM's mid-range phones with 4 GB RAM, Android 13/14 . Crashlytics shows nothing: no crash, no ANR. Logcat captured from a tester: ActivityManager: Killing 12345:com.music/u0a210 adj 0 : excessive wakelocks / OEM power policy The message is OEM-specific. The app uses the old MediaSessionCompat and a custom notification. The team wants to "add START STICKY and a boot receiver" and 'ask users to turn off battery optimization.'

title: FGS notification behavior across releases
text: How has the foreground service notification behavior changed in Android 12, 13 and 14 deferred display, dismissibility, POST NOTIFICATIONS ? What do you do to keep it reliable? Android 12 can delay the FGS notification by about 10 seconds unless the service is of an exempt type or I call setForegroundServiceBehavior FOREGROUND SERVICE IMMEDIATE . Android 13 makes the FGS notification dismissible by the user except for exempt categories like media sessions and calls , and adds POST NOTIFICATIONS: without it the notification is hidden, but the service still runs and appears in the "Active apps" Task Manager. Android 14 requires the FGS type, which also affects how the system classifies and shows it.

title: IntentService migration
text: Plan the migration. A fintech app 2M MAU, API 24-35 supported still uses JobIntentService for four tasks: 1 sync transactions after push, 2 upload KYC photos up to 10 MB , 3 refresh tokens, 4 clear cache nightly. After the team raised targetSdk to 34, QA reports: sync after push sometimes doesn't run when the app is in the background; the KYC upload fails with 3% rate after app switch; crash reports show IllegalStateException: Not allowed to start service Intent from a legacy receiver. You must remove the deprecated class without breaking live traffic: the release train is weekly with 10% staged rollout, and there are in-flight uploads from the previous version.

title: Ambiguous requirement
text: How do you turn this requirement into a design? What would you ask product, and what would you build? Product writes: "Our delivery partners must be tracked continuously while on a delivery, even if the app is closed. We must also know when they stop for more than 10 minutes." Fleet: 120k partners, 70% mid-range Android 11-14, 15% Xiaomi/Oppo. Constraints: battery drain target <5%/hour, Play policy, privacy review, location updates every 10 s while moving. Past attempt: a started service with START STICKY lost location after 15 minutes for 25% of partners.

title: Receiver registration
text: What is the difference between a manifest-declared receiver and a context-registered receiver, and how do you choose between them? A manifest receiver is declared statically, so the system can create my process and deliver a broadcast even if the app is not running. A context-registered receiver lives only while the registering component lives, so I must call registerReceiver and unregisterReceiver . Since API 26 most implicit broadcasts can only reach context-registered receivers, so I default to dynamic registration and keep manifest receivers for the small exempt list like BOOT COMPLETED or for explicit broadcasts.

title: ContentProvider basics
text: What is a ContentProvider, how does a client talk to it, and what does a content URI look like? A ContentProvider is a component that exposes structured data behind a URI and a CRUD-like interface query , insert , update , delete , getType . Clients never get the provider object, they use ContentResolver with a content://authority/path/id URI. The call crosses a Binder boundary, so it works across processes and apps, and access is controlled by manifest permissions and URI grants.

title: Implicit broadcast limits
text: What are the implicit broadcast restrictions introduced in Android 8.0, and how do they affect an app that listens for CONNECTIVITY ACTION or PACKAGE ADDED in its manifest? For apps targeting API 26 or higher, a manifest receiver can no longer receive most implicit broadcasts, meaning those that are not addressed to the app's package or component. There is a short exempt list, such as BOOT COMPLETED and LOCALE CHANGED . Everything else I register at runtime while a component is alive, or I switch to a purpose-built API such as ConnectivityManager.NetworkCallback or JobScheduler / WorkManager constraints.

title: Exported flags and RECEIVER_EXPORTED
text: What are the android:exported requirement Android 12 and the RECEIVER EXPORTED / RECEIVER NOT EXPORTED requirement for dynamically registered receivers Android 13/14 ? If I target API 31+, every activity, service or receiver with an intent filter must declare android:exported explicitly, otherwise the install fails. For context-registered receivers, the RECEIVER EXPORTED / RECEIVER NOT EXPORTED flags exist from API 33, and when I target API 34+ I must pass one of them for any non-system broadcast or registerReceiver throws SecurityException . I use ContextCompat.registerReceiver so older API levels also work.

title: Ordered, sticky and local broadcasts
text: Explain ordered, sticky and local broadcasts. Which ones should you still use today? Normal broadcasts go to all receivers in no defined order. Ordered ones sendOrderedBroadcast are delivered one receiver at a time by priority, and each can modify the result or abort it. Sticky broadcasts stay cached so late registrants get the last value; sendStickyBroadcast is deprecated since API 21, though reading ACTION BATTERY CHANGED that way still works. LocalBroadcastManager is deprecated too; in-process events should be a SharedFlow / StateFlow or observable.

title: goAsync and receiver timeouts
text: How long can onReceive run, what does goAsync change, and what should you do for work that takes longer? onReceive runs on the main thread and the broadcast is considered done when it returns. The system budget is on the order of 10 seconds for foreground-priority broadcasts and 60 for background ones, after which an ANR is raised. goAsync returns a PendingResult so I can finish on another thread, but it does not extend the budget meaningfully. For anything real I enqueue WorkManager or start a foreground service and return immediately.

title: BOOT_COMPLETED
text: Why might the boot broadcast not work for these users and how would you fix and verify it? A reminders app 800k DAU, 70% Samsung/Xiaomi/Oppo re-schedules alarms in a receiver on BOOT COMPLETED . After the release that targets API 34, support tickets say reminders vanish after reboot for about 12% of users. The manifest is below, there is no crash. Logcat on a Pixel emulator shows the receiver fires; on a Xiaomi test phone it never does. <receiver android:name=".BootReceiver" <intent-filter <action android:name="android.intent.action.BOOT COMPLETED"/ </intent-filter </receiver The receiver reads credentials from credential-encrypted storage and calls AlarmManager.setExactAndAllowWhileIdle .

title: FileProvider
text: Why can't you share a file:// URI with another app on modern Android, and how does FileProvider solve it? Since API 24, passing a file:// URI outside the app throws FileUriExposedException for apps targeting 24+, because the receiver would need raw filesystem access to my private storage. FileProvider is a ContentProvider subclass that maps a file to a content:// URI and lets me grant temporary read/write permission to just the receiving app via FLAG GRANT READ URI PERMISSION .

title: FileProvider exposure
text: What is wrong, how would an attacker exploit it, and how would you fix it? A security scan of a banking-lite app 1.2M MAU flags that another installed app can read internal files. The team uses FileProvider to share statement PDFs. Code review finds: <provider android:name="androidx.core.content.FileProvider" android:authorities="com.bank.lite.fp" android:exported="true" android:grantUriPermissions="true" <meta-data android:name="android.support.FILE PROVIDER PATHS" android:resource="@xml/paths"/ </provider <paths <root-path name="all" path="."/ </paths and fun shareStatement ctx: Context, name: String { val f = File ctx.filesDir, "statements/$name" // name comes from a deep link query param val uri = FileProvider.getUriForFile ctx, "com.bank.lite.fp", f ctx.startActivity Intent Intent.ACTION VIEW, uri .addFlags Intent.FLAG GRANT READ URI PERMISSION } Logcat on a test device shows: java.lang.SecurityException: Provider must not be exported on API 34 after a FileProvider update.

title: Provider init order
text: In what order do Application.attachBaseContext , ContentProvider onCreate and Application.onCreate run, and why does it matter? The Application object is created and attachBaseContext runs first, then the system installs all the app's ContentProviders in the process calling their onCreate , and only then Application.onCreate runs. So providers initialize before my Application code, on the main thread, adding to cold start. Libraries like Firebase and WorkManager used this to self-initialize, and AndroidX App Startup consolidates it in one provider.

title: Provider permissions and URI grants
text: How do ContentProvider permissions work: readPermission , writePermission , path-permission and grantUriPermissions ? An exported provider can require a permission for reading and another for writing, and path-permission can override these per path. Callers who lack the permission can still be granted temporary access to a specific URI if the provider allows grantUriPermissions , either globally or only for <grant-uri-permission paths. The grant is passed with FLAG GRANT READ/WRITE URI PERMISSION on an Intent, and the system enforces it on each Binder call.

title: Exported component security
text: What are the main security risks of exported components activities, services, receivers, providers , and how would you audit an app for them? Any exported component is a public API that any installed app can call with attacker-controlled input. Typical bugs are an exported activity that forwards a nested Intent intent redirection , an exported service acting on unvalidated extras, an exported receiver trusting a sender, and an exported provider with SQL injection or path traversal. I audit the merged manifest, treat each exported=true as a boundary, require a signature permission when a caller is known, and validate every input.

title: Dynamic receiver leak
text: Find all the bugs and give the fix. A news app's crash dashboard 2.5M sessions/day shows two issues after a refactor: IllegalArgumentException: Receiver not registered: ...ConnectivityFragment$receiver$1 0.4% of sessions and LeakCanary reports a leaked MainActivity retained by a ConnectivityFragment . Code: class ConnectivityFragment : Fragment R.layout.fragment conn { private val receiver = object : BroadcastReceiver { override fun onReceive c: Context, i: Intent { banner.isVisible = !isOnline c } } override fun onViewCreated view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle? { requireActivity .registerReceiver receiver, IntentFilter ConnectivityManager.CONNECTIVITY ACTION } override fun onDestroy { requireActivity .unregisterReceiver receiver super.onDestroy } } Crash happens mostly on rotation and back navigation; the app targets API 34.

title: LocalBroadcastManager migration
text: How would you migrate, what would you replace it with, and how do you do it safely? A 12-year-old app 4M DAU, 40 modules uses LocalBroadcastManager in 130 places for events like ACTION CART UPDATED , ACTION LOGOUT , ACTION SYNC DONE . The library is deprecated, and there are two incidents per quarter caused by missed events when an Activity is stopped receiver unregistered in onPause , plus an ANR path where an onReceive runs a DB query. Release cadence is weekly with staged rollouts; the team of 6 has one quarter. ACTION LOGOUT must reach three process-wide listeners including a Service .

title: ContentObserver and Cursor transport
text: How do change notifications work for ContentProviders notifyChange , ContentObserver , setNotificationUri , and how does a Cursor actually travel across processes? The provider calls ContentResolver.notifyChange uri, null after a write. The system's content service dispatches that to every registered ContentObserver whose URI matches, and cursors that called setNotificationUri are told to requery or mark themselves stale. Cursor data moves through a CursorWindow in shared memory, with the Binder only carrying the window handle and small control calls; rows are filled in chunks, and a window is about 2 MB by default.

title: Receiver ANR
text: Walk me through diagnosis and the fix. A fintech app 600k DAU sees ANR rate rise from 0.25% to 0.9% after release 8.12 Play bad-behaviour threshold is 0.47% user-perceived ANRs . Crashlytics/Play Console ANR clusters: "main" prio=5 tid=1 Native at android.database.sqlite.SQLiteConnection.nativeExecute at com.app.sync.SyncDao.insertAll SyncDao.kt:48 at com.app.sync.NetworkReceiver.onReceive NetworkReceiver.kt:31 at android.app.ActivityThread.handleReceiver ActivityThread.java:4xxx Reason: Broadcast of Intent { act=android.net.conn.CONNECTIVITY CHANGE flg=0x... cmp=com.app/.NetworkReceiver } The receiver is context-registered in Application.onCreate , so it is always alive. It is hit by 60 broadcasts/day per user on mobile networks. ANRs concentrate on devices with 2-3 GB RAM and users coming out of a lift/tunnel.

title: Provider security audit
text: Do a post-incident review: how did this get exploited, why does the manifest above matter, and what do you change? A note-taking app 3M installs receives a bug-bounty report: a malicious app, with no permissions, reads any user's notes and also reads shared prefs/auth.xml from the notes app's private storage. The app's provider, unchanged since 2014: <provider android:name=".NotesProvider" android:authorities="com.notes.provider"/ class NotesProvider : ContentProvider { override fun query uri: Uri, proj: Array<String ?, sel: String?, args: Array<String ?, sort: String? : Cursor? { val q = "SELECT FROM notes WHERE owner = '" + uri.getQueryParameter "user" + "'" return db.readableDatabase.rawQuery q, null } override fun openFile uri: Uri, mode: String : ParcelFileDescriptor? { val f = File context!!.filesDir, uri.lastPathSegment!! return ParcelFileDescriptor.open f, ParcelFileDescriptor.parseMode mode } // insert/update/delete omitted } The manifest merger report shows minSdk 21, targetSdk 33 . The app has no exported attribute on the provider.

title: Provider vs alternatives
text: When would you actually write your own ContentProvider, and when would you use MediaStore, the Storage Access Framework or a DocumentsProvider instead? I write a ContentProvider only when I must expose data or files to other apps or system features through a stable URI, such as FileProvider, search suggestions, a sync adapter or a widget data source. For private in-app data I use Room and a repository. For user media I use MediaStore; for user-chosen documents I use the Storage Access Framework; and if I want my app's files to appear in the system file picker as a storage backend, I implement a DocumentsProvider .

title: Explicit vs implicit intents
text: What is the difference between an explicit and an implicit intent, and when do you use each? An explicit intent names the exact target component class or package plus class , so the system skips resolution and delivers straight to it. An implicit intent only describes an action and data, and the system matches it against intent filters of installed apps. I use explicit for anything inside my own app, and implicit only when I want any capable app to handle it, such as ACTION VIEW or ACTION SEND.

title: Intent filters and resolution
text: How does the system resolve an implicit intent against intent filters? What are the three tests, and why is CATEGORY DEFAULT important? The intent must pass three tests against a filter: action, category, and data URI and MIME type . Action: the intent's action must be in the filter's list. Category: every category on the intent must be declared in the filter. Data: scheme/host/port/path and MIME type must match. For startActivity the system adds CATEGORY DEFAULT to the intent, so an activity must declare android.intent.category.DEFAULT to be reachable implicitly.

title: Intent extras and Bundle limits
text: How do intent extras work internally, what types can they hold, and what are the size limits? Extras live in a Bundle a typed key-value map backed by a Parcel . When the Intent crosses to another process it is parceled and sent through Binder, whose per-process transaction buffer is about 1 MB shared across all in-flight transactions. So extras should be small IDs or tiny values; large payloads go through a repository, file, or content URI.

title: Parcelable vs Serializable
text: Parcelable vs Serializable for passing objects in Intents: why is Parcelable preferred, and how do you implement it in Kotlin safely? Serializable uses reflection and creates lots of temporary objects, so it is slower and heavier on GC. Parcelable is Android's explicit, reflection-free IPC format, designed for Binder. In Kotlin I use @Parcelize from kotlin-parcelize so I do not hand-write writeToParcel . But Parcelable is not stable storage: never persist it, because the format can change between OS versions.

title: Package visibility (API 30)
text: What is package visibility in Android 11, what does <queries do, and which APIs does it affect? From Android 11 API 30 , apps targeting API 30+ can only see a filtered list of other installed apps. To see more I declare <queries in the manifest with specific packages, intent filters, or providers. It affects queryIntentActivities , resolveActivity , getPackageInfo , getInstalledApplications , getLaunchIntentForPackage ; they return empty or throw NameNotFoundException for invisible apps. Blindly adding QUERY ALL PACKAGES is restricted by Play policy.

title: android:exported
text: What does android:exported control, and what changed in Android 12 API 31 ? exported says whether components from other apps can start or bind to this component. If targeting API 31+, I must set android:exported explicitly on every activity, service, and receiver that has an <intent-filter , or the build and install fail. The old default true when a filter exists was a footgun, so Android removed the default.

title: PendingIntent identity
text: Find the bug, explain the mechanics, and fix it. A food-delivery app shows one notification per active order 5-10 per user at peak, about 1.2M DAU . Tapping a notification should open OrderActivity for that order. QA reports that "tapping any notification always opens the first order". The code: fun notify ctx: Context, order: Order { val intent = Intent ctx, OrderActivity::class.java .putExtra "orderId", order.id val pi = PendingIntent.getActivity ctx, 0, intent, PendingIntent.FLAG IMMUTABLE val n = NotificationCompat.Builder ctx, "orders" .setContentTitle "Order ${order.id}" .setSmallIcon R.drawable.ic stat .setContentIntent pi .setAutoCancel true .build NotificationManagerCompat.from ctx .notify order.id.toInt , n } Logs show correct notify ids, but OrderActivity.onCreate always receives the first orderId. It reproduces only after two or more orders are posted.

title: PendingIntent mutability flags
text: What is a PendingIntent, and what do FLAG IMMUTABLE and FLAG MUTABLE mean? What changed in API 31 and API 34? A PendingIntent is a token that lets another process NotificationManager, AlarmManager, a widget host run an Intent later, with my app's identity and permissions. FLAG IMMUTABLE means the receiver cannot fill in or change the Intent's fields; FLAG MUTABLE allows fillIn . Targeting API 31+, I must specify one of them or it throws. I default to IMMUTABLE and use MUTABLE only when the system must add data, like inline reply. On API 34, a mutable PendingIntent wrapping an implicit Intent no component/package throws.

title: PendingIntent hijack
text: How can a PendingIntent be abused, and how do you build one safely? A PendingIntent runs with my app's identity. If it is mutable and the base Intent is empty or implicit, whoever receives it can fill in the target component and make my app launch or broadcast to something I never intended, including non-exported components or permission-protected ones. So: explicit component, immutable by default, never hand a PendingIntent to untrusted code, and be careful about what I put in extras.

title: Intent redirection
text: What is an intent redirection vulnerability? Show how it arises in an exported component and how you prevent it. It occurs when an exported component takes an Intent from an untrusted extra and launches it with my app's identity. The attacker packs a nested Intent aimed at one of my private, non-exported components or a protected one , and my app starts it for them. Fix: do not launch attacker-supplied Intents; build my own from validated fields, and if I must, check the resolved component is allowed.

title: Chooser and share sheet
text: How do you implement sharing correctly with ACTION SEND and the system chooser? How do you share a file securely, and how does your app appear as a share target? I build an ACTION SEND Intent with a MIME type and EXTRA TEXT or EXTRA STREAM , wrap it in Intent.createChooser or ShareCompat.IntentBuilder , and start it. For files I never use file:// URIs; I use a FileProvider content URI with FLAG GRANT READ URI PERMISSION and ClipData. To receive shares, I declare an exported activity with an ACTION SEND filter and publish sharing shortcuts for Direct Share.

title: App Links verification
text: At the intent level, how does an HTTPS link open your app directly without a disambiguation dialog? How does verification work, and why does it fail? I declare an intent filter with autoVerify="true" , ACTION VIEW , DEFAULT , BROWSABLE , and http / https scheme with the host. The system downloads https://host/.well-known/assetlinks.json , and checks that it lists my package name and signing certificate SHA-256. If verified, links to that host open my app directly. Otherwise the user sees a chooser Android 6-11 or the link opens in the browser Android 12+ .

title: PendingIntent flags
text: Walk me through diagnosis and the fix, and how you decide what to do about the second crash. Release 6.12 of a ride-hailing app 9M MAU, 94% on Android 10-14 raises targetSdk 33 to 34. Within an hour Crashlytics shows a new top crash at 1.9% of sessions, almost entirely during ride start: java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: android.app.PendingIntent: com.example.rides: Targeting U+ version 34 and above disallows creating or retrieving a PendingIntent with FLAG MUTABLE, an implicit Intent within and without FLAG NO CREATE and FLAG ALLOW UNSAFE IMPLICIT INTENT for security reasons. at android.app.PendingIntent.checkFlags PendingIntent.java at com.example.rides.tracking.NotificationFactory.buildReply NotificationFactory.kt:88 Staged rollout is at 20%. Crash-free rate dropped from 99.6% to 98.4%. Another smaller crash shows SecurityException: Starting FGS ... , which began in the same release.

title: Extras and Binder limits
text: Explain the failure and propose a fix that survives process death. A photo-editor app 1.1M DAU passes selected media between screens. Crash reports: 0.9% of sessions on low-RAM devices 2-3 GB after the user selects around 150 photos and switches to another app and back. java.lang.RuntimeException: android.os.TransactionTooLargeException: data parcel size 1048252 bytes at android.app.servertransaction.TransactionExecutor.execute Caused by: android.os.TransactionTooLargeException Code: class GalleryActivity : AppCompatActivity { private var selected = ArrayList<MediaItem // MediaItem: Parcelable, 6 KB each thumb bytes inside override fun onSaveInstanceState out: Bundle { super.onSaveInstanceState out out.putParcelableArrayList "sel", selected } fun openEditor = startActivity Intent this, EditorActivity::class.java .putParcelableArrayListExtra "items", selected } The adb test with 20 photos never crashes. Another team suspects a Fragment leak red herring .

title: Intent redirection
text: How do you respond: triage, fix without breaking partners, and prevention? A fintech app 3M MAU receives a pentest report: "High: Intent redirection in AuthBridgeActivity ". Play Console also shows a security warning on the latest release. The activity is used by the partner SDK to hand over from a bank's app after login: class AuthBridgeActivity : AppCompatActivity { // exported=true, filter: com.fin.action.AUTH DONE override fun onCreate s: Bundle? { super.onCreate s val token = intent.getStringExtra "token" session.store token val next = intent.getParcelableExtra<Intent "redirect" // deprecated getter if next != null startActivity next finish } } The partner app 4 bank apps, 600k installs combined depends on redirect to resume a flow. A 2-week release freeze starts in 3 days. The pentester's PoC opened the internal, non-exported ExportStatementsActivity .

title: Package visibility
text: Diagnose, mitigate, and describe a fix that is Play-policy compliant. A super-app 6M DAU raises targetSdk 29 to 33 in one jump. Within two days of staged rollout at 50%, support tickets spike: "Pay with UPI app button missing", "cannot open Maps", "Invite via WhatsApp does nothing". Crash rate is flat at 0.3%, but UPI payment conversion on Android 11+ falls from 61% to 38%. The UPI code: val upi = Intent Intent.ACTION VIEW, Uri.parse "upi://pay?pa=$vpa&am=$amt" val apps = pm.queryIntentActivities upi, 0 // shows installed UPI apps as buttons if apps.isEmpty showCardOnly and getPackageInfo "com.whatsapp", 0 wrapped in try/catch returning false. Android 10 and below show no regression 35% of base .

title: Share target and exported surface
text: Design the intent-facing layer: components, filters, validation, and what you refuse to support. Your notes app 2M MAU wants to be a share target for text, images, and PDFs from any app, and to handle "Open with" for .md files. Product also wants a custom notes://new?title= scheme for automation apps. Security wants a minimal attack surface after last quarter's redirection finding. Constraints: images up to 25 MB, p95 share-to-editor under 400 ms on mid-range devices, Android 8 API 26 to 15.

title: App Links in production
text: Give your root-cause analysis and what you change in process and code. Post-incident review for a retail app 4M MAU . Last Tuesday an email campaign sent 2.4M links https://shop.example/p/123 . Expected: 35% open in the app. Measured: 4% on Android 12+, 31% on Android 10-11, and Chrome on iOS fine. No release shipped that week. Two days before, infra moved shop.example behind a CDN that now redirects /.well-known/assetlinks.json with a 302 to a regional path. Support also sees "Open with" chooser dialogs on old devices. The product manager asks whether to "just add a custom scheme."

title: Task and back stack model
text: What is a "task" in Android, and how does it relate to the back stack and to the process? Can one app have several tasks, and can one task hold activities from several apps? A task is a stack of activities the user experiences as one unit of work, and the back stack is that stack: last in, first out. A task is a UI/navigation concept owned by the system server ATMS , not a process. One app can have several tasks, and a task can contain activities from different apps, for example my app launches the system share sheet or a camera activity into the same task, and Back returns through them in order.

title: launchMode standard and singleTop
text: What are standard and singleTop launch modes? What happens when I start an activity that is already on top of the stack in each mode? In standard every startActivity creates a new instance on top of the caller's task, even if the same class is already on top. In singleTop , if an instance of that activity is already at the top of the task, the system does not create a new one; it delivers the new Intent to the existing instance via onNewIntent . If the instance exists but is not on top, singleTop behaves like standard and creates a new one.

title: launchMode singleTask
text: How does singleTask differ from singleTop ? What happens to the activities above an existing singleTask instance? singleTask means one instance of the activity in the system for its affinity's task. If it already exists, the system brings its task to the foreground, finishes every activity above it, and delivers the intent through onNewIntent . If it does not exist, it creates it in the task matching its affinity, becoming the root if a new task had to be created. Unlike singleTop , it does not care whether the instance is on top, and it clears what is above.

title: Back handling APIs
text: onBackPressed is deprecated. What replaces it, and why was it replaced? Activity.onBackPressed is deprecated from API 33. The replacement is OnBackPressedDispatcher from androidx.activity 1.0+ , which I use through onBackPressedDispatcher.addCallback owner { ... } with an OnBackPressedCallback . It was replaced because the old model is a synchronous "the user pressed back, do whatever" call that the system cannot predict, so it cannot animate or cancel the back gesture; predictive back needs a registered, enableable callback the system can query before the gesture finishes.

title: singleInstance and singleInstancePerTask
text: What are singleInstance and singleInstancePerTask ? When would you ever use them? singleInstance makes the activity the only member of its own task: it is always the root and nothing else ever joins that task; anything it starts goes to another task. singleInstancePerTask API 31 is like singleTask , but allows multiple instances if they live in different tasks for example with FLAG ACTIVITY MULTIPLE TASK or NEW DOCUMENT ; within one task there is only one. I use them rarely: launcher-like or overlay-like hosts, picture-in-picture host, or per-document tasks on large screens.

title: Intent flags for tasks
text: Explain FLAG ACTIVITY NEW TASK , FLAG ACTIVITY CLEAR TOP , FLAG ACTIVITY SINGLE TOP and FLAG ACTIVITY CLEAR TASK . How do they combine, and which combinations are valid? NEW TASK starts the activity in a task matching its affinity it does not always make a brand-new task; it reuses a matching one . CLEAR TOP brings an existing instance to the top and finishes everything above it. SINGLE TOP is the per-call version of singleTop. CLEAR TASK empties the whole task before the activity starts, and is only valid together with NEW TASK . A typical logout is NEW TASK CLEAR TASK ; "go back to Home screen" is CLEAR TOP SINGLE TOP .

title: onNewIntent handling
text: When is onNewIntent called, where does it sit in the lifecycle, and how do you handle it correctly? onNewIntent is called on an existing instance when it is re-targeted instead of re-created: singleTop on top, singleTask/singleInstance, or CLEAR TOP/SINGLE TOP flags. If the activity was in the background, the order is onNewIntent → onRestart → onStart → onResume ; if resumed, only onNewIntent . I always call setIntent intent , reset any per-request state, and route through one shared handler used by onCreate as well.

title: onNewIntent
text: What is wrong, how would you reproduce it, and what is the right fix? A food-delivery app 1.4M DAU has OrderTrackingActivity with launchMode="singleTop" . Push notifications deep link to it with an orderId extra. QA reports: when a user has order 1001 open and taps a notification for order 1002, the title changes to 1002 but the map and ETA still show 1001; after rotating, it jumps back to 1001. Crash rate is unchanged, so it was triaged as cosmetic. Here is the code: class OrderTrackingActivity : AppCompatActivity { private val vm: TrackingViewModel by viewModels override fun onCreate savedInstanceState: Bundle? { super.onCreate savedInstanceState setContentView R.layout.activity tracking vm.load intent.getStringExtra "orderId" !! } override fun onNewIntent intent: Intent { super.onNewIntent intent title = "Order " + intent.getStringExtra "orderId" } override fun onResume { super.onResume analytics.track "order viewed", intent.getStringExtra "orderId" } }

title: taskAffinity
text: What is taskAffinity , what is its default, and what do allowTaskReparenting and taskAffinity="" do? taskAffinity is a string saying which task an activity prefers to live in. The default is the application's package name or the taskAffinity set on <application , so by default all activities share one affinity and one task. It only matters in two cases: when the activity is launched with NEW TASK the system finds a task with a matching affinity or creates one and when allowTaskReparenting is true the activity can move to its affinity's task later . Setting taskAffinity="" gives the activity no affinity.

title: TaskStackBuilder and notification navigation
text: How do you make a notification tap open a deep screen with a sensible Back history? What does TaskStackBuilder do and what does it require? For an activity that is part of the normal app flow I build a PendingIntent with TaskStackBuilder , using addNextIntentWithParentStack intent . It reads each activity's android:parentActivityName from the manifest, adds the whole parent chain, and starts it as a new task, so Back goes Detail → parent → … → Home rather than exiting the app. For a "special" activity that only exists via the notification, I use a plain PendingIntent with a separate task NEW TASK + CLEAR TASK .

title: Notification back stack
text: Walk me through diagnosis and the fix. A messaging app 800K DAU, targetSdk 34 receives reports that tapping a chat notification opens the conversation, but pressing Back closes the app instead of showing the chat list about 12% of notification taps, 3.1 stars in the last release notes . Crashlytics is clean. In the latest release the team replaced TaskStackBuilder with a simple PendingIntent.getActivity ..., ChatActivity to "reduce complexity". Another change in the same release: ChatListActivity now declares taskAffinity="" to avoid a duplicate Recents card. Some users also say that when they were typing a message in the app and tapped a notification for another chat, the draft vanished.

title: OnBackPressedCallback
text: Why does Back do nothing on the Home tab, and how do you fix it? A single-activity app 2.2M DAU uses show/hide fragment transactions for its 4 bottom tabs to keep scroll position. CartFragment handles Back to close an expanded bottom sheet. After a refactor, users on the Home tab report that Back does nothing for several taps until it finally exits about 1 in 20 sessions, mostly users who visited Cart earlier . No crash, no ANR. Code: class CartFragment : Fragment R.layout.fragment cart { override fun onCreate savedInstanceState: Bundle? { super.onCreate savedInstanceState requireActivity .onBackPressedDispatcher.addCallback this { sheet.collapse // runs even when sheet is already collapsed } } } Navigation to tabs is done with supportFragmentManager.beginTransaction .hide current .show next .commit .

title: Root activity back behavior (Android 12)
text: On Android 12 and above, pressing Back on the last launcher activity no longer destroys it. What exactly changed, and what code does it break? Since Android 12 API 31 , when the user presses Back on a root launcher activity the only activity in its task, with a MAIN/LAUNCHER intent filter , the system moves the task to the background instead of finishing the activity, so the activity goes to onStop and stays alive in memory like a Home press. This applies to all apps on Android 12+, regardless of targetSdk, unless the app overrides back handling. Code that assumed Back = onDestroy ending sessions, stopping players, clearing state stops running.

title: Recents screen controls
text: How do you control what appears in Recents? When would you use excludeFromRecents , autoRemoveFromRecents , finishAndRemoveTask , or documentLaunchMode ? Recents shows tasks, so these controls apply per task via its root activity. android:excludeFromRecents="true" keeps the task out of Recents useful for short-lived pickers, share receivers, or overlays . autoRemoveFromRecents removes the entry when its last activity finishes. finishAndRemoveTask finishes the task and removes its card. documentLaunchMode lets one activity produce multiple Recents entries one per document , implemented with NEW DOCUMENT and MULTIPLE TASK .

title: Logout and CLEAR_TASK
text: What were the causes, what did we ship, and how do we prevent recurrence? A fintech app 1.1M DAU had a privacy incident: after Logout, pressing Back showed the previous user's account screen for about 0.3% of logouts roughly 3,000 per day . Another group reported that after logging out and signing in as a different user, a stale "Statements" screen from the first user was visible in Recents. The logout code: fun logout { session.clear startActivity Intent this, LoginActivity::class.java .addFlags Intent.FLAG ACTIVITY CLEAR TASK finish } StatementsActivity is opened from push notifications and from the share sheet via TaskStackBuilder , and has taskAffinity=".statements" so it appears as its own card. A security review is asking for a post-incident report.

title: Predictive back
text: Explain predictive back: how do you opt in, what changes for your code, and how has enforcement changed from Android 13 to 16? Predictive back lets the user peek at the destination during the back gesture and cancel it. It requires callbacks registered ahead of time rather than an after-the-fact onBackPressed . I opt in with android:enableOnBackInvokedCallback="true" application or per activity , register OnBackPressedCallback s, and for custom animations implement progress callbacks handleOnBackStarted/Progressed/Cancelled , AndroidX Activity 1.6+ . It began as a developer-option preview on Android 13 API 33 , got in-app and cross-activity/task animations on 14, and the system animations moved out of developer options on 15. For apps targeting Android 16 API 36 the behavior is on by default and legacy onBackPressed /KEYCODE BACK callbacks are no longer invoked; verify details and opt-out status on developer.android.com.

title: Activity transitions
text: What are the options for animating between activities, and what changed with overridePendingTransition in recent releases? Name the common pitfalls with shared element transitions. There are three layers: simple enter/exit animations overridePendingTransition , deprecated in API 34 in favor of overrideActivityTransition OVERRIDE TRANSITION OPEN/CLOSE, enter, exit , window content transitions Material container transform / fade , and shared element transitions using ActivityOptions.makeSceneTransitionAnimation . Predictive back's cross-activity animation uses the system's own transition and can conflict with custom ones, so on newer releases I'd prefer theme-defined or Material transitions.

title: Deep links and duplicate activities
text: How do you diagnose and fix this? A marketplace app 3M DAU sends product links in emails and WhatsApp shares. ProductActivity is standard . Analytics shows 4.5% of deep-link sessions end up with the same product screen stacked 2-3 times; Back from the last one shows the same product again, and users abandon bounce up 6 points on those sessions . Memory warnings also rise on low-end 2 GB devices because each product screen holds a gallery. Intent filter has autoVerify app links. Android Studio's Navigation graph is used inside the Product flow. Red herrings reported: "only on Android 13", "only when the app was already open", "happens more after the new image carousel".

title: How the system picks a task
text: Describe how the system decides which task and which instance to use when I call startActivity . Walk through the decision for launchMode, flags and affinity. The ActivityTaskManager ActivityStarter merges the target's launchMode and the intent flags into one effective set of launch flags, then decides: does this launch need a new task NEW TASK, singleTask, singleInstance, or a non-activity caller ? If so, it looks for an existing task with a matching affinity or root intent; if none, it creates one. Within the chosen task it applies instance rules: singleTop top only , singleTask / CLEAR TOP find existing, clear above, deliver onNewIntent , CLEAR TASK empty first , else create a new instance on top.

title: Choosing launch modes for multi-entry apps
text: Pick a design and defend the trade-offs. You are the tech lead for a social app 6M DAU moving from 14 activities to one MainActivity hosting Compose Navigation. Entry points: launcher, push notifications 5 types , deep links from web, a share target images and text , app shortcuts, and a home-screen widget. Requirements from product: 1 tapping a notification never throws away the user's in-progress compose screen without warning; 2 Back from a share target returns to the app that shared; 3 deep links always land on the right screen with a sensible Back path; 4 no duplicate Main in Recents. Today, Main is standard . Some teammates want singleTask , others singleTop .

title: Predictive back migration
text: Plan the migration without hurting live users. A travel app 4M DAU, 60% on Android 13+ has 9 activities overriding onBackPressed , 14 fragments with custom Back logic, three third-party SDK activities, and a custom dispatchKeyEvent in a base class that intercepts KEYCODE BACK for analytics. Product wants predictive back animations before targeting API 36. Last attempt to flip enableOnBackInvokedCallback="true" on the application in a beta caused: payment confirmation dialog not showing 0.8% of payment attempts failed to confirm in the beta cohort of 20K , Back doing nothing in a map screen, and an analytics drop of Back events by 100%. Release train is every 2 weeks; you cannot pause features.

title: Launcher duplicates
text: Explain the mechanism, fix it, and say how you would validate. After a new release, support gets reports that "the app opens twice": after installing from the store and tapping Open, then pressing Home and tapping the launcher icon, users see a second copy of the splash/login screen, and pressing Back shows the first one. Crash-free rate is 99.7%, nothing in logs. It reproduces on 8% of installs, mostly through sideloaded APKs and some OEM installers, rarely from Play. SplashActivity is the launcher activity and launchMode is standard . Product notes: "we turned on Android 12 root-back last week", which is likely unrelated.

title: App heap limit
text: Why does an Android app get an OutOfMemoryError when the phone still has gigabytes of free RAM? How do you find out your app's heap limit at runtime? Every app process gets a hard cap on its managed ART Java heap, set per device by system properties, not by free RAM. When the heap hits that cap and a GC can't free enough, ART throws OutOfMemoryError even if the device has plenty free. I read it with ActivityManager.getMemoryClass MB or Runtime.getRuntime .maxMemory bytes . It is typically 128 to 512 MB on modern phones and much lower on old or low-RAM devices, so I never hardcode sizes.

title: largeHeap
text: What does android:largeHeap="true" actually do, and when would you refuse to add it in a code review? largeHeap asks the system to use the larger dalvik.vm.heapsize cap instead of heapgrowthlimit for my process's Java heap. It is a request, not a guarantee, and on many devices the two values are equal. The costs are longer GC cycles on a bigger heap and a larger footprint that makes my process a better LMK victim. I only accept it for apps with a genuinely huge working set, such as a photo or video editor, and only after profiling shows the memory is justified.

title: Memory categories
text: Name the different kinds of memory an Android app process uses, and which of them are limited by the Java heap cap. A process has the ART Java heap my objects, capped , the native heap malloc, C++ libraries, and bitmap pixels from 8.0 , graphics memory GPU textures, surface buffers, hardware bitmaps , code mapped dex, oat/vdex, .so files , thread stacks, and other mmapped files. Only the Java heap has the per-app cap. The whole process is still subject to device pressure and LMK.

title: Bitmap memory
text: How much memory does a decoded bitmap take, and where does that memory live? Why can a 200 KB JPEG blow up a low-end phone? Memory is width x height x bytes per pixel , independent of file size. ARGB 8888 is 4 bytes per pixel, so a 4000x3000 photo is 12,000,000 x 4 = 48,000,000 bytes, about 45.8 MiB, even if the JPEG file is 2 MB. From Android 8.0 the pixel buffer is in native memory tracked so GC still reacts ; on 3.0 to 7.1 it was in the Java heap. Drawable resources can also be scaled up by density at decode time.

title: onTrimMemory
text: Explain onTrimMemory levels. What should an app actually release at each level, and how is it different from onLowMemory ? onTrimMemory level is a ComponentCallbacks2 hint from the system that it wants processes to shed memory. TRIM MEMORY UI HIDDEN 20 means my UI is no longer visible, so I drop view-related caches. The RUNNING levels 5, 10, 15 say I'm still in the foreground but the device is getting tight. The BACKGROUND/MODERATE/COMPLETE levels 40, 60, 80 say I'm cached and how close I am to being killed. It's advisory; LMK may kill me anyway. onLowMemory is the older coarse version, roughly the "complete" case.

title: PSS, RSS, USS in meminfo
text: In dumpsys meminfo , what do PSS, RSS, Private Dirty and USS mean, and which one do you trust to decide whether your app is "too big"? RSS counts every resident page the process maps, including pages shared with other processes, so it over-counts. PSS proportional set size divides shared pages among the processes that share them, so summing PSS across processes works. USS unique set size is only the private pages, which is what would be freed if the process died. For "how much does my app really cost", I use PSS for comparison and Private Dirty/USS for "what would a kill reclaim".

title: ART garbage collection basics
text: How does garbage collection work on modern Android ART ? What do the GC lines in logcat tell you, and when does GC actually hurt the UI? ART uses a mostly concurrent, compacting collector concurrent copying since Android 8.0 that does most work on a background thread with very short pauses. GC hurts when I allocate faster than it reclaims. Then an allocation can block waiting for a GC "GC FOR ALLOC" , or the GC thread steals CPU from the render path. I read the art log lines for cause, freed amount, heap utilization, and pause time to see which case I'm in.

title: Allocation churn
text: What is allocation churn, why does it cause jank even though the heap is not leaking, and what are the most common hidden allocations in Kotlin Android code? Churn is creating many short-lived objects rapidly. Nothing leaks, but the heap fills quickly, GC runs often, and on a busy main thread or a small CPU it competes with frame work. Hot paths such as onDraw , onBindViewHolder , scroll listeners, and per-item mapping are where it bites. Typical hidden allocators: boxing primitives in generic collections, string formatting and concatenation, capturing lambdas, Regex constructed in a loop, Paint / Rect created inside onDraw , and chained map/filter creating intermediate lists.

title: Low memory killer
text: How does Android decide which process to kill under memory pressure, and how can you tell in production that your app was killed for memory rather than crashing? Android keeps a score per process oom score adj that reflects importance: the foreground app is 0, visible about 100, perceptible about 200, services around 500, and cached processes 900+. The userspace daemon lmkd watches memory pressure PSI based on devices with kernel support, older versions used free-memory thresholds and kills the highest score first, which means cached background apps die first. A kill is a SIGKILL, so no exception or onDestroy . In production I use ApplicationExitInfo API 30+ and look for REASON LOW MEMORY .

title: Leak mechanics
text: What exactly is a memory leak in a garbage-collected runtime? Walk me through why a leaked Activity is so expensive and the platform-level patterns that create them. In a GC runtime a leak means an object I no longer need is still reachable from a GC root, so it is never collected. A leaked Activity keeps its entire view tree, any bitmaps in it, its ViewModel references, and anything captured by its listeners, so one leak often costs several MB. The common roots are static fields, singletons, long-lived threads, registered listeners and callbacks, and system services holding my objects.
