title: Build pipeline from source to installed code
text: Describe what happens to my Kotlin code from ./gradlew assembleRelease to code running on a device. Which tools touch it, and which of them can break a release build that works in debug? The Kotlin compiler produces .class files, then AGP merges them with library classes. R8 the default shrinker/optimiser shrinks, obfuscates and optimises, and its built-in D8 stage desugars and converts to DEX. AAPT2 compiles and links resources and the manifest; the pieces are packaged, zipaligned and signed into an APK or AAB. Release-only breakage typically comes from R8 reflection, missing keep rules , resource shrinking, manifest merge differences, and signing config.

title: Binder model
text: What is Binder, and why does Android use it for IPC instead of sockets, pipes or shared memory? Binder is Android's kernel-backed RPC mechanism. A client holds a proxy to an object living in another process; calling a method on it is marshalled into a Parcel, sent through the /dev/binder driver one copy into the target's mapped buffer , executed on a Binder thread in the server, and the reply comes back. Android picked it over sockets because the kernel stamps the caller's UID/PID on every transaction so identity cannot be forged, objects can be passed by reference with reference counting and death notification, and it costs one copy instead of two.

title: Parcelable
text: Parcelable vs Serializable: which do you use on Android and why? How does @Parcelize work, and can you persist a Parcel to disk? Parcelable, because it is designed for Binder marshalling: explicit field-by-field writes with no reflection, so it is faster and produces smaller payloads than Serializable. In Kotlin I use @Parcelize from the kotlin-parcelize plugin, which generates writeToParcel and the CREATOR . A Parcel must never be persisted: the format is not stable across OS versions and is not meant for storage; use a database, protobuf or JSON for that.

title: System services
text: What does context.getSystemService ... actually return, and how does it reach a service living in system server? It returns a client-side Manager object, for example ActivityManager or ConnectivityManager. The Manager wraps an AIDL proxy to the real service, whose IBinder was fetched from servicemanager by name. SystemServiceRegistry creates and caches these managers per Context, so most methods you call are Binder transactions into system server.

title: Binder threads and oneway
text: Explain the Binder thread pool and the oneway keyword. What happens if all Binder threads in a process are busy? Each process gets a pool of Binder threads, by default about 15 spawned plus the initial one, commonly quoted as 16. Incoming transactions run on those threads, not on your main thread. A normal call blocks the caller until the reply; oneway returns immediately, has no return value, and calls on the same binder object are delivered in order. If every Binder thread is busy, new incoming transactions queue in the driver and callers appear to hang, potentially cascading into ANRs.

title: Transaction buffer
text: What is the 1 MB Binder transaction buffer limit? What exactly is shared, what throws, and what are the non-obvious ways to blow through it? Each process gets one mapped Binder buffer of about 1 MB 1 MB minus two pages, so roughly 1016 KB with 4 KB pages . That buffer is shared by all transactions currently in flight for the process, not per call. If a transaction cannot get space, you get TransactionTooLargeException a RemoteException , and logcat shows "FAILED BINDER TRANSACTION". Intent extras, saved-state Bundles, fragment arguments and large IPC returns all count.

title: AIDL
text: How does AIDL work? What does the generated code look like, what do in/out/inout mean, and what threading rules apply? AIDL is an interface definition language; the tool generates a Java interface plus two classes: Stub server side, extends Binder, implements onTransact that unmarshals the Parcel and calls your implementation and Proxy client side, marshals arguments and calls transact . asInterface returns the local object in-process or a Proxy otherwise. Non-primitive parameters need a direction tag in, out, inout , and server methods run on Binder pool threads, so they must be thread-safe.

title: TransactionTooLargeException
text: How do you find the cause and fix it? A shopping app 1.2M DAU, 70% Android ships v8.4. Crashlytics shows a new crash cluster, 0.9% of sessions up from 0.1% , almost all on Android 8-13: java.lang.RuntimeException: android.os.TransactionTooLargeException: data parcel size 1187532 bytes at android.app.servertransaction.PendingTransactionActions$StopInfo.run Caused by: android.os.TransactionTooLargeException: data parcel size 1187532 bytes Logcat on a repro device also prints !!! FAILED BINDER TRANSACTION !!! parcel size = 1187532 . Crashes occur when users press Home or open another app, not while using the screen. v8.4 added "recently viewed" carousel and a filter screen. Product says "we did not touch navigation or startActivity". Big-memory flagship devices are affected as much as low-end ones.

title: Messenger vs AIDL
text: You need IPC between your app and a service in another process. When do you choose a local Binder, a Messenger, or AIDL? If the service is in the same process, return a local Binder subclass: no IPC at all. For cross-process with simple request/response messages and no need for concurrency, use Messenger : it wraps a Handler, so all calls are serialised on one thread. For richer typed APIs, concurrent calls, return values, or multiple clients, use AIDL with a thread-safe implementation.

title: DeadObjectException
text: Why does this crash happen, and how do you make the client robust? A navigation app runs its routing engine in a bound service in android:process=":engine" about 250 MB native memory . Clients bind from the UI process and call engine.reroute req sync AIDL . Since v3.2, crash rate is 1.4% on low-RAM devices 3 GB , mostly after the user has been in other apps for a while: android.os.DeadObjectException at android.os.BinderProxy.transactNative Native Method at com.acme.IEngine$Stub$Proxy.reroute IEngine.java:112 at com.acme.nav.RouteRepo.reroute RouteRepo.kt:58 Logcat before it: ActivityManager: Killing 4123:com.acme.nav:engine adj 900 : empty 17 lmkd kill a few minutes earlier. QA never reproduces because their devices have 8 GB.

title: Chatty IPC
text: How do you cut this without removing the features? A banking app's cold start p50 is 1.9 s, p95 3.4 s on mid-range devices 4 GB, Android 11-13 . A trace Perfetto of Application.onCreate plus first Activity shows 410 ms on the main thread inside "binder transaction" slices. Breakdown: a feature-flag SDK calls packageManager.getPackageInfo pkg, GET SIGNING CERTIFICATES for each of 12 partner apps about 14 ms each, 170 ms total , a device-fingerprint module calls getInstalledApplications 0 about 60 ms, 400 apps , a root-check calls getInstalledPackages three times about 150 ms , and ConnectivityManager.getActiveNetworkInfo is called around 30 times by different layers about 30 ms . Time on-CPU in the app is low. Product asks for p95 under 2.5 s.

title: Death recipients
text: How do you detect and handle the death of a process you hold a Binder reference to? Cover linkToDeath, DeadObjectException, and RemoteCallbackList. The driver tracks references. On a remote IBinder I can call linkToDeath recipient, 0 and get binderDied on a Binder thread when the hosting process dies; synchronous calls to a dead binder throw DeadObjectException . On the server side, a client callback is just a proxy, so I store callbacks in a RemoteCallbackList , which links to death for each entry, removes dead ones automatically and gives me a safe broadcast loop.

title: Large payload IPC
text: Design the data path between the two processes. What do you send through Binder, what not, and why? A document-scanning app moves its ML pipeline into an isolated process android:process=":ml" , isolatedProcess="true" for crash and security isolation. The UI process sends camera frames 1920x1080 YUV, about 3.1 MB each; 12 fps preview to :ml and receives detections about 2 KB . The first prototype passes ByteArray through AIDL. On a mid-range device you see TransactionTooLargeException immediately, and when downscaled to 640x480 about 460 KB frames are accepted but preview jank is 18% of frames, and 2-3% of sessions throw DeadObjectException when the ML process is killed. Product wants full-resolution captures up to 12 MP JPEG, 4-6 MB to be processed too.

title: Caller identity and permissions
text: In a service that other apps can bind to, how do you know who is calling and enforce permissions? Explain getCallingUid , enforceCallingPermission , checkCallingOrSelfPermission and clearCallingIdentity . The kernel stamps each Binder transaction with the sender's UID and PID, and Binder.getCallingUid returns it on the Binder thread handling that call. For access control I use <service android:permission="..." enforced when binding plus per-method checks with enforceCallingPermission against a signature-level permission. I avoid checkCallingOrSelfPermission for security checks, because my own process usually holds the permission, so it passes. clearCallingIdentity resets the identity to my own so downstream calls run as me; it must be restored in a finally block.

title: Exported service security
text: List every flaw, explain why the attack works, and fix it. How do you prevent this class in future? A fintech SDK ships in the host app com.acme.wallet 3M installs . Partner apps bind to its service to request a payment. A bug bounty report says any app on the device can read the user's last 10 transactions and trigger a refund. Here is the shipped code: // AndroidManifest.xml // <permission android:name="com.acme.PAY" android:protectionLevel="normal"/ // <service android:name=".PayService" android:exported="true"/ class PayService : Service { private val executor = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor private val binder = object : IPay.Stub { override fun lastTransactions callerPkg: String : List<Txn { if checkCallingOrSelfPermission "com.acme.PAY" != PackageManager.PERMISSION GRANTED throw SecurityException "no" return repo.last 10, callerPkg } override fun refund txnId: String, cb: IPayCallback { executor.execute { if checkCallingPermission "com.acme.PAY" == PackageManager.PERMISSION GRANTED { cb.onDone repo.refund txnId } } } } override fun onBind i: Intent : IBinder = binder } Logcat in the bounty PoC shows the attacker app calling both methods successfully from uid=10247 not signed with your key . Red herring: the team had just enabled R8 and thought "obfuscation broke permission checks".

title: Binder driver internals
text: Walk me through what happens, from the Kotlin call to the kernel and back, when app A makes a synchronous Binder call to a service in app B. What is mapped, what is copied, and which threads are involved? The Kotlin call goes to a Proxy that writes arguments into a Parcel and calls BinderProxy.transact , which goes through JNI to libbinder IPCThreadState , then an ioctl BINDER WRITE READ on /dev/binder . The driver finds the target by handle, copies the Parcel data once into the buffer that B mapped at startup, wakes a Binder thread in B spawning one if needed , and B runs Stub.onTransact . The reply goes back the same way; A's thread sleeps in the driver the whole time.

title: AIDL versioning
text: What went wrong, how do you migrate safely with clients on both old and new versions, and how do you stop this recurring? You own com.acme.pay , a host app exposing an AIDL service used by 40 partner apps about 2M combined installs; partners update on their own schedule, host updates roll weekly . Current AIDL: interface IPay { PayResult pay in PayRequest req ; // code 1 void cancel String id ; // code 2 int status String id ; // code 3 } // PayRequest.java hand-written Parcelable : writes amount, currency, merchant The team wants to add refund String id, long amountMinor and a new field idempotencyKey to PayRequest . A junior dev inserted refund between pay and cancel "for readability" and added idempotencyKey in the middle of writeToParcel . In the staging mix test, an old partner build built against the old AIDL calling cancel against the new host caused a refund; another old client crashed with RuntimeException: Parcel android.os.Parcel@...: Unmarshalling unknown type code when reading a PayRequest. Rollout to prod starts Monday.

title: Permission types
text: Explain normal, dangerous, signature and special permissions in Android. How does the system decide which are granted at install time and which need the user? Every permission has a protection level. Normal ones, like INTERNET, are low risk and granted automatically at install. Dangerous ones, like CAMERA or ACCESS FINE LOCATION, touch private data, so since API 23 the app must ask at runtime and the user can revoke later. Signature permissions are granted only if my app is signed with the same certificate as the app that declared the permission. Special permissions, like SYSTEM ALERT WINDOW or SCHEDULE EXACT ALARM, are not requested with a dialog at all; the user flips a toggle on a dedicated Settings screen.

title: Runtime request flow
text: Walk me through the correct way to request a runtime permission today. Why did the Activity Result API replace onRequestPermissionsResult ? I check checkSelfPermission first; if granted I proceed. Otherwise I launch a request through a contract registered with registerForActivityResult RequestPermission . The result lands in a callback, not in a request-code switch. Registration must happen before the owner is STARTED, typically as a property initializer, and the registry restores the callback after process death.

title: Rationale and permanent denial
text: How do shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale and "don't ask again" actually work, especially on Android 11+? How do you detect that a permission is permanently denied? shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale returns false before the first ask, true after one denial, and false again once the system will no longer show the dialog. On Android 11+, a second denial for the same permission acts as "don't ask again", and later launch calls return denied instantly with no dialog. To detect permanent denial I combine: result denied AND rationale false AND I have asked before, which I track myself.

title: Approximate vs precise location
text: What changed for location permissions in Android 12 API 31 , and how should an app request ACCESS COARSE LOCATION and ACCESS FINE LOCATION? From API 31, the user can choose "Approximate" or "Precise" on the dialog. An app targeting 31+ that wants precise must request COARSE and FINE together in one request; asking only for FINE is ignored. The user may grant only approximate, so I must work with coarse accuracy and ask for upgrade only when the feature truly needs it.

title: Request flow bugs
text: Find every bug, explain why each causes the symptoms, and fix it. A teammate's QR scanner screen crashes in 1.4% of sessions on first launch, and a QA note says "after denying camera, the app keeps showing the dialog and the screen is black". Android 13 and 14 devices only. Code: class ScanActivity : AppCompatActivity { private lateinit var cameraLauncher: ActivityResultLauncher<String override fun onCreate savedInstanceState: Bundle? { super.onCreate savedInstanceState setContentView R.layout.activity scan findViewById<Button R.id.start .setOnClickListener { cameraLauncher = registerForActivityResult ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission { granted - startCamera } cameraLauncher.launch Manifest.permission.CAMERA } } override fun onResume { super.onResume if checkSelfPermission Manifest.permission.CAMERA != PackageManager.PERMISSION GRANTED { requestPermissions arrayOf Manifest.permission.CAMERA , 7 } } private fun startCamera { / opens CameraX / } } Logcat excerpt: java.lang.IllegalStateException: LifecycleOwner ScanActivity is attempting to register while current state is RESUMED. LifecycleOwners must call register before they are STARTED.

title: One-time permissions and auto-reset
text: What are one-time permissions and permission auto-reset? How do they affect an app that assumes "granted once means granted forever"? Android 11 added "Only this time" for location, camera and microphone. The grant lasts while the app is in use and is revoked after the app leaves the foreground for a while or its process dies. Separately, auto-reset revokes runtime permissions of apps the user has not used for several months. In both cases the app must re-check at the point of use and be ready to ask again.

title: POST_NOTIFICATIONS (API 33)
text: How does the notification runtime permission in Android 13 work, and how does behavior differ for apps targeting 32 vs 33 or higher? POST NOTIFICATIONS is a dangerous permission from API 33. If I target 33+, I must declare it and request it myself; until granted, my notifications are not shown. If I target 32 or lower, the system prompts the user automatically the first time I create a notification channel while an activity is in the foreground. I should ask in context, after a moment of value, not at cold start.

title: Photo picker and READ_MEDIA_*
text: How did media access permissions change across Android 10, 13 and 14, and why is the photo picker the preferred answer for most apps? If the user just needs to choose photos or videos, I use the photo picker and need no permission at all. Android 13 split READ EXTERNAL STORAGE into READ MEDIA IMAGES, READ MEDIA VIDEO and READ MEDIA AUDIO. Android 14 added READ MEDIA VISUAL USER SELECTED so the user can grant access to only chosen items, which means I must treat "partial access" as a normal state.

title: Permanent denial UX
text: How would you redesign the flow, and what would you tell the PM? A 1.5M DAU expense-tracking app has a "scan receipt" flow that requires CAMERA. Analytics: 31% of users deny on first ask; of those, 55% tap the button again and see nothing happen. Support reports "camera is broken". On Android 11+, the second denial blocks future dialogs. A PM wants to "keep asking until they accept". Android 11 to 14 are 70% of the base.

title: Special permissions
text: How do special permissions like SYSTEM ALERT WINDOW and SCHEDULE EXACT ALARM differ from runtime permissions, and how do you request and check them? Special permissions are controlled by app ops and a dedicated Settings screen, not by a system dialog. I launch an Intent to the relevant screen, the user toggles, and I re-check on return, since there is no result callback with the answer. SYSTEM ALERT WINDOW uses Settings.canDrawOverlays ; exact alarms use AlarmManager.canScheduleExactAlarms .

title: Manifest permissions and libraries
text: A third-party SDK adds permissions you never asked for through manifest merging. How do you find, remove and control them? The manifest merger unions every <uses-permission from all AARs into the final APK. I inspect the merged manifest, remove what I do not need with tools:node="remove" , narrow with maxSdkVersion , and mark hardware features as required="false" so Play does not filter devices out.

title: Bluetooth permissions API 31
text: Diagnose and fix, and explain how you would ship it. A smart-lock companion app 400k MAU bumps targetSdk from 30 to 34. Within 48 hours, support tickets say "cannot find my lock" and Crashlytics shows a new top crash, 0.9% of sessions, all on Android 12 and above: java.lang.SecurityException: Need android.permission.BLUETOOTH SCAN permission for AttributionSource{...}: GattService startScan Android 11 and below users are fine. The manifest still declares BLUETOOTH , BLUETOOTH ADMIN and ACCESS FINE LOCATION ; the code checks only location permission before scanning. Red herrings: a BLE library update shipped the same day, and one OEM reports slow scans.

title: Testing permissions
text: How do you stabilize and speed this up without losing coverage of the permission flows? Your Espresso/UI Automator suite has 420 tests and runs on CI emulators API 30, 33 and 34 . Flake rate is 6%, and the top failing tests are anything involving the camera, location or notifications. Failures: UiObjectNotFoundException: no object with text "While using the app" . Different API levels and one OEM-skinned device farm show different button labels. Total run time is 48 minutes, a third of which is permission dialog handling.

title: Background location
text: Explain the two-step flow for background location ACCESS BACKGROUND LOCATION , how it differs across API 29, 30 and 31+, and when you can avoid it. Background location is a separate permission added in API 29. On API 30+, I cannot request it together with foreground location; I must first get foreground permission, then separately request background, and the system sends the user to Settings to choose "Allow all the time" rather than showing a dialog. Most use cases tracking during a run, navigation can use a foreground service with a location type and avoid the background permission altogether.

title: Revocation and process death
text: What happens to your app when the user revokes a runtime permission in system Settings while the app is running or in the background? How should you design for it? Permission state lives in the system, not in my app. Historically, revoking a runtime permission from Settings kills the app's process, so the user returns to a recreated process and an Activity restored from saved state. Behavior varies by permission and release some app-op based permissions can change without a kill , so I never cache "granted", I check at the point of use, and I handle SecurityException as a possible outcome.

title: Revocation crash
text: Run the post-incident review: cause, fix, prevention, and what changed in your process. A running-tracker app 900k DAU sees a new crash on Android 12 to 14: 0.42% of sessions, mostly "resume from recents". Stack: java.lang.SecurityException: uid 10456 does not have android.permission.ACCESS COARSE LOCATION or android.permission.ACCESS FINE LOCATION at com.google.android.gms.location.FusedLocationProviderClient.requestLocationUpdates called from TrackFragment.onStart . Facts: crash volume spiked after a "Privacy Dashboard" campaign by a phone vendor. The app was launched with Play services 24.x; QA cannot reproduce because testers grant location once on a fresh install. A red herring: the same release updated the maps SDK.

title: Custom and signature permissions
text: When would you define a custom permission, and how do protection levels, exported components and android:permission fit together? What attacks exist if you get it wrong? A custom permission lets me gate access to my exported components, such as a service or provider, so only trusted callers can use them. I choose signature when only my own apps same signing cert should have access, since the system enforces the cert match and the user never sees a prompt. A normal custom permission is nearly useless as protection because any app can request it.

title: checkSelfPermission vs PermissionChecker and app ops
text: What's the difference between ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission and PermissionChecker.checkSelfPermission , and why can a permission be "granted" but the access still fail? A runtime permission has a grant state, and many are also tied to an app-op that the system uses to track and restrict usage, such as "while in use" location or the user turning off a permission for background. checkSelfPermission reports only the grant. PermissionChecker also consults the app op and can return PERMISSION DENIED APP OP . For foreground-only location, checkSelfPermission says granted even when my app is in the background and the system will not deliver real data.

title: Notification permission rollout
text: Plan the targetSdk 33 migration and the permission strategy, and tell me what you'd measure. A commerce app with 2M DAU targets SDK 32 today and must move to 33 store requirement in 6 weeks . About 38% of users are on Android 13+. Currently on Android 13 the system prompt appears automatically at first channel creation cold start , with 72% opt-in. Marketing says "push drives 30% of orders; do not lose reach". Product also says "we want a nicer prompt, but no more than one extra screen". The requirement is ambiguous on whether existing users should be re-prompted.

title: Storage permission migration
text: Design the migration plan. A document-scanner app 3M MAU, 20% on Android 10 or lower targets SDK 29, uses WRITE EXTERNAL STORAGE with requestLegacyExternalStorage="true" , and saves PDFs to /sdcard/ScanPro/ . Play requires targetSdk 34 next quarter. Test builds on API 33 show FileNotFoundException: open failed: EACCES on old files, and a user-reported missing-files complaint appeared in the beta channel. Constraints: no data loss, exports must stay visible in the Files app, the app may not ask for MANAGE EXTERNAL STORAGE .

title: targetSdk vs OS behavior changes
text: What is the difference between compileSdk, targetSdk and minSdk, and how do you know whether a given Android behavior change hits your app only after you bump targetSdk or immediately when users update their OS? minSdk is the oldest OS I install on, compileSdk is the SDK I compile against APIs and lint , targetSdk is the OS version I promise my app was tested against. The platform gates many behavior changes on targetSdk, so they only turn on when I bump it. The rest apply to every app on that OS version regardless of targetSdk. Google publishes both lists per release: "Behavior changes: apps targeting API X" and "Behavior changes: all apps".

title: android:exported (Android 12)
text: What changed about android:exported in Android 12, what happens if you ignore it, and how do you decide the value for each component? For apps targeting API 31+, any activity, service or receiver that has an intent filter must declare android:exported explicitly. If missing, manifest merge fails at build time or the install fails on old tooling . Launcher activities must be true . Everything internal should be false . Exported means other apps can start or bind the component, so each true is public API plus an attack surface.

title: PendingIntent mutability
text: Explain PendingIntent mutability requirements across Android 12 and 14. When do you actually need FLAG MUTABLE , and what breaks if you use it wrong? Targeting API 31+, every PendingIntent must specify FLAG IMMUTABLE or FLAG MUTABLE , else IllegalArgumentException . I default to immutable. Mutable is needed only when the receiver of the PendingIntent must fill in extras, like inline-reply notification actions or bubbles. Targeting API 34+, a mutable PendingIntent whose base Intent has no component or package an implicit one throws.

title: Splash Screen API (Android 12)
text: What happened to splash screens in Android 12, and how do you implement one correctly for all API levels? From Android 12 the system always draws a splash screen on cold and warm starts, built from your theme window background color plus app icon . Custom splash Activities now show a double splash on 12+. The fix is androidx.core:core-splashscreen : set a splash theme, call installSplashScreen before super.onCreate , optionally hold it with setKeepOnScreenCondition .

title: Foreground service background start
text: Find the cause, stop the bleeding, and design the long-term fix. A ride-tracking app 900k DAU, 70 percent on Android 12 to 14 starts a location foreground service from an FCM data message handler so drivers resume tracking after reconnect. Last week Crashlytics shows a new top crash on Android 12+: android.app.ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException: startForegroundService not allowed due to mAllowStartForeground false: service com.example/.TrackingService , 0.6 percent of sessions, only when the app was swiped away or idle for hours. Release 5.14 changed the FCM priority from high to normal to save battery. Android 11 and below show nothing. The code was untouched in the same period.

title: targetSdk 34 bump
text: Find every bug, explain which is targetSdk-gated, and fix. After bumping targetSdk from 33 to 34, QA reports three issues on Android 14 only: 1 pressing a notification action closes the app silently; 2 opening Settings from an in-app link does nothing; 3 the app crashes on cold start for some users with SecurityException: ... One of RECEIVER EXPORTED or RECEIVER NOT EXPORTED should be specified when a receiver isn't being registered exclusively for system broadcasts . Code: // Application.onCreate registerReceiver syncReceiver, IntentFilter "com.example.SYNC DONE" // opening an internal screen startActivity Intent "com.example.OPEN SETTINGS" // manifest: exported=false, has intent filter // notification action val i = Intent "com.example.REPLY" val pi = PendingIntent.getBroadcast this, 0, i, PendingIntent.FLAG MUTABLE

title: POST_NOTIFICATIONS (Android 13)
text: How does the Android 13 notification runtime permission work, and does it behave differently depending on targetSdk? POST NOTIFICATIONS is a runtime permission on API 33+. If I target 33+, I declare it and request it myself at a good moment. If I target 32 or lower and run on Android 13, the system asks on my behalf the first time the app creates a notification channel while an activity is in the foreground , so I lose control over timing. Denied means no notifications, including the foreground service notification in the drawer, but FGS still shows in the Task Manager.

title: Media permissions (Android 13/14)
text: How did media access permissions change in Android 13 and 14, and what is the right architecture for picking photos today? Android 13 targeting 33+ replaced READ EXTERNAL STORAGE for media with READ MEDIA IMAGES , READ MEDIA VIDEO , READ MEDIA AUDIO . Android 14 targeting 34+ added READ MEDIA VISUAL USER SELECTED so the user can grant "selected photos only". The best design is not to ask at all: use the system Photo Picker PickVisualMedia , which needs no permission.

title: Per-app language and themed icons (Android 13)
text: What are per-app language preferences and themed icons in Android 13, and what does an app have to do to support them? Per-app language lets the user pick a language for my app in system Settings, different from the system language. To support it I declare android:localeConfig pointing to an XML of supported locales target 33+ , and I use AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales for pre-33 backport. Themed icons are a monochrome layer in the adaptive icon, which the launcher tints with the wallpaper palette.

title: Notification permission rollout
text: How do you handle this, technically and as a post-incident review? A food-delivery app 2.4M MAU, 55 percent on Android 13+ bumped targetSdk to 33 in release 8.2. Two weeks later Growth says push-reachable users fell from 71 percent to 38 percent among Android 13+ users, order-status engagement dropped, and support reports "I did not get my delivery update". Engineering shipped the standard permission request at first launch after the splash . Product wants "back to 70 percent reach" and says "just ask again every launch". Legal has not weighed in. Crash rates are unchanged.

title: Foreground service types (Android 14)
text: What does Android 14 require for foreground services, and what failures should you expect if you get it wrong? Targeting 34+, every foreground service must declare at least one android:foregroundServiceType in the manifest, pass a matching type or types to startForeground , and hold the type-specific FOREGROUND SERVICE <TYPE permission plus any runtime permission the type needs camera, microphone, location . Missing pieces throw MissingForegroundServiceTypeException or SecurityException .

title: Exact alarms (Android 12 to 14)
text: Walk through how exact alarm permissions evolved from Android 12 to Android 14 and how you decide between SCHEDULE EXACT ALARM , USE EXACT ALARM , and not using exact alarms at all. Android 12 introduced SCHEDULE EXACT ALARM : user-grantable "Alarms & reminders" special access for exact alarms. Android 13 added USE EXACT ALARM , auto-granted and non-revocable but only allowed for alarm clock and calendar apps under Play policy. Android 14 stopped pre-granting SCHEDULE EXACT ALARM for newly installed apps targeting 13+ denied by default , so I must check canScheduleExactAlarms and handle denial. For most apps the right answer is inexact alarms, WorkManager, or setAlarmClock .

title: Exact alarm denial on Android 14
text: Diagnose, mitigate, and fix without breaking patient trust or Play policy. A medication-reminder app 300k DAU, 62 percent Android 13 to 14 schedules daily doses with setExactAndAllowWhileIdle . Release 3.9 targetSdk 33 to 34 went live Tuesday. By Thursday: 1-star reviews "reminder never rang", support tickets up 5x, and Crashlytics shows SecurityException: Caller com.example needs to hold android.permission.SCHEDULE EXACT ALARM or android.permission.USE EXACT ALARM to set exact alarms at 1.8 percent of sessions, almost all new installs on Android 14. Users who updated from 3.8 are fine. The manifest declares SCHEDULE EXACT ALARM . A teammate says "the permission is in the manifest, so it must be an OEM bug".

title: Edge-to-edge (Android 15/16)
text: What does Android 15 enforce about edge-to-edge for apps targeting 35, what changes in Android 16, and how do you migrate a legacy View-based or Compose app? Targeting 35 on an Android 15 device, windows draw behind the status bar, navigation bar and cutout by default; the old color APIs stop having effect and content gets overlapped unless I apply insets. Android 15 had an opt-out windowOptOutEdgeToEdgeEnforcement ; targeting 36 on Android 16 disables that opt-out. The migration is: call enableEdgeToEdge , consume WindowInsets in layouts, fix IME and system bar icon contrast.

title: FGS timeouts and boot restrictions (Android 15)
text: What are the Android 15 foreground service timeout rules for dataSync and mediaProcessing , and which other FGS start restrictions did 15 add? For apps targeting 35, dataSync and mediaProcessing foreground services get a combined budget of 6 hours in 24 hours. When it is exhausted the system calls Service.onTimeout int, int ; I have a few seconds to call stopSelf or the app crashes with RemoteServiceException: A foreground service of type dataSync did not stop within its timeout . Starting one again after exhaustion throws ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException until the user brings the app to the foreground which resets the timer . Also, BOOT COMPLETED receivers cannot start several FGS types, and SYSTEM ALERT WINDOW now needs a visible overlay.

title: dataSync timeout crashes
text: Diagnose, mitigate, and re-architect. A notes app 1.2M DAU syncs large attachments through a dataSync foreground service. Release 7.0 bumps targetSdk to 35. Crashlytics on Android 15: top crash RemoteServiceException$ForegroundServiceDidNotStopInTimeException: A foreground service of type dataSync did not stop within its timeout: {com.example/.SyncService} at 0.9 percent of sessions, mostly overnight; second signal ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException: Time limit already exhausted for foreground service type dataSync at 0.4 percent. Users with big libraries 50k+ attachments are affected. Crashes were absent in QA and staging. SyncService has a retry loop that restarts itself via startForegroundService on any failure.

title: 16 KB page size
text: What is the 16 KB page size change, which apps does it actually break, and how do you check and fix an app that includes native libraries? Since Android 15, AOSP supports devices whose kernel uses 16 KB memory pages instead of 4 KB. Pure Kotlin/Java apps are fine. Apps with native code my own NDK code or SDK .so files must have ELF segments aligned to 16 KB and, if libraries are stored uncompressed, 16 KB zip-aligned; otherwise they crash at load or fail to install. Play requires apps targeting 35+ to support 16 KB on 64-bit devices.

title: 16 KB readiness plan
text: Plan the work, sequence risks, and tell Product what you will and will not promise. A fintech app 4M MAU, arm64 only in practice ships 11 native libraries: 2 are ours C++ crypto, built with NDK r25 , 9 come from SDKs analytics, payments, a face-liveness vendor, video player, crash reporter . The Play Console shows a warning that app updates must support 16 KB page sizes. Product wants to ship a feature release in 3 weeks. AGP is 8.2, useLegacyPackaging is false, the face-liveness vendor says "16 KB support coming Q3", and QA has no 16 KB device. On an Android 16 beta device with a 16 KB kernel, the app launches but shows the page-size compatibility dialog.

title: Predictive back
text: Explain the bug and fix it for 36, keeping pre-36 devices working. A support-chat app bumps targetSdk to 36. On Android 16 devices, QA reports: 1 pressing back on the chat screen with an unsent draft no longer shows the "Discard draft?" dialog and the draft is lost; 2 the system back-to-home animation plays for a screen that must confirm first; 3 the custom BackHandler in a Compose bottom sheet works but the legacy View screen does not. On Android 14 with targetSdk 36 everything still worked. Code: class ChatActivity : AppCompatActivity { override fun onBackPressed { if viewModel.hasDraft showDiscardDialog else super.onBackPressed } override fun onKeyDown keyCode: Int, event: KeyEvent? : Boolean { if keyCode == KeyEvent.KEYCODE BACK && viewModel.hasDraft { showDiscardDialog ; return true } return super.onKeyDown keyCode, event } } The manifest has no enableOnBackInvokedCallback attribute.

title: Android 16 adaptive layouts
text: What does Android 16 change about screen orientation and resizability restrictions, who is affected, and how do you prepare? For apps targeting 36 on displays with smallest width = 600dp, the system ignores screenOrientation , resizableActivity , minAspectRatio , maxAspectRatio , and setRequestedOrientation locks: the app fills the window and can rotate or be resized. Exceptions: games appCategory , user opt-in to the app's default behavior, and screens smaller than sw600dp. There is a temporary opt-out through a manifest property, and it will not apply when targeting 37.

title: Android 16 background work changes
text: What changes in Android 16 affect background work JobScheduler quota, scheduled executors, broadcasts , and which of them apply to all apps versus only apps targeting 36? Several are all-apps: JobScheduler runtime quota regular and expedited now depends on app standby bucket, whether the job started while the app was top, and whether it runs concurrently with a foreground service; setImportantWhileForeground is a no-op; ordered broadcast priority is only honored within a process; abandoned jobs get a new stop reason. One is target-36 only: ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor.scheduleAtFixedRate runs at most one missed execution on return to a valid lifecycle.

title: targetSdk bump playbook
text: Lay out your targetSdk bump playbook from 33 to 36 and how you will test behavior changes with compat flags. A marketplace app 6M MAU, targetSdk 33, 480 Gradle modules-equivalent codebase, 40 percent legacy View screens, 9 third-party SDKs must reach targetSdk 36 before the Play deadline in 10 weeks. Last year's 33 bump caused two incidents a crash cluster from notification handling and a login regression . The org wants a plan, a risk ranking, and a rollout that will not cause an incident. Crash-free sessions today: 99.62 percent, ANR 0.21 percent.

title: Doze
text: What is Doze mode? Explain light vs deep Doze, what it restricts, and what an app can still do. Doze is a battery saver the system enters when the device is idle. Deep Doze API 23 needs screen off, unplugged and stationary for a while; light Doze API 24 needs only screen off and unplugged. While dozing, the system defers network access, wake locks, standard alarms, JobScheduler jobs, syncs and Wi-Fi scans to periodic maintenance windows that get further apart over time. Exceptions are high-priority FCM, setAlarmClock, and setExactAndAllowWhileIdle/setAndAllowWhileIdle rate-limited . Anything that must reach the user at a specific time has to use one of those.

title: AlarmManager basics
text: Walk me through AlarmManager: the alarm types, inexact vs exact, and what happens to alarms on reboot, app update and force stop. AlarmManager fires a PendingIntent at a time, outside my process lifetime. There are two clock bases, RTC wall clock and ELAPSED REALTIME since boot , each with a WAKEUP variant that wakes the CPU. Since API 19 set and setRepeating are inexact so the system can batch them; setExact and friends need care and, from API 31, a permission. Alarms are wiped on reboot, on force stop, and on app update/uninstall, so I must reschedule from BOOT COMPLETED and my own state.

title: App Standby buckets
text: What are App Standby buckets, how does an app move between them, and what do they limit? Since API 28 the system ranks each app by recent usage into Active, Working Set, Frequent, Rare, and opt-in by the system Restricted. The lower the bucket, the stricter the limits on job run time, alarm frequency and high-priority FCM. Using the app, interacting with its notification, or a foreground service moves it up; days of no use move it down. Apps can query their bucket but not set it.

title: Background execution limits (API 26)
text: What did Android 8.0 API 26 change about background execution, and how does it differ from Doze? From API 26, an app that is not in the foreground can't freely call startService ; it throws IllegalStateException once the app is "idle" a minute or so after leaving the foreground , unless I use startForegroundService and call startForeground within about 5 seconds. Manifest-declared receivers also stopped getting most implicit broadcasts. Doze is different: it works on device idle state and defers network/alarms/jobs for every app. The limits depend on the app's state, Doze on the device's state.

title: Exact alarm permissions
text: Explain SCHEDULE EXACT ALARM vs USE EXACT ALARM. When do you need each, what is the default state per Android version, and how do you handle revocation? Since API 31, setExact requires SCHEDULE EXACT ALARM , a special app-access permission the user can toggle in Settings. For apps targeting 33+ and installed fresh on Android 14+, it's denied by default; on 12/13 it is granted by default. USE EXACT ALARM API 33 is granted automatically at install and can't be revoked, but Play only permits it for core alarm-clock, timer or calendar apps. I check canScheduleExactAlarms before scheduling, send the user to the settings page if needed, and re-schedule when the permission state changes, with an inexact fallback.

title: AlarmManager
text: Find every defect and give the corrected version. A medication-reminder app 200k DAU schedules daily reminders. After a release targeting API 34, Crashlytics shows IllegalArgumentException: targetSdkVersion ... requires that one of FLAG IMMUTABLE or FLAG MUTABLE be specified on some paths, and support tickets say reminders "come late at night" or "vanish after phone restarts". Review: object ReminderScheduler { fun schedule ctx: Context, medId: Long, atMillis: Long { val am = ctx.getSystemService AlarmManager::class.java val i = Intent ctx, ReminderReceiver::class.java .putExtra "med", medId val pi = PendingIntent.getBroadcast ctx, 0, i, 0 am.setExact AlarmManager.RTC, atMillis, pi } }

title: Alarm exemptions in Doze
text: Compare setAndAllowWhileIdle, setExactAndAllowWhileIdle, setAlarmClock and setWindow in the context of Doze. Which would you pick for a calendar reminder, a chat retry timer, and a wake-up alarm app? setAlarmClock is the strongest: exact, fires in Doze, shows an alarm icon, no exact-alarm permission, and the system exits Doze for it reserved for real alarm UX . setExactAndAllowWhileIdle is exact and works in Doze but needs the exact-alarm permission and is rate-limited about once per 9 minutes per app in Doze . setAndAllowWhileIdle fires in Doze but inexact and rate-limited. setExact / setWindow without AllowWhileIdle get deferred to maintenance windows. Calendar reminder: exact-and-allow-while-idle or alarm clock if the app is a calendar category . Retry timer: inexact allow-while-idle or a job. Wake-up app: setAlarmClock .

title: FCM priority and Doze
text: How do high-priority and normal-priority FCM messages behave in Doze and under App Standby, and what can the app do inside onMessageReceived? Normal-priority messages are deferred during Doze until a maintenance window. High-priority messages wake the device, give brief network access and a short temporary allowlist so I can finish work and, on API 31+, start a foreground service . I get roughly 10 seconds in onMessageReceived , so I post a notification or enqueue a job. High priority is meant to end in a user-visible notification; if it doesn't, FCM can downgrade future messages, and standby buckets cap how many high-priority messages an app gets per day in Frequent/Rare.

title: JobScheduler (platform level)
text: At the platform level, how does JobScheduler decide when to run a job, and what constraints and limits does it enforce? I describe a job with JobInfo network type, charging, battery-not-low, storage-not-low, idle, content-URI triggers, latency/deadline, periodic interval and the system runs it in my JobService when all constraints are met and quota allows, in a batch with other apps. onStartJob runs on the main thread, the job has about 10 minutes, then the system calls onStopJob , and I return true if I want a reschedule. Periodic jobs have a 15-minute minimum interval. Standby buckets, Doze and battery saver can delay it.

title: Battery optimization exemptions
text: What are battery-optimization exemptions in Android, how does an app request one, and when is it appropriate? An exemption puts the app on the Doze allowlist, so it keeps network and can hold partial wake locks in Doze and is less restricted by standby. I check isIgnoringBatteryOptimizations and, if truly necessary, launch ACTION REQUEST IGNORE BATTERY OPTIMIZATIONS with the package URI needs REQUEST IGNORE BATTERY OPTIMIZATIONS , or send the user to ACTION IGNORE BATTERY OPTIMIZATION SETTINGS . Google Play restricts the direct-request intent to apps whose core function breaks without it e.g. device automation, messaging/VoIP in some cases, companion/health devices . It is not a substitute for FCM, and OEM killers ignore it.

title: Testing Doze/standby
text: How do you reproduce and diagnose this, and what do you ask first? QA files: "Notifications for scheduled tasks don't show up overnight on a Pixel 7 Android 14 , but work when I test at my desk." The app 1.2M DAU uses an exact alarm to show a morning briefing at 07:00 plus an hourly WorkManager sync. Crash rate is fine 99.7% crash-free and no ANRs. Engineering says "can't reproduce". Logs from a bug report show Alarm ... deferred is absent; the device was on a charger overnight at 03:00 but unplugged at 05:30.

title: OEM background killers
text: Why do apps get killed or throttled on Xiaomi, Oppo/Vivo, Huawei and Samsung beyond stock Android's rules, and how do you design around it without hacks? Many OEMs add proprietary task killers and "autostart/sleeping app/battery saver" layers on top of AOSP to win battery benchmarks. They may kill the process when it's swiped from recents effectively force-stop, which cancels alarms and blocks pushes , block auto-start after boot, and throttle background work for apps not marked "unrestricted". I can't fix it in code. I design for it: rely on FCM high priority, make state recoverable, detect the likely problem from telemetry, and guide users to the right OEM setting with honest UX, without deep-linking undocumented settings blindly.

title: OEM killers + alarms
text: What is happening and what do you do this week and this quarter? A habit app 600k DAU, 55% India schedules a daily reminder with setExactAndAllowWhileIdle at user-chosen times. Support volume jumps: "reminder came 2-4 hours late or never". Analytics: scheduled-vs-fired lateness p50 = 3 s overall, but for Xiaomi/Redmi p50 = 4 min with 18% never firing, and Samsung p95 = 3 h. Crash-free rate 99.8%, no code change in the last 3 releases. The only recent change: marketing launched a campaign that doubled new installs. Logcat of a Redmi bug report shows the process was killed am kill ... reason: ... after the user swiped the app away.

title: Standby buckets
text: Why does "sync stop after three days unused", and how do you fix it? A news app 2M DAU prefetches articles via an hourly job and shows a "new for you" notification via silent FCM pushes. After an A/B test, the "returning after 3+ days" cohort shows: notification open rate -40%, "first load after open" p95 = 7.8 s was 2.1 s . Server logs: FCM delivery to this cohort is 91% but device-side onMessageReceived count is 62% of sent. Job success logs show the hourly job ran 1x per day for these users. No change in app code; Android 13/14 majority; crash rate stable.

title: Force stop vs swipe vs system kill
text: What is the difference between the user force-stopping an app, swiping it from recents, and the system killing it for memory? What survives each: alarms, jobs, FCM, broadcasts, services? On stock Android, swiping from recents only removes the task; the process may stay or be killed later, and alarms, jobs and FCM keep working. System LMK/memory kill ends the process but leaves scheduled alarms/jobs and pushes intact, and the process restarts on demand. Force stop Settings App info puts the package in the "stopped" state: alarms, jobs and notifications are cancelled, services stopped, and the app receives no broadcasts including BOOT COMPLETED and FCM until the user launches it explicitly. Many OEMs make swipe behave like force stop.

title: Choosing the mechanism
text: Pick the mechanism for each feature and defend it against the PM's proposal. You own scheduling for a super-app 8M DAU, 70% mid-range devices, 40% of users on Android 10-12 . Three features are being designed: 1 chat message delivery when the app is closed p95 target < 3 s , 2 a daily 08:00 medication reminder must be on time, safety-related , 3 a nightly photo backup of up to 400 MB on Wi-Fi + charging. The PM suggests "one foreground service for everything, keeps it simple."

title: targetSdk migration
text: Run the post-incident review: causes, fixes, and process changes. The team bumped targetSdk from 33 to 34 for 30% staged rollout. Within 6 hours: crash-free users fall 99.6% to 98.1%. Top crashes: 1 SecurityException: Caller com.example needs to hold android.permission.SCHEDULE EXACT ALARM or android.permission.USE EXACT ALARM to set exact alarms 2 ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException from a receiver 3 MissingForegroundServiceTypeException: Starting FGS without a type . All are Android 14 devices. The release was approved because "tests pass on emulators with API 33".

title: Evolution of background limits
text: Give me the timeline of Android's background-execution restrictions from API 23 to the latest, and the principle behind each step. Each release moved control from the app to the system: Doze 23 and light Doze 24 batch idle activity; Background limits 26 restrict services and broadcasts; Standby buckets 28 rank apps by use; API 30-31 add hibernation, exact alarm and FGS-start restrictions plus expedited jobs; API 33-34 add the exact-alarm permission defaults, FGS types, and user-visible job types; API 35+ adds FGS time limits and boot-launch limits. The principle is: background work must be user-visible, deferrable, or server-triggered, and the cost of guaranteed execution rises each release.

title: Context types
text: What exactly is a Context in Android, and what are the different kinds of Context you get in an app? "Context is the abstract gateway to the app environment: resources, assets, files, system services, starting components. ContextImpl is the real implementation; everything else wraps it. The Application context lives as long as the process and has no UI theme. Activity is a ContextThemeWrapper , so it carries a theme and can show windows. Service is a plain ContextWrapper without UI theme. Choosing between them is about lifetime and UI capability."

title: Context usage
text: When should I use the Activity context and when the Application context? Give concrete cases of each. "Anything that touches UI or themes uses the Activity context: inflating views, creating Dialogs, resolving theme attributes, startActivity without flags. Anything that outlives the screen, like a singleton, repository, Room/WorkManager/Retrofit setup, takes the Application context. So the rule is: match the context to the lifetime of the thing holding it, and use Activity only for what needs UI."

title: ContextWrapper / attachBaseContext
text: What is attachBaseContext used for, and how does ContextWrapper let you override locale or configuration for an Activity? " attachBaseContext newBase is called by the framework before onCreate hands the component its ContextImpl . Since Activity is a ContextWrapper , I can override it and pass a wrapped context built with createConfigurationContext config , so everything the Activity reads from resources uses my locale or font scale. It must be set before onCreate because views inflate from it."

title: Application class
text: What is the Application class for, when is onCreate called, and what should and should not go in it? "One Application instance exists per process, created before any Activity, Service, Receiver or Provider code runs, except providers' onCreate , which runs before Application.onCreate . It's the right place for process-wide singletons and light init like DI graph setup or crash reporting. It's the wrong place for disk, network or SDK-heavy work, because it runs on the main thread on every cold start, including cold starts caused by a broadcast or a WorkManager job."

title: ContentProvider / App Startup init
text: Why do many SDKs initialize through a ContentProvider, and how does Jetpack App Startup change that? "Providers are instantiated by the system at process start before Application.onCreate , with a Context, so libraries use them as an auto-init hook without asking you to touch your Application. The cost: each provider costs main-thread time on every cold start, and you can't control the order. App Startup replaces N providers with one InitializationProvider that runs Initializer s in dependency order, and you can disable or defer any initializer by removing its meta-data node in the manifest."

title: Manifest merge
text: How does the manifest merger work, in which priority order, and how do you resolve conflicts with tools: markers? "AGP merges manifests by priority: the app's variant manifests buildType, flavors override the main manifest, which overrides library and AAR manifests. Elements merge by key name, for components , attributes conflict when values differ. I resolve conflicts with tools:replace , tools:remove , tools:node markers in my manifest, and I always read the Merged Manifest tab and the merge report before release."

title: exported & permissions
text: Explain android:exported , component permissions and the API 31 changes. How do you secure an exported component? " exported=true lets other apps start or bind the component. Since targetSdk 31 you must set android:exported explicitly on any component with an intent-filter, else the app fails to install/parse. Default for providers with targetSdk 17+ is false. To secure an exported component I either need it exported for a reason, then guard with a signature-level permission and validate every incoming Intent, or I don't export it."

title: Package visibility
text: What changed in Android 11 for package visibility, and how do <queries work? "From API 30, with targetSdk 30+, PackageManager only returns apps that are auto-visible or that I declare under <queries . Without it, resolveActivity returns null and getPackageInfo throws NameNotFoundException even though the app is installed. I declare the specific package, intent filter, or provider authority I need; QUERY ALL PACKAGES is restricted by Play policy."

title: Resource qualifiers
text: How does Android pick a resource when multiple qualified versions exist values-night , drawable-xhdpi , layout-sw600dp , values-v31 ? Walk me through the resolution algorithm. "The system first throws away every directory that contradicts the current device configuration. Then it walks the qualifier precedence table from the top MCC, MNC, locale, layout direction, smallestWidth, available width/height, screen size, ratio, orientation, UI mode, night mode, density, ... platform version . At the first qualifier that any remaining directory uses, it keeps only the directories having it. It repeats until one directory remains. Density is special: no exact match scales the best neighbour."

title: Locale resolution & fallback
text: How does Android resolve the locale for resources, what is the fallback chain, and how does per-app language API 33 fit in? "Since API 24 the user has an ordered LocaleList. For each resource Android tries locale list entries in order against available qualifiers language+region, then language , falling back to the default values/ . Apps can override per app: API 33 LocaleManager.setApplicationLocales with a locales config.xml declared in the manifest, and AppCompat 1.6+ backports it to older versions."

title: Configuration, night mode & insets
text: What does Resources.getConfiguration contain, how does night mode actually get applied, and how does that differ between Application and Activity context? Where do window insets fit in? " Configuration holds locales, uiMode night bit, car/TV type , fontScale, orientation, screen size in dp, densityDpi. Each Resources object has its own copy. The system pushes changes to the process; an Activity without configChanges is recreated. AppCompat's night mode rewrites the Activity's override configuration, so the Activity sees night while the Application context may still see the system value. That mismatch is why using the Application context for colors is a bug."

title: App bundles & dynamic delivery
text: What is an Android App Bundle, how does Play build device-specific APKs from it, and what delivery options exist for dynamic feature modules? "An AAB is a publishing format, not installable. Play generates split APKs per device: a base APK plus config splits for ABI, screen density and language, plus optional dynamic feature module splits. Smaller downloads, but behavior changes: only the languages and densities Play thinks the device needs are installed. Dynamic features can be install-time, on-demand, or conditional."

title: Context leaks
text: What is wrong, how do you fix it correctly, and how do you stop it recurring? Crash rate is fine, but OOM-killed sessions rose from 0.4% to 1.1% after release 8.3 on 2 GB RAM devices about 38% of 900k DAU . LeakCanary in debug shows HomeActivity retained after back-press, leak trace: GC Root: static ImageLoader.instance - ImageLoader.ctx - HomeActivity . The relevant code: object ImageLoader { lateinit var ctx: Context fun init context: Context { ctx = context } fun placeholder = ctx.getDrawable R.drawable.ph } // HomeActivity.onCreate ImageLoader.init this A teammate says "just switch to a WeakReference".

title: Application init / startup
text: How do you cut cold start, in what order, and how do you prove it? Fintech app, 2M DAU, 55% on devices with 3-4 GB RAM. Android vitals reports cold start p90 at 3.4 s; Play's "excessive" threshold is 5 s we are under it , but product wants p90 below 2.2 s. Application.onCreate is 410 ms on a Redmi-class device Perfetto . Eight SDKs analytics, crash, ads, attribution, chat, maps, payments, feature flags each initialize in Application.onCreate , and three of them also add their own <provider . Before onCreate even starts, Perfetto shows 260 ms in installContentProviders . Home screen first frame at 1.1 s after onCreate . A second red herring: a BOOT COMPLETED receiver also triggers the same init.

title: Manifest merge / security
text: Run the post-incident review: how did it happen, how do you contain it, and how do you prevent it? Release 12.0 of a ride-hailing app 3M DAU was flagged by a pentest two weeks after rollout: another installed app can launch com.app.sdk.DebugOverlayActivity and a PushReceiver with crafted extras, reading the user's last-trip data in a log. The exported components are not in our source tree. Also Play Console warned about a new READ PHONE STATE permission. We upgraded an analytics SDK from 4.1 to 4.2 in this release. The debug manifest in CI looked fine; the release build uses a different flavor dependency releaseImplementation .

title: Locale override
text: What are the bugs and what is the right design? A matrimony app 1.2M DAU, 60% Hindi/regional shipped an in-app language picker. Support tickets: "I chose Hindi but notifications and the home-screen widget are English", and "after rotation, dialogs flip to English on Android 12". Code: class BaseActivity : AppCompatActivity { override fun attachBaseContext newBase: Context { val cfg = Configuration newBase.resources.configuration cfg.setLocale Locale.forLanguageTag Prefs.lang // Prefs uses a lateinit Application super.attachBaseContext newBase.createConfigurationContext cfg } } class NotifBuilder private val app: Application { fun title = app.getString R.string.match title } Crashlytics also shows a rare UninitializedPropertyAccessException: lateinit property app has not been initialized from Prefs , mostly from BaseActivity.attachBaseContext on Android 7-8 during process restore.

title: Night mode / context theming
text: Diagnose it, fix it, and explain why QA missed it. After adding an in-app Light/Dark/System toggle AppCompatDelegate.setDefaultNightMode , support receives screenshots: users who set app = Dark while system = Light see a dark screen with unreadable dark-grey text in the "Payment methods" bottom sheet and the toast-like snackbar helper. 9% of sessions use that sheet. System=Dark + app=Light shows the opposite. Helper code: class SheetHelper private val context: Context { // constructed with applicationContext fun inflate : View = LayoutInflater.from context .inflate R.layout.sheet payment, null fun textColor = context.getColor R.color.text primary } R.color.text primary has a values-night variant. QA tested only with matching system and app settings.

title: Bundles / language splits
text: What is happening and what is the durable fix? App on Play as an AAB, 4M MAU, with an in-app language picker en, hi, ta, te, bn, mr . After release 9.4 built with AGP 8.x, nothing in the bundle config changed , Crashlytics shows Resources$NotFoundException rate 0.3% and a flood of support tickets: "app is in English after I chose Tamil", concentrated on users whose system language is English 91% of reports . Fresh installs on internal test tracks look fine; the QA team always installs with a Tamil system language. The universal APK built by CI works for everyone. A new config.ta.apk split appears for only some users in Play Console device catalog.

title: Task removal vs process death vs configuration change
text: A user swipes your app away in Recents. Is that the same as the process being killed, and what survives in each case: rotation, swipe-away, and low-memory kill? "Three different events. Rotation recreates the Activity but the process and ViewModel survive. Swipe from Recents removes the task, finishes its activities and, on stock Android, usually kills the process unless something like a foreground service holds it; saved instance state is gone because the task is gone. A low-memory kill takes only the process while the task stays in Recents, so the user comes back to a restored back stack with a fresh process and the saved Bundle. Each needs a different test."

title: Process death + singleton
text: Find the root cause, reproduce it, and fix it so a user returning after an hour does not crash. A shopping app 300K DAU, mid-range devices shows a crash cluster in Crashlytics: 1.2% of sessions, almost entirely Android 13/14, only when the app is resumed after 30 min in background. Stack: java.lang.IllegalStateException: Session not initialised at com.shop.auth.SessionManager.requireToken SessionManager.kt:22 at com.shop.cart.CartViewModel.refresh CartViewModel.kt:41 at com.shop.cart.CartFragment.onViewCreated CartFragment.kt:58 The code: object SessionManager { private var token: String? = null fun login t: String { token = t } // called from LoginActivity fun requireToken : String = token ?: throw IllegalStateException "Session not initialised" } class CartFragment : Fragment R.layout.fragment cart { private val vm: CartViewModel by viewModels override fun onViewCreated v: View, s: Bundle? { vm.refresh } } QA cannot reproduce on emulator; "it works when I rotate". Red herring: crash rate jumped the week a new image-library update shipped.

title: Config change during network call
text: Why do duplicates happen and how do you fix it end to end? A food-order app 80K DAU shows a "Place order" button. Support tickets: 0.4% of orders are duplicated, charged twice. Backend logs show two POST /orders within 1.5 s from the same session. The button handler: class CheckoutActivity : AppCompatActivity { private var inFlight = false override fun onCreate s: Bundle? { super.onCreate s binding.pay.setOnClickListener { if inFlight return@setOnClickListener inFlight = true lifecycleScope.launch { api.placeOrder cart // 2-4 s on slow networks inFlight = false showSuccess } } } } Tickets mostly mention "I rotated my phone" or "I switched dark mode". Red herring: backend also retries on 5xx via the gateway.

title: Notification action + PendingIntent
text: Explain both bugs and design the fix. A messaging app 1.1M DAU shows a "Mark as read" action on notifications. Analytics: 3% of "mark as read" actions processed twice, and "Reply" sends the previous message's text on some devices. Code: val intent = Intent ctx, NotificationActionReceiver::class.java .setAction "com.chat.MARK READ" .putExtra "conversationId", convo.id val pi = PendingIntent.getBroadcast ctx, 0, intent, PendingIntent.FLAG UPDATE CURRENT or PendingIntent.FLAG IMMUTABLE builder.addAction R.drawable.ic check, "Mark read", pi Server logs show action requests arriving 40-300 ms apart. Targets API 34. Red herring: users on a flaky network.

title: Exported receivers audit
text: Plan the audit and the bump without breaking partners who legitimately send you broadcasts. The security team flags your app after a pentest. Findings: a manifest receiver PaymentResultReceiver has an intent filter and no exported attribute; a dynamically registered receiver DownloadDoneReceiver accepts broadcasts from any app; a service SyncService is exported with no permission. You also plan to bump targetSdk 33 - 34 next sprint. QA's smoke run on an Android 14 build after the bump produced: java.lang.SecurityException: com.shop: One of RECEIVER EXPORTED or RECEIVER NOT EXPORTED should be specified when a receiver isn't being registered exclusively for system broadcasts at android.app.ContextImpl.registerReceiverInternal Red herring: the crash only occurs on Android 14 devices.

title: Permission revoked in Settings
text: What is happening and how do you make the app robust to permission changes while it is running or backgrounded? A photo-scanner app 200K DAU crashes for 0.8% of users in the camera screen with: java.lang.SecurityException: Permission Denial: opening provider ... or java.lang.RuntimeException: Fail to connect to camera service at android.hardware.Camera.<init Support: "I turned off camera in Settings, switched back, app crashed / lost my work". Some reports say the app restarted with a blank screen. Red herring: the crash also shows on devices whose camera is in use by another app.

title: Reproducing platform-state bugs
text: Your crash dashboard shows issues that QA cannot reproduce. Give me a repeatable matrix of platform conditions to try before declaring "cannot reproduce". "I run the app under six forced conditions: process death, activity recreation, configuration changes, background restrictions, permission changes, and low memory. Each has a one-liner: Don't keep activities, am kill , wm density/size , locale and dark mode switches, cmd appops / pm revoke , and am send-trim-memory . If the crash correlates with time in background or with a specific OS version, I pick the condition from that signal."

title: Deep link + task model
text: Explain what the task system is doing and propose the fix. A news app 2M DAU sends push notifications with an https://news.example/article/123 deep link. Users report: tapping the notification while the app is open opens a second ArticleActivity on top; Back then walks through duplicate screens; from a cold start, Back exits to the launcher instead of the home feed. A habit-tracker app 500K DAU targets API 34 and schedules reminders: alarmManager.setExactAndAllowWhileIdle AlarmManager.RTC WAKEUP, triggerAt, pi Crash cluster on fresh installs on Android 14 2.3% of new users : java.lang.SecurityException: Caller com.habit needs to hold android.permission.SCHEDULE EXACT ALARM or android.permission.USE EXACT ALARM to set exact alarms. title: Standby buckets + FCM

Support: "after 3-4 days of not opening the app, data is stale for hours and syncs only after we open it." title: End-to-end: notification tap after process death
text: A user taps a notification two hours after the app was last used. Walk through everything the system and your app do from the tap to the first rendered frame, naming each platform component and each place state can be lost. "SystemUI fires the PendingIntent, which asks ActivityTaskManager to start the target activity. If no process exists, AMS asks Zygote to fork one, the process runs ActivityThread, creates the Application providers first , then the Activity gets created with whatever saved state the system holds. Any state in memory, singletons, or ViewModels is gone, so the screen must rebuild from the intent, saved state and persistent storage."

title: Post-incident review of a platform-blind release
text: Run the post-incident review. What went wrong at the platform-awareness level and what do you change? Release 8.4 targetSdk 34, 1.8M DAU went to 100% in 3 days, then a rollback. Timeline: day 1 crash-free users 99.7% - 98.9% on Android 14; day 2 ANR rate 0.3% - 1.1% on low-RAM devices; day 3 support spike: "notifications don't open the right chat" and "music stops after locking screen". Changes in the release: targetSdk bump, a new analytics SDK, a refactor moving the token into a singleton, and Media3 migration. Staged rollout was skipped due to a marketing date. QA ran on two Pixel emulators, API 33 and 34.

title: Background location requirement
text: Turn this into a workable platform design and push back where needed. Product says: "Our delivery app must track the courier's location continuously, even when the phone is locked or the app is closed, and it must be battery friendly, and it must not scare users with permission prompts." Fleet: 25K couriers on personal devices, Android 10-14, shifts of 6-8 h. Play review rejected the last submission for background location justification. Prior implementation: a started service plus wakelock; battery drain complaints at 18%/h on mid-range phones.

title: Background execution evolution (API 23 to 15)
text: Walk me through how Android's background-execution rules evolved from Doze to Android 15, and give me a decision rule for choosing between a foreground service, WorkManager, an alarm and FCM today. "Each release tightened what runs without the user: Doze in 6, background service limits in 8, background-start limits and FGS-start restrictions in 12, typed FGS and exact-alarm gating in 13/14, timeouts and boot limits in 15. Today: visible, user-started, ongoing work is a typed foreground service; deferrable, guaranteed work is WorkManager; a time-critical user-facing moment is an alarm or high-priority FCM; and server-triggered work is FCM."

title: Runtime memory areas
text: Walk me through the memory areas of a running HotSpot JVM. Which of them are inside -Xmx and which are not? I split it into heap, which -Xmx caps, and everything else, which it does not cap. Heap holds objects and arrays. Outside it: Metaspace for class metadata, the code cache for JIT-compiled code, one stack per thread, direct and mapped buffers, and GC and JVM internal structures. The process RSS is the sum of all of that, so the container limit has to cover the whole sum, not just -Xmx.

title: Stack vs heap
text: What exactly lives on the stack and what lives on the heap in Java? What causes StackOverflowError, and can you size the stack? Each thread has its own stack of frames; a frame holds local variables, the operand stack and return info. Primitives and references live in frames; every object and array lives on the heap escape analysis can sometimes eliminate the allocation, but that is an optimisation, not a semantic . StackOverflowError means the thread's stack ran out, normally from unbounded or very deep recursion. Size it with -Xss or -XX:ThreadStackSize ; default is 1 MB on Linux x64.

title: Class loading
text: Explain how a class gets loaded in the JVM: the phases, the loader hierarchy and parent delegation. Why does delegation exist? Loading reads the bytes and creates the Class; linking verifies, prepares static defaults and resolves; initialization runs static initializers, lazily, on first active use. Loaders delegate to their parent first, so core classes like java.lang.String always come from the bootstrap loader and cannot be spoofed by application code.

title: Object layout
text: How many bytes does new Object take on a 64-bit JVM? What is in an object header, and how much does an Integer , an int 1 , and an object with two int fields cost? On HotSpot 64-bit with default compressed class pointers, the header is 12 bytes 8-byte mark word plus 4-byte class pointer , and objects are aligned to 8 bytes, so new Object is 16 bytes. Integer is 12 + 4 = 16 bytes, an int 1 is 12 + 4 length + 4 data = 20, rounded to 24, and a two-int object is 12 + 8 = 20, rounded to 24. Without compressed class pointers the header is 16 bytes.

title: Compressed oops
text: What are compressed oops? Why do teams say "don't go above 32 GB heap", and what actually happens at that boundary? With compressed oops the JVM stores object references as 32-bit values, shifted left by 3 because objects are 8-byte aligned, so 32 bits address 2^35 bytes, about 32 GB. Cross that and references become 64-bit, which makes every reference field and array of references twice as large. A 33 GB heap can hold less live data than a 31 GB heap.

title: Container memory
text: Explain what is happening and how you would fix it. A Spring Boot order service runs on Kubernetes Java 17, G1 with resources.limits.memory: 2Gi and JAVA OPTS=-Xms2g -Xmx2g . Since Monday's release new Netty-based HTTP client and a larger Caffeine cache pods restart every 6-10 hours. kubectl describe pod shows Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137 . The application log has no OutOfMemoryError. Grafana's jvm memory used bytes{area="heap"} peaks at 1.4 GB. Traffic is 400 RPS, steady. A colleague says "Java is leaking, let's add -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError ".

title: JIT tiers
text: Explain HotSpot's tiered compilation. What are the tiers, what triggers promotion, and why does a Java service get faster after minutes of running? Code starts in the interpreter, which also collects counters. Hot methods go to C1 quick, lightly optimised , at level 3 with full profiling, and the hottest go to C2 slow to compile, heavily optimised using that profile at level 4. Performance rises as C2 finishes compiling the real hot paths, which is why a cold JVM is slow for the first seconds to minutes.

title: Metaspace and class unloading
text: What is stored in Metaspace, how does it grow and shrink, and when can a class actually be unloaded? Metaspace holds class metadata: method bytecode, constant pools, field and method descriptors, vtables. It lives in native memory and is unlimited by default, so unbounded class generation grows it until the OS stops you. A class is unloaded only when its defining class loader becomes unreachable and a GC cycle notices, so classes from the bootstrap, platform or app loaders effectively never unload.

title: Direct memory and off-heap
text: What is direct off-heap memory in Java? Why do Netty and Kafka clients use it, how is it freed, and how is it limited? ByteBuffer.allocateDirect allocates native memory outside the heap, avoiding a copy between a heap array and the kernel when doing I/O and keeping big buffers out of the GC's way. The JVM frees it only when the small heap-side DirectByteBuffer object is collected and its cleaner runs, so a quiet heap can delay freeing of lots of native memory. The total is capped by -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize , which when unset defaults to roughly the max heap size verify your version .

title: JIT warmup
text: Why do new pods perform badly, and what do you change? A Java 17 payment-lookup service G1, 4 vCPU request, limit 4 vCPU, 4 GiB averages p99 = 60 ms. HPA scales from 6 to 24 pods at a peak. Each new pod becomes Ready 25 s after start readiness probe hits /health , receives its fair share of traffic immediately, and for the first 2 minutes shows p99 = 900 ms and 10% timeouts client timeout 500 ms . Cluster-wide p99 triples during every scale-up. GC logs of new pods look normal young pauses 10-20 ms . CPU on new pods is pegged at 100% of limit for the first minute, then falls to 55%. A teammate wants to "tune G1".

title: Escape analysis
text: What is escape analysis in the JVM, and what does it enable? Does Java allocate objects on the stack? C2 analyses whether an object can be seen outside the method or thread that created it. If it cannot escape, C2 can eliminate the allocation by scalar replacement, splitting the object into its fields held in registers, and can remove locks on it lock elision . HotSpot does not do true stack allocation of objects; it removes the object entirely, and only when it can prove non-escape after inlining.

title: Object layout and footprint
text: Why is the live set so much larger than 800 MB, and what would you do? An ad-tech service keeps an in-memory lookup Map<Long, Long user id - segment bitmask refreshed daily. It holds 50 million entries. The service runs on Java 17 with G1 and a 16 GB heap; young pauses are 40-80 ms and full-heap marking takes several seconds. The team proposes moving to a 32 GB node and a 24 GB heap "because the map takes about 800 MB 50M x 16 bytes ". Observed live set after refresh is about 4.5 GB.

title: CDS, AppCDS and AOT cache
text: What is Class Data Sharing CDS/AppCDS , and how does it relate to the newer AOT cache? When would you use them for a containerised service? CDS stores pre-parsed, pre-verified class metadata in a memory-mapped archive so the JVM skips parsing and verification at startup and can share the pages between processes.
