The rules are the same as wait/notify: hold the lock, and always check the predicate in a loop.

title: tryLock / interruptible
text: How do you stop the cascade, and how would you redesign the lock usage? An order-matching API 800 RPS, 64 request threads on 8 vCPUs updates a per-account balance under a ReentrantLock per account. A batch job occasionally holds a hot account's lock for 4 s while recalculating. During it, request p99 climbs from 60 ms to 8 s, the thread pool saturates, the load balancer health check 2 s timeout fails and pods are restarted, making things worse. Thread dump excerpt: 60 threads WAITING parking at ReentrantLock.lock ReentrantLock.java . CPU is 15%.

title: ReadWriteLock
text: Why does it hang and how do you fix it? A config registry uses a ReentrantReadWriteLock . In staging all tests pass. In production, shortly after 20 threads began calling getOrLoad under traffic, the service hangs: no CPU, requests time out, and jstack shows threads WAITING in ReentrantReadWriteLock$WriteLock.lock , with the same threads also holding read locks. private final ReentrantReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock ; private final Map<String, Config map = new HashMap< ; Config getOrLoad String key { rw.readLock .lock ; try { Config c = map.get key ; if c == null { rw.writeLock .lock ; // "upgrade" try { c = load key ; map.put key, c ; } finally { rw.writeLock .unlock ; } } return c; } finally { rw.readLock .unlock ; } }

title: ReadWriteLock
text: What are the semantics of ReentrantReadWriteLock , and when does it actually help versus a plain lock? Many threads can hold the read lock at once, but the write lock is exclusive and excludes readers. It helps when reads are frequent, the read critical section is long enough to amortise the lock's overhead, and writes are rare. It does not support upgrading read to write, supports downgrading, and under heavy read load writers can be delayed. For short read sections, an immutable snapshot, volatile , or a concurrent collection usually beats it.

title: StampedLock
text: Explain StampedLock : optimistic reads, the three modes, and why it is dangerous to adopt casually. StampedLock returns a long stamp for every acquisition. Besides write and read locks it offers an optimistic read: tryOptimisticRead takes no lock at all, I read fields into locals, then validate stamp tells me whether a write happened in between. If validation fails I fall back to a real read lock. It is not reentrant, has no Condition s, and the optimistic path can observe inconsistent data until validated, so it needs careful code.

title: StampedLock
text: Identify every bug and describe the fix. A 16-core market-data service holds a mutable Quote bid, ask in a StampedLock . Reads run at 1.2M/s, writes 2k/s. After a refactor, a rare ArithmeticException: / by zero and occasional negative spreads appear, about 5 per hour, and one pod hung with 3 threads WAITING on StampedLock.readLock . class Quote { private double bid, ask; private int levels; private final StampedLock sl = new StampedLock ; double avgPerLevel { long s = sl.tryOptimisticRead ; double spread = ask - bid; double r = spread / levels; // levels may be 0 transiently if sl.validate s return r; s = sl.readLock ; try { return ask - bid / levels; } finally { sl.unlockRead s ; } } void update double b, double a, int l { long s = sl.writeLock ; try { bid = b; ask = a; levels = l; refresh ; } finally { sl.unlockWrite s ; } } void refresh { long s = sl.readLock ; // called inside update try { / recompute derived cache / } finally { sl.unlockRead s ; } } }

title: Lock granularity / striping
text: How do you scale it, and what are the traps in each option? A rate-limiter service keeps per-API-key counters in a HashMap<String, Counter guarded by one synchronized block. At 5k RPS on a 4-core pod it was fine lock hold 1 microsecond . Marketing expects 10x. In a load test at 40k RPS on 8 cores, throughput plateaus at 18k RPS, CPU shows 35%, and async-profiler lock mode attributes 70% of wait time to that one monitor. There are 200k distinct keys.

title: Lock ordering
text: Explain the deadlock, fix it, and make it robust for 3+ accounts. A wallet service transfers money between accounts. Each Account has its own ReentrantLock . At peak 1.5k transfers/s the service periodically freezes: p99 jumps from 80 ms to timeouts, CPU drops to 5%, and jcmd Thread.print ends with "Found one Java-level deadlock" listing two request threads, each owning one account's lock and waiting for the other's. void transfer Account from, Account to, long amt { from.lock.lock ; try { to.lock.lock ; try { from.debit amt ; to.credit amt ; } finally { to.lock.unlock ; } } finally { from.lock.unlock ; } } Thread A runs transfer x, y while thread B runs transfer y, x . After the deadlock, subsequent requests touching x or y queue up, and the pool of 200 threads saturates in under 90 seconds.

title: Semaphore
text: What is a Semaphore , and how would you use it to bound concurrency to a downstream dependency? A Semaphore holds a count of permits. acquire takes one blocking if none , release returns one. Unlike a lock, permits are not owned by a thread, so any thread can release. I use it to cap the number of concurrent calls to a limited resource, such as 20 in-flight calls to a payment provider. I always acquire before try and release in finally , and I prefer tryAcquire with a timeout so callers fail fast instead of piling up.

title: CountDownLatch vs CyclicBarrier
text: What is the difference between CountDownLatch and CyclicBarrier ? Give a use for each. CountDownLatch is a one-shot gate: threads call await until the count reaches zero through countDown calls, and it can't be reset. The counting threads and waiting threads can be different. CyclicBarrier makes a fixed set of N threads wait for each other at a rendezvous point; when the Nth arrives all are released, an optional barrier action runs, and the barrier resets for the next round.

title: Phaser
text: What does Phaser offer that CyclicBarrier and CountDownLatch don't? When would you reach for it? Phaser is a reusable barrier with a dynamic number of parties. Threads can register and deregister at any time, it tracks a phase number that advances each time all registered parties arrive, you can override onAdvance to run code at each phase and decide termination, and it supports arrive-without-waiting. It also supports a tree of phasers to reduce contention. I'd use it when the participant set changes over time, such as a recursive fork/join-style computation; for a fixed set of N workers, CyclicBarrier is simpler.

title: CountDownLatch
text: Diagnose and fix. What else would you change? A service starts 5 warm-up tasks cache load, config fetch, JIT warmup requests, etc. and blocks the readiness probe on a latch. Since a release on Tuesday, about 1 in 30 pod starts never becomes ready; the orchestrator kills them after 10 minutes and restarts them, making deployments take 40 minutes instead of 6. Logs show 4 tasks finishing; the fifth printed java.net.SocketTimeoutException: Read timed out once and then nothing. jstack shows main parked in CountDownLatch.await . CountDownLatch ready = new CountDownLatch 5 ; for Runnable t : warmups { pool.submit - { t.run ; // may throw ready.countDown ; } ; } ready.await ; // readiness waits here

title: synchronized vs ReentrantLock on virtual threads
text: Why is virtual-thread throughput capped, what do you do on JDK 21, and what changes on newer JDKs? A team migrates a Tomcat/Spring service from a 200-thread platform pool to virtual threads on JDK 21, expecting to handle 5x concurrency. After canary at 20% traffic, throughput stalls near the old number, and p99 grows from 120 ms to 900 ms. CPU is 30%. JFR shows many jdk.VirtualThreadPinned events with stack frames inside a vendor SDK's synchronized method that does a 150 ms blocking HTTP call. The DB pool maximum 30 is not exhausted.

title: Choosing the right tool
text: You need to coordinate threads: how do you decide between synchronized , ReentrantLock , ReadWriteLock / StampedLock , Semaphore , latches/barriers, and higher-level structures? Walk me through your decision process. I start by asking whether I need shared mutable state at all; immutable data, confinement, or a concurrent collection often removes the lock. If I do need mutual exclusion, I use synchronized by default for simplicity and move to ReentrantLock only for tryLock , interruptibility, fairness or multiple conditions. Read-write locks and StampedLock come only after profiling shows read contention on long-enough read sections. Semaphores bound concurrency, latches signal one-time events, barriers and phasers synchronise rounds. And for handoff between threads I prefer a BlockingQueue over hand-built wait/notify.

title: CAS and atomics
text: What is compare-and-swap, and how do the java.util.concurrent.atomic classes use it to be thread-safe without locks? CAS is a single CPU instruction: "set this memory location to NEW only if it currently equals EXPECTED, and tell me whether it worked". Atomic classes wrap a volatile field and run a loop: read the current value, compute the new one, CAS it in, retry if another thread got there first. No thread ever blocks or sleeps, so there is no lock to hold or deadlock on, but under heavy contention threads burn CPU on retries.

title: volatile vs atomic
text: volatile int count; count++ from 10 threads loses updates. Why, and what are the fixes? volatile guarantees visibility and ordering, not atomicity. count++ is three steps: read, add, write. Two threads can both read 5 and both write 6, losing an increment. Fix with AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet , LongAdder for hot counters, or a lock.

title: ABA problem
text: What is the ABA problem in CAS-based algorithms, and how do you solve it in Java? CAS only checks "is it still equal to what I read". If another thread changes A to B and back to A, my CAS succeeds although the state changed underneath me, which can corrupt structures like lock-free stacks that reuse nodes. In Java, AtomicStampedReference pairs the reference with an int version stamp, and AtomicMarkableReference pairs it with a boolean. Garbage collection already removes the worst form of ABA, because a node cannot be reused while someone still references it.

title: LongAdder vs AtomicLong
text: When would you use LongAdder instead of AtomicLong , and what is the cost? AtomicLong is one variable that every thread CASes, so under heavy write contention threads fight over one cache line and retry. LongAdder keeps a base plus a lazily grown array of cells; each thread tends to hit its own cell, so adds scale with cores. Reading with sum adds all cells, is not an atomic snapshot, and the class uses more memory. Use it for write-heavy, read-rarely statistics counters, not for sequence generators or anything needing compare-and-set.

title: AtomicReference and immutable state
text: How do you update a multi-field piece of shared state atomically without a lock? Explain the AtomicReference pattern and its limits. Put all the related fields in one immutable object and keep it in an AtomicReference . To update, read the reference, build a new object from it, and compareAndSet old, new in a loop. Readers always see a consistent snapshot. The limits: the update function must be pure and cheap because it may run multiple times, writers can livelock-ish under contention, and each update allocates.

title: Check-then-act on ConcurrentHashMap
text: What is wrong, how do you fix it, and what would you NOT do? A service caches per-tenant rate limiters. Under load 8 Tomcat threads per pod, 1,200 RPS , you notice that two requests for a new tenant sometimes end up with different limiter instances and the tenant exceeds quota by up to 2x right after first access. The code: private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, RateLimiter limiters = new ConcurrentHashMap< ; RateLimiter limiterFor String tenant { if !limiters.containsKey tenant { limiters.put tenant, RateLimiter.create 100 ; // 100 permits/s } return limiters.get tenant ; } The map is thread-safe, tests pass, and a code reviewer said "it's a ConcurrentHashMap, it's fine". Another dev suggests wrapping the method in synchronized .

title: ConcurrentHashMap internals
text: How does ConcurrentHashMap work internally in Java 8+, and how is it different from the Java 7 design? Java 7 split the table into 16 Segment s, each a lock. Java 8 removed segments: there is one array of bins. Inserting into an empty bin is a lock-free CAS of the first node; if the bin is occupied, I synchronized on that bin's head node, so writers only contend when they hit the same bin. Reads get take no locks and rely on volatile fields. Long bins turn into red-black trees, and resize is cooperative: threads that hit a moved bin help transfer it.

title: Hashtable vs synchronizedMap vs ConcurrentHashMap
text: Compare Hashtable , Collections.synchronizedMap new HashMap< and ConcurrentHashMap . Which do you use and why? Hashtable and synchronizedMap guard every method with one lock the object's monitor or a mutex , so all threads serialize, and iterating still requires manual locking. ConcurrentHashMap allows concurrent reads without locks and concurrent writes to different bins, offers atomic compound operations computeIfAbsent , merge , and has weakly consistent iterators that never throw ConcurrentModificationException . I default to ConcurrentHashMap for shared maps.

title: ConcurrentHashMap size and consistency
text: What does ConcurrentHashMap.size actually return under concurrent updates, and what are mappingCount and weakly consistent iterators? How should you use them in production? size is an estimate under concurrent modification: it sums a base counter and striped counter cells without freezing writers, so by the time it returns it may be stale. The Javadoc says such methods are suitable for monitoring, not program control. mappingCount is the same estimate as a long , preferred for huge maps. Iterators are weakly consistent: they traverse elements as they existed at creation and may or may not reflect later changes, but never throw CME or return an element twice.

title: computeIfAbsent pitfalls
text: Diagnose and fix. A pricing service Java 17, 16 vCPU, 4 GB heap, 2,500 RPS memoizes expensive rule evaluations: ConcurrentHashMap<String, Rule rules = new ConcurrentHashMap< ; Rule resolve String id { return rules.computeIfAbsent id, k - { Rule r = loadFromDb k ; // 120 ms, p99 900 ms for String dep : r.dependencies r.link resolve dep ; // recursive, same map return r; } ; } After a deploy that added rules with dependencies, p99 jumped from 80 ms to 12 s for some tenants, CPU on two pods sat at 100% and a few request threads never returned. jstack shows several threads in ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent and others BLOCKED / RUNNABLE in ConcurrentHashMap.transfer and ConcurrentHashMap.putVal . Heap and GC are normal. Someone says "the DB is slow".

title: CopyOnWriteArrayList
text: How does CopyOnWriteArrayList work and when is it the right or wrong choice? It stores elements in an array that's never modified in place. Every write takes a lock, copies the whole array, applies the change, and swaps the volatile reference. Readers just read the current array reference, lock-free. Iterators work on the array snapshot at creation, so they never throw CME and never see later writes. It's ideal for small, read-mostly collections like listener lists; terrible for write-heavy or large ones, since each write is O n and allocates.

title: ConcurrentModificationException
text: Why does ConcurrentModificationException happen, even in single-threaded code? How do fail-fast and weakly consistent iterators differ? ArrayList / HashMap keep a modCount that every structural change increments; the iterator remembers the value at creation and checks it on next . If the collection changed by anything other than the iterator itself, it throws CME. That can happen on one thread removing inside a for-each . It's best-effort detection, not a thread-safety guarantee. Concurrent collections use weakly consistent iterators: no CME, they reflect some state at or after creation.

title: BlockingQueue family
text: Walk through the BlockingQueue implementations ArrayBlockingQueue , LinkedBlockingQueue , PriorityBlockingQueue , LinkedTransferQueue , LinkedBlockingDeque and how you'd choose among them. ArrayBlockingQueue is a bounded ring buffer with one lock for both ends. LinkedBlockingQueue is linked nodes with separate put and take locks, optionally bounded default capacity is Integer.MAX VALUE , effectively unbounded . PriorityBlockingQueue is unbounded and orders by priority. LinkedBlockingDeque is a double-ended, bounded-optional queue. LinkedTransferQueue is unbounded and lock-free with transfer handoff. I choose bounded for backpressure, and unbounded only if the producer is naturally limited.

title: Executor queue choice
text: Explain what happened and redesign. A notification service Java 17, 2 GB container, -Xmx1g , 3 pods uses Executors.newFixedThreadPool 16 to send emails/webhooks. A partner SMTP gateway degrades: each send goes from 40 ms to 8 s. Inbound rate stays 600 tasks/s. Over 25 minutes: heap climbs from 300 MB to 1 GB, GC logs show repeated full GCs Pause Full G1 Compaction Pause 950ms , then java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space , pods restart, and the queued notifications are lost. CPU was low throughout; the API itself returned 200 to callers the whole time. The team's first idea: "double the pool to 32 threads".

title: SynchronousQueue and DelayQueue
text: What are SynchronousQueue and DelayQueue , how do they work, and where are they used inside the JDK or in real designs? SynchronousQueue has zero capacity: a put blocks until a take arrives and vice versa, a direct handoff. Executors.newCachedThreadPool uses it, so a task either goes to an idle thread or triggers a new thread. DelayQueue is an unbounded priority queue of Delayed elements; take blocks until the head's delay has expired, so items come out in expiry order. It is a natural fit for expiring entries, retries with backoff, and simple timers.

title: ConcurrentLinkedQueue and non-blocking queues
text: How does ConcurrentLinkedQueue work, and when would you choose it over a LinkedBlockingQueue ? ConcurrentLinkedQueue is an unbounded, non-blocking FIFO queue based on the Michael-Scott algorithm: head and tail pointers advanced with CAS, no locks. offer and poll never block, so consumers must handle "empty" themselves spin, sleep, or park . size is O n because it traverses. I choose it for many producers/consumers needing minimal latency with no need for blocking or capacity; when consumers should wait or I need backpressure, I use a BlockingQueue .

title: Disruptor and ring buffers
text: What is the LMAX Disruptor idea, and why can it outperform ArrayBlockingQueue for some workloads? When would you not use it? The Disruptor is a pre-allocated ring buffer with sequence numbers instead of locks. Producers claim a slot by incrementing a sequence, write into a reused event object, then publish; consumers track their own sequence and wait using a configurable strategy busy-spin, yield, block . Wins come from no locks, no per-event allocation, power-of-two index masking, cache-friendly sequential memory, and padding sequence counters to avoid false sharing. I'd use it for single-digit-microsecond pipelines trading, high-rate event processing ; for ordinary services a blocking queue is simpler and fast enough.

title: Producer-consumer design
text: Design the producer-consumer pipeline: queue type and size, consumer count, batching, shutdown, and failure handling. You are designing an ingestion stage: an HTTP endpoint receives 4,000 events/s peaks 12,000/s for 30 s , each event needs a 15 ms enrichment remote call and then a batched DB insert 500 rows per insert, 40 ms . The pod has 4 vCPU, 2 GB RAM, -Xmx1200m . The previous version used new Thread ... per event, then a switch to an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue with 8 consumers; staging OOMed after a peak. Latency target for the HTTP call is p99 < 200 ms; events may be dropped only with an explicit 429. Events cannot be lost once accepted HTTP 202 .

title: Collections.synchronizedX
text: What does Collections.synchronizedList give you, and what does it not? What are the compound-operation and iteration pitfalls? It wraps each method in synchronized mutex , so individual operations are atomic and visible. But compound actions check-then-add, get-then-set, iteration are not atomic unless I hold the same mutex around the whole sequence. Iterating without synchronized list can throw CME or see inconsistent data. For read-mostly use CopyOnWriteArrayList ; for maps use ConcurrentHashMap .

title: Lock-free progress guarantees
text: Explain the difference between blocking, obstruction-free, lock-free and wait-free algorithms, and where the JDK's structures fall. Blocking: a stalled thread holding a lock can stall everyone. Lock-free: some thread always makes progress in a finite number of steps, though a given thread can retry indefinitely. Wait-free: every thread finishes in a bounded number of steps. Obstruction-free: a thread completes if it runs alone. CAS-loop structures like AtomicInteger.updateAndGet , ConcurrentLinkedQueue are lock-free; getAndIncrement on x86 LOCK XADD and LongAdder.add in the uncontended path are effectively wait-free per op; ConcurrentHashMap.get is wait-free for readers in practice, but writes use locks.

title: LongAdder for hot counters
text: How do you confirm the diagnosis and what would you change? What are the risks? A gateway Java 17, 32 vCPU pod, 6,000 RPS per pod, 200 worker threads records per-request stats in a shared class: AtomicLong totalRequests , AtomicLong totalBytes , AtomicLong errors , all incremented on every request. CPU is 70% with p99 at 45 ms; the SLO is 30 ms and the team wants to avoid adding pods each costs about 1,400 USD/month; 40 pods . An async-profiler CPU flame graph -e cpu shows 11% of samples in AtomicLong.incrementAndGet / Unsafe.getAndAddLong frames, and perf stat shows a high cache-miss rate. A teammate proposes sharding the counters by hand with an array indexed by threadId % 8 .

title: Blocking inside compute
text: Why did a 97% hit rate not protect you, and what would you change? An inventory service Java 21, 8 vCPU, Tomcat with 200 threads uses a ConcurrentHashMap<Long, Product as a read-through cache of 2 million SKUs table size 4M bins : Product get long sku { return cache.computeIfAbsent sku, id - catalogClient.fetch id ; // HTTP, 30 ms typical } During a catalog slowdown fetch 30 ms - 4 s p99 , the service's p99 goes from 60 ms to 25 s, all 200 Tomcat threads are busy, and /health times out so Kubernetes restarts pods. Thread dumps show 190 threads blocked in ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent , 6 threads in SocketInputStream.read . Hit rate is 97%. Someone says: "97% hit rate, so the lock shouldn't matter".

title: Consumer shutdown and poison pill
text: Find the bugs and give a correct shutdown protocol. A batch exporter uses one producer thread filling a BlockingQueue<Row capacity 1,000 and 4 consumer threads writing to S3. On completion the main thread should flush and exit. In production the job sometimes hangs forever after the producer finishes about 1 run in 20 , and at other times it exits but the last 800 rows are missing. Code: volatile boolean done = false; BlockingQueue<Row q = new LinkedBlockingQueue< 1000 ; // consumer while !done { Row r = q.take ; write r ; } // main producer.join ; done = true; pool.shutdownNow ; jstack of the hung run shows consumers in LinkedBlockingQueue.take / AbstractQueuedSynchronizer$ConditionObject.await . An engineer suggests changing take to poll in a loop.

title: ConcurrentSkipListMap
text: What is ConcurrentSkipListMap , how does a skip list give you a concurrent sorted map, and when do you prefer it over ConcurrentHashMap or a synchronized TreeMap ? It's a lock-free sorted map and ConcurrentSkipListSet the set version built on a skip list: layered linked lists where higher layers skip over many nodes, giving expected O log n get/put/remove. Skip lists are easier to make concurrent than balanced trees because inserts and deletes touch only local pointers via CAS and never need global rebalancing. I use it when I need ordered iteration or range queries headMap , ceilingKey , subMap under concurrency; otherwise ConcurrentHashMap is faster and lighter.

title: Hot key and hash contention
text: Why does it plateau, will the larger capacity help, and what is your design? A real-time ad service Java 21, 16 vCPU, 300 worker threads tracks per-campaign spend in ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long spend using spend.merge campaignId, cents, Long::sum . Today: 20k merges/s, p99 4 ms. Marketing plans a launch expected to give 10x traffic with one flagship campaign receiving about 60% of impressions. Load test at 10x 200k merges/s, 120k/s on one key : p99 jumps to 180 ms, CPU in ConcurrentHashMap.merge and monitorenter frames rises, throughput plateaus at 90k/s. Table has 5,000 campaigns. A teammate suggests increasing the CHM initial capacity to 64k "to reduce collisions".

title: CopyOnWrite and snapshot semantics
text: Lead the post-incident review: root causes, contributing factors, why CME appeared elsewhere, and corrective actions. Post-incident review. An event-routing service kept subscriber callbacks in a CopyOnWriteArrayList<Subscriber . Normally 200 subscribers with a few changes per hour. A bug in a client library re-registered a new subscriber on every reconnect without unregistering the old one. Timeline: 10:00 a reconnect storm network flap starts at 300 reconnects/s across 40 clients; by 10:12 the list holds about 215,000 entries; each add copies the array 215k x 4 bytes compressed refs = 860 KB . Allocation rate hits 260 MB/s from that alone 300 adds/s x 860 KB , G1 logs Humongous Allocation warnings region size 2 MB so objects = 1 MB are humongous; here 860 KB is below, but the list reached 270k entries later, 1.08 MB , young GC pauses rise from 20 ms to 340 ms, event fan-out latency iterating 215k subscribers per event, many being dead connections goes from 2 ms to 900 ms, and a "ConcurrentModificationException" alert fired from a different component. Pods OOM at 10:41.

title: Deadlock conditions
text: What are the four conditions required for a deadlock, and how does each one map to a prevention technique in Java code? Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions at once: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Remove any one and deadlock is impossible. In practice I break circular wait with a global lock order, hold-and-wait by acquiring everything up front or using one coarser lock, and no-preemption with tryLock timeout and back-off. Mutual exclusion is usually what I want to keep, so I reduce it with immutability or lock-free structures where possible.

title: Lock ordering
text: Show a minimal two-lock deadlock in Java and fix it. Thread 1 locks A then B, thread 2 locks B then A; each ends up holding one and waiting for the other. The fix is a single global acquisition order. When the locks are chosen dynamically, like transfer from, to , I order by a stable unique key such as account id.

title: Thread dump analysis
text: A service hangs. Walk me through confirming a Java-level deadlock from a thread dump and what you look at in the output. I take 3 dumps 5-10 seconds apart with jcmd <pid Thread.print -l or jstack -l . If there is a monitor or j.u.c lock cycle, HotSpot prints "Found one Java-level deadlock" at the end listing each thread, the lock it waits for, and who holds it. I confirm the same threads are stuck in all dumps. If there is no such banner but threads are parked, it is a non-lock deadlock pool, latch, DB and I trace what they wait on.

title: Livelock
text: What is livelock, how does it differ from deadlock, and how did a tryLock -based fix produce one? In deadlock threads are blocked and make no progress; in livelock they are running, burning CPU, reacting to each other, and still make no progress. A classic cause is two threads using tryLock on two locks, both failing, both releasing and retrying in sync. Fix with randomized exponential back-off, or an ordering that makes one side always win.

title: Starvation
text: What is thread starvation, and how can it occur even though no deadlock exists? Does ReentrantLock true solve it? Starvation is a thread being perpetually denied a resource while others progress. Causes: unfair locks and barging, a writer starved by constant readers, high-priority tasks monopolizing a pool, or a long task hogging a single-thread queue. A fair lock gives FIFO-ish acquisition and prevents lock starvation but typically cuts throughput significantly, so I use it only when starvation is a proven problem.

title: Lock ordering
text: Find the bug and fix it. Why does it only show up once or twice a day? A wallet service runs in-memory per-user locks to keep a 2 ms critical section off the DB . After a release, once or twice a day a few hundred requests hang; the node needs a restart. CPU is 3%, heap fine. Dump shows two threads BLOCKED on UserLock objects. Code: void transfer String fromId, String toId, long amt { Object l1 = locks.computeIfAbsent fromId, k - new Object ; Object l2 = locks.computeIfAbsent toId, k - new Object ; Object first = fromId.hashCode < toId.hashCode ? l1 : l2; Object second = first == l1 ? l2 : l1; synchronized first { synchronized second { move fromId, toId, amt ; } } }

title: Thread pool deadlock
text: What is thread-pool starvation deadlock? Give an example and the ways to avoid it. A task running on a bounded pool submits subtasks to the same pool and blocks waiting for them. If every worker is occupied by such a parent, the children sit in the queue forever, so no worker ever frees up. The fix is to not block on same-pool children: use separate pools, compose asynchronously thenCompose , run children in the caller, or use a ForkJoinPool designed for join-with-helping.

title: Priority inversion
text: What is priority inversion, and does it matter in Java on Linux? Priority inversion is when a high-priority thread waits on a lock held by a low-priority thread that gets preempted by medium-priority threads, so the high-priority work is effectively delayed by lower-priority work. Famous from Mars Pathfinder, solved with priority inheritance. In Java on typical Linux, thread priorities are not generally honored by default HotSpot maps them but defaults to ignoring them for normal threads; verify per JDK , so classic inversion is rare, yet the same shape appears at application level: a low-importance job holding a lock or pool slot that critical requests need.

title: Blocked request threads
text: What do you do right now, and what is the root cause? Order API Spring MVC on Tomcat, 200 max threads, 6 pods, 1,800 RPS total, normal p99 120 ms . At 14:05 p99 jumps to 30 s then requests time out; the load balancer marks pods unhealthy one by one. CPU 4%, heap 55%, GC pauses < 20 ms. jcmd Thread.print on one pod shows 198 http-nio-8080-exec- threads: "http-nio-8080-exec-41" WAITING parking at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park at java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.park at com.zaxxer.hikari.util.ConcurrentBag.borrow at com.zaxxer.hikari.pool.HikariPool.getConnection No "Found one Java-level deadlock" banner. Hikari maximumPoolSize=20 , connectionTimeout=30000 . A new feature that day calls a partner API inside a @Transactional method with a 60 s read timeout.

title: Lock contention diagnosis
text: Throughput plateaus at 8 of 32 cores and CPU is only 25%. How do you prove lock contention is the cause and find which lock? Low CPU with a throughput ceiling and many threads BLOCKED or parked means waiting, not computing. I confirm with repeated thread dumps counting threads waiting to lock the same address , then identify the lock and its hold time with JFR jdk.JavaMonitorEnter , jdk.JavaMonitorWait , jdk.ThreadPark or async-profiler in lock mode -e lock . Then I shorten the critical section, shard the lock, or remove sharing.

title: Pool exhaustion cascades
text: Explain the failure mechanism and why recovery lagged the rollback. How do you make this system safe? Checkout Service A calls Inventory Service B over HTTP with 3 retries, 5 s timeout, no jitter. A has 8 pods x 200 Tomcat threads and a shared HTTP client pool of 100 connections per pod; B has 4 pods x 100 threads. Normal: 2,000 RPS into A, B p99 40 ms. At 02:10 a B deploy introduces a slow DB query: B p99 rises to 4 s. By 02:14 A p99 is 20 s, A returns 503, B's CPU at 95% and its request count is 3x normal, even though A's inbound RPS is flat. A's dumps: 190+ threads in PoolingHttpClientConnectionManager.leaseConnection /socket read. B rolled back at 02:20 but A and B stay degraded until 02:40.

title: Undetected deadlocks
text: The JVM printed no "Found one Java-level deadlock" but the app is clearly deadlocked. Give me the kinds of deadlock the built-in detector cannot see. The detector only finds cycles of threads blocked on object monitors and AbstractOwnableSynchronizer -based locks e.g. ReentrantLock . It misses waits on things that are not "owned" by a thread: latches, semaphores, Future.get / join , conditions never signalled, a bounded pool starved by its own tasks, DB row locks, distributed locks, and class-initialization cycles in some cases. For those I read what each parked thread waits for and find who should have released or signalled.

title: Nested connection acquisition
text: Why can a connection pool deadlock itself, and what pool size guarantees it can't HikariCP's guidance ? If a thread holds a connection and requests a second one nested transaction REQUIRES NEW , or a helper that opens its own connection , then under load all pool connections can be held by threads each waiting for another. Nobody can finish, nobody releases. Hikari's guidance for the guaranteed-safe minimum is pool size = Tn x Cm - 1 + 1, where Tn is max concurrent threads and Cm is max connections one thread holds simultaneously.

title: ReadWriteLock
text: What's wrong, why does it hang, and how do you fix it? A pricing cache refresh serves 5,000 RPS. After adding "refresh if stale" the service stalls permanently within minutes of deploy; CPU 1%. One thread dump line stands out in every worker: "http-exec-17" WAITING parking at ...ReentrantReadWriteLock$WriteLock.lock at PriceCache.get PriceCache.java:31 Code: private final ReentrantReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock ; Price get String sku { rw.readLock .lock ; try { Price p = map.get sku ; if p == null p.isStale { rw.writeLock .lock ; // upgrade try { p = load sku ; map.put sku, p ; } finally { rw.writeLock .unlock ; } } return p; } finally { rw.readLock .unlock ; } }

title: Class initialization deadlock
text: Can class initialization cause a deadlock? Explain how and how you'd spot it. Yes. The JVM guarantees a class is initialized once, by taking an initialization lock; if class A's static initializer touches class B while another thread initializes B whose static initializer touches A, each thread holds one init lock and waits for the other. Typical triggers are static singletons referencing each other, or static init spawning threads that use the class being initialized.

title: Lock contention
text: How do you redesign it to hold 50,000 RPS without moving to a new datastore? A rate limiter / metrics service keeps Map<String, Stats stats = Collections.synchronizedMap new HashMap< , with Stats fields updated under synchronized this . At 5,000 RPS across 3 pods 16 cores each CPU is 20% and p99 is 15 ms. Product expects 10x traffic 50,000 RPS via Black Friday. A load test at 20,000 RPS shows throughput flat at 17,000, CPU 35%, p99 380 ms; JFR shows jdk.JavaMonitorEnter dominated by the synchronized map; 1,500 distinct keys but 40% of traffic hits 5 hot keys.

title: Application vs database deadlocks
text: Two requests hit "Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction" in the database. How is this different from a JVM deadlock, and how do you handle it in application code? The DB detects a cycle of row/table locks between transactions and kills one as the victim, so the application sees an exception it must handle. Prevention is the same idea as in the JVM: consistent ordering of updates by primary key , short transactions, and appropriate indexes so fewer rows are locked . Handling: retry the whole transaction a bounded number of times with jitter, only if it is safe idempotent .

title: Post-incident review
text: Lead the review: root cause, contributing factors, and the action items you'd prioritize. Post-incident review of a 47-minute full outage of a payment-orchestration service 6 pods, 200 worker threads each, shared @Async executor core=max=32, queue=10,000 . Timeline: 11:02 traffic +30%; 11:05 p99 from 90 ms to 12 s; 11:09 pods fail liveness probes they run on the same executor ; 11:11 Kubernetes restarts pods in a loop; 11:49 recovered after manual scale-down of upstream. Dumps taken at 11:07 show 32 executor threads WAITING in CompletableFuture.join , queue length 9,870. No deadlock banner. The @Async method fans out to 3 sub-calls, each also @Async on the same executor, then join s.

title: Virtual vs platform threads
text: What is a virtual thread, and how is it different from a platform thread? "A platform thread is a thin wrapper over one OS thread, with a roughly fixed stack reserved by the OS and a scheduler in the kernel. A virtual thread is a java.lang.Thread implemented by the JVM: its stack lives on the heap, and the JDK schedules it onto a small pool of platform threads called carriers. It is final in Java 21. It doesn't run faster; it lets me have hundreds of thousands of blocked-waiting threads, so thread-per-request scales with I/O concurrency again."

title: Creating virtual threads
text: What are the ways to create and run virtual threads in Java 21, and which would you use in a service? " Thread.ofVirtual .start r or Thread.startVirtualThread r for a single one, Thread.ofVirtual .factory when a library wants a ThreadFactory , and Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor for services. That executor starts a fresh virtual thread per submitted task; it's not a pool, and since Java 19 ExecutorService is AutoCloseable , so try-with-resources waits for tasks."

title: Carriers & continuations
text: Explain how virtual threads are scheduled: what are carrier threads and continuations, and what happens when a virtual thread blocks? "Each virtual thread is a continuation, a stack of frames that can be suspended and resumed, plus a scheduler. The scheduler is a FIFO-mode ForkJoinPool of platform threads called carriers, parallelism defaulting to the CPU count. A virtual thread is mounted on a carrier to run; when it blocks in a JDK API it yields, its frames go to the heap, the carrier is freed, and when it's unblocked it's resubmitted to the pool, possibly resuming on a different carrier."

title: When they help
text: For which workloads do virtual threads improve throughput, and for which do they not? Quantify it. "They help when concurrency is limited by threads blocked on I/O. Concurrency L = throughput x latency, so if each request waits 200 ms and I want 5,000 RPS I need 1,000 requests in flight; with 200 platform threads I cap at 1,000 RPS. Virtual threads remove that cap. For CPU-bound work, throughput is limited by cores, so they add nothing and can hurt."

title: Pooling anti-pattern
text: Why is pooling virtual threads an anti-pattern, and how do you limit concurrency instead? "A pool exists to amortise the cost of an expensive resource and to cap how many exist. Virtual threads are cheap, so there's nothing to amortise, and pooling them also reintroduces queueing where a task waits for a free slot instead of just blocking cheaply. If I need to cap concurrent access to a resource, I use a Semaphore around the call, sized to the resource, not to the thread."

title: Bounding concurrency
text: The feature "worked" but the system is worse. Explain why and what you change. An order service runs Spring Boot 3.2 on Java 21 with Tomcat, 200 threads, a HikariCP pool of 30 connections maximumPoolSize=30 , p99 180 ms at 800 RPS. Marketing expects 8x traffic. A teammate enables spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true and load tests at 6,000 RPS. Results: CPU 35%, pod memory fine, but p99 jumps to 11 s, and logs show HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms and some 5xx at the gateway . Each request does 2 queries, 15 ms each, in one transaction.

title: Pinning (Java 21)
text: What is virtual thread pinning in Java 21, what causes it, and why does it matter? "Pinning means a virtual thread can't unmount from its carrier while blocked. In Java 21 that happens when it blocks inside a synchronized block or method, or inside a native method or foreign function frame. The carrier OS thread is then blocked too, and the scheduler doesn't add carriers to compensate. A few pinned threads waiting on slow I/O can consume all carriers and stall the whole app even though CPU is idle."

title: Pinning
text: Diagnose and fix without taking the service down. A notification service Java 21, Spring Boot 3.2, virtual threads on, 4 vCPU pods, 6 replicas calls an internal REST API. After a release, p99 goes from 120 ms to 9 s every few minutes, then recovers; CPU 8%; heap flat at 40%. Thread dumps via jstack show only 14 platform threads. Log excerpt every spike: Request timed out waiting for response from the gateway. The release added a "rate-limit shim": class ShimClient { private final HttpClientWrapper http; synchronized Response call Request r { // "to keep it simple and ordered" return http.send r ; // network call, 50 ms normally, 3 s when downstream is slow } } Red herring: a recent GC flag change.

title: JEP 491 and later pinning
text: What changed for pinning in Java 24, and what pinning remains? "JEP 491, delivered in Java 24, lets virtual threads acquire, hold and release monitors independently of their carrier, so a virtual thread can unmount while blocked inside synchronized , while waiting to enter a monitor, and in Object.wait . Pinning remains for native frames: native methods or FFM calls that call back into Java and block, plus blocking during class loading or class initialisation. jdk.tracePinnedThreads no longer works; the JFR pinning event stays for the remaining cases."

title: ThreadLocal
text: What is wrong, and what do you change? A service migrated to virtual threads Java 21, one virtual thread per request, 20,000 concurrent at peak . Code: public class Formatter { private static final ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat FMT = ThreadLocal.withInitial - new SimpleDateFormat "yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss" ; private static final ThreadLocal<byte BUF = ThreadLocal.withInitial - new byte 256 1024 ; // "avoid allocation per request" static String fmt Date d { return FMT.get .format d ; } } After the move, heap usage rises from 1.5 GB to 6 GB at peak, GC allocation rate triples, and p99 worsens. A tester notes MDC context sometimes appears in logs of other requests only when they use a hand-rolled platform worker pool.

title: ScopedValue
text: What is ScopedValue , how does it differ from ThreadLocal , and what is its status across Java versions? "A ScopedValue is an immutable binding that is visible only for the dynamic extent of a run / call , and is inherited by structured-concurrency child threads without copying. There's no set , so no mutation from callees and no leaks beyond the scope. It was preview in 21 JEP 446 , refined through 22-24, and finalised in Java 25 JEP 506 . Reading is usually as cheap as a local variable."

title: Structured concurrency
text: What is structured concurrency, what problem does StructuredTaskScope solve, and what is its status? "Structured concurrency says subtasks must finish within the scope that started them, like block-structured code. StructuredTaskScope forks subtasks as virtual threads, the owner join s, and on exit all children are done, so there are no leaked threads. With a fail-fast policy a failure cancels siblings and propagates. It is still a preview API: previewed from 21, with Java 25 delivering its fifth preview JEP 505 , where the API moved to StructuredTaskScope.open plus Joiner policies. So use it behind --enable-preview , and never assume the 21 API compiles on 25."

title: Structured concurrency
text: Find the bugs and explain the observed behaviors. A profile endpoint Java 21 with --enable-preview , 900 RPS fans out to three services. A reviewer approves this code; in staging it throws intermittently and, when a downstream fails, latency is 2 s longer than expected: Profile load String id throws Exception { try var scope = new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure { var user = scope.fork - userSvc.get id ; // 30 ms var orders = scope.fork - orderSvc.get id ; // 40 ms, fails fast on bad id var recs = scope.fork - recSvc.get id ; // 2 s, slow var u = user.get ; // line A scope.join ; scope.throwIfFailed ; return new Profile u, orders.get , recs.get ; } } Error in logs: java.lang.IllegalStateException: Owner did not join after forking subtasks . Red herring: recent upgrade of the HTTP client library.

title: Spring/Tomcat enablement
text: How do you enable virtual threads in a Spring Boot application on Tomcat, and what exactly changes? "On Java 21+ and Spring Boot 3.2+, set spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true . Boot then runs Tomcat or Jetty request handling on virtual threads and uses virtual threads for @Async /scheduled task executors it auto-configures. Each request gets its own virtual thread, so the 200-thread cap disappears. Everything downstream, notably the DB pool, still has its old limits."

title: Migration
text: Plan the migration. What goes wrong, in what order do you de-risk it? A payments-adjacent API Java 17, Spring Boot 3.1, Tomcat 300 threads, 12 pods x 4 vCPU, 2,500 RPS total, p99 220 ms must move to Java 21 + virtual threads to survive a 3x campaign without tripling pods. Dependencies: Postgres via HikariCP 20/pod; DB max connections 400, shared with another service using 150 , Redis, an old SOAP client library synchronized internally , and a metrics agent that uses ThreadLocals. Error budget is tight, no downtime allowed.

title: Virtual threads vs reactive
text: Virtual threads vs reactive programming WebFlux/Reactor : when would you pick each? "Both solve 'too many threads blocked on I/O'. Reactive does it by never blocking: async pipelines, operators, backpressure, a few event-loop threads. Virtual threads keep blocking style and let the JVM do the multiplexing. For most CRUD and orchestration services I'd choose virtual threads: simpler code, normal stack traces, normal debugging, existing blocking libraries. I'd still choose reactive for streaming, backpressure-centric pipelines, or when the stack is already reactive and working."

title: Virtual threads vs coroutines
text: How do virtual threads compare to Kotlin coroutines, and could one replace the other on a server? "Virtual threads are stackful and runtime-level: any blocking JDK call can suspend, no language support needed, and existing blocking libraries benefit. Coroutines are stackless, compiled into state machines, with suspend colouring the call graph. Coroutines give structured concurrency, cancellation, Flow and multiplatform that are shipping and mature, while Loom's structured concurrency is still preview. On the server I wouldn't rewrite coroutine code to virtual threads; I'd use them side by side, and for new Java code virtual threads are the natural default. Coroutine mechanics belong to the Kotlin chunk."

title: Observability
text: How do you see what the virtual threads are doing, and what tooling do you rely on? A Java 21 service on virtual threads hangs for 40 s at a time: health checks time out, RPS drops to near zero, CPU 3%. On-call runs jstack <pid and sees only 25 platform threads ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1..4 carriers, GC threads, Tomcat acceptor and no application stack traces. They conclude "nothing is running" and want to restart. Metrics from ThreadMXBean.getThreadCount also show 25 threads while the access log shows 6,000 in-flight requests.

title: CPU-bound work
text: Why didn't virtual threads help, and why did latency get worse? What would you do? A document-processing API Java 21, 8 vCPU pods, 10 pods parses PDFs: per request 400 ms of CPU text extraction plus 100 ms waiting on object storage. It was on a 64-thread platform pool; p99 was 1.4 s at 120 RPS/pod. To "save cost", the team moved all handling to newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor . Result: p50 doubled, p99 6 s, health-check endpoint same scheduler occasionally times out, throughput per pod unchanged at 15 RPS CPU 100% . Red herring: the object store SDK upgrade the same week.

title: Admission control & backpressure
text: With virtual threads, thread count no longer limits you. How do you design backpressure and overload protection? "I make limits explicit at three layers. At the edge, admission control caps in-flight requests a Semaphore or concurrency limiter and sheds excess with 429/503 quickly. Per dependency, a Semaphore bulkhead sized to what that dependency can take, with tryAcquire timeouts. And bounded queues wherever work is handed between stages. Plus timeouts on every outbound call, because a virtual thread waiting forever is a leak that holds memory."

title: Misconceptions
text: True or false, and why: "Virtual threads make my code faster", "I should use them everywhere", "they replace ExecutorService". "All three are false as stated. Virtual threads improve throughput for blocking I/O by allowing high concurrency; individual request latency doesn't drop. They shouldn't be used for CPU-bound work. And ExecutorService isn't replaced: I still use it, just with a per-task virtual-thread executor for blocking work and a fixed pool for CPU work."

title: Memory & lifecycle
text: Run the review: what failed, why wasn't it visible, and what changes? Post-incident review: an ingestion service Java 21, 4 GB heap, container limit 6 GB, G1 was moved to a virtual thread per message. A downstream outage lasted 12 minutes. Messages kept arriving at 8,000/s from Kafka consumers that handed each message to executor.submit ... on newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor ; each task did a HttpClient.send with the default no request timeout and held a 40 KB payload plus 10 KB of stack. Timeline: heap rose from 1.2 GB to 4 GB in 6 minutes, GC pauses grew Pause Young ... 450ms , then java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space , then the pod was restarted and reprocessed duplicates. Dashboards showed no thread-count growth platform threads steady at 40 .

title: Dispatchers on a server
text: On a Kotlin backend, what are Dispatchers.Default, Dispatchers.IO and Dispatchers.Unconfined, and how do you pick one for a request handler? Default is for CPU-bound work and has as many threads as cores minimum 2 . IO is for blocking calls like JDBC or file IO and by default allows max 64, cores concurrent blocking tasks. They share one underlying thread pool. Unconfined runs wherever the caller resumed and I basically never use it in server code. For a handler I run suspend code from non-blocking clients on whatever dispatcher the framework gives me, and wrap each blocking call in withContext Dispatchers.IO .

title: limitedParallelism and IO sizing
text: What does Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism n do, how is it different from a fixed thread pool dispatcher, and how would you size it for a service with a 20-connection HikariCP pool? limitedParallelism n returns a view that lets at most n coroutines of that view run at once, reusing the parent's threads. On Dispatchers.IO the views are elastic: their sum is not capped by IO's 64, so each dependency gets its own independent limit. For a 20-connection Hikari pool I would use a view of about 20, equal to the pool size, so excess coroutines queue in the dispatcher cheap rather than blocking threads waiting on getConnection .

title: Blocking calls in coroutines
text: Why is calling a blocking function from a coroutine dangerous, and what are the options when you must call blocking code? A coroutine suspension frees the thread, but a blocking call holds it. The dispatcher has few threads cores for Default, or Netty's small event-loop set , so a handful of blocked coroutines can freeze everything on that dispatcher. Options: wrap in withContext Dispatchers.IO or a limitedParallelism view, use a non-blocking client, or on JDK 21+ run the blocking code on virtual threads. runBlocking inside a coroutine is the worst option.

title: Blocking calls in coroutines
text: Find the bugs, explain the symptoms, and fix it. Ktor service, 4-core pods 2 GB RAM , 600 RPS peak. After shipping a new /orders/{id} endpoint, p99 goes from 80 ms to 9 s during a downstream blip, CPU stays at 15%, heap is fine, no GC pauses over 20 ms. Health checks /health , pure in-memory start timing out. The code: get "/orders/{id}" { val id = call.parameters "id" !! val order = withContext Dispatchers.Default { ordersDao.find id // blocking JDBC, Hikari max pool 10 } val items = coroutineScope { 1..5 .map { async { runBlocking { itemsClient.get order, it } } }.awaitAll } call.respond Response order, items } jstack shows 4 DefaultDispatcher-worker-N threads in HikariPool.getConnection or inside runBlocking /socket read.

title: Spring MVC/WebFlux coroutine support
text: How does Spring support Kotlin coroutines in controllers, and what differs between running them on Spring MVC and on WebFlux? With kotlinx-coroutines-core and kotlinx-coroutines-reactor on the classpath, Spring lets @RestController methods be suspend or return Flow , and coRouter for functional endpoints. Spring adapts the coroutine to a Mono / Flux internally. On WebFlux it runs on the Netty event loop, so any blocking there is fatal. On MVC the suspend method is run through async request handling; I would verify on my Spring version which thread executes it and keep blocking work behind withContext IO either way.

title: Ktor at a high level
text: At a high level, how does Ktor use coroutines to handle requests, and what should you know before putting blocking or long-running work in a route? Ktor runs on an engine Netty, CIO, Jetty, Tomcat . Each request is handled in a coroutine, and route handlers are suspend lambdas, so non-blocking calls free the thread while waiting. Plugins formerly features form a pipeline around handlers. Blocking calls must be moved off the engine threads with withContext . Request coroutines are tied to the call; work launched into an application-level scope outlives the request.

title: Context propagation (MDC)
text: Why does SLF4J MDC lose its values across coroutine suspension points, and how do you fix it? MDC is a ThreadLocal. A coroutine can suspend on one thread and resume on another, so the values stay behind or, worse, a different request's values are visible. The fix is MDCContext from kotlinx-coroutines-slf4j , a ThreadContextElement that copies the MDC map into the thread each time the coroutine resumes and restores the old state when it suspends. Children inherit it through the coroutine context.

title: Context propagation
text: How do you explain these symptoms, stop the leak of wrong userIds, and make it robust? A Spring Boot + Kotlin service on WebFlux 6 pods, 4 vCPU, 1,800 RPS . After a refactor that introduced withContext Dispatchers.IO for a legacy DAO, support reports two problems: 1 about 12% of log lines have no traceId , and these cluster around DB calls; 2 in audit logs, a handful of entries carry a userId belonging to a different user. Security is alarmed. The code sets MDC.put "userId", u in a WebFilter and reads SecurityContextHolder.getContext in a service method after withContext IO . Heap and GC are normal; no errors in logs.

title: Tracing, security and transaction context
text: Besides MDC, which other thread-bound things break inside coroutines on a server security context, tracing spans, JPA/JDBC transactions , and how do you handle each? Anything stored in a ThreadLocal is unsafe across suspension: Spring's SecurityContextHolder , @Transactional it binds a connection to a thread , tracing spans in Micrometer/OpenTelemetry. Per resume the dispatcher may pick another thread. Fixes: use a coroutine-aware mechanism. Tracing: PropagationContextElement or OTel's coroutine context extension. Security: reactive security context. Transactions: TransactionalOperator.executeAndAwait on reactive stack; with blocking JDBC keep the whole transaction inside one withContext Dispatchers.IO block without suspension.

title: Cancellation on client disconnect
text: A client closes the connection while your handler is waiting on three downstream calls and a DB query. What happens in a coroutine-based server, and what do you have to do for cancellation to be effective? If the engine/framework detects the disconnect it cancels the request coroutine's Job, and cancellation propagates to children. But cancellation is cooperative: a suspend call that is cancellable delay, Ktor client, await throws CancellationException at the suspension point. Blocking code does not stop. So I make downstream calls cancellable, never swallow CancellationException , and for blocking JDBC I use statement timeouts or runInterruptible .

title: Cancellation
text: What is wrong with this code and how do you fix it? A Ktor service with a pricing endpoint has a timeout of 2 s at the gateway. At 500 RPS, during a downstream slowdown, the DB shows 300 active sessions running the pricing query although gateway timeouts return 504 to users. Pod memory grows 400 MB over an hour. Code: suspend fun quote id: String : Quote { return try { withTimeout 2 000 { val base = withContext Dispatchers.IO { dao.basePrice id } // blocking JDBC val fx = fxClient.rate base.currency // suspend, Ktor client Quote base, fx } } catch e: Exception { log.warn "quote failed", e Quote.fallback id } finally { metrics.record id // suspend call } } Logs show TimeoutCancellationException stack traces logged as warnings, and also callers that cancelled still returning fallback quotes.

title: Structured concurrency fan-out
text: How do you call three services in parallel from a request handler with coroutines, and what happens if one of them fails? coroutineScope { val a = async { ... }; val b = async { ... }; ... } . The scope waits for all children, and if one throws, the scope cancels the siblings and rethrows. If I want partial results I use supervisorScope children fail independently and handle exceptions per await .

title: Fan-out and timeouts
text: Design the fan-out, timeouts and degradation. What would you do about overload? A product-page endpoint at 1,200 RPS fans out to 4 services: catalog p99 40 ms, required , price p99 60 ms, required , reviews p99 300 ms, optional , recs p99 800 ms, optional, occasionally 5 s . The SLO is p99 under 400 ms. Today a sequential implementation has p99 1.2 s. Product wants "always show something". A teammate proposes one withTimeout 400 around the whole fan-out.

title: Bulkheads
text: How would you implement bulkheads and concurrency limits per downstream dependency using coroutines, and when do you use a Semaphore versus limitedParallelism? A bulkhead caps concurrent in-flight calls per dependency so one slow service cannot eat all capacity. Use a Semaphore n for non-blocking suspend calls: coroutines waiting for a permit suspend cheaply, and permits are held across suspension. Use limitedParallelism n for blocking calls, since it limits threads actually running. Add a bounded wait timeout on acquire so queues cannot grow forever, and fail fast when full.

title: Coroutines vs virtual threads
text: On JDK 21+, why would you still use Kotlin coroutines on a server instead of just virtual threads, and when would you pick virtual threads? Both give cheap concurrency, but they sit at different layers. Virtual threads final in Java 21 make blocking code scale with zero code changes, but give no structured concurrency or built-in cancellation semantics beyond interrupts structured concurrency in the JDK is still a preview API, verify for your version . Coroutines give explicit suspension, structured concurrency, cancellation, Flow and dispatcher control. For a mostly blocking JDBC service I'd lean to virtual threads; for Kotlin-first code with heavy fan-out, cancellation and Flow I'd keep coroutines, and they can be combined.

title: Coroutines vs virtual threads
text: What do you propose, and how do you migrate with live traffic? A Kotlin Spring MVC service JDK 17, Tomcat 200 threads, JPA/Hibernate, HikariCP 30 handles 900 RPS. Calls to a slow partner p50 200 ms, p99 3 s cause Tomcat threads to saturate during partner incidents all 200 busy, queue grows, 503s . Management asks to "go reactive/coroutines" in one quarter. The team has 4 engineers and 40% of the code uses JPA lazy loading and @Transactional .

title: Testing coroutines
text: How do you test suspend code on the server deterministically, including delays, timeouts and dispatcher usage? Use runTest from kotlinx-coroutines-test . It runs the body with a test scheduler and skips delay in virtual time, so a 2-second timeout test runs instantly. I inject dispatchers into classes instead of hard-coding Dispatchers.IO , pass the test dispatcher, and use advanceTimeBy / runCurrent to step through. For real blocking calls I use a real dispatcher in integration tests.

title: Common production bugs
text: Run the post-incident review: root cause, fixes, and prevention. A notification service Kotlin, Ktor, 3 pods, 2 GB heap each slowly degrades. Over 6 days, heap use climbs from 600 MB to 1.7 GB; at day 6 pods hit OOM and restart, then the cycle repeats. Threads dumps show 4,000+ idle DefaultDispatcher-worker entries are not the issue only 64 , but a heap dump Eclipse MAT shows 1.1 M StandaloneCoroutine objects, each holding references to request payloads. Code review reveals: class Notifier private val sender: Sender { private val scope = CoroutineScope SupervisorJob + Dispatchers.IO fun enqueue n: Notification { scope.launch { sender.send n } } // called per request } sender.send has no timeout; the email provider occasionally hangs connections for minutes. Also a GlobalScope.launch in a retry helper.

title: JFR
text: What is Java Flight Recorder, and how would you run it continuously in production? JFR is an event recorder built into the JVM. The JVM and JDK libraries emit typed events GC, allocation samples, thread parks, monitor waits, I/O, CPU samples into thread-local buffers, which are flushed to a ring of chunk files. I run it always-on with the default settings designed for low overhead, roughly 1% by Oracle's docs, so verify on your workload and a bounded size and age. When an incident happens I dump the last N minutes with jcmd <pid JFR.dump and open it in JDK Mission Control or with the jfr CLI.

title: Thread dumps
text: How do you take a thread dump and what do you look for in it? jcmd <pid Thread.print or jstack <pid , or kill -3 which prints to stdout of the JVM . I take three dumps, 5-10 seconds apart, and compare: threads that stay in the same frame across dumps are stuck, not just passing through. I look at states RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED WAITING , what they wait on waiting to lock <0x... , parking to wait for , who holds the lock, and group identical stacks to see which pool is saturated.

title: jcmd, jstat, jmap
text: Which command-line JDK tools do you reach for to inspect a running JVM, and what does each answer? jcmd is the single entry point: Thread.print , GC.heap dump , GC.class histogram , VM.flags , VM.native memory , JFR. . jstat -gcutil <pid 1000 gives GC occupancy and counts cheaply, with no pause. jmap -histo and -dump are the older heap tools; both can pause the JVM. I go from cheap to expensive: metrics, jstat, class histogram, JFR, then heap dump.

title: GC logs
text: How do you enable and read GC logs on a modern JDK, and what are the first three things you check? Unified logging since JDK 9: -Xlog:gc :file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20m . First I check pause times against the SLO, then heap occupancy after GC the live set trend: if "after" keeps climbing it is a leak or undersizing , then the allocation rate and the cause of each collection Allocation Failure, G1 Humongous Allocation, Metadata GC Threshold, Evacuation Failure, full GC .

title: Safepoint bias
text: What is safepoint bias in profilers, and how do JFR and async-profiler avoid it? Classic profilers e.g. Thread.getAllStackTraces -based ones, older hprof, VisualVM sampling can only sample a thread at a safepoint, because the JVM must stop it to walk its stack consistently. Code only polls for safepoints at certain places method returns, loop back-edges of non-counted loops , so samples cluster at those locations and hot code between polls, such as tight counted loops, looks cold. JFR and async-profiler sample using signals plus AsyncGetCallTrace -style stack walking at arbitrary points, so they are not tied to safepoints.

title: High CPU
text: Walk me through finding what is burning the CPU. A Spring Boot order service 8 vCPU pods, 4 GB heap, JDK 17, G1 normally runs at 35% CPU at 600 RPS. After last night's release, 3 of 12 pods sit at 95-100% CPU, p99 went from 180 ms to 2.4 s, and the other pods are fine. Errors are timeouts only; no OOM. kubectl top confirms CPU, memory flat at 2.6 GB. GC logs show Young pauses 25 ms, one every 2 s. Release diff includes a new caching layer, a Jackson upgrade, and a changed log pattern.

title: async-profiler
text: Explain async-profiler's cpu, wall, alloc and lock modes. When do you use each? CPU mode samples threads that are actually running on a CPU, so it answers "where is CPU going". Wall-clock mode samples all threads at a fixed interval regardless of state running, sleeping, blocked , so it answers "where does a request spend its time", which is what I need for latency with I/O or lock waits. Alloc mode samples allocations via TLAB events to find who creates garbage. Lock mode samples contended monitor and ReentrantLock waits, to find who blocks whom.

title: Flame graphs
text: How do you read a flame graph, and what are the common misreadings? The x-axis is not time order; it is sample count, so frame width is the share of samples time or bytes, depending on mode that included that frame in the stack. The y-axis is stack depth: callers below, callees above. I look for wide plateaus at the top self time and wide towers in the middle cumulative cost . I never judge by height. I compare before/after with a differential graph.

title: Allocation profiling
text: How do you decide what to do? A pricing API JDK 21, G1, 6 GB heap, 4 vCPU pods, 40 pods at 1,200 RPS each costs too much. Finance wants 30% fewer pods. CPU averages 70%, p99 is 140 ms and spikes to 400 ms every few seconds. GC log excerpt: Pause Young Normal 2800M- 310M 6144M 18ms every 1.1 s. Live set after mixed GC is stable at 900 MB. Old gen is healthy. Someone proposes switching to ZGC and adding more heap.

title: Heap dump analysis
text: Walk me through the heap dump workflow for an OutOfMemoryError: capture, analysis in MAT, and what to look at. Prefer -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=... so you get the dump at the failure point; otherwise jcmd <pid GC.heap dump . Open it in Eclipse MAT, run the Leak Suspects report, then use the dominator tree sorted by retained heap, and "path to GC roots excluding weak/soft references" for the suspect. I compare two dumps taken hours apart to separate leak from large working set.

title: Native Memory Tracking
text: The container RSS is far above the Java heap size. How does Native Memory Tracking help, and what does it not cover? The process uses heap plus metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, GC data structures, symbol tables, direct buffers, and malloc arenas. NMT -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary tracks what the JVM itself allocates, by category. I take a baseline , wait, then run summary.diff to see which category grows. It does not see native allocations from JNI libraries, glibc fragmentation, or mmap-ed files outside the JVM's accounting, which I check with pmap , /proc/<pid /smaps , and malloc tuning.

title: Container memory
text: How do you find the cause and fix it? A Kotlin/Spring service JDK 17, 3 GB container limit, -Xmx2g , G1 restarts every 18 hours with OOMKilled exit 137 . Grafana: heap used oscillates 0.9-1.7 GB with healthy GC; no OutOfMemoryError in logs; no heap dump exists. Container working set climbs 35 MB/hour from 1.9 GB to 3.0 GB. The service uses Netty-based HTTP clients, Kafka client, and Jackson. Someone says "heap must be leaking, bump -Xmx to 2.5g".

title: Safe production profiling
text: How do you profile a production JVM safely, especially inside a container? I use low-overhead, sampling tools and time-box them: JFR default settings continuous, profile for a bounded window or async-profiler for 30-60 s on one canary pod, not the whole fleet. I take the pod out of the LB if the tool pauses heap dump, class histogram . In containers I verify the attach path works same UID, /tmp , that the profiler has needed permissions perf events may be blocked, so I use itimer/wall , and that output goes to a volume with space. I pre-enable what cannot be turned on later NMT, JFR flags, GC logs .

title: Micrometer JVM metrics
text: Which JVM metrics do you put on a dashboard and alert on for a Java service, and why? Memory: jvm.memory.used/max by pool and jvm.gc.live.data.size live set after GC trend; GC: jvm.gc.pause rate and max, jvm.gc.memory.allocated allocation rate and jvm.gc.memory.promoted ; threads: jvm.threads.live , jvm.threads.states blocked/waiting ; buffers: jvm.buffer.memory.used direct ; classes: jvm.classes.loaded ; CPU: process.cpu.usage , system.cpu.usage ; plus pool-level metrics: executor.queued , executor.active , hikaricp.connections.pending , and request latency percentiles. I alert on symptoms latency, errors, saturation and keep the JVM metrics as diagnosis panels, with a few leading indicators.

title: USE and RED
text: What are the USE and RED methods, and how do you apply them to a Java service incident? RED Rate, Errors, Duration describes request-facing symptoms of a service; USE Utilization, Saturation, Errors examines every resource: CPU, memory, disk, network, plus software resources like thread pools and connection pools. I start with RED to confirm user impact and which endpoint, then walk USE across resources to find the saturated one, then drill into the JVM with the right tool.

title: Incident methodology
text: Lead the diagnosis. What's your sequence and what do you say to the room? Black Friday, 15:02. A checkout service JDK 17, 16 pods x 4 vCPU, G1 4 GB heap, Tomcat max 200 threads, Hikari 30 connections sees p99 jump from 220 ms to 6 s; error rate 4% timeouts, 503s from the gateway . RPS is 2.5x normal. CPU per pod is 45%. GC: pauses < 40 ms. No deploys in 24 hours. Alerts channel is noisy. The on-call has already restarted two pods and it didn't help. The CTO is on the call.

title: JMH
text: Why can't you benchmark Java code with a main and System.nanoTime loop, and what does JMH do about it? The JIT changes the code as it runs: interpreter first, then C1, then C2 after profiling, with inlining and deoptimization. A naive loop measures warm-up, may get the whole computation eliminated if the result is unused dead-code elimination , or have inputs constant-folded. JMH forks fresh JVMs, runs warmup iterations before measured ones, provides Blackhole to consume results, @State for non-constant inputs, and reports score with error.

title: JMH pitfalls
text: What is wrong with this benchmark and how would you redo it? A teammate benchmarks two ways to join IDs and reports "approach B is 40x faster, merge it". The code: public class JoinBench { static final List<String IDS = List.of "a1", "b2", "c3", "d4" ; public static void main String args { for int i = 0; i < 1 000 000; i++ joinA ; // warm-up long t = System.nanoTime ; for int i = 0; i < 10 000 000; i++ joinA ; long a = System.nanoTime - t; t = System.nanoTime ; for int i = 0; i < 10 000 000; i++ joinB ; long b = System.nanoTime - t; System.out.println "A=" + a / 1e6 + "ms B=" + b / 1e6 + "ms" ; } static String joinA { String s = ""; for String id : IDS s += id + ","; return s; } static String joinB { return String.join ",", IDS ; } // result discarded by callers } Machine: a laptop on battery, JDK 17. The JVM was started once and both loops ran in the same process.

title: JFR events and streaming
text: Beyond a CPU profile, which JFR events do you use to diagnose latency, and how do you add your own application events? I use jdk.GCPhasePause / jdk.GarbageCollection for pauses, jdk.JavaMonitorEnter and jdk.ThreadPark for lock waits, jdk.SocketRead / SocketWrite and jdk.FileRead for I/O, jdk.ObjectAllocationSample for allocation, jdk.ExecutionSample for CPU stacks, and jdk.SafepointBegin/End or related safepoint events for stalls. For application context I define a custom Event subclass for example one per request or per downstream call so the timeline shows business operations next to the JVM events. I read them with JMC or jfr print .

title: Lock contention
text: Diagnose and fix. Why is CPU low while latency is terrible? A metrics-enrichment service JDK 21, 8 vCPU pod, 150 request threads, 1,500 RPS shows p50 12 ms but p99 1.8 s after a feature added "tenant-level rate counters". CPU is only 30%. Thread count is stable. GC pauses 15 ms. A sampled jstack shows many threads like: "http-exec-87" 187 BLOCKED on java.util.HashMap@6a4f a tenant counter map at com.acme.RateLimiter.record RateLimiter.java:52 - waiting to lock <0x00000007c1a0d2e0 a java.util.Collections$SynchronizedMap "http-exec-12" RUNNABLE at java.net.SocketInputStream.socketRead0 at com.acme.RateLimiter.record RateLimiter.java:58 - locked <0x00000007c1a0d2e0 The code: synchronized counters { counters.merge tenant, 1, Integer::sum ; audit.log tenant ; } , where audit.log makes a blocking call to a remote audit service.

title: Load testing measurement
text: What is coordinated omission and how can it make your latency measurements lie? Coordinated omission is when the load generator waits for a slow response before sending the next request, so the stall suppresses the very samples that would have shown the stall. A closed-loop client records one slow request instead of the hundreds that would have arrived during it, so percentiles look far better than reality. Open-loop generators fixed arrival rate, like wrk2 or k6 constant-arrival-rate executors and HdrHistogram's correction fix this.

title: Post-incident review
text: What changes do you make, and what do you say about how we'd find the root cause next time? A payments service JDK 17, 5 GB heap in a 7 GB pod, Kubernetes crashed twice in one week with java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space . Each time the pod restarted within 40 s and the team has no evidence: no heap dump the container has no volume for it and the JVM flags were -Xmx5g only , GC logs were stdout lines rotated away, and metrics scraped every 60 s show heap hitting max only in the last minute. You are asked to lead the post-incident review and make the next OOM diagnosable.

title: HashMap internals
text: Walk me through what happens when I call map.put key, value on a HashMap in Java 8+. How does it pick a bucket? "HashMap is an array of buckets. put calls key.hashCode , XORs the high 16 bits into the low 16 h ^ h 16 , then picks the bucket with n - 1 & hash where n is the power-of-two table length. If the bucket is empty it stores a node; otherwise it walks the chain comparing hash then equals , replacing the value on a match or appending a new node. When size exceeds capacity times load factor 0.75 the table doubles. A long chain can become a red-black tree."

title: equals/hashCode contract
text: What is the equals/hashCode contract, and what actually breaks if you override one without the other? "If a.equals b then a.hashCode == b.hashCode . equals must be reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent and false for null. If I override equals but not hashCode, two equal objects usually land in different buckets, so HashSet.contains and HashMap.get return false for a key that is logically present. The reverse is legal but slow: equal hashes for unequal objects is just a collision."

title: HashMap treeification
text: When and why does HashMap turn a bucket into a red-black tree? What are the thresholds and what happens if the keys are not Comparable? "When a single bin reaches 8 nodes and the table has at least 64 buckets, the bin is converted to a red-black tree, giving O log n instead of O n in that bin. If the table is smaller than 64, HashMap resizes instead. A tree bin reverts to a list when it shrinks to 6 or fewer checked on resize . Ordering inside the tree uses hash first, then Comparable if the keys share a class and implement it, and otherwise a tie-break that forces searching both subtrees, so non-Comparable keys with colliding hashes degrade back toward O n ."

title: ArrayList vs LinkedList
text: ArrayList or LinkedList: which do you use and why? Is the textbook "LinkedList is faster for inserts" true on the JVM? "Default to ArrayList. It is a contiguous array: O 1 random access, amortized O 1 append, O n mid insert via System.arraycopy , which is very fast memcpy. LinkedList gives O 1 insert only if you already hold the node/iterator position; finding the position is O n with pointer chasing and cache misses, and each element costs a 24-byte node. In practice ArrayList wins even for many middle inserts until lists get large. If I need a queue or deque I use ArrayDeque, not LinkedList."

title: Mutable keys
text: Find the bug, explain exactly why get and remove fail, and fix it. A session tracker keeps active sessions in a HashMap<SessionKey, Session ; about 40k entries, 800 RPS. After a recent change, ops see "session not found" errors for sessions that definitely exist, plus a slow memory leak: the map grows, never shrinks, and remove returns null. Code: class SessionKey { String userId; String deviceId; SessionKey String u, String d { userId = u; deviceId = d; } @Override public boolean equals Object o { return o instanceof SessionKey k && userId.equals k.userId && deviceId.equals k.deviceId ; } @Override public int hashCode { return java.util.Objects.hash userId, deviceId ; } } SessionKey key = new SessionKey user, "unknown" ; sessions.put key, session ; ... key.deviceId = reportedDevice; // device id learned later Session s = sessions.get key ; // null! sessions.remove key ; // no-op, entry leaks Red herring: the team suspects a recent Tomcat upgrade and GC settings.

title: HashMap resize, load factor and iteration
text: How does HashMap resize, why does the load factor default to 0.75, how should I presize one, and can I rely on its iteration order? "When size exceeds capacity times load factor 16 x 0.75 = 12 initially , the table doubles and entries are redistributed. Because capacity is a power of two, each entry either stays at index i or moves to i + oldCap, decided by one bit of its hash. 0.75 balances memory against collision probability.
