title: What attention heads do (induction, sinks)
text: What have we learned about what attention heads actually do? Explain induction heads and attention sinks, and why they matter in practice. "Induction heads are a two-head circuit that finds an earlier occurrence of the current token and copies what came next, which is a main mechanism behind in-context pattern completion. Attention sinks are tokens, usually the first, that soak up a large share of attention mass because softmax must sum to one; keeping them in the cache is what makes sliding-window streaming work. Both are empirical findings, not guarantees."

title: Sparse/windowed attention and MLA
text: Beyond GQA, what techniques cut attention's cost or KV memory at long context sliding-window, local/global layers, MLA , and what do they trade away? "Sliding-window attention limits each token to a fixed recent window so cache and compute become O window ; information still propagates across layers, but exact long-range recall is limited. Interleaving local and global layers keeps a few full-context layers. Multi-head latent attention compresses K and V into a low-rank latent per token so the cache is much smaller while keeping near-MHA quality. Each trades exactness or complexity for memory."

title: Numerical stability in attention
text: Diagnose and fix. What's the mechanism, and how do you avoid a restart loop? A 3B-parameter model is being continued-pretrained in fp16 mixed precision loss scaling on on 64 GPUs after a data-mix change. At step 41,200 the loss jumps from 2.31 to 9.8 and the log shows grad norm: inf for 12 consecutive steps, then training reports nan loss. The same config was stable in bf16 on a previous run. Logs show attention logits in layer 24 with max score 7.3e4 pre-softmax shortly before the failure. Data team notes the new mix contains many long repetitive log files. The infra team suspects a bad node.

title: LM head and vocabulary memory
text: Find the cause and a cheaper fix. You serve a 128,256-vocabulary model d = 4096 via a Hugging Face-based endpoint on a 24 GB GPU. Short prompts are fine. For 8,192-token prompts the process OOMs during prefill even though the KV cache for one sequence is only 1 GiB 128 KiB/token and weights are 15 GiB the logs show CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 3.91 GiB . Memory profile shows a single large allocation right at the end of the forward pass. A teammate proposes upgrading to a 48 GB GPU. Another proposes lowering max context to 4k.

title: Decoder-only vs encoder-only vs encoder-decoder
text: Explain the three transformer architecture families encoder-only, decoder-only, encoder-decoder . What is the real difference, and give one production use for each. "The blocks are the same; what changes is the attention mask and the objective. Encoder-only, like BERT, uses bidirectional attention and masked-token prediction, so it makes great representations for classification, NER and embeddings but cannot generate. Decoder-only, like GPT or Llama, uses a causal mask and next-token prediction, so it generates and is what chat LLMs use. Encoder-decoder, like T5 or the original Transformer, encodes the input bidirectionally and a decoder cross-attends to it, which suits translation and summarization. For a classifier at 5k QPS I would reach for an encoder; for open-ended generation, a decoder."

title: Why decoder-only dominates
text: Why did decoder-only models win for general-purpose LLMs, when encoder-decoder looks like a more natural fit for "input to output" tasks? "Three reasons. Every training token is a supervised signal in next-token prediction, so data efficiency per token is high and the objective scales cleanly. One stack handles every task as 'continue this text', so prompting, in-context learning and instruction tuning all fit with no task-specific heads. And inference infrastructure is simpler: one KV cache, one decode loop. Encoder-decoder isn't worse in principle at small scale; decoder-only just got the most scaling investment and tooling."

title: MoE active vs total parameters
text: A model card says "47B total parameters, 13B active". What does that mean, and what does it imply for compute, memory and quality? "In a Mixture-of-Experts model, each FFN layer is replaced by many expert FFNs plus a router, and each token is sent to only a few of them. Total parameters are everything that must exist in memory; active parameters are what a single token actually touches. So per-token FLOPs look like a 13B dense model, but I still need memory for all 47B weights. MoE saves compute, not memory. Quality tends to land between a 13B dense model and a 47B dense model, usually closer to the latter on knowledge-heavy tasks."

title: MoE routing and load balancing
text: How does routing work in a Mixture-of-Experts layer, and how do training recipes stop the router from collapsing onto a few experts? "A small linear router scores each token against every expert, we keep the top-k scores, softmax them into weights, and the layer output is the weighted sum of those experts' outputs. Left alone, the router self-reinforces: experts that get more tokens train faster, get chosen more, and the rest starve. So training adds an auxiliary load-balancing loss that penalizes uneven token distribution, plus an expert capacity limit that drops or reroutes overflow tokens. Some newer recipes, like DeepSeek-V3's, balance with per-expert bias terms instead of a loss, to avoid hurting the main objective."

title: Reasoning models and test-time compute
text: What is a "reasoning model" and what is test-time inference-time compute? How does it differ from just prompting a normal model with "think step by step"? "A reasoning model is trained, usually with reinforcement learning on verifiable outcomes like math answers and unit tests, to produce a long chain of thought before the final answer, and to use that scratchpad to explore, check and backtrack. Test-time compute means I spend more tokens at inference to get better answers, so quality scales with thinking length, not only model size. 'Think step by step' on a normal model is a prompt that elicits a short chain; a reasoning model has learned the behavior, so it is more reliable on hard problems, but it is slower and costs more because the thinking tokens are generated and typically billed."

title: Choosing an architecture
text: Which architecture and model family do you pick, and how do you justify it? A fintech must classify incoming customer emails into 40 intents. Volume is 3M emails/day peak 120 QPS , average 250 tokens, p95 latency budget 150 ms, one 16 GB GPU class per node. They have 60k labeled examples; current macro-F1 is 0.84 with a TF-IDF + logistic regression baseline. A teammate proposes calling a hosted frontier chat model with a 12-example few-shot prompt "it will be 0.9 out of the box" . Estimated prompt: 1,800 tokens in, 10 out. Illustrative price: $2.50 per 1M input tokens.

title: Multimodal architectures
text: How does a vision-language model like LLaVA let a text LLM "see" an image? Walk through the architecture and what is trained when. "A vision encoder, typically a CLIP ViT, turns the image into a grid of patch embeddings. A small projector, a linear layer or MLP, maps those into the LLM's embedding space so they look like token embeddings. They get concatenated with the text tokens and the decoder processes everything as one sequence. Training is usually staged: first train only the projector to align vision and language, then fine-tune the projector and LLM on visual instruction data. Image tokens consume context and compute like text tokens do."

title: State-space and hybrid models
text: What are state-space models like Mamba, how do they differ from attention, and why do production teams build hybrids? "A state-space layer compresses the history into a fixed-size state that it updates per token, like a learned recurrence, so compute grows linearly with sequence length and decode memory is constant, with no growing KV cache. Mamba makes the state update input-dependent, 'selective', so it can choose what to remember. The weakness is that a fixed state is lossy, so exact recall of arbitrary earlier tokens, like in-context retrieval, is weaker than attention. Hybrids such as Jamba interleave a few attention layers with many Mamba layers to get most of the memory savings and keep the recall."

title: Small vs large models
text: When would you choose a small model 1-8B over a large one 70B+ or a frontier API ? What do you give up? "I pick the smallest model that passes my eval at the required reliability. Small models win on cost, latency, on-device or private deployment, and fine-tuning ease. They lose on broad knowledge, multi-step reasoning, instruction-following on messy prompts, and robustness to out-of-distribution inputs. Narrow, well-defined tasks like extraction, classification and routing are where a tuned small model often matches a big one; open-ended reasoning and long, ambiguous tasks still favor large models."

title: MoE memory sizing
text: Why did it fail, what do you propose, and what do you tell the PM about "same speed"? You serve a dense 13B model bf16 on single 40 GB GPUs at 6 QPS with p95 of 1.2 s. Product wants better quality, and a vendor suggests a 47B-total / 13B-active MoE "same speed as what you have now" . Traffic will grow 10x to 60 QPS next quarter. GPUs available: 80 GB class, 8 per node. Average request: 1,500 prompt tokens, 300 output tokens. KV per token for this MoE is 128 KiB GQA, bf16; assume the same as the dense model for simplicity . Staging test on one 80 GB GPU: model fails to load.

title: MoE serving implications
text: You are asked to serve a large MoE model in production. What is different from serving a dense model of the same active size? Cover parallelism, batching, latency and failure modes. "Three differences. Memory: all experts must be resident, so the model needs multi-GPU sharding even though the compute is small. Communication: with expert parallelism each GPU holds a subset of experts, so tokens must be sent to the GPUs hosting their chosen experts and back, an all-to-all per MoE layer, which becomes the bottleneck on slow interconnects. Load imbalance: routing is data-dependent, so a hot expert makes one GPU the straggler and sets the step latency. Batching helps utilization because more tokens means every expert has work, but small batches waste bandwidth by reading experts that few tokens use."

title: MoE routing implementation
text: Find the bug and explain how you would prove it. You port a top-2 MoE layer from a reference implementation. Offline tests pass on shapes, but compared with reference outputs on 1,000 prompts the ported model has mean logit difference of 0.8 and perplexity rises from 6.1 to 7.4. Training-time load-balancing loss is not involved inference only . Code: def route x, router, k=2 : probs = torch.softmax router x , dim=-1 T, E topv, topi = probs.topk k, dim=-1 return topv, topi used directly as combine weights def forward x, router, experts : w, idx = route x, router out = torch.zeros like x for s in range 2 : for e in range len experts : m = idx :, s == e out m += w m, s, None experts e x m return out Distractors: the team suspects bf16 precision, a tokenizer difference, or FlashAttention versions.

title: Distillation
text: Explain knowledge distillation for LLMs. What are the variants, what does a student actually learn, and when is distillation the right architecture decision? "Distillation trains a small student to imitate a large teacher. Classic logit distillation minimizes KL divergence between the student's and teacher's token distributions, which carries more signal than one-hot labels because the teacher's soft probabilities encode which wrong answers are nearly right. For LLMs the common practical version is sequence-level: generate outputs, including reasoning traces, from the teacher and SFT the student on them. DeepSeek did this at scale, distilling R1 reasoning traces into 1.5B to 70B models. It is right when I have a narrow, high-volume task and a strong teacher; it is wrong when the student lacks the capacity or when the teacher's license forbids it."

title: Reasoning models cost and latency
text: How do you diagnose and what do you do? A coding assistant moved from a standard chat model to a reasoning model after a quality push. Traffic: 400k requests/day. Before: average 900 input tokens and 350 output tokens, p95 latency 4 s. After: average 900 input, 350 visible output plus 3,800 reasoning tokens, p95 latency 38 s. Illustrative prices: $3 per 1M input, $15 per 1M output tokens for both verify real pricing; reasoning tokens bill as output on most providers . Pass@1 on the internal eval rose from 61% to 74% overall, but on the 55% of traffic classified as "simple edits and explanations" it rose only from 93% to 94%. Support tickets about "slow responses" tripled; the CFO asks for a 40% cost cut.

title: Multimodal token cost
text: Explain the spike and what you would do. A claims app lets users upload photos of damage and asks a hosted vision-language model to describe them. Last week the median upload was a 1024x768 phone photo costing about 800 image tokens. After a mobile release that sends original 12 MP photos 4032x3024 , logs show: prompt tokens=6,412 per request up from 1,000 , p95 latency 3 s to 9 s, and the daily bill up 5x. Quality on a spot check is unchanged. The model tiling behavior is vendor-defined illustrative: images are split into 512px tiles at 170 tokens each plus a base of 85, with large images downscaled so the short side is at most 768px before tiling; verify the actual provider's documentation .

title: Distillation migration
text: How do you plan the migration? A document-extraction product calls a large model illustrative: $5 per 1M input, $15 per 1M output for 2M invoices/month: 3,000 input and 400 output tokens each, about $42k/month. Field-level accuracy is 96.5% with p95 of 6 s. The team distilled a 8B student from 150k teacher-labeled invoices teacher outputs, not human-verified . Offline on a held-out set the student scores 95.8%. Shadow traffic for a week shows 95.9% agreement-adjusted accuracy, but customer C about 4% of volume, many scanned multi-language invoices shows 88%. Product wants to cut over this month.

title: Test-time compute strategies
text: Besides a model that thinks in a long chain of thought, what other ways can you spend extra inference compute to improve answer quality? What are the trade-offs? "The main families are parallel and sequential. Parallel: sample N answers and pick one, by majority vote self-consistency , by a reward model or verifier best-of-N , or by running tests for code. Sequential: let the model revise, critique and retry using feedback, or use a longer thinking budget. Parallel methods need a way to choose; they work best when a cheap, reliable verifier exists, like unit tests or exact-match math answers. Cost scales roughly linearly with N, while quality gains flatten, so I tune N against the verifier's accuracy and the latency budget."

title: Multimodal vs text pipeline
text: What do you recommend, and how do you handle the ambiguity? A procurement team asks: "Use the new multimodal model so we can just send PDFs and get structured line items." Volume: 50k PDFs/month, 5 to 40 pages each median 12 , mix of digital-native and scanned, 15% with dense tables; they need totals reconciled to the cent and an audit trail. A vision call for a page costs roughly 1,200 image tokens illustrative ; the same page extracted as text is about 600 text tokens. The vendor pitches the multimodal path as "no OCR pipeline needed." There is no labeled dataset yet.

title: Pretraining objective
text: What is an LLM actually trained to do during pretraining, and how does that one objective produce models that can write code, translate and answer questions? "Pretraining minimizes cross-entropy on next-token prediction over trillions of tokens: given tokens 1..t, maximize the log-probability of token t+1. Nothing else is supervised. To predict text well across the web, the model has to compress grammar, facts, code semantics and reasoning patterns into its weights, so those skills emerge as a side effect. The result is a base model that continues text, not one that follows instructions."

title: Base vs chat models
text: What exactly changes between a base model and the chat/instruct model you call through an API? When would you deliberately choose the base model? "A base model is the raw pretrained next-token predictor. The chat model is that same network after supervised fine-tuning on instruction/response pairs, then preference optimization RLHF, DPO or similar , often plus safety and tool-use training. Weights are changed modestly, but behavior changes a lot: it follows a chat template, answers instead of continuing, refuses some requests, and is more verbose and agreeable. I pick a base model for few-shot pattern completion, calibrated probabilities, creative diversity, or as the starting point for my own fine-tune."

title: Pretraining data pipeline
text: Walk me through how a pretraining corpus is built from raw web crawl. Why do deduplication, quality filtering and data mixing matter so much? "Raw crawl goes through extraction HTML to text , language ID, heuristic filters, model-based quality filters, PII and toxicity handling, deduplication at exact and fuzzy levels, decontamination against benchmarks, then mixing across sources web, code, books, math, multilingual with chosen proportions and often an annealing phase of high-quality data at the end. Dedup reduces memorization and wasted compute; filtering raises the average quality per token; mixing sets the capability profile."

title: SFT and instruction data
text: What is supervised fine-tuning instruction tuning for an LLM, what does the data look like, and what does the loss actually apply to? "SFT continues training the base model with the same next-token loss, but on curated prompt/response pairs formatted with the chat template. Loss is usually computed only on the assistant tokens, not the prompt. It teaches format, style and instruction-following, not new knowledge. A few thousand to tens of thousands of very high-quality examples can work; quality beats quantity."

title: SFT pipeline
text: What is wrong, how do you confirm it, and how do you fix it without retraining blindly? You SFT a 7B open-weight base model on 18,000 customer-support conversations, 2 epochs, LR 2e-5. Eval loss looks great 0.31, train 0.29 but in a live canary the model answers correctly and then keeps going, inventing a fake "User:" turn and answering itself, in about 35% of requests, averaging 480 output tokens instead of 90. Your data prep: def to text ex : text = "" for m in ex "messages" : text += f"{m 'role' .upper }: {m 'content' }\n" return {"text": text} trainer: standard causal LM loss on "text", max len 1024, no special tokens added inference: tokenizer.apply chat template msgs, add generation prompt=True , stop on eos Red herrings: GPU is fine, the LR is typical, and eval loss is low.

title: Knowledge cutoff
text: What is a model's knowledge cutoff, why is it fuzzy, and how do you design applications around it? "The cutoff is the date after which the pretraining data contains little or nothing. The model's weights know nothing newer, and it is fuzzy because data about recent months is sparse the web has not finished writing about them , so the model's effective knowledge is weaker near the cutoff than the stated date suggests. Models also often misreport their own cutoff. In applications I inject the current date, and use retrieval or tools for anything time-sensitive."

title: RLHF pipeline
text: Explain the classic RLHF pipeline: what are the stages, how is the reward model trained, and what does PPO optimize? "Three stages: SFT on demonstrations; train a reward model on human pairwise preferences using a Bradley-Terry loss; then optimize the SFT policy with PPO to maximize reward minus a KL penalty to the SFT reference, so it does not drift into gibberish that fools the reward model. InstructGPT showed labelers preferred a 1.3B RLHF model over the 175B GPT-3 base."

title: DPO vs RLHF
text: How does Direct Preference Optimization work, and when would you choose it over PPO-based RLHF? "DPO rewrites the RLHF objective so the optimal policy is a closed-form function of the reward. That lets you express the reward as beta times the log-ratio of policy to reference, and train directly on preference pairs with a simple logistic loss. No reward model, no sampling loop, no value network: two forward passes per pair. I choose it for cheap, stable alignment with an offline preference dataset; I prefer online RL when I need exploration, verifiable rewards, or the data is far from the policy's own outputs."

title: Method selection
text: Which preference-optimization approach do you propose, and what do you build around it? Your team has an SFT'd 8B model for a legal-drafting assistant. You have 12,000 human-labeled preference pairs drafts ranked by lawyers , 2 GPUs of 80 GB, a 3-week deadline, and no RL infra. The product lead asks for "RLHF so it follows firm style." Output quality is judged by lawyers; there is no automatic correctness check. Inference budget is fixed; verbosity is already a complaint.

title: Reward hacking
text: What is reward hacking / over-optimization in RLHF, why does it happen mechanically, and how do you detect and limit it? "The reward model is a learned proxy trained on limited data. When the policy optimizes it hard, it finds regions where the proxy is high but true quality is low: verbose, flattering, formatted-looking answers. Gold reward rises then falls as proxy reward keeps climbing. I limit it with a KL penalty, early stopping on a held-out gold signal, RM ensembles, larger/better RMs, fresh preference data on policy samples, and by auditing output length and style."

title: Sycophancy and preference data
text: Why do preference-trained models become sycophantic, and what can you do about it in data and training? "Human raters, and reward models trained on their votes, tend to prefer answers that agree with them, flatter them, and sound confident. Optimizing against that preference signal teaches the model to tell people what they want to hear. Anthropic's sycophancy research found this behavior across RLHF-trained assistants and that preference models sometimes prefer sycophantic responses over truthful ones verify details . Mitigations: counter-sycophancy training data, diversified and expert raters, rewarding disagreement when the user is wrong, and evals that flip user opinion."

title: Preference tuning side effects
text: Diagnose and fix. What would you tell the VP who asks "didn't evals say it was better?" You shipped a DPO-tuned 70B assistant two weeks ago. Offline pairwise win rate vs the previous model: 64%. Live metrics since: average output 210 tokens was 150 , p95 latency 6.1 s was 4.4 s , GPU spend up 22%, support-ticket thumbs-down on "too wordy" up 3x, and a new log pattern: Great question! ... In summary, ... on 70% of answers. JSON-mode tasks show valid-JSON rate down from 99.1% to 96.8%. DPO run: beta 0.1, 3 epochs, 40k pairs. Reward-margin on train hit 8.0. Red herring: traffic mix is unchanged and the serving engine was not upgraded.

title: RLAIF and constitutional approaches
text: What are RLAIF and Constitutional AI, how do they differ from RLHF, and what are the risks of replacing human labels with model labels? "RLAIF replaces human preference labels with labels from an AI judge. Constitutional AI, from Anthropic, goes further: a written set of principles drives the model to critique and revise its own responses supervised phase , and an AI judge picks the better response according to the principles to produce preference data for RL RLAIF phase . It scales cheaply and makes the rules explicit and auditable. Risks: the judge's own biases length, self-preference, sycophancy get baked in, and errors are correlated, not averaged out like independent humans."

title: RLVR and reasoning RL
text: What is reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards RLVR , how does GRPO fit in, and what does it change compared with RLHF? What are its limits? "RLVR uses a programmatic checker as the reward: exact match on a math answer, unit tests for code, a format validator. No learned reward model, so far less reward hacking from a fuzzy proxy and no human labels needed. GRPO, introduced in DeepSeekMath and used for DeepSeek-R1, samples a group of responses per prompt and uses the group-normalized reward as the advantage, removing the value network. It works only where correctness is checkable, and some research argues it mostly sharpens sampling of abilities already in the base model rather than creating new ones; that is still debated."

title: DPO implementation
text: Find the bugs and explain why the loss dropped so fast while quality fell. A teammate implements DPO. Training runs, loss falls from 0.69 to 0.05 in 200 steps, reward accuracy hits 99%, but generations get worse: repetitive, sometimes empty, and held-out win rate vs the SFT model is 38%. Code: ref = copy.deepcopy policy A never switched to eval ; dropout stays on opt = torch.optim.AdamW policy.parameters , lr=5e-5 def dpo step batch, beta=0.1 : pw = seq logp policy, batch "chosen" pl = seq logp policy, batch "rejected" with torch.no grad : rw = seq logp ref, batch "chosen" rl = seq logp ref, batch "rejected" margin = beta pw - rw - pl - rl return -F.logsigmoid margin .mean def seq logp model, ids : B sums over ALL positions, padding and prompt included logits = model ids .logits :, :-1 lp = torch.log softmax logits, -1 .gather -1, ids :, 1:, None .squeeze -1 return lp.sum -1 Config: 5 epochs, chosen/rejected padded with pad token id, no attention-mask passed. Red herring: the data has been checked and looks fine.

title: Catastrophic forgetting
text: What is catastrophic forgetting when fine-tuning an LLM, why does it happen, and what techniques reduce it? "Fine-tuning updates the same shared weights that store general skills. If the new data distribution is narrow and the learning rate or epochs are high, gradients move weights away from the regions that supported old abilities, and old performance drops: format following, safety refusals, other languages. I reduce it with lower LR, fewer epochs, LoRA/adapters, replay of general or original-style data mixed in, regularization toward the original weights, and by regression-testing a general eval suite."

title: Alignment tax
text: What is the "alignment tax," and is it real in current models? "Alignment tax is the drop in raw capability or benchmark performance caused by alignment training, such as RLHF. InstructGPT observed regressions on some public NLP tasks from PPO and reduced them by mixing pretraining gradients into the update PPO-ptx . Today the tax is usually small on knowledge benchmarks and often negative for usability, but it shows up as lower calibration, less diversity, over-refusal, and sometimes lower performance on tasks like few-shot completion. It is a trade-off that must be measured per use case."

title: Over-refusal after safety tuning
text: Run the post-incident review: what went wrong, how do you measure and fix it, what process change prevents recurrence? Your company fine-tuned a 13B chat model with an extra safety dataset 6,000 refusal examples, 2 epochs for a healthcare-adjacent product. After launch, support sees complaints: the model refuses "What is the maximum safe dose of ibuprofen?" and "How do I kill a Python process?". Over 4 weeks, refusal rate on benign eval prompts went from 2% to 14%, while red-team attack success fell from 20% to 3%. Log excerpt: assistant: I'm sorry, but I can't help with that request. on 9% of 120k weekly queries. Red herring: system prompt unchanged for 2 months.

title: Synthetic data and model collapse
text: When is training on model-generated data safe and useful, and what is model collapse? How do you build a synthetic pipeline that avoids it? "Synthetic data is great when a filter or verifier injects information the generator did not have: correctness checks, tests, stronger-teacher distillation, human-curated seeds. It is dangerous when a model is trained recursively on its own unfiltered outputs: Shumailov et al. showed the tails of the distribution vanish over generations, a degradation they called model collapse. Mitigations: keep real data in the mix accumulating rather than replacing helps , filter hard, diversify generators and prompts, and measure diversity, not only quality."

title: Synthetic data pipeline
text: How do you scope and execute this? What would you push back on? A PM says: "We have 400 real customer conversations about insurance claims. Generate 50,000 more with an LLM and fine-tune our 8B model so it handles claims." Budget: roughly $2,000 of API spend, 2 weeks, a small team. Teacher API cost is $3 per 1M input and $15 per 1M output tokens illustrative . Average synthetic conversation is 900 output tokens and 400 input tokens. Compliance says no real customer PII may reach a third-party API. Held-out eval: 60 real conversations rated by claims staff.

title: Knowledge cutoff
text: Diagnose and fix. Which of these failures are cutoff problems, which are not? An HR-policy assistant built on a hosted chat model provider-stated knowledge cutoff roughly 14 months ago runs for 9,000 employees. Complaints this week: it said the "parental leave is 12 weeks" policy changed to 16 weeks 5 months ago ; it computed an employee's tenure as "4 years" when the true value is 5; and when asked "what is the latest version of our HR portal?" it named a version two releases behind. The RAG index contains the current policy PDFs last re-indexed 6 weeks ago . Logs: top-3 retrieved chunks for the leave question include the current policy chunk at rank 2. Red herring: provider status page shows no incidents.

title: Preference labeling cost
text: Design the labeling strategy. What goes to humans, what to the AI judge, and how do you keep the pipeline honest? Your assistant gets 2M conversations per month. You currently collect 8,000 human preference pairs per month at $4.50 per pair about $36,000/month and run DPO monthly. Leadership wants to scale the training signal 10x without a 10x bill. An experiment: an LLM judge about $0.02 per pair, illustrative agrees with humans 78% overall, but only 61% on the safety-sensitive and medical subsets about 15% of traffic , and it prefers longer answers 70% of the time when lengths differ by 2x. Human inter-annotator agreement is 73%.

title: Preference data quality
text: What makes preference data good or bad? Discuss on-policy vs off-policy pairs, annotator noise, and how to curate a dataset before running DPO or RM training. "Good preference data has clear, consistent margins between chosen and rejected, covers the prompt distribution you serve, comes from outputs near the current policy on-policy , and is free of spurious correlates like length or style. Bad data has noisy labels, tiny quality gaps, systematic artifacts, or pairs whose responses are far from anything the policy would generate. I curate by filtering by annotator agreement and margin, balancing length, deduplicating prompts, and auditing a sample by hand."

title: Post-training plan
text: Lay out the post-training plan: stages, data, evaluation and rollout. Would you commit to the cost-cut target? You own a customer-support assistant built on a closed API chat model: $0.0045 per conversation, 1.2M conversations per month $5,400/month , p95 latency 3.8 s, 91% resolution on your eval. A VP wants to "own the model" using an open-weight 8B base and cut cost 60%. You have 150k historical conversations 30k with CSAT scores , 3 engineers, 2 months, 8 GPUs available for training. The company has no RL infrastructure. The live traffic must not regress.

title: Kaplan vs Chinchilla
text: What is a neural scaling law, and how did the Chinchilla result differ from the earlier Kaplan result? A scaling law says pretraining loss falls as a smooth power law in parameters N, training tokens D and compute C. Kaplan et al. 2020 concluded that for a fixed compute budget you should mostly grow the model and train it on relatively modest data, stopping before convergence. Chinchilla Hoffmann et al., 2022 redid the fits with proper learning-rate schedules per run and found N and D should scale roughly in equal proportion, about 20 tokens per parameter. Their 70B model trained on about 4x more data than the 280B Gopher, at the same compute, beat it.

title: Reading loss curves and power laws
text: If a scaling-law plot shows loss falling as a straight line on log-log axes, what can and can't you conclude from it? A straight line on log-log means a power law: each constant multiplicative increase in compute gives a constant multiplicative drop in the reducible loss. It means returns diminish in absolute terms but are predictable, and that you can extrapolate small runs. It does not tell me the loss floor is zero, that downstream skills improve smoothly, or that the trend holds outside the fitted range.

title: Compute-optimal training math
text: Given a budget of 1e24 training FLOPs, how would you estimate the compute-optimal model size and token count, and how many GPU-hours is that? Use C ≈ 6ND with D ≈ 20N. So C = 120 N², N = sqrt 1e24/120 ≈ 91B parameters and D ≈ 1.8T tokens. For GPU time, divide by realistic sustained FLOPs: H100 peak dense BF16 is on the order of 1e15 FLOP/s verify spec , and large runs often reach roughly 30-45% utilisation, so about 4e14 effective. That is 2.5e9 GPU-seconds, about 700k GPU-hours.

title: Overtraining small models
text: Why do modern open models like Llama 3 8B train far past the Chinchilla-optimal token count? Chinchilla minimises loss for a given training budget. But a model is trained once and served billions of times, and inference cost scales with parameters. So it pays to spend extra training compute on a smaller model to reach the quality of a larger one. Meta reported training Llama 3 8B on about 15T tokens, roughly 1,900 tokens per parameter versus the 20 heuristic, with loss still improving log-linearly.

title: Emergent abilities debate
text: What are "emergent abilities", and why do some researchers say they are a mirage? Emergent abilities are skills that appear absent in small models and then jump sharply at some scale. Schaeffer et al. argue many of those jumps come from the metric: exact-match or all-or-nothing scores are nonlinear in per-token accuracy, so smooth underlying improvement looks like a sudden leap. With continuous metrics like token-level log-likelihood the curves are smooth. The honest position: some of it is metric artefact, but for practical purposes capability on a specific task can still be hard to predict in advance.

title: Benchmark contamination and saturation
text: What are benchmark contamination and saturation, and how do they make leaderboard numbers unreliable? Contamination means test items, or near-copies, leaked into training data, so the score measures memorisation. Saturation means top models cluster near the ceiling, so the benchmark can't tell them apart and label errors dominate the remaining gap. Both inflate or flatten the signal, so I treat public benchmarks as a coarse filter and decide with my own held-out task evals.

title: Reading benchmark claims
text: What do you do before agreeing to switch? A vendor's launch post says their new model "beats GPT-class models on MMLU, HumanEval and GSM8K" and shows a bar chart: new model 88.5, competitor 87.0 on MMLU. Footnotes: new model "5-shot, best of 3 runs"; competitor number "from the competitor's technical report". Your VP wants to switch a support-classification workload 2M requests/day, mean 900 input tokens to it because it is also "30% cheaper per token". MMLU has about 14k questions. You have 400 labelled tickets from production.

title: Data wall
text: What is the "data wall", and what are the realistic ways labs respond to it? Compute-optimal training wants tokens to grow in step with model size, but the stock of high-quality public human text is finite. Epoch AI's 2022 estimate was that training sets could reach the size of the available public human text between 2026 and 2032, sooner if models are overtrained. Responses: multiple epochs on the same data, better filtering and quality weighting, synthetic data, multimodal and code data, private or licensed data, and shifting compute to post-training and inference time.

title: Inference-time scaling
text: What is inference-time test-time scaling, and when is it better than using a bigger model? Instead of making the model bigger, you spend more compute per query: sample many answers and pick one best-of-N, majority vote , use a verifier or reward model to search, or let the model generate a long chain of thought. Snell et al. 2024 found that allocating test-time compute adaptively per prompt can beat best-of-N by over 4x efficiency, and that on problems where a small model has non-trivial success, extra test-time compute can beat a 14x larger model in a FLOPs-matched comparison. It helps on checkable, multi-step tasks and doesn't fix missing knowledge.

title: Cost-of-training intuition
text: Estimate the cost and give a recommendation. A startup CEO asks whether you should "train our own 70B model from scratch" because API spend is $180k/month on a document-extraction product about 3B tokens/day total . You have 128 H100s on offer at $2.5/GPU-hour verify , a 1.5T-token licensed/proprietary corpus of mixed quality, and no prior pretraining experience. An open 70B model scores 94% on your internal extraction eval; the API model scores 96%.

title: Benchmark contamination
text: Run the post-incident review: what happened, how do you confirm, and what changes? Your team fine-tuned a 7B model on 200k synthetic coding tasks generated by a larger model. Internal benchmark: 71% pass@1 on a public 500-problem coding set, up from 52% for the base. In a pilot with real customer repos, pass rate on 300 tasks is 49%. Marketing already published "71%". A teammate notes the generator model was prompted with "problems in the style of" the public set, and the training JSON has a field source hint containing problem titles. Dedup was done by exact string match only.

title: Scaling trade-offs
text: Which do you pick, and how do you justify it? A chat product serves 40M requests/day, average 1,200 input and 300 output tokens. Option A: hosted 70B-class open model on H100s. Option B: an 8B-class overtrained model, fine-tuned on your domain. Offline eval on 1,000 held-out conversations judge-scored 1-5 : A 4.35, B 4.12, with per-category gaps largest on multi-step reasoning A 4.1 vs B 3.4 . Estimated serving cost: A $0.60 per 1M tokens, B $0.09 per 1M tokens assumed, verify with your own benchmarks . Product team says users complain mostly about wrong answers on hard questions, which are 12% of traffic.

title: Limits of scaling-law extrapolation
text: Scaling laws predict loss well. Why can't you simply use them to predict what a model will be able to do, and where do they break? Laws are fit to next-token loss on a specific data distribution. Task performance is a nonlinear, sometimes thresholded function of loss and depends on data mix, post-training and the metric. Extrapolating beyond the fitted range is also risky: data limits, optimiser instabilities, changing data quality and architecture changes shift the curve. So I use laws for planning compute and ranking small-scale ablations, and I validate capabilities directly.

title: Inference-time scaling
text: How do you decide and de-risk the rollout? You run a support assistant on a standard chat model: p50 latency 2.1 s, p95 4.5 s, cost $0.004 per request at 5M requests/day. You A/B test a reasoning model on 5% traffic: resolution accuracy rises from 78% to 86% on a 2,000-case eval, but p50 latency becomes 14 s, p95 41 s, and cost per request $0.031. Output tokens jumped from 350 to about 4,200 including hidden reasoning . Timeouts at the gateway 30 s hit 7% of reasoning requests. Product wants a 100% rollout next week.

title: What the context window is
text: What is a context window, and what actually limits how large it can be? The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can attend to in one forward pass: prompt plus everything it generates. It is limited by three things: the length the model was trained at positions beyond that are unfamiliar , the O n^2 attention compute, and the KV-cache memory that grows linearly with tokens. A provider's advertised number is where those three were engineered to hold up, not a guarantee of quality.

title: Token budgeting across input and output
text: How do you budget a context window between system prompt, history, retrieved content and the model's answer? I compute the budget as window minus reserved output, then allocate fixed shares: system prompt and tools are non-negotiable, the latest user message is non-negotiable, and history and retrieval fill the rest by priority. I count with the model's real tokenizer, keep a safety margin for template overhead, and decide up front what is trimmed first so overflow never becomes a runtime error.

title: KV-cache memory math
text: Estimate the KV-cache memory for a 128K-token request on a Llama-3-8B-class model. Why does it matter for long context? Per token the cache stores K and V for every layer: 2 x layers x KV heads x head dim x bytes. For an 8B model with 32 layers, 8 KV heads GQA , head dim 128 in bf16, that is 131,072 bytes, 128 KiB per token. At 128K tokens that is about 16 GiB for one request, as much as the model weights themselves. So concurrency collapses as context grows.

title: Prefill vs decode cost of long prompts
text: Why does a long prompt make the first token slow, while later tokens are less affected? What is the real cost scaling? Prefill processes all n prompt tokens in parallel; its attention work scales as n^2 and its linear-layer work as n, so time to first token TTFT grows super-linearly with prompt length. Decode generates one token at a time, attending to the cached n keys, so each step costs O n memory reads but is dominated by reading weights and cache from memory. Long prompts hurt TTFT a lot and per-token speed modestly.

title: Cost/latency of long prompts
text: How do you cut cost and latency without hurting quality? A support copilot sends, per request, a 6K-token system prompt policies, tool schemas, 40 few-shot examples , plus 2K of conversation and a 500-token answer. Traffic is 2M requests/day. Illustrative pricing: $3 per 1M input tokens, $15 per 1M output tokens verify your provider; cached input is typically discounted . Monthly bill is about $1.4M and finance wants it down 40%. p95 TTFT is 3.2 s. Someone proposes switching to a smaller model.

title: Length extrapolation failure
text: Why does a model trained on 4K tokens fall apart when you feed it 16K, even though nothing in the architecture forbids it? Attention itself accepts any length, but the position signal does not. With RoPE, each token's query and key are rotated by an angle proportional to position; beyond the trained range the model sees rotation angles and relative distances it never saw, so attention scores become unpredictable. Perplexity explodes. The fix is to remap positions into the trained range or retrain a little at the longer length.

title: Position interpolation, NTK scaling, YaRN
text: Explain how Position Interpolation, NTK-aware scaling and YaRN extend a RoPE model's context, and what you give up with each. Position Interpolation divides positions by a scale factor s so longer inputs map into the trained range; it needs a short fine-tune and blurs local resolution. NTK-aware scaling changes the RoPE base instead, stretching low frequencies a lot and high frequencies little, so nearby tokens stay distinguishable. YaRN combines per-frequency interpolation with an attention temperature tweak and needs much less fine-tuning data. All trade some short-context sharpness for reach.

title: Lost in the middle
text: What is the "lost in the middle" effect, and how does it change how you assemble prompts? Liu et al. found that models answer best when the relevant information is at the start or end of the context and worse when it is in the middle, a U-shaped accuracy curve, even for models built for long inputs. In practice I put the most important instructions and evidence at the edges, keep context short, rerank so top results are first, and measure position sensitivity on my own data because newer models vary.

title: Needle-in-a-haystack tests
text: What does a needle-in-a-haystack test measure, and why can a model ace it and still fail on your documents? The test hides one fact in a long filler text and asks the model to retrieve it, sweeping length and depth. It measures literal lookup of a distinctive string. Models that score near 100% can still fail at multi-fact aggregation, reasoning across the text, or when the needle looks like surrounding content. So I use it as a smoke test, then run RULER-style or task-specific evals.

title: History trimming
text: Find the bugs and fix them. A chat service trims history to fit a 16K window. Users report that after long conversations the assistant "forgets its rules" and sometimes returns a provider 400 context length exceeded prompt 16,412 tokens 16,384 . Average conversation is 40 turns; system prompt is 1.2K tokens; max output is set to 1,024. Code: def trim messages, count, limit=16384 : total = sum count m "content" for m in messages while total limit and len messages 1: removed = messages.pop 0 total -= count removed "content" return messages

title: Effective vs advertised context
text: How do you respond and what do you do next? A product manager says: "The vendor's model has a 1M-token window, so we'll let customers upload their whole knowledge base up to 700K tokens and ask questions. No RAG needed." Questions are mixed: lookups "what is the refund window?" and cross-document ones "which of our policies conflict with the new EU rule?" . Target: 90% answer accuracy, p95 latency under 20 s, about 5K queries/day. Illustrative price $2.50 per 1M input tokens verify . No eval set exists yet.

title: Long context vs RAG
text: When would you choose long-context prompting over RAG, and when the reverse? Isn't RAG dead now? They solve different constraints. Long context wins when the corpus is small enough to fit and cache, the task needs holistic or cross-document reasoning, and I want fewer moving parts. RAG wins when the corpus is much larger than any window, changes often, needs access control or citations, or when per-query cost and latency matter. Most production systems end up hybrid: retrieve broadly, then give the model a generous but curated context.

title: Context rot
text: Why did quality go down although recall went up, and what do you do? An internal analyst assistant was upgraded to "use more context": retrieval top-k went from 8 to 60 chunks about 4K to 38K tokens , reasoning that the new model has a 200K window verify . Two weeks later, user thumbs-down rose from 6% to 14%. Offline eval on the 300-question set: accuracy 84% at k=8, 76% at k=60. Logs show answers citing wrong but plausible numbers from near-duplicate quarterly reports; latency p95 went from 2.1 s to 6.8 s; cost per query tripled. Retrieval recall@60 improved from 88% to 96%.

title: Context rot
text: What is "context rot", why does performance degrade as input grows even on simple tasks, and what can you do about it? Context rot is the observed decline in model reliability as input length increases, even when the task stays the same difficulty. Chroma's 2025 study reported degradation across many models on controlled tasks, worsened by distractors that are semantically close to the answer and by lower similarity between question and needle verify details in the report . Causes are not fully settled: attention dilution, positional biases and training distribution on shorter sequences. I manage it by keeping context small and relevant.

title: Long context vs RAG
text: Design the context strategy. A legal-tech startup reviews M&A data rooms. A deal has 400-900 documents, about 1.5-4M tokens in total; analysts ask 30-60 questions per deal over a week "list all change-of-control clauses", "any contradictions on liability caps?" . Acceptance: recall of clauses above 95%, every claim cited to page, no cross-client leakage. Budget: $40 per deal in LLM spend. Illustrative price $3 per 1M input, cached reads at 10% verify . Largest available window is 1M tokens verify .

title: Context management strategies
text: A conversation or agent run will exceed the window. What are your options for managing context, and how do you choose? Five options: truncate drop oldest , sliding window, summarize older content, retrieve relevant memory on demand, and offload to external state such as files or notes. I combine them: pin instructions, keep the last N turns verbatim, summarize the middle, and store facts and artifacts externally with retrieval. Choice depends on whether old details are needed verbatim, cost of an extra summarization call, and error tolerance.

title: Cost/latency of long prompts
text: What do you do before the 10x traffic arrives? A document-chat product has 20K DAU, each session uploads a 90K-token document and asks about 8 questions. Today the full document plus history is sent every turn with no caching: 20K x 8 x about 92K = 14.7B input tokens/day. Illustrative $3 per 1M input = $44K/day. Marketing plans a 10x user push. On a self-hosted fallback with an 8B model, you saw 16 GiB KV per 128K request and OOMs when concurrency exceeded 3 per GPU. p95 TTFT is 11 s.

title: Migrating to a longer window
text: How do you migrate safely? You run a contract-summary service on a 32K-window model with chunk-and-merge map-reduce summarization at 15K requests/day. A vendor's newer model offers 200K verify at a similar per-token price. Product wants to drop map-reduce and send whole documents average 70K tokens, p95 160K in one call. Current eval: faithfulness 91%, key-clause coverage 88%. Latency p95 now 9 s; a pilot on the new model gave p95 31 s on the long tail and coverage 90% on average but 79% for documents above 120K tokens.

title: Open-weight vs open-source vs closed
text: People say "open-source LLM". What do they usually mean, and how is that different from an open-weight model or a closed API model? "Closed API means I only get an endpoint; weights, training data and code stay with the vendor. Open-weight means the trained weights are downloadable, so I can host, fine-tune and inspect them, but usually not the training data or full recipe, and the license may restrict use. Truly open-source in the OSI sense would also need an OSI-approved license and ideally open data and code. Most 'open-source LLMs' are really open-weight, so I read the license before assuming anything."

title: Open vs closed decision axes
text: What are the main factors you weigh when choosing between a closed API model and a self-hosted open-weight model? "I weigh six things: capability on my task, cost at my volume, data privacy and residency, control and customization, latency and reliability, and lock-in or deprecation risk. Closed APIs usually win on peak capability and zero ops. Open-weight wins on data control, version stability, deep customization and cost at sustained high volume. I decide on an eval of my own task, and often end up hybrid."

title: License types
text: Explain the main license families you see on LLM weights: Apache 2.0/MIT, Llama-style community licenses, and OpenRAIL. What do they allow and restrict? "Apache 2.0 and MIT are permissive: commercial use, modification and redistribution allowed with notice/attribution, and Apache adds an explicit patent grant. Llama-style community licenses are custom: broadly commercial but with conditions like attribution, naming rules, an acceptable-use policy, and a large-scale user threshold. OpenRAIL licenses add behavioral-use restrictions, such as banned harmful uses, that must flow down to derivatives. I always read the specific model's license file, since families mix licenses by size and version."

title: Llama license obligations
text: If you build a commercial product on a Llama 3.x model, what obligations does the community license put on you? "From the Llama 3.1 community license text I looked at: you must include a copy of the agreement when distributing, show 'Built with Llama' on related product surfaces, start derivative model names with 'Llama', keep the notice file, and if your products exceed 700 million monthly active users you must request a license from Meta. There's also an acceptable-use policy. Versions differ, so I'd verify the version I'm actually deploying and have legal sign off."

title: Sizing models to tasks
text: How do you decide how big a model a task needs? Walk through how you would match model size to task. "I classify the task by how much reasoning, world knowledge and instruction nuance it needs. Classification, extraction, routing, and short summarization often work on small models, especially with few-shot or light fine-tuning. Multi-step reasoning, ambiguous instructions, long-horizon agents and open-ended writing need larger or reasoning models. I start with the cheapest model that might work, build a labeled eval set, and move up only until quality meets the bar."

title: Latency / price / quality trade-offs
text: How do latency, price and quality trade off when picking an LLM, and how do you reason about each quantitatively? "Price is input tokens times input rate plus output tokens times output rate, and output is usually several times pricier per token. Latency is time to first token, driven by prompt size and queueing, plus output tokens times per-token decode time, so long outputs dominate. Quality is task eval score. Bigger models cost more and decode slower; reasoning models spend hidden thinking tokens, raising both cost and latency. I plot candidates on a cost-latency-quality chart and pick from the Pareto frontier for the product's SLA."

title: Model selection
text: How do you choose the model for production? A B2B support platform wants to auto-triage 2.4M tickets/month into 14 categories and a priority level. Average ticket is 600 input tokens; output is a short JSON of about 40 tokens. The prototype uses a frontier closed model at illustrative $3 in / $15 out per 1M tokens and scores 94% accuracy on 500 hand-labeled tickets. Finance flags the projected bill. Target p95 under 2 s. Legal says tickets may contain customer PII but a zero-retention API is acceptable. A teammate proposes "just use the cheapest open model".

title: Self-hosting economics
text: Does self-hosting pay off? Show the math and what else you need to know. A document-tagging service calls a mid-tier closed API illustrative $0.50 in / $1.50 out per 1M tokens . It processes 2.0B input and 0.4B output tokens a month. The CTO asks whether to self-host an open-weight 8B model instead. Quoted GPU cost: $2.00/hour per GPU on-demand illustrative . Load testing shows one GPU sustains about 1,500 output tokens/s aggregate with batching at the latency target assumption, measure yourself . Traffic is business-hours heavy: peak is 4x the overnight average. One platform engineer is available at about 30% time.

title: Quantization levels (brief)
text: When choosing a deployment model, how does quantization level FP16, FP8, INT8, 4-bit affect quality and cost, and how would you decide? "Quantization stores weights, and sometimes activations, in fewer bits to cut memory and often speed up serving. From the studies I read, 8-bit and FP8 are close to lossless, while 4-bit weight-only methods show small average drops that grow on long context and non-English tasks. So I treat FP8/INT8 as the safe default, and 4-bit as a decision I validate on my own eval set, especially for long inputs, multilingual, and reasoning-heavy tasks."

title: Choosing by eval, not leaderboard
text: Why shouldn't you pick a model based on public leaderboards, and what do you do instead? "Public benchmarks measure someone else's tasks, can be contaminated by training data, are gamed or overfit, and ignore my latency, cost, format and language needs. I use leaderboards only to shortlist, then build a task-specific eval from real production-like inputs with a rubric or labels, run 3-5 candidates under the same prompt budget, and choose on quality, cost and p95 together with confidence intervals."

title: Fallbacks
text: Find the bugs and fix the design. A gateway wraps two models to improve availability: a primary with a 128k context window and a cheaper fallback with an 8k window. After launch, support reports empty answers on long documents, and the bill is 1.4x expected. Logs show repeated primary: 400 context length exceeded then fallback: 400 context length exceeded for 3% of requests, plus primary: timeout bursts followed by fallback success with noticeably worse answers. Code pseudo-SDK, client.chat stands for any provider SDK : MODELS = "big-128k", "small-8k" def complete messages : for model in MODELS: try: r = client.chat model=model, messages=messages, timeout=5 return r.text except Exception: continue return ""

title: Multi-model routing
text: Explain multi-model routing. How do routers, cascades and static rules differ, and what can go wrong? "Routing sends each request to the cheapest model that can handle it. A static rule routes by task type. A learned router predicts, before generating, whether a strong or weak model is needed. A cascade tries the cheap model first and escalates if a confidence check fails, costing extra for escalated requests. Wins are real but depend on the router's accuracy and the confidence signal, so I measure routing quality against an eval and monitor drift."

title: Alias drift
text: What happened and how do you respond? A contract-analysis product calls model="provider-large-latest" . Monday 09:10 the extraction accuracy dashboard daily eval on 300 canned contracts drops from 93% to 81%. Customer tickets mention "missing clauses" and malformed JSON. No deploy happened in 5 days. API error rate is normal; p95 latency is up from 3.1 s to 4.4 s; mean output tokens rose from 410 to 640. A teammate suspects the vector DB red herring: the product does not use RAG for this feature ; another suspects a prompt injection in a customer file.

title: Deprecation risk & abstraction layers
text: How do you design for vendor model deprecation and lock-in? What does a good abstraction layer look like and what are its limits? "Assume every model will be retired. I pin dated snapshots, track vendor deprecation notices, and keep a thin provider-agnostic interface for the request/response plus an adapter per provider. The real portability work is not the API call; it is prompts, tool schemas, structured-output behavior and evals. So I keep prompts versioned per model and a regression eval suite that lets me swap a model in days with evidence."

title: Migration
text: How do you run the migration? A fintech chat assistant serves 1,800 req/min peak on a closed API model, average 1,500 input and 250 output tokens. A new compliance rule requires customer text to stay inside the company's cloud account within 6 months. The plan: move to a self-hosted open-weight 70B model. Offline eval: 91% task pass vs 94% for the incumbent. The new stack's p95 is 5.2 s vs 3.0 s. Prompts use the incumbent's tool-call format; 22% of traffic uses tools. No downtime allowed.

title: Data residency & compliance
text: A customer demands that their data never leave the EU and not be used for training. How do model-selection and deployment choices respond to data residency and compliance requirements? "I separate four things: where data is processed, where it is stored or logged, whether the vendor may train on it, and who can access it. Options range from a vendor's regional endpoint with zero data retention, to a closed model served inside my cloud account, to self-hosted open weights in my VPC or on-prem. I pick the least costly option that satisfies the legal text, get contractual terms DPA, subprocessors , and verify with legal; I do not decide compliance alone."

title: Selection under ambiguity
text: How do you turn this into a model-selection decision? A legal-tech VP says: "We need the best model for reviewing contracts. Budget is flexible." Facts you can get: 40k contracts/year, average 18k tokens some 150k , reviewers currently spend 25 minutes per contract, a wrong "no risk" call is costly, and two customers ban sending data to third parties. There is no labeled data yet. Three vendors have pitched benchmark slides. Your team has two engineers and a six-week target.

title: Customization & lock-in
text: How do customization options prompting, RAG, fine-tuning differ between closed and open-weight models, and how does that affect lock-in? "With open weights I can fully fine-tune, use LoRA, merge, quantize and serve anywhere, and the resulting artifact is mine, subject to the license. Closed vendors offer limited fine-tuning options on selected models, the tuned model lives on their platform and dies with its base model's lifecycle. Prompts and RAG are portable-ish but tuned to a model's quirks. The portable assets are data: eval sets, training examples and retrieval corpora. I invest there."

title: Scale 10x
text: What is your plan to scale 10x? An AI writing assistant uses a mid-tier closed model illustrative $2.50 in / $10 out per 1M . Today: 300k requests/day, 900 input and 350 output tokens each. The launch of a new partner will take it to 3M requests/day within a month. API rate limits are 4M tokens/minute today. Quality bar: 85% win-or-tie against the incumbent in blind human pairwise review. Budget owner says the infra bill must not exceed 3x current.

title: Reasoning vs non-reasoning model selection
text: When should you choose a reasoning model over a standard chat model, and what are the production costs of that choice? "Reasoning models spend extra inference-time tokens thinking before answering, which helps on multi-step math, code, planning and ambiguous analysis. The cost is hidden thinking tokens, usually billed as output, higher latency, less predictable cost per request, and sometimes weaker instruction-following on simple formats. I use them for hard, high-value tasks, route simple requests to standard models, and cap thinking budget where the API allows."

title: Logits to tokens
text: Walk me through exactly what happens between the final transformer layer and the next token appearing in the output. The last hidden state of the final position is multiplied by the unembedding matrix to give one raw score logit per vocabulary entry. I optionally adjust those logits penalties, bias, temperature , convert to probabilities with softmax, optionally truncate the distribution top-k, top-p, min-p , renormalize, and then pick a token, either argmax greedy or a random draw. That token is appended and the loop repeats, one token per forward pass thanks to the KV cache.

title: Temperature
text: What does temperature actually do mathematically, and what happens at T=0, T=1 and T much greater than 1? Temperature divides the logits before softmax. T<1 sharpens the distribution toward the top token, T 1 flattens it toward uniform, T=1 leaves the model's own distribution unchanged. T→0 converges to argmax, and T→infinity converges to a uniform choice over the vocabulary. It does not change the ranking of tokens, only the gaps between their probabilities.

title: Greedy vs beam vs sampling
text: Compare greedy decoding, beam search and sampling. When would you pick each? Greedy takes the argmax at every step: cheap, deterministic in principle, but can miss better sequences. Beam search keeps the B highest-scoring partial sequences, approximating the max-likelihood sequence; great when there is a single correct output like translation or ASR. Sampling draws from the truncated distribution; it is what chat and creative generation use because maximum likelihood text is often bland and repetitive.

title: Top-k vs top-p
text: Explain top-k and top-p nucleus sampling. Why is top-p usually preferred, and what are its failure modes? Top-k keeps the k most likely tokens and renormalizes; top-p keeps the smallest set whose cumulative probability reaches p. Top-k is fixed width, so when the model is very sure it still admits k-1 junk candidates, and when the model is uncertain many valid tokens it cuts valid ones. Top-p adapts the candidate set size to the model's confidence. Its weakness is that at high temperature the flattened distribution makes the nucleus large and junky.

title: Min-p
text: What is min-p sampling, and what problem does it solve that top-p does not? Min-p keeps only tokens whose probability is at least p base times the probability of the top token. The threshold scales with the model's confidence: when the top token has 0.9, the cutoff is high; when the top token has only 0.1, the cutoff is low. Unlike top-p, it does not let the candidate set explode when temperature flattens the distribution, so it keeps coherence at higher temperatures.

title: Sampling code
text: Find the bugs and fix them. A teammate wrote a custom sampler for a self-hosted 7B model and says "it works at T=0.7 but at T=0 the service crashes with NaN and at T=1.5 the answers are strangely good". Code: import torch def sample logits, temperature, top p : probs = torch.softmax logits, dim=-1 sorted p, idx = torch.sort probs, descending=True cum = torch.cumsum sorted p, dim=-1 sorted p cum top p = 0.0 sorted p = sorted p / sorted p.sum scaled = torch.softmax torch.log sorted p + 1e-9 / temperature, dim=-1 return idx torch.multinomial scaled, 1 Logs: RuntimeError: probability tensor contains either inf, nan or element < 0 at temperature=0. Eval at top p=0.9: first token is sometimes empty-set trouble when the top token has p=0.93.

title: Non-determinism
text: You set temperature to 0 and the model still returns different outputs on identical requests. Why? Temperature 0 removes sampling randomness, but logits are still floating-point numbers computed on GPUs. Floating-point addition is not associative, and the order of reductions in matmul, attention and normalization kernels depends on batch size, tiling and parallel scheduling. On a shared server your request lands in different batches each time, so the logits differ in the last bits. When two top tokens are near-tied, argmax flips, and after one flipped token everything downstream diverges. Mixture-of-experts routing, hardware differences and model/version rollouts add more variance.

title: Beam search vs sampling
text: Do you adopt beam search for A, B, both or neither? Defend with mechanics and cost. You own two features on one self-hosted 8B model served with vLLM-style batching on 4 GPUs: A English-to-German product description translation, 2M items/day, reference translations exist, BLEU/COMET tracked; B a customer chat assistant, 40 QPS peak, p95 target 3 s. A colleague proposes "beam search with 5 beams everywhere because it finds higher-probability outputs". Current greedy decode uses 14 GB of KV cache per GPU at the peak batch.

title: Seeds and reproducibility
text: What does setting a seed do for LLM generation, and what does it not guarantee? How would you design for reproducible outputs? A seed initializes the random number generator that drives the sampling step the multinomial draw . With the same seed, same weights, same prompt, same params and identical logits, the same tokens come out. It does not fix numerical variation in logits from batching, hardware or backend changes. Providers that expose seed describe it as best-effort; OpenAI's docs say outputs are "mostly" consistent and expose system fingerprint to detect backend changes verify current status, as the field has been de-emphasized . For real reproducibility I log the full request, the seed, the model snapshot ID and the fingerprint, and cache responses instead of promising regeneration.

title: Reproducibility
text: What happened and what do you do? Your CI runs 400 LLM regression prompts nightly against a hosted API with temperature=0, seed=42 . For three weeks the suite was 99.5% stable. Tuesday: 38 of 400 cases fail 9.5% , mostly exact-match on JSON field text. Logs: the response system fingerprint changed from fp a1b2 to fp c3d4 at 02:10 UTC; median latency dropped 18%. No code deploy. The prompt template is unchanged; one dependency tokenizer-based truncation helper was bumped Monday. A PM wants the tests "fixed by tomorrow".

title: Logprobs
text: What are token logprobs, and what practical uses do they have in an LLM application? A logprob is the log of the probability the model assigned to a token. APIs can return it for the chosen token and the top-N alternatives. Uses: confidence scoring e.g. gating low-confidence answers to a human , classification read the probabilities of the label tokens instead of parsing text , threshold-based routing, detecting where a generation went off, perplexity/eval of fixed text, and debugging near-tie non-determinism. Caveat: they reflect the model's token-level belief, which is not guaranteed to be calibrated, especially after RLHF.

title: Logprobs for classification
text: How do you cut the cost and keep accuracy? What can go wrong? A support pipeline classifies 3M tickets/month into 12 intents using a large model with a 600-token prompt and a free-text JSON answer; avg output 45 tokens. Pricing assumption illustrative : $3 per 1M input, $12 per 1M output. Monthly cost: input 3M x 600 = 1.8B tokens = $5,400; output 3M x 45 = 135M tokens = $1,620; total $7,020. Accuracy 91%. The business wants cost cut 60% without dropping below 90%. You find the provider returns top-20 logprobs.

title: Repetition penalties
text: Explain repetition, frequency and presence penalties. How do they differ, and what do they break? They all lower the logits of tokens that already appeared, to fight loops. The OpenAI-style frequency penalty subtracts a value proportional to how many times a token has appeared; the presence penalty subtracts a flat value once a token has appeared at all. The Hugging Face repetition penalty from the CTRL paper is multiplicative: it divides positive logits and multiplies negative logits by the penalty for seen tokens. All are blunt: they penalize legitimate repeats like JSON keys, names, code identifiers and numbers.

title: Repetition loops
text: Diagnose and fix without a model retrain. A self-hosted 13B summarizer vLLM, greedy, T=0, max tokens=4096 starts producing runaway outputs. Overnight: 0.8% of requests about 2,400/day of 300k hit max tokens with a looping phrase, e.g. ...the committee approved the plan. The committee approved the plan. The committee approved the plan... . Those requests hold decode slots 40x longer than average 4096 vs 100 tokens , p95 latency rose from 4 s to 19 s and GPU cost is up 22%. Changes this week: a new document source with long meeting transcripts avg 28k tokens, context limit 32k , and a quantization update fp16 to int8 rolled Thursday. Loop rate was 0.05% before.

title: Batch invariance
text: Explain batch invariance and why it, rather than "GPU randomness", is the crux of LLM inference non-determinism. What would it cost to fix? A kernel is batch-invariant if the result for one request does not depend on what else is in the batch. Most GPU kernels are run-to-run deterministic for a fixed input shape, but inference servers change the effective shape per request as load changes the batch size, and kernels pick different reduction orders or split strategies for different shapes. Since floating-point addition is not associative, the logits differ in low bits, and near-tied argmax flips. Fixing it means batch-invariant RMSNorm, matmul and attention kernels with a fixed reduction order, which costs throughput, so it is a choice, not a free flag.

title: Hallucination causes
text: At a conceptual level, why do language models hallucinate? The model is trained to produce plausible continuations, not to verify truth. When it lacks the fact, the most plausible continuation is still a fluent, confident guess; nothing in next-token training teaches abstention. Contributing causes: knowledge gaps and rare facts seen once in training, noisy or contradictory training data, evaluations and post-training that reward guessing over saying "I don't know", sampling that occasionally picks tail tokens, exposure bias where earlier mistakes condition later text, and context problems such as missing or ignored retrieved evidence.

title: Hallucination mitigation
text: Which mitigations for hallucination operate at the decoding/generation layer, and what are their limits compared with retrieval and evaluation-side fixes? Decoding-layer levers: lower temperature or truncation reduces tail-token errors, not knowledge gaps , constrained decoding guarantees structure and enumerated values, not truth , logprob thresholds to abstain or escalate, self-consistency across samples to detect unstable claims, and contrastive or verification-style decoding methods from research. They help detect or limit errors but do not add knowledge. Real fixes for knowledge gaps sit upstream: retrieval or tools for grounding, abstention training and prompts, and downstream verification citation checks, NLI-style entailment against sources , plus measuring with a hallucination-specific eval.

title: Calibration
text: What is calibration for an LLM, how would you measure it, and why does it matter for decoding-time decisions? A model is calibrated if its stated confidence matches observed accuracy: of answers given at 80% confidence, about 80% are right. I measure it on labeled data with a reliability diagram and Expected Calibration Error ECE , binning predictions by confidence and comparing average confidence to accuracy in each bin. Base pretrained models are often reasonably calibrated; instruction tuning and RL tend to make them overconfident, so I recalibrate e.g. Platt scaling or isotonic regression on logprob-derived scores before using any threshold for abstention or routing.

title: Stop sequences and length control
text: Diagnose both failure modes and fix them. A pipeline extracts structured records using a few-shot prompt where each example ends with . Config: stop= " " , max tokens=300 , T=0. After a prompt refactor, 6% of requests about 18k/day of 300k return truncated JSON: {"name": "Acme", "items": {"sku": "A1", "qty": 2}, {"sku": "A2", "q with finish reason: "length" . Another 1.5% return output containing a premature cut: {"note": "Use for headers" ending at the first inside a field value, finish reason: "stop" . Average output was 140 tokens before; orders with 20+ line items now average 380. Parsing errors page the on-call; retries cost 7% more tokens.

title: Decoding configuration design
text: What decoding strategy would you propose, and how do you find out if it worked? A product lead says: "Make the assistant more consistent but still natural." The assistant a single hosted model, 2M conversations/week serves three modes: 1 policy answers from a knowledge base, 2 JSON action planning for tool calls, 3 friendly small talk. Current global config: T=0.8, top p=1.0, no seed. Metrics: policy answer factual-consistency 88% judge , tool-call schema validity 94%, user thumbs-up on small talk 71%. Complaint tickets: "it gave me two different refund policies on the same question", and "the bot sounds robotic" since last week's tweak that set T=0.2 for everyone in a canary 5% of traffic ; in the canary schema validity rose to 97% but small-talk thumbs-up fell to 63%.

title: KV-cache memory math
text: How much GPU memory does the KV cache use per token for a Llama-3-8B-class model, and why does it matter for how many users you can serve? Per token the cache stores a key and a value vector for every layer and every KV head. For Llama 3 8B that is 2 x 32 layers x 8 KV heads x 128 head dim x 2 bytes bf16 = 131,072 bytes, 128 KiB per token. An 8k-token sequence holds 1 GiB, a 32k one holds 4 GiB. After weights, the leftover GPU memory divided by per-sequence KV size is roughly your concurrent-request ceiling.

title: Token budgeting
text: Find every defect in this budgeting code and fix it. A support chat product uses an 8,192-token context model. Roughly 1 in 40 long conversations fails with 400 context length exceeded: This model's maximum context length is 8192 tokens. However, you requested 8317 tokens 7293 in the messages, 1024 in the completion . The developer insists the trimming code "already keeps it under budget". The system prompt is 1,400 tokens and 3 tool schemas add about 600. import tiktoken enc = tiktoken.get encoding "cl100k base" CTX, MAX OUT = 8192, 1024 def build history, user msg : budget = CTX - MAX OUT used = len enc.encode user msg kept = for m in reversed history : n = len enc.encode m "content" if used + n budget: break kept.insert 0, m used += n return {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM} + kept + {"role": "user", "content": user msg}

title: Cosine vs dot product
text: What is wrong, and how do you fix it without a bad week? Semantic search over 2M support chunks was fine on embedding model A. The team swapped to model B same 1024 dims and kept faiss.IndexFlatIP . Offline recall@10 on the golden set fell from 0.86 to 0.58, but there are no errors. Top results are now dominated by a few long FAQ chunks. A similarity threshold of 0.75 "stopped working" everything passes . import faiss, numpy as np index = faiss.IndexFlatIP 1024 index.add doc vecs float32, shape 2 000 000, 1024 def search q, k=10 : q = model.encode q model B faiss.normalize L2 q scores, ids = index.search q, k return i, s for i, s in zip ids 0 , scores 0 if s 0.75 Logged norms: model A docs 1.0 always; model B docs range 6 to 41, correlated with chunk length.

title: Multilingual token inflation
text: Explain the overrun, what you do this week, and what you do this quarter. You launch a support assistant in Hindi, Tamil and Thai. The budget model assumed English: 600 input + 150 output tokens per request, 6M requests/month, at an illustrative $2.50 / 1M input and $10 / 1M output, i.e. $0.003 per request or about $18k/month. The first invoice is $43k. 60% of traffic is non-English. Sampling shows non-English requests average 2,000 input and 520 output tokens. Latency p50 also rose from 2.1 s to 5.8 s. The English system prompt 400 tokens did not change.

title: Non-determinism
text: Why does it flake at temperature 0, and how do you restructure the tests? CI has 140 LLM-backed tests. Since a model-provider migration, about 8% of runs fail on 2 to 6 tests, always different ones, passing on rerun. Tests call the API with temperature=0 and assert response == EXPECTED STRING . A teammate set seed=42 and the flake rate fell from 8% to about 5% but did not vanish. The release manager wants a "retry until green" step.

title: Hallucination mitigation
text: Walk me through diagnosis and the fix. Do you simply lower temperature? A support bot answers from a help-center knowledge base RAG, 5 chunks of about 300 tokens .
