text: How do you respond? An enterprise prospect, worth about 30% of next year's revenue, demands a 99.99% availability SLA with service credits of 100% of monthly fees if breached. Current performance on the platform over 12 months: 99.93% measured at the load balancer. Architecture is a single region with multi-AZ and a Postgres primary with manual promotion. Sales says "just sign it".

title: correlated failure
text: Review the incident. What was wrong with the availability math and what changes? The design doc claimed: two app instances at 99% each in parallel give 99.99%. Last Tuesday both instances went down for 41 minutes after a deploy introduced a null pointer on a rarely used code path, hit by a nightly job. Logs: 14:02:11 deploy v412 rolled to app-1 and app-2 both, 30 s apart 14:09:40 NullPointerException OrderMapper.map OrderMapper.java:88 app-1 14:09:52 NullPointerException ... app-2 14:10:05 LB: 0 healthy backends 14:51:10 rollback to v411 complete The deploy pipeline had no canary.

title: SLO alerting
text: Redesign the alerting. Show the thresholds. On-call receives about 40 pages a week from "error rate 1% for 5 minutes" for a service with SLO 99.9% / 30 days. Most pages auto-resolve in under 10 minutes. Last week a slow leak ran at 0.25% errors for 5 days with no page; the monthly budget was 60% gone by the time someone noticed. Traffic is 1,000 req/s.

title: single points of failure
text: What is a single point of failure and how do you find them in a design? A SPOF is any component whose failure takes the whole system down. I find them by walking a request path and asking at every box "if this dies, what happens?" The usual suspects are the load balancer, the database primary, DNS, a config or auth service, a single region, an expiring certificate, and even a single person who knows how to deploy.

title: redundancy models
text: Compare active-passive and active-active redundancy. When would you pick each, and what is the N+1 rule? Active-passive: one node serves, a standby waits; simple, failover takes seconds to minutes, standby is idle cost. It fits primary databases. Active-active: all nodes serve; better utilisation and near-instant loss tolerance, but stateful data needs conflict handling. N+1 means I provision enough that after losing one node the survivors still carry peak load.

title: failover and split brain
text: Walk me through a database failover end to end. What is split brain and how is it prevented? How do RTO and RPO fit in? Three steps: detect heartbeats, health checks, lease expiry , decide consensus such as etcd or Raft picks exactly one leader , switch promote the replica, move the VIP or DNS, reconnect clients . Split brain is two nodes both believing they are primary and accepting writes. I prevent it with quorum, odd voter counts, and fencing so the old primary cannot write. RTO is how long I can be down; RPO is how much data I can lose: async replication gives RPO greater than zero, sync gives zero at a latency and availability cost.

title: finding SPOFs
text: List the SPOFs, rank them, and say what you would change first. Design review for a new B2B API. The proposal: 3 app pods across 3 AZs behind a cloud load balancer; one Postgres instance with nightly backups; Redis single node for sessions; auth through a company SSO service reached on every request; secrets fetched at startup from a single vault; DNS at one provider; TLS certificate renewed manually each year; deployments by a script run from one engineer's laptop. Target 99.95%.

title: retries
text: List every problem and the corrected design. Code review of a payment client: Languages: Java, Kotlin tab Response charge Order o { for int i = 0; i < 5; i++ { try { return http.post "/charge", o ; // no timeout set } catch Exception e { Thread.sleep 100 ; // fixed delay } } throw new PaymentFailed ; } tab fun charge o: Order : Response { repeat 5 { try { return http.post "/charge", o } // no timeout set catch e: Exception { Thread.sleep 100 } } throw PaymentFailed } The service sits in a call chain: gateway 3 retries - orders this code - payments provider.

title: health checks
text: Why did a 40 s DB blip become a 5 minute outage and what do you change? Kubernetes deployment of 40 pods. The liveness probe calls /healthz , which runs SELECT 1 against Postgres periodSeconds 10, failureThreshold 3 . The DB had a 40 second failover. Events: 10:14:05 db primary unreachable 10:14:35 40/40 pods: Liveness probe failed - Killing container 10:14:50 40 pods restarting; 0 ready endpoints; 503 from ingress 10:15:10 db new primary ready 35 s 10:15:20 pods up, cache cold, DB CPU 100%, connection errors 10:19:40 recovery

title: timeouts, retries, circuit breakers
text: Explain timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, circuit breakers and bulkheads. How do they work together and how do they go wrong? A timeout bounds how long I wait, shorter than my caller's own budget. A retry with exponential backoff and jitter handles transient failures, limited to 2 or 3 attempts and only for idempotent calls. A circuit breaker opens after a failure rate threshold and fails fast so a sick dependency can recover. A bulkhead gives each dependency its own pool so one cannot drain everything. Wrongly combined, retries multiply: 3 layers of 3 retries is 27 calls for one user action.

title: graceful degradation
text: How do you design the page for failure and what is the availability gain? A product page calls six services: price, inventory, reviews, recommendations, ads, personalisation. Each is 99.9% available. Today any failure returns a 500 for the page. Page latency budget is 400 ms. Product owner says all six are "important".

title: retry storm
text: Why does it stay down after the trigger is gone and how do you recover and prevent it? Inventory service: normal 3,000 req/s, capacity 5,000 req/s. At 11:02 a slow query pushed p50 to 900 ms for 30 seconds, then the query was fixed. Metrics: 11:02 inventory req/s 3000, errors 2% timeouts client timeout 1 s 11:03 inventory req/s 11800, errors 61% 11:06 inventory req/s 12100, errors 64% root cause fixed at 11:03 clients: 3 attempts, 100 ms fixed backoff, no breaker, on 3 layers app, gateway, mesh The query fix is deployed and healthy but the service does not recover.

title: split brain
text: What failed in the design and how do you recover and prevent a repeat? MySQL pair with async replication across two zones and automatic failover by an orchestrator that uses a simple 5 second ping from one monitor host. At 09:40 a 45 second network blip isolates the monitor from the primary, though the primary remains reachable by the app servers in its own zone. 09:40:05 monitor: primary unreachable x5 - promoting replica lag 1.8 s 09:40:11 replica promoted, VIP moved 09:40:12 old primary still accepting writes from zone-A apps did not receive demote 09:40:50 network healed: two writable primaries, about 2.1k divergent writes on each 09:55 both frozen; support receives duplicate-order tickets

title: active-active migration
text: How do you approach the migration and what do you say about "active-active"? A booking service has Postgres primary in region A with an async replica in region B active-passive, RTO 15 min, RPO about 5 s . Leadership wants "multi-region active-active" so that a region loss is invisible, within two quarters. 40% of traffic is in region B's geography. Data: user profiles rarely edited , bookings with inventory counts that must not oversell, an audit log.

title: restore drills and game days
text: What does this tell you and what do you do about it? A drill, finally scheduled after a near miss: restore last night's production Postgres backup 1.8 TB into staging. Findings: 00:00 start restore from nightly snapshot 00:20 restore finished: error "WAL segment 000000010000004A000000F3 missing" 02:40 second attempt from previous snapshot: ok, but 6 h 10 min total backups bucket: same account and region as production; delete role shared with the app deploy role alerts: backup job "success" alerts only on exit code; no restore ever tested Stated RTO is 1 hour, RPO 5 minutes.

title: hash mod N
text: Why is server = hash key mod N a bad way to spread keys over a cache cluster that changes size? "Mod N ties every key's location to N itself. Go from N to N+1 and a key stays put only if k mod N equals k mod N+1 , so about N/ N+1 of all keys move. For a cache that means nearly everything misses at once, the database takes a miss storm, and latency spikes."

title: ring
text: Explain how a consistent hashing ring works and what happens to keys when a node is added. "Servers and keys are hashed onto the same circle. A key belongs to the first server clockwise from its position. Adding a server only takes over the arc between it and its predecessor, so on average 1/N of keys move, and keys owned by everyone else stay put."

title: mod N in production
text: What happened, what do you do right now, and how do you prevent it? A product cache fleet has 6 memcached nodes. Client libraries pick hash key % 6 . Peak is 200k reads/s, normal hit ratio 95%, the primary DB handles at most 30k QPS. To handle growth, an engineer adds a 7th node during the evening peak and bumps N to 7 in the client config. Within a minute: cache hit ratio 95% - 14% db qps 10k - 172k db p99 ms 12 - 4,800 app 5xx 0.1% - 38% Cache node CPU and network look normal.

title: ring lookup
text: List the bugs and fix the code. A teammate wrote a ring for a client-side cache router. In staging, some keys throw a NullPointerException and, after scaling from 4 to 5 nodes, more keys move than expected. Code review is today. Languages: Java, Kotlin tab class Ring { private final TreeMap<Long, String ring = new TreeMap< ; void add String node, int vnodes { for int i = 0; i < vnodes; i++ ring.put hash node + i , node ; } String owner String key { Long p = ring.floorKey hash key ; return ring.get p ; } } tab class Ring { private val ring = java.util.TreeMap<Long, String fun add node: String, vnodes: Int { for i in 0 until vnodes ring hash node + i = node } fun owner key: String : String? = ring ring.floorKey hash key }

title: virtual nodes
text: What are virtual nodes, what problems do they solve in consistent hashing, and what do they not solve? "With one point per server, arcs are uneven and a dead server dumps all its load on one neighbour. Vnodes give each physical server many points, so load evens out and a failure spreads over many nodes. They fix uneven key ranges, not a single hot key."

title: sizing vnodes
text: Which vnode count do you pick, and how do you justify it with numbers? You are designing a 20-node key-value tier. Nodes are identical. The SRE target: no node more than 15% above average load in steady state. A colleague proposes 8 vnodes per node "to keep metadata small"; another proposes 1,000 "for perfect balance". The store streams data per range on node add and repairs per range.

title: cascading failure
text: Why did a single failure cascade, and how do you redesign it? A 4-node cache tier uses a consistent hash ring with 1 point per node. All nodes run at 65% CPU at peak. Node B crashes OOM . Over the next 4 minutes: t+0:00 B down. C cpu 65% - 98% t+1:30 C p99 800 ms, timeouts, C OOM-killed t+2:00 D cpu 62% - 96% took C's arcs t+3:30 D down. Only A left, DB at 100%. Restart of B and C later makes things worse: they come up empty.

title: hot key
text: How do you fix it, and why will the obvious fix not work? A livestream platform caches viewer-count and stream metadata in Redis, sharded by consistent hashing over 20 nodes. A celebrity goes live: one key stream:meta:777 receives 1M reads/s. One Redis node serves about 100k ops/s and sits at 100% CPU, with p99 over 900 ms; the other 19 nodes are at 8%. Adding nodes changes nothing. The app has 400 servers. The key is updated about once every 5 seconds.

title: alternatives
text: Compare ring-based consistent hashing with rendezvous hashing, jump consistent hash, Maglev and Redis Cluster's fixed hash slots. When would you choose each? "Ring with vnodes for elastic membership and replication on preference lists. Rendezvous for small N, simple and balanced, O N per lookup. Jump hash when buckets are numbered and only grow at the end, zero memory. Maglev for L4 load balancers where balance and minimal disruption matter. Fixed slots like Redis Cluster's 16,384 when I want explicit, controllable data movement."

title: Kafka key partitioning
text: What went wrong and how do you scale partitions safely? An orders topic has 12 partitions; producers key by orderId and the default partitioner computes hash key mod partitions verify for your client . Consumers rely on per-order ordering CREATED before PAID before SHIPPED . Lag is growing at peak 350k msgs/s , and the team wants 24 partitions. The platform engineer runs kafka-topics --alter --partitions 24 on a Tuesday. By Wednesday support sees orders marked SHIPPED before PAID.

title: when not to use
text: How do you respond and what do you propose? A PM says: "Our orders table 3 TB, growing 100 GB/month is too big for one Postgres. Shard it with consistent hashing, we will add shards every quarter. Also finance runs daily reports by date range and the support tool lists a customer's orders newest first." There are 5 engineers and no existing sharding infrastructure.

title: replica placement
text: Run the post-incident review: cause, impact estimate, fix and prevention. An in-house KV store replicates each key to the next 3 ring points clockwise RF=3 . The ring has 5 hosts x 128 vnodes. During a host failure test, host H3 is powered off. Reads at QUORUM 2 of 3 fail for a large share of keys: unavailable errors quorum : 0 - 21% of requests logs: "only 1 live replica for token range 0x4a..0x5c replicas: H3,H3,H1 " Writes at QUORUM also fail on those ranges. Dashboards claim "RF=3".

title: CAP
text: What does the CAP theorem actually say, and why is "pick two of three" misleading? "Partitions will happen on any real network, so P is not optional. CAP says that during a partition each side must either refuse requests to stay consistent, meaning linearizable, or answer with possibly stale data to stay available. With no partition you can have both, so it is a choice made during failure, not a permanent menu."

title: per-feature choice
text: Answer the interviewer. You are designing a shopping app: product browsing and reviews, a cart, inventory reservation for the last unit, payment, "likes" on reviews, and a typing indicator in customer chat. The interviewer says: "Is your system CP or AP?"

title: PACELC
text: What does PACELC add on top of CAP, and how does it change how you evaluate a database? "If Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, in normal operation, choose Latency or Consistency. Even with a healthy network, keeping replicas in sync means waiting for them, which costs latency, so I ask what a write must wait for."

title: read-your-writes
text: Diagnose and fix without sending all reads to the primary. A social app serves reads from 3 async MySQL replicas and writes to the primary. Users complain: "I changed my display name, saved successfully, and the profile still shows the old name; after a refresh it is right, sometimes wrong again." Metrics: replica lag ms p50 40 p99 310 max 2,900 during batch job profile update 200 OK, redirect to GET /profile GET /profile routed round-robin to any replica Support tickets: 1,100/day.

title: quorum math
text: Which configuration do you choose and why? What does R + W N buy you and what does it not? A Dynamo-style store has N=5 replicas in one region. Workload: 95% reads, 5% writes, read p99 target 10 ms, write p99 target 30 ms. The team debates W=5, R=1 , W=3, R=3 and W=4, R=2 . One node is down for patching about 2% of the time and sometimes two are.

title: consistency ladder
text: Walk me through the consistency models from linearizable to eventual. Which would you use for a payment ledger, a profile page and a like counter? "Linearizable: one global real-time order, reads see the latest write. Sequential: one order everybody agrees on, not tied to real time. Causal: cause before effect everywhere. Session guarantees: read-your-writes, monotonic reads. Eventual: replicas converge if writes stop. Ledger: linearizable. Profile: eventual plus read-your-writes. Like counter: eventual, ideally a CRDT."

title: cross-region writes
text: Pick one and defend it with numbers. Is it a one-way door? An order service must survive the loss of a whole region. Regions: Mumbai primary users , Singapore RTT 60 ms from Mumbai , Frankfurt RTT 120 ms from Mumbai . Orders are about 2,000 writes/s. Product wants "zero lost orders" and checkout p99 under 400 ms, of which 150 ms is already used elsewhere. Options: A async replication to the other two, B majority sync Mumbai plus nearest , C wait for all three.

title: last-write-wins
text: Explain and fix it. How would you decide whether LWW is acceptable anywhere? A Cassandra-backed profile service uses client-supplied timestamps default last-write-wins per cell . Customers report: "I changed my shipping address twice within a minute; the first wrong address came back." Logs for one user: 12:00:01.200 app-3 UPDATE addr='B' ts=1700000001200000 ack ok 12:00:01.900 app-7 UPDATE addr='C' ts=1700000001100000 ack ok read at 12:00:05 - addr='B' chronyc tracking app-7 : System time 0.8 s slow of NTP time About 0.3% of profile updates are affected.

title: split brain
text: What failure mode is this, how do you reconcile now, and how do you redesign? A wallet service runs a primary in Region A and a hot standby in Region B with an automatic failover script: "if the primary does not answer health checks for 20 s, promote B". The WAN link flaps for 90 seconds. Region A stays healthy and keeps serving its clients; B promotes itself and serves its clients. After the link heals: wallet-A: 41,200 writes during window wallet-B: 13,800 writes during window conflicting balances detected: 1,412 wallets negative balances: 187

title: conflict resolution
text: If an AP database accepts writes on both sides of a partition, how are the conflicts resolved afterwards? Compare last-write-wins, vector clocks and CRDTs, and say when each is appropriate. "LWW keeps the highest timestamp: simple but loses data and trusts clocks. Vector clocks detect that two writes were truly concurrent and keep siblings for the application to merge. CRDTs are data types whose merge is commutative, associative and idempotent, so replicas converge without coordination: counters, sets. Read repair, hinted handoff and Merkle-tree anti-entropy bring replicas together."

title: sloppy quorum
text: R + W = 4 N = 3, so why was the read stale? What do you change? A Dynamo-style store N=3, W=2, R=2 is used for a feature-flag service. During a rack outage, an engineer toggled a flag off. The write was acknowledged. For 6 minutes afterwards some read requests R=2 still returned the old "on" value, and users continued to see the feature. Notes from the incident: write coordinator: "W=2 satisfied: replicas n4 hinted , n2" preference list for key: n1, n2, n3 n1 and n3 were in the failed rack reads: coordinator contacted n1 and n3 after rack restored - both stale hinted data on n4 delivered 6 min later

title: inventory across regions
text: How do you respond? The interviewer says: "Make inventory highly available across two regions, and never oversell." Flash sales sell 500 units of a SKU in 2 minutes with 40k requests/s peak. Regions: US and EU, inter-region RTT 90 ms. Customers are 60% US, 40% EU.

title: request journey
text: What happens between typing https://api.shop.com/orders in an app and the first byte of the response? Where does the time go? "First DNS turns the name into an IP, then TCP opens a connection 1 round trip , then TLS secures it 1 more with TLS 1.3 , then the HTTP request goes out and the server works. On a cold request that is several round trips before my code runs; on a warm path with DNS cached and the connection reused only the last step remains."

title: DNS resolution
text: Describe how a DNS lookup for api.shop.com works, including who asks whom, and what is cached. "The app asks the OS or browser cache, then the recursive resolver ISP or 8.8.8.8 . If the resolver has no cached answer it walks the tree: root server points to the .com TLD server, which points to the authoritative server for shop.com, which returns the record. Each answer is cached along the way for its TTL."

title: zone apex
text: What is wrong, and how do you fix it? A startup moves its marketing site to a CDN. The CDN docs say "point your domain at d123.cdn-vendor.net with a CNAME". The engineer edits the zone for shop.com : shop.com. 300 IN CNAME d123.cdn-vendor.net. shop.com. 300 IN MX 10 mail.shop.com. shop.com. 172800 IN NS ns1.dnsprovider.example. www.shop.com. 300 IN CNAME shop.com. The DNS provider rejects the change, or if it accepts it, email delivery starts bouncing.

title: negative caching
text: Why is the partner still failing and what do you do? At 10:00 you deploy payments-v2.shop.com . Someone tested the URL at 09:50 before the record existed and got NXDOMAIN. You create the record at 10:00 TTL 60 s . At 10:30 a partner still gets "unknown host" while others work. $ dig payments-v2.shop.com @ns1.dnsprovider.example +short 203.0.113.40 $ dig payments-v2.shop.com @partner-resolver status: NXDOMAIN SOA ... minimum 3600

title: TTL
text: What is DNS TTL and why is "DNS propagation" a misleading term? How should you plan a change? "TTL is how long a resolver or client may cache an answer. Nothing is pushed; old copies simply expire, so a change is visible when the last cache holding the old answer expires. I lower the TTL ahead of a planned change, switch, keep the old target alive until traffic drains, then raise the TTL again."

title: CIDR planning
text: Review the plan. You are creating a VPC for a Kubernetes platform where pods get VPC IPs from subnets as with some cloud CNIs . Plans: 600 nodes with about 30 pods each at peak 18,000 pod IPs , three AZs, growth 3x in two years, peering to a corporate network that uses 10.0.0.0/8 . A teammate proposes VPC 10.0.0.0/20 "4,096 is plenty" with /24 subnets.

title: NAT port exhaustion
text: Diagnose and fix. A batch fleet in private subnets calls a partner API at one IP and port through a single NAT gateway. At 02:00 the job ramps to about 2,000 new HTTPS connections/s no connection reuse . From 02:10: app log: connect timeout to 198.51.100.9:443 sporadic, 35% NAT gateway CloudWatch: ErrorPortAllocation 0 - 41,000/min NAT gateway: ActiveConnectionCount 55,000 CPU on app servers: low; partner status page: green

title: Kubernetes ndots
text: Explain both symptoms and fix. After migrating a service to Kubernetes, calls to api.partner.com show random 5 s stalls p99 5.2 s, p50 40 ms . CoreDNS runs 2 replicas at 85% CPU; query rate 6k/s. In a pod: $ cat /etc/resolv.conf search default.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local nameserver 10.96.0.10 options ndots:5 $ tcpdump port 53 for one lookup of api.partner.com: A? api.partner.com.default.svc.cluster.local NXDOMAIN A? api.partner.com.svc.cluster.local NXDOMAIN A? api.partner.com.cluster.local NXDOMAIN A? api.partner.com NOERROR Some lookups show a missing reply and a 5 s retry.

title: anycast
text: How does anycast routing work and how does it compare to DNS-based global traffic steering? What are its failure modes? "Anycast announces the same IP prefix from many sites through BGP; routers send each client to the nearest announcing site, and a dead site withdraws its route so traffic shifts in seconds to a minute, no TTL wait. It gives nearest, not balanced, routing. The risk is route changes mid-connection, which can break long TCP flows to a different site."

title: DNS failover
text: Why did it not meet the SLO and what do you do? Your SLO is 99.99% about 4.3 minutes of downtime per month . The design: active-passive regions, Route 53 failover records with health checks, TTL 60 s. In a game day you fail the primary region at 12:00: 12:00:30 health check marks primary unhealthy, DNS answer switched 12:01:30 60% of traffic on secondary 12:05:00 82% on secondary 12:15:00 93% on secondary; 7% still hitting dead region JVM services, some mobile clients

title: DNS provider outage
text: What do you change, and what are the traps in the fix? Your only authoritative DNS vendor suffers a large DDoS. Timeline from your side: 10:00 vendor degraded 10:05 NXDOMAIN/SERVFAIL for shop.com begins for resolvers whose cache expired TTL 300 10:20 70% of lookups failing; app and API both unreachable 12:10 vendor recovers Servers were healthy throughout. The postmortem asks for a redesign.

title: geo DNS
text: What is going on and what do you change? You enable latency-based DNS routing between Mumbai and Singapore for an API. After the change, p95 latency for a large share of Indian users rises from 60 ms to 190 ms. Region-level dashboards look fine. Sampling shows: Client IP Delhi, ISP X - resolver 8.8.8.8 anycast node in Singapore - answer: Singapore Share of traffic served from SG: 38% expected 3% Only some ISPs are affected.

title: TCP handshake and TIME_WAIT
text: Walk me through how a TCP connection starts and ends. Why does it matter for latency in a system design? TCP opens with SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, which costs one round trip before I can send data data can ride on the final ACK . Closing uses FIN/ACK in each direction, and whoever closes first sits in TIME WAIT, about 60 s on Linux. So a new connection per request pays one RTT every time, plus TLS on top, and burns ports. I reuse connections with pools and keep-alive.

title: Flow control vs congestion control
text: What is the difference between TCP flow control and congestion control, and what limits how fast one connection can send? Flow control protects the receiver: it advertises a window of free buffer. Congestion control protects the network: the sender keeps a congestion window cwnd that starts small and grows, shrinking on loss. Sending rate is bounded by the smaller of the two windows divided by RTT. Hence on a long fat link the limit is round trips, not bandwidth.

title: UDP vs TCP
text: What transport do you propose, and what do you ask first? Product says: "We are building a multiplayer game for mobile. Players send position updates 30 times per second to a game server. Use TCP so nothing gets lost, right?" About 50k concurrent players, 60-byte updates, typical mobile loss 1-2%, RTT 80 ms.

title: Idle timeouts
text: Find the cause and fix it. Order API behind an AWS ALB, clients are mobile backends using a pooled HTTP/1.1 client. About 1,500 req/s at peak, but quiet periods at night. Error rate alert fires every morning at 06:00 right after quiet hours: 0.3% of requests fail, then it fades. 06:00:02 ERROR java.net.SocketException: Connection reset 06:00:02 ELB 502 count=41 target 200 OK, backend CPU 12% nginx keepalive timeout 75s; ALB idle timeout 60s; client pool idle eviction 120s A teammate blames the new deploy from yesterday.

title: Slow start and round trips
text: Why is it slow and what do you do? A download service in Mumbai serves 2 MB JSON bundles to apps in Virginia. Customers have 1 Gbps links, RTT 200 ms, yet each fetch takes about 2.5 s. Server CPU and network are idle. The infra team proposes upgrading everyone to a 10 Gbps link. Each fetch opens a fresh connection.

title: Head-of-line blocking across HTTP versions
text: HTTP/2 multiplexes requests, yet people say it still has head-of-line blocking. Explain, and say how HTTP/3 changes that. HTTP/1.1 had HOL at the HTTP layer one request at a time per connection . HTTP/2 fixed that by interleaving streams, but all streams share one TCP connection, which delivers bytes strictly in order. One lost packet stalls every stream until it is resent. HTTP/3 runs on QUIC, where each stream has its own ordering, so loss stalls only the stream that owned the packet.

title: HTTP/2 and gRPC load balancing
text: Why is the load lopsided and how do you fix it? Service A calls Service B over gRPC. B has 8 pods behind an L4 TCP load balancer. A has 4 pods, each opens a few long-lived connections. Traffic is 6,000 RPC/s. pod cpu rps b-1 92% 3900 b-2 85% 2100 b-3-8 2% 0 Autoscaler keeps adding pods but the new ones stay idle. Latency p99 is 1.8 s.

title: Ephemeral ports and TIME_WAIT
text: What is going on and what do you change? A report-rendering service calls an internal PDF API at 1 fixed IP:port, about 800 req/s, using a new HTTP/1.1 connection per call with Connection: close . At peak: java.net.BindException: Cannot assign requested address $ ss -s - TCP: 31204 estab 210, closed 30650, timewait 30610 $ sysctl net.ipv4.ip local port range - 32768 60999 CPU and memory are fine; the PDF API is healthy.

title: HTTP/3 rollout
text: Interpret these numbers and decide the rollout plan. You front a mobile app 6M DAU, peak 12k req/s with a CDN. Product wants HTTP/3 to cut tail latency. After enabling it for 10% of traffic: metric h2 h3 p50 latency ms 180 170 p99 latency mobile ms 2400 1500 p99 latency wifi ms 420 430 edge CPU per req 1.0x 1.6x h3 share of requests - 4.1% expected about 10% A VP says the rollout "does not work" because only 4.1% used h3.

title: QUIC 0-RTT and connection IDs
text: What does QUIC give you over TCP+TLS, and what are the risks of 0-RTT? Would you run QUIC inside your data centre? QUIC runs on UDP in user space and merges transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes: 1 RTT for a new connection versus 2 for TCP+TLS1.3 and 0-RTT on resumption. Streams are independent, and a connection ID lets the connection survive IP changes. The risk of 0-RTT is replay, so only idempotent requests. Inside a data centre I would usually not: RTT is tiny, CPU cost is higher, tooling less mature; I keep it at the edge.

title: Reconnect storm
text: Give the review: causes, contributing factors and actions. A rolling deploy of the API tier 200 pods, 50k persistent client connections, mostly mobile apps restarted all pods in 3 minutes. At 14:02: 14:02 new TLS handshakes/s: 400 - 38,000 14:02 api cpu: 35% - 98% kernel + crypto 14:03 connect timeouts 1s - clients retry immediately - 61,000 handshakes/s 14:07 error rate 41%, recovers 14:19 after manual scale to 3x Postmortem is on Monday.

title: HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/2 migration
text: Decide: what do you change, in what order, and what could go wrong? A legacy web shop serves about 60 assets per page over HTTP/1.1 using domain sharding img1..img4.shop.com , sprite sheets and a single 2 MB JS bundle. Users are 70% mobile, RTT 50 ms, loss 1%. The CDN supports h2 and h3. An architect says: "Enable h2 and delete the sharding; it will fix everything." Another says: "Leave it; it works."

title: What TLS protects
text: What does HTTPS actually protect, and what does it not protect? HTTPS is HTTP carried inside TLS. TLS gives me three things: confidentiality nobody on the path can read the bytes , integrity any change is detected and authentication the server proves it owns the hostname through a certificate . It protects data in transit only. It does not make the server code safe, it does not hide the destination IP, and the hostname is usually visible through SNI unless ECH is used.

title: Symmetric vs asymmetric and forward secrecy
text: Why does TLS use both asymmetric and symmetric cryptography, and what is forward secrecy? Asymmetric crypto is slow but lets two strangers agree on a secret and prove identity with signatures. Symmetric crypto like AES-GCM is fast but needs a shared key. So TLS uses ECDHE key exchange plus a signature to agree on a session key, then encrypts all data with AES or ChaCha20. Forward secrecy means the key exchange uses throwaway ephemeral keys, so if the server's long-term key leaks later, recorded old traffic still cannot be decrypted.

title: Certificate chain
text: What is wrong, how do you confirm it, and what do you do? Your team renewed the certificate for api.shop.com on the load balancer at 10:00. Chrome and Safari work. Within minutes the support channel reports that the Android app and a partner's Java service fail. Error rate from Android is 100%, web is 0%. The new cert came from the same CA and has 60 days left. Logs: okhttp: javax.net.ssl.SSLHandshakeException: Trust anchor for certification path not found. curl: 60 SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate Someone suggests it is a CDN problem. Someone else suggests turning off verification in the app config as a hotfix.

title: Handshake latency math
text: Where does the time go and what would you change, in order? Your product manager says: "Users in Sydney complain the first load of the app feels slow, about 1 second before anything appears. Make the TLS faster." Your origin is in Virginia. Measured RTT Sydney to Virginia is 200 ms. The load balancer currently allows TLS 1.2 and 1.3. The server time for the first API call is 40 ms. The browser shows connect 200 ms, SSL 200 ms, wait 440 ms.

title: 0-RTT replay
text: What is the bug, and how do you fix it without giving up the latency win everywhere? A payments team enabled 0-RTT on their nginx edge to shave 100 ms from mobile checkout. Two weeks later reconciliation finds 31 duplicate charges out of 4 million orders, all on flaky mobile networks. Config: nginx.conf excerpt, shown as YAML-ish key/value for readability ssl protocols: TLSv1.3 ssl early data: "on" location /v1/payments: proxy pass: http://payments pool no Early-Data header forwarded The payments service has no idempotency keys. The load balancer retries once on connection reset.

title: Termination choice
text: Which option do you pick and how do you decide? You run an e-commerce API at 8,000 requests/s behind an AWS ALB that terminates TLS using ACM certificates; traffic to the pods is plain HTTP inside the VPC. A new payments compliance review says "card data must be encrypted in transit on every hop". Engineering has three options: keep it, re-encrypt to the pods, or switch to an L4 passthrough NLB with TLS on the pods. The platform team prefers the service mesh with mTLS. You have 6 weeks.

title: Resumption and 0-RTT
text: How do TLS session tickets and 0-RTT work, and why is 0-RTT considered risky? After the first handshake the server hands the client an encrypted ticket holding the session state. On reconnect the client sends the ticket, both sides derive keys from a pre-shared key, and the server can skip the certificate and signature, which saves CPU. It still costs 1 RTT. 0-RTT lets the client send the request in the very first flight with zero extra round trip, but that data is replayable, so I allow it only for idempotent requests like GET.

title: TLS 1.3 handshake
text: Walk me through the TLS 1.3 handshake. Why is it one round trip, and what is encrypted? In TLS 1.3 the client guesses the key exchange group and sends its ECDHE public value in the ClientHello along with SNI and ALPN. The server replies with its own key share, so both compute keys right then. Everything after ServerHello, including the certificate, is already encrypted. The server adds a signature over the transcript and Finished, the client sends Finished and can include the HTTP request in the same flight. One round trip, versus two in TLS 1.2, plus the TCP handshake before it.

title: Resumption failure
text: What happened and what do you do? A mobile API on nginx was scaled from 1 node to 6 behind an L4 NLB to handle a campaign. CPU on the TLS tier went from 35% to 78% with traffic only 2x higher. Metrics: before 1 node after 6 nodes req/s 3,000 6,000 full hs/s 300 1,850 resumed hs/s 2,700 350 node CPU 35% 78% The new nodes are a smaller instance type. A dev says the NLB must be dropping packets.

title: Certificate expiry
text: Lead the post-incident review: what failed and what changes? Saturday 00:00 UTC, the public API returned handshake failures for 3 hours 40 minutes error rate 100%, servers healthy, CPU 4% . The cert was issued by an ACME client on a single bastion VM with a cron job. A firewall change two months ago blocked port 80 so renewals silently failed. Monitoring: the internal uptime check calls https://localhost/health with curl -k . On-call needed 90 minutes to find the cause because the dashboards were green.

title: Pinning rotation
text: How do you rotate the key without an outage, and what do you change structurally? Your Android and iOS apps hard-pin the SPKI hash of the server's leaf key. 2.4 million monthly users; 18% are on app versions older than 12 months and release adoption takes about 6 months to reach 95%. Security wants to rotate the server key after an employee departure in 3 weeks. Last year a similar rotation broke 9% of the user base for two days. The pin set contains only the one current key. There is no remote kill switch.

title: Handshake storm
text: Size it, then tell me what you change so this never causes an outage. A push notification campaign and a load balancer restart cause 2 million phone clients to reconnect within 60 seconds. The TLS tier is 16-core nodes; each core can do about 1,000 RSA-2048 full handshakes/s about 1 ms or about 20,000 ECDSA P-256 handshakes/s about 0.05 ms . You have 4 nodes. Last time the TLS tier hit 100% CPU and p99 went from 80 ms to 9 s. Cert is RSA-2048. Resumption rate in steady state is about 60%.

title: L4 vs L7
text: What is the difference between an L4 and an L7 load balancer, and when would you pick each? An L4 balancer works on TCP/UDP connections: it sees IP and port, picks a backend when the connection starts and forwards packets. It is very fast and protocol-agnostic. An L7 balancer terminates the connection, parses HTTP, and balances each request, so it can route by path or header, terminate TLS, retry and canary. I use L7 for web and API traffic, L4 for non-HTTP protocols or as a fast front layer that gives stable IPs and absorbs floods.

title: Balancing algorithms
text: Compare round robin, least connections, power of two choices and consistent hashing. When does each fit? Round robin is simple and fine when requests are similar and short. Least connections or least outstanding requests is better when request time varies or connections are long. Power of two choices picks two random backends and takes the less loaded: nearly as good as global least-loaded without shared state, and it avoids herding. Consistent hashing sends the same key to the same backend, great for caches and sharded services, and moves only about 1/N of keys when backends change.

title: Sticky sessions behind NAT
text: What is going on and what do you do? A B2B web app has 10 backend servers, sticky sessions by source-IP hash. Each normally serves about 1,000 users at 35% CPU. After onboarding a large enterprise customer whose 2,000 employees all egress through one corporate NAT IP, one server web-7 runs at 95% CPU with p99 of 6 s; the others sit at 30%. Dashboards: server active users cpu p99 web-1 800 30% 120ms ... web-7 3,000 95% 6.1s A teammate wants to add 5 more servers.

title: Health check cascade
text: What happened and how would you redesign health checks? 12:04: the primary Postgres failed over took 35 s . The API cluster of 30 instances sits behind an ALB; the /health endpoint runs SELECT 1 and returns 500 if it fails timeout 3 s, unhealthy threshold 3, interval 10 s . At 12:05 the ALB shows 0 healthy hosts, all requests get 503. The DB recovered at 12:05 but the service did not recover until 12:09. CPU on the API was 5% the whole time. Endpoints serving cached catalogue data could have worked during the failover.

title: Graceful deploy
text: Find what is wrong and fix the deploy. Every rolling deploy of a 12-pod API about 250 requests/s per pod, p99 400 ms, 2% of requests are 20 s uploads produces a spike of 502s and connection resets, roughly 1,500 failed requests each time. Manifest and behaviour: spec: terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30 containers: - name: api image: api:2.14 no lifecycle.preStop readinessProbe: httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 } periodSeconds: 10 failureThreshold: 3 The app exits immediately on SIGTERM. ALB deregistration delay is 300 s. The dev says "Kubernetes handles it".

title: Pool sizing
text: How many servers do you run and how do you justify it? You are asked to size a pool for a ticketing API: peak 18,000 requests/s flash sales , one server handles 1,500 requests/s at 100% CPU, you want 60% target CPU, 3 AZs. The business states "we must survive losing an AZ during a sale". It also says "the budget is tight". Autoscaling takes about 4 minutes to add capacity.

title: Liveness, readiness, startup
text: Explain active and passive health checks, and the difference between liveness, readiness and startup probes. What should /health check? Active checks are probes the LB sends every few seconds; passive checks watch real traffic and eject a backend after consecutive failures. Liveness asks "should this process be restarted", readiness asks "can it take traffic now", startup protects slow-starting apps from being killed. A health endpoint should be shallow: it must not check a dependency shared by all instances, because then one blip removes every node at once.

title: LB high availability
text: The load balancer is a single point of failure. How do you make it highly available, and what limits its capacity? In cloud I use a managed multi-AZ LB. When self-managing, I run active-passive with VRRP and a floating IP failover in 1 to 3 s, half the capacity idle , or active-active: several LB IPs in DNS, or ECMP routing where the router spreads flows over many L4 nodes announcing a VIP via BGP. Large L4 systems like Maglev and Katran use consistent hashing so existing connections keep their backend when an LB node dies. I also watch limits: connections, TLS handshakes per second, bandwidth and ephemeral ports to backends.

title: Idle timeout mismatch
text: Diagnose and fix. Behind an ALB idle timeout 60 s , a Node.js service sees rare, unreproducible 502s: about 0.03% of requests, more at low traffic hours. Access log excerpt: elb status=502 target status=- request processing time=0.000 target processing time=-1 response processing time=-1 error reason=- App CPU 20%, no exceptions logged. The Node server uses the default keep-alive timeout of 5 s. Someone proposes adding retries in the client and someone else proposes upgrading Node.

title: gRPC and L4
text: Explain and fix. A new gRPC service runs on 40 pods behind a Kubernetes Service and an L4 NLB. Under 20,000 calls/s: pod cpu rps pod-17 95% 9,800 pod-03 12% 300 ... 38 others 8-12% 250 each The 25 client instances each open one HTTP/2 connection. Autoscaler adds pods but the hot pod stays hot. A teammate says the LB algorithm is broken and wants to switch to least connections.

title: Regional failover capacity
text: What utilisation do you allow, what do you do about the data, and what is reversible? Three regions Mumbai, Singapore, Frankfurt each serve about 90,000 requests/s at peak. Each region is provisioned for 120,000 requests/s. Finance asks to remove "wasted capacity". The SLO requires surviving the loss of one region. Mumbai failed last quarter for 25 minutes and the surviving regions hit 100% CPU, latency tripled. Data is regional with async replication to the others.

title: Least-connections herd
text: Why does this happen and what do you change? A pool of 20 JVM API nodes uses least conn in two LB nodes. During a rolling deploy, each time a new node joins it gets a burst of connections, goes to 100% CPU for 90 s cold JIT , p99 on that node hits 8 s, some requests time out, and the retries make neighbours busy too: t=0 node-21 joins, active conn=0 others 180 t=3s node-21 active conn=410 cpu 100% t=40s timeouts, LB retries onto node-04 .. node-09 t=90s node-21 cpu 35% A teammate wants more nodes. Another says switch to round robin.

title: Proxy types
text: What is the difference between a forward proxy, a reverse proxy, an API gateway and a CDN? A forward proxy represents the client: clients send traffic through it to the internet, used for egress control, fixed IPs and caching. A reverse proxy represents the server: clients think they talk to the site, and the proxy fronts hidden backends for TLS termination, balancing and buffering. An API gateway is a reverse proxy plus API jobs like auth, rate limits and routing to services. A CDN is a global fleet of caching reverse proxies near users.

title: Cache-Control semantics
text: What do no-cache , no-store , private , max-age and s-maxage mean? max-age is how long any cache may reuse the response; s-maxage overrides that for shared caches like a CDN. private means only the browser may store it, never a CDN. no-cache means store it but revalidate before every reuse; no-store is the real "never keep this". For personal data I use private, no-store .

title: Trusting X-Forwarded-For
text: What is the bug and how do you fix it? An API sits behind an NGINX reverse proxy that appends the real client address to X-Forwarded-For . A rate limiter 100 requests/min per IP was added in the app. Attackers bypass it and one scraper made 40,000 requests/min. Code: Languages: Java, Kotlin tab String clientIp HttpServletRequest req { String xff = req.getHeader "X-Forwarded-For" ; if xff != null && !xff.isEmpty { return xff.split "," 0 .trim ; // first value } return req.getRemoteAddr ; } tab fun clientIp req: HttpServletRequest : String { val xff = req.getHeader "X-Forwarded-For" if !xff.isNullOrEmpty { return xff.split "," 0 .trim // first value } return req.remoteAddr } Nginx config: proxy set header X-Forwarded-For $proxy add x forwarded for; . Logs show the same attacker with many "client IPs" such as 1.2.3.4 , 5.6.7.8 .

title: Cache key fragmentation
text: Why is hit ratio low, what do you expect after the fix, and what could go wrong? A product API GET /v1/products?id=7 is cached at the CDN with s-maxage=300 . Hit ratio is only 31% and origin sees 14,000 requests/s edge total 20,000 requests/s . Marketing campaigns append utm source , utm campaign and a random cb=<timestamp that a mobile SDK adds. There are 10,000 products. Origin egress cost is a worry.

title: Private data cached
text: Handle this incident. After enabling a CDN, support gets tickets: "I see another user's order history". 11 confirmed cases within 40 minutes. The /v1/orders endpoint returns Cache-Control: public, max-age=60 added by a framework default for GET and authentication is by cookie. The CDN default cache key is host + path + query; cookies are not in the key. Origin CPU dropped 60%, which the team had celebrated.

title: Egress proxy and port exhaustion
text: Diagnose and fix. A payments partner only accepts calls from two allow-listed IPs. Your autoscaling services route outbound calls through two NAT proxies with Elastic IPs. During a sale the partner call volume rises to 3,000 requests/s, each connection held about 30 s because the partner is slow. Errors start: connect timeout to partner:443 rate 18% nat: ErrorPortAllocation count rising Proxy CPU is 10%. The partner confirms nothing is wrong on their side.

title: Invalidation strategies
text: How do you update content that is already cached on a CDN? Compare your options. My first choice is fingerprinted URLs like app.3f9a1c.js cached forever, so nothing needs invalidation; only the small HTML that references them has a short TTL. For APIs I use a short TTL with stale-while-revalidate. When freshness matters I purge by tag or surrogate key triggered by an event. Purge-all is a last resort because it sends all traffic to the origin at once.

title: Origin protection
text: What is a cache stampede at a CDN and how do origin shield, request coalescing and stale serving protect the origin? When a popular object expires or is purged, thousands of users miss at once and each miss goes to the origin: a stampede. Request coalescing makes the cache send one origin request and hold the others until it answers. An origin shield adds a mid-tier so that 200 edge POPs asking for the same object become one origin request. Stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error serve old content during refresh or origin failure, and origin lockdown stops attackers bypassing the CDN.

title: Gateway scope
text: What do you recommend? You have 40 microservices behind a gateway at 30,000 requests/s. A principal engineer proposes adding order aggregation and discount rules to the gateway "so mobile makes one call". The mobile team agrees; backend teams worry. The gateway currently does JWT checks RS256, about 0.1 ms each , per-user rate limits in Redis and routing. It is owned by a 4-person platform team. Deadline: 6 weeks.

title: Fast price update
text: Design the update path and call out the failure modes. Flash sale: prices must update for all users within 5 seconds of an admin change. Product pages are cached at the CDN with s-maxage=60 . Traffic is 25,000 requests/s with a 95% hit ratio on product pages. The admin writes to a primary Postgres; pages are rendered from a read replica with lag usually 200 ms, up to 3 s under write load. A tag purge API call takes about 1 to 2 s globally.

title: Purge-all incident
text: Lead the review. What failed and what do you change? At 11:02 an engineer ran "purge everything" to fix a bad banner. Metrics: 11:02 CDN hit ratio 95% - 12% 11:03 origin req/s 1,100 - 21,000 origin sized for about 3,000 11:04 origin CPU 100%, DB connections 480/500, p99 12 s 11:05 5xx 38%, CDN serves errors, retries from clients 11:21 recovery after manual rate limiting and rollback of nothing No origin shield, no stale-if-error, origin reachable directly.

title: Layered timeouts and retries
text: Explain the amplification and the fix. Stack: CDN, ALB, API gateway, orders service, Postgres. A payments dependency slows from 80 ms to 6 s. Settings: layer timeout retries client app 10 s 3 API gateway 5 s 2 orders svc 3 s 3 to payments Orders traffic is 2,000 requests/s. Within a minute the payments service gets about 50,000 requests/s and falls over; the gateway and orders pods show thread pool exhaustion. A teammate says "payments is just slow, nothing to do".

title: Safe vs idempotent methods
text: What is the difference between a safe and an idempotent HTTP method, and why does it matter for a mobile client? Safe means the call does not change server state, like GET. Idempotent means calling it N times leaves the same state as calling it once, like PUT and DELETE. Every safe method is idempotent but not the other way round. It matters because networks drop responses: I can blindly retry an idempotent call, but a POST retry can create a duplicate, so POST needs an idempotency key.

title: 401 vs 403 vs 400 vs 422
text: When do you return 401 versus 403, and 400 versus 422? How should the client react to each? 401 means I do not know who you are, so missing or expired token; the client refreshes the token and retries once. 403 means I know who you are and you are not allowed; no retry. 400 is malformed or invalid input, 422 is well-formed but violates a business rule; either is fine if the team is consistent. Neither is retried, because the same request fails the same way.

title: URL design for non-CRUD actions
text: How do you design URLs for an order that can be cancelled, refunded and re-delivered, without putting verbs everywhere? How deep should nesting go? URLs are plural nouns, the method is the verb. For actions that are not CRUD I model the action as a resource: POST /orders/42/cancellation or POST /payments/99/refunds , which creates a refund. Google's POST /orders/42:cancel is an acceptable escape hatch; I pick one style and keep it. I nest at most two levels, because once a thing has a global id, /orders/42 is enough.

title: Status codes
text: What is wrong, and what do you change? The Orders API wraps every response so the Android team has one parser. Controller snippet and the on-call dashboard: Languages: Java, Kotlin tab @PostMapping "/orders" public ResponseEntity<? create @RequestBody OrderReq r { try { return ResponseEntity.ok service.create r ; } catch ValidationException e { return ResponseEntity.ok Map.of "error", e.getMessage ; } catch Exception e { return ResponseEntity.ok Map.of "error", "failed: " + e ; } } tab @PostMapping "/orders" fun create @RequestBody r: OrderReq : ResponseEntity<Any = try { ResponseEntity.ok service.create r } catch e: ValidationException { ResponseEntity.ok mapOf "error" to e.message } catch e: Exception { ResponseEntity.ok mapOf "error" to "failed: $e" } orders-api 5xx rate: 0.0% p99: 180ms status=200: 100% support tickets "order not created": 340 this week

title: BOLA / IDOR
text: What are the vulnerabilities and how do you fix them? A security review of the ride-history API flags the endpoint below. 400K DAU, JWT auth, ids are sequential bigints. Languages: Java, Kotlin tab @GetMapping "/rides/{id}" public Ride get @PathVariable long id, @AuthenticationPrincipal User u { return rideRepo.findById id .orElseThrow NotFound::new ; } @PutMapping "/users/me" public User update @RequestBody User body { return userRepo.save body ; // body bound straight to entity } tab @GetMapping "/rides/{id}" fun get @PathVariable id: Long, @AuthenticationPrincipal u: User : Ride = rideRepo.findById id .orElseThrow { NotFound } @PutMapping "/users/me" fun update @RequestBody body: User : User = userRepo.save body GET /rides/100234 - 200 my ride GET /rides/100235 - 200 someone else's ride, with pickup address

title: Async operations
text: How do you design this, and what do you ask before you start? Product says: "Add a Download my statement button; it is sometimes slow." Backend today builds a PDF inline in GET /statements?month=... . 20K exports/day, p50 3 s, p99 70 s. The load balancer idle timeout is 60 s and you see this: GET /statements 504 upstream timed out 60s count=410 last hour

title: Error response design
text: How would you design the error format for a public API used by Android, iOS and web clients? One shape for every error, following RFC 9457 problem details: type , title , status , detail , plus a stable machine-readable code , a request id , and field-level errors for validation. Clients switch on code , never on message text. Return all field errors in one response and never leak stack traces or SQL.

title: Payload design
text: List what is wrong with this contract and how you fix it without breaking shipped apps. A payments dashboard web, JavaScript and the Android app show wrong numbers for some customers. Sample response and complaints: { "id": 9007199254740993, "amount": 19.99, "created": 1731146130, "status": "PAID", "items": { "price": 0.1 }, { "price": 0.2 } } Web: id shows 9007199254740992 off by one - refund API returns 404 Android: total shows 0.30000000000000004 on receipt Another dev: "created" is seconds in one service and millis in another iOS crash: new status "PARTIALLY REFUNDED" - exhaustive enum switch

title: Optimistic locking with ETags
text: Why did this happen and how do you prevent it at the API level? An admin console lets support staff edit a customer profile. Two agents opened Priya's record; agent A changed the address, agent B changed the phone and saved afterwards. The address edit vanished. 60 edits/s peak, PUT /customers/{id} replaces the whole object, no concurrency control. Customer complaint volume: 25 per day, "my update disappeared". 10:02:11 A GET /customers/7 - {addr:"Old", phone:"111"} 10:02:15 B GET /customers/7 - {addr:"Old", phone:"111"} 10:03:01 A PUT /customers/7 {addr:"New", phone:"111"} 200 10:03:40 B PUT /customers/7 {addr:"Old", phone:"222"} 200 <- overwrites A

title: Retry behaviour and codes
text: What went wrong at each layer and what do you change? Post-incident review. Release 5.8 of the Android app sent quantity: "two" string due to a form bug. The API returned 500 because a parse exception was uncaught. The app retried 5xx up to 5 times without backoff. 300K devices on 5.8, 40% hit the form. 12:00 POST /orders 500 rate 800/s baseline 600/s total 12:05 POST /orders 500 rate 6,200/s 12:08 p99 for all endpoints 9s, DB pool exhausted, healthy endpoints 503 12:20 rolled back server, client unaffected, still retrying

title: Changing URLs and shapes
text: How do you migrate without breaking anyone, and what is the decision gravity? Your public API uses /getUserOrders?id=7 and returns a bare array of orders with price in float rupees. You want /users/7/orders returning {data, next cursor} with amount minor ints. Traffic: 40M requests/day, 6 mobile app versions live; versions older than 2 years are 8% of calls, plus 30 partner integrations you cannot force to move.

title: Payload size and caching
text: Estimate savings and propose changes in order of effort. The feed endpoint returns 20 items, 2 KB JSON each 40 KB per page to Android users, most on 1 Mbps 3G in your target market. 5M DAU, each opens the feed 6 times a day. egress cost is about 0.08 USD/GB verify your own price . Median screen time-to-content is 1.4 s; 60% of requests re-fetch data that has not changed. Only 600 bytes per item are shown on screen. GET /feed?limit=20 200 40,000 B no Content-Encoding, no ETag

title: What gRPC is
text: What is gRPC and how does it differ from a REST/JSON API? gRPC is Protocol Buffers plus HTTP/2 plus generated client and server stubs. I write a .proto contract, generate code, and call remote functions like GetUser id . Compared with REST/JSON it is binary and smaller, strongly typed, multiplexes calls on one connection and supports four streaming modes. The cost is browser support needs gRPC-Web and harder debugging.

title: GraphQL and N+1
text: What is the N+1 problem in GraphQL and how do you solve it? GraphQL runs a resolver per field. If I query 50 users and each has orders , the orders resolver runs 50 times, so 1 + 50 = 51 DB queries. The fix is batching with a DataLoader: collect all user ids during one tick, run one WHERE user id IN ... , then give each parent its slice. That gives 2 queries.

title: Protobuf compatibility
text: Which protobuf changes are backward compatible and which break old clients? Why are field numbers special? The wire format identifies fields by number. Adding a field is safe, old readers ignore it. Removing a field is safe if I reserved its number and name so nobody reuses it. Reusing a number with a different meaning silently corrupts data. Changing types is mostly breaking: int32 to int64 is wire-compatible, int to string is not. New enum values show up as unknown/default to old clients.

title: gRPC load balancing
text: Why did scale-out not help, and how do you fix it? Orders service moved from REST to gRPC on Kubernetes, behind a ClusterIP Service. Traffic doubled so you scaled from 4 to 12 pods. Ten minutes later: pod orders-0 cpu 94% rps 5,100 pod orders-1 cpu 91% rps 4,900 pod orders-2..11 cpu 3% rps 0 new pods latency p99: 1.8s was 120 ms ; GC pauses normal ; DB healthy The client is a long-lived Java service with 2 channels.

title: GraphQL resolvers
text: What is the bug and what is your fix? A mobile team ships a feed screen via GraphQL. After launch DB CPU is 80%. Resolver and query log: Languages: Java, Kotlin tab @SchemaMapping typeName = "Post", field = "author" public User author Post p { return userRepo.findById p.authorId .orElse null ; // runs per post } tab @SchemaMapping typeName = "Post", field = "author" fun author p: Post : User? = userRepo.findById p.authorId .orElse null query { feed first: 50 { id text author { name avatar } } } SQL log for one request: 1 x SELECT posts ... ; 50 x SELECT users WHERE id = ? requests: 2,000/s - 102,000 SQL/s

title: Picking the API style
text: What API style do you pick for each leg and why? A ride-hailing app has 500,000 online drivers sending location every 4 s: 125,000 updates/s. Riders, an admin web console and 12 internal microservices consume these. A teammate proposes plain POST /locations with JSON for everything.

title: REST vs gRPC vs GraphQL
text: Compare REST, gRPC and GraphQL across caching, typing, streaming, browser support and versioning. How do they coexist in one system? REST: HTTP/JSON, universal, best HTTP caching, weak typing unless OpenAPI. gRPC: protobuf over HTTP/2, strict contract, native streaming, smallest payload, needs gRPC-Web for browsers, poor HTTP caching. GraphQL: one endpoint, client picks fields, fixes over/under-fetching, weak HTTP caching, needs N+1 and cost control. A typical layout is REST or GraphQL at the edge and gRPC between services.

title: Proto evolution
text: What went wrong and what is the safe way to make this change? During a refactor an engineer edits payment.proto . Order-service is still on the old build for another 3 hours rolling deploy . // before message Payment { int64 id = 1; int64 amount = 2; // paise string upi ref = 3; bool refunded = 4; } // after message Payment { int64 id = 1; string amount = 2; // now "19.99" string upi ref = 3; string refund state = 4; // "NONE" "FULL" } payment-service new - order-service old : warning: unknown/invalid wire type for field 2, order totals = 0 refunds show as "true" for 40% of orders

title: GraphQL abuse and cost
text: Mitigate now, find the root cause and design the defences. Public GraphQL API for a social app, 8M DAU. At 02:10 DB CPU hits 100% and p99 goes from 200 ms to 25 s. Gateway shows only 900 rps normal 1,500 . Slow-query log and the offending query: query { user id:"1" { friends first:100 { friends first:100 { friends first:100 { friends first:100 { name posts first:100 { comments first:100 { text }}}}}}}} rows touched: 10^8 per query ; 6 clients using it ; all HTTP 200 WAF: no alerts valid JSON, POST /graphql

title: Choosing under ambiguity
text: What do you say and what do you recommend? A new CTO says: "Our Android app makes five REST calls to render the home screen and it is slow. Let us move everything to GraphQL." You have 18 engineers, a REST API with 90 endpoints used by Android, iOS, web and 30 partners, 3M DAU, mostly 4G, median RTT 150 ms. Home screen calls: /me , /feed , /notifications , /ads , /config .

title: gRPC deadlines and retries
text: What is wrong with the setup and how do you make the migration safe? You are moving the checkout path Gateway - Cart - Pricing - Inventory from REST to gRPC, one hop at a time, at 8,000 rps. Early canary at Cart - Pricing shows: Gateway timeout 3s ; Cart client no deadline ; Pricing - Inventory deadline 10s Inventory p99 6s during a cache flush threads in Cart: 200/200 busy, queue growing ; Gateway 504 rate 18% retry policy: 3 attempts on UNAVAILABLE and DEADLINE EXCEEDED, incl. ReserveStock

title: GraphQL operations
text: What failed in the platform choices and what do you change? Post-incident review of a Saturday outage of a product-search feature served by GraphQL at 20K rps. Findings: - Uptime check: HTTP 200 for the entire 4h incident - Body: {"data":{"search":null},"errors": {"message":"upstream timeout"} } - 31% of requests - CDN hit ratio fell from 78% old REST /search?q= to 4% after the GraphQL move - Origin egress cost +3.1x; p50 latency +90 ms - Alert fired only after customers tweeted, 52 minutes in

title: Offset vs keyset
text: What are the problems with offset pagination and what does keyset pagination do differently? Offset says "skip N rows, give M", so OFFSET 1000000 makes the database walk and discard a million rows; latency grows with page number. It is also unstable: an insert at the top shifts everything and I see a duplicate or miss a row. Keyset says "give me rows after this last key", using an index seek, so every page costs the same and it is stable under inserts. The trade-off is no jump to page 57 and no cheap total.

title: Idempotency key
text: What is an idempotency key and how does the server implement it? The client generates a unique key per logical operation, such as a UUID created when the user taps Pay, and sends it as Idempotency-Key . The server atomically inserts the key with a unique constraint, does the work once, stores the response, and on any retry with the same key returns the stored response. A key seen while still in progress gets 409, and the same key with a different body is rejected.

title: Backward compatibility
text: Which API changes are backward compatible and which are breaking? Does "adding a field is always safe" hold? Adding an optional request field, a new response field or a new endpoint is usually safe, provided clients are tolerant readers that ignore unknown fields. Removing or renaming a field, changing a type, unit or meaning, making an optional field required, tightening validation, changing error codes, default sort or page size, or making a non-null field nullable are breaking. "Adding is always safe" is false: strict deserializers and exhaustive enum switches can crash.

title: Deep offset
text: Why does latency grow and what do you do? A back-office orders export UI paginates with LIMIT 50 OFFSET page-1 50 on a 120M-row table. Ops scripts crawl all pages. DB shows: GET /orders?page=1 18 ms GET /orders?page=2000 210 ms GET /orders?page=40000 2.9 s OFFSET 1,999,950 Primary CPU 85%, replica lag 12 s, 6 concurrent crawlers EXPLAIN: Index Scan on orders created idx rows=2000000 discarded ... Limit

title: Cursor correctness
text: Find all the bugs. A feed API uses a keyset cursor on created at only. Users report duplicates and "missing posts" in infinite scroll. Import jobs insert hundreds of posts with the same timestamp. Languages: Java, Kotlin tab List<Post next Instant after, int limit { return jdbc.query "SELECT FROM posts WHERE created at < ? ORDER BY created at DESC LIMIT ?", mapper, after, limit ; } // cursor = base64 created at of last row , unsigned tab fun next after: Instant, limit: Int : List<Post = jdbc.query "SELECT FROM posts WHERE created at < ? ORDER BY created at DESC LIMIT ?", mapper, after, limit // cursor = base64 created at of last row , unsigned page 1 ends at created at = 10:00:00.000 rows A,B,C share it; only A fits on page 1 page 2: WHERE created at < 10:00:00.000 - B and C are never shown limit param: no maximum ; cursor: plain base64

title: Idempotency race
text: What is the bug and how do you fix it? A payments endpoint claims idempotency. Production sees occasional double charges when the Android app taps twice. Code: Languages: Java, Kotlin tab @PostMapping "/payments" public Response pay @RequestHeader "Idempotency-Key" String key, @RequestBody PayReq r { var saved = keyRepo.find key ; // 1 check if saved != null return saved.response ; var resp = gateway.charge r ; // 2 side effect keyRepo.save key, resp ; // 3 store return resp; } tab @PostMapping "/payments" fun pay @RequestHeader "Idempotency-Key" key: String, @RequestBody r: PayReq : Response { keyRepo.find key ?.let { return it.response } // check val resp = gateway.charge r // side effect keyRepo.save key, resp // store return resp } 10:01:02.100 key=abc find - null thread 1 10:01:02.104 key=abc find - null thread 2 10:01:02.900 charge OK x2 duplicate

title: Versioning strategies
text: What are the main API versioning strategies, and how would you choose for a mobile-first public API? URL path /v1 , header/media type, query parameter, date-based Stripe's account-pinned version or none with strictly additive evolution. For a mobile-first API I prefer additive evolution as the default and a URL major version only for real breaks, because old app versions can stay at 5 to 10% of traffic for years. Whatever I choose, I publish a deprecation policy and measure usage per version.

title: Offline sync API
text: How do you design the API, and what do you ask first? The PM says: "Make the notes app work offline and keep phones in sync." Server has 2M users, 300 notes each on average, phones come online irregularly. Today the app calls GET /notes?page=N and replaces the local Room table with everything.

title: Idempotency under failure
text: Explain what is going on, how you unstick users now and how you design it to be safe. Payments API with idempotency keys, 1M payments/day. After a database failover at 03:12 support sees customers with a pending payment that never resolves: idempotency keys: key=k91 status=IN PROGRESS created at=03:12:04 rows stuck: 212 provider ledger: charge for k91 SUCCEEDED client retries: POST /payments key=k91 - 409 "request in progress" for 40 minutes The service crashed after the provider call and before saving the response.

title: Field rename migration
text: Give the migration plan with sequencing and exit criteria. Orders API returns price as float rupees for example 199.5 . Finance wants integer paise as amount minor after a rounding discrepancy of 0.01 on 0.3% of invoices. Usage by app version in the last 7 days: v7 current 61%, v6 24%, v5 11%, older 4%. Server and apps deploy independently; 2M DAU.

title: Switching to cursors at scale
text: How do you move to cursor pagination without breaking clients, and what do you size? Public API GET /transactions?page=N&size=50 serves 12K rps on a 2B-row table. Traffic will grow 10x after a partner launch. Today: p99 450 ms; the DB spends 70% of time on offsets over 10,000. 200 partners and 3 app versions use page . Partners need an end date for any change.

title: Version sunset decision
text: How do you decide and execute? What is the gravity? You run /v1 through /v4 of a public API. Cost review: version traffic clients eng cost/quarter v1 0.8% 2 partners, old apps 3 eng-weeks security patches, tests v2 3% old apps 2 eng-weeks v3 41% current apps shared core v4 55% new apps shared core v1 hit by a vulnerability scanner; fix needed in v1 and v2 handlers Leadership asks: "Kill v1 and v2 next month?"

title: Why rate limit and what key to use
text: Why do we rate limit an API, and how do you decide what to limit on? I rate limit to stop one caller from hurting everyone else: abuse like password guessing, client bugs that retry in a loop, cost blowups on paid downstream calls, and plain overload. Before the algorithm I pick three things: who is limited user id, API key, tenant, IP , what is counted requests, bytes, cost units and what happens at the limit reject with 429, queue, slow down . The key matters most: IP alone punishes a whole office behind one NAT.

title: Fixed window vs sliding window counter
text: What is the boundary burst problem in a fixed window rate limiter, and how does a sliding window counter fix it? A fixed window counts per clock minute and resets at the boundary, so a client can send 100 requests at 12:00:59 and 100 more at 12:01:00: 200 in two seconds while obeying a limit of 100/min. The sliding window counter keeps the current and previous window counts and estimates current + previous 1 - elapsed fraction , so there is no sharp reset and memory is still two counters.

title: Atomicity
text: Find the bugs and fix them. 10 API pods share a Redis limiter. Limit is 100 req/min per user. Support reports a bulk-export customer got 380 requests through in one minute. This is the code: boolean allow String userId { String key = "rl:" + userId + ":" + System.currentTimeMillis / 60000 ; String v = redis.get key ; int count = v == null ? 0 : Integer.parseInt v ; if count = 100 return false; redis.set key, String.valueOf count + 1 ; redis.expire key, 60 ; return true; } fun allow userId: String : Boolean { val key = "rl:$userId:${System.currentTimeMillis / 60000}" val count = redis.get key ?.toInt ?: 0 if count = 100 return false redis.set key, count + 1 .toString redis.expire key, 60 return true } Redis CPU is 15%, replication lag is 2 ms. The customer fires 40 parallel requests.

title: Token vs leaky bucket
text: Why did the token bucket not protect you, and what would you use instead? Your notification service calls an SMS vendor that accepts exactly 100 messages/s and returns 429 plus a 60-second ban if you exceed it. Marketing sometimes fires 5,000 messages in one second. Today you use a token bucket with B=200, R=100/s in front of the vendor client. Last week a campaign caused two bans, and 3,000 messages failed.

title: 429 and backoff
text: What is happening and what do you do? Public API, limit 100/min per key. A mobile release 4.2 ships at 10:00. By 10:20 the dashboard shows: 429 rate: 4% - 63% unique API keys: 18,000 flat requests/s: 3,000 - 21,000 per-key request histogram: spikes every 50 ms backend CPU: 40% - 95% The limiter itself is healthy. The 4.2 changelog says "improved network resilience".

title: Sliding window log memory
text: Estimate memory at 10M users and propose a fix. What accuracy do you give up? A team built a sliding window log limiter on Redis sorted sets: limit 600 requests/hour per user, ZADD per request. It worked at 200k users. Marketing expects 10M users next quarter, with about 30% active per hour. Redis shows: used memory human: 41G maxmemory: 64G evicted keys: 0 - 5,200/min latency p99: 2 ms - 11 ms Each sorted-set member is a request id.

title: Token bucket mechanics
text: Explain how a token bucket works and how you implement it without a timer thread per bucket. A bucket holds up to B tokens and refills at R per second. Each request takes a token; no token means reject. B is the burst size and R is the sustained rate. I do not run a timer: I store tokens and last ts , and on each request compute tokens = min B, tokens + now - last R then try to take one. Two numbers per key, O 1 .

title: Distributed limiter and failure policy
text: How do you build a rate limiter that works across 20 API servers, and what do you do when the limiter store is down? Per-server counters give N times the limit, so all servers consult shared state, usually Redis. Updates must be atomic: INCR for fixed windows, a Lua script for token bucket or sliding window, with Redis TIME as the clock and a TTL on every key. Shard keys across a Redis Cluster since one node does roughly 100k ops/s. If Redis is down I decide per route: fail open with a local fallback limiter for general APIs, fail closed for login and money paths, and alert either way.

title: Ambiguous requirement
text: What do you ask, and what do you propose? Your PM says: "We are opening the API to partners next month. Add rate limiting so nobody can take us down." Facts you find: capacity is about 60,000 req/s at 70% CPU. Today 5,000 paying customers average 10 req/s each 50,000 req/s in total , plus 10,000 req/s from free users. There is no published limit, no API keys per partner yet, and some partners sit behind corporate NATs.

title: Hot key on limiter shard
text: Diagnose and fix, and say what failing open means here. Your limiter is a 6-shard Redis Cluster sharded by tenant id . At 14:05 API latency for all tenants rises. You see: shard-3: cpu 100%, ops/s 118k, p99 18 ms shard-1,2,4,5,6: cpu 35%, ops/s 40k, p99 0.6 ms top key on shard-3: rl:tenant:7781 95k ops/s gateway log: limiter timeout 10ms - failing open Tenant 7781 is a new enterprise customer running a load test. Redis memory is fine and there was no failover.

title: Changing limits live
text: How do you roll this out without breaking customers? Your API has had no limits for 3 years. Traffic is 25,000 req/s with 40,000 active keys. A runaway client caused a 9-minute outage, so leadership wants 100 req/s per key within 2 weeks. You suspect some keys exceed 100 req/s legitimately. You also have a token bucket library but no per-key data.

title: Layered limits
text: Lead the review: what went wrong and what is the corrected limiter design? Post-incident review. Black Friday, 09:12 to 09:40: checkout API errors hit 38%. Facts: a per-IP limit of 60/min at the CDN returned 429 to a large college campus 4,000 students on one NAT and to a mobile carrier CGNAT range. Separately, an internal recommendation service called the cart service at 9,000 req/s with a bug, saturating its DB; that traffic never crossed the CDN. Gateway per-key limits were healthy. The CDN 429s were 12% of the errors; the cart DB saturation was 26%.

title: The five real-time options
text: HTTP is request-response. How do you get server-side events to a client quickly? Compare the options. The server cannot speak first in plain HTTP, so there are five tricks. Short polling asks every few seconds. Long polling asks and the server holds the request until there is news. SSE is one long HTTP response streaming events one way. WebSocket is a two-way connection after an HTTP upgrade. Push FCM/APNs wakes the app when it is closed. I pick the simplest one that meets the latency and direction I need.

title: SSE mechanics
text: How does Server-Sent Events work, and what are its limits compared to WebSockets? SSE is one long HTTP response with Content-Type: text/event-stream where the server writes small text events. The client auto-reconnects and sends Last-Event-ID so the server can resume. It is one-way, text only, and works through ordinary HTTP infrastructure. Limits: no binary, no client-to-server channel on the same stream, a six-connection cap per domain on HTTP/1.1 browsers, and proxy buffering that can clump events.

title: SSE through a proxy
text: Find the problems. A job-progress page uses SSE. Works on localhost. In production, progress jumps 0% to 100% after 40 s instead of updating each second; and every 60 s the console shows a reconnect. Setup: browser - ALB idle timeout 60 s - NGINX - app. NGINX config: location /events { proxy pass http://app; } App response headers: Content-Type: text/event-stream . App emits an event every 1 s and nothing else.

title: Short polling cost
text: How do you cut cost and battery without moving to WebSockets? Order-tracking screen of a food app: 200,000 concurrent active orders, the Android client polls GET /orders/{id}/status every 3 s. Status changes about 6 times per order over 40 minutes. Backend: 6,700 req/s at 12% CPU but the DB read replica is at 60%. Users complain the app drains battery. Product wants "live" updates but with no big rewrite this quarter.

title: Long polling gaps
text: Explain what is wrong and fix it. Support chat widget uses long polling: GET /poll?timeout=60 . Since a load balancer change on Monday, users report "messages arrive late or not at all". Metrics: LB idle timeout: 60 s was 120 s poll responses 504 every 60.0 s: 4,100/min server held requests: 52,000 ; app threads blocked: 52,000/200 pool messages table: rows with delivered=false age 5 min: growing The client re-issues /poll immediately on any response and does not send any cursor.

title: Connection capacity
text: Size the fleet, name the limits you will hit first, and describe the routing layer. A chat app has 500k concurrent WebSocket connections on 10 gateway nodes 50k each, 16 GB RAM, 8 cores . Marketing plans a launch for 5M concurrent. Each user sends about 1 message per minute of 300 bytes. Node metrics at 50k connections: memory 3 GB, CPU 12%, file descriptors 51k of 65k limit. A teammate says "scale linearly: 100 nodes".

title: WebSocket handshake and what you must build
text: How does a WebSocket connection start, and what does the protocol not give you? It starts as an HTTP GET with Upgrade: websocket ; the server replies 101 Switching Protocols , and from then on both sides send small frames in either direction over the same TCP connection. The protocol gives full duplex and low overhead 2 to 14 bytes per frame . It does not give reconnect, message replay, ordering across reconnects, auth beyond the handshake, or caching; I build those myself.

title: Heartbeats, reconnect, resume
text: How do you detect a dead connection and reconnect without losing or duplicating messages?
