TCP may not notice a dead peer for minutes, so I send a ping every 20 to 30 s and treat a missing pong within about 10 s as dead; the interval stays below the shortest NAT or LB idle timeout. On reconnect I use exponential backoff with full jitter, then resume by sending the last sequence number so the server replays what I missed; if the gap is too large I do a full REST resync. Messages carry server ids and client send ids so duplicates are dropped.

title: Reconnect storm
text: Stabilize the system and fix the design. A gateway node with 100k connections crashes at 20:00. The remaining 19 nodes hold 1.9M connections. Within 30 s: connect rate: 200/s - 38,000/s gateway CPU: 30% - 98% TLS handshakes auth DB QPS: 500 - 41,000, p99 2.3 s connection count: sawtooth, nodes dropping 20-60k then re-adding client log: reconnect attempt=1 delay=1000 ... attempt=2 delay=2000 no jitter Total connections trending down, not up.

title: Push at scale
text: Redesign the sender. A news app has 10M installs. A breaking-news push must reach users within 2 minutes. The current job loops over device tokens with one FCM HTTP call per token from a single worker at 800 sends/s. It takes 3.5 hours. Logs show 8% of calls return UNREGISTERED / NOT FOUND , and during the last campaign some calls returned 429/503. Delivery receipts show many users got it after the 40-minute mark.

title: Resume and dedupe
text: Find all the bugs. A chat client reconnects on failure. Users report that after a tunnel they see messages twice, and sometimes a message they sent shows twice to the recipient. Client code: override fun onFailure ws: WebSocket, t: Throwable, r: Response? { connect // immediately } override fun onOpen ws: WebSocket, r: Response { ws.send """{"type":"sync","since":${lastSeenTime}}""" pending.forEach { ws.send it.json } // resend unsent messages } override fun onMessage ws: WebSocket, text: String { ui.add parse text ; lastSeenTime = now } Server replays everything newer than since and persists every send it receives. Messages have no ids.

title: Choosing the technique
text: What do you ask, and what do you build? "Build live cricket scores for our app." No further detail. Peak: 2M concurrent viewers, a score update every 3 s about 200 bytes . Some users also post emoji reactions, the app is often in the background, and the CTO wants it live in 4 weeks with a team of 4.

title: When SQL is the right choice
text: When would you pick a relational database for a new system, and when would you not? I choose SQL when I need correctness across several rows or tables, flexible queries, or I do not yet know the future queries: payments, orders, bookings, inventory, accounts. One good Postgres or MySQL node does about 20,000 to 50,000 indexed reads/s and 5,000 to 15,000 transactional writes/s benchmark it , far more than most products need. I look elsewhere for giant append-only streams millions of writes/s , pure key lookups at huge QPS Redis , or deep graph traversals.

title: Primary key choice
text: What primary key would you use for a table expected to reach billions of rows, and why? A 64-bit, roughly time-ordered ID: BIGINT identity if a single database generates it, or a Snowflake-style or UUIDv7 ID if multiple writers or shards need to generate without coordination. I avoid random UUIDv4 as the clustered key on a huge table because every insert lands on a random page; I never use 32-bit INT for growing tables overflow at about 2.1B rows . I do not expose sequential IDs publicly.

title: Integer overflow
text: Stop the bleeding and plan the real fix. At 02:14 an e-commerce platform starts failing every order insert: ERROR: integer out of range DETAIL: nextval: reached maximum value of sequence "order events id seq" 2147483647 order events has 2.1B rows and 900 GB, grows 30M rows/day, and is written by 12 services. A hotfix must be live before the 09:00 peak. Replication to two replicas is healthy; CPU is 20%.

title: Connection pool sizing
text: What is happening and what is the right pool design? Postgres on 16 vCPU, max connections = 1000 raised last month. 60 app pods autoscale; each has a Hikari pool of maximum-pool-size: 30 . During a sale the HPA scales to 60 pods. Symptoms: p99 latency 80 ms - 2.4 s pg stat activity: 1,620 connections requested, 1000 max - "FATAL: sorry, too many clients already" CPU 100%, load average 70, context switches 600k/s app log: HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 3000ms queries avg 6 ms, QPS 3,000

title: Query shape and indexes
text: Explain each problem and fix it. A support console lists orders for a customer. With 120M rows the page "load more" gets slower the deeper you go page 400 takes 9 s . Search by email also seems slow. Code and plan: -- list SELECT FROM orders WHERE customer id = 42 ORDER BY created at DESC OFFSET 20000 LIMIT 25; -- search SELECT id FROM customers WHERE lower email = 'a@b.com'; Limit cost=... actual time=8870..8870 rows=25 - Sort actual time=8210..8700 rows=20025 - Seq Scan on orders Filter: customer id = 42 Rows Removed by Filter: 119,979,975 Seq Scan on customers actual time=1900 ms Indexes: orders pkey, customers pkey, customers email key email

title: Read replicas and lag
text: Why does this happen and how do you fix it without giving up the replicas? Reads were moved to 2 replicas to relieve the primary 20,000 read QPS, 500 write QPS . Since then support gets tickets: "I updated my address and the page shows the old one", and sometimes an order disappears from "My orders" for a few seconds after checkout. Metrics: replica lag seconds: p50 0.04 p99 3.8 max 21 during nightly batch primary CPU: 70% - 25% error rate: none

title: Normalise vs denormalise
text: When do you normalise and when do you deliberately denormalise? I normalise the source of truth to about 3NF so each fact lives once: no duplicated addresses, no update anomalies. I denormalise only a derived read copy for a measured hot path: a summary column, a materialised view or a read-model table fed by a change stream. The source stays normalised and the copy can be rebuilt; if the copy becomes the only truth, it is dangerous.

title: Expand and contract migrations
text: How do you change the schema of a table with 500M rows while serving production traffic? I use expand and contract so every deploy is backward compatible: add the new nullable column metadata only , deploy code that writes both, backfill in small batches with pauses, switch reads, and drop the old column in a later release. I build indexes with CONCURRENTLY , add constraints as NOT VALID then VALIDATE , and set lock timeout so a migration fails fast instead of queuing behind a long query and blocking everyone.

title: Migration lock
text: Handle the incident and design the retry. 14:02 a deploy runs ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN gift note TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT ''; on a 500M row Postgres table. At 14:03 writes hang. pg stat activity: pid 811 state=active query='SELECT ... FROM orders ...' running 14 min, analytics pid 904 state=active wait event=Lock query='ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN ...' pids 1,100+ state=active wait event=Lock query='INSERT INTO orders ...' API 5xx: 41% pool timeouts rising DB CPU 8% The team asks to kill the migration, then wants to retry it.

title: Hot counter row
text: Fix it and explain trade-offs. A social app stores posts.likes count and increments it with UPDATE posts SET likes count = likes count + 1 WHERE id = :id on every like. A celebrity post goes viral: 4,000 likes/s on one row. pg stat activity: 380 sessions waiting wait event type=Lock transactionid tps overall: 9,000 - 1,100 p99 like API: 4.8 s dead tuples on posts: 2.1M and rising, autovacuum busy CPU 35% Other posts are fine. Product wants the count to be "roughly right, within seconds".

title: When to shard
text: Do you shard now? What do you do, and what shard key? A B2B SaaS has one Postgres primary 32 vCPU, 256 GB RAM, 8 TB, 3 replicas . Growth is 15% per month. Today: writes 4,000/s limit tested at about 9,000 , reads 25,000/s served mostly by replicas, buffer cache hit ratio 93% and falling, vacuum struggling on two 2 TB tables. A principal engineer proposes sharding by user id now. Customers are companies with 1 to 50,000 users; a few big tenants make 40% of traffic. Many queries join across a tenant's users.

title: Schema choice for a new product
text: What do you ask and what do you recommend? A founder says: "We are building a marketplace. We will have millions of users, so we need a scalable database; the CTO says use MongoDB. Launch in 3 months." You learn: orders and payments with refunds, sellers with inventory counts, buyer search with filters, and a reporting need from finance. Expected year-one numbers: 200k users, 2,000 orders/day, 50 writes/s peak.

title: The four NoSQL families
text: What are the main NoSQL families and what is each one good at? Each is a data structure with a network in front. Key-value Redis, DynamoDB is a distributed hash map: fast lookup by key only. Document MongoDB, Firestore is a map of JSON documents: one read returns a whole entity. Wide-column Cassandra, Bigtable is a sorted map of sorted maps: huge write rates, queries by partition key. Graph Neo4j is nodes and edges: cheap multi-hop traversals. They trade joins and ad-hoc queries for scale or a flexible shape, so you design data around queries.

title: Embed vs reference in documents
text: In a document database, how do you decide between embedding and referencing related data? I embed data that is read together and bounded in size, like order line items inside the order, so one read returns everything. I reference data that is large, shared, unbounded or changes independently, like the product catalogue or all reviews of a viral product. Documents have size limits MongoDB 16 MB and every update rewrites more as a document grows, so I never embed an unbounded list.

title: Wide-column modeling
text: What is wrong and how do you change the model? You model chat history on Cassandra: "show the latest 50 messages of a conversation, newest first". First attempt: CREATE TABLE messages conversation id uuid, sent at timeuuid, sender id bigint, body text, PRIMARY KEY conversation id, sent at WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY sent at DESC ; Six months in, one company-wide channel has 40M messages; queries on it time out. nodetool tablehistograms shows partition size max 38 GB and p99 read latency 2.1 s for that channel; other conversations are fine at 4 ms.

title: Redis big key
text: Diagnose and fix. Redis single primary, 3 replicas backs sessions and a leaderboard. Every day at 18:00 API latency spikes for 4 to 6 seconds across all services. Metrics: slowlog: ZRANGE leaderboard:global 0 -1 WITHSCORES duration 3,840,000 us slowlog: KEYS session: duration 1,210,000 us used memory 21 GB ; leaderboard:global = 4.8 GB sorted set, 31M members connected clients 4,200 ; blocked on single thread; CPU 100% on one core Nothing else changed; the 18:00 job is a "weekly report" cron.

title: Document model bug
text: Find the design bugs and fix them. A forum stores each thread as a MongoDB document and shards the threads collection on { createdAt: 1 } : { " id": "t 77", "title": "Launch day", "createdAt": "2026-11-09T10:15:00Z", "posts": {"user": "u1", "text": "...", "at": "..."} } After a viral thread: update latency for it goes 4 ms to 900 ms, and writes errors appear: BSONObj size: 16793600 is invalid . Sharding stats show one shard taking 100% of inserts; the other 3 shards idle.

title: Quorum and stale reads
text: Explain the anomaly and decide. Cassandra, RF=3, one datacenter. An inventory-like counter "seats left" is written and read at consistency ONE for speed. Users occasionally see seats available when a show is sold out; two buyers got the same last seat. Metrics: write CL=ONE, read CL=ONE read repair: 3.1% of reads trigger repair hint backlog on node-5: 2.4M hints node-5 was down 40 min last night nodetool status: all UN now The team asks whether to "just use QUORUM".

title: CAP, PACELC, quorum
text: Explain CAP correctly, and how quorum reads and writes give consistency in a replicated store. CAP says that during a network partition a distributed store must choose consistency everyone sees the latest write, some requests may be refused or availability every request answers, possibly with stale data . Partitions happen, so the real choice is C or A while one is happening; day to day the trade is latency versus consistency PACELC . With N replicas, writing to W and reading from R replicas with R + W N makes the read set overlap the latest write.

title: Choosing by access pattern, polyglot
text: How do you choose a datastore for a new feature, and when is using several stores justified? I start from the top three queries with their QPS and latency, then ask about multi-row transactions or joins, size and write rate in one and three years, staleness the business tolerates, and what the team already runs well. Money and stock go to SQL; cache, sessions and counters to Redis; flexible catalogues to a document store; huge keyed write streams to wide-column; deep relationships to a graph; text search to a search engine. If I use several stores I name one system of record and treat the rest as derived and rebuildable.

title: DynamoDB hot partition
text: Explain and fix. A flash-sale app stores product stock counters in DynamoDB, table keyed by productId . Provisioned: 40,000 WCU. During a sale on one product: ConsumedWriteCapacityUnits table : 11,000 / 40,000 27% ThrottledRequests: 9,400/s on PutItem/UpdateItem ThrottlingException: Rate of requests exceeds the allowed throughput hot key: productId=P-8812 receiving 6,000 writes/s Other products succeed. Finance asks why throttling happens when "we have 73% capacity free".

title: Tombstones
text: Diagnose and fix. A team uses Cassandra as a job queue: insert a row into pending jobs partitioned by queue name , workers read the first 100 rows and delete each after processing. After 3 weeks, p99 read latency goes 5 ms to 4 s and workers time out. Logs: WARN ReadCommand: Read 100 live rows and 1,874,332 tombstone cells for query SELECT FROM pending jobs WHERE queue name='emails' LIMIT 100 tombstone failure threshold: 100000 aborts query Compaction is running; gc grace seconds is the default 10 days. Disk is at 55%.

title: Graph store fit and super-nodes
text: Do you move to a graph database? What do you do? A social app wants "people you may know": friends of friends ranked by mutual friends. 20M users, average 150 follows, some celebrities with 30M followers. The SQL prototype: SELECT f2.followee id, count AS mutuals FROM follows f1 JOIN follows f2 ON f2.follower id = f1.followee id WHERE f1.follower id = :me AND f2.followee id < :me GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY mutuals DESC LIMIT 10; It takes 40 ms for typical users but 11 s for users who follow a celebrity. Depth-2 expansion: 150 x 150 = 22,500 paths normally. A proposal: "move to Neo4j".

title: Source of truth and drift
text: Lead the review: root cause and corrected architecture. Post-incident review of a retailer. Stores: Postgres orders , Elasticsearch product search , Redis cart and prices cache , and MongoDB product details, added by a different team . On a sale day customers were charged 499 for products shown at 399 in search; 2,300 orders were affected. Findings: Postgres price: 499 updated 09:58 by pricing service MongoDB price: 399 updated by CMS import at 09:40, never overwritten Elasticsearch: 399 indexed from MongoDB Redis price: 499 TTL 24h, from Postgres at 09:59 no job compares the stores; the "price" field exists in 4 places

title: LSM write and read path
text: Walk me through what happens when you write a key to an LSM-tree database like Cassandra or RocksDB, and then how a read finds it again. I append the record to a write-ahead log for durability, then insert it into an in-memory sorted memtable and acknowledge. When the memtable hits a size like 64 MB it is frozen and flushed as an immutable sorted file, an SSTable. Reads check the memtable, then SSTables newest to oldest, using Bloom filters to skip files that cannot hold the key. Background compaction merges files and drops overwritten and deleted entries.

title: Write amplification
text: What are write, read and space amplification, and why can you not minimise all three at once? Write amplification is physical bytes written per logical byte the app wrote. Read amplification is disk reads per logical read, and space amplification is bytes on disk per byte of live data. They trade against each other the RUM conjecture : leveled compaction gives low read and space amp but high write amp, size-tiered gives low write amp but high read and space amp.

title: Engine choice
text: Which engine family do you pick, with the numbers, and how reversible is the decision? You are designing storage for a metrics platform. 200,000 devices each send one 100-byte data point per second: 20 MB/s of ingest, about 1.7 TB/day. Queries are "last 24 hours for one device" point-range and a nightly rollup. Retention is 30 days. The team proposes Postgres because "everyone knows SQL". One engineer proposes Cassandra with TWCS. Budget: 6 NVMe nodes.

title: Bloom filters
text: What do you change, and how much memory does it cost? A RocksDB-backed service holds 2 billion keys over 5 levels. 60 percent of lookups are for keys that do not exist a dedup check . Today bloom filters are disabled. p99 lookup is 18 ms, disk read IOPS are at 90 percent of the NVMe limit. The node has 64 GB RAM, 40 GB is used by the block cache. An engineer proposes buying more NVMe.

title: Compaction choice
text: What is wrong, and what do you do? A Cassandra table stores user profile documents. Each user is updated about 20 times per day. 300 million users. The schema was copied from a logging table: compaction: class: SizeTieredCompactionStrategy min threshold: 4 max threshold: 32 Symptoms after three months: nodetool tablehistograms users.profile SSTables per read: p50=7 p99=19 Read latency p99: 85 ms target 15 ms Disk used: 6.1 TB of 8 TB; compaction needs temp space A teammate suggests adding more read replicas reads are 70 percent of traffic .

title: Write stalls
text: Walk me through the incident. A RocksDB-based event store leveled compaction normally takes 40,000 writes/s at p99 5 ms. After a marketing event ingest rises to 90,000 writes/s. Within 20 minutes p99 write latency hits 4 seconds and some writes are rejected. Metrics: rocksdb.num-files-at-level0 : 38 slowdown=20, stop=36 rocksdb.estimate-pending-compaction-bytes : 410 GB rising rocksdb.is-write-stopped : 1 disk util: 100% cpu: 45% mem: normal rocksdb.actual-delayed-write-rate : 16 MB/s Reads are unaffected. A teammate wants to restart the process because "it looks hung".

title: B-tree page splits
text: How does a B-tree insert work, and why do random UUID primary keys hurt a B-tree table? A B-tree finds the leaf page for the key and inserts there; if the page is full it splits into two and pushes a separator key to the parent. With sequential keys inserts always hit the rightmost leaf, which stays hot in cache and fills pages. With random UUIDs inserts land on random leaves all over the tree, so the working set is the whole index, pages split everywhere and end about 50 to 70 percent full.

title: Compaction strategies
text: Compare size-tiered, leveled, time-window and FIFO compaction. When would you pick each, and what does each cost you? Size-tiered merges similar-sized files: lowest write amp, but high read amp and up to 2x space during merges, good for write-heavy data. Leveled keeps non-overlapping files per level with a 10x size ratio: low read and space amp, high write amp, good for read- or update-heavy. Time-window compacts only within a time bucket and drops whole expired windows, ideal for TTL time-series. FIFO just deletes the oldest files, for caches and disposable streams.

title: Engine choice
text: How do you approach the choice? A product manager says: "We are building chat history storage. It must scale to 50 million users and be fast." Nothing else is specified. The team is split: Postgres or Cassandra/ScyllaDB.

title: Write amplification and SSD wear
text: Do the math and propose a fix. A RocksDB cluster stores 4 KB blobs thumbnails with a 32 B key . The app writes 300 GB/day of logical data. The leveled LSM measures a write amplification of 18. Drives are 3.84 TB NVMe rated for 1 DWPD over 5 years, and the SMART data shows 40 percent of lifetime endurance used after 8 months. Finance asks why drives are being replaced so fast.

title: Tombstones
text: Explain what is happening and how you fix it. A Cassandra table inbox holds per-user notifications. A cleanup job deleted 70 percent of rows last night about 4 billion rows . Today: disk usage did not fall, and a read path that normally takes 8 ms now times out for some users: WARN Read 1 live rows and 148320 tombstone cells for query SELECT ... WHERE user id=? LIMIT 20 ERROR Scanned over 100001 tombstones; query aborted tombstone failure threshold nodetool tablestats: SSTable count 412, pending compactions 9,800 A teammate says "the delete must not have worked, run it again".

title: Changing compaction under live traffic
text: Plan the migration. A 24-node Cassandra cluster stores 90 days of click events on SizeTiered compaction, 65 percent disk full, 120,000 writes/s sustained, read SLO p99 20 ms. Retention is enforced by a nightly DELETE job. You want to move to TimeWindowCompactionStrategy with TTL. Business: no downtime, no latency regression beyond 10 percent, and the change must be rollback-able.

title: Cost of an index
text: What does an index buy you and what does it cost? Why not index every column? An index lets the database seek to rows instead of scanning the table, turning tens of seconds into about a millisecond on a 100M-row table. The cost: every insert, delete and update of an indexed column must also update each index, and each index takes disk and RAM. So I index for the queries that matter and drop the rest.

title: Composite index column order
text: You have WHERE customer id = ? AND status = ? AND created at ? ORDER BY created at . How do you order the columns in a composite index and why? A composite index sorts by the first column, then the second within equal first values, and so on. So it helps queries that use a leftmost prefix. My rule is equality columns first, then the sort column, then range columns: customer id, status, created at . Selectivity is only a tiebreaker.

title: Index not used
text: What is wrong with each query and what do you do? A login endpoint is slow after a deploy, p99 jumped from 5 ms to 900 ms. The users table has 40M rows and an index on email . The new code: SELECT id, password hash FROM users WHERE lower email = lower $1 ; and a second endpoint: SELECT FROM users WHERE phone = 9876543210; -- phone is varchar 15 , indexed EXPLAIN shows Seq Scan on users for both. A teammate says "the index is corrupted, rebuild it".

title: Index design for a feed
text: Design the index and justify it. A notifications table has 500M rows. The hot query serves 3,000 QPS: SELECT id, type, created at FROM notifications WHERE user id = $1 AND read = false ORDER BY created at DESC LIMIT 20; Current index: user id . A typical user has 4,000 notifications, 3 percent unread. p99 is 60 ms; EXPLAIN shows Sort and Rows Removed by Filter: 3880 .

title: Partial index for a job queue
text: What indexes would you create, and what are the pitfalls? A jobs table has 100M rows, of which about 2 percent are status = 'PENDING' . Workers poll constantly: SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'PENDING' ORDER BY created at LIMIT 100; The full index on status, created at is 3.4 GB, and index maintenance on completed jobs is hot. A second requirement: usernames must be unique among non-deleted users deleted at IS NULL but a deleted user's name can be reused.

title: Index verification
text: Handle the incident and design the fix. After a Tuesday deploy, a Postgres primary 16 vCPU, 128 GB RAM goes from 30 percent to 95 percent CPU, p99 API latency 40 ms to 3 s. Deploy touched a reporting endpoint. pg stat statements top entry: query: SELECT ... FROM events WHERE tenant id = $1 AND created at = $2 AND type = ANY $3 ORDER BY created at DESC LIMIT 50 calls: 9,200/min mean exec time: 1,850 ms shared blks read: 42,000,000 Limit - Sort - Seq Scan on events rows=412M Filter: tenant id = .. Rows Removed by Filter: 411,998,000 Existing index: created at . Table is 380 GB, taking 8,000 writes/s. The team wants to add tenant id , type , and created at, tenant id indexes to be safe.

title: Covering indexes
text: What is a covering index? Why might an index-only scan in Postgres still hit the table? A covering index holds every column the query needs, so the database answers from the index without fetching table rows. In Postgres I add payload columns with INCLUDE . An index-only scan still visits the heap for pages the visibility map does not mark all-visible, so stale VACUUM makes it quietly degrade.

title: Inverted indexes and search
text: How does an inverted index work, and when would you use Postgres full-text search versus Elasticsearch? An inverted index maps each term to a sorted posting list of document IDs. Text is analysed tokenised, lowercased, stemmed at index time and again at query time; a AND b intersects two posting lists, and results are ranked with TF-IDF or BM25. Postgres FTS with a GIN index is enough for small to medium workloads; Elasticsearch is for large corpora, faceting and relevance tuning, but it is a derived store fed from the source of truth, near real time, not a primary database.

title: Geo indexes
text: What is wrong, and how would you redesign it? A ride-hailing service has 5 million drivers, each reporting location every 4 s 1.25M writes/s globally . A rider request needs "the 10 nearest available drivers within 2 km", under 50 ms. The first design stores lat and lng in Postgres with two B-tree indexes and queries lat BETWEEN ... AND lng BETWEEN ... . At 5,000 requests/s the DB falls over. A geohash cell prototype works but support tickets say drivers just across a street are missed.

title: Too many indexes
text: How do you decide what to drop and how do you do it safely? A Postgres payments table 900M rows, 700 GB data has 14 indexes totalling 1.1 TB. Insert rate is 6,000 rows/s at peak with p99 insert latency 120 ms target 20 ms . Replica lag spikes to 40 s during peaks. Autovacuum runs constantly. The DBA's stats: indexrelname idx scan size pay user idx 8,900,000 64 GB pay user created idx 0 91 GB pay status idx 12 48 GB pay created idx 210,000 52 GB pay merchant idx 5,300,000 71 GB ... 9 more, 6 with idx scan < 100 The stats were last reset 11 days ago. A lead says "drop all with low scans today".

title: Search design
text: How would you decide, and what are the risks of the option you pick? Product asks for "a search box on our catalogue". 8 million products, descriptions of about 50 words, 300 queries/s at peak, 50 new or changed products per second. Today the app uses WHERE name ILIKE '%' $1 '%' and takes 4 s. Engineering is debating Postgres full-text search versus a new Elasticsearch cluster.

title: Changing an index under live traffic
text: How do you ship the new index with no outage, and how do you retire the old one? A MySQL 8 InnoDB table events has 2 billion rows 900 GB and takes 12,000 writes/s. The current index user id is too weak: the hot query filters by user id and type and sorts by created at . Plan: replace it with user id, type, created at . Last quarter a plain ALTER TABLE ... ADD INDEX on a smaller table caused 20 minutes of replica lag and a spike in deadlocks. There is a 99.95 percent availability SLO.

title: ACID and durability
text: Explain ACID. How does a database actually guarantee durability when COMMIT returns? Atomicity is all or nothing, done with an undo log or by never exposing uncommitted versions. Consistency means constraints hold, and is mostly the schema and the application's job, not CAP consistency. Isolation means concurrent transactions do not see half-finished work, at a tunable level. Durability means that once COMMIT returns the data survives a crash: the engine appends to the write-ahead log and calls fsync before acknowledging.

title: Lost update vs write skew
text: Explain lost update and write skew with an example each. Why doesn't a row lock fix write skew, and what does? Lost update: two transactions read the same value, both modify it, the second write overwrites the first. Write skew: two transactions read overlapping data, each updates a different row, and together they break a rule neither broke alone. Row locks do not help write skew because there is no shared row to lock; I need Serializable isolation, a lock on the shared parent or a constraint that makes the invariant checkable.

title: Oversell and lost update
text: What is the bug, and what is the best fix? A ticketing service sells the last seats. Postgres, default isolation. Code: Languages: Java, Kotlin tab @Transactional public void book long eventId, int qty { int left = jdbc.queryForObject "SELECT seats left FROM events WHERE id = ?", Integer.class, eventId ; if left = qty { jdbc.update "UPDATE events SET seats left = ? WHERE id = ?", left - qty, eventId ; jdbc.update "INSERT INTO tickets event id, qty VALUES ?, ? ", eventId, qty ; } else throw new SoldOutException ; } tab @Transactional fun book eventId: Long, qty: Int { val left = jdbc.queryForObject "SELECT seats left FROM events WHERE id = ?", Int::class.java, eventId !! if left = qty { jdbc.update "UPDATE events SET seats left = ? WHERE id = ?", left - qty, eventId jdbc.update "INSERT INTO tickets event id, qty VALUES ?, ? ", eventId, qty } else throw SoldOutException } Event capacity 500. After a sale burst: 523 tickets issued, seats left = -3 in some rows and 11 in others. The team proposes SERIALIZABLE globally.

title: Write skew under Repeatable Read
text: Explain what happened and how to fix it. A scheduling app requires at least 1 nurse on every shift. Postgres at REPEATABLE READ . Code in a transaction: SELECT count FROM assignments WHERE shift id = 9 AND status = 'ON'; -- app: if count = 2 then UPDATE assignments SET status = 'OFF' WHERE shift id = 9 AND nurse id = :me; Audit finds 14 shifts last month with zero nurses on duty. Logs show two requests overlapping by milliseconds each time. Developer: "Repeatable Read gives a stable snapshot, so this cannot happen."

title: Deadlocks
text: Why do the deadlocks happen and how do you eliminate them? A wallet service transfers money between accounts. Under load you see: ERROR: deadlock detected DETAIL: Process 4121 waits for ShareLock on transaction 99812; blocked by process 4377. Process 4377 waits for ShareLock on transaction 99811; blocked by process 4121. HINT: See server log for query details. about 40 per minute at 2,000 transfers/s. The code: Languages: Java, Kotlin tab @Transactional void transfer long from, long to, long amt { jdbc.update "UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - ? WHERE id = ?", amt, from ; jdbc.update "UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + ? WHERE id = ?", amt, to ; } tab @Transactional fun transfer from: Long, to: Long, amt: Long { jdbc.update "UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - ? WHERE id = ?", amt, from jdbc.update "UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + ? WHERE id = ?", amt, to } A teammate wants to raise deadlock timeout to reduce the errors.

title: Long transactions and MVCC
text: What is happening and how do you respond? A Postgres orders database 10M-row hot table, 5,000 updates/s slowly degrades over a week: table size grew from 20 GB to 55 GB, queries slow, autovacuum is running constantly but not finishing its work. SELECT pid, now -xact start AS age, state, left query,40 FROM pg stat activity WHERE xact start IS NOT NULL ORDER BY age DESC LIMIT 3; pid age state left 8812 6 days idle in transaction SELECT FROM config WHERE ... 9020 00:00:41 active UPDATE orders SET ... pg stat user tables: orders n live tup=10.2M n dead tup=412M A teammate wants to run VACUUM FULL orders immediately.

title: Isolation levels per engine
text: The SQL standard has four isolation levels. How do Postgres and MySQL InnoDB actually behave at Read Committed, Repeatable Read and Serializable? Postgres defaults to Read Committed, where each statement sees a fresh snapshot. Its Repeatable Read is snapshot isolation: no phantoms, but write skew is still possible. Its Serializable uses SSI, which detects dangerous patterns and aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE 40001, so the app must retry. InnoDB defaults to Repeatable Read, with a consistent snapshot for plain reads and next-key/gap locks for locking reads. Oracle has no true Repeatable Read and its SERIALIZABLE is snapshot isolation.

title: MVCC mechanics and cost
text: How does MVCC work in Postgres versus InnoDB, and what are the design consequences? MVCC keeps several versions of a row so readers do not block writers. Postgres stores each version in the heap with xmin creator and xmax deleter , and an UPDATE inserts a new version; VACUUM removes dead ones. InnoDB keeps the latest version in the clustered index and rebuilds older versions from undo logs, with a purge thread cleaning them. The design consequences: long transactions pin old versions and cause bloat, hot rows still serialise writers, and Postgres needs vacuum to keep ahead of transaction ID wraparound.

title: Hot row contention
text: How do you redesign it to survive 5,000 buyers? A flash sale of 100 units of one SKU expects 5,000 concurrent buyers. The current code uses pessimistic locking: BEGIN; SELECT FROM inventory WHERE sku = 'A1' FOR UPDATE; -- call pricing service about 30 ms UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = 'A1'; COMMIT; During last sale: throughput about 25 purchases/s, p99 latency 14 s, DB connection pool exhausted, many 500s. A teammate proposes optimistic locking with a version column instead.

title: Outbox
text: Run the post-incident review: root cause, fix and prevention. An order service writes the order to Postgres, then publishes OrderPlaced to Kafka: Languages: Java, Kotlin tab @Transactional public void place Order o { orderRepo.save o ; kafka.send "orders", o.id , o.toEvent ; // fire and forget } tab @Transactional fun place o: Order { orderRepo.save o kafka.send "orders", o.id , o.toEvent // fire and forget } Incident: during a Kafka broker restart 0.4 percent of 2M orders in one hour about 8,000 were saved but never published, so no payment or shipping was triggered. Also, 150 orders were published but then rolled back in the DB because a later step failed. A reconciliation job found the gaps three days later.

title: Saga vs 2PC
text: Which do you choose and how do you design it? You are splitting a monolith. An order flow now crosses three services with their own databases: Inventory reserve stock, 5 ms , Payment external card charge, about 800 ms, 2 percent failure , Shipping create shipment, 20 ms . Volume: 300 orders/s. The architect proposes XA two-phase commit across the three databases "to keep it ACID". Another engineer proposes a saga.

title: Durability vs latency
text: What do you recommend and what do you tell compliance? A payments ledger on Postgres has 4,000 commits/s at peak. p99 commit latency is 38 ms, mostly waiting on a synchronous standby in another availability zone RTT about 2 ms plus WAL fsync on a network disk about 4 ms . The product team wants p99 under 10 ms and proposes synchronous commit = off . Compliance says no acknowledged payment may be lost. Primary failure rate: about once a year.

title: Why replicate
text: Our primary database is at 90% CPU. A teammate says "add two replicas and we are done." When is that right and when is it wrong? Replication keeps copies of the same data on several machines. It helps with three things: surviving a machine failure, serving more reads, and putting data near users. It does not scale writes, because every replica still applies every write. So if the CPU is from reads, replicas help. If it is from writes, they do not, and I would look at sharding, batching or a bigger box.

title: Sync, async, semi-sync and failover
text: Explain synchronous, asynchronous and semi-synchronous replication, and what actually happens to your data when the leader dies in each case. In sync mode the leader waits for a follower before acknowledging the client, so no acknowledged write is lost, but a slow follower stalls writes. In async mode the leader acknowledges right away, so it is fast but writes not yet shipped are lost if the leader dies. Semi-sync waits for exactly one follower and leaves the rest async, which is the usual compromise. On failover I promote the most up-to-date follower and must fence the old leader to prevent split brain.

title: Replication lag
text: What is the bug, and how do you fix it without sending all traffic back to the primary? A comments feature writes to the primary and reads from a pool of 3 replicas. Support tickets: "I posted a comment, the page reloaded and my comment is gone, then it appears after a few seconds." Replica lag dashboard shows a steady 200 to 400 ms. The code: Comment c = commentRepo.save newComment ; // goes to primary return redirect "/post/" + c.getPostId ; // later, in the GET handler: List<Comment list = readPool.pick .findByPost postId ; // random replica val c = commentRepo.save newComment // goes to primary return redirect "/post/${c.postId}" // later, in the GET handler: val list = readPool.pick .findByPost postId // random replica

title: Replication lag
text: What is happening and what do you do now and next? Tuesday 02:10. A nightly job runs UPDATE orders SET archived = true WHERE created at < now - interval '1 year' touching 40M rows about 2 GB of WAL . At 02:14 the alert fires: replica lag 90 s and climbing. The customer app reads order status from replicas; support reports "order shows Pending but I paid". Primary CPU is 35%, replica CPU is 100% on a single core. replay lag write lag flush lag ---------------+-----------+---------- 00:01:32 00:00:00.2 00:00:00.4 Network shows no loss.

title: Sync vs async
text: Do you configure the Singapore standby as synchronous? What would you propose? A payments ledger runs a Postgres primary in Mumbai ap-south-1a . The CTO asks for RPO = 0 across a regional disaster and wants a second region in Singapore about 60 ms RTT as a standby. The ledger does 1,500 writes/s at peak, each write transaction currently commits in about 3 ms. The SLO is p99 write latency under 50 ms.

title: Failover and split brain
text: What do you do in the first 15 minutes, and how do you stop this recurring? A MySQL cluster 1 primary, 2 replicas, async, orchestrator-managed in one region. At 14:03 a switch flaps; the orchestrator cannot reach the primary for 12 s and promotes replica-2. The old primary is fine, just partitioned from the orchestrator, and app servers in rack B still reach it. At 14:05 the network heals. Now two nodes accept writes. 14:03:12 orchestrator: primary db-1 unreachable heartbeat timeout 10s 14:03:14 orchestrator: promoting db-2 gtid 7f3a:1-884213 14:03:15 app-b: connected to db-1 read only=OFF 14:05:20 app-a/app-b: 1,100 INSERT conflicts ... duplicate key on orders.id

title: Quorum math
text: In a Dynamo-style store with N, W and R, why does W + R N matter, and what does it not guarantee? N is the number of replicas holding a key, W is how many must acknowledge a write and R how many must answer a read. If W + R N, any read set shares at least one node with any write set, so a read sees the latest acknowledged write. It is not a strong-consistency guarantee: concurrent writes, sloppy quorums, partially failed writes and clock-skewed last-write-wins can all still give stale or lost data.

title: Multi-leader conflicts
text: When is multi-leader replication justified, and how do you handle write conflicts? I use multi-leader when writes must be local in several regions or must work offline, and a cross-region round trip on each write is not acceptable. The cost is conflicts: two regions accept different writes to the same record. I first avoid conflicts by routing a record's writes to its home region, then use a merge CRDT, siblings or custom resolution, and treat last-write-wins as lossy.

title: Quorum
text: Explain how this read returned the old value, and what you would change. A Cassandra cluster, RF=3, one DC. Reads and writes use LOCAL QUORUM QUORUM = 2 . A node n3 goes down at 09:00 for 4 hours of maintenance. At 11:30 a user changes their email; a support agent immediately reads the old email once, then the new one on retry. The team says "quorum should have prevented this". Logs: 09:00 n3 DOWN 11:30:01.120 write email=new@x.com acks: n1, n2 ok 11:30:01.310 read CL=LOCAL QUORUM contacted: n1, n3? - old@x.com n3 was restarted at 11:29 and is still replaying hints.

title: Multi-leader
text: How do you respond to this requirement, and what would you propose? A product manager says: "We are launching in Mumbai, Frankfurt and Virginia next quarter. Users in all three must see fast writes and the app must survive a region outage. Let's go active-active." Today you have one Postgres primary in Virginia with 3 replicas. Traffic: 30M DAU, 8,000 writes/s peak, 85% of users stay in one region, data includes profiles, orders and a wallet balance.

title: Choosing replication
text: What replication style and settings would you pick for each, and why? You own two new services. A A payments ledger: 3,000 writes/s, balances must never be wrong, single region, RPO = 0, RTO < 2 min. B A chat message history: 120,000 writes/s, reads by conversation, a message appearing 100 ms late is fine, must stay writable when a node or AZ is down, 3 AZs.

title: Failover data loss
text: Walk through what happened, what you would tell the business, and the corrective actions. Last Friday a primary in an async-replicated Postgres cluster lost its disk controller at 19:41. Patroni promoted replica-1 in 38 s. Customers reported missing data: 1,240 orders accepted by the app between 19:40:57 and 19:41:03 do not exist after failover. Metrics from before the crash: replica-1 replay lsn lag: 6.1 MB about 4 s of WAL at peak replica-2 lag: 11 MB sync standby: none configured Payment gateway captured payments for those orders. The VP asks for a post-incident review.

title: Why shard
text: What is sharding, how does it differ from replication, and when do you actually shard? Replication copies the same data to several machines; sharding splits different data across machines, each owning a slice. I shard when data or write volume no longer fits one machine, for example a few TB, or writes beyond what one primary can fsync, or a working set bigger than RAM. Before that I exhaust cheaper steps: indexes, caching, read replicas, a bigger machine, archiving old data.

title: Hash partitioning and consistent hashing
text: Why is hash key % N a poor way to map keys to shards, and what do you use instead? With modulo, changing N remaps almost every key: going from 4 to 5 shards moves about 80% of the data. Instead I use many fixed slots for example 16,384 in Redis Cluster assigned to nodes, or a consistent-hash ring with virtual nodes. Adding a node then moves only about 1/N of the keys.

title: Range partitioning
text: What is wrong and how do you fix it? An IoT platform stores sensor readings in a range-partitioned store, key = timestamp , one partition per day. 50,000 inserts/s all day, 29 older partitions are only read occasionally. Dashboards: one partition node at 95% CPU and 8 ms write p99 on that node going to 400 ms; the other 29 nodes at 3% CPU. Total cluster looks "fine" at 12% average.

title: Shard key choice
text: Pick a shard key and handle the awkward queries. A B2B SaaS has 20,000 tenants and 600M rows. The largest tenant has 12% of all rows; the top 10 have 35%. The main queries: 1 all records for a tenant 95% of traffic , 2 lookup a user by email at login before the tenant is known , 3 a nightly admin report over all tenants. Candidate shard keys: tenant id , country , record id auto-increment .

title: Hash partitioning
text: List all bugs/risks in this design and fix them. A session cache layer uses client-side sharding over 4 Redis nodes. Next week traffic doubles, and a teammate's change to 5 nodes goes to production at noon. Code: int shardFor String key, int nodes { return Math.abs key.hashCode % nodes; } Redis pick String key { return pool.get shardFor key, pool.size ; } fun shardFor key: String, nodes: Int : Int = Math.abs key.hashCode % nodes fun pick key: String : Redis = pool shardFor key, pool.size After the change: cache hit ratio drops from 96% to 21%, DB CPU goes from 30% to 100%, users get logged out.

title: Scatter-gather
text: Why is the endpoint slow when the shards look healthy, and what do you do? An order-search endpoint fans out to 32 shards and merges. Per-shard latency: median 10 ms, p99 200 ms. After a feature launch, API p99 climbs from 90 ms to 650 ms and timeouts hit 3% of requests. Shard CPU is only 40%. A red herring: one shard shows a 5 minute compaction in its logs. endpoint /orders/search p50=48ms p95=210ms p99=650ms fanout=32 timeout=500ms retries=1

title: Directory-based partitioning
text: What is directory-based partitioning, what are logical shards, and what can go wrong with the directory? A directory is a lookup table that says which shard owns which key or tenant, instead of a formula. A common compromise is logical shards: hash the key into, say, 1,024 logical shards and keep a small table mapping each to a physical server, so moving data means moving one logical shard. The risks are the directory becoming a single point of failure or a per-request bottleneck, and updating it safely during a migration.

title: Cross-shard transactions
text: How do you handle a business operation that must change data on two shards? Compare 2PC and sagas. First choice is to design the shard key so one business transaction stays on one shard. If not, 2PC is correct but blocks if the coordinator dies and is slow. A saga runs local transactions in sequence with compensating actions refund if shipping fails : no locks, eventually consistent, but you must handle intermediate states and idempotency.

title: Cross-shard pagination
text: Why is it so costly and how do you fix it? An admin screen lists orders across 16 shards with ORDER BY created at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET :off . Staff paging deep OFFSET 50,000 trigger alerts: coordinator memory 6 GB, shard CPU spikes, request takes 14 s. The query planner is not the problem. Per shard receives: ORDER BY created at DESC LIMIT 50020 16 shards x 50,020 rows = 800,320 rows to the coordinator, 20 returned

title: Why shard
text: What do you say about sharding now, and what is your plan? A founder says: "We hit 400 GB in Postgres and growth is 8% a month. Our CTO says we must shard now to be web-scale." Facts: 1 primary 16 vCPU, 64 GB RAM , 2 replicas, peak 1,800 writes/s, 9,000 reads/s, p99 query 40 ms, CPU averages 35%, the biggest table has 230 GB and a bloated index, and no query has been tuned in a year.

title: Shard key choice
text: Explain each defect and the fixes. After sharding users and orders by user id across 8 PostgreSQL shards, these defects appear in the first week: duplicate emails across accounts, a foreign key error when creating an order for a user on another shard, and two different orders with id = 1042 . The schema was copied to every shard unchanged: CREATE TABLE users id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, email text UNIQUE, ... ; CREATE TABLE orders id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, user id bigint REFERENCES users id , ... ;

title: Directory partitioning
text: Describe the migration, including the directory flip and how you handle stale caches. Tenant "BigCorp" generates 40% of load on shard 3 p99 write 180 ms, CPU 92% . You use a directory tenant id - shard id cached in 60 app servers 60 s TTL . You must move BigCorp 900 GB, 4,000 writes/s to a new dedicated shard 9 with no downtime and no lost writes.

title: Hot partitions
text: What is a hot partition, what causes it, and why does adding shards not fix it? A hot partition is one shard getting far more traffic than the rest, so it saturates while the others idle. Causes are a hot key a celebrity or viral item , skewed distribution sequential keys on a range partition, one giant tenant , time hotspots everyone reads today and plain bad hashing luck. More shards do not help because the extra capacity is not where the load is; one key always lives on one shard.

title: Fixing hot keys
text: Name your toolbox for a hot key, in the order you would try it, with the cost of each. Cheapest first: cache in front with a short TTL, replicate the hot key under several names and read a random copy, salt counter writes across N sub-keys and sum on read, coalesce requests so a miss hits the database once, isolate the whale on its own shard, and queue and batch writes. Each fix trades something: staleness, read amplification, or complexity.

title: Hot partitions
text: Why does doubling not fix it, and what do you do? A DynamoDB table provisioned at 20,000 RCU, evenly across about 10 partitions holds user profiles. A celebrity posts and their profile gets 8,000 reads/s. Errors appear immediately: ProvisionedThroughputExceededException for 85% of requests on userId=celeb 77 Table consumed RCU: 11,000 / 20,000 CloudWatch: ThrottledRequests spikes, ReadThrottleEvents on one partition The on-call proposes doubling the provisioned capacity to 40,000 RCU.

title: Salting hot writes
text: Find the problems and improve it. A like counter for viral posts was salted across 10 sub-keys to spread writes. After launch: post pages sometimes show "0 likes" for a few seconds, the like count goes backwards, and the read path adds 10 round trips p99 from 4 ms to 38 ms . Code: void like String postId { int salt = ThreadLocalRandom.current .nextInt 10 ; redis.incr "likes:" + postId + ":" + salt ; } long count String postId { long sum = 0; for int i = 0; i < 10; i++ { String v = redis.get "likes:" + postId + ":" + i ; sum += v == null ? 0 : Long.parseLong v ; } return sum; } fun like postId: String { val salt = ThreadLocalRandom.current .nextInt 10 redis.incr "likes:$postId:$salt" } fun count postId: String : Long = 0 until 10 .sumOf { redis.get "likes:$postId:$it" ?.toLong ?: 0L }

title: Rebalancing
text: How much data moves, how long will it take, and how do you run it safely? A 3-node Cassandra-like cluster, 300 GB per node, 48 partitions 16 per node . Disks 70% full, so you add node D. Link: 1 Gbps about 100 MB/s usable . Daytime traffic already uses 60% of the network. Your manager asks "how long and when?"

title: Hot key stampede
text: Explain the pattern and design a fix. A flash-sale product page reads product:991 from Redis TTL 60 s and falls back to MySQL. At peak, 30,000 reads/s. Every 60 s the DB connection pool 200 saturates for about 3 seconds; p99 jumps to 4 s and 2% of requests fail. Logs: 12:00:00.000 cache MISS product:991 expired 12:00:00.001..12:00:00.040 4,100 concurrent DB queries for product:991 mysql: Threads running = 198, Aborted connects rising Red herring: the DB slow log shows the query itself takes only 6 ms.

title: Rebalancing strategies
text: Compare fixed-partition, dynamic-splitting and proportional vnode rebalancing. Should rebalancing be automatic? Fixed partitions: create many more partitions than nodes up front and let a new node steal whole partitions Kafka, Redis slots, Couchbase vBuckets, Elasticsearch primary shards . Dynamic splitting: a partition splits when it passes a size or load threshold HBase, Bigtable, MongoDB chunks, CockroachDB ranges . Proportional: each new node takes random token ranges Cassandra vnodes . Automatic rebalancing is convenient but can worsen a load spike or storm after a false failure, so many teams throttle or require approval.

title: Online resharding
text: Describe the standard pattern for resharding a live system with no downtime, and where it can go wrong. Provision the new layout, backfill existing data from a consistent snapshot, stream changes since the snapshot with CDC so the new shards stay current, verify with counts and checksums and optionally shadow reads , then cut over behind a router flag, with a brief write pause. Keep reverse replication to the old layout for days as a rollback, then delete. The usual failures: missing writes during backfill, no verification, no rollback and dual writes with partial failures.

title: Capacity planning
text: When must you start and what would you set up? A shard is at 1.8 TB of 3 TB disk, growing 100 GB/week, with p99 latency still good. The team plans to "reshard when it gets close". Backfill for this shard takes about 2 weeks and planning another 2 weeks. A PM adds: a marketing campaign in 6 weeks may double the write rate.

title: Resharding
text: What went wrong and what is the corrected plan? You are moving from 4 to 8 shards 2 TB, 500 GB per old shard with hash user id into 1,024 logical shards. The plan: backfill, then flip. Rehearsal in staging found a discrepancy: after cutover, 1,900 rows written during the copy are missing from the new shards. backfill: 500 GB at 40 MB/s = 3.5 h per shard snapshot at 02:00:00; cutover at 05:40:00 new shard row count: 123,410,022 old: 123,411,922 diff: 1,900

title: Partition count decision
text: What shard count do you choose and why? You create a new Elasticsearch index for logs: 3 TB now, expected 12 TB in two years, 6 data nodes 2 TB disk each growing to maybe 24. A colleague proposes 3 primary shards "one per two nodes, keep it simple" ; another proposes 5,000 shards "so we never reshard". Target shard size guidance: tens of GB verify current vendor guidance, commonly 10 to 50 GB .

title: Rebalancing storm
text: Run the post-incident review: root cause, contributing factors and corrective actions. A 12-node cluster with automatic rebalancing. During a busy Saturday, a 40 s network blip made node 7 look dead. The cluster began re-replicating its 600 GB to other nodes. Node 7 came back after 2 minutes. Timeline and metrics: 19:02 node7 unreachable blip, 40s 19:02 cluster marks node7 down, starts re-replicating its partitions 19:03 node7 back; cluster continues streaming no cancel 19:05 p99 latency 25ms - 1,400ms on 8 nodes; disk util 98%, network 85% 19:20 two more nodes slow, marked down - more streaming cascade 19:45 manual: set rebalance throttle to 20MB/s and delay timeout to 10 min; recovery at 20:30

title: Object vs block vs file storage
text: Why would you store user photos in S3 instead of the Postgres database or a mounted file system? What do you give up? Photos are large, immutable, read whole, and there are millions of them. Object storage is the cheapest per GB, scales almost without limit and serves bytes over HTTP, so I keep the bytes there and only a small key in Postgres. I give up in-place edits, real folders, POSIX semantics and low-latency random writes: you replace the whole object.

title: Replication vs erasure coding
text: How does an S3-like system achieve eleven nines of durability, and when would you choose erasure coding over 3x replication? Durability comes from redundancy across failure domains at least 3 AZs , checksums on every read and write, and constant scrubbing and repair after a disk dies. Replication is simple and fast to read and repair but costs 3x. Erasure coding such as 10+4 costs 1.4x and survives 4 lost pieces, at the price of CPU and slower, more network-heavy repair, so I use it for big, cold, mostly-read data.

title: Presigned URLs
text: List every problem and give the corrected design. A profile-photo service issues presigned PUT URLs. Security review flags this endpoint. Read it. Languages: Java, Kotlin tab @PostMapping "/upload-url" public Map<String, String uploadUrl @RequestParam String path, @RequestParam String contentType { PutObjectRequest put = PutObjectRequest.builder .bucket "media-prod" .key path .contentType contentType .build ; String url = presigner.presignPutObject r - r .signatureDuration Duration.ofDays 7 .putObjectRequest put .url .toString ; return Map.of "url", url ; } tab @PostMapping "/upload-url" fun uploadUrl @RequestParam path: String, @RequestParam contentType: String : Map<String, String { val put = PutObjectRequest.builder .bucket "media-prod" .key path .contentType contentType .build val url = presigner.presignPutObject { it .signatureDuration Duration.ofDays 7 .putObjectRequest put }.url .toString return mapOf "url" to url } The endpoint has no auth check beyond a logged-in session. Uploads land in the same bucket that serves the public CDN.

title: Cost and storage classes
text: Estimate month-12 storage cost with and without tiering and say what you would check before turning tiering on. A photo app gets 1M uploads/day averaging 2 MB, kept forever. Finance asks for a 12-month storage bill forecast and ways to cut it. Product says photos older than 30 days are viewed rarely under 5% ever . Prices: Standard about $0.023/GB-month, Standard-IA about $0.0125/GB-month 30-day minimum, retrieval fee per GB: verify current . Ignore request and egress cost for now.

title: Multipart orphans
text: Explain the gap, fix it, and prevent it. Month-end bill: S3 storage is $3,600 above forecast. The bucket inventory report shows 120 TB of objects, but billing shows 158 TB-months. Mobile uploads of 1 to 4 GB videos use multipart with 16 MB parts. Android crash rate on the upload screen was elevated after release 8.4. $ aws s3api list-multipart-uploads --bucket media-prod --max-items 5 Uploads: {Initiated: 2026-08-02, Key: raw/u/881/...mp4, UploadId: ...}, ... count older than 30 days: 9,412 Nothing visible in the console object list explains the gap.

title: Multipart upload mechanics
text: Walk me through how multipart upload works, how you would make a mobile upload resumable, and how part size is chosen. I start an upload session and get an UploadId, upload numbered parts in parallel, each returning an ETag, then complete with the ordered list. A failed part is retried alone. For resumability I persist the UploadId and finished parts and ask the server which parts it has before continuing. I pick 5 to 8 MB parts on mobile and larger in a datacenter, and verify checksums at the end.

title: Upload design
text: How do you approach designing this? Product manager: "Let users upload videos from their phones. Should be fast and reliable." No further detail. Expected 200k DAU, 5% upload one video per day.

title: Lifecycle and Glacier
text: What went wrong and how do you fix it without more disruption? A data platform has 200 TB of Parquet event files in S3 Standard $4,600/month . A cost project adds a lifecycle rule: transition to Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 30 days. Two weeks later the data science team reports that backfill jobs fail with InvalidObjectState and the bill shows a retrieval spike. Their weekly model-training job reads 20% of last 6 months data.

title: Egress and CDN
text: Explain the spike and fix it without exposing private images. Image-heavy app. Monthly AWS bill jumps from $4k to $19k. Cost Explorer: the whole increase is "Data Transfer Out" from S3 and CloudFront origin fetches. CloudFront cache hit ratio dropped from 96% to 41% three weeks ago. A release that week changed image URLs to use S3 presigned GET URLs 1 hour expiry behind CloudFront for "privacy". GET /u/42/cat.jpg?X-Amz-Signature=a91f...&X-Amz-Date=20261105T101500Z GET /u/42/cat.jpg?X-Amz-Signature=77c2...&X-Amz-Date=20261105T111500Z Egress price about $0.09/GB.

title: Metadata layer and consistency
text: In an S3-like system, why is the metadata service the hard part, and what does strong read-after-write consistency change for clients? Bytes are easy to spread and replicate, but every key needs a lookup that must be correct, fast and sharded across billions or trillions of entries, including ordered LIST by prefix. That index must be strongly consistent or clients see missing or stale objects. Since December 2020 S3 gives read-after-write for PUT, DELETE and LIST, so clients no longer need retry-until-visible hacks or external consistency layers.

title: Request limits and hot prefixes
text: Diagnose, mitigate, and redesign. A mobile config service stores config/latest.json in S3 and clients fetch it directly on app start. After a push notification campaign, 40k devices open the app within a minute: about 12k GET/s for a single key. Errors: 503 Slow Down Code: SlowDown rate=38% p99 latency 2.4 s, up from 60 ms Same bucket also serves user uploads without issue on other prefixes.

title: Build vs buy storage
text: What do you recommend and how do you decide? A photo-sharing company stores 50 PB in S3 Standard at list price about $0.023/GB-month, roughly $1.15M/month before discounts and egress. The CFO asks whether to build an own storage system like Dropbox did on rented or owned servers. Team: 40 engineers, none with storage-systems experience. Growth: 40%/year.

title: Why not LIKE
text: Why can't we just use WHERE title LIKE '%running shoes%' for product search? A B-tree sorts whole values, so a leading wildcard cannot use it and the database scans every row. On 50M titles that is seconds. A search engine builds an inverted index from words to documents so lookup is instant, and adds stemming, typo tolerance and relevance ranking, which LIKE has no concept of.

title: Inverted index and segments
text: Explain how an inverted index is built and queried, and what Lucene segments are. Each document is analyzed tokenize, lowercase, stem, synonyms and each term maps to a sorted posting list of doc ids with frequencies and positions. A query runs the same analyzer and intersects or unions lists. Lucene writes immutable segments; updates are delete plus insert, and background merges compact segments and drop deleted docs.

title: Analyzer mismatch
text: Why no results, and how do you fix it without downtime? Search for "Running Shoes" returns 0 hits although documents titled "Nike running shoes" exist. The mapping: PUT /products { "mappings": { "properties": { "title": { "type": "keyword" }, "brand": { "type": "text" } } } } and the query: GET /products/ search { "query": { "match": { "title": "Running Shoes" } } } Dev says "the data is there, I can see it in source ". A colleague suggests increasing replicas.

title: Shard sizing
text: Choose shard and node counts and defend them. Product catalog: 600 GB now, growing 20%/year, plan for 3 years. Query load 800/s peak, p99 target 100 ms. A junior proposes number of shards: 100 "so we never have to reshard". Each data node: 64 GB RAM, 1 TB NVMe usable keep 30% headroom .

title: BM25 and ranking signals
text: How does BM25 rank documents, and how does a production system go beyond it? BM25 scores a match by term frequency with diminishing returns, rarity of the term across the corpus IDF and field length normalization. Production adds field boosts, business signals like popularity and stock, a rerank step learning to rank on the top few hundred, and often vector search merged with BM25. I measure with NDCG offline and click and conversion in A/B tests.

title: Relevance complaints
text: What do you do first? Head of product: "Search is bad. Users say they can't find things. Fix it." The site has 3M products, 80k searches/day. Engineers want to switch to a vector database.

title: Near real-time and durability
text: A document was indexed successfully but a search a moment later does not find it. Why, and how does Elasticsearch keep that document from being lost on a crash? Elasticsearch is near real-time: a new document sits in an in-memory buffer and becomes searchable only after a refresh creates a new segment, by default every 1 second. Durability is separate: each write is appended to the translog, fsynced per request by default, and periodic flush commits segments to disk. So indexed means durable, not yet searchable.

title: Deep pagination
text: Diagnose and fix. A SEO crawler and an "export results" feature page deep through results using from / size . Alert: search p99 from 80 ms to 6 s, JVM heap 92%, GC pauses 4 s. Index: 24 primary shards, 1 replica. GET /products/ search?from=90000&size=100 took: 5400 circuit breaking exception: parent Data too large, data for <search would be larger than limit rejected search tasks: 3,100 in 5 min Normal traffic is unchanged. Another team suspects "too many new products".

title: Sync pipeline
text: Write the post-incident review and the target design. An e-commerce app dual-writes: save product in Postgres, then call Elasticsearch index . Incident: prices changed to Rs 999 in Postgres but search showed old Rs 1,999 for 6 hours for 12,000 products; customers saw the wrong price in listings. Logs: ES had a 4-minute brownout; app swallowed the exception catch Exception e { log.warn ... } . A second symptom: two quick updates arrived at ES out of order for some SKUs. Peak rate 5,000 updates/s.

title: Reindexing
text: Plan the migration end to end. You need to add an edge n-gram analyzer for autocomplete and change the language analyzer, on products v7 : 80M documents, 700 GB, 6,000 updates/s peak, search traffic 1,500 QPS that cannot be interrupted. Cluster has 25% free capacity. Change window: no downtime allowed.

title: 10x traffic
text: Plan capacity and protections. Sale event in 3 weeks: expected search traffic 20x, from 500 to 10,000 QPS, autocomplete adds about 3x requests per search session. Cluster: 6 primaries, 1 replica, 4 data nodes; each node handles about 1,500 QPS at p99 under 80 ms for this index. Today CPU is 35% at peak. Top 1,000 queries are about 40% of traffic.

title: Choosing a search stack
text: Recommend one and say what would make you change your mind. A B2B SaaS app has 3M documents average 5 KB, 15 GB , 150 QPS, text search with filters by tenant and a few facets. Team of 6 backend engineers, no one has operated Elasticsearch. Already running Postgres 15 on managed RDS. The CTO is deciding between Postgres full-text, self-managed Elasticsearch, managed Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, or Algolia. Budget: modest.

title: OLTP vs OLAP
text: What is the difference between OLTP and OLAP, and why not run reports on the production database? OLTP serves the live app with many tiny key-based reads and writes at millisecond latency on a normalized row store. OLAP answers questions over history, scanning millions or billions of rows but few columns, on a columnar, denormalized store. A long scan on the production database evicts the cache, burns I/O and spikes latency for customers, so I copy data to a separate analytical system.

title: Column stores
text: Why are column stores fast for analytics and slow for OLTP, and how does a cloud warehouse separate storage from compute? Analytics reads few columns of many rows, so storing each column together lets the engine read only what it needs, compress similar values 5 to 10x, process batches with SIMD and skip blocks via min-max metadata. Updating or fetching one whole row touches every column file, which is why OLTP suffers. Cloud warehouses keep columnar data in object storage and spin compute clusters up independently, so they scale and pause separately.

title: Analytics on OLTP
text: Diagnose and fix. Every Monday 09:00 the checkout API p99 jumps from 120 ms to 3 s for about 8 minutes. Postgres primary r6g.4xlarge, 2 TB orders table . Metrics at 09:02: active connections: 310 max 400 cache hit ratio: 99.2% - 71% iowait 38% longest running query: 7m 12s "SELECT city, avg total FROM orders WHERE created at now - interval '12 months' GROUP BY city" A new weekly report by the analytics team runs at 09:00. The team proposes "just add an index on city".

title: Warehouse cost
text: Quantify and cut the cost. BigQuery on-demand bill is $9,400 this month, up from $1,100. Top query by bytes scanned: SELECT FROM analytics.events WHERE JSON VALUE payload, '$.user id' = '8812' events is a 5 TB unpartitioned table, run 60 times a day by a support tool. Pricing about $6.25 per TB scanned verify current .

title: Idempotent pipelines
text: Find every bug and give a corrected design. Nightly job loads orders into the warehouse. Finance reports revenue 2x on days after a retry, and deleted cancelled orders still counted. -- load orders.sql, run by Airflow at 02:00 with retries=3 INSERT INTO warehouse.fact orders SELECT order id, customer id, total, updated at FROM source.orders WHERE updated at SELECT MAX updated at FROM warehouse.fact orders ; The task failed at 02:40 after loading and was retried at 02:45. The source hard-deletes cancelled orders.

title: Freshness requirement
text: How do you respond? Operations lead: "We need real-time dashboards for orders." There are 40 ops staff, orders 20/s, and decisions are made every 15 to 30 minutes staffing, courier allocation . The data team wants to adopt Flink and Pinot.

title: Table formats
text: What problem do Iceberg, Delta and Hudi solve on top of Parquet files in object storage? A plain lake is just files: no transactions, no row-level updates or deletes, no safe schema change, and readers can see half-written data. Table formats add a transaction log or manifests over the Parquet files, giving ACID commits, snapshot isolation, time travel, schema evolution, upserts and compaction, and let several engines read the same tables.

title: Small files
text: Explain and fix the performance, including how you avoid it recurring. A streaming job writes Parquet into s3://lake/events/dt=.../hour=.../ every 30 s from 40 tasks. After 3 months, a Trino query for one day went from 20 s to 6 minutes. Stats: files for last 7 days: 2,350,000 avg size: 2.1 MB query planning: 3m 10s S3 LIST requests: 18,000 S3 503 SlowDown: sporadic Storage cost is flat; data volume is about 120 GB/day.

title: Late events and watermarks
text: Diagnose and fix without making the dashboard useless. A Flink job computes orders per city per 1-minute tumbling window on event time and feeds a live dashboard. Support: "Numbers are 4% lower than the nightly batch total, worse for rural cities." Job config: watermark = max event time minus 5 s, allowed lateness 0. Telemetry: mobile apps buffer events offline and upload in bursts; 6% of events arrive 30 s to 10 min late. Late-event metric: numLateRecordsDropped = 412,000 last 24 h.

title: Delivery semantics
text: What does "exactly-once" mean in stream processing, and why is end-to-end exactly-once harder than it sounds? Delivery is at-most-once, at-least-once or exactly-once. Engines like Flink achieve exactly-once state updates with checkpoints, but the outside world only sees effects through sources and sinks. End to end it needs a replayable source, checkpointed offsets and either an idempotent sink upsert by key or a transactional two-phase-commit sink, otherwise a recovery can duplicate or lose output.

title: Schema drift and backfills
text: Run the post-incident review: fix, backfill, and prevent. For 9 days the executive "active users" dashboard dropped 18% with no real change in behavior. Root cause found: an upstream team renamed user id to account id in the events topic. The bronze-to-silver job used SELECT user id ... which evaluated to NULL for new data; a downstream COUNT DISTINCT user id silently excluded NULLs. No tests failed, jobs were green. Raw data in the lake is intact. The nightly job takes 12 minutes for one day 300 GB .

title: Warehouse vs lakehouse
text: What do you recommend and how do you migrate? A company has 80 TB in a proprietary-format cloud warehouse costing about $60k/month compute $40k, storage $20k . Growth is 4 TB/month. A new ML team needs raw events 500M/day, about 250 GB/day JSON and unstructured data; BI teams use SQL dashboards with 200 users. Compliance requires GDPR deletes within 30 days. Leadership asks whether to move to a lakehouse Iceberg on S3 with Trino/Spark and leave the warehouse.

title: why a cache helps
text: Why does adding a cache in front of a database help, and when would it not help? Access is skewed: a few keys take most reads. I keep those in RAM, so most requests never reach the database. That cuts latency about 1 ms vs 5-20 ms and, more importantly, cuts database load to QPS x miss rate. It does not help when access is near-uniform over a key space far bigger than the cache, or when the real problem is a missing index.

title: cache-aside write path
text: In cache-aside, why do we delete the cache key on write instead of updating it? Cache-aside means the app reads cache, on miss reads the DB and fills the cache. On write I commit to the DB and then delete the key. Updating the cache instead lets two concurrent writers leave the older value last. Deleting is idempotent: the next read reloads from the DB. A TTL still bounds the rare stale case.

title: hit-ratio capacity math
text: Do the math and tell me whether a 90% hit ratio is enough. A product-detail API serves 12,000 reads/s at peak. The Postgres replica does about 4,000 of these reads/s with p99 under 20 ms; beyond that p99 climbs past 200 ms. A cache read costs 1 ms, a DB read 15 ms. The product asks: "What hit ratio do we need, and what is the average latency?" The team proposes a 5-minute TTL on every product.

title: write-back vs write-through
text: Do you agree? Which pattern for each? A live-streaming app has two features: 1 a "likes" counter, up to 50,000 increments/s on one viral stream; 2 a wallet balance for tipping creators, about 300 writes/s. An engineer proposes write-back Redis first, flush to MySQL every 5 s for both "to keep MySQL cool". Redis runs as a primary plus one async replica, AOF everysec .

title: invalidation ordering
text: Find the bug, explain the interleaving, fix it. Users report that after changing their email, the old email shows for up to an hour, roughly 1 in 300 updates. The code: Languages: Java, Kotlin tab void updateEmail long uid, String email { cache.delete "user:" + uid ; // invalidate first db.updateEmail uid, email ; // then commit } User getUser long uid { User u = cache.get "user:" + uid ; if u == null { u = db.load uid ; cache.set "user:" + uid, u, 3600 ; } return u; } tab fun updateEmail uid: Long, email: String { cache.delete "user:$uid" // invalidate first db.updateEmail uid, email // then commit } fun getUser uid: Long : User = cache.get "user:$uid" ?: db.load uid .also { cache.set "user:$uid", it, 3600 } The profile page makes three concurrent requests header, settings, API so reads overlap writes often.

title: eviction policy and OOM
text: Walk me through diagnosis and the fix. Checkout starts failing at 14:05 with 500s. App logs show: OOM command not allowed when used memory 'maxmemory' . The Redis box has 16 GB RAM; config is maxmemory 14gb , maxmemory-policy noeviction . INFO shows used memory 14.0G , evicted keys 0 , keyspace hits falling and DB CPU at 85%. A new feature released at 13:30 caches search results with TTL 24 h.

title: cache write patterns compared
text: Compare cache-aside, read-through, write-through and write-back. How do you choose? Cache-aside: the app manages the cache, DB-speed writes, no loss. Read-through: the cache loads on a miss, the app only talks to the cache. Write-through: each write hits cache and DB synchronously, always fresh, slower writes. Write-back: ack from the cache, flush later, fastest but loses data on a crash. I default to cache-aside, use write-back only for data I can lose.

title: LRU vs LFU
text: When would you choose LFU over LRU, and how does Redis actually implement LRU? LRU evicts what was untouched longest; it is a good default. A big one-time scan batch job, crawler touches everything once and flushes the hot set from plain LRU. LFU evicts the least frequently used, so a few long-lived hot items survive scans. Redis does not keep an exact LRU list; it samples maxmemory-samples keys default 5 and evicts the best candidate.

title: staleness per data type
text: How do you respond and what do you design? A PM says: "Search is slow. Just cache everything for 10 minutes." The catalogue API serves item title, image URL, price, stock count and seller rating at 8,000 QPS. Price changes happen about 50 times/hour and a wrong price shown at checkout is a legal complaint. Stock hits 0 for popular items several times a day, and overselling costs refunds.

title: cold start and migration
text: Plan the migration so users see nothing. You are moving a 40 GB self-managed Redis single primary to a managed cluster. Traffic is 25,000 reads/s at 96% hit ratio; the DB handles 3,000 reads/s comfortably, 6,000 at the edge. Cutting the app over directly will start the new cluster empty. Last quarter a cache flush pushed DB CPU to 100% for 12 minutes.

title: stale data after invalidation
text: Explain how stale data is cached even though the delete always runs after commit, and fix it. Support reports that about 0.2% of users see an old plan after upgrading, until their cache entry expires after 24 h. Logs show writes: UPDATE plans ... COMMIT then DEL plan:u:8812 , both successful. The DB is Postgres with a streaming read replica; reads for the cache refill go to the replica. pg stat replication shows replay lag of 50 ms normally and 2-4 s during a nightly batch. Red herring: the CDN also caches static assets for 24 h.

title: memory sizing and cost
text: Where is the money best spent: cache memory or DB capacity? Show numbers. A recommendation cache: 200M items x 2 KB = 400 GB of data; the hot set items read in the last day is about 60 GB. Managed Redis costs about 8 USD per GB-month verify . Current config: 200 GB cache, hit ratio 91%, 40,000 reads/s, DB load 3,600/s on a cluster that scales at about 1,500 reads/s per 1,000 USD/month. Finance wants a 30% cost cut. Metrics: evicted keys 2,000/s, p99 miss path 80 ms.

title: stampede vs penetration vs avalanche
text: What is the difference between cache stampede, penetration and avalanche, and what is the first fix for each? Stampede: one hot key expires and thousands of requests rebuild it at once; fix with single-flight or stale-while-revalidate. Penetration: requests for keys that exist nowhere, so every one reaches the DB; fix with negative caching and a Bloom filter. Avalanche: many keys expire together or the whole cache dies; fix with TTL jitter, replicas, layered caches and warm-up.

title: Redis Cluster slots
text: How does Redis Cluster decide which node owns a key, and what happens when a client asks the wrong node? The key space is 16,384 hash slots. A key's slot is CRC16 key mod 16384, and each master owns a range of slots. The client caches the slot map and talks to the owner directly. A wrong node replies MOVED slot host:port and the client refreshes its map. Adding a node moves slots, not every key.

title: stampede on a hot key
text: Diagnose and fix. Every day at about 10:00:00 the home page latency spikes from 40 ms to 6 s for 20 seconds; DB CPU hits 100%. The home page JSON is cached under home:v3 with EX 600 , written by a cache-aside loader. Traffic: 20,000 reads/s on that key. The loader runs a 900 ms aggregation query. Slow query log shows 15,000+ identical copies of the aggregation at 10:00:00. Red herring: a deploy happened at 09:50.

title: penetration and Bloom filters
text: What is happening and how do you stop it without breaking real users? An API GET /orders/{id} sees a sudden 40,000 req/s. The legitimate rate is 2,000/s.
