Cache hit ratio drops to 5%; the DB shows 38,000 lookups/s returning zero rows. Requests come from 300 IPs with sequential-looking random 12-digit IDs. There are 100M valid order IDs. Redis memory is flat. Red herring: a marketing email went out an hour ago.

title: mass expiry
text: What is wrong, and what would you change? Every night at 02:00 a job warms the cache with 1.5M product keys. Exactly one hour after 03:00 the DB CPU goes to 100% for about 4 minutes, with 5,000 reads/s of misses vs the usual 300/s. Loader code: Languages: Java, Kotlin tab void warm List<Product all { for Product p : all { redis.setex "p:" + p.id, 3600, serialize p ; // same TTL for all } } tab fun warm all: List<Product { all.forEach { redis.setex "p:${it.id}", 3600, serialize it } // same TTL for all }

title: Memcached vs Redis
text: What do you recommend and why? Is it a reversible decision? A team caches rendered HTML fragments avg 40 KB for a media site: 200 GB, 400,000 gets/s, no persistence needed, a plain get/set. They run on 32-core boxes. A second team wants a per-user rate limiter and a leaderboard on the same infrastructure. The CTO asks "Memcached or Redis?" and wants one answer.

title: hot keys and big keys
text: What are hot keys and big keys in a sharded Redis, why does adding nodes not fix them, and how do you find and mitigate each? A hot key gets more traffic than one node can serve; hashing pins it to one shard, so more nodes do not help. A big key is one huge value a list with millions of entries whose commands block the single-threaded event loop. For hot keys I add a local in-process cache or split the key into copies; for big keys I split into buckets and use UNLINK . I detect both with --hotkeys / --bigkeys and client metrics.

title: durability of Redis as cache
text: Can you treat Redis as a durable store? What can be lost on a crash or a failover? Not by default. RDB snapshots lose everything since the last snapshot. AOF with appendfsync everysec loses up to about one second; always loses almost nothing but is slow. Replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose acknowledged writes that did not reach the replica. Good for caches and ephemeral state; for data I cannot lose I write to a real DB first.

title: celebrity hot key
text: Mitigate now, and design the fix for good. A social app runs a 10-shard Redis Cluster at about 40,000 ops/s per shard. During a live event, one celebrity profile key profile:777 jumps to 300,000 reads/s. Shard 4 shows 100% CPU, p99 latency 900 ms, connected clients climbing; the other 9 shards are at 25% CPU. App servers: 60. The profile JSON is 3 KB and changes about once per hour. Red herring: network is fine shard 4 NIC at 40% utilisation .

title: single node to cluster
text: What is your plan and what do you change in the key design? You must move a 180 GB single-primary Redis about 90k ops/s, maxed at 85% CPU to Redis Cluster. Code uses MGET , a Lua script reserve stock.lua touching stock:{sku} and reserved:{sku} , and SUNIONSTORE across user sets. The test cluster returns: error CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot . The product owner wants zero downtime.

title: cache node loss
text: Walk me through the first 15 minutes and the long-term fix. At 19:12 one of 3 Redis cluster masters crashes and its replica is also lost both on the same rack . Slots 5461-10922 a third of the key space are empty after a restart at 19:14. App p99 goes 30 ms - 4 s; DB connection pool exhausted FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved ; error rate 18%. Metrics: DB QPS jumped from 800 to 9,000; the DB limit is about 3,000. Traffic is 30,000 reads/s.

title: single-flight lock
text: List the bugs and give a corrected version. You review a stampede fix. After deploy, once a week a key report:daily returns 503 for about 5 minutes until someone deletes lock:report:daily by hand. Code: Languages: Java, Kotlin tab String get String key { String v = redis.get key ; if v != null return v; if redis.setnx "lock:" + key, "1" == 1 { // acquire v = loadFromDb key ; // can take 20 s or throw redis.set key, v, 600 ; redis.del "lock:" + key ; // release return v; } while redis.get key == null { } // wait return redis.get key ; } tab fun get key: String : String { redis.get key ?.let { return it } if redis.setnx "lock:$key", "1" == 1L { // acquire val v = loadFromDb key // can take 20 s or throw redis.set key, v, 600 redis.del "lock:$key" // release return v } while redis.get key == null { } // wait return redis.get key !! }

title: queue vs log
text: What is the core difference between a message queue like SQS or RabbitMQ and a log like Kafka? A queue deletes a message once it is acknowledged, and each message goes to one consumer: it distributes jobs. A log is an append-only ordered file kept for a retention period; consumers only track an offset, so many independent readers can read the same data and replay by resetting the offset. Queue for "do this job once", log for "many systems need these events, and I may replay".

title: Kafka consumer groups
text: How do partitions and consumer groups work in Kafka, and what limits consumer parallelism? A topic is split into partitions, each an ordered log. In a consumer group, each partition is read by exactly one consumer, so parallelism is at most the number of partitions: 12 partitions allow 12 active consumers; a 13th sits idle. Different groups are independent and each receives every message. When members join or leave, a rebalance reassigns partitions.

title: backlog and drain math
text: Will a queue meet the 10-minute target? How big does the backlog get and when does it drain? What would you change if not? A flash sale produces 5,000 orders/s for 90 seconds, then drops to 300/s. The email/receipt worker pool can process 800 messages/s each 1 KB . Normal traffic is 300/s. The product owner wants the receipt email within 10 minutes of the order for 99% of orders. Queue is SQS Standard.

title: SQS visibility timeout
text: Diagnose and fix. A video-transcoding service on SQS Standard sees customers getting two copies of the same output and the bill for compute doubling. A transcode takes 30 s to 4 min. Queue settings: visibility timeout 30 s default , no DLQ. CloudWatch: ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible oscillates; NumberOfMessagesReceived is 1.8x NumberOfMessagesDeleted . Red herring: the producer sometimes retries on 5xx.

title: choosing a broker
text: What do you pick for each and what is the decision gravity? An e-commerce company wants two features: 1 "send receipt email" after an order, one consumer, retries and failure handling; 2 an "OrderPlaced" event that billing, inventory, search indexing, analytics and a fraud model all consume, where the fraud model is retrained monthly and must replay the last 30 days. Volume: 800 orders/s at peak. The team has no Kafka experience and runs on AWS. An architect proposes "one Kafka for everything".

title: partition ceiling and lag
text: Why did scaling fail and what is the right fix? Consumer group payments-indexer on topic payments 12 partitions has growing lag: 4.2M messages and rising 5,000/s. The team scaled the deployment from 8 to 20 pods; lag did not change. kafka-consumer-groups --describe : GROUP TOPIC PARTITION CURRENT-OFFSET LOG-END-OFFSET LAG CONSUMER-ID payments-indexer payments 0 9812000 9990000 178000 c-1 payments-indexer payments 1 9500100 9980000 479900 c-2 ... payments-indexer payments 11 9700500 9970000 269500 c-12 Pods 13 to 20 show 0 assigned partitions. Each message takes 4 ms to index.

title: ordering in Kafka
text: What ordering does Kafka guarantee, and how do you get per-entity order with retries and multiple consumers? Only within one partition. For per-entity order I use the entity ID as the message key so all its events hash to the same partition: partition = hash key mod numPartitions . On the producer I set enable.idempotence=true so retries cannot duplicate or reorder with max in-flight at most 5 . The consumer must process a partition sequentially; handing messages to a random thread pool breaks order.

title: delivery semantics and DLQs
text: Queues are "at-least-once". What does that mean for consumer design, and how do DLQs and idempotency fit in? At-least-once means a message is delivered one or more times: if I do not ack in time visibility timeout in SQS, no ack in RabbitMQ , it is redelivered. So handlers must be idempotent, for example by recording a processed ID or making the write conditional. Messages that fail repeatedly go to a dead-letter queue after maxReceiveCount so one poison message does not block or loop forever.

title: consumer reorders events
text: List every way order and delivery can break here, and fix it. Customers occasionally see an order as "Shipped" and then "Paid" in their timeline. Events are keyed by orderId on a 24-partition Kafka topic producer config acks=1 , retries=5, max.in.flight=5 , idempotence off . The consumer: Languages: Java, Kotlin tab ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool 16 ; while true { for var r : consumer.poll Duration.ofMillis 200 { pool.submit - timeline.apply r.value ; // parallel handling } consumer.commitSync ; // commits before tasks finish } tab val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool 16 while true { consumer.poll Duration.ofMillis 200 .forEach { r - pool.submit { timeline.apply r.value } // parallel handling } consumer.commitSync // commits before tasks finish }

title: hot partition from a bad key
text: Explain the lag pattern and redesign the key and capacity. A ride-hailing platform keys driver-location events by city . The topic has 60 partitions, 50,000 events/s total. Mumbai makes up 30% of events 15,000/s , Delhi 20%. Consumers handle 2,500 events/s each. Lag is zero for most partitions but 3 partitions show growing lag; one consumer is at 100% CPU, with the topic's max lag at 2.4M. Next quarter volume is 10x for a festival. Red herring: broker disk usage is balanced.

title: poison message and retry storm
text: Run the post-incident review: causes, timeline lessons, and the specific changes. Post-incident: at 03:10 a malformed message amount: null entered an SQS queue feeding the billing worker. The worker threw an exception before deleting it. Visibility timeout was 30 s, no DLQ. The message was received 11,000 times over 91 hours; each attempt wrote a partial row and sent an alert email. Worse, the exception path also released a DB lock late and the queue depth tripled as 40 workers kept failing. Metrics: error rate 100% for that message, 3% overall; DB lock waits up 6x.

title: RabbitMQ to Kafka migration
text: Should you move to Kafka, and how would you migrate safely? A logistics company runs RabbitMQ topic exchange, 6 queues, 25,000 msg/s peak, quorum queues for shipment events. Three new teams ETA model, billing audit, customer notifications want the same events, one needs a 14-day replay. The broker is at 70% CPU and adding queues for each consumer duplicated the publish work. Existing consumers rely on per-shipment order and use priorities on one queue. Zero downtime is required; the producers are 11 services.

title: Partition and segment layout
text: Kafka stores everything on disk, yet it does hundreds of MB/s. Why is it fast, and what exactly is a partition on the broker? A partition is a directory of append-only segment files; each message gets an increasing offset. It is fast because writes are sequential, the broker leans on the OS page cache instead of its own heap, messages are batched and compressed, and reads use zero-copy sendfile from page cache to the socket. Old data is removed by deleting whole segment files.

title: Replication, ISR and acks
text: Explain leader, followers and ISR. What do acks , min.insync.replicas and unclean.leader.election.enable do together, and what is the safe setup for payments? Each partition has one leader that serves reads and writes; followers copy from it. The ISR is the set of replicas that are caught up. With RF=3, min.insync.replicas=2 , producer acks=all and unclean election off, a write is confirmed only when at least 2 replicas have it, so I survive one broker loss with no data loss and still accept writes. If the ISR drops to 1, writes are rejected rather than stored unsafely.

title: Offset commits
text: Find the bug and fix it. A billing consumer uses defaults enable.auto.commit=true , 5 s interval . After a pod OOM-kill during a deploy, finance says 212 invoices were never generated, yet consumer lag is 0. Languages: Java, Kotlin tab while true { var records = consumer.poll Duration.ofMillis 500 ; for var r : records executor.submit - generateInvoice r.value ; // async } tab while true { val records = consumer.poll Duration.ofMillis 500 for r in records executor.submit { generateInvoice r.value } // async }

title: Cluster sizing
text: How many brokers and partitions? Show the math. A new ride-events pipeline: 30,000 msgs/s at 800 bytes, retention 3 days, RF=3, 4 consumer groups one is a 3 ms/msg enricher . Brokers have 6 TB usable disk and 10 GbE. Product wants 30% headroom.

title: Retention vs compaction
text: When would you choose cleanup.policy=compact over delete retention, and how do tombstones work? Delete policy removes old segments by age or size, right for event streams like clicks. Compaction keeps at least the latest record per key, right for changelogs and state such as user profiles or CDC. A tombstone is a key with a null value that marks deletion; it is itself removed after delete.retention.ms .

title: Offsets and rebalance
text: Diagnose and fix. An image-resize consumer group 8 consumers, 16 partitions shows constant rebalancing. Logs: WARN Member consumer-7 sending LeaveGroup because consumer poll timeout has expired max.poll.interval.ms=10000 INFO Revoking previously assigned partitions resize-3 INFO Re- joining group ERROR CommitFailedException: group has already rebalanced max.poll.records is 500 default . Each image takes 80 ms. Lag keeps growing despite CPU being only 30%. Brokers look healthy.

title: ISR shrink
text: What do you do, and what is going on? A payments topic RF=3, min.insync.replicas=2 , producers acks=all at 12k msgs/s. At 14:02 producers log NotEnoughReplicasException ; checkout error rate hits 40%. Metrics: UnderReplicatedPartitions: 0 - 118 ISR size payments- : 3 - 1 on 118 partitions broker-2: disk await 450 ms, CPU 20% broker-3: network OK, GC pause 9 s at 14:01 A teammate proposes setting min.insync.replicas=1 right now.

title: Partition count and ordering
text: How do you choose the number of partitions for a topic, and what happens if you need to change it later? I derive it from the target throughput divided by what one consumer handles, then add headroom, rather than from broker count. Partitions can be increased but never decreased, and increasing changes the key-to-partition mapping so ordering per key is broken across the change. I start moderately say 12 or 24 and grow deliberately.

title: Page cache and replay
text: Explain and fix. Cluster: 6 brokers, 64 GB RAM each 16 GB heap , 50 MB/s ingest. At 10:15 a data-science team starts a backfill reading a topic from 3 days ago at full speed. Immediately, p99 produce latency jumps from 8 ms to 400 ms and real-time consumers show lag rising. Metrics: broker CPU: 25% network: 40% disk read IOPS: 300 - 9,000 on broker-1,4 page cache hit ratio node exporter : 98% - 61% GC: normal

title: Retention vs lag
text: What happened and how should retention and consumer config be set? A clickstream topic has 1-hour retention to save disk 100 MB/s ingest, RF=3 . The downstream consumer is down for a 3-hour outage after a bad release. When it recovers, it logs OffsetOutOfRangeException and, because auto.offset.reset=latest , jumps to the end. Analytics later shows a 2-hour hole. Disk use was 8% so nobody objected to longer retention.

title: Compacted topic design
text: What do you ask, and what do you propose? Product says: "New services must start with every customer's current profile, and when a customer deletes their account we must stop serving their data." There are 4M customers, about 20 updates each per year, 2 KB per record. The architect proposes a delete-retention topic with 365 days.

title: Partition growth under live traffic
text: Plan the migration. The keyed orders topic key=orderId, 12 partitions, 20 MB/s is saturating its 12 consumers each at 95% CPU . You must go to 48 partitions with zero downtime. Order events for the same order must stay in order CREATED, PAID, SHIPPED . Peak traffic is in 3 hours.

title: Stream vs batch
text: What is stream processing, how does it differ from a nightly batch job, and when would you NOT use it? Stream processing computes results continuously as events arrive, so a fraud score can be ready in 200 ms or a dashboard can update every few seconds. Batch waits and processes a bounded chunk, like yesterday's data. I use streaming when the value of the result decays fast, and batch when an hourly or daily result is enough, because streaming adds state, checkpoints and 24/7 operations.

title: Windows
text: Explain tumbling, sliding and session windows. Which would you use for "orders per minute", "rolling 5-minute average updated every minute" and "user visit length"? Tumbling windows are fixed and non-overlapping, so "orders per minute". Sliding windows have a fixed size but move by a smaller step, so each event lands in several windows: the rolling 5-minute average every minute. Session windows close after a gap of inactivity, so their length varies per user: "visit length".

title: Choosing a window
text: What do you ask, and what do you build? A PM says: "Show me how many users are active right now." The product has 2M daily users and 8,000 events/s at peak. Events carry a user id and an event timestamp.

title: Event time and watermarks
text: What is the difference between event time and processing time, and what is a watermark? How do you handle late events? Event time is when the thing happened the phone's timestamp ; processing time is when my system saw it. A watermark is the processor's claim that no events older than T will arrive, normally max event time seen - allowed bound . When it passes the end of a window, the window fires. The bound trades latency against completeness, and late events are dropped, sent to a side output or applied as an update with allowed lateness.

title: Consumer lag math
text: How much time do you have, and what do you do? Pager: "orders-consumer lag 2.1M". Producers write 10,000 msg/s and consumers handle 6,000 msg/s since a deploy 30 minutes ago. Topic retention is 1 hour. The DB team says the DB is healthy. consumer-group orders-cg PARTITION CURRENT-OFFSET LOG-END-OFFSET LAG 0 81,203,110 81,950,004 746,894 1 80,000,515 80,200,100 199,585 ... Lag is uneven across partitions.

title: Poison messages
text: Fix it now and design it properly. At 03:12 the orders consumer stops making progress: lag grows 3,000/s on partition 5 only, other partitions are fine. Logs: ERROR OrderHandler - Failed offset=8421 partition=5: JsonParseException: Unexpected character '<' INFO Retrying offset=8421 attempt 1412 The handler has while true retry on any exception.

title: Sliding window cost
text: Will it survive 10x? What do you change? A Flink job computes a per-user "events in the last 10 minutes" using a sliding window 10 min / 1 s step at 5,000 events/s. It works at present, but traffic will grow 10x for a campaign. Heap use is already 70% and checkpoint time is 40 s.

title: Backpressure
text: What is backpressure? Compare how it works with a Kafka consumer versus inside a Flink job, and what you do when lag keeps rising. Backpressure is a slow downstream stage forcing upstream to slow down. Kafka never pushes back on producers: the log is the buffer, so lag simply grows until retention deletes unread data. Inside Flink, bounded network buffers propagate backpressure upstream to the source, which then reads Kafka more slowly. When lag rises, I check whether it is a burst or a trend, scale consumers to the partition count, fix the slow handler batch, async I/O , then add partitions or shed low-value work.

title: Idle partition watermark
text: Why are no windows firing, and how do you fix and prevent it? A Flink job windows per minute over a topic with 12 partitions and 4,000 events/s. After a regional rollout at 02:00, output windows freeze at 01:58 for 25 minutes although events keep flowing. No errors. Partition stats: partition 0..10: 360 events/s each partition 11 : 0 events/s since 01:58 producer for that shard stopped checkpoint OK, backpressure OK, lag normal

title: Late data
text: Critique and propose a design. A mobile app emits events; 98% arrive within 5 s, 99.9% within 3 minutes, a tail up to 6 hours offline users . Finance needs hourly revenue by region, and the live dashboard needs 1-minute freshness. The team sets a 6-hour watermark delay "to be correct".

title: Retry topics and ordering
text: Redesign the retry path. A notification consumer calls a flaky SMS vendor 3% of calls fail transiently, vendor outages of 10 minutes happen . Volume: 2,000 msg/s. Currently: 5 immediate retries then crash. During the last outage all consumers crash-looped and caused a retry storm on the vendor when it recovered: 12:04 vendor 503 - consumers retry 5x with no delay - 10,000 calls/s 12:05 consumers crash, restart, reprocess same batch 12:15 vendor recovers, sees 40,000 calls/s, rate limits 429

title: Lag and cost
text: How do you serve 96,000 msg/s without 48 consumers or repartitioning? A topic has 24 partitions, 24 consumers each 4 vCPU, 8 GB , handling 48,000 msg/s; each message does one DB lookup 4 ms and one HTTP call 6 ms . Peak lag stays at 0 but the cloud bill is high and CPU is 15%. Next quarter volume doubles, and the topic cannot exceed 24 partitions without a migration.

title: Why duplicates happen
text: Why can't a message system guarantee that a message is delivered exactly once? Where exactly do duplicates come from? Networks lose packets and acknowledgements, and processes crash between doing the work and telling anyone. The sender cannot distinguish "the message was lost" from "the ack was lost" the Two Generals problem . So a reliable system retries, and a retry after a lost ack duplicates the work. The key crash window is after the side effect and before the commit/ack.

title: Delivery guarantees
text: Define at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once. How do offset commits map to each, and which do you default to? At-most-once: commit first, then process; a crash loses messages but never duplicates. At-least-once: process, then commit; a crash causes redelivery, so duplicates are possible but loss is not. Exactly-once is not achievable as pure delivery; I achieve it as an effect by combining at-least-once with idempotent or transactional processing. My default is at-least-once with idempotent consumers.

title: Choosing a guarantee
text: Choose a guarantee for each and push back on the global setting. Three consumers on one platform: 1 GPS pings from 1M scooters every 2 s for a live map; 2 a "like" counter; 3 wallet transfers between users. An engineer wants a single global setting: "exactly-once everywhere, it is the safest".

title: Idempotency keys
text: How do you design an idempotent endpoint or consumer using an idempotency key? What are the pitfalls? The client generates a unique key per intended action and reuses it on every retry. The server stores the key with a unique constraint, in the same transaction as the side effect. A repeat key returns the stored result without redoing the work. Keys expire after a window longer than the worst redelivery delay.

title: Dedup race
text: What are the bugs and how do you fix them? Consumers are idempotent "by design" yet customers occasionally receive two refunds. Two consumers partition rebalance during a deploy process the same refund event concurrently. Languages: Java, Kotlin tab void onRefund RefundEvent e { if !db.exists "processed", e.id { // 1. check paymentApi.refund e.orderId , e.amount ; // 2. side effect db.insert "processed", e.id ; // 3. record } } tab fun onRefund e: RefundEvent { if !db.exists "processed", e.id { // 1. check paymentApi.refund e.orderId, e.amount // 2. side effect db.insert "processed", e.id // 3. record } }

title: Kafka EOS boundary
text: What went wrong and what is the right design? A Kafka Streams job reads orders , enriches, writes order totals , and also calls an email vendor and updates a MySQL table. The architect writes in the design doc: " processing.guarantee=exactly once v2 , so every email is sent exactly once". After a broker failover, a few customers got two confirmation emails and a MySQL counter is off by 17.

title: Kafka transactions and idempotent producer
text: How do the Kafka idempotent producer and transactions work, and what exactly do they guarantee? With enable.idempotence=true each producer gets a producer ID and per-partition sequence numbers, so the broker drops duplicates caused by retries and keeps order. Transactions transactional.id let me atomically write to several partitions and commit consumer offsets together; consumers with isolation.level=read committed see only committed data. Together they give exactly-once for consume-process-produce inside Kafka only; external side effects are not covered.

title: Dedup window
text: Root cause, fix, and how do you clean up? A webhook receiver dedups events in a table with a 5-minute TTL on event id copied from an SQS FIFO setup . A partner's system had an outage; when it recovered it replayed events from the last 6 hours. Result: 9,300 orders created twice. Logs: INSERT processed event id=evt 7731 ok at 09:02 ... INSERT processed event id=evt 7731 ok at 14:41 -- key already expired

title: Double charge incident
text: Write the review: causes, contributing factors, fixes. Postmortem: 412 customers were debited twice in 90 minutes. Timeline: 11:03 deploy of payment-consumer v52 rolling 11:04 consumers rebalance; max.poll.interval.ms=30000; batch processing takes 45 s 11:05 consumer-3 evicted; its batch reassigned to consumer-5 while consumer-3 still running 11:05 both consumers call the ledger: debit applied twice 11:40 offset commits fail: CommitFailedException Handler: debit account, amt , then commitSync .

title: Dedup store choice
text: Evaluate the design and propose an alternative. A team proposes: "Check Redis SETNX msg:{id} first; if it was set, skip. Then write to Postgres." Throughput is 5,000 msg/s; they say Redis is faster than a DB unique key. Last month a Redis failover happened, and a handful of orders went missing while others duplicated.

title: Dedup table growth
text: Why is it slow and how do you fix it for 10x? A processed messages table msg id UUID PK, result JSONB averaging 400 B holds 90 days of keys at 20M msgs/day. Inserts have slowed from 1 ms to 25 ms, autovacuum is constantly running and the table is 900 GB. Traffic will grow to 200M/day. Max replay horizon is 3 days.

title: Safe consumer review
text: List every problem and show the corrected version. Code review of a consumer for an order-fulfilment service 1,000 msg/s, 0.1% duplicates expected : Languages: Java, Kotlin tab void onMessage ConsumerRecord<String, Event r { ack r ; // A try var tx = db.begin { applyBusinessLogic r.value , tx ; // B tx.commit ; } catch Exception e { log.error "failed", e ; // C } } tab fun onMessage r: ConsumerRecord<String, Event { ack r // A try { db.begin .use { tx - applyBusinessLogic r.value , tx // B tx.commit } } catch e: Exception { log.error "failed", e // C } }

title: Dual writes
text: What is the dual-write problem, and why can't you just retry the publish? Saving to the database and publishing to a broker are two separate systems with no shared transaction, so one can succeed while the other fails. If the DB write succeeds and the publish fails, downstream never hears about the order; reverse the order and a crash leaves an event for data that was never saved. Retrying in the same process does not help if the process dies, because nobody remembers to retry.

title: Transactional outbox
text: How does the transactional outbox pattern work, what delivery guarantee does it give, and what are its limits? I write the business row and an outbox row in the same local DB transaction, so they commit or roll back together. A separate relay a polling publisher or CDC reads the outbox and publishes to the broker. Publishing is at-least-once because the relay may crash after publishing and before marking the row, so consumers must dedup using the outbox id.

title: Fix a dual write
text: What are the bugs and what do you change? A checkout service occasionally has orders in the DB with no OrderPlaced event, so inventory is never reserved. Broker was healthy during most failures; a few coincided with pod restarts. Languages: Java, Kotlin tab @Transactional public void placeOrder Order o { orderRepo.save o ; kafka.send "orders", o.id , toEvent o ; // fire-and-forget } tab @Transactional fun placeOrder o: Order { orderRepo.save o kafka.send "orders", o.id, toEvent o // fire-and-forget }

title: CDC
text: What is change data capture, how does Debezium do it, and what operational risks does it carry? CDC turns the database's commit log Postgres WAL, MySQL binlog into a stream of row-change events, with low load on the DB. Debezium reads the log, publishes one topic per table to Kafka, and downstream consumers keep search, caches or a warehouse in sync or act as the outbox relay. The main risk is an abandoned replication slot, which makes Postgres retain WAL until the disk fills.

title: Polling relay at scale
text: What do you do? A polling outbox relay single instance, 100 ms poll, batch 100 works at 300 events/s. Marketing plans a 10x event; expected 3,000/s. Metrics at 300/s: relay: 3 polls/s x 100 = max 300 events/s batch-bound outbox backlog: 0 DB CPU due to polling: 8% At 1,000/s in a load test the backlog grows by 700/s.

title: Choreography vs orchestration
text: Would you change the coordination style, and how do you handle failure? Order flow: Order, Inventory, Payment, Shipping, Notification services. Currently choreographed with events. Problems: nobody can answer "where is order 8812?"; adding a fraud check needed changes in 3 services; failures leave stuck PENDING orders about 0.3% = 150/day at 50k orders/day .

title: Sagas and durable workflows
text: How does a durable workflow engine Temporal or Step Functions style survive crashes and week-long waits, and what rules must your code follow? The engine records every step in an event history. After a crash or a deploy it replays the workflow code deterministically against that history to rebuild state, skipping activities already completed. So workflow code must be deterministic no random, wall clock or direct I/O; use the workflow APIs , and activities have at-least-once execution, so they must be idempotent. Timers are durable, so a 7-day sleep survives restarts.

title: Replication slot lag
text: What do you do in the next hour, and how do you prevent it? Sunday 04:10 pager: primary Postgres disk at 94% 2 TB volume . Application traffic is normal. Findings: SELECT slot name, active, pg size pretty pg wal lsn diff pg current wal lsn , restart lsn FROM pg replication slots; slot name active retained debezium orders f 1.4 TB old analytics test f 220 GB The Debezium connector crashed Friday evening after a schema change; nobody was paged because Kafka lag alerts looked fine no new messages .

title: Saga compensation
text: What is wrong with the saga design and how do you fix it? A travel saga: book flight, book hotel, book car. The car service was down 20 minutes. The orchestrator compensated hotel then flight, but the flight cancellation endpoint timed out; the orchestrator logged the error and marked the saga FAILED. Customers kept flight tickets they were never charged for in the final state, while the airline charged cancellation fees on a different subset. Support got 300 tickets. saga 77a1: bookFlight OK, bookHotel OK, bookCar FAIL cancelHotel OK, cancelFlight TIMEOUT - state=FAILED no retry

title: Workflow versioning
text: Mitigate and explain how to deploy such changes properly. A Temporal-style OnboardingWorkflow has 40,000 in-flight executions many waiting on a 3-day timer . A deploy inserts a new activity runFraudCheck between createAccount and sendWelcome , and replaces a UUID.randomUUID call with System.currentTimeMillis . After deploy: ERROR WorkflowTaskFailure: NonDeterministicException: history event 7 ActivityTaskScheduled sendWelcome != command ScheduleActivity runFraudCheck tasks failing: 38,900, workflow stuck, retried every 10 s

title: Outbox migration
text: Plan the migration. A monolith writes orders to MySQL and calls kafka.send afterwards dual write . Reconciliation shows 0.05% of 400,000 daily orders 200 lack events. You must adopt the outbox with zero downtime and no duplicated downstream effects. Consumers are not all idempotent yet; 12 teams consume orders .

title: Outbox ordering
text: Explain, fix, and say what ordering you can actually promise. Outbox at 20,000 events/s with 4 relay instances FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED , batch 500 . Consumers report that for some orders OrderShipped arrives before OrderPaid . Outbox ids are auto-increment. Another team insists "ids are monotonic so order is guaranteed". Observed: tx A paid : outbox id 9,001 inserted at 10:00:00.001, commits 10:00:00.250 tx B shipped : outbox id 9,002 inserted at 10:00:00.010, commits 10:00:00.040 relay 1 reads at 10:00:00.100: sees id 9,002 committed , not 9,001 not yet

title: Why wall clocks cannot order events
text: Two services on different machines both stamp their writes with now . Why can't I just sort by those timestamps to know which write came first? Every machine's clock drifts and is only corrected approximately by NTP, so two clocks can disagree by milliseconds to hundreds of milliseconds. If two writes are closer together than that error, the timestamp order can be the opposite of the real order. For ordering across machines I use causal order logical clocks , a single sequencer, or clocks with a bounded error, not raw wall-clock time.

title: Wall vs monotonic clock
text: What is the difference between a wall clock and a monotonic clock, and which one do I use to measure a timeout? A wall clock tells the date and time and can jump forwards or backwards when NTP steps it or an admin changes it. A monotonic clock only counts elapsed time and never goes back, but its absolute value means nothing and cannot be compared across machines. I use monotonic for durations, timeouts and rate limits, wall clock only when I need a calendar time.

title: Clock skew and last-write-wins
text: Find the cause, say how you would confirm it and what you would change. A user-profile service runs on a Cassandra-like store with last-write-wins by coordinator timestamp, 6 nodes, about 3,000 writes/s. Support reports that about 20 users per day see their "display name" revert to an older value minutes after they changed it. The app has no error logs. Two clients web and mobile sometimes update the same profile within a few hundred ms of each other. Dashboards show CPU 30% and replication healthy. chronyc tracking on one node shows System time: 0.180 seconds fast of NTP time .

title: Monotonic time for leases
text: What is the bug, what exactly happened in the incident, and how do you fix it? A cache entry and a worker lease are implemented as below. Ops see that after a maintenance window where NTP stepped the clock back by 30 s, some cache entries lived about 30 s too long and one worker kept running a job after its lease should have expired. Lease is 20 s. Languages: Java, Kotlin tab class Lease { private final long expiresAt; // epoch millis Lease long ttlMs { this.expiresAt = System.currentTimeMillis + ttlMs; } boolean isValid { return System.currentTimeMillis < expiresAt; } } tab class Lease ttlMs: Long { private val expiresAt = System.currentTimeMillis + ttlMs // epoch millis fun isValid = System.currentTimeMillis < expiresAt }

title: Lamport vs vector clocks
text: What can a vector clock tell me that a Lamport clock cannot, and what does it cost? A Lamport timestamp guarantees that if A happened-before B then L A < L B , but the reverse does not hold, so it cannot tell "A caused B" from "A and B were concurrent". A vector clock keeps one counter per node, so comparing two vectors says before, after or concurrent. The cost is O N size per timestamp, and detection only: the application still has to merge conflicts.

title: Ordering with a single authority
text: How do you proceed? Assume the interviewer wants to see you handle the ambiguity. Product says: "Messages in a chat must always show in the right order." The chat has 2M DAU, about 15,000 messages/s at peak, 1:1 and group conversations up to 500 members, multi-region US, EU . The first design stamps each message with the sender's phone clock and sorts by it. Beta users see replies appear above the messages they reply to.

title: Vector clocks vs LWW
text: Which do you choose and why? State the decision gravity. You own a shopping-cart service on a Dynamo-style store, 3 replicas, 40,000 carts updated per minute at peak. Customers on phone and laptop sometimes edit the same cart within seconds while a network blip separates two replicas. Option A: last-write-wins by timestamp current . Option B: vector clocks that return siblings, with the app merging by union of items. Complaints: "I removed an item and it came back" and "my new item vanished".

title: HLC and external consistency
text: Explain a hybrid logical clock. Does it give external consistency like Spanner's TrueTime? Why or why not? An HLC timestamp is l, c : l is the max physical time this node has seen and c is a counter for events with the same l . It fits in 64 bits, tracks real time within the clock skew, and respects causality: if A happened-before B then HLC A < HLC B . It does not give external consistency, because there is no bounded uncertainty and no commit wait; two non-causally-related transactions can be ordered differently from real time. TrueTime gets that by exposing an interval and waiting it out.

title: Snowflake IDs and clock regression
text: Explain why IDs collided, how many, and what you change. Order IDs come from a Snowflake-style generator: 41 bits ms timestamp, 10 bits worker ID, 12 bits sequence. After an NTP step the clock on worker 17 jumped back 2.3 s. For the next 2.3 s, about 600 orders/s were created. Afterwards the DB shows duplicate key value violates unique constraint "orders pkey" errors and a few orders were silently attached to the wrong customer because an upsert-by-ID path was used. The generator code is ts = now ; if ts == last { seq = seq+1 & 4095 } else { seq = 0 }; last = ts .

title: TrueTime vs timestamp oracle
text: Compare the two on latency, throughput, failure and decision gravity. Which do you pick? You are designing a globally distributed ledger database: 3 regions US-East, EU, AP , 5,000 read-write commits/s, p50 commit budget 60 ms, requirement "if transaction T1 commits before T2 starts, T2 must see T1" external consistency . Option A: bounded-uncertainty clocks GPS/atomic or cloud time sync with a published bound, assume uncertainty 7 ms with commit wait. Option B: a single timestamp oracle in US-East handing out increasing timestamps; EU and AP are about 80 ms and 150 ms RTT from it illustrative .

title: NTP, leap smear and HLC offset
text: Why are nodes dying, what do you do right now, and how do you prevent it? A 9-node HLC-based SQL database max clock offset configured at 500 ms loses 3 nodes in 10 minutes, each exiting with clock synchronization error: this node is more than 500ms away from at least half of the known nodes . Nodes 1-6 sync to the cloud provider's NTP leap-smearing and nodes 7-9 were recently added from an image configured with pool.ntp.org no smear . A leap second is being smeared over the next 24 hours. chronyc tracking on node 8 shows Last offset: -0.31 s and growing.

title: Migrating from LWW to HLC
text: Design the migration and name the risks. A metadata service stores 800M records with writer-supplied wall-clock timestamps LWW . Lost updates under skew are a recurring incident. You must move to HLC timestamps with no downtime. 60 app servers write at about 25,000 writes/s. Old readers/writers some mobile clients on old app versions, up to 3 months old still send wall-clock millis. The column is an int64 of epoch millis.

title: What consensus solves
text: What problem does consensus solve, and what does the FLP result say about it? Consensus lets several machines agree on one value, or one ordered log of values, even if some crash and messages are delayed. It needs agreement no two decide differently , validity the value was proposed and termination. FLP proves no deterministic algorithm can guarantee all three in a fully asynchronous network with one possible crash, so Raft and Paxos always keep safety and give up guaranteed liveness: they may stall during chaos but never decide wrongly.

title: Quorums and cluster size
text: Why do consensus clusters use majority quorums and odd sizes? Why is a 4-node cluster no better than 3? A majority is floor N/2 +1 . Any two majorities share at least one node, so a new decision always overlaps the previous one and learns about it; that overlap is the safety argument. 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure, 4 also tolerate only 1 majority is 3 , so the fourth node adds cost and write latency but no tolerance. I use 3 or 5 nodes spread across 3 failure domains.

title: Quorum placement
text: Explain, restore service, and fix the design. Your 3-node etcd cluster runs in two availability zones: etcd-1 and etcd-2 in zone A, etcd-3 in zone B. At 14:02 zone A loses power. Kubernetes API calls start failing: etcdserver: request timed out . From etcd-3: etcdctl endpoint health returns unhealthy: failed to commit proposal: context deadline exceeded . Workloads already running on nodes in zone B keep serving traffic. Management asks: "we had a replica in zone B, why is the cluster down?"

title: Split brain
text: What happens in the next cut, and what would you ask and propose? A team says: "We have a Postgres primary and one standby in two datacenters. We want automatic failover: if the standby sees no heartbeat from the primary for 10 s it promotes itself. Management wants zero data loss and no downtime." Last quarter a network cut lasting 40 s between the datacenters happened; the primary was healthy and serving clients in DC1 the whole time.

title: Raft leader election
text: Walk me through a Raft leader election after the leader dies. Why are election timeouts randomized, and why is there a log check on votes? A follower that hears no heartbeat for its election timeout increments its term, votes for itself and sends RequestVote term, lastLogIndex, lastLogTerm . A peer votes yes if the term is at least its own, it has not voted this term, and the candidate's log is at least as up to date. A majority makes it leader and it sends heartbeats immediately. Timeouts are randomized so nodes do not all become candidates together and split the votes. The log check guarantees a leader already holds every committed entry.

title: Leader flapping
text: Diagnose and fix. Which signals are red herrings? A 3-node etcd cluster backing a Kubernetes cluster shows API timeouts every few minutes. etcd server leader changes seen total rose by 14 in the last hour. Logs: etcdserver: failed to send out heartbeat on time exceeded the 100ms timeout for 412ms and slow fdatasync took 1.3s . etcd disk wal fsync duration seconds p99 is 180 ms. CPU on nodes is 20%. A nightly backup job uploads a 4 GB file from the same volume. Heartbeat is 100 ms and election timeout 1000 ms.

title: Raft vote handling
text: List the bugs and the corrected logic. A teammate wrote a toy Raft RequestVote handler. In a chaos test, two nodes both won term 7, and a node that crashed and restarted voted for a second candidate in the same term. Find every bug. Languages: Java, Kotlin tab synchronized boolean handleRequestVote long term, String candidateId, long lastLogIndex, long lastLogTerm { if term < currentTerm return false; if votedFor == null { votedFor = candidateId; // in memory only return true; } return false; } tab @Synchronized fun handleRequestVote term: Long, candidateId: String, lastLogIndex: Long, lastLogTerm: Long : Boolean { if term < currentTerm return false if votedFor == null { votedFor = candidateId // in memory only return true } return false }

title: Linearizable reads in Raft
text: Why can't a Raft leader just answer reads from its local state? How do ReadIndex and leader leases fix it, and what does each cost? A leader may have been deposed by a partition and not know it, so a local read can return stale data and violate linearizability. ReadIndex records the commit index, confirms leadership with a heartbeat round to a majority, waits until that index is applied, then reads: one network round trip but no log write. A leader lease skips the round by trusting a time-bounded lease, which is faster but depends on bounded clock drift. Follower or serializable reads are fastest but may be stale.

title: Membership change
text: Is that plan safe? Give the safe plan and the risks. Your 3-node etcd cluster nodes e1, e2, e3, e1 is leader serves 4,000 writes/s. You are replacing e2's failing disk and growing to 5 nodes add e4 and e5 in the same maintenance, without downtime. A colleague proposes: "add e4 and e5 simultaneously with member add , then remove e2." Current DB size is 1.4 GB.

title: Scaling a Raft group
text: Evaluate both, show the math, and say what happens with the second region. A metadata service runs one 3-node Raft group same region, RTT 0.5 ms, SSD fsync 2 ms at 3,000 writes/s, p99 commit 9 ms. Product expects 10x growth to 30,000 writes/s and a second region with 80 ms RTT to the existing one. Proposal 1: "add 4 more nodes to the group for capacity." Proposal 2: shard into many Raft groups. Data is 400 GB.

title: Raft vs alternatives, multi-region
text: Which do you recommend? Reason about the latency of a write issued in AP. You will build a configuration store used by services in three regions US 80 ms from EU, 150 ms from AP, 200 ms EU to AP; illustrative . It stores 50 MB of config, 200 writes/s, strongly consistent reads wanted. The team debates: A embed a Raft library in the service, 5 voters 2/2/1; B run etcd or Consul as a managed dependency; C a leaderless protocol like EPaxos; D Byzantine-tolerant PBFT "for safety".

title: etcd space quota and compaction
text: Write the post-incident review: timeline of actions to recover, root cause, and action items. At 03:10 a Kubernetes cluster stopped accepting changes: etcdserver: mvcc: database space exceeded . Existing pods kept running. etcdctl alarm list shows memberID:... alarm:NOSPACE . etcdctl endpoint status shows DB size 2.1 GB quota 2 GB, default; verify for your version , 3 members, healthy leader. Disk free is 70%. Over the last week DB size rose from 400 MB to 2.1 GB. Root cause found later: a controller rewrote a status field of 50,000 objects every second after a bug.

title: Do I need a lock
text: When would you use a distributed lock, and what would you try first instead? A distributed lock makes sure only one process across many machines does a job at a time. First I ask whether I need one: a unique constraint or conditional update, an idempotent operation, a single consumer per partition, or optimistic concurrency often do the job. Then I ask why I lock: for efficiency avoid duplicate work; a failure only wastes CPU, so a simple Redis lock is fine or for correctness two holders corrupt data; then I need a consensus-backed lock with fencing .

title: Correct Redis lock
text: How do you implement a safe single-instance Redis lock, and where does it still fail? Acquire with one atomic command, SET lock:billing <random-id NX PX 30000 : NX sets only if absent, PX is the TTL. Release with a Lua script that deletes the key only if its value still equals my random id, so I never delete someone else's lock. It still fails when Redis fails over asynchronously the lock write may not have reached the replica , when the holder pauses past the TTL, and because there is no fencing token. So it is fine for efficiency, not for correctness.

title: Avoiding locks
text: How do you approach this? Evaluate the lock and propose alternatives. Your service runs 20 pods. At 02:00 a cron in every pod sends a "daily digest" email to 1M users; the job takes about 10 minutes when run by one pod. Today users get up to 20 emails. A teammate proposes a Redis lock with a 15-minute TTL. You are told only: "make sure exactly one email per user per day."

title: Redis lock mistakes
text: List every bug and fix them. Operations notice that once a month the nightly billing job never runs again until someone deletes the lock key by hand, and twice the job ran concurrently on two hosts. The lock helper does this sequence shown as redis-cli commands : acquire redis-cli SETNX lock:billing 1 redis-cli EXPIRE lock:billing 30 ... run job that usually takes 20 s but sometimes 70 s ... release redis-cli DEL lock:billing

title: Paused lock holder
text: Explain what happened and fix it. A JVM service uses a lease lock TTL 30 s, renewed every 10 s around updating a customer's ledger file in object storage. During a nightly spike, duplicated and overwritten entries appear for about 15 customers. Log excerpt: 02:14:07.100 acquired lock cust-881 ttl=30s 02:14:09.800 gc pause 41.2 s G1 Full GC 02:14:38.000 other pod acquired lock cust-881 02:14:40.400 other pod wrote ledger cust-881 version=412 02:14:51.100 writing ledger cust-881 version=412 Heap is 28 GB on a 32 GB container; GC pause p99 is about 30 s at night. Lock service dashboards show no errors.

title: Fencing tokens
text: What is a fencing token, who generates it, who checks it, and why can't the lock service alone make a lock safe? A fencing token is a number that increases every time the lock is granted. The lock service issues it; the protected resource remembers the highest token it has seen and rejects any request with a lower one. A paused holder wakes up believing it holds the lock, but its token is old, so the resource refuses the write. The lock service alone cannot do this because it has no control over what the stale holder does after the lease expired; the check must live at the resource.

title: Choosing a lock service
text: Pick a mechanism for each use and justify, including failure behaviour. You need a lock for three different uses in one platform: 1 a nightly report generator duplicate runs just waste 5 minutes of CPU , 2 ensuring one worker at a time rebuilds a search index a double rebuild corrupts the index unless fenced , 3 a job queue where 50 workers each claim 10 jobs at a time from a Postgres jobs table at about 2,000 jobs/s. Available: Redis existing , etcd used by Kubernetes, not by your app , Postgres primary store .

title: ZooKeeper lock recipe
text: Describe the ZooKeeper distributed lock recipe. Why does each waiter watch only its predecessor, and how does etcd do the equivalent? Each client creates an ephemeral, sequential znode under /lock , such as /lock/node-0000042 . It lists the children; if its node has the lowest sequence number it holds the lock, otherwise it sets a watch on the node just before its own and waits. Watching only the predecessor means a release wakes exactly one waiter instead of all no thundering herd . The ephemeral node disappears when the session dies, so a crash frees the lock. etcd does this with leases and key creation revisions: lowest revision wins, attached to a lease.

title: Redis failover double holder
text: Explain the failure, how you contain the money impact now, and what the long-term design is. A payouts job takes a Redis lock SET payout:lock <id NX PX 60000 so only one worker issues settlement transfers. During a Redis maintenance failover primary to replica with async replication , two workers ran the payout concurrently for about 40 seconds. 37 merchants were paid twice, total about 52,000 in duplicate payouts. Redis logs show the old primary accepted SET 80 ms before it was demoted; the new primary had no such key. App logs: both workers logged lock acquired .

title: Leader election timing
text: Can you hit 3 s by changing the settings? Reason it through and give the options. A scheduler runs 3 replicas with Kubernetes-style leader election leaseDuration: 15s , renewDeadline: 10s , retryPeriod: 2s . Failover after a leader crash takes about 17 s of scheduling stall. Product now wants failover under 3 s. Observed on this service: JVM full-GC pauses up to 4 s at p99 on a busy day; API server lease store p99 latency 800 ms with occasional 3 s spikes.

title: Advisory locks and poolers
text: Explain exactly why this happened and fix it, both now and permanently. A singleton job takes SELECT pg try advisory lock 42 at start and pg advisory unlock 42 at end, behind PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode. After a deploy, the job runs once and then never again; try lock returns false everywhere. Postgres warnings in logs: WARNING: you don't own a lock of type ExclusiveLock . SELECT FROM pg locks WHERE locktype='advisory' shows objid=42 held by backend pid 9114 which is idle, and no application owns it. Connection count looks normal.

title: Fencing without resource support
text: Write the post-incident analysis and design the fix when the storage cannot check fencing tokens natively. A compaction service rewrites a table-manifest file in object storage under a leader lease etcd, 20 s TTL . In an incident, a leader paused for 70 s VM live migration , woke up and overwrote the manifest written by the new leader; 6 hours of compaction results were lost and queries returned stale file lists. The lock service logs are clean: the old leader's lease had expired and a new leader revision 5,210 was elected. The object store accepts plain PUTs; nobody reads tokens.

title: Three signals
text: What is the difference between monitoring and observability, and when do you reach for metrics, logs or traces? Monitoring tells me THAT something is wrong, for failure modes I predicted. Observability lets me ask new questions about a running system, using the data it emits, to find WHY, without shipping new code. Metrics are cheap aggregated numbers, good for alerting and dashboards. Logs are detailed events, good for the exact error. Traces follow one request across services, good for "where did the 800 ms go". I use them in that order: metric to detect, trace to locate, log to explain.

title: Percentiles and histograms
text: Why do we alert on p99 rather than the average, and why can you not average p99 values across servers? The average hides the tail. If 99 requests take 100 ms and one takes 10 s, the mean is 199 ms and looks fine while 1% of users wait 10 s. With a page making 20 calls, 1 - 0.99^20 is about 18% of page loads hit a p99 outlier. A percentile is a property of a whole distribution, so the mean of two servers' p99 is not the p99 of the combined traffic. I use histograms: each instance exports bucket counts, I sum the buckets across instances, then compute the quantile.

title: RED, USE, golden signals
text: Explain RED and USE. Which would you apply to a REST service and which to a database connection pool, and why is saturation the signal people skip? RED is for request-driven services: Rate, Errors, Duration. USE is for resources like CPU, disk, network and connection pools: Utilization, Saturation, Errors. Google's four golden signals are RED plus saturation. So RED on the REST service, USE on its pool. Saturation is the early warning because queueing makes latency explode before utilization hits 100%: waiting work threads blocked on a connection shows up in saturation while CPU still looks calm.

title: Cardinality
text: Explain what happened, how you stop the bleeding, and how you still let people debug one customer. A team adds a user id label to http requests total "to debug one customer". Before: services 50 x endpoints 40 x status 5 = 10,000 series. There are 2M daily active users. Two days later Prometheus memory goes from 8 GB to 40 GB, scrapes take 25 s of a 15 s interval, and the OOM killer restarts it every few hours. Dashboards time out. Your vendor-hosted equivalent would bill per active series.

title: Log pipeline cost
text: Do the capacity math and propose a plan that cuts cost by at least 70% without losing the ability to debug incidents. Platform has 100 pods emitting 50 lines/s each at 500 B. Logs go through Fluent Bit to Elasticsearch with 1 replica, hot retention 30 days. The monthly bill is 3x budget and queries are slow. Breakdown: 40% DEBUG, 45% INFO health-check and per-request lines, 15% WARN/ERROR. A security review also found a full email address and a bearer token in some lines.

title: Broken traces
text: Why are traces broken and why are rare errors missing? What do you change? Tracing is on for the API gateway, order-service and payment-service all OpenTelemetry auto-instrumented . Traces for checkout show gateway - order-service, but the Kafka consumer invoice-worker that sends the invoice appears as separate one-span traces with no parent. Also, inside order-service, spans created in a thread pool task are missing from the request trace. Head sampling is 1%, and "the rare payment timeout never shows up in tracing". Code in order-service Java : // request thread has the active span; executor and Kafka produce lose context executor.submit - inventoryClient.reserve orderId ; producer.send new ProducerRecord< "invoices", orderId, payload ; Languages: Java, Kotlin executor.submit { inventoryClient.reserve orderId } producer.send ProducerRecord "invoices", orderId, payload

title: Burn rate alerts
text: Explain multi-window, multi-burn-rate SLO alerting. Why is it better than "error rate 2% for 5 minutes"? An SLI measures quality, say the fraction of requests that succeed in under 300 ms. The SLO is the target, say 99.9% over 30 days, so the error budget is 0.1%. Burn rate is how fast I consume that budget relative to an even spend: burn 1 would exhaust it exactly at the end of the window, burn 14.4 would exhaust it in about 50 hours. I page when burn is 14.4 over both 1 hour and 5 minutes, page when burn is 6 over both 6 hours and 30 minutes, and ticket when it is 1 over 3 days. A fixed threshold either pages on trivial blips or misses a slow leak, and has no notion of how much budget is at stake.

title: Alert fatigue
text: Run the post-incident review for the alerting side and propose a redesign. On-call gets about 50 pages a week; the weekly review shows 45 are auto-resolved before anyone looks CPU 85% for 1 minute, a single pod restart, disk 80% . Last Tuesday a real disk-full on the payments DB host took checkout down for 40 minutes; the page was acknowledged after 18 minutes because it looked like the daily disk warning. Two engineers have asked to leave the rotation.

title: SLO budget math
text: Compute the damage, say which burn-rate alerts would have fired, and answer product. Checkout SLO: 99.9% of requests succeed in under 300 ms over 30 days. Traffic is 100 req/s average about 259M requests per month . At 14:00 a deploy raises the 5xx rate to 5% for 10 minutes before rollback. A batch job in the same window raised DB CPU to 80% possible red herring . Product asks: "do we still have budget to ship the big migration this month?"

title: Debugging with the three signals
text: Walk through the incident from alert to cause and say what you do. At 09:12 the checkout burn-rate alert pages. Facts: p99 went from 400 ms to 3.8 s; error ratio is 3%; traffic is normal at 1,200 rps; only region eu-west is affected; a deploy of pricing-service happened at 09:05; DB CPU is 40%. http request duration seconds p99{service="checkout",region="eu-west"} 3.8 http request duration seconds p99{service="checkout",region="us-east"} 0.41 trace 7f3a...: checkout 3.7s - pricing 3.4s - cache GET 3.3s timeout log: {"msg":"cache timeout","trace id":"7f3a...","host":"redis-eu-2","timeout ms":3000}

title: Ambiguous requirement
text: How do you respond and what is your plan for the first 90 days? A CTO says: "We keep finding out about outages from Twitter. Set up observability for our 60 microservices Kotlin on Kubernetes, a mobile app, Postgres, Kafka . Budget: 15% of the current commercial-vendor bill of about $40k/month." No further detail.

title: Observability that dies with the system
text: Redesign the stack so it survives this failure and meets the retention goal. Which choices are reversible? Prometheus, Grafana, Loki and Alertmanager all run in the same Kubernetes cluster as the product. During a control-plane incident the cluster lost networking for 25 minutes: apps degraded, dashboards unreachable, no pages sent, engineers debugged blind. Metrics retention is 15 days at full resolution; leadership also wants a year of history cheaply.

title: Deploy vs release
text: What is the difference between deploying code and releasing a feature, and why does it matter for risk? Deploy means the new binary is running on servers. Release means users can actually see the new behaviour. If I wrap new behaviour in a feature flag, I can deploy at 2pm on a Tuesday with the flag off, then release to 1%, 10%, 100% and turn it off in seconds if it breaks. Small batches plus separable release give a small blast radius and fast recovery.

title: Rolling updates
text: How does a Kubernetes rolling update work, and what must be true of the app for it to be zero-downtime? The Deployment replaces pods a few at a time, controlled by maxSurge and maxUnavailable. It starts new pods, waits for readiness, then kills old ones. For zero downtime I need a real readiness probe, graceful shutdown stop accepting, finish in-flight, a preStop sleep so the load balancer drains , and code and schema that work with old and new versions side by side.

title: Blue-green trade-offs
text: When would you choose blue-green over canary, and what does blue-green not protect you from? Blue-green gives an instant switch and instant rollback because the old environment stays warm, so I pick it when the flip must be atomic and the service is mostly stateless. It does not give gradual exposure, it needs double capacity during the window, and both colours share the same database, so schema changes must be compatible with both. Canary is better when I want a small blast radius and have good metrics.

title: Feature flag design
text: How would you design feature flag evaluation so that it is fast, consistent per user, and safe if the flag service is down? Evaluate locally in the SDK from a cached ruleset, not with a network call per check. Bucket by hash userId + flagName so a user's experience is stable as the percentage grows. Default off, and if the flag service is down use the last-known cached value or the safe default. Give every flag an owner and expiry so they are deleted.

title: Rolling update
text: Diagnose and fix without changing the deployment strategy. A checkout API runs 10 pods on Kubernetes. Every deploy produces a 20 to 40 second burst of 502 responses about 1.5% of requests at 3,000 req/s and then recovers. Error budget for the month is nearly gone. Deployment YAML: maxSurge: 25% , maxUnavailable: 25% , no readiness probe, terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30 , no preStop hook. Load balancer logs show 502s from the ingress with upstream prematurely closed connection . The app handles SIGTERM by calling System.exit 0 immediately. The team suspects "bad code in the new version".

title: Canary sizing
text: Is a blanket 1% canary right? How would you design canary gates per service? A video platform serves 100,000 req/s globally and 40 req/s on a niche admin API. The team wants "a 1% canary with a 10 minute bake" as company policy for both. Business tolerates about 0.1% error rate normally. A recent regression had a 2% error rate that nobody noticed on the admin API for hours. The canary comparison uses the long-running fleet as baseline.

title: Schema migration
text: List everything that will go wrong and rewrite the plan. You review this migration that will run automatically in the same deploy as the code change, on a Postgres 14 orders table with 300M rows doing 4,000 writes/s. The deploy renames status to state , and the new code only reads state . Rollout is a 10-pod rolling update. BEGIN; ALTER TABLE orders RENAME COLUMN status TO state; ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN archived boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false; CREATE INDEX idx orders state ON orders state ; ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT fk customer FOREIGN KEY customer id REFERENCES customers id ; COMMIT;

title: Rollback limits
text: Run the post-incident review: why did rollback make it worse, and what changes? At 14:05 a release of the orders service goes to 100% over 30 minutes. At 14:40 p99 latency rises and 3% of orders fail validation. On-call runs kubectl rollout undo at 14:45; pods revert, but errors rise to 8%. Findings: v2 started writing price cents as a new Avro field into a Kafka topic and changed the DB column price to numeric 12,2 using a one-step ALTER; v1 consumers throw on the new schema. v2 also sent 1,900 confirmation emails during the window. Rollback took 6 minutes to execute. Error budget is burned.

title: Blue-green cutover
text: What happened, and how would you redesign the cutover? An e-commerce site 50 pods, 4 vCPU each does blue-green on AWS with a Route 53 weighted DNS record TTL 60 s . At 10:00 the team flips 100% to green. By 10:03 green shows 2.5% errors and p99 of 4 s; they flip back at 10:04, but dashboards show blue still receiving only about 40% of traffic at 10:08 and green still receiving 60%. Green's cache hit rate is 12% against 96% on blue. Database CPU on the shared primary spiked from 30% to 85% at 10:01.

title: Flag kill switch
text: Design the kill switch. What do you ask first and what would you build? Product asks: "We want a big red button to disable the new recommendations carousel in the Android and iOS apps if it misbehaves." The backend is a flagged feature already. The mobile apps have 8M DAU, 40% on versions older than 4 weeks, and a store review takes 1 to 3 days. The flag service SDK is called per screen render. Last month the flag vendor had a 25 minute outage; apps crashed because the SDK blocked on startup.

title: Live migration
text: Plan the migration, and the numbers you would check. A MySQL 8 events table has 2.4 billion rows 1.8 TB , 6,000 writes/s, with a replica for reads. You must change user id INT to BIGINT because IDs will overflow in about 5 months. A plain ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY on a staging copy took 11 hours and rebuilt the table. Replica lag already hits 20 s at peak. The business allows no maintenance window.

title: Strategy choice
text: Choose strategies per system and defend the decision. How reversible is each choice? You own the release process for three systems: 1 a stateless pricing API at 20k req/s, 2 a rewrite of the recommendations engine that must be validated against real production behaviour before users see it, 3 a mobile banking app with 3M installs. Leadership wants "one deployment strategy to rule them all" to simplify the platform. Past incidents: bad config pushed to all clusters at once; a rewrite that passed tests but gave worse results in production.

title: Cascading failure
text: What is a cascading failure, and why is a slow dependency often worse than a dead one? A cascading failure is when one sick service makes its callers sick, which makes their callers sick. A dead dependency fails fast and frees the caller's thread. A slow one holds the thread, so callers run out of threads or connections, become slow themselves, and the whole chain collapses although only one service was unhealthy. Resilience patterns exist to cap how long and how much we wait.

title: Timeouts and deadlines
text: How do you choose a timeout for a downstream call, and what is deadline propagation? I set connect timeouts small 100 to 500 ms in a datacenter and the read timeout just above the dependency's observed p99.9, for example p99.9 = 300 ms gives 400 to 500 ms. On top I keep one overall deadline for the user request and pass the remaining budget downstream, so the next hop gets 800 ms left, not a fresh 2 s. That stops work nobody is waiting for.

title: Retries
text: Explain exponential backoff with jitter and why retries can make an outage worse. Retries help only for transient, idempotent failures. I use exponential backoff capped at some maximum, with full jitter sleep random between 0 and the current backoff so clients do not retry in sync, limit to 2 or 3 attempts, add a retry budget of about 10% of normal traffic, and retry at one layer only. Without these, three layers each retrying three times turn one request into 27 calls just when the dependency is weakest.

title: Circuit breaker
text: How does a circuit breaker work, and what makes a good configuration? It has three states. Closed: calls flow and failures are counted. Open: calls are rejected immediately for a cool-down such as 30 s. Half-open: a few trial calls are allowed; success closes it, failure re-opens it. I trip on failure rate say over 50% across the last 20 calls with at least 10 calls and on slow-call rate, one breaker per dependency, and I always pair it with a fallback and emit state-change metrics.

title: Retry storm
text: Explain the numbers and how you recover and prevent. A user service at normal 1,200 req/s depends on an inventory service. At 09:12 inventory briefly slows a 40 s GC pause . Afterwards inventory CPU stays at 100% and its request rate reads 9,800 req/s for 25 minutes even though user-facing traffic is flat at 1,200 req/s. Config: the mobile app retries 3 times with no delay; the API gateway retries 2 times on 5xx; the user service HTTP client retries 3 times with a fixed 100 ms delay. Inventory p99 is 6 s, caller timeout is 2 s.

title: Bulkhead sizing
text: Size the bulkheads with numbers, and describe the trade-off. A checkout service uses one shared thread pool of 200 for three dependencies: payments p99 120 ms, 300 req/s , recommendations p99 800 ms, 600 req/s and email p99 300 ms, 100 req/s . Last Friday recommendations hung and checkout failed for 18 minutes. You are asked to split the pool. Leadership wants "the minimum extra capacity".

title: Load shedding
text: What do you do now and how do you design for this? An API has capacity of 1,000 req/s autoscaler needs about 4 minutes to add pods . A marketing push brings 1,500 req/s for 20 minutes. Metrics during the first 5 minutes: CPU 100%, queue wait 9 s, p50 latency 11 s, error rate 0.5% but the success rate by users is dropping because clients time out at 3 s and retry. Goodput responses delivered within 3 s is about 60 req/s. The team proposes "just raise the autoscaler max".

title: Backpressure
text: Explain the failure and redesign for the 10,000 events/s case. An ingestion service reads events from an HTTP endpoint and puts them on an in-memory unbounded queue; 4 workers write to a database. Normal: 2,000 events/s in and out. After a partner migration inflow is 10,000 events/s while the DB handles 2,000/s. Heap is 4 GB; each event is 1 KB. Symptoms: heap grows 8 MB/s, GC time rises from 2% to 70%, p99 ingest latency is 40 s, then pods are OOM-killed and the queue contents are lost; the partner retries everything on connection errors.

title: Layering retries and timeouts
text: List the defects, estimate the worst-case behaviour and rewrite the call. Review this code for a service called by a mobile app with a 2 s user-facing budget. Traffic is 800 req/s; the pricing dependency has p99 of 300 ms normally and 5 s when degraded. public Price getPrice String sku { for int i = 0; i < 5; i++ { try { return pricingClient.get sku ; // client readTimeout = 10s, no breaker } catch Exception e { // retry immediately } } throw new PricingUnavailable ; } fun getPrice sku: String : Price { repeat 5 { try { return pricingClient.get sku } // readTimeout = 10s catch e: Exception { / retry immediately / } } throw PricingUnavailable }

title: Graceful degradation
text: Ask the right clarifying questions, then design what "never down" means, with numbers. The CTO says: "The product page must never be down." The page needs price, inventory, reviews, personalised recommendations and a promo banner, from five services each at 99.9% availability. Today the page is a single orchestrated call; any failure returns an error page. Availability measured: 99.5%. Fraud/auth is not involved in this page.

title: Breaker tuning
text: Why is the breaker not helping, and how would you reconfigure? A search service calls a ranking service through a Resilience4j breaker: slidingWindowSize: 10 , minimumNumberOfCalls: 5 , failureRateThreshold: 50 , waitDurationInOpenState: 2s , permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState: 1 . Traffic is 300 req/s. Logs over 3 minutes: state changes CLOSED - OPEN - HALF OPEN - OPEN about 40 times; ranking CPU stays at 95%; p99 on search is 1.8 s with intermittent errors. A single bad host in ranking 1 of 12 returns errors 100% of the time. The breaker is one instance for the whole ranking cluster.

title: Metastable failure
text: Lead the review: why did the incident outlast its trigger, and what are the action items? Timeline from a post-incident document: 20:00 a 2-minute traffic spike 3x normal saturated the order service; 20:02 spike ended but p99 stayed at 12 s and error rate at 35% for 70 minutes. During that time the database cache hit rate dropped from 97% to 40%, clients retried 3 times with no jitter, and the load balancer had ejected 6 of 20 healthy-but-slow pods, concentrating load on the rest. Recovery came at 21:12 when the team blocked traffic at the CDN for 4 minutes, restarted pods, and let traffic ramp. Autoscaler had added 10 pods at 20:08 with no effect.

title: RPO, RTO, HA and backup
text: Define RPO and RTO, and explain how high availability, disaster recovery and backups differ. RPO is how much data I can afford to lose, measured in time. RTO is how long I can be down. HA survives component failures inside a site automatically; DR survives loss of a whole site or region, often with a human decision; backups protect against corruption and deletion, which replication does not because it copies the bad delete everywhere. Business sets the numbers, and each step lower costs roughly 10x.

title: Four DR strategies
text: Compare backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby and active-active. How do you pick? From cheap and slow to expensive and fast: backup and restore hours of RPO and RTO, nothing running , pilot light data replicated, core infrastructure defined but off , warm standby full stack at reduced capacity running , active-active full stack serving traffic, near zero RPO and RTO . I pick by the business cost of downtime against the extra cost, roughly 2%, 10 to 15%, 30 to 50% and 100%+ of the primary's bill.

title: Active-active
text: What makes active-active hard, and how do you handle writes and capacity? Routing is easy; concurrent writes are hard. I choose among partitioning users by home region no conflicts, simple, failover moves ownership , multi-leader replication with conflict resolution LWW, CRDTs, app merge , or cross-region consensus Spanner, CockroachDB, paying 50 to 150 ms per write . Capacity: with 2 regions each must hold 100% so run at 50% utilisation; with 3 regions each takes 50% on loss, so about 66% utilisation.

title: Replication modes and PITR
text: Explain synchronous, asynchronous and quorum replication, and how point-in-time recovery works. Synchronous commit waits for the replica: RPO 0 but write latency includes the RTT and availability depends on the replica. Asynchronous returns immediately: faster but RPO equals the lag at failure. Quorum commit waits for any k of n replicas. PITR is a periodic base backup plus continuously archived write-ahead log; I restore the base and replay the log to just before the mistake.

title: PITR
text: Walk through recovery, with the time estimate and what you would not do. At 10:43:05 an engineer runs DELETE FROM payments WHERE status = 'pending' against production without a WHERE on the right environment filter, removing 1.2M rows. Three read replicas applied it within 200 ms. The database is Postgres 15, 2 TB, with pgBackRest: nightly base backup at 02:00 about 600 GB compressed and WAL archived to S3 every 60 s. Restore throughput from S3 is 500 MB/s and WAL replay about 100 MB/s; 24 h of WAL is about 50 GB. The system is still serving other tables.

title: Async failover and RPO
text: Explain the loss, what you do now, and how you would redesign. An orders database in region A has an async replica in region B. Writes are 5,000 per second; replication lag shows 200 ms normally and 3 s at peak. Region A fails at 14:00:00 with a power event. The team promotes region B at 14:07. After promotion the business reports 14,000 missing orders. The runbook says RPO = 0 because "we have a replica". A manager asks whether the data is recoverable.

title: Choosing a DR strategy
text: Assign DR strategies, with RPO/RTO and rough costs, and defend the plan. A SaaS company with 100K USD per month infrastructure has three systems: a customer-facing API an hour of downtime costs about 80K USD revenue and trust , an internal analytics warehouse 8 TB, used by analysts and a billing batch system runs nightly, a missed run delays invoices by a day . The CFO says "make everything survive a region loss, budget is 40K USD per month extra." Current DR: nightly snapshots in the same region.

title: Fencing and split brain
text: What went wrong and how do you recover and prevent a repeat? A Postgres primary in zone A loses connectivity to the monitor for 40 s because of a network partition, though it still serves some app servers. The automatic failover health check 3 failures x 10 s promotes the standby in zone B. For 6 minutes both nodes accept writes: 2,300 orders on A and 1,900 on B, with overlapping order numbers sequences . After the network heals, replication cannot resume timelines diverged . Customers see missing and duplicate orders.

title: Restore drill
text: What do you conclude and what changes? The first-ever restore drill of a 1.5 TB production database. The documented RTO is 1 hour. Timeline: 00:00 start; 00:20 the restore role cannot read the KMS key 45 minutes lost granting access ; 01:05 download begins on an instance type with 2x less network and disk than production restore takes 1 h 10 min ; 02:15 starting the database fails because max connections and a parameter group differ from production; 03:05 a runbook step references a retired bastion host; 03:20 the database is up and checks pass. The drill ran in staging, not the DR region.

title: Multi-region writes
text: Ask clarifying questions, then design the data layer. Product wants a chat app for 50M users in the US, EU and Asia: "messages should feel instant everywhere, nothing lost, usernames unique globally, and EU data must stay in the EU." Round-trip times: US-EU about 80 ms, US-Asia about 180 ms. The team proposes one globally replicated SQL database with synchronous replication.

title: Region-loss capacity
