text: Do the capacity math and recommend options. An active-active service runs in 2 regions, each at 60% CPU at peak with 100 pods 4 vCPU each , total traffic 40,000 req/s. During a drill, region 2 was removed and region 1 hit 100% CPU, p99 went from 80 ms to 3.4 s and 35% of requests failed. Autoscaling reached its limit of 150 pods after 12 minutes. The CFO asks whether adding a third region would be cheaper than raising utilisation headroom.

title: DNS failover and control plane
text: Run the post-incident review and propose the redesign. Region A suffers a network failure at 03:10. The runbook says: use the deployment tool hosted in region A to scale up region B, then update Route 53 records TTL 60 s . The deployment tool is unreachable; engineers lose 25 minutes finding credentials in a secrets manager that also lives in region A. When DNS finally changes at 03:41, about 20% of mobile and corporate clients keep hitting A for another 15 minutes. Region B scales from 20% to 100% at 03:55 and its database falls over from a cold cache and 3x connection spike. RTO target was 15 minutes; actual was 58.

title: N+1 queries
text: What is the N+1 query problem, why does it hurt, and how do you fix and detect it? One query loads a list of N items, then the code issues one more query per item for related data, so N+1 round trips instead of 1 or 2. Each round trip costs 0.3 to 1 ms plus parse and plan, so 100 orders is 101 queries, and at 1,000 req/s that is 101,000 queries/s on the database. I fix it with a join or join fetch, or a batched IN query 2 queries total , or a DataLoader in GraphQL. I detect it by counting SQL per request: Hibernate statistics, pg stat statements showing one statement with a huge call count and a tiny mean time, APM traces with hundreds of identical sibling DB spans, and tests that assert query counts.

title: Cache stampede
text: What is a cache stampede, and what are your options to prevent it? Which do you combine? A hot key expires and thousands of requests miss at once and all recompute from the database. The DB was sized for a 95% hit rate and suddenly gets 100% of traffic, which keeps the cache from refilling. Fixes: single flight only one request recomputes, the rest wait , a lock or lease on the key, serve stale while one refresher updates it, TTL jitter so keys do not expire together, probabilistic early refresh, pre-warming after deploys or failovers, and background refresh for extremely hot keys. In practice I combine jitter, single flight and stale-while-revalidate.

title: N+1 in production
text: Diagnose and fix, and say how you stop it from coming back. After a release, GET /orders p99 goes from 120 ms to 2.4 s for users with many orders. DB CPU rises from 30% to 85%; app CPU is 20%. pg stat statements excerpt: query calls mean ms total ms select from customers where id = $1 4,820,000 0.38 1,831,600 select from orders where created at $1 41,000 21.0 861,000 Release notes mention a new "customer name" field in the order list DTO. Another change in the same release raised the connection pool from 20 to 40 possible red herring .

title: Chatty services
text: Design the fix and show the numbers. The mobile home screen makes 12 sequential REST calls profile, orders, recs, banners... at 80 ms mobile RTT each, about 960 ms plus TLS setup when connections are not reused. Product wants under 300 ms to first content and will 10x traffic to 20,000 req/s next quarter. Each call is 99.9% available. The backend team proposes "make each service faster".

title: Pagination and indexes
text: Explain the symptoms and fix them. An admin export endpoint pages through a 40M-row events table using LIMIT 50 OFFSET :n ordered by id . Page 1 takes 2 ms; page 20,000 offset 1,000,000 takes 900 ms; scraping scripts crawl deep and DB CPU spikes. The query selects including a 5 KB JSON column. Also, a separate query filtering WHERE tenant id = ? ORDER BY created at DESC is doing a sequential scan. Limit cost=... actual time=902.1..902.2 rows=50 - Index Scan using events pkey actual time=0.03..851.4 rows=1000050

title: Stampede after cache flush
text: Explain why recovery was slow and how you would redesign. During a Redis maintenance window the cache is flushed at 10:00 peak: 8,000 req/s . Before: hit ratio 96%, DB at 400 qps. After: hit ratio 0%, DB attempts 8,000 qps and its connection pool saturates; p99 goes 90 ms to 12 s, then clients retry retry rate 3x and the site is down for 9 minutes even after Redis is healthy. db connections in use 200/200 waiting threads 1,900 cache hit ratio 0.00 retries total rate 24,000/s

title: Unbounded queues and Little's law
text: Why is "just add a queue to absorb the load" dangerous? Use Little's law and name concrete unbounded things in a JVM service. A queue only absorbs the difference between arrival and service rate while memory lasts. Latency becomes queue length over service rate: a backlog of 600,000 items at 1,000 items/s is a 10-minute wait, so every item is stale and users have retried, and then the process OOMs and the queue is lost. Little's law says in-flight items = arrival rate x time in system, so 1,000 req/s at 2 s latency is 2,000 concurrent requests; if latency goes to 20 s it is 20,000, and memory and threads explode. So I bound every queue, pool and cache and choose the overflow policy explicitly: block, reject with 503, drop, or spill to a durable queue.

title: Queue backlog
text: Explain what happened, the immediate mitigation, and the redesign. An image-processing service has an in-memory LinkedBlockingQueue default fixed pool, 32 threads . Normal arrival is 800 jobs/s, service rate 1,000/s. A downstream storage slowdown cuts service rate to 400/s for 30 minutes. Heap is 4 GB, each job is 1 KB. Metrics: queue depth 0 - 1.2M - 2.9M p99 job latency 40 ms - 90 s jvm heap used 1.1 GB - 3.9 GB gc pause 20 ms - 6 s back-to-back full GC pod restarts: OOMKilled x3 Clients retry after 10 s timeouts. CPU is at 35%.

title: Lock contention
text: Diagnose both problems and fix them. A pricing service on a 32-core host handles 480 ops/s at 8% CPU; adding threads does not help. Thread dumps taken 5 s apart show 28 of 32 threads BLOCKED on one monitor. A separate SQL counter for "orders today" is also slow under load UPDATE stats SET orders = orders + 1 WHERE id = 1; with lock waits . // shared cache guarded by one lock synchronized lock { Price p = db.load sku ; // 1.8 ms network call log.info "loaded {}", sku ; // 0.15 ms cache.put sku, p ; } Languages: Java, Kotlin synchronized lock { val p = db.load sku // 1.8 ms network call log.info "loaded {}", sku // 0.15 ms cache sku = p }

title: GC pauses and failure detection
text: How can a garbage-collection pause cause an outage in a distributed system that is otherwise healthy, and how do you prevent it? A stop-the-world pause freezes the app. If it lasts longer than the health-check timeout, heartbeat interval or lock lease, the node looks dead: the load balancer ejects it, the cluster fails over, a lease expires and a second holder takes over, and the paused node wakes up believing it still owns something. That can cascade into retry storms or split brain. Prevention: pick a modern collector G1 with a pause goal, or ZGC/Shenandoah for low pauses , size the heap right a bigger heap with an old collector means longer pauses , reduce allocation, fix leaks, and keep timeouts above the worst realistic pause. Use fencing tokens for locks.

title: Reconnect and retry storm
text: Plan the rollout so it does not cause an outage, and fix the client behavior. A WebSocket gateway fleet 40 nodes, 2M concurrent mobile clients must be restarted for a TLS library patch. The last restart caused 2M reconnects within 20 seconds, auth service CPU hit 100%, and 30% of clients saw errors for 12 minutes. Clients reconnect immediately on close with a fixed 1 s delay and no backoff. Reconnect handshake costs about 15 ms of auth CPU; the auth tier handles about 20,000 handshakes/s.

title: Measure first
text: How do you respond, and what do you investigate first? Use Amdahl's law in your answer. Your manager says: "The API is slow, p99 went from 250 ms to 1.4 s last week. We should double the pods." Data you can see: 60 pods, CPU at 30%, p50 unchanged at 40 ms, DB active connections at the max 100 with 40 clients waiting for a connection, one endpoint /search accounts for 85% of the p99 outliers, GC pauses average 25 ms. A deploy last Tuesday added a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in the order path.

title: authn vs authz
text: What is the difference between authentication and authorization, and which HTTP status codes map to each? Authentication is "who are you", done once per login or token. Authorization is "what may you do to this resource", done on every request. Not authenticated is 401, authenticated but not allowed is 403. Authz must be checked per object, not just per endpoint.

title: password storage
text: How should a system store user passwords, and why not SHA-256 or encryption? Store a per-user salted hash from a slow, memory-hard function: argon2id, or bcrypt/scrypt if that is what the platform has. Never plain SHA-256 too fast to brute-force and never reversible encryption a key leak exposes all . Optionally add a pepper held outside the DB.

title: sessions vs JWT
text: Which do you choose, and what is the decision gravity? You are designing auth for a B2C app: web, iOS and Android, 5M DAU, 40 requests per user per day about 2,300/s average, 7k/s peak . Product asks for "ban a abusive user within 30 seconds" and "keep users logged in for 30 days". A teammate wants stateless JWTs with a 30-day expiry because "no session store, no scaling problem". Another wants server-side sessions in Redis.

title: JWT validation
text: What is wrong, how would an attacker exploit it, and what is the corrected check? A code review shows this token check in an API gateway filter. The service handles money movement. Languages: Java, Kotlin tab public Claims authenticate String token { DecodedJWT jwt = JWT.decode token ; // parses only if jwt.getExpiresAt .before new Date { throw new Unauthorized ; } return jwt.getClaims ; } tab fun authenticate token: String : Map<String, Claim { val jwt = JWT.decode token // parses only if jwt.expiresAt.before Date throw Unauthorized return jwt.claims }

title: server-side sessions
text: Walk me through diagnosis, mitigation and the permanent fix. A web app with 2M active sessions stores them in a single Redis node maxmemory 8 GB, policy allkeys-lru . At 14:02 an unrelated team deploys a cache feature that fills the same Redis. Support gets 4,000 tickets in 20 minutes: "I was logged out". Metrics: redis evicted keys total 0 - 9,800/s from 14:02 used memory 7.99 GB / 8 GB session lookup miss rate 0.1% - 38% login endpoint QPS 150/s - 2,900/s argon2 CPU 30% - 100%, login p99 12 s

title: OAuth redirect flow
text: List what is wrong and what flow you would use instead. A single-page app adds "Sign in with Google". A reviewer finds this config and flow: oauth client: response type: token implicit flow, token returned in URL fragment redirect uris: - https:// .example.com/callback state: null scopes: openid, email, profile, drive The app never sends a state parameter, stores the access token in localStorage , and the product only needs the user's email.

title: OAuth vs OIDC
text: What is the difference between OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, and what are the ID token, access token and refresh token each for? OAuth 2.0 is delegated authorization: it gives a client an access token to call an API on the user's behalf. OIDC is an identity layer on top that adds an ID token a signed JWT saying who logged in, for the client and a userinfo endpoint. Access token is for the resource server, ID token is for the client, refresh token gets new access tokens.

title: refresh token rotation
text: What happened, what do you do now, and how do you redesign refresh? Mobile app, access token 10 minutes, refresh token 60 days, non-rotating, stored in plain app storage. Security notices a surge: auth-service log, one refresh token rt 9f..a1 : 10:01:04 refresh ok ip=49.x.x.12 device=Pixel-7 10:01:09 refresh ok ip=185.x.x.88 device=unknown ua=python-requests 10:07:11 refresh ok ip=185.x.x.88 ... 185.x.x.88 shows 1,100 refreshes in 6 hours across 340 distinct tokens

title: revocation
text: Design revocation with numbers and trade-offs. A platform with 20M MAU uses 15-minute JWT access tokens, verified locally by 60 services. Security now requires "logout everywhere, account compromise lock, and employee offboarding take effect in under 10 seconds". Peak 50k requests/s across services. A proposal: every service calls the auth service to validate each token. Another: a denylist in Redis.

title: RBAC vs ABAC vs ReBAC
text: Compare RBAC, ABAC and relationship-based access control. When would you use each, and how do you make the decision at scale? RBAC grants permissions to roles, simple and auditable but it explodes with fine-grained or per-object rules. ABAC evaluates attributes of user, resource and context against policy, flexible but harder to reason about. ReBAC Zanzibar style derives access from relationships like "member of group that owns folder", ideal for sharing graphs like Docs or Drive. Most systems start with RBAC and add attributes or relations where needed.

title: role explosion
text: How do you fix the model and migrate it live? A B2B SaaS has 3,000 tenants. Every customer asked for custom permissions, so engineering created roles per request. Now there are 410 roles, 1,900 role-permission rows per tenant on average, and a permission check query joins 4 tables: SELECT 1 FROM user roles ur JOIN role perms rp ON ... JOIN perms p ON ... WHERE ur.user id=? AND p.name=? authz p99: 4 ms - 38 ms at 12k checks/s peak; DB CPU 70% support: "Why can Maria delete invoices?" takes an hour to answer You want to restructure without downtime.

title: enforcement points
text: Run the post-incident review: root causes, fixes, and detection. Post-incident review. An attacker with a free account called GET /api/orders/{id} on the order service by iterating ids and downloaded 41,000 orders of other customers over three days about 1 request/s, so no rate alarm . The API gateway validated the JWT and checked the orders:read scope. The order service "trusts the gateway" and loads any order by id. The attacker also reached the order service directly through a mistakenly public load balancer, bypassing the gateway.

title: threat modelling
text: In a design interview, how do you do threat modelling, and why before picking controls? I draw the data flow, mark trust boundaries, list assets what an attacker wants , then walk STRIDE spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege at each boundary, rank by likelihood times impact and only then choose controls. Spending effort follows the risk, not the fashion.

title: TLS
text: What does TLS provide and how does the handshake work at a high level? Where do you terminate it? TLS gives confidentiality, integrity and server authentication and optionally client authentication . The client and server agree on a cipher, the server proves identity with a certificate chained to a trusted CA, they derive a shared session key with ephemeral Diffie-Hellman forward secrecy , then use fast symmetric encryption. I usually terminate at the edge load balancer and re-encrypt inside for sensitive traffic.

title: certificate expiry
text: Mitigate, find root cause and prevent recurrence. Saturday 03:12. Your public API 6k rps returns errors for mobile clients, while the web app seems fine. Logs and a client trace: mobile: javax.net.ssl.SSLHandshakeException: PKIX path validation failed: certificate expired $ echo openssl s client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com 2 /dev/null openssl x509 -noout -dates notBefore=Aug 15 00:00:00 2025 GMT notAfter =Nov 13 00:00:00 2025 GMT Web browsers work because the CDN serves a different, auto-renewed cert. The API hostname bypasses the CDN and uses a cert renewed by hand 90 days ago by an engineer who left.

title: leaked secrets
text: What do you do in the first hour and what changes after? A secret scanner flags that an AWS access key and a Stripe live key were committed to a public GitHub repo 41 minutes ago by an intern in config/prod.env . The key belongs to a service role with S3 read/write on the customer-uploads bucket. CloudTrail already shows: 10:42:11 GetCallerIdentity src=203.0.113.50 unfamiliar IP 10:42:40 ListBuckets 10:43:02 ListObjectsV2 bucket=prod-customer-uploads 10:44:15 GetObject x 18,200 over 6 minutes

title: injection and mass assignment
text: Find every vulnerability, class it by OWASP category, and fix it. Review of a user-profile update endpoint: Languages: Java, Kotlin tab @PutMapping "/users/{id}" public User update @PathVariable long id, @RequestBody User body { String sql = "UPDATE users SET name='" + body.getName + "' WHERE id=" + id; jdbc.execute sql ; userRepo.save body ; // User has fields: id, name, email, role, isAdmin return body; } tab @PutMapping "/users/{id}" fun update @PathVariable id: Long, @RequestBody body: User : User { jdbc.execute "UPDATE users SET name='${body.name}' WHERE id=$id" userRepo.save body // User has: id, name, email, role, isAdmin return body }

title: encryption at rest
text: Explain envelope encryption. How do you encrypt data at rest at scale, and what does it actually protect against? Each object or record is encrypted with a data key DEK ; the DEK is itself encrypted by a master key KEK held in a KMS/HSM. You store the wrapped DEK next to the ciphertext. This makes rotation and access control cheap and keeps the master key off the data path. Disk or database-level encryption protects against stolen disks and backups, not against a compromised app with valid credentials.

title: web hardening
text: Which are real risks, in what order do you fix them, and what is the target configuration? A pentest report on a SPA plus API lists these findings. Config excerpts: Set-Cookie: session=9a8f...; Path=/ Access-Control-Allow-Origin: Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true server reflects the Origin header in practice No Content-Security-Policy, no X-Frame-Options POST /transfer works with a cookie and no CSRF token JWT stored in localStorage

title: mTLS rollout
text: Plan the rollout with numbers and failure modes. 80 microservices in Kubernetes talk plain HTTP inside the cluster; peak 120k internal rps. A compliance audit requires encrypted and mutually authenticated service traffic within 6 months, without downtime. Some services are legacy and cannot be changed. You are evaluating a service mesh sidecar mTLS versus library-level TLS.

title: encryption requirements
text: How do you turn the vague requirement into a design, and what do you encrypt where? A healthcare startup's enterprise customer writes: "All patient data must be encrypted." You run Postgres on managed cloud storage 500 GB , S3 for scans 20 TB , Kafka between services, and an analytics warehouse. The CTO wants the cheapest approach that passes the customer's security review in four weeks.

title: KMS throttling
text: Diagnose and fix it. After enabling application-level encryption, checkout latency p99 rises from 80 ms to 2.4 s at peak 9k rps. Logs: ERROR KmsThrottlingException: Rate exceeded ThrottlingException region=eu-west-1 kms.Decrypt calls: 9,300/s account quota in this region: about 5,500/s shared - verify cache: none; each request decrypts a wrapped DEK retry: 3 immediate retries, no jitter

title: SSRF
text: Contain, explain and fix it. A "fetch image from URL" feature in your profile service lets users paste an image URL; the server downloads it for resizing. GuardDuty alerts on unusual use of an instance role from an external IP. Request logs show: POST /profile/avatar {"url":"http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/profile-svc-role"} 200 OK response body returned to caller in an error message The role has s3: and dynamodb: on production resources. IMDSv1 is enabled.

title: key rotation
text: How do you design key management and rotation: for signing keys, data-encryption keys and the master key? What happens when a key is compromised? Keep a hierarchy: root keys in an HSM/KMS, key-encrypting keys below, data keys per object or tenant. Rotate on a schedule and on compromise, with versioned keys so old data stays readable. For signing keys, publish multiple public keys JWKS with kid , overlap old and new for the token lifetime, then retire. For compromise, revoke, re-encrypt affected data and treat it as an incident, not a config change.

title: rate limiting algorithms
text: Compare fixed window, sliding window, token bucket and leaky bucket rate limiting. Which would you pick for a public API? Fixed window is simplest but allows 2x bursts at window edges. Sliding window log is exact but stores every timestamp. Sliding window counter approximates cheaply. Token bucket allows controlled bursts at a steady average and is my default for APIs. Leaky bucket smooths output to a constant rate, good for protecting a downstream.

title: GDPR
text: What are the GDPR basics an engineer must design for? Lawful basis and consent for processing, data minimisation, purpose limitation, user rights access, rectification, erasure, portability , breach notification within 72 hours, and privacy by design. For engineers that means knowing where personal data lives, being able to export and delete it per user, setting retention limits and keeping an audit trail.

title: limiter race condition
text: What bugs exist and how do you fix them? A Redis-backed fixed-window limiter 100 requests per minute per API key is deployed on 12 gateway pods. Ops notes some keys get no limit at all and Redis memory slowly grows with keys with no TTL. Languages: Java, Kotlin tab boolean allow String key { long count = redis.incr "rl:" + key ; // step 1 if count == 1 { redis.expire "rl:" + key, 60 ; // step 2 } return count <= 100; } tab fun allow key: String : Boolean { val count = redis.incr "rl:$key" // step 1 if count == 1L redis.expire "rl:$key", 60 // step 2 return count <= 100 }

title: L7 DDoS
text: Mitigate and design for the next one. Tuesday 11:20. Normal traffic is 3k rps. Suddenly 140k rps hits /search?q=<random . Origin CPU 100%, DB connection pool exhausted. Edge logs: requests/s by country: 62% from 40 countries, each under 3% share user agents: 9 distinct, all "Mozilla/5.0 ... Chrome/118" query strings: all unique cache hit ratio 0.1% bandwidth: 280 Mbps small - not a volumetric flood TLS fingerprint JA3 : 3 values cover 90% of requests

title: WAF rollout
text: How do you roll out the WAF safely? Your org is putting a managed WAF OWASP core rule set in front of an API at 8k rps and a checkout flow. Last time a team enabled blocking mode in one go and lost 3% of legitimate orders for two hours because a rule flagged JSON bodies containing SELECT -like product names and a SOAP integration. Security wants coverage in two weeks.

title: scraping and bots
text: What do you ask, and what do you build? A retail site sees 35% of product-page traffic from non-human clients. Marketing says "stop the scrapers", but SEO needs Googlebot, partners use an affiliate feed, and a price comparison site is a customer. Logs: IP 198.51.100.7 : 4,800 req/hour, sequential product ids, no cookies, UA "python-requests/2.31" residential proxy pool: 20,000 IPs, each 8 req/hour, headless Chrome, same navigation pattern real users: median 14 pages/session

title: distributed limiting and load shedding
text: How do you do rate limiting across many gateway nodes, and how is load shedding different from rate limiting? Options: a central store like Redis with atomic scripts accurate, adds a hop , local limits at limit/N per node cheap, inaccurate , or hybrid with local token batches synced periodically. Rate limiting is per-client fairness; load shedding protects the server when overall demand exceeds capacity by dropping low-priority requests early, regardless of who sent them.

title: credential stuffing
text: Respond, then design the long-term defences. Login service normal: 400 logins/min, 94% success. Now: logins/min: 38,000 success rate: 1.8% distinct IPs: 210,000 in 1 hour about 3 attempts each distinct usernames: 36,000, each tried once or twice many usernames match a recent third-party breach list support: 120 accounts report unauthorised gift-card purchases per-IP limit: 20/min never triggers ; argon2 CPU: 100%

title: distributed limiter at scale
text: Redesign the limiter for 400k rps and the hot key. Your Redis-backed per-API-key limiter handles 40k rps with one Redis primary about 55% CPU . Traffic is going to 10x for a launch 400k rps . One enterprise customer sends about 25% of all traffic under one key. Gateway to Redis adds 1.2 ms p50; the product SLO budget for the limiter is 2 ms. redis ops/s now: 40k after launch: 400k hot key "rl:acme": 100k ops/s on one shard

title: right to erasure
text: Design the erasure pipeline and handle the awkward stores. You receive 300 erasure requests per month, growing to 3,000. User data lives in: Postgres 3 services , Elasticsearch search index , Redis, a Kafka topic with 30 days retention, a Snowflake warehouse, S3 log archives 400 days , nightly DB backups 35 days and two SaaS vendors email, support desk . Today a developer runs manual SQL for each request and misses systems. Legal says: complete within 30 days, prove it, keep invoices for 7 years tax law .

title: abuse by design
text: How do you design the abuse defences, starting from the requirement? Product wants a "free 30-day trial, no card needed" with 50 GB of storage and an invite-a-friend bonus. Expected 200k signups a month. Last year a similar promo lost money to fake accounts. The PM says: "Make it frictionless, but don't let it be abused."

title: PII classification
text: How do you classify and handle PII in a large system: tagging, minimisation, tokenisation, logs and access? Classify data into tiers public, internal, confidential, restricted , tag fields in schemas, collect and keep the minimum, tokenise or pseudonymise high-risk values, encrypt, restrict access by purpose with audit, and keep PII out of logs, URLs and analytics by default.

title: Redis basics
text: Why is Redis fast, what is it good and bad at, and how durable is it? Redis keeps data in memory and runs commands on a single thread atomic, no locks , giving about 100k ops/s per node at sub-millisecond latency. Great for caches, sessions, counters, rate limits, leaderboards. Bad as the only copy of data you cannot lose or for datasets bigger than RAM. Durability is optional via RDB snapshots and AOF, and replication is asynchronous.

title: back-of-envelope numbers
text: How do you use rough throughput numbers for Redis, Kafka, Postgres and so on in a design discussion without sounding like you are guessing? I convert the requirement to per-second numbers 1M requests/day is about 12 rps, peak 2 to 3x , compare to per-node ballpark capacity, state the assumption, and add headroom. I say "roughly" and name what I would benchmark. Then I pick the technology whose limit I am safely below.

title: Redis latency spike
text: Identify the causes and fix them. Product catalog service uses one Redis node 24 GB used, 80k ops/s . Every few minutes API p99 jumps from 5 ms to 1.5 s for about 3 seconds. Evidence: redis-cli --latency-history - spikes to 1,400 ms SLOWLOG GET: HGETALL catalog:category:all duration 1,380,000 us hash with 1.8M fields INFO: latest fork usec 900000 during BGSAVE every 5 min used memory 24 GB, host RAM 32 GB, transparent hugepage enabled

title: Kafka consumer lag
text: Why is lag growing and how do you fix it? An order-events topic has 12 partitions. Producers write 25k msgs/s 1 KB each, 25 MB/s . A consumer group of 20 pods processes each message in about 8 ms calls a payment API . Lag grows 40k per minute and notifications arrive 25 minutes late. kafka-consumer-groups --describe: partition 0-11 LAG rising CONSUMER-ID: assigned to 12 pods; 8 pods have no partitions max.poll.interval.ms=300000, session timeouts: rebalances every few minutes

title: Postgres connection exhaustion
text: Evaluate that and propose the right fix. A Postgres primary 16 vCPU, 64 GB, max connections=500 serves 60 app pods, each with a pool of 20 connections. During a sale, errors begin: FATAL: sorry, too many clients already pg stat activity: 497 connections, 410 state='idle in transaction'? no: 410 'idle', 70 'active', 17 'idle in transaction' load average 38, cpu 100%, TPS 9k, p99 query 900 ms The team's reaction: raise max connections to 2000.

title: DynamoDB throttling
text: Why throttling at 70% utilisation and how to fix? A DynamoDB table events partition key tenant id , sort key ts has 20,000 WCU provisioned. Writes of 2 KB items average 9,000/s but throttle at peak: WriteThrottleEvents rising; ConsumedWriteCapacity 14,000 of 20,000 WCU Contributor Insights: tenant id=acme = 78% of writes about 7,000 writes/s = 14,000 WCU per partition limit: about 1,000 WCU

title: Cassandra data modelling
text: How does Cassandra store and distribute data, and how do you model tables for it? What are tombstones and why are they a problem? Cassandra is a leaderless, AP wide-column store. Data is partitioned by the partition key on a consistent-hash ring with replication factor 3, writes go to a commit log and memtable then flush to immutable SSTables merged by compaction. You design one table per query, keep partitions bounded, and avoid heavy deletes because deletes write tombstones that slow reads until compaction purges them.

title: Elasticsearch shard sizing
text: What is wrong and how do you restructure? Product search cluster: 6 data nodes 64 GB RAM, 30 GB heap each . A daily index per tenant creates 14,000 indices, 5 primary shards each with 1 replica 140,000 shards ; the data is only 900 GB total. Symptoms: GET cluster/health - status yellow, number of pending tasks 4,800 master node: heap 92%, cluster state 380 MB, GC pauses 6 s search p99 2.8 s; indexing rejected with es rejected execution exception

title: S3 cost and uploads
text: How do you cut cost and fix uploads? A video app stores 800 TB in S3 Standard and serves downloads directly from S3 to the internet. Monthly bill: storage about $18,000, egress about $140,000 verify current prices; roughly $0.023 per GB-month storage and $0.09 per GB egress . Mobile uploads of 2 GB videos fail often over flaky networks and are retried from byte zero; support complains.

title: Nginx 502 and limits
text: Diagnose and fix. Nginx fronts 12 app pods; at 35k rps during a promotion users see intermittent 502/504: error.log: 2026/11/13 12:04:11 alert 31 31: 1024 worker connections are not enough error.log: upstream prematurely closed connection while reading response header error.log: connect failed 99: Cannot assign requested address while connecting to upstream worker processes 4; worker connections 1024; no keepalive to upstream; ulimit -n 1024 ss -s: TIME-WAIT 61,000

title: etcd/ZooKeeper misuse
text: What is wrong and what is the right architecture? A team uses a 3-node etcd cluster for leader election and config, and has also begun storing per-user feature flags 6M keys, 4 GB plus high-frequency heartbeats 8,000 writes/s . Symptoms: etcdserver: request timed out; "apply request took too long" 1.2s mvcc: database space exceeded quota 8 GB wal fsync duration p99 = 210 ms disk shared with other workloads, HDD-backed volume leader changes: 14 in the last hour; services lose leadership and flap

title: choosing technologies
text: Given a chat app with 50M DAU sending 40 messages/day each, how do you pick the data stores and what do the numbers tell you? 50M x 40 = 2B messages/day, about 23k writes/s average and about 70k at peak. That is beyond one Postgres node, so messages go in a partitioned store Cassandra or DynamoDB keyed by chat and time. Presence and counters in Redis, fan-out and async work on Kafka, search in Elasticsearch fed from Kafka, attachments in S3 behind a CDN, coordination leader election in etcd or ZooKeeper, and Postgres for accounts and billing.

title: CQRS basics
text: What is CQRS and why would you separate the read model from the write model? CQRS means one model changes data commands and a different model serves reads queries . Writes need validation, invariants and transactions on a normalised schema. Reads need speed and pre-joined shapes. When one schema serves both, you get slow joins and read load hurting writes. CQRS has levels: separate code paths on one DB, read replicas or materialised views, or a fully separate read store fed asynchronously. I start at the cheapest level.

title: Event sourcing basics
text: What is event sourcing, and how is the current state of an aggregate obtained? Instead of overwriting balance = 70 , I append immutable events like Deposited 100 and Withdrew 30 to an append-only event store keyed by stream id and version. To get current state I load the stream and apply each event in order. Changes validate the command against current state, then append new events with optimistic concurrency on the expected version. It gives audit and replay, but it adds replay cost and needs projections for queries.

title: Read-your-writes
text: How do you fix the user-visible symptom without giving up the read store? An e-commerce team added a read store Elasticsearch fed by a projector. Users now click "Place order", get redirected to "My orders", and the order is missing. Support gets 300 tickets/day, "my order disappeared", and some users order twice. Projection lag p50 = 150 ms, p99 = 2.5 s. The write DB shows the order. The CPU on the projector is 30%. Someone proposes "read from the write DB for everything".

title: Projections
text: How does a projection work, and what must be true of a projection handler? A projector subscribes to the event stream from a stored checkpoint, applies each event to a read store and advances the checkpoint, ideally in the same transaction. Delivery is at-least-once, so handlers must be idempotent and deterministic: no now , no external calls, time comes from the event. To change a projection I deploy new code and replay from event 0 into a new table, then swap. I monitor lag as latest event version minus applied version.

title: Optimistic concurrency
text: What is the bug and how do you fix it, including the retry path? A wallet service uses event sourcing. Two parallel withdrawals of 80 on a balance of 100 both succeeded; the balance is -60. Code: Languages: Java, Kotlin tab void withdraw String id, long amt { List<Event events = store.load id ; Wallet w = Wallet.replay events ; if w.balance < amt throw new InsufficientFunds ; store.append id, List.of new Withdrew amt ; // no expected version } tab fun withdraw id: String, amt: Long { val events = store.load id val w = Wallet.replay events if w.balance < amt throw InsufficientFunds store.append id, listOf Withdrew amt // no expected version } The table has version INT but only an index on stream id , not a unique key.

title: Snapshots
text: What do you do? A trading account aggregate has 1M events. Loading it for each command takes 2 s 2 us per event apply, plus read time . Command p99 SLO is 100 ms. A teammate says "add snapshots every 1,000 events". Another says "we will never need snapshots, just cache the aggregate in memory". A third notes the 1M events came from one account being used as a catch-all stream for all of a customer's activity over 4 years.

title: Schema evolution
text: How do you introduce the new shape? An event-sourced order service has 200M stored OrderPlaced events. V1 stored total: 4999 implicit rupees . Product now sells in USD and EUR, so total must carry a currency. Three consumers billing, search, analytics read the events from Kafka. A developer proposes a one-off SQL UPDATE over the event table at night. The release is in 2 weeks and downtime is not allowed.

title: Sagas
text: How do sagas replace distributed transactions, and how do you choose between choreography and orchestration? A saga is a sequence of local transactions across services; if a step fails, earlier steps are undone by compensating actions, which are business-level undos like a refund, not a DB rollback. Choreography has services react to each other's events: fine for 2 or 3 steps, hard to follow beyond that. Orchestration uses a process manager Temporal, Step Functions that sends commands and owns timeouts and retries. Every step must be idempotent, because a timeout may still have succeeded.

title: Outbox and delivery
text: Explain both symptoms and fix them. Orders service: repo.save order then kafka.send OrderPlaced . At 1,000 orders/s, a rolling deploy kills pods. Next day finance reports 1,400 orders in the DB with no shipment, and shipping reports 90 duplicate shipments. Kafka is healthy. Logs excerpt: 12:01:03 INFO order o-88121 saved 12:01:03 WARN SIGTERM received, shutting down 12:01:04 INFO kafka producer closed Another service shows ack timeout retries around the same time.

title: When not to use
text: What do you recommend, and what questions do you ask first? A 12-engineer startup runs an internal-tools SaaS: 200 writes/s, 2k reads/s, one Postgres, Redis cache. A new architect proposes event sourcing plus CQRS for "auditability and scale". The CTO asks you: yes or no? Compliance only requires "who changed what and when" for 3 account-setting tables. Nobody on the team has run Kafka in production. Page load p95 is 400 ms, with the slow query being a 5-table join.

title: Saga failure handling
text: Write the post-incident review: causes and fixes. Order saga: ReserveStock - ChargePayment - ShipOrder. During a payment-provider brownout p99 from 300 ms to 35 s , 4,200 customers were charged twice and 1,100 orders have stock reserved forever. Saga log: ChargePayment sent key=none ChargePayment timeout after 30s - retry 1 ChargePayment timeout after 30s - retry 2 saga marked FAILED - ReleaseStock sent ReleaseStock failed: stock-svc 503 Provider later confirmed 3 of the charges had succeeded.

title: Rebuild and replay
text: Plan the rebuild. Search projection over 200M events processes 20k events/s; live traffic adds 2k events/s. A bug shows wrong totals for refunded orders. You must rebuild the projection with no downtime. A junior suggests truncating the table and replaying. The projector also calls a tax API and sends a "refund processed" email.

title: Monolith vs microservices
text: What are the real trade-offs between a monolith and microservices? A monolith is one deployable with usually one database: simple to build, debug and test, with free cross-feature transactions and nanosecond calls. Microservices split into independently deployed services that own their data and talk over the network. The benefit is team and scaling independence; the price is latency, partial failure, distributed data consistency and a platform investment tracing, CI/CD per service, on-call . I choose microservices for team scaling or very different scaling shapes, never for fashion.

title: Modular monolith
text: What is a modular monolith and why is it often the best default? A modular monolith is one deployable made of modules with strict boundaries: each module exposes a public interface, hides its internals and its tables, and does not reach into others. You get local calls and one DB transaction, but also clear ownership. Boundaries drawn wrong are cheap to redraw inside a monolith and very expensive across services. When a module needs independent scaling, I extract it behind its existing interface.

title: Choosing a style
text: What architecture do you propose, and how do you push back? Series A startup, 8 engineers, one Rails/Spring monolith, 300 req/s peak, 99.95% SLO. The new CTO wants to move to 20 microservices "to scale". Deploys are weekly because of a flaky test suite, not because of coupling. The only real hotspot is image processing that spikes 10x and needs GPUs. Hiring plan: 20 engineers in 12 months.

title: API gateway and composition
text: What does an API gateway do, and how does API composition differ from a gateway? A gateway is the single entry point handling cross-cutting concerns: routing, TLS, authentication, rate limiting, request shaping. API composition is aggregating data from several services into one response a BFF or composer . Composition calls services in parallel with timeouts and returns partial results on failure. I keep the gateway thin; business logic does not belong there.

title: Latency and availability tax
text: Why is the SLO missed and what do you change? Checkout calls Cart - Pricing - Inventory - Tax - Payments - Notifications in sequence. Each service is 99.9% available with p50 20 ms and p99 50 ms. Checkout SLO: 99.9% availability and p99 under 200 ms. The monitoring shows checkout availability at 99.4% and p99 at 310 ms. A 7th service called Loyalty is proposed in the chain.

title: Shared database trap
text: What is wrong architecturally, and what is the plan? Orders service and Reporting service both read and write the customers table in one shared Postgres. Reporting added a nightly job that does UPDATE customers SET segment = ... with a long transaction. The Orders team can't add a NOT NULL column because Reporting breaks, and last Tuesday the job locked rows for 40 minutes: ERROR: deadlock detected / lock wait timeout on customers Orders p99: 120 ms - 9 s "We are microservices, but ..."

title: Strangler fig
text: How do you migrate safely? Billing lives in a 10-year-old monolith 8k invoices/hour, money involved . Leadership wants a billing service in 10 weeks. Someone proposes a rewrite and a weekend cutover. Past shadow experiments in another team showed 0.5% mismatches on rounding.

title: Service mesh
text: What does a service mesh give you, what does it cost, and when is it not worth it? A service mesh moves service-to-service networking into sidecar or node proxies: mTLS, retries, timeouts, traffic shifting, and telemetry without code changes. With 300 services in many languages, enforcing mTLS means one policy instead of 300 code changes. The cost is latency per hop, resource overhead, operational complexity and a platform team. It is worth it around 50+ services across languages; for 5 services a library like Resilience4j is enough.

title: Retry storm
text: What do you do right now and what is the root cause? Pricing service p99 rose from 80 ms to 4 s after a deploy. Within 3 minutes Orders, Cart and Checkout all alarm. Traffic into Pricing: 5k/s normal, 16k/s now. Mesh config: 3 retries on 5xx and timeouts, app SDK also retries 2 times; per-try timeout 2 s. CPU on Pricing is 98%. pricing rps in=16210 5xx=41% p99=4.1s checkout rps out to pricing=15980 Someone suggests scaling Pricing 4x.

title: Cross-service consistency
text: Design the data flow and explain the consistency trade-off. Order list screen shows 50 orders with customer names. Orders and Users are separate services. Current implementation calls Users 50 times 5 ms each, sequential : 250 ms. Users has a rate limit that is hit at peak. A rename currently shows instantly. Product says the list must load under 100 ms.

title: Extracting from a modular monolith
text: How do you extract search? In a 40-engineer modular monolith, the search module needs independent scaling: it uses 70% of the CPU on instances and its indexing batch jobs slow down checkout. Search reads products and orders summary tables owned by other modules via direct SQL joins. Deploys are daily. You have 4 weeks.

title: Gateway as bottleneck
text: Write the review: contributing factors and fixes. The API gateway ran product-page composition: calls Catalog, Pricing, Inventory, Reviews sequentially, and contains discount rules written by 3 teams. Black Friday: gateway p99 3.8 s, error rate 6%, and a Reviews slowdown p99 400 ms took down the whole page. Deploys of the gateway needed approval from 5 teams and blocked a hotfix for 6 hours.

title: Multi-tenancy basics
text: What is multi-tenancy, and why must tenant id be there from day one? Multi-tenancy means one running system serves many customers tenants whose data and performance must stay separate. Sharing infrastructure is cheap but creates risks: data leaks between tenants and one tenant hurting others. I carry a tenant id through schema, auth, caches, queues, search and files from day one, because retrofitting it later across all those stores is very expensive. The isolation model is a one-way door: it ends up in schema, backups and pricing.

title: Isolation models
text: Compare shared tables, schema per tenant, and database per tenant. When do you pick each? Shared tables with a tenant id column pool are cheapest and easiest to operate but have the weakest isolation. Schema per tenant is the middle path. Database per tenant silo gives the strongest isolation, per-tenant backup and restore, and noisy-neighbour protection, at a high cost. For 100k small tenants, I pool; for the top 20 whales and regulated customers I use silos, and a tenant directory lets me move a tenant between them.

title: Tenant data leak
text: List the bugs and the systematic fix. A support engineer reports seeing another customer's invoice. The code: Languages: Java, Kotlin tab @GetMapping "/invoices/{id}" Invoice get @PathVariable String id { return invoiceRepo.findById id .orElseThrow NotFound::new ; // no tenant check } private final Cache<String, Invoice cache = ...; // key = invoice id only tab @GetMapping "/invoices/{id}" fun get @PathVariable id: String : Invoice = invoiceRepo.findById id ?: throw NotFound // no tenant check private val cache: Cache<String, Invoice = ... // key = invoice id only Invoice ids are sequential integers. A nightly report job also iterates all invoices with no tenant set.

title: Noisy neighbour
text: What is the noisy neighbour problem and how do you detect it before customers report it? One tenant's heavy usage consumes shared resources threads, CPU, DB connections, IOPS, cache and degrades others. Example: a shared 100-thread worker pool where tenant A's export holds 95 threads for 10 minutes pushes everybody else's p99 from 80 ms to 12 s. Detection needs per-tenant metrics from day one: requests, latency, queue time, resource use, top-N tenants by consumption. Without them you see only aggregate degradation.

title: Noisy neighbour incident
text: Mitigate, then fix. At 10:02 all tenants report slow dashboards: p99 80 ms to 12 s. 500 tenants share a pool of 100 workers. Metrics excerpt: workers busy 100/100 queue wait p99 11.7s tenant=acme workers held=95 job=bulk export started=10:00 db cpu 35% network normal CPU on web nodes is low. The first suggestion is "restart everything".

title: Metering and billing
text: Redesign metering. A usage-based SaaS bills per API call. Today usage is counted by a usage table with UPDATE ... SET count = count + 1 per request. At 2,800 events/s, the table is a hotspot, and after a queue redelivery, customers were over-billed and an enterprise customer disputes an invoice. Finance wants hourly usage per tenant and per metric.

title: Strategy by tier
text: What is your tenancy strategy and your answer to sales? Revenue per tenant per month: free $0, pro $50, enterprise $10,000. Infrastructure cost per pooled tenant is $0.20/month; a dedicated database costs $300/month. Sales promised "dedicated database" to a pro customer as a perk. 20 enterprise tenants also demand it for compliance.

title: Tenant sharding and cells
text: How do you shard a multi-tenant system by tenant, and what are cells? I shard by tenant using a tenant directory: a table mapping tenant to shard or cell, cached in routers. A cell is a complete, self-contained copy of the stack app, DB, cache, queue serving a subset of tenants, so a bad deploy or failure affects only that cell's tenants. I avoid hash-mod-N routing because adding a shard remaps everyone. Capacity planning is per cell: add a cell when average utilisation hits about 60%.

title: Resharding
text: Plan the move. Tenant data is sharded with shard = hash tenant id % 4 . Four shards are at 85% disk and 70% CPU; growth is 8% monthly. Adding a fifth shard remaps about 80% of tenants. The business forbids downtime longer than a minute per tenant. Whales: 10 tenants hold 60% of the data.

title: Promoting a tenant to a silo
text: How do you move them? Tenant "Globex" pooled, 120 GB, 30% of the shared DB's IO signs an enterprise deal requiring isolation and a 4-hour RPO restore of only their data. Today all tenants are in shared tables with tenant id ; no directory exists. Cutover window: max 5 minutes of read-only mode. Foreign keys cross tenant tables; some reference shared lookup tables.

title: Blast radius
text: Write the review: what went right, what went wrong, what changes. A schema migration rolled out to all 20 cells at once. In cell 7 an index build took an exclusive lock for 25 minutes; cell 7 5% of tenants was down. Other cells were fine, but the incident was only noticed after 9 minutes because dashboards were aggregated across cells and showed a 5% error rate within normal noise.

title: Introducing quotas
text: How do you introduce limits safely? After two noisy-neighbour incidents the CEO says "add rate limits tomorrow". The API has 500 tenants and no limits. Top tenants send 2k req/s legitimately, the median sends 5 req/s. Last quarter, 3 enterprise customers ran batch imports at 800 req/s. Sales fears breaking them. You have per-tenant metrics for 6 weeks.

title: Bloom filter
text: What is a Bloom filter, what guarantees does it give, and where is it used? A Bloom filter is a bit array plus k hash functions that answers "is this key in the set?" with either "definitely not" or "probably yes". It has no false negatives, only false positives, and uses a few bits per element. You can add but not remove a counting variant allows removal . It sits in front of an expensive lookup: Cassandra and LSM stores use one per SSTable to skip disk reads for missing keys.

title: HyperLogLog
text: What does HyperLogLog do, and what do you give up when using it? HyperLogLog estimates the number of distinct elements using tiny, fixed memory. Redis HLL uses 12 KB per counter with about 0.81% standard error, regardless of whether you count a thousand or a billion items. The idea: hash each item, track the longest run of leading zeros per register; rare long runs imply many distinct items. You give up exactness, membership listing and removal. Counters merge by taking register-wise maximum, which makes it great for unions across servers or days.

title: Fan-out on write math
text: Do the math and decide. A social feed app: 100M active users, average 200 followers, 5M posts/day, peak 3x average. Feed shows the latest 800 post ids per user kept in Redis. Read SLO: p99 under 50 ms. Entry cost is about 50 B in Redis including overhead. The architect asks whether push is feasible and what it costs.

title: Sharded counters
text: How do sharded counters work and what do you trade for the write throughput? One counter row serialises writes on a row lock, so a single row tolerates roughly 1k to 2k updates per second. I split the counter into N shards, write to a random shard, and read by summing all N. With 50 shards, 50k likes/s means about 1k/s per shard. I trade simple reads and instant exactness for write throughput: reads sum N values, usually cached, and may be briefly stale but eventually exact.

title: Hot counter
text: Diagnose and fix. A viral video receives 50k likes/s. Postgres UPDATE posts SET likes = likes + 1 WHERE id = $1 shows: lock wait: 12.4s on relation posts, tuple 4411,7 pg stat activity: 1,800 sessions waiting, app connection pool exhausted db cpu 22%, iops normal All API endpoints now time out; the team suspects a DB upgrade from last week and wants to roll it back.

title: Bloom filter drift
text: Explain and fix it. A signup service uses a Bloom filter of taken usernames in front of the DB check. Sized for 10M names at 1% false positive. Two years on there are 38M names. Complaint volume: "username taken" shown for names that are free, up to 25% of attempts. DB load for existence checks also rose. filter: m=96M bits, k=7, inserted=38M estimated false positive rate 90%+

title: Approximate vs exact
text: What do you build, and what do you ask first? A product manager asks for "unique visitors per page" on 100,000 pages with 1B pageviews/day. Another stakeholder says the same number will be used to bill advertisers per unique viewer. The data team proposes a SET of user ids per page-day in Redis: estimated 8 GB per day for large pages alone.

title: Geohash vs quadtree
text: Compare geohash and quadtree for a nearby-search system, including the edge cases. Geohash encodes a lat/lng cell as a string where a shared prefix means nearby, so it's trivial to store in Redis or a DB index and shard by prefix. A quadtree recursively splits space into four, only splitting cells that exceed a point limit, so dense areas Manhattan get fine cells and empty areas stay coarse. Geohash is simple and static; a quadtree adapts to density. Both need neighbour-cell queries because of boundary problems.

title: Celebrity fan-out
text: Diagnose and redesign. The feed uses pure fan-out on write. A celebrity with 50M followers posts. Fan-out workers process 100k writes/s. Queue metrics: fanout queue depth: 0 - 38M over 6 min feed write latency p99: 40ms - 9s normal users' posts delayed 8-12 min Redis cluster CPU 91% Support: "my friends' posts are missing". An engineer proposes doubling workers.

title: Trending with Count-Min Sketch
text: Design it and explain the error behaviour. Trending hashtags over 1B events/hour with 100M distinct tags in the window. The exact HashMap approach needs about 5 GB per server 50 B per tag and several servers each see a subset. Product wants the top 20 per hour per region, near real time, errors on rare tags acceptable. A teammate proposes Count-Min Sketch alone, a second proposes sampling 1%.

title: Hot geohash shard
text: Explain both problems and the fix. Ride-hail location service: 1M drivers, an update each 4 s 250k writes/s , sharded by 4-character geohash prefix across 24 Redis shards. After launching in a big city, one shard shows 100% CPU while others sit at 15%. Complaints: "no drivers nearby" at cell borders even when drivers are 300 m away across the street. shard-07 prefix 'ttnf'... dense downtown ops/s 61k p99 480ms shard-12 ops/s 4k nearby lat,lng,2km returns drivers only from the query point's own cell

title: Choosing blocks
text: Pick structures per metric and give the memory estimate. Design "post analytics" for 1M active posts: total views high rate , unique viewers per day, top referrers, "has this user already seen this post?" for the feed, and "events near me". Budget: a small Redis cluster. Peak 40k views/s across posts, one viral post at 50k views/s alone. The interviewer says "do not say approximate for everything".

title: 301 vs 302 redirects
text: In a URL shortener, should the redirect return 301 or 302? What does each cost you? I use 302 if we care about click analytics or may change the target. A 301 is permanent, so browsers and proxies cache it and never ask us again: no click counts, and we can never repoint the link for users who already visited. A 302 costs one request per click, which our redirect service is built to handle anyway.

title: Code length and ID generation
text: Compare hashing the long URL, a counter with base62, and a pre-generated key service for creating short codes. Which would you pick and why? Hashing is simple but collides and needs a check-and-retry. A plain counter never collides but codes are sequential, scrapeable, and the counter is a bottleneck. I would use a range allocator: each app server leases a block of, say, 10,000 ids, then I scramble each number with a reversible permutation and base62 it, and I still use a conditional insert as a safety net.

title: Capacity estimate
text: Do the capacity math for the new scale and say what, if anything, must change in the architecture. Your shortener serves 100M new links a month and 100:1 reads, running on one Postgres primary plus Redis. Product now says the campaign business will push it to a Bitly-class service: 1M new links a day, 1B redirects a day, 1B stored links, peak 5x average. The interviewer gives you five minutes and a whiteboard.

title: Ambiguous requirement
text: What do you do in the first five minutes? The interviewer says only: "Design a URL shortener." No numbers, no other requirements. You have 40 minutes.

title: Atomic creation
text: Find the bug, explain how it shows up, and fix it. A teammate wrote custom-alias creation. Under load tests two users occasionally both get a 201 for summer-sale , and one of them later sees the other's link. Languages: Java, Kotlin tab public Link create String alias, String longUrl { if repo.exists alias { throw new Conflict "alias taken" ; } Link link = new Link alias, longUrl ; repo.save link ; // plain upsert by primary key return link; } tab fun create alias: String, longUrl: String : Link { if repo.exists alias throw Conflict "alias taken" val link = Link alias, longUrl repo.save link // plain upsert by primary key return link }

title: Cache stampede on a viral link
text: Diagnose and fix it. A celebrity tweets a short link at 14:02. Within a minute: redirect p99 goes from 12 ms to 2.4 s, DB CPU 95%, and one Redis shard is pinned. 14:01 redis shard-2 cpu 38% db qps 900 hit ratio 93% 14:03 redis shard-2 cpu 100% db qps 11,400 hit ratio 71% 14:03 redirect-svc timeouts: 4,200/s Kafka producer errors: 0 Link aZ3k9Q is getting about 40,000 clicks/s. The cache TTL on it was 60 s and it just expired. Someone suggests "add more DB replicas".

title: Analytics under failure
text: Redesign the click path. What do you tell marketing about accuracy? Click analytics are written synchronously into the Link DB in the same transaction as the redirect lookup UPDATE links SET clicks = clicks + 1 . Last week the analytics Kafka cluster was replaced; this week redirect error rate hit 8% during a broker maintenance because an intermediate "events" call was added in the request path. Marketing insists they cannot lose clicks.

title: Pastebin variant and migration
text: Describe the target design and the migration plan. Your Pastebin stores paste bodies average 10 KB, up to 10 MB in a Postgres bytea column. 1M pastes/day: 10 GB/day, table now 4 TB, vacuum takes hours, backups take 18 hours, p99 reads are 400 ms. Reads are 50:1. You must move bodies to object storage with zero downtime and no lost pastes.

title: Token bucket vs fixed window
text: What is the token bucket algorithm, and why is it usually preferred over a fixed window counter? A bucket holds up to B tokens and refills at rate r. Each request takes a token; no token means 429. It allows short bursts up to B but enforces the average rate r, and uses O 1 memory. A fixed window counter is simpler, but a client can send the full limit at the end of one window and again at the start of the next, getting 2x the limit in a short time.

title: Atomic distributed check
text: You have 20 API gateway servers sharing one Redis for limits. Why can a GET-then-SET token check be wrong, and how do you make it correct and fast? Two gateways can both read "1 token left" and both spend it, so the limit is exceeded. I run the whole refill, check and decrement as one Redis Lua script; Redis is single-threaded per shard, so scripts do not interleave. That is one round trip per request, key sharded by user so it hits one shard.

title: Fail-open vs fail-closed
text: What is the right policy and how do you implement it? Tuesday 10:12: the Redis cluster behind the limiter loses its primary and fails over about 20 s . The API gateways are configured fail-closed everywhere. Metrics: 10:12:05 gateway 5xx rate: 0.1% - 61% 10:12:05 limiter check timeout 200 ms : 14,800/s 10:12:25 redis failover complete, 5xx rate returns to 0.2% after 40 s The checkout flow was down for about a minute. The business asks you to make sure this never happens again, but also does not want login brute force to be easier.

title: Algorithm choice and memory
text: Evaluate it and propose a cheaper design. A teammate implemented a sliding window log a Redis sorted set of timestamps for the public API. 10M active keys, limit 100 requests/min, Redis memory is 41 GB and growing, ZADD/ZREMRANGEBYSCORE CPU is 70%. They say "it is the most accurate".

title: Hot key and abusive client
text: How do you protect the shard and the other users? One IP sends 110k requests/s at POST /login . Redis Cluster has 3 primaries; one is at 100% CPU, the others at 15%. Limiter latency p99 went from 1 ms to 90 ms for everyone whose keys live on that shard. redis-2 cpu 100% ops 118k/s slowlog: EVALSHA rl:ip:203.0.113.9:login redis-1 cpu 14% ops 17k/s redis-3 cpu 16% ops 18k/s

title: Capacity and design for stated scale
text: Does the design still work? What changes? Today: 500M API requests/day, average 5.8k/s, peak 17k/s, 10M active keys, one Redis primary with replica handles it with 12% CPU. Next year a partner program will make it 10x: 170k/s peak, 100M active keys. p99 limiter budget is 2 ms; latency budget on the network is about 0.5 ms intra-region.

title: Changing algorithm under live traffic
text: How do you migrate without breaking customers or the system? Customers currently get a fixed window limit of 1,000/hour. You are moving to a token bucket rate 1,000/h, burst 100 to stop boundary bursts. Two weeks after the change plan was announced, support is worried: customers have built batch jobs that fire at the top of each hour and rely on getting all 1,000 at once.

title: Retry storm and Retry-After
text: Write the post-incident analysis: causes, actions, and what you change in the API contract. Post-incident: a deploy slowed the API; the limiter started returning 429 to many clients. Instead of recovering, load tripled for 15 minutes. Logs: 11:03:00 requests/s 18k 429s/s 1.1k 11:03:30 requests/s 41k 429s/s 24k 11:04:00 requests/s 55k 429s/s 38k retry-after header: absent client sdk v1.2: retries immediately, up to 5 times, no backoff The limiter latency stayed at 1 ms; the app servers fell over from the extra connection handling.

title: Consistent hashing and virtual nodes
text: Why does a distributed key-value store use consistent hashing with virtual nodes instead of hash key % N ? With modulo, changing N remaps almost every key, so adding a node causes a massive data shuffle. Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a ring; a key belongs to the next node clockwise, so adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the keys. Virtual nodes 128 to 256 points per physical node even out the load and spread a failed node's data across many peers.

title: Quorums and vector clocks
text: With N=3, W=2, R=2, do you get strong consistency? How are conflicting concurrent writes detected and resolved? R + W N guarantees that read and write sets overlap, so a read sees at least one replica with the latest acknowledged write, but it is not linearizability: sloppy quorums, concurrent writes, clock skew and failed partial writes can still produce stale or conflicting reads. Concurrent writes are detected with vector clocks, and resolved by the application merging siblings, by last-write-wins simple but loses writes or by CRDTs.

title: Capacity estimate
text: Do the math and size the cluster. Design the cluster for 10B keys, 1 KB average value, RF=3, peak 200k ops/s with 80% reads, p99 under 10 ms. Nodes have 2 TB usable SSD. The interviewer says "give me a node count and tell me what the constraint is."

title: Tombstones and zombie data
text: Explain what happened and fix it. Users report deleted records coming back. A node was down for 12 days during a data-centre issue and rejoined yesterday. Config: gc grace seconds = 10 days, repairs not run on schedule for that range. nodetool status: node7 UN back 20h ago read key=user:991 CL=ONE - returns deleted record from node7 read key=user:991 CL=QUORUM - returns record on 1 of 3, tombstone on 2 of 3 - deleted

title: Choose consistency per use case
text: What do you recommend? Two teams want to use the store. Team A runs a shopping cart: "never refuse an add-to-cart". Team B runs account balances for a wallet and wants "no double-spend, ever". Both ask if they can use the same cluster with the same settings N=3, W=1, R=1 .

title: Hot partition and replica overload
text: What do you do now and what is the long-term design? During a flash sale, one product key product:777 gets 60k reads/s. The three replicas holding it show CPU 98%, p99 latency 450 ms, while the other 33 nodes are at 20%. node11 cpu 98% reads/s 20,100 p99 430ms node19 cpu 97% reads/s 19,800 node27 cpu 98% reads/s 20,000 others cpu 20% Someone suggests adding more nodes to the cluster.

title: LSM compaction lag
text: Diagnose, stabilise and prevent a repeat. Read p99 climbed from 6 ms to 70 ms over 5 days. Disk usage rose from 55% to 88%. pending compactions: 1,840 was 12 sstables per read p99 : 34 was 4 compaction throughput limit: 16 MB/s write rate: 3x higher since a backfill job started 6 days ago tombstone scans per read: 9,000 on table events by user

title: Replacing a failed node
text: Walk through the recovery. Rack 2 loses power. Three nodes are down for 4 hours; the rack comes back. Meanwhile coordinators used sloppy quorums and hinted handoff. Hints expire after 3 hours. Writes continued at 40k/s during the outage. The interviewer asks how you bring the cluster back to full consistency without a customer-visible impact.

title: Log vs queue
text: What is the difference between a Kafka-style log and a classic queue like RabbitMQ or SQS, and why does it matter for design? A log is append-only and retained; each consumer group keeps its own offset and can replay old messages, and many groups read the same data independently. A classic queue deletes a message after it is acked, supports per-message redelivery and often priorities, but you cannot replay. I pick a log when I need replay, fan-out to many consumers and high throughput; a queue when I need per-message ack, delays or priorities.

title: ISR and acks
text: Explain acks, ISR and min.insync.replicas. What settings give you "no committed message is lost when one broker dies"? Each partition has a leader and followers; the ISR is the set of followers caught up with the leader. A message is committed once all ISR members have it. With RF=3, acks=all , min.insync.replicas=2 and unclean leader election disabled, any single broker can die with no loss of committed data and no downtime; if two die, writes stop safety over availability but committed data remains.

title: Capacity estimate
text: Size brokers, partitions and storage. State what you size for peak vs average. Peak 1M messages/s, 1 KB each, average load is 100k msg/s, retention 7 days, RF=3, three consumer groups read everything. Brokers handle about 100 MB/s write each including replication conservative .

title: Consumer lag and rebalance storms
text: Diagnose and fix. Order-processing consumers in group billing show lag climbing and processing pausing in waves every few minutes. records-lag-max: 2.1M was 5k rebalance count last hour: 38 consumer log: "Member ... sending LeaveGroup request ... consumer poll timeout has expired" max.poll.interval.ms=300000 max.poll.records=500 avg processing per record: 1.4 s after a new fraud-check API call was added

title: Hot partition and ordering
text: What do you change? Topic orders has 24 partitions keyed by customerId . One enterprise customer generates 35% of traffic. That partition's broker is at 90% disk throughput and the consumer for it lags by 40 minutes while 23 others are idle. Business requires order of events per order, not per customer.

title: Exactly-once vs duplicates
text: What do you promise and what do you build? A payment service consumes payment-requests and writes to Postgres and a bank API. The product manager says: "we need exactly-once". During a broker leader change last week, 312 requests were processed twice and 41 customers were charged twice.

title: Broker failure and under-replicated partitions
text: What happens, and what do you do? RF=3, acks=all , min.insync.replicas=2 . Broker 4 and broker 7 both in rack B go down at 03:10. Alerts: UnderReplicatedPartitions: 112 OfflinePartitionsCount: 0 producer errors: NotEnoughReplicasException on 31 partitions producer errors: none on the rest Some partitions had both followers on brokers 4 and 7.

title: Partition count change under live traffic
text: How do you go from 12 to 48 partitions? Topic clicks has 12 partitions, 40 MB/s, consumers cannot keep up and you need 48 parallel consumers. Messages are keyed by sessionId and downstream aggregation depends on per-session order. You cannot lose data or order, and cannot have downtime.

title: Top-K per trie node
text: How do you return the top 5 suggestions for a prefix quickly? Why not just traverse the trie subtree? Store the precomputed top K at every trie node. A query then walks as many nodes as the prefix is long and returns the stored list: O prefix length . Traversing the subtree and sorting is far too slow for a short prefix like "a", which sits above millions of queries.

title: Offline index build and atomic swap
text: Why build the suggestion index offline in snapshots, and how do you publish a new one without downtime or a bad release? Reads are the hot path and need a simple, immutable, in-memory index. So search events flow through Kafka to an aggregation job that counts queries, filters them and builds a versioned snapshot in S3. Servers load it beside the old one and swap a pointer atomically, and I keep the last few snapshots for instant rollback. The price is freshness, which I cover with a small real-time trending overlay.

title: Estimates and sizing
text: Estimate QPS, index size and answer the sharding question. 100M DAU, 500M searches/day, average query 20 characters, users get suggestions after the first character with client debounce of about 150 ms. Interviewer: "does this need sharding?"

title: Offensive suggestions
text: What do you do now, and what do you change? A news event makes an offensive, defamatory query trend; it appears as suggestion 2 for a person's name. Hourly index build is 40 minutes from finishing and then publishes. Legal wants it gone in minutes. Index version age is 14 hours a build failed overnight and nobody noticed . index version age: 14h last good build: 2026-11-08T22:00 blocklist file updated: 2026-11-09T11:58 not applied; applied at build time only

title: Caching layers
text: How do you cut cost without hurting latency or quality? The suggestion fleet has 40 servers and costs a lot; peak is 90k req/s. CDN hit rate is only 22%, and p99 at origin is 45 ms. Cache key currently includes userId , timestamp and the full query string. GET /v1/suggest?q=iph&limit=5&lang=en&userId=42& =1731150000123 Cache-Control: no-store

title: Freshness vs cost
text: Pick one and justify, including reversibility. Product wants "trending now" suggestions within 2 minutes of a spike election night, a celebrity event . Current design rebuilds hourly. Engineering is split: A move the whole pipeline to streaming and rebuild every 2 minutes; B keep hourly snapshots and add a real-time overlay. Budget is limited; the index is 12 GB.

title: Multi-language sharding
text: Design the new serving topology. The product expands from English to 30 languages. Index grows from 12 GB to 400 GB. Peak is 400k req/s globally, distributed over regions. One engineer proposes sharding by first character; another proposes sharding by language and region. Latency target stays p99 under 50 ms at the server.

title: Bad ranking release
text: Write the post-incident actions. Post-incident: a ranking change recency boost x3 shipped with the 14:00 snapshot. Click-through on suggestions fell from 31% to 22% over 3 hours, and searches per session dropped 6%. It took 3 hours for anyone to notice; rollback took 20 minutes because snapshots were pruned to the last one only. suggestion ctr: 31% - 22% 14:00 - 17:00 index version: 2026-11-09-14 prev snapshot deleted at 14:10 alert: none configured on CTR

title: What a CDN does, pull vs push
text: What does a CDN actually do for a website, and what is the difference between a pull CDN and a push CDN? I'd say a CDN keeps copies of content on servers close to users, so a request is answered from a nearby edge instead of travelling to the origin. That cuts latency Mumbai to Virginia is about 200 ms round trip, Mumbai to a Mumbai edge about 5 ms and keeps most traffic off the origin. In a pull CDN the edge fetches from the origin on the first miss and caches it. In a push CDN the customer uploads content to the edge ahead of time. Pull is the web default; push suits large, predictable media.

title: Scoping the problem
text: How do you start? The interviewer says only: "Design a CDN for our company." The company has a marketing site mostly static , a logged-in web app, a public JSON API and a growing video library. No other numbers are given.

title: Cache keys, Vary, TTL and revalidation
text: How does a CDN decide two requests are "the same" object, and how does it decide how long to keep it? Where does this go wrong? The cache key is scheme plus host plus path plus a normalised query plus the headers I choose, for example Accept-Encoding . Freshness comes from Cache-Control : max-age for everyone, s-maxage for shared caches such as the CDN. After expiry the edge revalidates with If-None-Match and usually gets a cheap 304. It goes wrong when the key is too wide tracking parameters, Vary: User-Agent so the cache fragments, or too narrow so one user's variant is served to another.

title: Hit ratio collapse
text: What do you do, and what do you suspect? A CDN-fronted shop normally shows a 96% edge hit ratio. After a 14:05 release the dashboard shows: time hit ratio origin rps origin cpu p99 ttfb 14:00 0.96 14k 22% 48 ms 14:10 0.31 240k 91% 1,900 ms The release changed the front-end bundle, added a tracking cookie via Set-Cookie: sid=... on every response, and the team also upgraded the origin framework. The CDN vendor status page is green.

title: Capacity for a live event
text: Do the math and say what you would verify. A streaming customer expects 10M concurrent viewers for a live match at an average of 4 Mbps, with 4 s segments in 5 renditions. Your edge server has 2 x 100 Gbps NICs and about 100 Gbps effective throughput. You run roughly 50 PoPs. The finance lead asks how many edge servers are needed and how much traffic hits the origin.

title: PoP failure and cold cache
text: What is happening, what do you do right now, and what would you change? At 20:12 a power event takes the Mumbai PoP offline. Anycast withdraws the route and traffic moves to Chennai and Singapore. Over the next minutes: 20:12 mumbai rps 0 chennai rps 40k - 95k singapore rps 30k - 70k 20:13 chennai hit ratio 0.95 - 0.62 origin rps 12k - 118k 20:14 origin 5xx 0.2% - 9% chennai p99 ttfb 60ms - 1,400ms Chennai CPU is at 88%. Origin is a single region.

title: Routing choice
text: Which do you choose and how do you justify the decision gravity? You are choosing how users reach edges: DNS steering authoritative DNS picks a PoP from the resolver IP or EDNS Client Subnet, TTL 30 s or anycast one IP announced from every PoP via BGP . Telemetry shows 18% of your Indian users resolve through a public resolver abroad. A past attack of 600 Gbps saturated one PoP. Some customers have long-lived WebSocket and large downloads.

title: Private data leak
text: Run the post-incident review: cause, contributing factors, and the controls you add. For 35 minutes yesterday, about 1,200 users of a banking-style dashboard saw another user's account summary. A rule added for performance cached /dashboard for 5 minutes. A log excerpt: GET /dashboard cookie: session=abc 200 x-cache: MISS cache-control: public, max-age=300 GET /dashboard cookie: session=xyz 200 x-cache: HIT age: 143 The origin had recently been upgraded; its default response header changed from private to public .

title: Inverted index vs SQL LIKE
text: Why can't we just search products with WHERE title LIKE '%shoe%' in the main database? What does a search engine do differently? A leading-wildcard LIKE cannot use a normal B-tree index, so the database scans every row; at 50M products that takes seconds and burns the primary's CPU. A search engine builds an inverted index: for each token it keeps a list of document IDs. A query looks up the tokens and intersects the lists, so cost depends on matches, not on catalog size. It also scores by relevance BM25 , handles typos, synonyms and facets. The catalog stays in the primary DB; the index is a derived copy I can rebuild.

title: Scoping search
text: What do you ask, and what do you decide about consistency? "Design product search for our store." No numbers, no description of what is searchable. The business owner mentions "price and stock must always be right".

title: Filters, facets and scoring
text: Explain how a query like "red running shoes" with brand and price filters, plus facet counts, is executed. Why are filters different from the text match? The text part is scored BM25 on title and description with boosts . Filters like brand = nike and a price range go into a filter context: they don't affect the score, so the engine can cache their result as a bitset and apply it quickly. Facet counts are aggregations over the matching documents, usually on keyword fields with doc values. High-cardinality facets, like seller ID, are expensive, so I limit them to the top N or approximate.

title: Pagination
text: Find the problems and redesign pagination. A bot and some real users scroll deep into results. The API is GET /v1/search?q=shoes&from=24000&size=24 . Logs: ERROR Result window is too large, from + size must be less than or equal to: 10000 but was 24024 . See the scroll api for a more efficient way to request large data sets. search p99: 180 ms - 2.4 s during the bot's crawl, data nodes CPU 85% Customers also report that page 3 sometimes repeats items from page 2 when prices change.

title: Sizing shards and nodes
text: Size the cluster and say what you'd double-check. The business is acquiring a competitor: the catalog goes from 50M to 100M products and peak search QPS from 20k to 40k. Documents average 3 KB indexed. Target shard size 20-40 GB, one replica. A previous load test showed that a set of nodes holding one full copy of the index every primary shard on its own node sustained about 4k QPS at p99 under 200 ms. That number is an assumption from the test and should be re-measured.

title: Index drift and ordering
text: Diagnose the drift and explain how you repair and prevent it. After a Kafka broker outage and recovery, customers report items showing "in stock" in search but sold out at checkout, and some prices are old. Metrics: indexer consumer lag: 0 recovered search p99: 120 ms normal index doc count: 50,012,340 catalog rows: 50,016,905 product p 9981: DB version 417 price 3295 / index version 412 price 3495 indexer log: 4,100 events rejected "version conflict" in last hour

title: Analyzer change under live traffic
