text: How do you ship this without downtime or relevance regressions? Search quality review says "running" does not match "run", and the team wants a better stemmer plus a synonym list. The index is 150 GB in 6 primary shards, serving 20k QPS. The same release should also move to 12 shards because shards are now 25 GB at 100M documents planned. A sale starts in 3 weeks.

title: Heap pressure and tail latency
text: What is the cause and what do you do? During an afternoon, search p99 climbs from 180 ms to 4 s. Data nodes show: node-7 jvm old gen 91% gc pause 3.8 s search rejected 1,204 node-3 jvm old gen 88% gc pause 2.9 s bulk indexing: running since 13:00 nightly feed rerun by a seller cpu 40% new dashboard widget: facet "seller" terms agg size 10000 enabled at 12:40 Traffic is normal at 18k QPS.

title: The crawl loop and why the frontier matters
text: Describe the basic loop of a web crawler. Why is a plain FIFO queue not good enough for the URL frontier? The loop is: take a URL from the frontier, fetch the page, parse out text and links, dedupe the links, and put new ones back into the frontier, while storing the raw page for indexing. A single FIFO queue fails because it has no priority news home pages matter more than a forgotten archive , no per-host politeness it may hit one site 100 times a second , and it is a single machine's queue for billions of URLs. So the frontier is priority queues feeding per-host queues, partitioned across machines.

title: URL dedupe with a Bloom filter
text: Why does the HashSet not work, and how would you size and use a Bloom filter? Your crawler has seen about 5B unique URLs. A teammate proposes an in-memory HashSet<String for dedupe. URLs average 80 bytes. You can afford roughly 10 GB of RAM across the dedupe tier. A 1% false-positive rate is acceptable for low-priority URLs.

title: Politeness with front and back queues
text: How does a crawler stay polite to each website while still fetching 400+ pages per second? Politeness means never hitting a host faster than its crawl delay, and obeying robots.txt. I use front queues ordered by importance and back queues, one per host. A min-heap keyed by "next allowed fetch time" tells fetchers which host may be hit now. Because 400 fetches/s with a 1 s delay needs at least 400 distinct hosts active, the heap ensures workers always have a ready host. I partition the frontier by host hash so one machine owns a host and no distributed lock is needed.

title: Overloading a host
text: Explain what happened and fix it. A site owner emails you: your bot took their server down. Your logs: host: shop.example.org requests/min: 6,300 105 req/s status 503: 38% avg latency 4.1 s frontier shard 3: host queue depth 2.1M lease timeouts: 9,800/h robots.txt for host: fetched 3 days ago, Crawl-delay: 2 You had recently increased the fetcher fleet from 20 to 80 workers and moved from host-hash to URL-hash partitioning "for better balance".

title: Crawler traps
text: What is this, and how do you stop it and prevent it? Dashboards show the seen-set growing 3x faster than usual, with fetch throughput flat: host: events.example.net new urls/hour: 4.2M distinct pages content hash : 1,900 sample urls: /calendar/2031/04/17?view=month&session=a81f /calendar/2031/04/18?view=month&session=c92b /calendar/2031/04/19?view=month&session=e07d frontier depth for host: 14 - 4,100

title: 10x scale
text: What numbers change, what breaks first, and what do you redesign? The crawler works at 1B pages per month about 400 pages/s average, 1,000/s peak . The business now wants 10B pages per month with the same freshness policy. Average page 500 KB raw, about 100 KB gzipped. Fetcher nodes realistically reach about 100 pages/s each.

title: Mega-host imbalance
text: Is this a bug? What do you change, and what is the decision gravity? Frontier partitioning is by host hash across 64 shards. One shard holds 10x the queued URLs of the others because a single large site tens of millions of pages landed on it. shard 17: queued 410M fetch rate 12/s oldest URL age 19 days shard 18: queued 38M fetch rate 110/s oldest URL age 2 hours The big site allows only 1 request/second per the crawl delay and this is correct policy.

title: Freshness and JS-rendered pages
text: How do you meet the requirement without blowing the budget? Product now needs news sites updated within 5 minutes and a set of 20,000 e-commerce domains that render content client-side with JavaScript. Currently every page is recrawled on a fixed 7-day cycle with a plain HTTP fetch. A headless browser render costs about 10-50x a plain fetch. The budget allows 20% more compute.

title: Adaptive bitrate streaming
text: Why don't video platforms just serve one MP4 file? What is adaptive bitrate streaming and how does a player use it? One big file forces every viewer to the same quality: too heavy for a weak network, wasteful on a strong one. With adaptive bitrate HLS or MPEG-DASH the platform transcodes each video into a ladder of renditions say 144p to 4K , cuts each into 2-6 second segments, and publishes a manifest listing them. The player measures its throughput and buffer and picks the rendition for each next segment, switching at segment boundaries. Segments are small, immutable files, so a CDN can cache them for a year.

title: Resumable upload
text: Redesign the upload path. Creators upload files of up to 5 GB over mobile networks. Today the app does one PUT of the whole file to your API server. Support tickets: "upload failed at 92%, had to start over". The API servers also hit 90% CPU during the evening upload window.

title: Transcoding as a parallel DAG
text: How would you design the transcoding pipeline so a 10-minute video is ready in about a minute, and retries are safe? I don't encode a video as one job. I validate it, split it at keyframes into GOP-aligned chunks, encode each chunk for each rendition in parallel across many workers, then merge and package into HLS/DASH segments with a manifest and thumbnails. Tasks are idempotent, keyed by videoId, rendition, chunk , so a retry is harmless. A queue delivers tasks with visibility timeouts. If a video fails three times I mark it FAILED and notify the creator.

title: Codec choice and egress cost
text: What do you decide? Egress is the largest line in your bill. The team proposes encoding every upload in AV1, which is much smaller than H.264 but costs far more CPU to encode assume 10x; verify with your own benchmark . Data: 95% of videos get fewer than 100 views in their lifetime, while the top 2% account for most watch time. Many older devices lack AV1 hardware decode.

title: Ingest and transcode capacity
text: Do the math and call out the assumptions. The platform receives 500 hours of video per minute, average source 1080p at 8 Mbps. A rendition ladder takes about 5x the realtime work of the source, and one CPU core encodes 1080p at roughly 0.75x realtime a benchmark to verify . The CFO asks for the daily storage, ingest bandwidth and core count.

title: Transcoding backlog
text: Mitigate, diagnose, and fix the design. After a festival, uploads triple. Creators complain that videos stay in "Processing" for hours. transcode queue: depth 1.9M tasks oldest task age: 5h 40m workers: 12,000 autoscaler max worker task time p50: 38 s p99: 9 min retries/hour: 41,000 upload service: healthy object store: healthy top producers: 3 channels uploading 4K 3-hour streams

title: Viral video and cold caches
text: What is happening and how do you fix it now and structurally? A video goes viral in a region that had no prior traffic. Within 3 minutes: region sa-east: edge hit ratio 0.97 - 0.58 origin egress: 40 Gbit/s - 700 Gbit/s origin object store 503 SlowDown rate: 12% rebuffer ratio: 1.1% - 9% segments requested: 1080p/seg 00001..00180, same objects, from 340 edge servers The CDN hierarchy is edge - regional - origin, with no shield and no request collapsing configured.

title: View counts and hot rows
text: What is wrong, and what is the right design for counts? A code review shows the play handler doing this on every view: UPDATE videos SET views = views + 1 WHERE video id = 'v 8Hq2'; During a premiere the metrics read: videos table: row lock wait p99 6.2 s db cpu 35% active connections 1,900 / 2,000 v 8Hq2 plays: 90,000 per second playback API p99: 8 s was 120 ms Metadata reads for video pages are also served from the same database.

title: Delivery semantics and push vs poll
text: For live comments on a stream with millions of viewers, should delivery be guaranteed and ordered? How should viewers receive new comments: push or polling? Best-effort. No viewer can read 50,000 comments a second, so guaranteed, ordered delivery of every comment to every viewer is extremely costly and useless. I'd sample on the server, batch, and tolerate a few lost comments, but never lose the whole chat. For receiving, naive polling every second from 25M viewers is 25M requests/s. I'd push over WebSockets or SSE , or for the very biggest streams use polling of CDN-cached batches 2 s TTL if a latency of 3-5 s is acceptable.

title: Fan-out bandwidth
text: Show why that fails and size a workable design. Mega-event: 25M concurrent viewers, 50k comments/s at peak, 100 bytes per comment. A gateway box holds about 100k connections a figure to verify with a load test . The product owner says "just send everything to everyone".

title: Sampling, batching and ordering
text: Where in the pipeline do you sample and batch comments, how do you choose which ones to show, and how do you order them? A stream aggregator reads that stream's Kafka partition and, per 500 ms window, picks the top K comments by a score: recency, author priority moderator, creator, subscriber , mentions and engagement, after de-duplicating spam like repeated "GG GG GG". It writes one batch to the pub/sub tier, and gateways fan the same bytes out to their sockets. Order is by time-sortable id ULID or Snowflake within a batch; strict global order across partitions isn't needed.

title: Reconnect storm
text: What happened and how do you stabilise and prevent it? You deploy a new gateway version during a live match, restarting 250 gateways in two waves. Metrics: 14:02:10 gateways restarted 14:02:12 connection accepts/s: 8k - 410k gateway cpu: 35% - 98% 14:02:20 tls handshake failures 22% LB 5xx 14% 14:02:40 clients retrying every 1 s with no backoff; connected users 25M - 6M ulimit -n and kernel settings were verified earlier this week.

title: WebSocket vs CDN polling
text: Which do you choose and what is the decision gravity? For a one-off 25M-viewer stream the infra team estimates 250 WebSocket gateways plus a relay tree. A product engineer suggests: "Let clients poll /comments?since= every 3 seconds, and let the CDN cache the response with a 2 s TTL." Latency requirement: comments visible within about 2 s p99, but a stakeholder says 4-5 s would be acceptable for this event only. Infra budget is tight and the team has never operated that many sockets.

title: Bot raid and moderation
text: Write the review: what failed and which controls do you add? During a streamer's launch, a raid posted abusive spam. Timeline: 20:00 new accounts < 1 h old comments/s: 40 - 9,500 spam share of sampled comments: 63% 20:03 sync keyword filter catches 18% async ML classifier lag: 7 min 20:05 moderators delete 4,000 comments; deletes reach viewers after 45-90 s 20:07 legit viewers complain they see only spam; creator's own comments often not displayed

title: Why a sorted set
text: You are asked to build a live leaderboard for 50M players. Why not just run SELECT ... ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 100 and COUNT WHERE score x against a SQL table? Rank means "how many players have a higher score", and in SQL that is a range count over millions of rows per request. Even with an index it is O n in the worst case, and at 100k reads/s it dies. A Redis sorted set keeps members ordered in a skiplist with span counters, so update and rank are both O log n , around 20 comparisons for 50M members. I keep SQL as the durable source of truth and treat Redis as a rebuildable view.

title: Tie-breaking
text: Two players both have 1,000 points. Who is ranked higher in Redis, and how do you make "first to reach the score wins" deterministic? Redis orders equal scores by member string, lexicographically, which is arbitrary for users. To get "earlier wins" I encode a composite score: points 2^20 + WINDOW - secondsSinceStart , so an earlier time gives a bigger low part. Scores are doubles with 53 bits of exact integer precision, so the points part gets at most 33 bits about 8.6 billion . I must decide this before launch because every stored score changes shape.

title: Windows and TTL
text: What is happening and how do you fix it without losing live data? Daily and weekly boards use keys lb:global:d:<date and lb:global:w:<week . Redis used memory rose from 6 GB to 21 GB over three weeks and the box is at 85 percent of maxmemory with noeviction . Write errors OOM command not allowed have started for the score updater. A recent change moved window rollover into a nightly cron. 127.0.0.1:6379 INFO memory used memory human:20.9G maxmemory human:24G 127.0.0.1:6379 DBSIZE integer 41 127.0.0.1:6379 TTL lb:global:d:2026-10-20 integer -1 Traffic and QPS are unchanged. The team suspects a memory leak in the client library.

A new game launches and the plan says 500M members, 200k score updates/s and 1M reads/s at peak. Every update writes three keys daily, weekly, all-time . Read p99 SLO is 50 ms.

Rank queries SELECT count FROM scores WHERE score $1 take 1.5 s and the DB is at 70 percent CPU at 3k rank reads/s. You must move ranks to Redis with zero downtime during a live season, and there is no event log today.

text: Run the review: what failed, how do you repair the board, and what changes? Postmortem: for 40 minutes 9 accounts held ranks 1-9 with scores near 4 million, where the previous top was 99,120. The score API accepted delta values up to 450,000 from one game-server token. The eventId dedupe blocked replays but each call used a fresh id. A client mod had found a leaked staging token still accepted in production. Paid rewards are distributed at week end. POST /v1/boards/global-weekly/scores token=gs-staging-01 delta=450000 eventId=e aa1... 200 {"score": 3998020, "rank": 1}

title: Count-Min Sketch
text: How does a Count-Min Sketch count items, why does it take the minimum of its cells, and why can it only overestimate? It is a 2-D array of d rows by w columns of counters. To add an item I hash it with d different hash functions and increment one cell per row. To estimate, I read its d cells and take the minimum. Collisions with other items only add to a cell, never subtract, so every cell is at least the true count and the minimum is the least-polluted one. The estimate is at most true + epsilon N with probability 1 - delta , where w = e/epsilon and d = ln 1/delta .

title: Trending versus popular
text: " love" has the highest count every hour. Why is it not trending, and how do you rank what is trending? Trending means a surge relative to normal, not the biggest count. I keep a fast window count and a slow baseline per item, and rank by how far the current window exceeds expectation, for example current - expected / sqrt expected + 1 or a ratio against the same hour over the last 7 days. Always-popular items have high expected values so they score low. I also filter spam and blocklisted topics before publishing.

title: Scale and sketch sizing
text: Does the sketch still work at 10x, and what is the sizing and architecture change? Today: 1M events/s peak, sketch per window, region of w=2^20, d=4 16 MB . The product now wants 10M events/s, 200 regions, windows of 1 min, 1 h and 24 h. A reviewer says "the error bound will eat our top 100". Current hourly global N is 3.6 billion; the 100th item has about 400,000 hits in the hour.

title: Hot key
text: Diagnose and fix without restarting the pipeline from scratch. During a cup final, trending freshness jumps from 3 s to 4 minutes. Kafka consumer lag is high on exactly one of 32 partitions; the other 31 are at zero lag. Worker CPU for that partition's consumer is at 100 percent and its heap is 90 percent full. group trend-workers partition 17 lag 18,400,000 group trend-workers partition 0..16,18..31 lag 0 Topic is keyed by hash item ; cupfinal is getting 12 percent of all events.

title: Publishing results
text: Why did nothing alert, and how do you harden publishing? Users report the trending list is "stuck" on yesterday's evening topics. The API is healthy p99 8 ms and returns 200. The aggregator pod was OOM-killed 40 minutes ago and its replacement is crash-looping on startup. Redis shows: GET trend:global:1h - {"computedAt":"2026-11-09T13:20:04Z", ...} TTL trend:global:1h - -1 Stream workers and Kafka are fine.

title: Spam and distinct counting
text: Redesign counting so a coordinated burst does not dominate, within memory and latency limits. A political hashtag vote2026xyz is rank 1 in trending, with 480,000 posts in an hour. Moderators say 94 percent of its posts come from about 600 accounts. Meanwhile rainstorm has 210,000 posts from 190,000 distinct accounts and is rank 6. Users complain the trends are being gamed. Each item currently has a sketch count only.

title: Exactness and late events
text: What do you propose: pure stream, Lambda or Kappa, and how do you handle late data? The ads team wants the trending feed to also drive a paid "sponsored trend" product with invoices, so they ask for "exact" counts for the last hour and an audit trail. Mobile clients upload events up to 10 minutes late when offline. The current system is streaming Kafka, Flink with sketches and a 30 s watermark; late events are dropped.

title: Spot the bug
text: Find the bugs and give a correct design. A worker keeps a sketch and a "top K" heap. In production the top-10 is often a single item repeated, and old items never leave. Review: K = 10 cms = CMS heap = estimate, item def on event item : cms.add item est = cms.est item if len heap < K or est heap 0 0 : heapq.heappush heap, est, item if len heap K: heapq.heappop heap def top : return sorted heap, reverse=True Traffic: worldcup gets 100k events/s.

title: Location versus trips
text: Why would you store live driver locations and trips in two different systems for a ride-hailing service? Driver locations are a huge, lossy, short-lived firehose: millions of pings per second where losing one is harmless because the next arrives in 4 seconds. Trips are low volume but must be correct and durable: no double assignment, no lost payment. So locations go to an in-memory geo index sharded by city, and trips go to a transactional database with a state machine. Putting both in one SQL table would push a million writes per second through the database that guards your money.

title: Geo index choices
text: Compare geohash, quadtree and H3 for finding drivers near a rider. What goes wrong at cell boundaries? A geo index buckets the earth into cells so "who is near me" is a lookup of my cell plus neighbours instead of a scan. Geohash interleaves lat/lng bits into a base-32 string; same prefix means same rectangle, simple and in Redis GEO, but rectangles distort and two close points can have different prefixes. A quadtree splits a cell when it holds more than N drivers, so it adapts to density but needs rebalancing as drivers move. H3 uses hexagons with equidistant neighbours, so a k-ring query is uniform. Whatever I pick, I query the rider's cell and its neighbours, because the nearest driver may be 10 m away in the next cell.

title: Ingestion capacity
text: Do the numbers, say how many gateways and index shards you need, and challenge the one-cluster plan. You are sizing the location tier for 5M drivers online at peak, one ping per 4 s while idle, one per 1 s on trip assume 20 percent on trip . A candidate answer says "use Redis GEO, one cluster". Ping is 40 B payload, about 100 B on the wire. A gateway holds about 150k connections.

title: Double booking
text: What is the bug, and how do you make assignment safe without a global lock? Support reports that two riders were offered the same driver in the same second, and one driver app showed two offers. The matching service runs 8 workers. Code under review: // per-driver state lives in a shared in-memory map on the shard boolean tryOffer String driverId, String tripId { Driver d = drivers.get driverId ; if d.status == Status.AVAILABLE { d.status = Status.OFFERED; d.tripId = tripId; push driverId, tripId ; return true; } return false; } Kotlin equivalent: fun tryOffer driverId: String, tripId: String : Boolean { val d = drivers driverId !! if d.status == Status.AVAILABLE { d.status = Status.OFFERED; d.tripId = tripId; push driverId, tripId ; return true } return false }

title: Reconnect storm
text: Diagnose, mitigate and prevent. At 18:02 a gateway deploy restarts all 40 location gateways in one wave. Within a minute riders see cars frozen on the map and "nearby drivers" shows cars that left 10 minutes ago. Metrics: gateway connections 4.9M - 0.3M - 4.6M over 6 min kafka ping ingest lag 0 s - 95 s newest ping age p50 4 s - 71 s location shard CPU 40% - 97% The CDN and API gateway look healthy; a recent change reduced the staleness TTL to 5 minutes.

title: ETA cost and latency
text: What is the daily cost ceiling and how do you restructure ETA computation? Matching queries about 5,000 nearby searches per second at peak. For each, the service calls a third-party Directions API for the top 10 candidates. Assume list price of 5 USD per 1,000 calls verify current pricing . p99 request-to-offer is 7.8 s against a 5 s target; the vendor p95 is 220 ms per call and calls are made serially.

title: Hot cell and batched matching
text: What changes in the architecture and the matching policy? A concert ends at 23:00 and 25,000 riders open the app within five minutes at one stadium, where about 2,500 drivers are within 3 km. The shard that owns that geography is at 100 percent CPU; match latency p95 goes to 40 s, and drivers are offered rides they decline because pickups are far from the gate. Greedy sequential matching assigns each rider the nearest driver.

title: Cell scheme migration
text: Plan the migration and say what you refuse to change. The system started with geohash precision 6 cells keyed in every shard, offer, and analytics table. Cells near the equator are fine but rectangles distort, boundary misses cause "no cars nearby" complaints, and the team wants H3 resolution 8. 120 cities run in production; you cannot take downtime and surge pricing, matching and analytics all read cell ids.

title: Saga versus one transaction
text: Why is a food order modelled as a saga with a state machine instead of one database transaction? One ACID transaction cannot span a payment provider, a restaurant tablet and a rider who may take 40 minutes. So I model the order as a state machine PLACED, PAID, ACCEPTED, PREPARING, READY, PICKED UP, DELIVERED, plus CANCELLED/REJECTED , advance it step by step with compare-and-set, and give every state a timeout and a compensation void the authorisation, refund . I orchestrate it from one service so timeouts and debugging live in one place.

title: Outbox and CAS
text: What is the transactional outbox, and how does compare-and-set on order state stop races? Show the SQL. The outbox writes the order state change and an event row in the same DB transaction, and a relay publishes outbox rows to Kafka, so I never have "saved but not published". Compare-and-set updates state only if the current state and version match, so two concurrent transitions cannot both succeed: one updates one row, the other updates zero rows and gets an error.

title: Stuck orders
text: Diagnose and fix; what is the red herring? Complaints: 1,900 customers in the last hour were charged but see "waiting for restaurant". Dashboard excerpts: orders in PAID older than 5 min: 1,873 orders in ACCEPTED: normal payment auth success rate: 99.2% order-service deploy: 14:42 new outbox relay kafka topic order-events: produce errors 0.3% Restaurants say tablets never rang.

text: Where is the real load, and what do you scale or throttle? Average 5M orders/day, 70 percent in two 2-hour peaks. A cup final is expected to produce 10x dinner load in some cities. Browse sessions run about 40 per order. The proposal: "autoscale all services 10x". Cost budget does not allow 10x compute everywhere.

title: Idempotent ordering and quote
text: Redesign the API contract and explain the failure cases. On a flaky mobile network a customer taps "Place order" three times. Support sees 112 duplicate orders last week and 40 complaints "price changed at checkout". Current flow: POST /orders accepts items and recomputes price at the server at order time; no idempotency key. POST /v1/orders {"restaurantId":"r 12","items": ... ,"paymentMethodId":"pm 3"} 201 {"orderId":"o 9001"} client times out, retries 201 {"orderId":"o 9002"}

title: Dispatch timing
text: What do you change in dispatch, and what do you measure? Rider idle time at restaurants is rising and order delivery time p90 is 52 min versus a 40 min target. Data: avg rider wait at restaurant: 11.4 min was 5.1 dispatch trigger: at ORDER ACCEPTED restaurant-reported prep: 12 min actual median: 19 min dinner rider travel to restaurant: 6 min The team wants to add more riders.

title: Payments
text: Choose a payment flow and defend it. Finance wants to charge at order time to cut payment risk. Ops says restaurants reject 6 percent of orders after payment out of stock , producing refunds that take 5 to 7 days and about 12,000 support tickets a month. Most customers use UPI or wallets, which do not support card-style holds, and cards authorisations expire after about 7 days.

title: Discovery freshness and cache
text: What went wrong and how do you fix it? After launching personalised ranking, restaurant list p95 rises from 140 ms to 900 ms and the search cluster CPU doubles. Users also see closed restaurants as "open". Details: discovery cache hit ratio: 82% - 9% ES query p95: 60 ms - 640 ms is open field refresh: reindex every 15 min cache key: userId, cell, filters The team wants to add search nodes.

title: Immutable raw data
text: Why keep the raw uploaded file as an immutable source of truth and treat stats, segment efforts and maps as derived data? A ride is irreplaceable, and my smoothing, elevation and segment-matching code will change. If I store only derived numbers, a bug or an improvement can never be fixed. So I keep the original FIT/GPX file in object storage untouched, and every derived record distance, elevation, efforts, polylines can be recomputed from it. I also stamp each derived record with a pipelineVersion , so reprocessing a range is routine instead of a crisis.

title: Segment matching
text: With millions of segments and millions of activities per day, how do you find which segments an activity passed through without checking every pair? I index segments by geo cell S2, H3 or geohash . For each activity I collect the cells its track crosses a one-hour ride is maybe 200 cells , fetch the few hundred candidate segments in those cells, and only then do precise matching: the track must pass within about 15 m of the segment start, follow the segment path direction and distance , and reach the end. Elapsed time is interpolated time at the end minus at the start, stored as an effort.

title: Storage tiering
text: Do the capacity math and propose a lifecycle policy with its risks. 5M activities/day, average raw file 500 KB. The CFO asks why storage is 40 percent of the bill. Today everything is in the standard object storage class with no lifecycle. Assume list prices of about 23 USD/TB-month standard, about 12.5 infrequent access, and about 4 archive verify current pricing . Old raw files are read rarely reprocessing, user export .

title: Idempotent uploads
text: Why does this happen and how do you fix it at every layer? After a mobile release users report duplicate rides in their feed and doubled kudos. Metrics: duplicate activities same athlete, same start +/- 5 s, distance within 1% : 18,400 / day was 600 uploads/complete called twice with same uploadId: 31% of duplicates ride synced from watch AND phone: 58% of duplicates The retry policy in the new app version retries complete on any timeout, without checking status.

text: Run the review: detection, repair and prevention. Postmortem: for six days after pipeline v41 shipped, running distances were 3 to 5 percent high and elevation gain 30 percent high for about 4.2M activities. Athletes noticed personal records they could not reproduce. Metric review: distance/duration ratio daily median : v40 = 3.02 m/s v41 = 3.17 m/s elevation gain per km median : v40 = 9 m v41 = 12 m change in v41: smoothing window 5 - 1 point, elevation threshold 3 m - 0 m The change passed unit tests because tests used clean synthetic tracks.

title: Privacy
text: What failed, and how do you redesign so privacy is safe by construction? A journalist shows that an athlete's home address can be derived: the public activity map trims the first 200 m, but the streams endpoint returns raw latlng to followers, the segment Hill-Start-12 begins at the athlete's street and the public leaderboard lists name and time, and the "recent efforts" panel lists the segment. The privacy zone is only applied in the mobile UI. GET /v1/activities/a 5001/streams?keys=latlng - first point 12.9716,77.5946 home GET /v1/segments/s 9/leaderboard - "Priya K., 04:12"

title: Ambiguous requirement
text: How do you respond before drawing any boxes? Product says: "Add live tracking so family can watch my run in real time." The existing system is upload-after-finish, with 58 uploads/s average and a processing pipeline for finished files. Marketing expects 1M concurrent live sessions on New Year's Day.

title: Popular segment leaderboard
text: Why are bad times still there, and how do you correct and harden the leaderboard? Segment s 9 a famous climb has 9.8M efforts. Redis key segment:9:alltime uses ZADD LT elapsedS athlete to keep each athlete's best time. A matcher bug v41 matched a car-accelerating route and wrote 2,300 impossible times under 60 s for a 4 km climb before it was fixed in v42. After the fix, the impossible times are still at the top. The same key uses about 1 GB of memory on a shared Redis. ZRANGE segment:9:alltime 0 2 WITHSCORES - athlete 8812 41, athlete 9120 44, athlete 2210 52 efforts table: those rows are marked invalid=true since the v42 fix

title: Why a buffer sits between agents and the search store
text: In a logging pipeline, why put Kafka between the host agents and the indexers instead of letting agents write straight into Elasticsearch? Logs are bursty and the search cluster is the slowest, most fragile part. Kafka is a durable, replayable buffer: it absorbs error storms, lets indexers be down or slow without losing lines, lets several consumers indexer, archiver, alerting read the same stream, and lets me replay after a mapping mistake. The cost is about a second of latency and a Kafka cluster to run.

title: Agent delivery guarantees without blocking the app
text: What delivery guarantee does a log agent give, and how do you make sure logging never slows down the application that produces the logs? The app writes to stdout or a local file, which is cheap. The agent tails the file, remembers its offset, batches, and commits the offset only after Kafka acks, so a crash causes duplicates but not loss: at-least-once. Each entry gets a unique id so duplicates can be dropped at the index. If the pipeline is slow, the agent's bounded buffer fills, not the app's thread; in-process appenders use a bounded queue that drops on overflow, with a drop counter.

title: Capacity math
text: Give the ingest rate, daily volume, hot and cold storage and Kafka size, and say what you would cut first if the bill is too high. You are asked to size logging for a mid-size company: 2,000 hosts, average 60 lines/s each, 250 bytes per line. Incident mode multiplies volume by 4. Requirements: 7 days searchable on SSD, 1 year cold, Kafka buffer of 24 h at peak. Text compresses about 6x; index overhead roughly offsets compression for hot data; Kafka RF is 3.

title: Pipeline lag during an outage
text: What do you do right now, and what is the root cause? During a checkout outage engineers report no logs for the last 20 minutes. Dashboards show: Kafka cluster healthy, broker CPU 35%, topic logs consumer lag for group indexer at 480M messages and rising. Indexer logs show repeated bulk rejected: es rejected execution exception 429 . Search cluster write thread pool queue is full. Log volume is 10x normal because a retry loop is logging a stack trace per attempt. A teammate wants to restart Kafka.

title: Vague requirement
text: How do you start? The interviewer says only: "Design logging for our company. We have a lot of microservices and engineers complain they cannot find anything." No numbers, no stack named.

title: Mapping explosion
text: What is wrong, and how do you fix it without losing data? The Elasticsearch cluster turns slow, master node GC is long, and indexers log Limit of total fields 1000 has been exceeded for some indices. A new service logs requests like this, and the template allows dynamic fields: { "ts":1731150000123, "service":"search-api", "level":"INFO", "msg":"query done", "fields": { "req 9f31a": 12, "req 77be2": 9, "tenant 41": "ok" } } PUT index template/logs { "index patterns": "logs- " , "template":{ "mappings":{ "dynamic":true } } } Cluster state is 900 MB. Daily indices have a single shard each.

title: Index engine migration
text: Choose a target and describe a safe migration. Is this reversible? Elasticsearch hot storage costs 70% of the observability bill: 90 TB hot SSD at 26 TB/day raw. Query analysis shows 92% of queries are "service + level + 15 min window + keyword"; 3% scan weeks. The team proposes moving to Loki-style label index with chunks in S3, or ClickHouse. Engineers use the tool during incidents and cannot lose it. Kafka retains 48 h.

title: Query isolation
text: Run the post-incident review: causes, fixes, and what to change in the design. Post-incident review. At 14:05 an engineer ran msg: timeout over 30 days. Search cluster CPU hit 100%, search thread pool queue depth 800, bulk indexing latency rose from 80 ms to 9 s, indexer consumer lag climbed to 12 minutes. The query returned after 9 minutes; the engineer retried twice. Another team's secrets appeared in the results because all teams share one index pattern.

title: Why log-based CDC
text: We need to keep a search index in sync with our orders database. Why not just poll for rows where updated at is newer than the last run? Polling cannot see deletes, misses rows whose transaction committed late a row with an older updated at appears after my cursor moved , depends on clocks, and hammers the database with queries. Log-based CDC reads the database's own commit log WAL or binlog , so it sees every insert, update and delete in commit order with almost no load on the source.

title: Snapshot then stream without a gap
text: A table already holds 500 GB. How do you give a new consumer the full state and then the live changes with no gaps and no long lock on production? Record the current log position first, take a consistent snapshot read at that position, emit those rows as snapshot events, then start streaming from the recorded position. For re-snapshots without stopping the stream, use incremental snapshots: read primary-key chunks between low and high watermark writes and drop chunk rows that the live log also changed in that window.

title: Replication slot retention
text: Handle the incident and prevent it. Friday 02:10, the Postgres primary 2 TB disk pages at 92% disk and rising 18 GB per hour. Query load is normal, autovacuum looks fine, table sizes are unchanged. The Debezium connector task shows FAILED since Thursday 17:00 a network ACL change . Slot check: slot name active retained orders slot f 410 GB The checkout service writes 5 MB/s of WAL. A teammate says to run VACUUM FULL on the biggest tables.

title: Out-of-order and duplicate sink writes
text: What happened and how do you fix it? Product reports that cancelled orders still appear in search. A sample row: source DB shows order 9001 deleted. The topic shows events for key 9001: u status=PAID lsn=300 , u status=SHIPPED lsn=310 , d lsn=320 . The sink code is: INSERT INTO orders search id, status VALUES $1,$2 ON CONFLICT id DO UPDATE SET status = EXCLUDED.status; The connector restarted at 11:02 and replayed about 40 seconds of events. Topic partitions were increased from 12 to 24 last month.

title: Dual write vs outbox
text: Which design do you propose and why? Is it a one-way door? The orders service must update its database and publish OrderPaid for the shipping, email and analytics services. A teammate proposes: commit the DB transaction, then kafka.send in the next line. Last quarter 0.02% of 3M daily orders about 600 per day never produced an event because the pod was killed between the two calls. Another teammate suggests sending to Kafka first, then writing the DB.

title: Schema change
text: Stabilise, then design how schema changes should flow. 10:40 a deploy renames orders.total to orders.total amount and changes discount from int to string. At 10:41 the warehouse loader task goes FAILED, DLQ rate rises to 2,000/min, search sink keeps working but shows null totals. Connector logs: Schema being registered is incompatible with an earlier schema . Schema registry compatibility mode is NONE . 14 downstream consumers exist, owned by 9 teams.

title: Source failover
text: Restore CDC correctly and say what you tell downstream owners. The Postgres primary hardware fails; the standby is promoted in 40 s. Applications recover. But the Debezium connector reports replication slot "orders slot" does not exist and stops. Slot state was not present on the promoted standby version predates slot sync, verify for your version . 8 minutes of writes happened on the old primary after the last confirmed LSN; the new primary has a few seconds fewer than the old one. Downstreams: search, cache, warehouse.

title: 10x write volume
text: What breaks first and how do you plan for 50k writes/s and the backfill? Orders DB grows from 5,000 to 50,000 writes/s at peak a flash-sale season , avg event 1 KB. Today one connector task, topic with 12 partitions, 5 consumer groups. A nightly backfill updates 80M rows. Observations in rehearsal: MilliSecondsBehindSource reaches 90 s at 20k writes/s, Kafka brokers at 25% CPU, connector worker CPU at 100% on one core.

title: Fan-out on write vs read
text: Explain fan-out on write versus fan-out on read for a home feed, and which you would pick. Push: when someone posts, insert the post id into every follower's feed list, so a read is one cache call but a write costs as many inserts as followers. Pull: on read, fetch recent posts from each followee and merge: cheap writes, expensive reads. I pick hybrid: push for normal authors, pull for authors above a follower threshold, merging their recent posts at read time.

title: Cursor pagination with time-sortable ids
text: Why should a feed use cursor pagination with Snowflake-style ids rather than page numbers or OFFSET? New posts keep arriving at the top, so offsets shift and the user sees duplicates or misses items. A cursor says "continue after this post id". Snowflake ids embed a timestamp in the high bits, so id order is time order, ids are generated without coordination, and the same id serves as cursor and as the sort key in the Redis feed.

title: Celebrity post fan-out storm
text: Mitigate and fix the design. A celebrity with 80M followers posts at 20:00. By 20:03 normal users report their own posts take 6 minutes to appear for followers. Metrics: fan-out Kafka consumer lag 900M, fan-out workers CPU 85%, Redis cluster CPU 55%, post service latency normal, social graph read p99 up from 8 ms to 140 ms. The team notices Redis memory growth 2% and suggests adding Redis nodes.

title: Deleted and blocked content
text: What is wrong and what is the corrected design? Users complain that a deleted post keeps appearing, and a blocked user's posts still show for 2 hours. Each feed entry in Redis is stored as the full post JSON about 1.2 KB pushed at write time. The delete flow calls DELETE FROM posts WHERE id=? only. At 800 entries for 300M users that would be roughly 290 TB, so only a fraction of users are cached and the rest are rebuilt.

title: Small-scale ambiguity
text: What do you design, and what do you ask first? A startup CTO says: "We need a news feed for our fitness app. We have 2M registered users, maybe 150k DAU, people follow about 40 others, 30k posts a day. Design it like Twitter." Team size is 5 engineers on Postgres and Redis.

title: Redis node loss stampede
text: Recover and make the design resilient. At 09:00 one Redis shard holding feeds for 10M users crashes; the replica was also being resynced after a maintenance restart. Feed service error rate hits 30% and p99 rises from 120 ms to 6 s. The rebuild path followees + recent posts from the Posts DB runs per user on a cache miss. Posts DB CPU 95%, connection pool exhausted, graph service latency 10x. 800k users per minute are opening the app.

title: Hot post counters
text: What is wrong, and what is the corrected design? A post goes viral at 120k likes/s. The like handler is: BEGIN; INSERT INTO likes user id, post id VALUES $1,$2 ; UPDATE posts SET like count = like count + 1 WHERE post id = $2; COMMIT; Symptoms: Postgres shows 3,000 sessions waiting on transactionid / tuple locks, like API p99 22 s, other writes to posts new posts, edits on the same shard time out. CPU on the DB is only 30%. Users double-tapping sometimes see +2.

title: Ranking latency budget
text: Bring it back under budget and make it safe. After launching a ranked feed, feed p99 rose from 180 ms to 780 ms, SLO 200 ms. Trace breakdown for p99: Redis candidates 6 ms, post hydration 190 ms cache hit ratio 62%, misses fetch posts one by one , feature fetch 210 ms per-candidate calls for 500 candidates , model scoring 300 ms CPU model server at 90% CPU . The ranker is called synchronously and has no fallback.

title: Persist before ack and the tick ladder
text: Walk me through what the single tick, double tick and blue tick mean in the server, and why the server must persist before acknowledging the sender. One tick means the server persisted the message and now owns it. Two ticks mean the recipient's device acked delivery. Blue ticks mean the recipient read it. I persist before acking because the ack is a durability promise: if I ack and then crash before writing, the sender believes it is safe and the message is gone.

title: Group fan-out strategies
text: How do you deliver one message to a 1,000-member group versus a 1,000,000-member channel? For up to about a thousand members I fan out on write: copy a reference into each member's inbox, 1,024 small writes, fast reads. For huge channels I store the message once in the group stream and each member keeps a cursor lastReadSeq ; writes are one, reads happen only for active members. Group E2EE uses sender keys so the server stores one ciphertext, not N.

title: Connection capacity
text: Size the gateway fleet and the message path, and correct the manager. Launch in a new market: 20M DAU, peak 6M concurrent connections, 30 messages per user per day, average 1.4 recipients per message. Proposed gateway servers: 16 cores, 64 GB RAM, tuned to 400k connections each. A manager says "20M DAU is about 7,000 requests per second, we need 4 servers".

title: Duplicate messages
text: Explain the bug and the fix, including the receiver side. On poor networks users see the same message twice and the sender sees it sent twice. Server log excerpt: 10:01:02.100 recv send chatId=551 clientMsgId=<none from=u 3 ts=1731150062100 10:01:02.130 persist seq=412 server msg id=m 90017 10:01:02.131 ack-write FAILED connection reset 10:01:07.400 recv send chatId=551 clientMsgId=<none from=u 3 ts=1731150067400 10:01:07.431 persist seq=413 server msg id=m 90018 The client retries a send if no ack arrives within 5 s. The send frame has no client-generated id.

title: Ordering and gaps
text: Diagnose both problems and redesign ordering. Users report conversations showing replies before questions, but only for people on two different phones. The client sorts messages by the sender's local ts . One sender's phone clock is 3 minutes fast. Also, after a flaky reconnect a recipient shows seq 410, 411, 415 with 412 to 414 missing until app restart.

title: Reconnect storm
text: What is happening, and what do you change in the client, the deploy and the server? A rolling deploy of 200 gateways restarts them 20 at a time every 2 minutes with 90 s draining. After the third batch, auth latency goes from 20 ms to 4 s, Redis session registry CPU at 98%, delivery delay "minutes", gateway accept queue overflowing netstat -s: 1.2M SYNs to LISTEN sockets dropped . Clients reconnect immediately on disconnect with a fixed 1 s retry. 100M clients are connected; each batch drops about 10M.

title: Stale session registry
text: Explain how messages were mis-acknowledged or stuck, and fix the delivery path. A gateway host crashes at 14:00. Over the next minutes the support desk sees: senders show two ticks delivered but recipients never received messages; some messages show one tick forever. The registry still maps 400k users to the dead gateway for 90 s TTL heartbeat TTL 90 s . Router logs: push to gw-77 timed out repeated. Redis registry is healthy.

title: E2EE and new feature requests
text: What do you recommend for each request, and what do you refuse? Product wants three things for the E2EE chat: server-side message search for users, automatic spam and scam scanning, and keeping history on a new phone. Security says E2EE is a non-negotiable promise. The server today stores ciphertext and routing metadata only. Backups are plaintext in cloud storage "for now".

title: Idempotency keys
text: What is an idempotency key in a payments API, and how do you implement it so a retry can never charge a customer twice? The client sends a unique key a UUID per logical operation with each mutating request. The server inserts a row keyed by merchant, key with a unique constraint before doing anything. If the key exists, it returns the stored response same body or a conflict different body, or still in progress . The payment and the key row are written in the same database transaction, and the same reference is passed to the PSP so it also dedupes.

title: Why a double-entry ledger
text: Why model money with an append-only double-entry ledger instead of a payments table with a balance column? Every movement is a transaction of at least two immutable entries whose debits equal credits, so the books always balance and errors are visible. History is kept, audits are easy, and mistakes are fixed by new compensating entries rather than by overwriting. A mutable balance column loses the why behind each change and cannot prove itself.

title: Double charges
text: Find the cause, remediate customers and fix the system. During a bank latency spike auth p99 2 s to 14 s , support receives 340 tickets of double charges in one hour. Metrics: client SDK retry count up 6x, payments created per order id: 2 for about 0.4% of orders, idempotency-key hit rate unchanged at 0.2%. The mobile SDK was updated last week. Gateway had a 10 s timeout. Database CPU is normal.

title: Timeouts and UNKNOWN state
text: Explain the failure and redesign the handling of external calls. During a deploy, 1,900 orders were marked FAILED and inventory released, yet 1,100 customers were charged. Logs: psp.authorize timeout after 5s followed by status=FAILED reason=timeout . The PSP callbacks payment.succeeded arrived at 3 to 40 seconds later while pods were restarting; some returned 502. The state machine has only CREATED, SUCCEEDED, FAILED.

title: Idempotency race
text: List every bug and write the corrected flow. Code review of the payment creation handler language-neutral pseudocode . In production two identical requests 40 ms apart sometimes both charge. handle req : row = db.query "SELECT FROM idempotency keys WHERE merchant=? AND key=?", ... if row != null: return row.response payment = psp.charge req.amount, req.method takes 1 to 3 s db.exec "INSERT INTO idempotency keys merchant,key,response VALUES ?,?,? ", ... return payment The table has no unique constraint. The PSP call does not send a reference.

title: Reconciliation breaks
text: Run the review: classify breaks, fix customers and the system. Daily reconciliation after a callback-handler release shows out of 8.4M payments : matched 8,361,000; in PSP only 2,900 money taken, we show failure ; in us only 600; amount mismatches 1,150. Query excerpt: ref ours theirs note pay 77x 49900 49900 matched pay 81c NULL 120000 psp only, status=captured pay 93d 75000 NULL ours only, status=SUCCEEDED pay 95e 49900 49410 fee deducted? currency INR Settlement is T+2 and the bank statement has not arrived for the last day. A finance lead asks if the system is safe to keep running.

title: Hot ledger accounts at 10x
text: What is the bottleneck and how do you scale the ledger without breaking correctness? Festival sale: payments go from 600/s to 6,000/s peak. Each payment writes 5 ledger lines, including a credit to the single platform fee revenue account and a debit to psp clearing . Postgres shows lock waits on balances rows for those two accounts, ledger insert p99 3 s, CPU 40%, WAL fine. Payments DB is one primary with a synchronous replica. Ledger and payments are in the same database.

title: Adding a second PSP
text: Design the rollout and the failure handling; what is one-way here? Single acquirer A has 96.1% authorisation success and went down twice last quarter 45 and 70 minutes . Acquirer B is cheaper by 0.1% per transaction and claims 97.0% success. Volume is 600/s peak. Integration work and separate reconciliation files are required. Finance asks if routing can be switched dynamically and whether it is reversible.

title: CI vs CD
text: What is the difference between Continuous Integration, Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment? CI is merging small changes often and having a machine build and test every one. Continuous Delivery means every passing change is ready to release at the push of a button. Continuous Deployment removes the button: every passing change goes to production automatically.

title: Why CI/CD
text: Why do small, frequent releases reduce risk instead of increasing it? A small change is easy to review, easy to test, and when it breaks you know exactly which commit did it, so rollback is quick. A huge release mixes hundreds of changes, so failures are hard to find and fix, which makes people release even less often.

title: Branching
text: Compare trunk-based development with GitFlow. When would you pick each? Trunk-based means tiny branches merged to main within a day or two, with unfinished work hidden behind feature flags; it fits services deployed continuously. GitFlow uses long-lived develop and release branches and fits versioned products that must be patched for years, like on-prem software or some mobile releases.

title: Merge queue
text: Two pull requests each pass CI, but main breaks after both merge. How do you prevent this? Each PR was tested against an older main, so combined they can fail even without textual conflicts. A merge queue GitHub Merge Queue, GitLab Merge Trains, Bors tests each PR on top of the latest main plus the PRs ahead of it, and only merges if green.

title: Build once
text: What does "build once, deploy many" mean and why does it matter? You build the artifact for example a Docker image one time, identify it by digest or commit SHA, and promote that exact artifact through dev, staging and production. Only configuration changes between environments. If you rebuilt per environment, what you tested would not be what you ship.

title: Slow feedback
text: How would you improve the delivery process over the next quarter? A 25-engineer team has long-lived feature branches average 9 days , merges take 1-2 days of conflict fixing, and the CI pipeline takes 45 minutes. Releases happen every 3 weeks and about 1 in 4 causes a rollback.

title: Conventional commits
text: What are Conventional Commits and how do they help automation? A commit message convention such as feat: , fix: and feat!: for breaking changes. Tools like semantic-release or release-please read the prefixes to choose the next version number and generate the changelog automatically.

title: SemVer
text: Explain semantic versioning and why release tags should be immutable. MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: patch for bug fixes, minor for backwards-compatible features, major for breaking changes. A git tag marks exactly which commit was released, so moving it would make "what is running?" unanswerable and break reproducibility.

title: Monorepo
text: What are the CI implications of a monorepo compared with many repositories? A monorepo gives atomic cross-service changes and shared tooling, but CI must run only what a change affects, using a dependency graph Bazel, Nx, Gradle, Turborepo and remote caches. Polyrepo gives simple per-repo pipelines and clear ownership but makes cross-repo changes and version alignment painful.

title: DevOps culture
text: What does DevOps mean to you, and what is platform engineering? DevOps is a way of working: teams share responsibility for building and running software, automate the path to production, and learn from failures without blame. Platform engineering builds an internal developer platform with golden-path templates and self-service, so product teams get pipelines, deployments and dashboards without mastering every tool.

title: Mobile releases
text: How does releasing a mobile app differ from releasing a web service? Users hold old versions and store review plus update lag delay fixes, so you use release trains on a fixed cadence, staged store rollouts with crash-free thresholds, server-side feature flags and remote config as kill switches, force-update for dangerously old versions, and keep the backend API backward compatible.

title: Pipeline stages
text: What are the typical stages of a CI/CD pipeline and why does their order matter? Checkout, restore cache, build, unit test, lint and static analysis, security scan, package into an artifact or image, publish, deploy, then smoke test. Cheap and fast checks go first so a bad change fails in a minute, not after a 30-minute test suite.

title: GitHub Actions
text: Explain workflows, jobs, steps and runners in GitHub Actions. How do you make one job wait for another? A workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows triggered by events. It contains jobs, which run in parallel on runners machines . A job has steps that run shell commands or reusable actions. To order jobs you use needs: , for example deploy needs: test .

title: Tool comparison
text: How do Jenkins, GitLab CI and GitHub Actions differ, and what stays the same? The concepts are identical: a config file in the repo, jobs run on agents or runners, stages, artifacts, caches, secrets. Differences are syntax and operations. Jenkins uses a Groovy Jenkinsfile and you host, patch and scale it yourself, with a big plugin ecosystem. GitLab CI uses .gitlab-ci.yml built into GitLab. Actions uses YAML in .github/workflows and is built into GitHub.

title: Caching
text: How would you speed up a slow CI pipeline? Explain caching keys. Cache dependency downloads keyed by a hash of the lockfile so the cache is reused until dependencies change, run independent jobs in parallel, shard big test suites across runners, pass build outputs as artifacts instead of rebuilding, and use Docker layer caching.

title: Secrets and OIDC
text: How should a pipeline authenticate to a cloud provider to deploy? Why is OIDC preferred over stored access keys? With OIDC the pipeline gets a signed identity token from the CI platform, exchanges it with the cloud for a short-lived role, and uses it for the job. No long-lived key is stored, so there is nothing to leak or rotate, and the role can be scoped to one repo, branch and environment.

title: Compromised pipeline
text: What do you do, and how do you prevent a repeat? Your cloud bill spikes 8x overnight. Instances in an unused region are mining cryptocurrency. CloudTrail shows the actions came from the access key stored in the CI system for the deploy user, which has AdministratorAccess. The last change to the pipeline was a new third-party build step added two days ago.

title: Reusable pipelines
text: How do you avoid copy-pasting pipelines across 100 repositories? Publish a reusable workflow GitHub , include: template GitLab or shared library Jenkins owned by a platform team. Repos call it with a few inputs. Version the template for example @v3 so a change does not break every repo at once, and roll upgrades out gradually.

title: Runners
text: When would you use self-hosted runners, and what must you do to secure them? Use them for private network access, GPUs or special hardware, large machines, or lower cost at scale. Secure them by making each job run in a fresh ephemeral container or VM, never running untrusted fork code on persistent runners, giving minimal credentials, and autoscaling so queues stay short.

title: Artifact registries
text: Why use an internal artifact repository or proxy registry? It stores your immutable, traceable release artifacts and proxies public registries. Builds keep working when npm or Maven Central is down or a package disappears, and you can block malicious or typosquatted packages and enforce retention and scanning.

title: Android CI
text: Describe a CI/CD pipeline for an Android app. On each PR run lint and unit tests with Gradle. After merge run instrumented tests on an emulator or device farm. For release build a signed AAB with the keystore from a secrets store, upload to the Play internal track Fastlane or Gradle Play Publisher , then staged rollout, watching crash-free sessions.

title: Monorepo filters
text: A PR in a monorepo cannot merge because a required check never ran due to path filters. Why, and how do you fix it? A workflow skipped by path filters never reports a status, so branch protection waits for a check that never appears. Fix by having an always-running gate job that decides what to run and reports success when nothing needed to run, and make that gate the required check.

title: Broken main
text: What do you do and what changes afterwards? main has been red for 3 days. Eleven PRs have merged on top of the broken build, each author assuming "someone else will fix it". The failing test is in a module owned by a team on leave. Release is scheduled for Friday.

title: Containers vs VMs
text: What is a container and how is it different from a virtual machine? A container is an isolated process that shares the host's kernel. Linux namespaces limit what it can see processes, network, filesystem and cgroups limit what it can use CPU, memory . A VM runs a full guest OS on a hypervisor, so it is heavier and slower to start.

title: Dockerfile layers
text: How does Docker layer caching work, and how would you structure a Dockerfile for fast rebuilds and a small image? Each instruction makes a layer cached by its content and everything above it. Put rarely changing steps first base image, dependency install and frequently changing steps last copy source . Use multi-stage builds so compilers and dev tools stay in the build stage and the final image holds only what runs.

title: Tags vs digests
text: Why should you not deploy the latest tag to production? A tag is a movable label. latest can point to different images over time, so two nodes may run different code under the same name and you cannot tell what to roll back to. Deploy an immutable tag such as the commit SHA, or the content digest @sha256:... .

title: Container security
text: List practical steps to harden a container image and its runtime. Small base image slim or distroless , run as non-root, drop capabilities and use a read-only filesystem, scan images in CI and on a schedule, keep secrets out of the image, sign images and generate an SBOM.

title: Compose and data
text: Your integration tests need Postgres and Redis. How do you run them in CI, and what happens to the data when the container stops? Use Docker Compose or Testcontainers to start real Postgres and Redis for the test run. Data in a container's writable layer disappears when the container is removed; for tests that is desirable, and anything that must persist uses a named volume.

title: Image bloat
text: How would you fix both image size and build time? A Java service image is 1.4 GB. Pulling it on a fresh Kubernetes node takes 90 seconds, so autoscaling reacts slowly during traffic spikes. The Dockerfile uses FROM ubuntu , installs the JDK and Maven, copies the repo and runs mvn package inside the final image. Every commit rebuilds all layers 11 minutes .

title: Runtime internals
text: What are namespaces and cgroups, and what do containerd and runc do? Namespaces isolate what a process can see PIDs, network, mounts, hostname, users ; cgroups limit what it can use CPU, memory, I/O . runc is the low-level tool that creates a container process from an OCI spec; containerd manages images and container lifecycle and is what Kubernetes uses through the CRI.

title: Container networking
text: Your app container cannot reach Postgres at localhost:5432 even though the database container is running. Why? Each container has its own network namespace, so localhost inside the app container is the app container itself. Put both on the same user-defined network and connect using the service name, for example db:5432 , resolved by Docker's built-in DNS.

title: State
text: After each deployment users' uploaded files disappear. What is wrong and how do you fix it? Files were written to the container's ephemeral writable layer, which is deleted when the pod is replaced. Keep containers stateless: store uploads in object storage like S3, data in managed databases, and use volumes or persistent volumes only for state that must live on disk.

title: BuildKit
text: How do you speed up Docker builds in CI where runners are ephemeral? Use BuildKit with a remote cache --cache-from/--cache-to to a registry or the CI cache , order the Dockerfile so dependency layers are stable, use cache mounts for package managers, add a .dockerignore , and build multi-stage so only changed stages rebuild. Use secret mounts so credentials never land in layers.

title: OOMKilled JVM
text: Diagnose and fix. A Java service runs in Kubernetes with a 512 MiB memory limit and -Xmx512m . Pods restart about every 4 hours with OOMKilled exit 137 . Heap dumps taken before the kill look healthy at 380 MiB. CPU is normal and the restarts cause brief error spikes.

title: Architecture
text: What problem does Kubernetes solve, and what are its main components? It runs and manages containers across many machines. You declare the desired state, such as five replicas of an image, and controllers continuously make reality match it, restarting failed pods and rescheduling them. Control plane: API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager. Each node runs kubelet, a container runtime and kube-proxy.

title: Objects
text: What is the difference between a Pod, a Deployment and a Service? A Pod is the smallest unit, one or more containers sharing network and storage, and it is disposable. A Deployment manages replicas of identical pods and handles rolling updates and rollbacks. A Service gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name that load-balances to whichever pods match its label selector.

title: Probes
text: Explain readiness, liveness and startup probes. What goes wrong if you configure them badly? Readiness decides whether a pod receives traffic; failing it removes the pod from the Service without restarting. Liveness decides whether the container is stuck; failing it restarts the container. Startup gives slow-starting apps time before liveness begins. A liveness probe that checks a dependency like the database can restart every pod during a DB blip and turn a small problem into a full outage.

title: Resources and scaling
text: What are resource requests and limits, and how does the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler decide to scale? Requests are what the scheduler reserves for a pod; limits are the maximum. Exceeding the memory limit kills the container OOMKilled ; exceeding the CPU limit only throttles it. HPA computes desired replicas as ceil current × currentMetric / targetMetric , bounded by min and max, using CPU, memory or custom metrics.

title: Config and secrets
text: Are Kubernetes Secrets secure? How do you manage secrets properly? By default Secrets are only base64-encoded, not encrypted, and anyone with API read access to them can decode them. Enable encryption at rest, restrict access with RBAC, and ideally keep real secrets in an external manager Vault, AWS or GCP Secret Manager synced by the External Secrets Operator or a CSI driver. For GitOps use Sealed Secrets or SOPS so nothing plain lives in Git.

title: Rollout failing
text: Walk me through diagnosing and resolving this. You deploy a new image to production. kubectl get pods shows the new pods in CrashLoopBackOff with 6 restarts, while the 3 old pods are still serving traffic. The old ReplicaSet is not being scaled down. Users are unaffected so far. Logs from the current container are empty.

title: Scheduling
text: Three replicas of your service all land in the same availability zone. How do you make them highly available? Use topology spread constraints or pod anti-affinity so replicas spread across zones and nodes, together with a PodDisruptionBudget. Taints and tolerations and node affinity control which nodes pods may use; PriorityClass decides who is preempted when resources are tight.

title: NetworkPolicy
text: Are Kubernetes namespaces a network security boundary? How do you restrict traffic? No. By default every pod can reach every other pod across namespaces. Use NetworkPolicies: start with default-deny and allow only required paths, for example frontend to API to database. Policies only work if the CNI enforces them Calico, Cilium .

title: Ingress and TLS
text: How does external traffic reach a service in Kubernetes, and how are TLS certificates managed? An Ingress or Gateway API resource, implemented by a controller NGINX, Traefik, Envoy, cloud load balancer , routes external HTTP S by host and path to Services and terminates TLS. cert-manager issues and renews certificates automatically, for example from Let's Encrypt, so they do not expire.

title: RBAC
text: How do you give a CI system or developers appropriate access to a cluster? Least privilege with RBAC: Roles and RoleBindings scoped to a namespace, ServiceAccounts for pods and tooling, no day-to-day cluster-admin . In a GitOps setup only the GitOps controller changes production and developers get read access. Add ResourceQuotas, LimitRanges and Pod Security Standards for multi-tenancy.

title: Workload types
text: When would you use a Job, CronJob, DaemonSet and StatefulSet instead of a Deployment? Job for run-to-completion work like a data migration; CronJob for scheduled Jobs with concurrencyPolicy to prevent overlap; DaemonSet for one pod per node such as log shippers; StatefulSet for stable identity and per-pod persistent storage, as in databases or Kafka.

title: Service mesh
text: What does a service mesh provide and when would you not adopt one? A mesh Istio, Linkerd, Cilium adds a proxy per pod or node giving mTLS between services, retries and timeouts, traffic splitting for canaries, and uniform telemetry without app changes. The cost is extra CPU and memory, operational complexity and harder debugging, so I would adopt it only for a clear need such as zero-trust mTLS or fine-grained traffic control.

title: Pending pods
text: What do you check and fix? During a traffic spike the HPA scales a Deployment from 6 to 20 replicas, but 9 new pods stay Pending . Latency climbs and error rate hits 3%. kubectl describe pod says "0/12 nodes are available: insufficient cpu". Cluster Autoscaler is installed but no new nodes appear.

title: Strategies
text: Compare rolling, blue-green and canary deployments. Rolling replaces instances gradually in place. Blue-green runs a full second environment and flips traffic at once, so rollback is flipping back, at the price of double capacity. Canary sends a small percentage of traffic to the new version and promotes it only if metrics look good, limiting the blast radius.

title: Graceful rolling updates
text: Users see 502 errors during every rolling update. What could be wrong? Pods are being terminated while still receiving requests. Fix with graceful shutdown: handle SIGTERM by finishing in-flight requests, add a preStop sleep so the load balancer deregisters the pod first, set a sufficient terminationGracePeriodSeconds , and make sure readiness only passes when the app can really serve.

title: Feature flags
text: What is the difference between deploying and releasing, and how do feature flags help? Deploy means the code is running in production; release means users can use the feature. Flags let you ship code dark, enable it for staff, then a percentage, then everyone, and turn it off in seconds without redeploying, which also enables trunk-based development.

title: Migrations
text: How do you rename a database column with zero downtime? Never rename in one step. Use expand/contract: add the new column; deploy code that writes to both; backfill old rows in small batches; switch reads to the new column; and only in a later release drop the old column when no running version uses it.

title: Automated rollback
text: How would you automate canary promotion and rollback? Use a progressive delivery controller Argo Rollouts, Flagger, Spinnaker with Kayenta that shifts traffic in steps and queries metrics at each step, such as 5xx rate and p99 latency compared with the baseline. If the analysis fails, it aborts and returns traffic to the stable version; if it passes, it promotes.

title: Bad release
text: You are on call. What do you do? At 14:02 a deploy goes to 100% of a checkout service. By 14:05 the 5xx rate rises from 0.2% to 6%, p99 latency doubles, and support tickets begin. The release included a code change and a database migration that dropped an unused-looking column.

title: Traffic shifting
text: How do you implement a 5% canary in practice? Use weighted routing at a load balancer, ingress or service mesh, driven by a progressive delivery tool Argo Rollouts, Flagger that steps the weight and checks metrics. Make routing sticky by hashing on user or session so a user does not flip between versions. DNS weights are coarse and slow because of TTLs.

title: Shadow vs A/B
text: What is the difference between a canary, shadow traffic and an A/B test? A canary tests safety by giving a small share of real users the new version and watching error and latency metrics. Shadow traffic copies real requests to the new version and discards its responses, so users are unaffected. An A/B test measures a product metric such as conversion between variants with statistical significance.

title: Config changes
text: Why are configuration changes a leading cause of outages and how do you make them safe? Config often bypasses review, tests and staged rollout, yet a bad value can take everything down at once. Treat config like code: version it, review it, validate against a schema, roll it out progressively one cell or region first , watch SLOs, and be able to roll it back in seconds.

title: Regional waves
text: How would you roll out a change across many regions safely? In waves: one-box a single instance , then one small region or cell, then a few regions, then the rest, with a bake time between waves and automatic halt on alarms. A cell-based architecture limits any failure to one cell. Start with low-traffic regions and never deploy everywhere at once.

title: Chaos engineering
text: What is chaos engineering and how do you do it safely? Deliberately injecting controlled failures kill pods, add latency, drop a dependency, fail a zone to verify the system handles them. Start with a hypothesis, a small blast radius, monitoring and an abort button, and run in staging first before production. Game days rehearse incident response and restores.

title: Mobile crash
text: What do you do right now? Version 5.2 of your Android app is at 8% staged rollout. Crashlytics shows crash-free sessions at 97.1% baseline 99.6% , concentrated on Android 12 devices when opening the payments screen. Reviews are dropping. A fix will take two days including store review.

title: GitOps
text: What is GitOps and how does it differ from a traditional CI pipeline deploying with kubectl? In GitOps the desired state lives in Git and an agent inside the cluster Argo CD or Flux continuously pulls it and reconciles the cluster to match. Traditional push CI holds cluster credentials and runs kubectl apply . GitOps removes production credentials from CI, gives a full audit history, corrects drift automatically, and rolls back with git revert .

title: Argo CD
text: What do automated , prune and selfHeal do in an Argo CD sync policy? automated syncs when Git changes without a manual click. prune deletes cluster resources that were removed from Git. selfHeal reverts manual changes made directly in the cluster so it always matches Git.

title: Terraform state
text: What is Terraform state, and why must it be stored remotely with locking? State maps the resources in your code to real cloud resources and records their attributes. It must be remote for example S3 with DynamoDB locking, or Terraform Cloud so the team shares one truth and a lock stops two people applying simultaneously and corrupting it. It can contain secrets, so encrypt it and restrict access.

title: Secrets in Git
text: How do you store secrets safely in a GitOps workflow? Never plain text. Either commit encrypted secrets Sealed Secrets, SOPS with KMS or age that only the cluster can decrypt, or keep secrets in an external manager Vault, AWS or GCP Secret Manager and commit only a reference that the External Secrets Operator resolves at runtime.

title: Policy as code
text: What is policy as code and where would you enforce it? Policy as code expresses guardrails as machine-checked rules, for example "no root containers", "images only from our registry", "every pod has resource limits". Enforce them in the PR Conftest, Checkov, tfsec , and at deploy time in the cluster OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno admission control so violating resources are rejected.

title: Terraform mishap
text: What do you do now, and how do you prevent it? During an apply for a "small tagging change", Terraform destroys and recreates a production RDS database because an immutable field was modified in the same change. The plan output was long and was approved without close reading. Automated backups exist; the last snapshot is 3 hours old.

title: Helm vs Kustomize
text: Compare Helm and Kustomize. When would you use each? Helm packages manifests as templated charts with values and tracks releases with rollback; it suits third-party software and heavy parameterisation. Kustomize keeps plain YAML and applies overlays and patches per environment, with no templating language. A common split is Helm for community software, either tool for your own services; Argo CD supports both.

title: Environment promotion
text: How do you structure environments and promotion in GitOps, and why avoid a branch per environment? Use a folder or overlay per environment on one branch and promote the same image digest by a PR or automation changing the tag for the next environment after checks pass. A branch per environment drifts, produces confusing merges and makes diffs hard to review.

title: CI to CD handoff
text: How does CI hand an image off to a GitOps deployment? CI builds, tests, scans and pushes an immutable image, then commits the new image reference to the config repo through a PR or bot commit, or an image-updater tool watches the registry and writes it. The GitOps controller then syncs the cluster. The commit should link back to the source commit and build.

title: Terraform practice
text: How would you structure Terraform for multiple environments and keep it safe? Reusable, versioned modules; separate state and directory per environment and component to limit blast radius; remote state with locking; plan on PR and apply after approval; pinned provider and module versions; policy checks on plans; prevent destroy on stateful resources; and moved blocks for refactors.

title: Cloud basics
text: A pod in a private subnet cannot pull images from the internet. What do you check? The route table for the private subnet is there a route to a NAT gateway , the NAT gateway itself, security group and network ACL rules allowing outbound 443, DNS resolution, and registry permissions via IAM. Better still, use VPC endpoints or a private registry mirror to avoid internet egress.

title: Cloud bill
text: How do you bring costs under control without hurting reliability? The monthly cloud bill rose 45% in a quarter with no matching traffic growth. Kubernetes nodes run at 25% average CPU utilisation, 40 preview environments from old PRs are still running, and no resources are tagged with an owner.

title: Test pyramid
text: What is the test pyramid and which tests run at which stage of the pipeline? Many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests with real dependencies in the middle, and a few slow end-to-end tests at the top. Unit tests run on every commit, integration tests on every PR, and a small set of E2E or smoke tests after deploy to staging or production. Contract tests keep service interfaces compatible; load tests run on a schedule.

title: Quality gates
text: What is a quality gate and why apply it to "new code" instead of the whole codebase? A quality gate is a pass/fail rule, such as no new critical issues and at least 80% coverage on changed code, that blocks merging. Applying it to new code lets a team with a messy legacy codebase stop adding debt immediately without being blocked by thousands of old issues.

title: DevSecOps
text: What are SAST, SCA and DAST, and where does each fit in a pipeline? SAST analyses source code for insecure patterns CodeQL, Semgrep on every PR. SCA checks dependencies for known vulnerabilities Dependabot, Snyk on every PR and on a schedule. DAST attacks the running application OWASP ZAP against staging. Add secret scanning, container image scanning Trivy and IaC scanning Checkov .

title: Flaky tests
text: How do you deal with flaky tests in CI? Track and reproduce them run many times , find the cause, and fix it: timing sleeps, shared state or ordering, real network calls, uncontrolled time or randomness. Quarantine confirmed flaky tests out of the blocking set with an owner and deadline so they do not block everyone, and measure flake rate over time. Retries are a stopgap, not a fix.

title: Release gates
text: How do you balance manual approvals with automation in a regulated environment? Automate everything repeatable tests, scans, deployments and keep humans for judgement.
