The network team says "link is nowhere near full".

title: CLOSE_WAIT leak
text: Why CLOSE WAIT and what is the bug? A Java service's file descriptor count climbs by 40/min until Too many open files at 65,535, then it restarts every 27 hours . Evidence: $ ss -tan state close-wait wc -l 48211 $ ss -tanp state close-wait head -2 0 0 10.1.2.5:51822 10.1.9.9:8443 users: "java",pid=912,fd=1204 $ lsof -p 912 wc -l 65310 The suspicious code in the client wrapper: public String fetch String url throws IOException { HttpURLConnection c = HttpURLConnection new URL url .openConnection ; if c.getResponseCode != 200 { return null; // error path } try InputStream in = c.getInputStream { return new String in.readAllBytes ; } } Upstream 10.1.9.9 closes idle connections after 30 s. Error rate to upstream is about 1%.

title: What UDP gives you
text: What does UDP actually guarantee, and what does it leave to the application? UDP gives me ports and a checksum on top of IP, nothing else. Each sendto is one datagram: no connection, no ordering, no retransmission, no congestion control, no flow control. If I need any of those, I build them or pick another protocol.

title: Choosing a transport
text: When would you pick UDP over TCP? Give real examples. I pick UDP when late data is worthless or when I need control TCP will not give me: live voice/video, game state, DNS lookups, telemetry, and as the base for QUIC. I pick TCP when I need every byte in order and don't want to reimplement reliability.

title: MTU and MSS
text: What is MTU, what is MSS, and how are they related? MTU is the largest IP packet a link can carry, typically 1500 bytes on Ethernet. MSS is the largest TCP payload per segment, so MSS = MTU - 20 IP - 20 TCP = 1460. Peers announce MSS in the SYN.

title: Reliability over UDP
text: If you had to add reliability on top of UDP, what mechanisms would you need, and what's the hard part? Sequence numbers, ACKs, retransmit timers with RTT estimation, a reorder buffer, flow control, and congestion control. The hard part isn't the ACKs, it's congestion control and loss detection, which decide whether you are a good citizen or melt the network.

title: MTU black hole
text: What's wrong and how do you fix it without touching every host? You migrated an API behind a new site-to-site VPN. Health checks tiny GETs are green. Users report that uploads and large JSON responses hang forever; small calls are fine. curl -v shows the TLS handshake completing, then the request stalls. The ops team also recently "hardened" the firewall by dropping all ICMP. Tunnel MTU is 1400; hosts use 1500. Red herring: CPU on the gateway is 10%. $ tcpdump -ni eth0 host 10.2.0.5 12:01:01 10.1.0.9 10.2.0.5: Flags P. , len 1448 retransmitted x6, no ACK 12:01:03 10.1.0.9 10.2.0.5: Flags P. , len 1448

title: UDP packet loss
text: Why are metrics missing and what would you change? A StatsD-style metrics ingester receives 120k UDP packets/s on a 4-core box. Dashboards show gaps; senders report no errors UDP never does . Network team says the NIC shows no drops. CPU is 60% on one core, others idle. $ netstat -su Udp: 9,884,102 packets received 412,330 packet receive errors RcvbufErrors: 412,330 $ cat /proc/sys/net/core/rmem max 212992

title: Choosing a protocol for a new product
text: Which transport s would you propose and why? You're designing a real-time collaborative whiteboard: 50k concurrent rooms, up to 20 users each, cursor positions at 30 Hz, drawing strokes that must never be lost or reordered, and occasional 5 MB image uploads. Users are mostly on mobile networks 3-5% loss, 80-200 ms RTT, frequent Wi-Fi/LTE handoffs . The PM asks "WebSockets or UDP?". Enterprise customers sit behind proxies that often block non-HTTPS traffic.

title: UDP amplification
text: What is happening and how do you stop it permanently? Your public UDP service a game-lobby discovery endpoint suddenly shows 8 Gbps outbound with only 200 Mbps inbound. Your transit provider threatens to null-route your IP. Requests are 40 bytes and responses are 1,200 bytes. Source IPs in the logs are from all over the world, including residential ranges that don't play your game. $ tcpdump -ni eth0 udp port 27015 -c 3 IP 203.0.113.7.4444 192.0.2.10.27015: UDP, length 40 IP 192.0.2.10.27015 203.0.113.7.4444: UDP, length 1200

title: Why QUIC exists
text: Why was QUIC built on UDP instead of being a new transport protocol, and what does it fix over TCP+TLS? New IP protocols get dropped by middleboxes and TCP lives in kernels, so evolving it takes years. QUIC runs in user space over UDP, which every network passes. It combines the transport and TLS 1.3 handshake in 1 RTT 0-RTT on resumption , has independent streams so one loss doesn't stall the rest, and connection IDs so connections survive IP changes.

title: Reliability trade-offs
text: Compare TCP, UDP and QUIC on ordering, loss recovery, congestion control and head-of-line blocking. How do you decide? TCP: reliable, ordered byte stream, kernel congestion control, HoL blocking across the whole connection. UDP: nothing, you own everything. QUIC: reliable per stream, ordering only within a stream, built-in congestion control in user space, encrypted. I choose by what loss means for the data and who I want to own the logic.

title: QUIC rollout
text: What do you investigate, and do you keep HTTP/3 on? You enabled HTTP/3 alt-svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400 on your CDN edge. Metrics after 24 h: overall p50 latency improved 8%, but p99 got worse by 12%, and 6% of requests show "protocol=h2" despite alt-svc advertisement. A large enterprise customer reports intermittent 5 s delays on first page load. Edge CPU rose from 35% to 48%. Red herring: origin latency is flat.

title: Voice quality over lossy links
text: Evaluate the two proposals and suggest what to do. Your in-app voice calls UDP, 20 ms Opus frames, 50 packets/s get complaints in emerging markets: robotic audio, 4-6% loss, RTT 250 ms, jitter 80 ms. The team proposes "just retransmit lost packets" and separately "move audio to TCP for reliability". Bandwidth per call is 32 kbps; users are on metered data. rtp stats: loss=5.1% jitter=82ms rtt=251ms concealed samples=14%

title: Spot the bug in a UDP sender
text: What's the bug, why do only some customers fail, and how do you fix it? A telemetry client sends batches of events as one UDP datagram per batch. After a feature added more fields, a few customers on VPNs report missing data while most work. Review this code. The server logs show no errors. Packet capture shows IP fragments from this host, and none of the fragments arrive at the server for the failing customers. import socket, json s = socket.socket socket.AF INET, socket.SOCK DGRAM def flush events : payload = json.dumps events .encode grows with batch size s.sendto payload, "telemetry.example.com", 8125 events.clear

title: Choosing reliability for internal RPC
text: How do you respond to the proposal? A teammate proposes replacing gRPC/TCP between services with a custom UDP protocol "to cut latency" for a hot path doing 200k small RPCs/s inside one datacenter RTT 0.2 ms, loss 0.001% . Current p99 is 6 ms, p50 1.2 ms. Profiling shows 40% of time in TLS and serialization, 10% in kernel TCP. There is no written SLO, only "make it faster". Mixed replies include a Kubernetes service mesh sidecar adding 1 ms per hop.

title: Recursive vs authoritative
text: What is the difference between a recursive resolver and an authoritative name server? An authoritative server holds the actual records for a zone and answers with the final truth for it. A recursive resolver works on behalf of clients: it walks the hierarchy root, TLD, authoritative , caches results, and returns the answer. Clients talk to recursive resolvers, resolvers talk to authoritative servers.

title: Record types
text: Explain A, AAAA, CNAME, NS, MX, TXT and SRV records. Which restrictions on CNAME matter? A/AAAA map a name to IPv4/IPv6. CNAME makes a name an alias of another name. NS delegates a zone. MX routes mail. TXT holds arbitrary text SPF, verification . SRV gives host, port, priority and weight for a service. A CNAME cannot coexist with other records at the same name, so it cannot sit at the zone apex.

title: TTL
text: What is DNS TTL and how does it affect a planned migration? TTL is how many seconds a resolver may cache an answer. Before migrating, I lower the TTL say from 24 h to 60 s at least one old-TTL period ahead, make the change, watch traffic drain, then raise TTL again. Lowering it at the time of the change is too late because caches hold the old long TTL.

title: Full lookup path
text: Walk me through everything that happens from typing a hostname in a program to getting an IP, including the caches. The app calls getaddrinfo; libc checks /etc/hosts and nsswitch order, then asks the stub/system resolver maybe systemd-resolved or a local cache , which asks the configured recursive resolver over UDP/53 TCP on truncation . The resolver checks its cache, otherwise walks root, TLD, authoritative. The answer returns up the chain, each layer caching by TTL.

title: Stale DNS after migration
text: Why is traffic still hitting the old IP and what do you do? You moved a payments API from 198.51.100.10 to a new load balancer 203.0.113.50 at 02:00. TTL was 300 s lowered from 3600 the day before, 20 hours earlier . At 03:00 the old servers still receive 15% of traffic. At 06:00 still 4%. You planned to decommission the old box at 03:00. Clients are mobile apps and a few partner servers. Red herring: Route 53 shows the new record correct and dig @8.8.8.8 returns the new IP. $ dig +short api.pay.example.com @1.1.1.1 203.0.113.50 old LB access log source mix: 60% Java partner servers, 40% Android app

title: Intermittent 5 s delays
text: Diagnose and fix. A service on Linux glibc sometimes takes exactly 5 seconds for its first call to a downstream API; subsequent calls are fast. About 1 in 200 lookups. The VPC resolver is healthy per the cloud provider. Strace of the slow call: sendto 5, "...api.internal.example.com A...", ... sendto 5, "...api.internal.example.com AAAA...", ... recvfrom 5, ... A answer ... poll {fd=5, events=POLLIN} , 1, 5000 = 0 Timeout sendto 5, ...AAAA again... after 5s Red herring: CPU and network look normal.

title: Resolver outage design
text: What do you conclude, and what changes do you propose? Last night your authoritative DNS provider had a 90-minute outage. Your site TTL 60 s on A records, 300 s on NS from registrar went fully dark after about 5 minutes, even though your servers were healthy. A competitor with TTL 3600 stayed partly reachable. Status page: the provider's anycast network was hit by a DDoS. You get to present the post-incident review. Traffic: 40k req/s, SLO 99.95%.

title: GeoDNS
text: How does GeoDNS or latency-based DNS routing work, and what are its limits? The authoritative server returns different answers based on where the query seems to come from. But it sees the recursive resolver's IP, not the user's, unless EDNS Client Subnet ECS is passed. So steering is only as good as the resolver location and cached for the TTL.

title: DNS failure modes
text: Explain NXDOMAIN, SERVFAIL, REFUSED and timeouts. What does each tell you? NXDOMAIN: the name doesn't exist authoritative said so . SERVFAIL: the resolver couldn't get a valid answer upstream failure, DNSSEC validation failure, lame delegation . REFUSED: the server won't answer you ACL/recursion off . Timeout: nothing came back network, firewall, dead server . Each points to a different layer.

title: Weird failure for one customer
text: What happened and how do you fix it without breaking the website? After the marketing team pointed example.com apex to a SaaS landing page using a CNAME in the DNS UI the UI allowed it , outbound mail from the company starts bouncing with "no MX for example.com" for some recipients, and Google Search Console verification via TXT also fails. Website works. DNS provider is a small vendor. dig example.com MX returns different results from different resolvers. $ dig example.com CNAME +short landing.saas-vendor.io. $ dig example.com MX +short empty on some resolvers; old MX on others

title: Kubernetes DNS load
text: Why is the load so high and how do you scale it to 60k QPS? A cluster with 3 CoreDNS pods handles 6k QPS. Traffic is growing 10x next quarter. Today p99 DNS latency is 8 ms, but CoreDNS CPU is 70% and shows many NXDOMAIN answers. coredns dns responses total{rcode="NXDOMAIN"} 72% sample query log: api.payments.svc.cluster.local.default.svc.cluster.local NXDOMAIN api.payments.svc.cluster.local.svc.cluster.local NXDOMAIN api.payments.svc.cluster.local. NOERROR Pods' resolv.conf has ndots:5 . Red herring: the upstream resolver latency is flat.

title: Failover through DNS
text: Can DNS meet this requirement? What would you build? You run active-active in us-east and eu-west serving 25k req/s each. Product wants "automatic failover within 30 seconds if a region dies" using DNS health checks. You have TTL 30 s records with health checks every 10 s and 3 consecutive failures to mark unhealthy. Clients include browsers, mobile SDKs with their own DNS caching, and partners with connection pools.

title: Spot-the-bug in resolver config
text: Find all the bugs and fix them. A Java 17 service resolves a backend through DNS with weights shifted by a service registry that updates A records with TTL 30 s. During a blue/green cut, 100% of the traffic should shift within a minute, but the service keeps hitting blue for hours. A teammate shows the setup: // startup java.security.Security.setProperty "networkaddress.cache.ttl", "-1" ; // client static final InetAddress BACKEND = InetAddress.getByName "backend.internal.example.com" ; HttpClient client = HttpClient.newHttpClient ; URI uri = URI.create "http://" + BACKEND.getHostAddress + ":8080/v1/items" ; Red herring: the DNS records do update correctly.

title: DNSSEC / resolver attack surface
text: What happened and what do you do now and after? At 09:10 customers using one ISP report your site resolves to an unknown IP serving a login look-alike page. Your authoritative zone is unchanged. Users on other ISPs are fine. The look-alike IP is in a hosting range in another country. Your zone is not DNSSEC-signed. TTL is 3600 s. Security asks for a response plan within 15 minutes. $ dig @isp-resolver.example.net www.example.com +short 192.0.2.250 $ dig @ns1.example.com www.example.com +short 203.0.113.50

title: Methods, safety and idempotency
text: What do "safe" and "idempotent" mean for HTTP methods, and why does it matter for retries? Safe means no state change GET, HEAD, OPTIONS . Idempotent means repeating gives the same server state as doing it once GET, PUT, DELETE, plus the safe ones . POST is neither, PATCH is not guaranteed idempotent. Proxies and clients may retry idempotent requests automatically, so a non-idempotent POST needs an idempotency key.

title: Cache-Control basics
text: Explain Cache-Control, ETag and conditional requests. How is no-cache different from no-store ? max-age says how long a response is fresh. After that the cache revalidates using If-None-Match ETag or If-Modified-Since , and the server answers 304 with no body if unchanged. no-cache means "store it but revalidate before use"; no-store means "never store it". private restricts to the browser; public allows shared caches.

title: Keep-alive
text: What does HTTP keep-alive solve and what limits remain in HTTP/1.1? Keep-alive reuses a TCP and TLS connection for multiple requests, avoiding repeated handshakes and slow-start restarts. But HTTP/1.1 still handles one request at a time per connection: responses must come back in order, so a slow response blocks the ones behind it. Browsers work around this with about 6 parallel connections per host.

title: HoL blocking across versions
text: How do HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 each deal with head-of-line blocking? HTTP/1.1 blocks at the request level within a connection. HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection, which fixes request-level blocking but one lost TCP segment still stalls all streams. HTTP/3 uses QUIC where streams are independent, so loss only blocks the affected stream.

title: CORS failure
text: Why does it fail and what is the correct configuration? A new SPA at https://app.example.com calls https://api.example.com/v1/orders with fetch url, {method:'PUT', headers:{'Authorization':'Bearer ...','Content-Type':'application/json'}, credentials:'include'} . In the browser console: "blocked by CORS policy: Response to preflight request doesn't pass access control check". But curl works fine, and Postman too. Backend dev says "I added Access-Control-Allow-Origin: ." Network tab: OPTIONS /v1/orders - 403 no CORS headers Red herring: API gateway logs show 200s for GETs.

title: Cache bug
text: What's wrong and how do you fix it safely? After a release, some users see an old JavaScript bundle for days and the app breaks with API mismatch errors; a hard refresh fixes it. The CDN config and responses: GET /index.html - 200 Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400 GET /static/main.js - 200 Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable Build output: static/main.js same filename every build CDN hit ratio is 98%. Red herring: the service worker was recently disabled.

title: HTTP/2 behind a load balancer
text: Why is load unbalanced and how do you fix it? You moved internal gRPC/HTTP2 traffic through a layer-4 NLB to a pool of 12 pods. Total 3k req/s via 8 client pods. After scaling the backend from 6 to 12 pods, the new pods receive almost no traffic, and two old pods run at 90% CPU. Connection counts: pod-1: 8 conns CPU 91% pod-2: 8 conns CPU 88% pod-7: 0 conns CPU 3% Red herring: pod readiness is fine and the NLB reports all targets healthy.

title: Cookies and SameSite
text: How do cookie attributes HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, Domain protect a session, and how do sessions work with cookies? The server sets a session ID in Set-Cookie ; the browser returns it on each request, and the server looks up the session. HttpOnly hides it from JavaScript limits XSS theft , Secure sends only over HTTPS, SameSite=Lax/Strict stops cross-site sends limits CSRF , and Domain / Path scope where it goes.

title: Headers that matter
text: Which request and response headers matter most in a production HTTP setup, and why? Host virtual hosting , Content-Type / Content-Length / Transfer-Encoding framing , Accept-Encoding / Content-Encoding compression , Authorization , X-Forwarded-For / Forwarded client IP behind proxies , Cache-Control / ETag / Vary , Strict-Transport-Security , Content-Security-Policy , and Retry-After / 429 for backoff.

title: Intermittent 502s
text: Why do the 502s happen and how do you fix them? Behind an ALB idle timeout 60 s your Node.js service returns 0.1% 502s at low traffic, mostly after quiet periods; at high traffic it is rare. Logs: ALB target connection error / 502 ... backend closed connection . App is Node's default HTTP server. Red herring: CPU, memory and GC are fine. Node: server.keepAliveTimeout = 5000 default 5 s ALB idle timeout = 60 s

title: Cache poisoning risk
text: Explain the vulnerability, immediate response, and a durable fix. A CDN fronts your site. Security reports that https://shop.example.com/? sometimes returns a page whose links point to https://evil.example.net/ . The origin builds absolute URLs from the X-Forwarded-Host header when present. CDN cache key: path + query only. Hit ratio 95%, TTL 10 min. A researcher shows one crafted request poisons the cache for all users for 10 minutes. GET / HTTP/1.1 Host: shop.example.com X-Forwarded-Host: evil.example.net

title: Migrating to HTTP/3 and tuning
text: Would you adopt HTTP/3, and what else would you do first? A news site 80% mobile, p75 RTT 120 ms, loss 2% on 4G wants to cut load time. Current: HTTP/2 over TLS 1.3, 90 requests per page, 1.8 MB, TTFB p75 480 ms. A vendor pitches HTTP/3 as "30% faster". Budget allows one quarter of work. RUM data shows 35% of sessions are repeat visits with TLS session resumption.

title: Sessions at scale
text: Which approach do you choose and why? Your monolith uses in-memory sessions on 6 instances with sticky load balancing; deploys log users out and scale-out is uneven. Traffic: 20k concurrent sessions, 5k req/s, peak 3x. Proposals: a Redis session store, b stateless JWT in a cookie with 24 h life, c keep sticky sessions. Security requires "log out everywhere" and revocation within 1 minute. Cookies currently 600 bytes.

title: Misconfigured proxy and upload failures
text: Diagnose each symptom and redesign the upload path. Users uploading 20-80 MB videos via POST /upload through nginx to a Java app sometimes get 413 , sometimes a hang followed by 504 at exactly 60 s, and mobile users get connection resets halfway. Smaller files are fine. Config excerpts: nginx: client max body size 50m; proxy read timeout 60s; proxy request buffering on; app: Tomcat maxPostSize default; upload handler writes to disk after reading all Red herring: object storage is healthy.

title: Push options
text: HTTP is request/response. How do you get data from server to client the moment it exists, and what are your options? HTTP lets only the client speak first, so I have four options. Polling asks every N seconds: simple but wasteful. Long polling holds the request open until data exists: works everywhere, but a request cycle per message. SSE is one long-lived response streaming events down: one-way, auto-reconnect. WebSocket is an upgraded two-way connection. I pick by direction and by what the proxies in the path allow.

title: WebSocket handshake
text: How does a WebSocket connection get established, and what is different on the wire afterwards? The client sends a normal HTTP/1.1 GET with Upgrade: websocket and a random Sec-WebSocket-Key . If the server agrees it answers 101 Switching Protocols with Sec-WebSocket-Accept , a hash of that key. From then on the same TCP connection carries small framed messages in both directions, 2 to 14 bytes of overhead instead of HTTP headers.

title: SSE resume
text: What is Server-Sent Events, and how does it recover after a dropped connection? SSE is one long-lived HTTP response with Content-Type: text/event-stream ; the server writes id: , event: and data: lines and the browser's EventSource parses them. On a drop, the browser reconnects automatically and sends Last-Event-ID , so the server can replay what was missed. It is one-way and text-only.

title: gRPC internals
text: What is gRPC actually built on, and why can a browser not call it directly? gRPC is Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2. You define services in a .proto , codegen makes clients and servers, and each call is an HTTP/2 stream with a length-prefixed protobuf message, with the status sent in trailers. Browsers cannot control HTTP/2 framing or read trailers, so they use gRPC-Web through a proxy such as Envoy.

title: WebSocket idle timeout
text: Find the bug s and fix them without redeploying clients. A trading-alerts service uses WebSockets behind nginx. Users on desktop report the feed "freezes" and the app reconnects roughly once a minute, but only when the market is quiet. Server logs show nothing. Config: location /ws/ { proxy pass http://ws backend; proxy set header Upgrade $http upgrade; proxy set header Connection "upgrade"; } Browser console: WebSocket closed: code=1006 at 60-second intervals. nginx error log: upstream timed out 110: Connection timed out while reading upstream . The app sends no heartbeats; during busy hours it works fine. A colleague blames the CDN in front.

title: SSE buffering
text: What is happening and how do you fix it without changing protocol? A live-score page uses SSE. In staging, events arrive instantly. In production, behind nginx and a gzip-enabled CDN rule, viewers see nothing for 20 to 30 seconds, then a burst of 5 to 6 events at once. Direct to the app: $ curl -N -s https://origin.score.example/stream id: 811 data: {"over":14.2} id: 812 data: {"over":14.3} prints each event the moment it is produced. Through the public hostname the same command prints nothing for 25 s. App CPU is 8%. A teammate suggests moving to WebSocket.

title: ALB 502 keep-alive race
text: Explain the 502s and fix them. Checkout API on Node.js behind an AWS ALB. After a recent upgrade, ALB shows HTTPCode ELB 502 Count at about 0.15% of requests 300/hour at 55 rps average , no pattern by URL. App logs show no errors for those requests. ALB idle timeout is 60 s. ALB access log lines: http 2026-11-03T10:14:07 ... 10.0.3.21:8080 -1 -1 -1 502 - ... target status code=- request processing time=0.000 target processing time=-1 . ss -tn state established ' sport = :8080 ' wc -l is stable at 180. Node server.keepAliveTimeout is default 5 s. CPU is 30%, memory fine. A teammate wants to increase pod count.

title: L4 vs L7 load balancing
text: What is the difference between an L4 and an L7 load balancer, and when do you pick each? An L4 balancer sees IPs and ports and forwards TCP/UDP bytes; it is very fast, holds millions of connections, and cannot see HTTP. An L7 balancer parses the protocol, so it can route by host, path or header, terminate TLS, retry, rate-limit and cache, at higher CPU cost. I use L4 at the edge for raw throughput or non-HTTP protocols, and L7 where routing, retries or gRPC balancing matter.

title: Choosing a protocol
text: What protocol do you choose for each, and what do you ask before deciding? Product asks for "live" features in a brokerage app: a price ticks for a watchlist, 50 symbols per user, 3 updates/s each, 400k concurrent users at peak; b order status updates a few per order ; c a chat with the support agent; d internal services order, risk, ledger calling each other at 25k rps. Mobile and web clients. The PM says "just use WebSockets everywhere, it's real time".

title: Scaling WebSockets
text: Your WebSocket service is stateful. How do you scale it across 20 servers, deliver a message to user B who is connected somewhere else, and survive deploys? Connections pin to one node, so I keep a presence map user to node in Redis and use pub/sub or a stream to route a message to the right node, which writes to the local socket. Delivery is at-least-once with message ids and acks; clients resume with a last-seen id. Deploys drain gracefully and clients reconnect with jittered backoff to avoid a thundering herd.

title: gRPC load imbalance
text: Why did adding pods not help, and how do you fix it? Pricing service gRPC, 6 pods behind a Kubernetes ClusterIP Service. After adding 6 more pods for a sale, p99 latency stays at 900 ms and one pod is at 95% CPU while others sit at 8%. Metrics per pod: pod rps cpu p-0 4120 95% p-1 60 6% p-2 55 5% p-3 0 0% new p-4 0 0% new ... On the client order-service, 3 pods ss -tn dst 10.96.14.22:50051 shows exactly 1 ESTABLISHED connection per client pod. The Service uses kube-proxy iptables mode. A teammate suspects a noisy neighbor and wants to add a bigger node.

title: Retry storm
text: Why did a 6 s blip become a 14 minute outage, and what do you change before next sale? Edge Envoy retries upstream failures retry on: 5xx,reset,connect-failure , num retries: 3 and clients also retry 3 times. Inventory API normally 2k rps, 40 ms p50. Black Friday traffic goes to 20k rps; a DB failover causes inventory to return 503 for 6 seconds. Envoy stats: cluster.inventory.upstream rq total: 138402 cluster.inventory.upstream rq retry: 96311 cluster.inventory.upstream rq pending overflow: 18770 After the DB recovers, the API stays overloaded for 14 minutes CPU 100%, latency 12 s . The DB is healthy. Queue depth grows then decays slowly.

title: WebSocket reconnect storm
text: Plan the migration. You are migrating a WebSocket gateway 1.2M concurrent connections on 8 nodes from nginx to Envoy and from one Kubernetes cluster to another, with zero visible downtime. Each client auto-reconnects on close with a fixed 1 s delay cannot be changed quickly, mobile release takes weeks . Past deploy: 8 nodes restarted in sequence, and the first node took 400k reconnects in 20 s: node-1 CPU 100% for 90 s handshakes/s: 21,500 limit about 6,000 SSL do handshake queue growing; accept queue Recv-Q 4096/4096 nstat: TcpExtListenOverflows 188204 Target: no more than 5% of users see a disconnect longer than 10 s.

title: REST to gRPC cost
text: Is the gRPC migration the right first step? What would you do? Internal calls between order, pricing and inventory services run as JSON over HTTP/1.1, 20,000 calls/s, average payload 1 KB JSON. The platform lead proposes migrating all 40 services to gRPC "to cut latency". Profiling of order-service : CPU flame graph: jackson serialization 18%, GC 11%, TLS 9%, handler logic 40% p50 end-to-end: 38 ms; of which downstream network + parse about 3 ms New connection per call: 34% of calls no keepalive pool Cloud inter-AZ egress is $0.01/GB each way. Team size 6.

title: What TLS guarantees
text: What does TLS give you, and why does it use both asymmetric and symmetric cryptography? TLS gives confidentiality data is encrypted , integrity tampering is detected and authentication the server proves identity with a certificate, optionally the client too . Asymmetric crypto is slow, around thousands of signatures per second per core, so TLS uses it once to agree on a shared key and authenticate, then switches to fast symmetric encryption like AES-GCM, several GB/s per core with AES-NI.

title: TLS 1.3 round trips
text: Walk through the TLS 1.3 handshake and tell me how many round trips it adds to a new HTTPS request. After the TCP handshake, TLS 1.3 needs one round trip. The client sends ClientHello with its ephemeral key share; the server answers ServerHello with its key share, then certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished, all encrypted; the client sends Finished plus the HTTP request. TLS 1.2 needed two round trips, so TLS 1.3 saves one RTT.

title: Certificate chain validation
text: How does a client decide to trust a server's certificate? The client builds a chain from the server's leaf certificate through intermediates to a root already in its trust store, verifying each signature. It also checks that the hostname matches a Subject Alternative Name, the dates are valid, the certificate is not revoked, and Chrome that it appears in Certificate Transparency logs. The server must send the leaf and intermediates, not the root.

title: Forward secrecy and 0-RTT
text: What is forward secrecy, and why is TLS 1.3 0-RTT dangerous? Forward secrecy means each connection uses an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key, so if the server's long-term private key leaks later, previously recorded traffic still cannot be decrypted. TLS 1.3 mandates it. 0-RTT lets a resuming client send data in its first flight using the previous session's secret, but an attacker can replay that first flight, so I only allow it for idempotent requests.

title: Missing intermediate
text: Diagnose and fix, and explain why Chrome works. After renewing a certificate, the mobile team reports "SSL handshake failed" on Android 9 and the partner's Java batch job throws PKIX path building failed . Chrome and Safari on laptops are fine. Monitoring an HTTP check from a Chrome-based probe is green. You run: $ openssl s client -connect api.shop.com:443 -servername api.shop.com </dev/null 2 /dev/null grep -E 's: i: Verify' 0 s:CN = api.shop.com i:C = US, O = Let's Encrypt, CN = R3 Verify return code: 21 unable to verify the first certificate Only one certificate is shown in the chain. Expiry is Jan 2027. The ops engineer says "the cert is valid, the clients are broken".

title: Certificate expiry
text: Run the post-incident review: causes, actions, and how you would make this class of outage impossible. At 03:14 on a Sunday, every call to the internal billing API failed with x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid: current time 2026-10-18T03:14:02Z is after 2026-10-18T03:00:00Z . Time to detect: 41 minutes a customer ticket . Time to fix: 2 h 10 min because only one engineer knew where the cert lived. Facts from the review: $ openssl x509 -in /etc/billing/tls.crt -noout -enddate notAfter=Oct 18 03:00:00 2026 GMT cert-manager Certificate status: "Issuing... Order failed: DNS-01 challenge TXT record not found" last successful renewal: Jul 20 2026 90 day cert cert-manager logs had warned for 25 days. Nobody was subscribed to them. An exemption existed because the DNS API token was rotated in September.

title: Security group vs NACL
text: What is wrong and why does SG-only checking miss it? A new private subnet for a reporting service connects to an RDS Postgres 10.1.5.20:5432 . The SG on RDS allows 5432 from the reporting SG. The team also added a custom NACL on the DB subnet: Inbound rule 100 ALLOW tcp 5432 from 10.1.8.0/24 Inbound rule DENY all Outbound rule 100 ALLOW tcp 5432 to 10.1.8.0/24 Outbound rule DENY all From a reporting host: $ nc -zv -w 5 10.1.5.20 5432 nc: connect to 10.1.5.20 port 5432 tcp timed out: Operation now in progress $ sudo tcpdump -nn -i any host 10.1.5.20 10:02:11.1 IP 10.1.8.14.51234 10.1.5.20.5432: Flags S 10:02:12.1 IP 10.1.8.14.51234 10.1.5.20.5432: Flags S 10:02:14.1 IP 10.1.8.14.51234 10.1.5.20.5432: Flags S The SGs have been checked three times and look right.

title: HSTS rollout
text: What does HSTS protect against, and how would you roll it out safely? HSTS is a response header that tells the browser to use HTTPS only for this host for the next max-age seconds, which defeats SSL-stripping on the first plain-HTTP hop. I roll it out gradually: max-age 300, then a day, a week, a month, a year; add includeSubDomains only after every subdomain serves valid HTTPS; consider preload last because it is nearly permanent.

title: Site-to-site VPN
text: What is your plan, and what would you avoid? You are connecting the company's 10.0.0.0/16 on-prem network to an AWS VPC and to an acquired company's network, via two IPsec tunnels each. The VPC was created with the default 10.0.0.0/16. The acquired company uses 10.0.0.0/16 and 10.1.0.0/16. Users report that after a prototype link, internal DNS names resolve but pings go to the wrong machines: $ ip route get 10.0.4.22 10.0.4.22 dev eth0 src 10.0.1.5 $ ping 10.0.4.22 64 bytes from 10.0.4.22: icmp seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.4 ms answered by a LOCAL host The team wants to use NAT between networks to avoid renumbering. Throughput needed: 800 Mbit/s, one tunnel 1.25 Gbit/s max.

title: mTLS in a service mesh
text: How does mTLS work in a service mesh, what does it actually prove, and what are its failure modes? In mTLS the server sends a CertificateRequest and the client presents its own certificate plus a CertificateVerify, so both sides are authenticated. In a mesh, each sidecar gets a short-lived certificate from the mesh CA carrying a SPIFFE identity such as spiffe://prod/ns/payments/sa/api , rotates it automatically, and an authorization policy says which identities may call which service. It proves which workload is calling, not which user; and if the CA is down longer than the cert lifetime, workloads lose identity.

title: mTLS migration
text: What went wrong and how do you complete the rollout safely? You must turn on mesh-wide mTLS STRICT for 180 services about 40k rps total in 6 weeks for a compliance audit, with no customer-visible errors. Today the mesh is in PERMISSIVE. Telemetry after enabling STRICT in one pilot namespace payments for 5 minutes: istio requests total{response code="0", response flags="UC", destination service="payments-api"} +2,140 envoy log: upstream connect error or disconnect/reset before headers. reset reason: connection termination curl from legacy-batch no sidecar - payments-api:8080: curl: 56 Recv failure: Connection reset by peer kube-probe liveness for payments-api: Get "http://10.4.2.9:8080/health": connection reset by peer The pilot was rolled back after pod restarts began.

title: HSTS preload blast radius
text: What happened, how do you restore service, and what do you tell leadership? Security enabled Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload on the apex shop.com and submitted it to the preload list on Monday. Thursday, support gets reports that status.shop.com and ops.shop.com are unreachable for many Chrome and Firefox users. Edge/Safari mobile users on older versions are fine. $ curl -sI https://status.shop.com curl: 60 SSL: no alternative certificate subject name matches target host name 'status.shop.com' $ curl -sI http://ops.shop.com HTTP/1.1 200 OK plain HTTP only, port 443 closed browser: NET::ERR CERT COMMON NAME INVALID no "Proceed anyway" button status.shop.com is a third-party hosted page with a cert for shop.statuspage.example . ops.shop.com is an internal tool served over HTTP.

title: conntrack exhaustion
text: Explain the cause and fix it. A Linux NAT/egress gateway VM 8 vCPU, 16 GB for 400 app servers starts dropping new connections at peak 18k new conns/s . Existing connections work. Intermittent client symptom: connect timeout . Gateway evidence: $ dmesg -T tail -3 Tue Nov 10 14:02:11 nf conntrack: nf conntrack: table full, dropping packet $ sysctl net.netfilter.nf conntrack max net.netfilter.nf conntrack count net.netfilter.nf conntrack max = 262144 net.netfilter.nf conntrack count = 262144 $ conntrack -S head -2 cpu=0 found=1830 invalid=9 insert failed=41022 drop=41022 early drop=0 ... $ sysctl net.netfilter.nf conntrack tcp timeout time wait net.netfilter.nf conntrack tcp timeout established net.netfilter.nf conntrack tcp timeout time wait = 120 net.netfilter.nf conntrack tcp timeout established = 432000 CPU 35%, bandwidth 1.2 Gbit/s of 10. Red herring: a recent change added a UDP DNS rule.

title: TLS handshake cost
text: How do you survive 10x handshakes without 10x servers? An API edge terminates TLS on 6 nodes 16 vCPU each and sees 12k new connections/s at peak, using about 55% CPU. A campaign expects 10x. Perf output on one node: perf top: 31% libcrypto: rsaz 2048 sqr / ossl ecp nistz256 openssl speed rsa2048: sign 1,450/s per core Session reuse ratio ssl session reused : 12% Most traffic: mobile apps opening a new connection per request over 4G RTT 80 ms Certificate: RSA 2048. HTTP/1.1 with Connection: close on 40% of client libraries.

title: Debugging method
text: "Service A cannot reach service B." How do you debug it, in order? I go bottom-up, one layer at a time: does the name resolve dig , can packets reach it ping , mtr , is the port open nc -zv , ss , does TLS work openssl s client , curl -v , what does the app answer and how fast curl -w , and only then packets tcpdump . I always run the same test from a healthy client and the failing one, from the failing client's own environment, and compare.

title: Reading ping
text: What does ping tell you, and what does it not? Ping sends ICMP echo requests and reports round-trip time and loss. It proves a path exists at the IP layer; it does not prove any port or app works. Many networks block or deprioritize ICMP, so no reply does not mean down and a reply does not mean the service is up. I read min/avg/max and mdev, because large jitter or a high max matters more than the average.

title: Timeout vs refused
text: What is the difference between "connection timed out" and "connection refused", and what does each suggest? Refused means the host answered with an RST: the machine is reachable but nothing is listening on that port or a policy actively rejects . Timed out means silence: packets were dropped by a firewall, security group, NAT allow-list or routing, or the host is down. So refused points me at the server process ss -tlnp , timeout points me at the path mtr -T , rules, tcpdump for SYNs without replies .

title: Reading mtr
text: How do you read an mtr report, and when is loss at an intermediate hop real? traceroute raises the TTL one at a time so each router returns "time exceeded", revealing the path; mtr repeats this continuously with loss and latency per hop. Loss at a middle hop that disappears at later hops is just that router rate-limiting ICMP replies; ignore it. Loss that starts at hop N and persists to the destination, or a latency jump that persists, means the problem is at or after N.

title: Slow request breakdown
text: Where is the time going, and how do you find the culprit? The mobile team says /orders is "slow, must be the network" with p95 650 ms vs 120 ms last month. Both ends are in the same region. From a pod: $ curl -o /dev/null -s -w 'dns:%{time namelookup} connect:%{time connect} tls:%{time appconnect} ttfb:%{time starttransfer} total:%{time total}\n' https://api.shop.com/orders dns:0.012 connect:0.034 tls:0.071 ttfb:0.610 total:0.655 $ ping -c 3 api.shop.com tail -1 rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 20.9/21.4/22.3/0.6 ms The LB has three backends. Repeated runs of the same curl vary from 0.14 s to 0.7 s.

title: CLOSE-WAIT leak
text: What do these numbers say and what is the fix? An order service Java slowly degrades over 3 days, then throws java.net.SocketException: Too many open files and stops accepting traffic. Restarting fixes it. ulimit -n is 65,536. Output on the sick host: $ ss -s TCP: 61877 estab 410, closed 160, orphaned 0, timewait 120 $ ss -tan state close-wait wc -l 60912 $ ss -tn state close-wait awk '{print $5}' cut -d: -f1 sort uniq -c sort -rn head -2 60790 10.0.7.31 $ ss -tnp state close-wait head -2 0 0 10.0.3.4:48122 10.0.7.31:8443 users: "java",pid=2113,fd=412 10.0.7.31 is the payment provider's gateway. A colleague proposes lowering tcp fin timeout and enabling tcp tw reuse .

title: Stale DNS after migration
text: Explain what is happening, and how you would have run this migration better. You moved api.shop.com from old IP 198.51.100.10 to new 203.0.113.10 at 10:00. At 11:30, about half of users still hit the old now degraded stack. Checks: $ dig +short @ns1.dnsprov.net api.shop.com 203.0.113.10 $ dig @8.8.8.8 api.shop.com +noall +answer api.shop.com. 3100 IN A 198.51.100.10 $ dig @10.0.0.2 api.shop.com +noall +answer api.shop.com. 412 IN A 198.51.100.10 The TTL was 3600 s before the change. Some corporate clients use their own resolvers that ignore TTL for 24 h. A teammate wants to "flush DNS" on your servers.

title: TCP socket states
text: Which TCP states do you look at with ss when debugging, and what does a pile-up in each one mean? ss -s and ss -tan give the counts. SYN-SENT piling up means the remote isn't answering firewall or down . SYN-RECV piling up means a SYN flood or slow clients. TIME-WAIT is normal after an active close and lasts 60 s; tens of thousands can exhaust ephemeral ports. CLOSE-WAIT piling up means the peer closed and my app never called close : an application leak. On a LISTEN socket, Recv-Q is the accept queue depth, so growth means the app is not accepting fast enough.

title: Reading SYN retries in tcpdump
text: What does this capture say, and what do you do next? A new service in subnet 10.4.7.0/24 must call a vendor at 198.51.100.7:443. From the pod it fails after a long wait. The vendor says "we see nothing". On the node: $ sudo tcpdump -i any -nn host 198.51.100.7 14:02:11.201 IP 10.4.7.9.51234 198.51.100.7.443: Flags S , seq 1000, win 64240, length 0 14:02:12.205 IP 10.4.7.9.51234 198.51.100.7.443: Flags S , seq 1000, win 64240, length 0 14:02:14.213 IP 10.4.7.9.51234 198.51.100.7.443: Flags S , seq 1000, win 64240, length 0 14:02:18.229 IP 10.4.7.9.51234 198.51.100.7.443: Flags S , seq 1000, win 64240, length 0 dig vendor.example.com returns 198.51.100.7. An old subnet calls the vendor fine. ping 198.51.100.7 times out from both subnets.

title: Network vs application latency in a capture
text: You have a packet capture of a slow request. How do you prove whether the network or the application is slow, and what other patterns in Wireshark should you recognize? I look at the timestamps on one TCP stream: the SYN to SYN-ACK and request to server ACK give the network RTT. The gap between the server's ACK of the request and the first response data is application think time. If the ACK comes back in 21 ms and the data arrives 540 ms later, the network took 21 ms and the app took 540 ms. I also check retransmissions, dup ACKs, zero-window and RST patterns.

title: Kubernetes egress timeout
text: Find the root cause and fix it for good. You added a node group for a data-science team. Pods on the new nodes fail to call a partner API: Connection timed out , p99 30 s, 100% error rate. Old nodes work. Timeline and outputs: $ kubectl exec -it ds-pod -- sh -c 'dig +short partner.com; nc -zv -w 5 198.51.100.7 443' 198.51.100.7 nc: connect to 198.51.100.7 port 443 tcp timed out $ ssh node-new 'nc -zv -w 5 198.51.100.7 443' Connection to 198.51.100.7 443 port tcp/ succeeded! $ ssh node-new 'sudo tcpdump -i any -nn host 198.51.100.7 -c 4' IP 10.4.7.9.51234 198.51.100.7.443: Flags S IP 10.4.7.9.51234 198.51.100.7.443: Flags S retransmit CNI is Calico with natOutgoing: false for the new pool. Partner allow-lists one NAT IP.

title: NAT idle timeout resets
text: Do the post-incident review: cause, fix and prevention. A nightly batch job uses long-lived Postgres connections through an AWS NAT gateway to an on-prem DB. About 03:00 each night, 6 to 12 of 200 workers fail with could not receive data from server: Connection reset by peer , always after a step that runs silently for 6 minutes. Postgres logs show no error. Evidence: $ sudo tcpdump -nn -i eth0 'host 10.20.0.5 and port 5432 and tcp tcpflags & tcp-rst != 0 ' 03:07:41.118 IP 10.20.0.5.5432 10.0.3.44.50712: Flags R , seq 912331, length 0 $ sysctl net.ipv4.tcp keepalive time net.ipv4.tcp keepalive intvl net.ipv4.tcp keepalive time = 7200 net.ipv4.tcp keepalive intvl = 75 The last packet before the RST was the worker's query at 03:01:20, 381 s earlier. NAT gateway idle timeout is 350 s. Connection pool max lifetime 1 h.

title: Exactly 5 second stalls
text: Diagnose and fix, and say how to prevent a repeat. After a 10:05 deploy, 20% of requests to the checkout service hang for exactly 5 s, then succeed. Only inside Kubernetes; CPU and network graphs are normal. Evidence: $ kubectl exec checkout-7d9 -- curl -o /dev/null -s -w 'dns:%{time namelookup} total:%{time total}\n' http://inventory/health dns:5.012 total:5.231 $ kubectl exec checkout-7d9 -- cat /etc/resolv.conf nameserver 10.96.0.10 options ndots:5 $ kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns coredns-5c4d... 1/1 Running node-a coredns-8f2a... 1/1 Running node-b $ sudo tcpdump -i any -nn udp port 53 on a failing pod's node 10:21:07.1 IP 10.4.2.9.38811 10.96.0.10.53: A? inventory.default.svc.cluster.local. no answer 10:21:12.1 IP 10.4.2.9.38811 10.96.0.10.53: A? inventory.default.svc.cluster.local. 10:21:12.1 IP 10.96.0.10.53 10.4.2.9.38811: A 10.100.3.5 The deploy changed a NetworkPolicy. The DNS fault only occurs for pods on node-c.

title: MTU black hole
text: Diagnose and fix without a client change. A WireGuard tunnel wg0 links an office to a VPC. SSH and small API calls work; file uploads over 1 KB and large JSON responses hang forever. ping works. TLS to some internal sites stalls after ClientHello. $ ping -M do -s 1472 10.0.0.5 ping: local error: message too long, mtu=1420 $ ping -M do -s 1372 10.0.0.5 64 bytes from 10.0.0.5: icmp seq=1 ttl=62 time=19.8 ms $ tracepath 10.0.0.5 1?: LOCALHOST pmtu 1420 $ sudo tcpdump -nn -i eth0 icmp on the VPC-side gateway no "unreachable - need to frag" seen $ sudo tcpdump -nn -i eth0 'host 10.0.0.5 and tcp tcpflags & tcp-syn != 0' 10.1.2.3.50321 10.0.0.5.443: Flags S , options mss 1460,... wg0 MTU is 1500 on the VPC gateway; the cloud firewall drops all ICMP. Red herring: a recent TCP buffer tuning.

title: Role of the OS and containers
text: What does an operating system actually do for your application, and is a Docker container a small virtual machine? The OS shares the CPU, memory and devices between programs and protects them from each other. It gives each process a private address space, hides disks and NICs behind files and sockets, and enforces permissions. A container is not a VM: it is an ordinary Linux process with namespaces and cgroups, so it shares the host kernel. A VM has its own kernel on virtual hardware.

title: User mode vs kernel mode
text: What is the difference between user mode and kernel mode, and is a process running as root in kernel mode? The CPU has privilege levels: ring 3 for user code, ring 0 for the kernel on x86. User mode cannot run privileged instructions like touching device ports, changing page tables or halting the CPU. Root is not kernel mode. Root is a permission level inside the OS; a root process still runs in user mode and must ask the kernel through system calls.

title: What a syscall does
text: Walk me through what happens when your program calls read fd, buf, n . read is a libc wrapper. It puts the syscall number in rax and arguments in rdi , rsi , rdx , then executes the syscall instruction. The CPU switches to ring 0 and jumps to the kernel entry. The kernel validates the fd and the user pointer, looks in the page cache, and if the data is missing it blocks the task and asks the disk. It copies bytes to my buffer, puts the result in rax , and sysret returns to user mode. libc converts a negative result into -1 plus errno .

title: Syscall cost
text: What is wrong, how do you prove it, and how much faster can you get? A nightly job copies 1 GB files between volumes. After a rewrite from a shell cp to an in-house tool, the copy takes 8 minutes instead of 4 seconds. CPU shows 100% on one core, mostly system time. strace -c on a 10 MB sample: % time seconds usecs/call calls errors syscall 52.10 2.100000 0 10485760 read 47.50 1.915000 0 10485760 write The code: Languages: C++, Java, Kotlin, Python tab char c; while read in, &c, 1 == 1 write out, &c, 1 ; tab int b; while b = in.read != -1 out.write b ; // in/out are raw FileInputStream/FileOutputStream tab while true { val b = input.read ; if b == -1 break; output.write b } // raw file streams tab while b := f in.read 1 : f in opened with buffering=0 f out.write b Disk throughput is fine iostat shows 5% util . A colleague suggests a faster SSD.

title: Interrupts, traps, exceptions
text: Besides system calls, how else does the CPU enter the kernel? And how can the OS take the CPU back from a program stuck in while true {} ? Three doors: syscalls deliberate traps , hardware interrupts a device or timer says "attend to me", asynchronous , and exceptions or faults the current instruction needs the kernel, like a page fault or divide by zero, synchronous . The timer interrupt fires every 1 to 10 ms, the kernel runs, sees the task has used its slice and switches to another. That preemption is why one infinite loop cannot hang the machine.

title: top CPU split
text: What does this output say, and what do you do? An API service on an 8-core VM has p95 up from 40 ms to 300 ms after a deploy that moved from 50 to 800 worker threads. Traffic is unchanged at 1,200 rps. Dashboards show CPU at 85%. top and vmstat : %Cpu s : 18.0 us, 47.0 sy, 0.0 ni, 31.0 id, 1.5 wa, 0.0 hi, 2.5 si, 0.0 st procs -----------cpu------ -system-- r b us sy id wa st in cs 24 0 18 47 31 1 0 9000 310000 The team suspects the new JSON library red herring because it was upgraded in the same release. GC logs look normal.

title: strace for latency
text: What is happening and what would you change? An order service on one host has p99 latency of 2.1 s while p50 is 20 ms. CPU is 6%, memory fine, the DB is healthy query p99 12 ms . Only some requests are slow, about 1 in 40. A short, filtered strace on one worker thread: $ strace -f -tt -T -e trace=connect,sendto,recvfrom -p 4121 10:02:11.100 connect 9, {sa family=AF INET, sin port=htons 53 , sin addr=inet addr "10.0.0.2" }, 16 = 0 <0.000030 10:02:11.101 sendto 9, "\x..." , 40, 0, NULL, 0 = 40 <0.000020 10:02:13.103 recvfrom 9, "\x...", 512, 0, NULL, NULL = 80 <2.002100 A teammate wants to add retries and a bigger HTTP client pool.

title: strace safety and alternatives
text: How does strace work, why is it risky on a production process, and what would you use instead? strace uses ptrace : the kernel stops the tracee at every syscall entry and exit and wakes the tracer, so each syscall costs extra context switches. That can slow the target 10x to 100x. On a latency-critical process I would avoid it, or use a tight -e trace= filter for seconds. I prefer perf trace , or eBPF tools like bpftrace and bcc, which run in the kernel and add little overhead.

title: Steal time on cloud VMs
text: How do you diagnose and what do you do about it? A batch-processing fleet of 40 VMs 16 vCPU each runs the same job. 6 VMs consistently take 2.4x longer than the rest. Same image, same data size. On a slow VM: %Cpu s : 41.0 us, 3.0 sy, 0.0 ni, 6.0 id, 0.0 wa, 0.0 hi, 0.0 si, 50.0 st load average: 15.9, 15.5, 15.2 On a healthy VM st is 0.1. Disks and network look the same everywhere. Someone proposes rewriting the hot loop.

title: Reducing syscall overhead
text: What does a system call cost, where does the cost come from, and how do high-performance systems reduce the number or the price of crossings? A trivial syscall like getppid is about 100 to 300 ns versus 1 to 5 ns for a function call, more with Spectre and Meltdown mitigations; I would measure on the target machine. Cost comes from the mode switch, register save, argument validation and cache and TLB disturbance, plus the real work. To cut it, batch bigger buffers, writev , sendmmsg , use the vDSO for clock gettime , epoll instead of per-fd polling, io uring for submission and completion rings, and kernel bypass DPDK, RDMA for extreme network cases.

title: Softirq saturation
text: Diagnose and fix without replacing hardware. A UDP ingestion box 16 cores, 25 Gbit NIC drops packets at 600k packets/s. top shows one core pinned and the rest idle: %Cpu0 : 1.0 us, 4.0 sy, 0.0 ni, 0.0 id, 0.0 wa, 2.0 hi, 93.0 si %Cpu1 : 35.0 us, 5.0 sy, 0.0 ni, 58.0 id ... $ cat /proc/interrupts grep eth0 120: 98234112 0 0 0 ... IR-PCI-MSI eth0-TxRx-0 $ ethtool -S eth0 grep -i drop rx queue 0 drops: 1881233 The app is multithreaded and its CPU use is low. Someone suggests more worker threads.

title: Monolithic vs microkernel, isolation
text: Which do you recommend and why? You run a platform where customers upload and run their own code about 5,000 sandboxes per region, mostly idle, bursts of CPU . Today they run in plain Docker containers on shared hosts. A security audit found a recent Linux kernel local privilege escalation that a container could exploit. Options on the table: 1. Keep containers, add seccomp and drop capabilities. 2. gVisor syscalls intercepted by a user-space kernel . 3. Firecracker-style microVMs a guest kernel per sandbox . Benchmarks: syscall-heavy workloads slow about 2x under gVisor verify on your workload ; microVM boots in about 125 ms with about 5 MB overhead per VM vendor figure, verify .

title: Syscall return values
text: List every bug and how you would fix and test them. A log forwarder works in tests but corrupts data in production when the downstream pipe fills and during deploys SIGTERM/SIGHUP handlers installed . Code: void send all int fd, const char p, size t n { ssize t w = write fd, p, n ; if w < 0 { perror "write" ; return; // drop and move on } } ssize t read line int fd, char buf, size t cap { ssize t r = read fd, buf, cap ; if r == 0 return -1; // EOF return r; // assume r bytes form one record } Symptoms: 1 in about 20,000 records truncated, write: Interrupted system call appears in logs during deploys, and once write: Resource temporarily unavailable when the fd was non-blocking. Another engineer says the code is fine because it works under strace .

title: Post-incident review of a strace outage
text: Run the review. What went wrong, what are the contributing factors, and what changes? Postmortem: payments API p99 rose from 90 ms to 6 s for 11 minutes, error rate hit 34%. Timeline: 14:02 alert on latency CPU 40% . 14:05 an on-call engineer ran sudo strace -f -p 2210 on the busiest worker a JVM with 300 threads without a filter to see "what it is doing". 14:07 latency worsened, the load balancer started marking instances unhealthy, 14:09 retries amplified load 3x. 14:13 strace was killed and recovery began; root cause a slow upstream was found later in logs. Output tail at the time: pid 2299 futex 0x7f3c..., FUTEX WAIT PRIVATE, 0, NULL <unfinished ... pid 2301 futex 0x7f3c..., FUTEX WAKE PRIVATE, 1 = 0 pid 2310 write 14, "...", 312 = 312 Management asks whether to ban strace.

title: Process vs program vs thread
text: What is the difference between a program, a process and a thread? What does a process own? A program is a file on disk: instructions and data. A process is a running instance of it with its own virtual address space, open file descriptors, credentials, environment and signal handlers. A thread is a unit of execution inside a process: threads share the address space and fds, but each has its own stack, registers and program counter. Run one program twice and you get two processes.

title: Process states, zombies and D state
text: What process states does Linux show in ps , and what do a zombie and a D -state process mean? R running or runnable, S interruptible sleep, D uninterruptible sleep usually blocked on disk or NFS, ignores signals , T stopped, Z zombie. A zombie has exited but its parent has not called wait , so only its PCB and PID remain; it uses no CPU and kill -9 cannot remove it. A D process counts toward load average and cannot be killed until the I/O returns.

title: fork and exec
text: How does Unix create a new process? Why are fork and exec separate calls? fork clones the calling process: the child gets a copy of the address space, fds and environment, and fork returns 0 in the child and the child's PID in the parent. execve replaces the child's program with a new one; the PID stays and fds stay open unless marked close-on-exec. The parent calls wait to collect the exit status. They are separate so the child can rearrange its fds between the two, which is how ls out.txt and pipes work.

title: Zombies and PID 1
text: Diagnose, fix, and prevent. A containerised image-conversion service starts failing with fork: retry: Resource temporarily unavailable after about 3 days uptime. Pod restarts fix it for 3 days. Memory and CPU are normal 30% / 15% . Inside the pod: $ ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,cmd awk '$3 /Z/' wc -l 31872 $ ps -o pid,ppid,cmd -p 1 PID PPID CMD 1 0 python app.py $ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/pids.max 32768 The app spawns ffmpeg through subprocess.Popen ... per job and checks the exit code with poll only for jobs that time out. A teammate suspects a memory leak and wants to raise memory limits.

title: Copy-on-write mechanism
text: Explain copy-on-write. Why is fork fast even for a 20 GB process, and what is the hidden cost? After fork , parent and child share the same physical pages, marked read-only. The kernel copies only page tables, not data. When either side writes, a page fault fires, the kernel allocates a new frame, copies that 4 KB, maps it writable for the writer, and resumes. So fork costs page-table copying, tens of milliseconds for 20 GB, but later writes cause page copies, so memory use grows with the write rate.

title: Threads vs processes
text: What do threads share and not share, how are they implemented in Linux, and when would you choose processes over threads? Threads share the heap, globals, code and open files; each has its own stack, registers, thread-local storage and signal mask. In Linux a thread is just a task created with clone CLONE VM CLONE FILES CLONE FS CLONE SIGHAND CLONE THREAD , and the kernel schedules threads, not processes. I choose threads for cheap sharing and communication, and processes for fault isolation and security boundaries, because a segfault or data race in one thread takes down the whole process.

title: COW memory spike
text: Will the 10x load be safe? What do you change? A Redis primary holds 20 GB on a 32 GB VM and snapshots every 15 minutes. Traffic is about to grow 10x in writes from 5k to 50k writes/s, working set spread across all keys . Today INFO shows latest fork usec: 38000 and used memory peak: 20.3G . During the last snapshot the VM showed: $ grep -E 'Private Dirty Rss' /proc/<redis-child /smaps rollup Rss: 9437184 kB Private Dirty: 8650000 kB A teammate says "the snapshot child uses 9 GB? Redis is leaking memory." The VM has THP enabled=always .

title: Thread leak
text: Explain the error, find the cause, fix it. A Java service on Linux runs fine for hours, then fails with: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread while heap usage is only 35% and the container has 4 GB free. Metrics show the thread count climbing about 600 per hour. $ ps -o nlwp= -p 3120 18204 $ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/pids.max 20000 $ jstack 3120 grep -c 'pool- 0-9 -thread-1' 5120 The code creates Executors.newFixedThreadPool 8 inside the request handler for some endpoints. A teammate wants to raise -Xmx because the error says OutOfMemoryError.

title: Thread models 1:1, N:1, M:N
text: Explain 1:1, N:1 and M:N thread models. Where do Java platform threads, goroutines and Kotlin coroutines sit, and what does a blocking call do in each? In 1:1 every language thread is an OS thread pthreads, Java platform threads : real parallelism, but each costs a stack and kernel structures, so a few thousand is the practical ceiling. In N:1 many user threads share one OS thread: cheap, but no multicore, and one blocking syscall stalls everyone. M:N schedules many cheap tasks onto a small pool of OS threads: Go goroutines, Erlang processes, Java 21 virtual threads, Kotlin coroutines. The catch with M:N is a blocking call can pin an OS thread unless the runtime handles it.

title: Context switch storm
text: What is wrong, what do you change, and how do you size the pool? A pricing service 8 cores, 2,000-thread pool in Tomcat after "we need more concurrency" hits 800 rps and p99 climbs to 1.8 s. Calls are CPU-heavy JSON plus a 3 ms cache lookup. pidstat -w 1 and vmstat 1 : 11:20:02 UID PID cswch/s nvcswch/s Command 11:20:02 1000 4410 12000.00 9500.00 java r b swpd free cache in cs us sy id wa 60 0 0 812344 4123400 5100 45000 62 30 6 2 GC is normal young GC 15 ms . top -H shows hundreds of threads at 1 to 2% each. Management asks to add 8 more cores.

title: Concurrency model choice
text: Which model would you pick and why? You are designing a WebSocket gateway for a chat product: 200,000 concurrent mostly-idle connections per region, each sending a small message every 30 s on average, with occasional fan-out to 5,000 connections. The team knows Java and Kotlin; options: 1. Thread-per-connection on Tomcat platform threads, 1 MB stacks . 2. Netty event loop with a small thread pool. 3. Java 21 virtual threads with blocking-style code. 4. Rewrite in Go. Constraints: p99 delivery under 100 ms, 8-core nodes with 16 GB RAM, cost matters.

title: fork in multithreaded process
text: Find the bug, explain why it is rare, and fix it. A C++ server logs from many threads through a mutex-protected logger. To run a helper, a worker thread does a classic fork and then logs in the child before exec . About once per 5,000 helper launches, the child hangs forever; top shows the child stuck in S , 0% CPU, and the parent keeps waiting. std::mutex g log mu; void log const std::string& s { std::lock guard<std::mutex g g log mu ; fputs s.c str , stderr ; } void run helper { pid t pid = fork ; if pid == 0 { log "child starting" ; // BUG execlp "helper", "helper", nullptr ; exit 127 ; } int st; waitpid pid, &st, 0 ; } cat /proc/<child /stack is empty, strace -p <child shows futex 0x55d0..., FUTEX WAIT PRIVATE, 2, NULL . It never reproduces in tests with one thread.

title: Process-per-connection scaling
text: How would you migrate safely? A PostgreSQL primary 64 GB RAM, 32 cores serves a microservice fleet. Connections grew from 300 to 2,400 as services scaled out. Symptoms: query latency doubled, free shows 40 GB used by backends, and: $ ps -eo pid,rss,cmd grep 'postgres:' wc -l 2417 $ vmstat 1 r b free cs us sy id 48 0 3.1G 190000 55 30 14 Each backend is a separate process of 8 to 15 MB. Most connections are idle. You must introduce connection pooling without downtime; services use session features some SET statements, a few prepared statements, advisory locks in two services .

title: fork latency in big processes
text: Why is spawning slow and flaky and how do you fix it? A 24 GB-heap JVM service shells out to ffprobe for each uploaded file using ProcessBuilder . At 200 uploads/min p99 request latency has random 300 to 600 ms spikes, and perf trace shows: clone child stack=NULL, flags=CLONE CHILD CLEARTID CLONE CHILD SETTID SIGCHLD = 8120 <0.412000 The same call for a 100 MB process takes under 1 ms. Memory is at 85% of a 32 GB container, with vm.overcommit memory=0 . Occasionally spawns fail with Cannot allocate memory .

title: Purpose of scheduling
text: What does the CPU scheduler do, what goals conflict, and what is the difference between preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling? The scheduler decides which runnable task gets which core and for how long. There are nearly always more runnable tasks than cores, so it time-slices them. Goals conflict: throughput, low latency for interactive tasks, fairness, short turnaround for batch work, and low scheduler overhead. A preemptive scheduler can take the CPU away using the timer interrupt; a non-preemptive one waits until the task yields or blocks. Blocked tasks are not in the run queue.

title: FCFS, SJF, round robin
text: Compare FCFS, SJF and round robin. Three jobs arrive together with lengths 24 ms, 3 ms and 3 ms; compute the average waiting time for each. FCFS runs in arrival order with no preemption: simple, but the convoy effect makes short jobs wait behind a long one. SJF runs the shortest next: provably minimal average wait, but it needs job lengths which we do not know and starves long jobs. Round robin gives each task a quantum then moves it to the back: fair with good response time, but too large a quantum degrades to FCFS and too small drowns in context switches. For the example: FCFS A,B,C average wait is 0+24+27 /3 = 17 ms; SJF B,C,A is 0+3+6 /3 = 3 ms; RR with quantum 4 ms is about 5.7 ms.

title: Reading load average
text: What does load average actually measure, and how do you tell whether high load means a CPU problem or an I/O problem? Load average is the exponentially weighted average, over 1, 5 and 15 minutes, of tasks that are runnable or in uninterruptible sleep. It is not CPU percent. Compare it to core count: load 8 on 8 cores is roughly full. On Linux it includes D tasks, so a hung disk can give load 50 with idle CPUs. To split the cause I look at vmstat : r runnable high means CPU pressure, b blocked in D high means I/O pressure. Newer kernels also give PSI in /proc/pressure/ .

title: High load, idle CPU
text: What is happening and what do you do? At 03:10 an on-call page says "load average 40 on 8 cores, API latency 30 s". Output: $ uptime 03:12:01 up 41 days, load average: 41.2, 38.7, 22.5 $ top -bn1 head -4 %Cpu s : 4.0 us, 2.0 sy, 0.0 ni, 4.0 id, 90.0 wa, 0.0 hi, 0.0 si, 0.0 st $ vmstat 1 3 r b swpd free ... us sy id wa 1 39 0 2200000 ... 4 2 4 90 $ ps -eo pid,stat,wchan:22,cmd awk '$2 /^D/' head -3 6101 D nfs wait bit killable /usr/bin/exporter 6240 D jbd2 log wait commit postgres: writer $ iostat -x 1 2 grep nvme1n1 nvme1n1 ... await 4800.00 %util 100.0 The team is about to double the instance size and wants kill -9 on the stuck processes.

title: Starvation vs priority inversion
text: What is the difference between starvation and priority inversion, and how are each solved? Starvation: a strict priority scheduler always runs higher-priority tasks, so a low-priority one may never run. Fixes: aging raise priority of waiting tasks or a multilevel feedback queue. Priority inversion: a low-priority task holds a lock the high-priority task needs, and a medium-priority task preempts the low one, so the high task is blocked by the medium one. Fix: priority inheritance, where the lock holder temporarily runs at the waiter's priority. The 1997 Mars Pathfinder resets were this.

title: CFS quota throttling
text: Diagnose and fix. A Java service on Kubernetes requests.cpu: 1 , limits.cpu: 2 runs on 64-core nodes. Average CPU is 25% of the limit but p99 spikes to 800 ms every few seconds; p50 is 15 ms. No GC pauses beyond 20 ms. Metrics: $ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat usage usec 91233444000 nr periods 640000 nr throttled 210000 throttled usec 41220000000 $ jcmd 1 VM.info grep -i 'active processor' active processor count: 64 A teammate wants to double the pod's memory since "it must be GC".

title: CFS vruntime and EEVDF
text: How does Linux's CFS decide which task runs next, and what changed with EEVDF? CFS gives each task a fair share of CPU instead of a fixed quantum. It tracks vruntime , the weighted CPU time a task has consumed, keeps runnable tasks in a red-black tree ordered by it, and always runs the leftmost smallest vruntime . Lower nice means a higher weight, so vruntime grows slower and the task runs more. Tasks that slept get placed near the minimum so interactive tasks run promptly. EEVDF Linux 6.6 keeps the fair share but adds per-task virtual deadlines derived from requested slice length: among eligible tasks, the one with the earliest deadline runs, which improves latency fairness with fewer heuristics.

title: Quantum and convoy effect
text: What is happening and how would you redesign scheduling? You own a custom job runner single worker pool of 4 threads, FIFO queue . Job mix: 95% are 5 ms jobs, 5% are 3 s report jobs. Users complain that simple lookups sometimes take 6+ seconds. Queue metrics at peak: arrival: 20 jobs/s workers: 4 queue depth p99: 55 wait time p50: 40 ms p99: 6,200 ms Mean service time is 0.95 x 5 ms + 0.05 x 3000 ms, about 155 ms. Worker utilisation at peak is about 78% 20 jobs/s x 155 ms = 3.1 of 4 workers , so the long jobs dominate the load. Someone proposes making the pool bigger; another suggests time-slicing the reports.

title: Affinity, NUMA, hyperthreads
text: On a multicore server, what do CPU affinity, NUMA and hyperthreading mean for scheduling and performance? With many cores the scheduler also decides where a task runs. Moving a task loses warm L1/L2 cache; on a multi-socket NUMA machine, accessing memory attached to another node costs roughly 1.5x to 2x the latency. Affinity taskset , sched setaffinity pins tasks to cores to keep caches warm or keep interrupts separate. Hyperthreads share one core's execution units, so two threads give about 1.2x to 1.3x throughput, not 2x, and a cloud vCPU is usually one hyperthread. Load balancing must trade idle cores against cache thrash.

title: Priority inversion
text: Diagnose and fix. An industrial controller Linux, PREEMPT RT not enabled runs a 1 kHz control loop SCHED FIFO priority 80 , a telemetry uploader nice 0, normal , and a logger thread SCHED FIFO priority 20 sharing a std::mutex protecting a ring buffer that the control loop writes to. Occasionally the control loop misses its 1 ms deadline by 40 to 200 ms. A trace excerpt: control-loop prio 80 blocked on mutex 0x5e10 held by logger logger prio 20 runnable, waiting for CPU metrics-agent prio 50 running 120 ms SCHED FIFO busy loop CPU usage is 35% overall. Someone says "just raise the logger's priority to 99".

title: NUMA imbalance
text: Diagnose and fix. A 2-socket server 2 x 24 cores, 256 GB, 128 GB per node hosts a single large MySQL-style database with a 180 GB buffer pool. After a restart, queries are 40% slower than before and kswapd is active even though free -g shows plenty of memory overall: $ numastat -m egrep 'MemFree MemUsed' Node 0 Node 1 MemFree 1200 118000 MemUsed 126800 10000 $ vmstat 1 si so 450 1900 $ numactl --hardware grep size node 0 size: 131072 MB node 1 size: 131072 MB The service was started under numactl --cpunodebind=0 , copied from an old runbook for a smaller host. The team wants to add swap or lower innodb buffer pool size .

title: Isolating batch from latency work
text: What do you ask, and how do you configure this? Product says: "The nightly analytics batch must not slow down the checkout API on the same 32-core host, but it also must finish before 06:00." Today the batch 24 threads starts at 01:00 and checkout p99 goes from 80 ms to 400 ms. Containers are used cgroup v2 . Batch needs about 20 core-hours; there are 5 hours available. Checkout peaks at about 6 cores.

title: Utilisation and tail latency
text: Is 80 pods right? How would you plan capacity? A recommendation API has 12 pods at 8 cores each. At 4,000 rps overall CPU is 55% and p99 is 120 ms. Marketing plans a campaign for 10x traffic. Capacity plan from the team: "CPU is 55% at 4k, so 100% at about 7.3k; we need about 5.5x more capacity for 40k rps, plus a safety margin, so 80 pods". Load test at 6,500 rps on the current cluster: rps cpu% p50 p99 4000 55 22ms 120ms 5000 69 25ms 180ms 6000 83 31ms 520ms 6500 90 40ms 2100ms The service is a CPU-bound request handler with a 2 s client timeout.

title: SCHED_FIFO misuse
text: Run the review: causes, timeline lessons, and action items. Postmortem for a 25-minute partial outage. A feature team, to "guarantee low latency", set their event-processing threads to SCHED FIFO priority 50 via chrt in the startup script on shared 8-core hosts. A bug in a retry loop no sleep on error turned one thread into a busy loop. Timeline: 09:14 deploy; 09:20 SSH to the host became unresponsive; 09:23 other services on the host missed health checks; 09:26 monitoring agent silent. After some time the host recovered partially: $ dmesg tail sched: RT throttling activated $ cat /proc/sys/kernel/sched rt runtime us /proc/sys/kernel/sched rt period us 950000 1000000 $ top -H PID USER PR NI S %CPU COMMAND 8821 app -51 0 R 94.0 worker-3 Management asks: "How was one thread able to take down other services?"

title: Pipe semantics
text: What is a pipe, and what happens when the writer is faster than the reader, or when one end is closed? A pipe is a kernel buffer, 64 KB by default on Linux, with a write fd and a read fd. Bytes come out in the order they went in. If the buffer is full the writer blocks, which is free backpressure. If the buffer is empty the reader blocks. When every writer closes, the reader gets EOF read returns 0 . When every reader closes, the writer gets SIGPIPE or EPIPE.

title: Message passing vs shared memory
text: Why do processes need IPC at all, and what is the difference between message passing and shared memory? Processes have separate address spaces on purpose, so they cannot touch each other's memory. IPC is a controlled channel the kernel provides. Message passing pipes, sockets, queues copies data through the kernel: simple and safe, but each message costs syscalls and copies. Shared memory maps the same physical pages into both processes: no copies after setup and the fastest option, but I must synchronise myself.

title: SIGTERM vs SIGKILL
text: What is a signal, and what is the difference between SIGTERM and SIGKILL? Why does it matter in a rolling deploy? A signal is an asynchronous notification with a number but no payload. SIGTERM 15 is a polite request: the process can catch it, drain in-flight requests and exit. SIGKILL 9 cannot be caught or ignored; the kernel just removes the process. In Kubernetes the kubelet sends SIGTERM, waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds 30 s default , then SIGKILL. If my app ignores SIGTERM I drop requests or get force-killed.

title: Pipe deadlock
text: Find the bug, explain why only large outputs hang, and fix it. A nightly job shells out to a media converter and has started hanging for hours on a few large files; small files work. CPU is idle. The code: import subprocess def convert path : p = subprocess.Popen "ffconv", path, "-" , stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE p.wait wait for it to finish return p.stdout.read $ ls -l /proc/<converter pid /fd grep pipe l-wx------ 1 app app 64 1 - pipe: 88231 l-wx------ 1 app app 64 2 - pipe: 88232 $ cat /proc/<converter pid /wchan pipe write Failing inputs are all above 60 KB of output. Disk space is fine, and the converter works when run by hand.

title: Sockets, framing and epoll
text: How does a server handle 50,000 concurrent TCP connections on a few threads, and what pitfalls come with reading from TCP sockets? I make sockets non-blocking and register them with epoll ; one thread calls epoll wait , gets the list of ready sockets, and reads or writes until EAGAIN . That avoids a thread per connection. The pitfalls: TCP is a byte stream, so a recv can return half a message or two, so I need framing such as a length prefix; with edge-triggered epoll I must drain until EAGAIN ; and every socket costs a file descriptor, so ulimit -n must be raised.

title: Signals and graceful shutdown
text: Explain what is happening and how you would fix it. A Java service on Kubernetes 30 pods drops about 0.5% of requests on every deploy. Rolling update, terminationGracePeriodSeconds is the default. Pods show: $ kubectl describe pod orders-7d9f grep -A4 'Last State' Last State: Terminated Reason: Error Exit Code: 137 $ kubectl get events grep orders-7d9f Killing: Stopping container orders 30s later container did not terminate in time Dockerfile: CMD ./start.sh . start.sh runs some env setup and then java -jar app.jar . The app has a JVM shutdown hook that drains the HTTP server in about 5 s. A teammate says "memory leak, exit 137 is OOM". dmesg on the node shows no OOM kills.

title: Shared memory correctness
text: List what is wrong and how you would fix it. Two processes share a queue in a POSIX shared memory segment for a market-data feed 200k msgs/s . It works in tests, but in production the consumer occasionally crashes with SIGSEGV or reads garbage prices a few times a day. struct Msg { double price; int qty; }; struct Shared { Msg head; // pointer to the next message slot int count; Msg slots 4096 ; }; // Producer Shared s = Shared mmap nullptr, sizeof Shared , PROT READ PROT WRITE, MAP SHARED, fd, 0 ; s- head = &s- slots s- count % 4096 ; s- head- price = p; s- head- qty = q; s- count++; // consumer polls count // Consumer separate process, own mmap of the same fd while last < s- count { use s- head ; last++; } Both run on x86 with 8 cores. The segment is created by the producer with shm open and ftruncate .

title: POSIX shared memory setup and pitfalls
text: Walk me through how two unrelated processes share memory on Linux, and what operational pitfalls come with it. One process calls shm open "/name" , which creates a file under /dev/shm a tmpfs , then ftruncate to set the size; every process then mmap s it with MAP SHARED . After that they read and write the same physical pages with no syscalls. I add a process-shared mutex or semaphore, or a lock-free ring. Pitfalls: segments outlive the process so they leak, Docker caps /dev/shm at 64 MB by default, and the memory counts toward the cgroup limit.

title: Socket fd exhaustion
text: What is going on, how do you stop it now, and how do you stop it recurring? An API gateway Java, 4 cores, 8 GB starts failing at 14:10 with "Too many open files" and refused connections while CPU is 20% and memory is fine. Traffic is normal, 1,800 rps. On the box: $ ulimit -n inside the service's systemd unit 1024 $ ls /proc/4410/fd wc -l 1021 $ ss -tan awk '{print $1}' sort uniq -c 88 ESTAB 903 CLOSE-WAIT 20 TIME-WAIT A deploy of the gateway went out at 13:40 with a new upstream HTTP client.
