A teammate wants to raise the thread pool from 200 to 800. Another says it's a DDoS because there are many connections.

title: Choosing IPC
text: Which IPC mechanism s do you choose and why? What would make you change your mind? You are designing a host-level agent a sidecar that collects metrics from 40 application processes on the same machine. Each app emits roughly 5,000 small events per second 100 bytes each and occasionally a 20 MB profile dump. Requirements: the agent must tell when an app has died, an app must never be blocked or slowed by a slow agent, apps are written in Java, Go and Python, and some apps are in containers while the agent runs on the host. The security team wants only the right users to be able to connect.

title: Async-signal-safety and signal delivery
text: Why can't you call printf or malloc in a signal handler, and how do you write signal handling for a multithreaded daemon correctly? A handler can interrupt the program at any instruction, including inside malloc or printf holding an internal lock. If the handler calls the same function, it deadlocks or corrupts state. So handlers may only call async-signal-safe functions, in practice setting a volatile sig atomic t flag or write ing a byte to a self-pipe. For a multithreaded daemon I block signals in all worker threads and dedicate one thread to sigwait , so signals become ordinary events.

title: Listen backlog overflow
text: Diagnose this and propose fixes in order. A Go API behind an L4 load balancer handles 25k rps across 12 nodes. During a marketing push 3x traffic in 2 minutes clients see connect timeouts of 1 s, 3 s, 7 s, but the app's own latency graphs look normal and CPU is 45%. One node: $ ss -lnt sport = :8080 State Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port LISTEN 129 128 0.0.0.0:8080 $ nstat -az TcpExtListenOverflows TcpExtListenDrops TcpExtListenOverflows 48213 0.0 TcpExtListenDrops 48213 0.0 $ sysctl net.core.somaxconn net.core.somaxconn = 128 The service calls net.Listen Go uses somaxconn as the backlog . The LB health checks still pass. Someone suggests adding more pods; someone else suspects packet loss in the network.

title: Scale 10x with shared memory
text: How would you re-architect for 10x throughput and 9x lower latency? What new risks appear? A feed-normalisation service passes quotes from a network-receiver process to 6 strategy processes on one 32-core host via local TCP sockets. Today it moves 300k msgs/s 64 bytes with p99 latency of 180 microseconds, CPU in kernel networking about 30%. The business expects 3M msgs/s and wants p99 under 20 microseconds. Profile: $ perf top -p <receiver 18.2% kernel tcp sendmsg 11.5% kernel copy user 9.7% kernel tcp write xmit 7.0% kernel sock def readable $ strace -c -p <receiver 5 s % time calls syscall 71.2% 1.4M sendto Strategies only read; each needs every message. The team proposes Kafka, "since it scales".

title: Dead peers and leaked segments
text: Reconstruct the failure, and say what you would change in design, operations and monitoring. Post-incident review. A video-processing service has an ingest process and 4 encoder workers sharing frames via a POSIX shm segment guarded by a process-shared pthread mutex. At 03:20 an encoder was OOM-killed dmesg : Killed process 9120 encoder . From then on all workers hung and the ingest process stopped; the pipeline was dead for 4 hours until a human restarted things. After restart, the new instance failed with "cannot allocate memory" even though the host had 20 GB free. $ ls -l /dev/shm -rw------- 1 svc svc 1073741824 Nov 10 03:01 frames <- 1 GB, old -rw------- 1 svc svc 1073741824 Nov 10 07:20 frames.1 ... 9 files, total 9 GB; /dev/shm is a 16 GB tmpfs $ cat /proc/<ingest /wchan futex wait queue There was no alert; the process was alive, the container healthy.

title: What virtual memory is
text: What is virtual memory and why do operating systems use it? Why can ps show 8 GB VSZ for a process using 300 MB? Virtual memory gives each process its own private, contiguous-looking address space, and the MMU plus the OS map those virtual addresses to physical RAM frames. It gives isolation, a uniform layout for every program, sharing of common pages like libc , lazy allocation, and the ability to use more memory than RAM. VSZ counts address space that is reserved or mapped; RSS counts only pages actually resident in RAM, so a process can reserve 8 GB and touch 300 MB.

title: Page fault types
text: What is a page fault? Distinguish minor, major and invalid faults and say which should worry you. A page fault is a CPU trap when a process touches a virtual page that is not currently mapped to a usable frame. A minor fault is resolved without disk I/O first touch of zero page, copy-on-write, a file page already in cache and costs about a microsecond. A major fault needs disk I/O swap-in or cold mmapped file and costs 0.1 ms on SSD to ms on HDD. An invalid fault is a bad address or permission violation and becomes SIGSEGV. Major faults are the ones to worry about.

title: TLB purpose and cost
text: What is the TLB, and why does a TLB miss cost more than an ordinary cache miss? The TLB is a small, fast cache inside the CPU of recent virtual-to-physical translations. Without it every memory access would first walk the multi-level page table, up to 4 extra memory reads on x86-64. A hit adds about a cycle. On a miss, hardware walks the page table, which can cost tens to hundreds of cycles, and the data access cannot start until the translation finishes.

title: Thrashing
text: Diagnose and fix. At 09:00 a 16 GB analytics API node JVM heap 6 GB, plus a Redis cache and a batch job added yesterday goes from p99 120 ms to 9 s. CPU shows 5% user, 40% iowait. Disk is a network SSD. $ vmstat 1 r b swpd free buff cache si so bi bo 1 6 3201344 31244 1204 80200 5200 7400 5300 7600 0 7 3405120 29110 1180 79100 6100 8100 6200 8000 $ cat /proc/pressure/memory some avg10=71.20 full avg10=48.30 $ top PID USER %CPU COMMAND 45 root 98.7 kswapd0 A teammate says "iowait is high so the disk is slow; upgrade the disk." Another says "free is only 30 MB, add a swap file." The batch job's RSS is 7 GB.

title: Multi-level page tables
text: Why does x86-64 use a 4-level page table instead of a flat one, and how much memory do page tables take for a process with 1 GB resident? A flat table for a 48-bit space with 4 KB pages needs 2^36 entries x 8 bytes = 512 GB per process, which is absurd. A radix tree of four levels PGD, PUD, PMD, PTE , each a 4 KB table of 512 entries, only allocates the pieces in use. For 1 GB resident, that is 262,144 pages x 8 bytes = 2 MB of leaf PTEs plus a few KB of upper levels.

title: Segfault
text: List every memory bug here, say which one produced the logged crash, and how to find these in practice. A small C++ tool crashes with a segmentation fault only on some inputs, and only in release builds. Logs: $ dmesg tail -1 tool 4410 : segfault at 7ffd3a2f9000 ip 000055b1c8a0123a sp 00007ffd3a2f9010 error 6 in tool 55b1c8a00000+2000 Code: include <cstring include <cstdio char greeting { char buf 16 ; std::strcpy buf, "hello" ; return buf; } void deep int n { char pad 4096 ; pad 0 = char n; if n deep n - 1 ; } int main int argc, char argv { char s = char "hello world"; s 0 = 'J'; // 1 printf "%s\n", greeting ; // 2 deep argc 1 ? atoi argv 1 : 10 ; // 3 char name 8 ; strcpy name, argv 1 ; // 4 } Run with ulimit -s = 8192 KB . A teammate says it must be a compiler optimisation bug.

title: VSZ vs RSS
text: What do you tell the manager, and what do you change? A manager asks you: "Our monitoring says each of our 40 Java microservices uses about 6 GB of memory, but the nodes only have 32 GB and each hosts 8 of them, which would be 48 GB. Is this a capacity problem? Do we need bigger nodes? We got an alert at 90% memory on two nodes." You have: $ ps -o pid,vsz,rss,cmd -C java head -3 PID VSZ RSS CMD 4410 6291456 1810432 java -Xmx4g -jar orders.jar 4415 6389120 1752064 java -Xmx4g -jar users.jar $ free -m total used free shared buff/cache available Mem: 32000 16400 2100 300 13500 14800 $ grep -E 'Pss Rss' /proc/4410/smaps rollup Rss: 1810432 kB Pss: 1650000 kB The alert fires on total - free / total .

title: Page replacement algorithms
text: Compare OPT, FIFO, LRU and Clock page replacement. What does Linux actually do? When RAM is full the kernel must evict a page, writing it out first if dirty. OPT evicts the page used furthest in the future: optimal but impossible, only a benchmark. FIFO is simple but can fault more with more frames Belady's anomaly . LRU is good but exact tracking is too expensive per access, so systems use Clock, an approximation: pages sit in a circle with an accessed bit, and the hand clears bits until it finds a page with 0. Linux keeps active and inactive lists for file and anonymous pages, and kswapd reclaims in the background.

title: Page table overhead
text: Explain where the memory went and propose a cheaper fix, including how to roll it out safely. A PostgreSQL primary 64 GB RAM runs shared buffers = 32GB and max connections = 400 , with typically 350 active. The kernel memory looks wrong: $ grep -E 'PageTables MemAvailable Hugepage' /proc/meminfo MemAvailable: 11200000 kB PageTables: 21500000 kB Hugepagesize: 2048 kB HugePages Total: 0 $ grep VmPTE /proc/$ pgrep -f 'postgres: app' head -1 /status VmPTE: 61000 kB $ cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent hugepage/enabled always madvise never The box occasionally gets OOM-killed under connection spikes. The team wants to move to a 128 GB instance.

title: THP latency spikes
text: What is happening and what do you change? A Redis cluster r6 instances, 64 GB, 20 GB dataset shows p99 latency of 2 ms, but every few minutes some commands stall 300-900 ms. CPU is low, network is fine. After the AMI was updated last week, spikes appeared. $ redis-cli --intrinsic-latency 60 Max latency so far: 872 microseconds host is healthy $ redis-cli latency doctor fork: 3 events; latency 410 ms ... $ cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent hugepage/enabled always madvise never $ grep -E 'thp fault alloc thp collapse compact stall' /proc/vmstat compact stall 18211 thp collapse alloc 9920 $ grep AnonHugePages /proc/meminfo AnonHugePages: 21000000 kB BGSAVE runs hourly. The spikes also occur between saves. Someone suspects the network; someone wants to add replicas.

title: TLB shootdowns
text: Diagnose this and fix it. A 64-core ingest service C++ memory-maps and unmaps 8 MB buffers per request across 48 worker threads. Throughput stops scaling at about 16 threads and adding cores makes it slower. CPU profile: $ perf top -g 22.1% kernel smp call function many cond 14.0% kernel flush tlb mm range 11.3% kernel unmap page range $ grep TLB /proc/interrupts head -2 TLB: 8812334 9120011 9023009 ... TLB shootdowns per CPU, +1.3M/s $ perf stat -e dTLB-load-misses ./svc moderate Disk, network and locks perf lock look fine. The service allocates buffers with mmap / munmap each request. Someone proposes pinning threads to cores and upgrading the NIC.

title: Explicit huge pages vs THP
text: When would you use explicit hugetlbfs huge pages versus Transparent Huge Pages, and what are the failure modes of each? Huge pages 2 MB, or 1 GB cut TLB misses and page-table size. Explicit hugetlbfs pages are reserved up front, never swapped, and predictable, so I use them for large fixed shared memory like a database buffer pool or DPDK. THP is automatic kernel and khugepaged merge ranges , convenient but can cause latency spikes from compaction, memory bloat and large COW copies, so latency-sensitive stores like Redis and MongoDB recommend madvise or never .

title: Direct reclaim stalls
text: Explain the stalls and propose a plan to proceed with the consolidation safely. You are consolidating two services onto shared 32 GB nodes in Kubernetes to save cost: a latency-sensitive API p99 target 50 ms, 8 GB working set and a batch exporter that reads large files and writes 3-4 GB of output per run. You migrate 10% of API traffic to a consolidated node and see 150 ms stalls during exporter runs, with no CPU contention. $ vmstat 1 during export r b swpd free buff cache si so bi bo 2 1 0 112000 4000 21000000 0 0 120000 95000 $ cat /proc/pressure/memory some avg10=18.40 full avg10=6.20 $ grep -E 'allocstall pgscan direct pgsteal direct' /proc/vmstat allocstall normal 48210 pgscan direct 9120000 $ sysctl vm.min free kbytes vm.dirty ratio vm.min free kbytes = 67584 vm.dirty ratio = 20 Swap is disabled, no OOM kills. The exporter writes through the page cache and uses a lot of readahead.

title: Native crash debugging
text: Run the post-incident review: what happened, what evidence was missing, and what do you change? Post-incident review. A Java service using a JNI image library crashed 14 times across a week, each time the container vanished and restarted. App logs end abruptly; no OutOfMemoryError . Kubernetes showed exit code 134 on two of the restarts and 139 on the rest. The node's dmesg : java 4410 : segfault at 10 ip 00007f1a2c3b4a12 sp 00007f1a1d7fe8f0 error 4 in libimgproc.so 7f1a2c390000+4e000 A hs err pid4410.log file was found in the container's working dir on one occasion, but the pod filesystem was ephemeral so most were lost. The first responder restarted pods and closed the ticket as "Java flakiness".

title: malloc and the kernel
text: What happens when you call malloc 100 or new , and what does free really do? malloc is a library function, not a syscall. The allocator glibc, jemalloc, tcmalloc serves the request from free blocks it already holds. Only when it has none does it ask the kernel to grow the heap with brk or map fresh memory with mmap ; large requests glibc default threshold 128 KB, dynamic go straight to mmap . Neither syscall commits RAM: frames arrive on first touch via page faults. free usually just returns the block to the allocator's free list, not to the OS.

title: free vs available and page cache
text: free -m shows only 300 MB free on a 16 GB server. Is the server out of memory? What is the page cache? Not necessarily. Linux uses otherwise idle RAM as page cache, keeping recently read and written file data so most file I/O never touches disk, and gives it back under pressure. free is the wrong column; I look at available , an estimate of what can be allocated without swapping. If available is 9 GB, the box is fine.

title: Swap
text: What is swap, when is it useful, and why do many latency-critical services still avoid it? Swap is disk space that holds anonymous memory pages evicted from RAM; clean file-backed pages never need swap, they are dropped and re-read. It is useful because it lets the kernel push cold pages an idle daemon's heap out so RAM serves the hot working set and cache, and it cushions short spikes. Latency-critical services avoid it because a swapped-in page is a major fault costing 0.1 to 10 ms, and a swapping JVM stalls GC badly. The signal of trouble is active swap traffic si/so , not the amount of swap used.

title: Container OOM
text: Why is the pod being OOM killed and what do you do? A Spring Boot service in Kubernetes limit 4 GiB, request 4 GiB, -Xmx3g restarts every 6-8 hours. Heap dashboards show 1.8 to 2.4 GB used, never near 3 GB, and no OutOfMemoryError in logs. $ kubectl describe pod payments-5c7 grep -A3 'Last State' Last State: Terminated Reason: OOMKilled Exit Code: 137 $ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.events oom kill 3 $ jcmd 1 VM.native memory summary grep -E 'committed' head Java Heap: committed=3145728KB Thread: 410 threads committed=420000KB Class: committed=250000KB Code: committed=240000KB Internal/Other direct buffers : committed=620000KB Total committed is about 4.7 GB. A teammate proposes raising -Xmx to 3.5g "so it has more room" and another suspects a heap leak.

title: Allocator internals
text: How does a general-purpose allocator like glibc malloc or jemalloc work internally, and why do multithreaded servers care which one they use? The allocator carves large chunks from the kernel into blocks with a small size header. Free blocks sit in bins by size class; freed neighbours coalesce into larger blocks. To avoid a global lock on every call, each thread has a cache or arena tcache in glibc, thread caches in tcmalloc/jemalloc , trading some memory for speed. For long-running multithreaded servers, jemalloc and tcmalloc usually show less fragmentation and lock contention than glibc, and switching is as simple as LD PRELOAD .

title: RSS creep with stable heap
text: What is the likely cause and how do you confirm and fix it? A Python/C++ hybrid ingestion service gunicorn plus a native extension, 64 threads in a pool, 16-core node has steadily growing memory: 1.2 GB after deploy, 3.9 GB after 4 days, and then it is OOM-killed limit 4 GB . Python object counts tracemalloc , gc are flat. The native extension's own allocation counter says 120 MB live. $ pmap -x <pid awk '$3 20000' head 00007f2c40000000 65404 65320 65320 rw--- anon 00007f2c44000000 65412 64900 64900 rw--- anon ... about 40 anonymous 64 MB regions $ cat /proc/<pid /status grep Threads Threads: 66 Leak checkers valgrind on a short run show nothing. The next step proposed is "rewrite the extension".

title: Overcommit and OOM killer
text: Explain Linux memory overcommit modes and how the OOM killer chooses a victim. How does this differ inside a container? By default vm.overcommit memory=0 Linux lets processes allocate more virtual memory than exists, betting most will never touch it all; only absurd requests are refused. Mode 1 always allows Redis recommends it so fork does not fail ; mode 2 is strict and fails allocations up front. If physical memory runs out, the OOM killer scores processes by memory use adjusted by oom score adj and sends SIGKILL to the highest. In a container, hitting the cgroup memory.max triggers an OOM kill inside that cgroup even when the host has free RAM; Kubernetes reports OOMKilled , exit 137.

title: Dirty page write-back stalls
text: Explain the periodic spikes and how you would fix them. A write-heavy ingestion node 32 GB RAM, NVMe shows p99 write latency flat at 4 ms, then every 30 seconds a spike to 800 ms for 2-3 seconds. CPU is idle during spikes. The application appends to files via write and never calls fsync. $ while sleep 1; do grep -E '^ Dirty Writeback :' /proc/meminfo tr '\n' ' '; echo; done Dirty: 410000 kB Writeback: 0 kB Dirty: 3150000 kB Writeback: 0 kB Dirty: 6400000 kB Writeback: 980000 kB <- spike here Dirty: 900000 kB Writeback: 2400000 kB $ sysctl vm.dirty ratio vm.dirty background ratio vm.dirty expire centisecs vm.dirty ratio = 20 vm.dirty background ratio = 10 vm.dirty expire centisecs = 3000 $ iostat -x 1 - nvme0n1 wkB/s 1.9 GB/s, %util 100 during spikes Someone proposes faster disks; someone else wants to call fsync after every write.

title: Redis fragmentation
text: Explain the gap, propose the cheapest fix, and what you would monitor. A Redis primary on a 32 GB instance is at 90% memory and the team wants to double the instance size $$ . INFO memory : used memory: 10737418240 10.0 GB used memory rss: 17179869184 16.0 GB mem fragmentation ratio:1.60 mem allocator: jemalloc-5.2.1 active defrag running: 0 maxmemory: 0 The workload has many keys with varying value sizes and heavy expiry/deletes. A replica on an identical instance has used memory 10.0 GB and RSS 11.2 GB. Another engineer says "RSS 16 GB means we really use 16 GB; we need 64 GB nodes."

title: mmap vs read/write
text: When is mmap better than read / write for file I/O, and what are its hidden costs and failure modes? mmap maps file pages into the address space so I access them as memory; the kernel loads pages lazily through page faults and the page cache page is mapped directly, avoiding the copy that read does into a user buffer. It shines for random access to large files, sharing one cached copy across many processes, and simple code. Costs: page faults replace explicit I/O so latency is unpredictable a cold miss is a major fault , I/O errors arrive as SIGBUS rather than error codes, TLB shootdowns on unmap, and write-back timing is out of my control msync . For sequential streaming, read with large buffers is about as fast.

title: Durability and fsync
text: Identify every durability bug and describe the correct design, including cost. A small order-ingest service writes each accepted order to a journal file, acks the client, and replays the journal on restart. After a host power loss, 4 seconds of acknowledged orders were missing and the last record was half-written. The code: import os, json class Journal: def init self, path : self.f = open path, "ab" def append self, order : data = json.dumps order + "\n" .encode self.f.write data buffered Python file object self.f.flush return True caller acks the client now def rotate self, new path : os.rename self.f.name, new path self.f = open self.f.name, "ab" The disk is an NVMe SSD; the filesystem is ext4 with default options; the team says "flush writes it to disk".

title: Cache eviction by bulk copy
text: Explain the slowdown and how you'd fix the backup without a hardware change. Every night at 02:00 a nightly backup cp of a 400 GB database directory to a network volume runs on the primary of a 128 GB-RAM PostgreSQL server. Between 02:00 and about 05:30 query latency rises 8x, and the morning dashboards are slow until about 08:00. Evidence: $ free -m 01:55 Mem: 128000 45000 900 4100 82000 80000 $ free -m 03:00 Mem: 128000 45500 1100 4100 81400 79000 <- cache size the same! $ pg buffercache / pg stats: shared buffers hit ratio 99.7% - 94% $ vmtouch -v /pgdata/base/16384 tail -2 03:00 Resident Pages: 5100000/48000000 10% of hot DB files cached; was 70% $ iostat -x 1 - nvme0n1 r/s 21000, await 1.9 ms The team says "cache is the same size so it can't be a cache problem" and wants to add RAM.

title: Swap policy decision
text: Do you enable swap? Design the policy and the rollout, and say what evidence would change your mind. You run a fleet of 200 Kubernetes nodes 64 GB with swap disabled the historical default . Pods are a mix: latency-sensitive APIs Guaranteed QoS , Burstable batch workers, and many idle sidecars and JVM services that sit at 30% of requested memory. Finance wants better bin-packing denser nodes . Last quarter, OOM kills hit mostly bursty batch pods during spikes, costing retries. A proposal on the table: enable swap on all nodes e.g., 16 GB zram or NVMe swap, swappiness=60 . SRE worries swap will cause latency regressions for APIs.

title: Memory triage and incident review
text: Run the review: what are the real problems, what did the team miss, and what's the corrected triage process? Post-incident review of a recurring problem: a Go-and-Java platform node has had "memory alerts" for three weeks. The on-call's usual response was to restart the biggest process. Yesterday the node OOM-killed its logging agent and the database sidecar, causing data gaps. Facts from the timeline: RSS of 'ingest' process: Nov 1: 1.1 GB Nov 8: 2.9 GB Nov 15: 5.8 GB restart $ dmesg -T grep -i oom Nov 15, after the restart notes were lost Out of memory: Killed process 2211 fluent-bit total-vm:... anon-rss:380MB Out of memory: Killed process 3098 pgsidecar ... anon-rss:910MB $ cat /proc/meminfo grep -E 'Slab PageTables SUnreclaim' Slab: 9100000 kB SUnreclaim: 8800000 kB PageTables: 140000 kB $ slabtop -o head -4 OBJS ACTIVE USE OBJ SIZE SLABS 41000000 40900000 99% 192 bytes dentry The ticket history says "restarted ingest, memory back to normal" six times with no data captured.

title: Data race vs race condition
text: What is a race condition, and how is it different from a data race? Is counter++ thread-safe? A race condition is a bug where correctness depends on the timing of threads. A data race is the narrower, formal case: two threads touch the same memory, at least one writes, and nothing orders them. counter++ is not thread-safe: it is load, add, store, so two threads can both load 5 and both store 6 and one increment is lost. You can also have a race condition with no data race, for example check-balance then withdraw done in two separately locked steps.

title: Mutex and futex
text: How does a mutex work on Linux, and why is an uncontended lock cheap but a contended one expensive? On Linux a mutex is a futex: one integer in user memory. Uncontended lock is a single atomic compare-and-swap, around 20 ns, no syscall. If the CAS fails, the thread calls futex FUTEX WAIT and the kernel parks it; unlock sees waiters and calls FUTEX WAKE . A contended lock therefore costs a syscall plus a context switch, 2 to 10 microseconds.

title: Semaphore vs mutex
text: What is a semaphore, and when would you use one instead of a mutex? A semaphore is a counter with wait decrement, sleep if it would go below zero and signal increment, wake a sleeper . It has no owner, so one thread can signal what another waited on. I use a counting semaphore to limit N concurrent users of a resource, such as 20 connections, and a semaphore starting at 0 to signal "event happened". For protecting data I use a mutex, because it has an owner and priority inheritance.

title: Condition variable protocol
text: Why must a condition variable wait sit in a while loop, and what does wait do with the mutex? wait cv, m atomically releases the mutex and sleeps, then reacquires the mutex before returning. The condition can be false when you wake: spurious wake-ups exist, and another consumer may take the item between the signal and my reacquire. So I always re-check in a while . The condition is changed and signalled under the same mutex that wait uses.

title: Atomics and CAS
text: How does compare-and-swap work, what is the ABA problem, and are atomics always faster than locks? CAS says "set to new only if the value is still expected, and tell me whether it worked", done by one hardware instruction lock cmpxchg on x86, LL/SC or LSE on ARM . Lock-free code loops: read, compute, CAS, retry on failure. ABA: the value goes A to B to A, my CAS succeeds although the structure changed; fix with version stamps, hazard pointers or epoch/RCU reclamation. Atomics are not always faster: under heavy contention all cores fight for one cache line, so hot counters should be sharded.

title: Memory ordering and visibility
text: Why can one thread fail to see another thread's write, and what do release/acquire and volatile guarantee? Compilers keep values in registers and reorder, and CPUs have store buffers and reorder execution, so another thread may see writes late or in a different order. A release store guarantees all earlier writes are visible to a thread whose acquire load sees that store. Java volatile is acquire on read and release on write; C/C++ volatile is not a thread tool, use std::atomic . A mutex lock is acquire, unlock is release, so data under a mutex needs no extra fences.

title: Race condition without a data race
text: Find the bug, explain why TSan is silent, and fix it. A wallet service passes TSan cleanly, yet reconciliation shows 0.02% of accounts with negative balances at 3,000 withdrawals/s. class Wallet { private long balance; synchronized long get { return balance; } synchronized void set long v { balance = v; } } void withdraw Wallet w, long amt { if w.get = amt { // check w.set w.get - amt ; // act } } Red herring: the team already "made everything synchronized" last quarter.

title: Lost wake-up
text: Explain both failure modes and give a corrected version including shutdown. A hand-rolled job queue in C++ occasionally hangs: one worker sleeps forever while jobs sit in the queue. Happens about once per 50 million jobs, never in unit tests. std::mutex m; std::condition variable cv; std::queue<Job q; bool done = false; void push Job j { { std::lock guard<std::mutex g m ; q.push j ; } cv.notify one ; } Job pop { std::unique lock<std::mutex lk m ; if q.empty cv.wait lk ; // line A Job j = q.front ; q.pop ; // sometimes crashes: pop on empty return j; } With 8 workers, top shows low CPU and strace -f shows several threads in futex wait .

title: Critical section size and Amdahl
text: Explain the numbers and what you change. A request handler takes about 255 microseconds: 50 us parsing, 5 us updating a shared stats map, 200 us writing the response. A refactor wrapped the whole handler body in the stats mutex "for safety". The service on a 32-core box now peaks at 4,900 req/s and CPU sits at 12%, whereas before it hit 120,000 req/s. strace -c shows futex at 88% of syscall time.

title: Spinlock in user space
text: Why did a 100 ns lock become a disaster, and what do you do? A C++ in-memory cache uses a home-grown test-and-set spinlock while flag.exchange 1 {} around a hash lookup 100 ns . It ran fine on 8-core VMs. After moving to Kubernetes with 4-CPU limits on a 64-core host and a pool of 32 worker threads, p99 went from 2 ms to 600 ms and CPU is pegged at 400%. $ perf top 71.3% cache . SpinLock::lock $ pidstat -w -t 1 per thread nvcswch/s low ... nivcswch/s 2400 <- involuntary context switches high Throttling shows in cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat : nr throttled growing fast. The lock is held for 100 ns.

title: Finding lock contention
text: Walk me through diagnosis and the fix, then say how you would pick the final design. A Java order service doubled traffic after a promotion. p99 goes 80 ms to 1.4 s, error rate is flat, CPU 38%, memory fine. Heap GC logs show pauses under 20 ms. $ vmstat 1 3 r b swpd free cache ... in cs us sy id wa 14 0 0 812304 2210032 ... 9120 118000 21 17 62 0 $ perf trace -s -p 2310 -- sleep 5 summary futex calls 410,220 total 38,900 ms $ jstack 2310 grep -c BLOCKED 147 The latest release added a shared Map<String, Rate guarded by one synchronized method for currency conversion.

title: Hot atomic counter
text: Why does a lock-free increment cost 18% of CPU, and how do you fix it without losing accuracy? A metrics library increments one AtomicLong requests on every request. At 20k req/s on 8 cores it was invisible. The service is being scaled to 200k req/s on 64-core machines. A perf profile at the new load shows: 18.2% libmetrics Counter::inc lock xadd 9.1% app Handler::serve L1d cache misses: 31% of loads on cores that touch the counter Adjacent in the same object are AtomicLong errors and AtomicLong bytes , each updated by different request paths.

title: Visibility after hardware change
text: Why did this surface only on ARM, and what do you change? You are migrating a Java and C++ pricing service from x86 to ARM Graviton-class instances, 10% canary. After one hour, 3 of 40 canary pods publish stale prices, about one in 10 million reads, and one pod never stops on shutdown. Unit and integration tests pass. The code: class PriceBook { private Map<String, Price book = new HashMap< ; private boolean stop; // read in worker loop void publish Map<String, Price fresh { book = fresh; } // called from refresher Price get String k { return book.get k ; } void run { while !stop { work ; } } void shutdown { stop = true; } } static Foo inst; static Foo get { if inst == null { synchronized X.class { if inst == null inst = new Foo ; } } return inst; }

title: Priority inversion
text: Explain the failure and fix it without rewriting the architecture. A soft real-time telemetry gateway on Linux runs a control thread SCHED FIFO priority 80 , a logging thread nice 0 , and 6 medium-priority SCHED FIFO 50 compression threads. Once or twice a day the control loop misses its 5 ms deadline by 300 to 900 ms and the watchdog resets the unit. perf sched latency: control loop max delay 812 ms stack of control loop cat /proc/PID/stack : futex wait queue - ... pthread mutex lock log mutex logger thread state: runnable, not running preempted by compress- log mutex protects a shared ring buffer that both the logger and control thread write to; hold time is 10 us.

title: Coffman conditions
text: What is a deadlock, and what four conditions must hold for it to occur? A deadlock is a set of threads each waiting for something another in the set holds, so none can ever proceed; no crash, no CPU, just a stopped service. It needs all four Coffman conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Because all four are needed, breaking any one makes deadlock impossible. In practice breaking circular wait with a global lock order is cheapest.

title: Deadlock vs livelock vs starvation
text: What is the difference between deadlock, livelock and starvation, and how does each look in monitoring? Deadlock: threads wait forever for each other, so CPU is near zero and throughput hits zero. Livelock: threads keep running and reacting to each other but make no progress, so CPU is high and work done is zero. Starvation: the system makes progress overall but one thread or class of work never gets served, for example writers behind endless readers.

title: Lock ordering
text: How does a global lock ordering prevent deadlock, and how would you apply it to a two-account transfer? If every thread acquires locks in the same global order, a cycle cannot form, so circular wait is impossible. For a transfer I lock the account with the lower id first, then the higher, and I handle the from == to case separately so I never lock the same object twice. Keep critical sections short and never call unknown code while holding the lock.

title: Banker's algorithm and safe state
text: What is a safe state, how does the Banker's algorithm use it, and why does almost no real system use it? A state is safe if some order exists in which every thread can get its remaining maximum need and finish. The Banker's algorithm pretends to grant a request and grants it only if a safe sequence still exists. It needs each thread's maximum claim in advance, a fixed thread set, and costs O m x n^2 , so real systems use lock ordering, detection and retry, or admission control instead. An unsafe state does not mean deadlock now, just that one is possible.

title: Deadlock detection and recovery
text: How do databases detect and recover from deadlocks, and what must the application do? The DB keeps a wait-for graph: a node per transaction, an edge when one waits for a lock another holds. A cycle is a deadlock. It picks a victim usually the cheapest to roll back , aborts it and releases its locks. The application must catch the deadlock error and retry the whole transaction, typically 3 attempts with jitter. This is normal behaviour, not a DB bug.

title: Dining philosophers
text: Walk through the dining philosophers problem, three ways to solve it, and what each costs. Where does it show up in real systems? Five philosophers, five forks, each needs both adjacent forks. If all grab the left fork, all wait for the right one: deadlock with all four Coffman conditions. Fixes: order the forks and always take the lower number first breaks circular wait , allow at most four diners with a semaphore some philosopher can always eat , or use a single waiter that grants both forks together breaks hold-and-wait but serialises . In real systems it is a thread that needs two locks, or a transaction updating two rows.

title: Bounded buffer semaphores
text: Find the bug, explain why it only appears when the buffer fills, and fix it. What else would you check? A teammate implements a bounded buffer with semaphores empty = N , full = 0 , mutex = 1 . Under load the process hangs: 100% of threads idle, queue length constant at N. def producer item : mutex.acquire line 1 empty.acquire line 2 buf.append item mutex.release full.release def consumer : full.acquire mutex.acquire item = buf.pop 0 mutex.release empty.release return item Thread dump shows: one producer blocked in empty.acquire while holding mutex ; 8 consumers blocked in mutex.acquire .

title: Lock ordering bug
text: What are the two or three remaining bugs? After "fixing" deadlocks with ordering, the transfer service still freezes about twice a month, and sometimes a thread hangs alone. void transfer Account from, Account to, long amt { Account first = from.id < to.id ? from : to; Account second = from.id < to.id ? to : from; synchronized first { synchronized second { from.debit amt ; // calls listener.onChange from to.credit amt ; } } } // elsewhere void audit Account a { synchronized auditLock { synchronized a { ... } } } // AccountListener.onChange { synchronized auditLock { log ... ; } } jstack shows a cycle between a transfer thread holds account, wants auditLock and an audit thread holds auditLock , wants account . One hung thread has from == to .

title: Database deadlock errors
text: Why are deadlocks happening, and how do you drive them to near zero? After a flash-sale launch, 1.3% of checkouts fail with ERROR 1213 40001 : Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction MySQL InnoDB . Traffic is 800 checkouts/s. SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS : 1 TRANSACTION: UPDATE stock SET qty=qty-1 WHERE sku=8812 1 WAITING FOR THIS LOCK TO BE GRANTED: index PRIMARY of table shop . stock rec lock 2 TRANSACTION: UPDATE stock SET qty=qty-1 WHERE sku=4410 WE ROLL BACK TRANSACTION 2 Each checkout updates stock rows for up to 6 items in cart order; the cart UI lets users add items in any order. CPU on the DB is 55%.

title: Thread pool self-deadlock
text: Diagnose and fix. What do you do about the restarts? A pricing API using a fixed pool of 10 threads Executors.newFixedThreadPool 10 hangs every Friday at peak. Health checks time out, CPU is 3%, no locks are held in the usual sense. Kubernetes restarts the pod after 3 failed probes and it recovers for a day. $ jstack 2310 grep -c "pool-1-thread" - 10 $ jstack 2310 grep -A4 "pool-1-thread-3" java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING parking at java.util.concurrent.FutureTask.get FutureTask.java:191 at com.shop.PriceService.compute PriceService.java:57 A recent change made compute fan out three sub-requests to the same executor and wait for all.

title: Read-mostly routing table
text: Explain the symptoms and choose a better design. What about the read-to-write upgrade? A router service holds an in-memory routing table of 200k entries. 400k lookups/s across 32 threads each lookup about 0.3 microseconds , updates arrive 5 times per second rebuild of a few entries, 2 ms . The team used ReentrantReadWriteLock . Observations: throughput saturates at 1.1M lookups/s total instead of expected 10M+; occasionally an update takes 800 ms to start. perf: 42% of cycles in ReentrantReadWriteLock$Sync.tryAcquireShared cmpxchg Another developer added code that takes the read lock, finds a stale entry and then calls writeLock .lock to update it.

title: fork with locks
text: Why is the child stuck on a lock nobody holds, and how do you fix it without removing the feature? A Python 3 + C extension service multi-threaded, 16 threads shells out to an image tool using os.fork followed by exec in Python code, but a legacy C helper in the same process calls fork and then does snprintf / malloc in the child before execve . About once per 20,000 calls the child hangs forever; the parent waits on waitpid and request threads pile up. The child's stack: $ gdb -p 9731 -batch -ex "bt" 0 lll lock wait private 1 malloc 2 child setup at helper.c:58 3 spawn tool at helper.c:44 No other thread exists in the child.

title: Cyclic service calls
text: What happened, why did scaling and retries make it worse, and what should change? Post-incident review of a 41-minute outage. Services: Orders calls Inventory sync , Inventory calls Pricing , and a recent change made Pricing call Orders to check bundle eligibility. Client timeouts are 30 s everywhere with 3 retries. Timeline: 14:02 deploy; 14:05 p99 ramps; 14:09 all three services show 100% worker threads busy, CPU 5%; 14:12 autoscaler adds pods, no effect; 14:20 error rate 78%; 14:43 rollback restores service. Orders: pool active 200/200, queue 4,100 Inventory: 200/200 Pricing: 200/200 traces: Orders - Inventory - Pricing - Orders - ... depth 3, repeated

title: Unbounded queue at 10x
text: What happens at the peak, and how would you redesign the buffering, including shutdown and what to do when it is full? An ingestion service accepts events 1 KB each into an in-memory LinkedBlockingQueue with no bound, drained by 8 workers writing to a database. Normal: 3,000 events/s in, 3,000 out. A partner integration will raise peaks to 30,000 events/s for 10 minutes at a time, workers can sustain 5,000/s per instance. Heap is 4 GB.

title: What happens on read()
text: Walk me through what happens on Linux when a program calls read on a file, from the syscall down to the disk. read enters the VFS, which resolves the path through cached dentries to an inode and calls the concrete file system ext4, XFS . The file system looks up the data in the page cache; on a hit it copies from RAM. On a miss it maps the file offset to disk blocks through extents, the block layer queues the I/O, and read-ahead prefetches following pages. The disk only ever sees "read block N".

title: Inodes, links and unlink
text: What is an inode, what is a directory, and what actually happens when you rm a file? An inode holds a file's metadata: owner, permissions, size, timestamps, link count, and where its data blocks extents are. It does not hold the name. A directory is a file mapping names to inode numbers, so two hard links are two names for one inode. rm is unlink : it removes a name and decrements the link count; space is freed only when the count is 0 and no process still has the file open.

title: write vs durable write
text: When write returns success, is your data on disk? What does the page cache do on writes? No. write copies data into page-cache pages marked dirty and returns; the kernel flusher threads write them to disk later, after about 30 s dirty expire centisecs or when thresholds are hit. A kernel crash or power loss in between loses the data; a process crash does not, since the kernel still holds it. To make it durable you call fsync or fdatasync .

title: Journaling modes
text: What problem does journaling solve, how do ext4's ordered, writeback and journal modes differ, and does a journal protect your data? Creating a file updates several structures bitmaps, inode, directory, data ; a crash mid-way leaves a corrupt file system, and fsck over a big disk takes hours. A journal is a write-ahead log: log the change, commit it, then apply it, so recovery just replays committed transactions in seconds. ext4's default ordered journals metadata only but writes data blocks first; writeback has no data ordering; journal logs data too and roughly halves write throughput. The journal protects file-system structure, not your last seconds of data; that needs fsync .

title: ext4 vs XFS
text: How would you choose between ext4, XFS and a copy-on-write file system for a database or Kafka volume? Both are journaled and extent-based. ext4 is a safe general default, can shrink offline, and is simple. XFS has allocation groups with separate locks, so it scales better with many cores and large files or volumes, but it can only grow. For a database or Kafka I would usually pick XFS or ext4 with noatime . CoW systems ZFS, Btrfs give snapshots and checksums but can fragment and amplify writes on write-heavy databases. Block size and inode count are set at mkfs , so choose carefully; changing the file system later means copy out and recreate.

title: fsync and atomic replace
text: What exactly does fsync guarantee, and how do you safely replace a config file so a crash never leaves a half-written file? fsync fd forces that file's dirty data and the metadata needed to find it to stable storage before returning. fdatasync skips non-essential metadata like timestamps. For atomic replace: write a temp file in the same directory, fsync it, rename it over the target atomic on POSIX , then fsync the parent directory so the rename itself is durable. An fsync error must be treated as fatal; retrying can falsely succeed.

title: Disk full with free space
text: What is wrong, and how do you fix it now and for good? A build server's /var shows errors at 02:10: No space left on device . A teammate sees: $ df -h /var /dev/sda3 100G 34G 62G 36% /var $ touch /var/x touch: cannot create '/var/x': No space left on device $ df -i /var /dev/sda3 6553600 6553600 0 100% /var $ du -s /var/cache/ci/ sort -n tail -2 2.1G /var/cache/ci/layers 9.8M /var/cache/ci/tmp 4.9 million files A CI job started creating one tiny file per cache entry last week.

title: Deleted but held log
text: Why didn't the space come back, and how do you reclaim it safely without restarting a latency-sensitive service? Disk alert at 98% on /var . An on-call engineer deleted /var/log/app.log 21 GB at 11:00, but df still shows 98% and the service is writing normally. $ df -h /var - Use% 98% $ du -sh /var - 12G used column says 98G, du says 12G $ lsof +L1 COMMAND PID USER FD TYPE SIZE/OFF NLINK NODE NAME java 2310 app 7w REG 21474836480 0 9921 /var/log/app.log deleted

title: Atomic file replace
text: What is wrong with both versions, and what is the correct implementation? A deploy agent writes /etc/app/config.json on 2,000 hosts. After a rack power event, 37 hosts boot with an empty or truncated config and the app crashes; fsck was clean. def save config path, data : with open path, "w" as f: truncates the target first f.write data file closed here def save config v2 path, data : tmp = "/tmp/config.tmp" different file system tmpfs with open tmp, "w" as f: f.write data os.rename tmp, path v2 was "the fix" and a second power test still lost the file on some hosts or raised EXDEV .

title: Slow disk incident
text: Diagnose and propose fixes by cost. An API's p99 jumps from 40 ms to 2 s every few minutes; CPU is 20%. The service writes an audit log and a Postgres database on the same NVMe volume. $ iostat -x 1 Device r/s w/s rkB/s wkB/s await aqu-sz %util nvme0n1 45 2900 360 185000 18.4 53.2 99.8 $ cat /proc/pressure/io some avg10=62.40 avg60=48.10 avg300=30.00 $ grep -E 'Dirty Writeback:' /proc/meminfo Dirty: 3145728 kB Writeback: 982000 kB $ perf trace -s -p 4012 -- sleep 5 grep fsync fsync 812 calls total 3910.2 ms max 640.3 ms Heap and GC look normal.

title: Dirty page throttling
text: Why do the neighbour's write calls stall, and how do you fix it at the lowest cost? A batch ETL writes 200 MB/s of output files in 30 s bursts onto a disk that sustains 150 MB/s. The host has 16 GB RAM and defaults dirty ratio=20 , dirty background ratio=10 . A latency-sensitive neighbour process on the same host sees p99 spikes of 3 to 6 seconds on its small log writes during bursts. top shows kworker/flush busy and the neighbour in D state. $ grep -E 'Dirty Writeback' /proc/meminfo Dirty: 3354624 kB about 3.2 GB

title: fsync-bound commit rate
text: What is the ceiling and how do you hit 5,000/s without breaking durability? Which options would you refuse? A payments ledger service commits each transaction with an fsync on its WAL. Measured with strace: fdatasync 12 = 0 <0.004912 fdatasync 12 = 0 <0.005104 Throughput tops out at 200 commits/s per instance on a cheap cloud SSD; the business needs 5,000 commits/s per instance and must not lose acknowledged payments. The team proposes synchronous commit=off Postgres or appendfsync no Redis .

title: Changing file system under live traffic
text: Plan the migration and say what you change in mount options and tuning. A 12-broker Kafka cluster each broker an 8 TB ext4 volume, 5% reserved, about 86% full shows long segment deletes and allocation contention. Leadership wants XFS and better disk use, with no downtime and a 3-replica setup min.insync.replicas=2 , acks=all . Retention is 3 days; cluster traffic is 400 MB/s in. $ tune2fs -l /dev/nvme1n1 grep -E 'Reserved block count Block count' Reserved block count: 107374182 5% $ mount grep kafka /dev/nvme1n1 on /data/kafka type ext4 rw,relatime

title: Zero-length files after power loss
text: What happened, whose fault is it, and what do you change? Post-incident review: a datacenter lost power for 8 seconds. On 14 ext4 hosts running a metadata service, the file system recovered cleanly recovery complete , fsck clean , yet 3 hosts had zero-length index files created in the final seconds, and the application restarted with missing data. The service writes with plain write and close , journal mode is the default, commit=5 . $ dmesg grep -i ext4 EXT4-fs sda3 : recovery complete EXT4-fs sda3 : mounted filesystem with ordered data mode. $ ls -l /data/index/seg-9912.idx -rw-r--r-- 1 app app 0 ... seg-9912.idx

title: Blocking vs non-blocking vs asynchronous
text: What is the difference between blocking, non-blocking and asynchronous I/O? With blocking I/O my thread sleeps inside the call until the data is there. With non-blocking I/O the call returns immediately with "not ready" EAGAIN and I have to come back and ask again. With asynchronous I/O I submit the whole operation, keep working, and the kernel tells me when it is complete and the data is already in my buffer.

title: Thread-per-connection cost
text: Why does a thread-per-connection server struggle at 10,000 connections, even though sleeping threads use no CPU? A blocked thread does not burn CPU, but each one holds a stack Java defaults to 1 MB virtual plus kernel structures, and the scheduler has to track thousands of entities. At 10,000 threads that is gigabytes of address space, 100+ MB real memory, rising context switches and poor cache locality. An event loop uses one thread for all of them.

title: Thread pool exhaustion
text: Explain what is happening and what you would do. A Spring Boot service runs on 4 vCPUs with the Tomcat default of 200 worker threads. Normally each request calls a database for 100 ms. Peak traffic is 1,500 req/s. At 15:10 the DB gets slow 1 s per query . The dashboard shows: CPU: 12% tomcat.threads.busy: 200/200 http p99: 9.8 s requests/s: 198 DB CPU: 95% Someone proposes raising CPU to 16 vCPUs.

title: select vs poll vs epoll
text: How do select, poll and epoll differ, and why does epoll scale better? select and poll make me hand the kernel the whole list of descriptors on every call, and then I scan the whole list to find the ready ones, so each wake-up is O n . select is also limited to 1024 fds. epoll lets me register each fd once in a kernel structure and epoll wait returns only the ready ones, so the cost is O ready , not O watched .

title: Edge-triggered epoll
text: Find the bug and fix it. A custom TCP proxy uses edge-triggered epoll for performance. Under light load it works. Under load testing, some clients hang forever even though they sent complete requests; the server shows sockets in ESTABLISHED with Recv-Q of several KB on ss . CPU is idle. epoll event ev{}; ev.events = EPOLLIN EPOLLET; ev.data.fd = cfd; epoll ctl ep, EPOLL CTL ADD, cfd, &ev ; void on readable int fd { char buf 4096 ; ssize t n = read fd, buf, sizeof buf ; // fd is non-blocking if n 0 process buf, n ; } A red herring: the team suspects a kernel bug because it "only fails at high throughput".

title: Redis single-threaded design
text: Redis executes commands on a single thread. Why is it still so fast, and what is the catch? Commands are microsecond operations on in-memory structures, and one thread driving an epoll loop needs no locks, has no context switches, keeps caches warm, and gets atomic commands for free. The bottleneck becomes the network, not the CPU. The catch is that any slow command blocks every client, such as KEYS or a big SMEMBERS .

title: Event loop blocked
text: Diagnose and fix without taking the cache down. A shared Redis one primary, 6 GB dataset, 20k ops/s is used by 30 services. Every few minutes all clients see a latency spike to 300 ms, then it recovers. Redis CPU on the core shows 100% during the spike; network and memory look fine. Excerpts: $ redis-cli --latency min: 0, max: 312, avg: 0.9 $ redis-cli slowlog get 2 1 1 integer 207 3 integer 298114 4 1 "SMEMBERS" 2 "feed:global" 2 1 integer 206 3 integer 41200 4 1 "KEYS" 2 "session: " $ redis-cli scard feed:global integer 4800000 Red herring: the hosting team points to a noisy neighbour st is 0.2% .

title: Download server CPU cost
text: What would you change and what are the limits? A media service serves 800 MB video files from local NVMe over plain HTTP from a custom Java server using FileInputStream.read buf then socket.write buf with an 8 KB buffer. One box has a 10 Gbit NIC and 16 cores. At 6 Gbit/s the box is at 85% CPU, mostly in the app and kernel; the NIC is not saturated. perf top shows: 31% kernel copy user enhanced fast string 18% kernel tcp sendmsg 11% libjvm.so JNI copy to/from heap Management wants to double throughput without buying hardware. Someone suggests more threads.

title: How sendfile works
text: What does "zero-copy" actually mean for sendfile, and how many copies happen in a normal read-then-write file transfer? A normal read then write copies data four times: DMA disk to page cache, CPU copy to my buffer, CPU copy to the socket buffer, DMA to the NIC, with two syscalls and two mode switches. sendfile lets the kernel move data from page cache to socket without it entering user space. "Zero-copy" means zero CPU copies between user and kernel; DMA transfers still happen.

title: Accept queue overflow
text: Why are clients failing and how do you fix it? After a marketing push, a Node/Express API behind a load balancer sees clients timing out on connect 3 s . The app node shows CPU 35%, memory fine, p50 latency of served requests is 20 ms. The LB reports many connect failures to this node. On the node: $ ss -ltn State Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port LISTEN 512 511 0.0.0.0:3000 $ nstat -az TcpExtListenOverflows TcpExtListenDrops TcpExtListenOverflows 48210 TcpExtListenDrops 48210 $ top -H -p $ pgrep node PID %CPU COMMAND 2310 99.0 node <- the main thread 2318 4.0 node libuv workers $ cat /proc/sys/net/core/somaxconn 128 Red herring: an engineer notes "only 35% CPU, so we have headroom".

title: io_uring vs epoll
text: How is io uring different from epoll, and when would you actually adopt it? epoll tells me a socket is ready and then I make the syscall to do the read. io uring is completion-based: I put requests in a shared submission ring, the kernel performs them, and results appear in a completion ring, so I can batch dozens of operations per syscall, or none with SQPOLL. It also does real async file I/O, which epoll cannot. I would adopt it for heavy disk I/O or extreme syscall rates on kernels I control; epoll remains the default for ordinary network servers.

title: Event loop lag in Node
text: Explain every way this blocks and redesign it. A Node.js service reads uploaded CSV files up to 200 MB from local disk, parses them and streams results. The team believes "everything is non-blocking". During report generation, health checks from the LB time out 2 s and the whole instance flaps. Metrics: event loop delay p99: 3.4 s CPU main thread : 100% libuv threadpool queue: 128 pending fs ops UV THREADPOOL SIZE: default 4 Code snippet in the handler: const txt = fs.readFileSync path, "utf8" ; // used "for simplicity" const rows = JSON.parse convert txt ; // 150 MB string await Promise.all files.map f = fs.promises.readFile f ; // 500 files

title: Model migration under traffic
text: Which do you pick and how do you migrate with live traffic? A Java 17 payment-notification service uses Tomcat with 400 threads. Each request fans out to 3 slow partner APIs each p50 300 ms, p99 4 s . Traffic is doubling to 6,000 req/s in three months. Today at 3,000 req/s the pool is often exhausted; heap is 4 GB, 400 threads. The team has three options: A migrate to Netty/WebFlux, B upgrade to Java 21 and enable virtual threads, C keep threads and shard to 4x more nodes. The code base is 250k lines of blocking JDBC and Spring MVC.

title: 1M connection capacity
text: Is 1M feasible on one node? What breaks first and what do you change? A push-notification gateway holds 100,000 idle long-lived WebSocket connections per node today one Netty event loop group . Product wants 10x connections on the same fleet size "let each node hold 1M" . Average 1 message per connection per 5 minutes. At 100k connections the node shows: RSS 7.2 GB fds 100,312 / limit 1,048,576 CPU 6% ss -s: estab 99810, timewait 8 net.ipv4.ip local port range = 32768 60999 the node is a server, not a client Recv-Q/Send-Q kernel buffers: 40 KB avg per socket A peer says "TCP port limit of 65,535 means you cannot go above 65k connections."

title: Container vs VM
text: What is a container, and how is it different from a virtual machine? A container is an ordinary Linux process that the kernel has been told to show a limited view of the system namespaces and to limit in resource use cgroups . There is no guest OS: all containers share the host kernel. A VM runs its own kernel on virtual hardware, so it is heavier but has much stronger isolation.

title: Namespaces vs cgroups
text: What is the difference between namespaces and cgroups? Give an example of each. Namespaces control what a process can see: its own PIDs, network interfaces, mounts, hostname, users. cgroups control how much it can use: CPU, memory, I/O, number of processes. A PID namespace makes my process think it is PID 1; a memory cgroup makes the kernel kill it if it exceeds 512 MiB.

title: PID 1 and signals
text: Why does it behave like this and how do you fix it? A service runs in Docker with CMD ./start.sh , where start.sh does some setup and then runs java -jar app.jar . During rolling deploys, each pod takes exactly 30 s to terminate in Kubernetes the default grace period , in-flight requests are cut, and the app's shutdown hook that flushes a queue never logs "flush complete". Logs of the previous run: 10:01:05 Received SIGTERM <- not present no shutdown hook output kubectl describe: Last State: Terminated Reason: Error Exit Code: 137 Red herring: someone suspects the JVM shutdown hook has a bug.

title: Kubernetes requests and limits
text: How do Kubernetes CPU and memory requests and limits map onto cgroups, and what happens at the limit? Requests are for scheduling and, for CPU, a relative weight cpu.weight that only matters under contention; limits are hard caps. A CPU limit becomes a quota in cpu.max ; hitting it throttles all threads until the next period. A memory limit is memory.max ; hitting it after reclaim fails gets the process OOM-killed with SIGKILL.

title: Dockerfile bugs
text: List what is wrong and fix the Dockerfile. CI builds take 11 minutes on every commit even for a one-line change, the final image is 1.4 GB, and a security review flags that the process runs as root. Dockerfile: FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk WORKDIR /app COPY . . RUN mvn -B package -DskipTests EXPOSE 8080 CMD java -jar target/app.jar The registry also shows .git and test fixtures inside the image. A red herring: the team blames the slow Maven mirror.

title: Image layers and overlayfs
text: How do image layers and overlayfs work, and why is writing heavily inside a container slow? An image is a stack of read-only layers, each a tarball of file changes identified by a SHA-256 digest. overlayfs merges them: lower dirs are read-only layers, the upper dir is the container's writable layer, merged is what the process sees. Writing to a file from a lower layer triggers copy-up: the whole file is copied into the upper layer first. Heavy writes are slow and vanish with the container, so data goes on volumes.

title: CPU throttling
text: What is happening and what would you change? An API pod has requests.cpu: 1, limits.cpu: 1 , runs 8 worker threads and normally serves 500 rps. p99 jumped from 40 ms to 280 ms after a deploy, but the dashboards look healthy: kubectl top pod api-7d9f CPU: 310m / 1000m Memory: 410Mi node CPU: 22% $ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/.../cpu.stat nr periods 612300 nr throttled 301220 throttled usec 4812001299 Red herring: heap and GC logs look normal.

title: JVM OOMKilled
text: Why is it dying and how do you size it? A Java 21 service has limits.memory: 1Gi and starts with -Xmx1g . Every few hours the pod restarts. kubectl get pod shows RESTARTS climbing; heap dumps and app logs show no OutOfMemoryError . $ kubectl describe pod api-7d9f grep -A4 'Last State' Last State: Terminated Reason: OOMKilled Exit Code: 137 $ dmesg -T grep -i killed Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process 18211 java anon-rss:1048200kB file-rss:12288kB JVM metrics: heap used 900 MiB, threads 210, direct buffers 150 MiB Red herring: someone suspects a memory leak in business code.

title: CPU quota and runtime awareness
text: Why can a container with a 1-CPU limit running on a 64-core node behave badly, and what do you do about the runtime? A CPU limit is a time quota per 100 ms period, not a number of cores. A runtime that sizes its thread pools by the visible 64 cores starts 64 GC and worker threads that burn the quota in a couple of milliseconds, and then the whole group is paused until the next period. So I make the runtime quota-aware or set pool sizes explicitly.

title: Debugging a distroless crash loop
text: How do you find out what is wrong with no shell and no useful logs? A Go service in a distroless image no shell, no curl enters CrashLoopBackOff at 02:00 after a config change. On-call sees: $ kubectl get pod payments-6f8 0/1 CrashLoopBackOff 7 45s ago $ kubectl logs payments-6f8 empty $ kubectl exec -it payments-6f8 -- sh OCI runtime exec failed: exec: "sh": executable file not found $ kubectl describe pod payments-6f8 grep -E 'Reason Exit Liveness' Reason: Error Exit Code: 1 Liveness probe failed: Get "http://10.2.1.9:8080/healthz": context deadline exceeded Red herring: the node was also upgraded the same night.

title: Container OOM vs node OOM
text: What are the different kinds of out-of-memory events with containers on Kubernetes, and how do you tell them apart? A container OOM happens inside one cgroup: the container hit its own memory.max , the cgroup OOM killer SIGKILLs a process, exit code 137 and Kubernetes shows OOMKilled ; only that container dies. A node-level event is the host being out of memory: the kubelet evicts pods by QoS Evicted , BestEffort first or, if it is too slow, the global kernel OOM killer picks victims by oom score . The first is a sizing problem for one workload, the second a node-packing and requests problem.

title: Probe-induced restarts
text: Write the root cause analysis and the action items. Postmortem draft: "At 11:20 a traffic burst 2x caused 40% of pods in the checkout deployment to restart within 3 minutes, which reduced capacity and caused a full outage for 14 minutes." Facts: liveness: httpGet /healthz timeoutSeconds: 1 periodSeconds: 5 failureThreshold: 3 resources: requests.cpu 500m limits.cpu 500m JVM, 8 threads Events: "Liveness probe failed: context deadline exceeded" x3 - "Killing container" cpu.stat: throttled in 70% of periods during the incident No OOMKilled, exit code 143 Autoscaler HPA target is 70% average CPU; HPA reacted 4 minutes after the burst.

title: Isolation and security
text: What is wrong with this design, and what would you propose? You are building a "run your own code" feature for customers a CI-like service . Today an engineer proposes: every job runs in a Docker container started by the API server, which mounts /var/run/docker.sock to start siblings; containers run as root with --privileged so jobs can build Docker images; all jobs share one node pool with other internal services. Expected load: 5,000 jobs/hour, jobs up to 30 min, some from free-tier anonymous users.

title: Debugging network and pid limits
text: Explain both symptoms and how you would investigate from the node. A pod in Kubernetes intermittently shows 5-second delays on outbound calls to internal services; at other times the pod throws fork: Resource temporarily unavailable and Too many open files . Facts: $ kubectl exec app -- cat /etc/resolv.conf nameserver 10.96.0.10 search ns.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local options ndots:5 $ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/.../pids.current /sys/fs/cgroup/.../pids.max 4093 4096 $ nsenter -t $PID -n ss -s estab 12, timewait 3 $ nstat -az grep -i insert failed IpExtInInsertFailed ... conntrack insert failed 18433 Red herring: CPU and memory are comfortable.

title: USE method
text: A Linux server is "slow". How do you decide where to start, and what is the USE method? I work from broad to narrow: one resource, then one process, then one function. The USE method says for every resource CPU, memory, disk, network check Utilisation how busy , Saturation is work queueing and Errors. Saturation is the key signal: 100% busy with a queue is a bottleneck; 60% with no queue is not.

title: Load average
text: What does load average mean on Linux, and how do you interpret load average: 18.4, 12.1, 6.3 on an 8-core machine? Load average is the average number of tasks that are running, waiting to run, or on Linux in uninterruptible I/O sleep, over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. On 8 cores a load of 8 is full. 18.4/12.1/6.3 means it is rising fast and has more than twice as many tasks as cores. But because D-state tasks count, I must check whether it is CPU demand or I/O wait before deciding.

title: High load, low CPU
text: What is wrong and what do you do first? Alert: load average 22 on a 4-core database host; the application times out. Quick look: $ uptime load average: 22.1, 15.0, 7.2 $ top -b -n1 head -12 %Cpu s : 6.0 us, 3.0 sy, 0.0 ni, 10.0 id, 80.0 wa, 0.0 hi, 0.5 si, 0.5 st MiB Mem: 15900 total, 410 free, 3100 used, 12390 buff/cache PID S %CPU COMMAND 910 D 2.0 postgres: writer 944 D 1.0 postgres: checkpointer ... 18 more postgres processes in D $ iostat -xz 1 Device w/s w await aqu-sz %util sda 310 480.0 148.0 100.0 Red herring: a teammate says "buff/cache is 12 GB, memory is nearly full".

title: Reading a flame graph
text: How do you read a flame graph, and what are its limits? A profiler samples stack traces at, say, 99 Hz and the flame graph merges them: the x axis is the share of samples not time order , the y axis is stack depth, and width is how often a function and its children were on-CPU. I look for wide plateaus at the top: that is where CPU is actually spent. It only shows on-CPU time, so for a slow process with low CPU I need an off-CPU graph.

title: Memory pressure vs free memory
text: Is this host in trouble? What would you tell the on-call and what would you check on the other host? A monitoring alert says "memory 97% used" on a 32 GB application server and the SRE on call wants to restart the service and request a bigger instance. Output: $ free -m total used free shared buff/cache available Mem: 31900 9100 410 120 22390 22400 Swap: 2048 0 2048 $ vmstat 1 5 r b swpd free buff cache si so bi bo in cs us sy id wa 3 0 0 410 120 22390 0 0 0 4 9120 8100 38 9 52 1 $ sar -B 1 3 majflt/s 0.0 pgscand/s 0.0 Another host in the same fleet shows so 5,100 and majflt/s 900.

title: strace cost and alternatives
text: What can you learn with strace, what are its dangers, and what do you use instead on a busy production system? strace shows every system call a process makes with arguments, return values and time spent, so I can see which file, which connection and which wait. It uses ptrace and can slow the target 10 to 100 times, so on a hot production process I use strace -c for a few seconds, or perf trace , bpftrace or BCC tools, which have almost no overhead.

title: Disk saturation on a cloud volume
text: What is the bottleneck, and how do you fix it cheaply? A log-heavy ingestion service on an EC2-like VM with a 500 GB gp3-style volume baseline 3,000 IOPS, 125 MB/s sees write latency spikes every few minutes. Metrics: $ iostat -xz 1 Device r/s w/s rkB/s wkB/s r await w await aqu-sz wareq-sz %util nvme1n1 20 2980 320 11900 1.1 64.0 190 4.0 99.9 Cloud: VolumeWriteOps 3,000/s flat line , VolumeThroughput 12 MB/s Instance CPU 18%. The team proposes buying a 4x bigger instance.

title: Disk full but files small
text: Where did the space go and how do you recover without restarting? A service host reports No space left on device . Yet: $ df -h /var /dev/sda2 100G 100G 0 100% /var $ du -sh /var/ sort -h tail -3 2.1G /var/lib 1.4G /var/cache 900M /var/log $ ls /proc/2310/fd wc -l ; grep 'open files' /proc/2310/limits 2217 Max open files 4096 4096 files Logrotate ran last night and compressed old logs. Red herring: someone suspects inode exhaustion df -i shows 3% used .

title: Reading iostat
text: How do you read iostat -x output, and why can %util be misleading? I look at await time a request spends queued plus serviced , aqu-sz average queue length , request size and IOPS against the device or cloud limit. %util is just the fraction of time at least one request was in flight, so on NVMe or RAID, which serve many requests in parallel, 100% does not mean there is no headroom. Latency plus queue depth tell me saturation.

title: Fork, copy-on-write and THP
text: Explain the failure and fix it without losing durability. A Redis primary with 24 GB data on a 32 GB host works fine for weeks. Every day at 02:00, during BGSAVE , it gets OOM-killed or shows 2-second latency spikes. Excerpts: $ dmesg -T grep -i oom Out of memory: Killed process 5120 redis-server total-vm: 31457280kB anon-rss: 29360128kB $ cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent hugepage/enabled always madvise never $ redis-cli info persistence grep -E 'fork cow' latest fork usec:2310000 $ vmstat 1 so 12000 bi 8000 during the fork Writes during the snapshot are about 40,000/s. Red herring: the team suspects a memory leak because the dump is "only 24 GB".

title: On-CPU vs off-CPU profiling
text: A service has high latency but CPU is only 15%. A CPU flame graph looks flat. What do you do next? A CPU flame graph only samples threads that are running, so time spent waiting on locks, I/O or a downstream never shows up. I would switch to off-CPU analysis: an off-CPU flame graph built with offcputime-bpfcc /bpftrace shows where threads block and for how long. Alongside it I'd check thread dumps, strace -c -T , futex activity and ss -ti for slow downstream calls.

title: Lock contention
text: Why did more workers make it slower and what do you do? After raising the worker count from 16 to 64 on a 16-core host to "use more parallelism", throughput fell 35% and p99 tripled. Observations: $ vmstat 1 r b swpd free si so bi bo in cs us sy id wa 9 0 0 4.1G 0 0 0 4 41000 310000 31 24 45 0 $ sudo strace -c -f -p 2310 -- sleep 5 % time seconds usecs/call calls errors syscall 71.00 14.1 310 45500 18200 futex 12.00 2.4 ... $ perf top -p 2310 18% kernel raw spin lock 11% libc pthread mutex lock Red herring: memory and disk are fine.

title: Steal time and interrupts
text: What do you conclude and what is your plan, given only these symptoms? Vague report: "API latency doubled since Tuesday, nothing was deployed." You have SSH to one of 12 identical VMs on a public cloud 8 vCPU each . Excerpts from the slow VM and a healthy one: slow: %Cpu s : 31 us, 9 sy, 0 wa, 2 si, 18 st load 6.1 r=7 good: %Cpu s : 33 us, 8 sy, 0 wa, 2 si, 0 st load 5.9 r=7 $ mpstat -P ALL 1 slow VM CPU3: %irq 0 %soft 96 others normal $ cat /proc/interrupts grep eth0 CPU3: 41203018 ... CPU0..2,4..7: 1000 each $ ss -ti dst 10.0.3.7 retrans:0/12 rtt:18/9 Red herring: application GC logs show normal pauses.

title: Mitigate, capture, fix
text: Walk through what should have happened and which action items you would propose. Postmortem review. At 14:02 checkout p99 went from 80 ms to 6 s with 4% timeouts, 10 minutes after a deploy. The first responder restarted all pods at 14:06, latency recovered for 3 minutes, then returned. At 14:11 a second responder disabled the recommendations feature flag and everything normalised by 14:13. Evidence collected: none from before the restart. Later analysis of one surviving pod's thread dump and a profile shows 58% of samples in Pattern$Branch.match under RecommendationService.rank . Leadership asks: "Why did it take 11 minutes, and what should the team do differently?"

title: References and pass-by-value
text: Is Java pass-by-reference or pass-by-value for objects? What actually lives in a variable that "holds" an object? Java is always pass-by-value. For objects, the value copied is the reference, a handle to the heap object. So the callee can mutate the object through its copy of the handle, but reassigning the parameter does not change the caller's variable.

title: How a virtual call works
text: Animal a = new Dog ; a.speak ; How does the JVM decide which speak to run? Each class has a vtable, an array of method pointers. The call loads the object's class pointer, indexes the slot for speak , and jumps. Dog copied Animal 's table and replaced the overridden slot, so the runtime class decides, not the declared type.

title: equals and hashCode contract
text: Why must you override hashCode whenever you override equals ? HashMap and HashSet use hashCode to choose a bucket and then equals to confirm. If two equal objects have different hashes they land in different buckets, so contains and get silently miss. The rule: equal objects must have equal hash codes.

title: Constructor order
text: Why does it crash, and how do you fix it without changing the public API? A settings screen base class and a subclass are shipped. In staging it crashes at startup with an NPE; in unit tests with a mocked subclass it passes. abstract class Panel { Panel { System.out.println "Panel ctor" ; render ; } abstract void render ; } class TitlePanel extends Panel { private final String title = "Settings"; private final StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder ; TitlePanel { System.out.println "TitlePanel ctor" ; } @Override void render { out.append title.toUpperCase ; } } Panel ctor Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "java.lang.StringBuilder.append" because "this.out" is null at TitlePanel.render TitlePanel.java:6 at Panel.<init Panel.java:3 The team suspects the title constant, the JDK version, and a missing @Override .

title: Immutability recipe
text: What makes a class truly immutable in Java? Is a class with only final fields immutable? Final class, private final fields, no setters, and no leaking of mutable internals copy in, copy out . final fields alone are not enough: a final List field can still be mutated, and a non-final class lets a subclass add mutability.

title: equals/hashCode
text: Find all bugs and explain why it is only intermittent. A dedupe job collects User records into a HashSet<User to skip already-processed users. Most duplicates pass through testers saw it as intermittent , so a customer gets two welcome emails. Fully reproducible only with large input. class User { final long id; final String email; User long id, String email { this.id = id; this.email = email; } public boolean equals User o { return o != null && id == o.id; } } // seen.add u1 ; seen.contains new User 1, "a@x.com" - sometimes true, mostly false Red herrings: "the set is not thread-safe" it is single-threaded , "Java 21 regression".

title: Defensive copies
text: What remains wrong, and what is the right API shape? A shopping Cart exposes its items. A UI bug clears the displayed list and the cart silently empties. A fix attempt wraps the getter in Collections.unmodifiableList , but a nightly report still sees items change mid-iteration ConcurrentModificationException , 3 times in 1,000 runs . class Cart { private final List<Item items = new ArrayList< ; Cart List<Item initial { items.addAll initial ; } List<Item items { return Collections.unmodifiableList items ; } void add Item i { items.add i ; } } // report thread: for Item i : cart.items total += i.price ; Red herring: "ArrayList is slow".

title: Object memory cost
text: Explain where the memory goes and how you would cut it. A map-tile service keeps 20 million Point int x, int y objects in an ArrayList<Point . Heap is 4 GB, GC logs show young pauses of 80 ms and old-gen at 85% after warm-up. Product wants 3x more points next quarter. GC pause G1 Evacuation 3071M- 2890M 4096M 84.2ms jcmd GC.class histogram: Point 20,000,000 instances 480,000,000 bytes Object ... 80,000,000 bytes Red herrings: "switch GC to ZGC", "give the box more RAM".

title: What is not polymorphic
text: Which parts of a Java class hierarchy are bound at compile time rather than dispatched at runtime, and why does that matter? Static, private and final methods, constructors, and fields are not virtual. Overloads are chosen at compile time from the declared argument types. Only overridable instance methods dispatch on the runtime class.

title: Mutable hash keys
text: Diagnose the leak and the missing lookups, and fix it safely. A session cache Map<SessionKey, Session grows from 200 MB to 3 GB over a week and then OOMs. Lookups for a fraction of active sessions return null, so users are re-authenticated. Heap dump shows 4.1 million SessionKey entries; business says there are 90k active sessions. class SessionKey { String userId; String device; // device changes on re-login @Override public int hashCode { return Objects.hash userId, device ; } @Override public boolean equals Object o { / userId + device / } } // on device change: key.device = newDevice; // key is already in the map cache.get key - null Red herrings: "the TTL eviction is broken", "Caffeine bug".

title: equals symmetry and LSP
text: What contract is violated, what are the options, and which would you choose? A geometry library adds ColorPoint extends Point . A unit test in the checkout module intermittently fails depending on argument order. class Point { final int x, y; @Override public boolean equals Object o { if ! o instanceof Point p return false; return x == p.x && y == p.y; } } class ColorPoint extends Point { final String color; @Override public boolean equals Object o { if ! o instanceof ColorPoint c return false; return super.equals o && color.equals c.color ; } } Point p = new Point 1, 2 ; ColorPoint cp = new ColorPoint 1, 2, "red" ; p.equals cp // true cp.equals p // false Red herring: "make ColorPoint ignore color".

title: Entity equality
text: How would you design equals and hashCode for a JPA entity with a database-generated id? Why is the naive version risky? Never hash on a generated id that is null before persist, and never use all mutable fields. Either use a stable business key, or use identity-style equality with a constant hashCode per class. Do not use a Kotlin data class blindly for entities.

title: Immutability under concurrency
text: The class is "immutable". Why does it misbehave, and what do you change? A pricing RateTable is declared immutable "final fields, no setters" and shared by 200 request threads. Occasionally, one request returns a price computed from half-updated rates error rate 0.02% , and a reload thread throws ConcurrentModificationException once a day. public final class RateTable { private final Map<String, Double rates; public RateTable Map<String, Double src { this.rates = src; } // src is the loader's working map public Map<String, Double rates { return rates; } public double rate String k { return rates.get k ; } } // loader: working.put "EUR", 0.92 ; table = new RateTable working ; // later working.put "EUR", 0.91 Red herrings: "make rate synchronized", "use volatile on table".

title: Megamorphic call sites
text: Why did adding one implementation slow the loop and what would you do? A rules engine evaluates Rule.apply ctx over 100 million events per run. When the fifth Rule implementation shipped, the batch time went from 38 s to 61 s.
