CPU profile shows the time inside Rule.apply stubs, not the rule bodies. -XX:+PrintInlining @ 17 Engine::run 63 bytes @ 22 Rule::apply interface virtual call too many receiver types Red herrings: "the new rule is slow" it takes 40 ns , "GC".

title: Type erasure
text: What is type erasure, and what can't you do in Java because of it? The compiler checks generic types, then removes them: List<String and List<Integer are the same class at runtime, with casts inserted where needed. So you cannot do new T , new T n , x instanceof List<String , or overload on the type argument, and primitives can't be type arguments.

title: Checked vs unchecked
text: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions, and which would you throw from your own API? Checked exceptions are forced by the compiler for conditions the caller can reasonably recover from; unchecked ones signal programming errors or unrecoverable states. In my APIs I use unchecked by default, checked when callers must make a recovery decision, and return types Optional or a sealed result for expected outcomes like "not found".

title: Interface or abstract class
text: When do you use an interface and when an abstract class? Interface for a capability or contract; abstract class when subclasses share state or a fixed algorithm skeleton and I control all subclasses. Default to the interface because a class can implement many but extend only one. Often I offer both: an interface plus an optional abstract skeleton.

title: Raw types and heap pollution
text: What happened and how do you prevent this class of bug? A report job fails at 02:10 nightly with a ClassCastException deep inside a formatter, 4 stack frames away from where bad data entered. List<String names = loadNames ; // returns List<String addIds names ; // legacy helper for String n : names out.print n.trim ; // boom static void addIds List list { list.add 42 ; } // raw type java.lang.ClassCastException: class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.lang.String at Report.format Report.java:57 Red herrings: "bad DB data", "a recent JDK upgrade".

title: PECS and variance
text: Explain PECS. Why isn't List<Dog a List<Animal ? If I could pass a List<Dog as List<Animal , someone could add a Cat to it. So generics are invariant. If I only read from it producer I use ? extends T ; if I only write to it consumer I use ? super T . Producer Extends, Consumer Super.

title: Exception handling bugs
text: Explain what happened and what you change. An order service is returning HTTP 200 with an empty body for about 0.8% of requests during a database failover. Logs show nothing at ERROR. The code: Order load long id { try { return repo.find id ; } catch Exception e { // TODO handle } return null; } String parse String s { try { return Json.parse s ; } finally { return "{}"; } } Metrics: db connection errors total rose by 4,100 during the same 6 minutes; 5xx rate flat.

title: Default method conflicts
text: Explain the failure and how to roll this out safely. Your platform library ships interface Audit { default void log String m {...} } . Another team's module has class Service implements Logger, Audit where Logger already had default void log String . The upgrade to library 2.0 breaks their build; 14 services fail to compile on Friday before a release. error: types Logger and Audit are incompatible; class Service inherits unrelated defaults for log String from types Logger and Audit Red herring: "pin the old library forever".

title: Sealed types and exhaustiveness
text: Why did the compiler not help, and how do you prevent a repeat? An Android app models screen state. A new Empty state is added for a zero-result search. QA reports that the search screen shows an endless spinner for empty results, 3 of 6 screens affected. No compile error. sealed interface UiState { object Loading : UiState data class Success val items: List<Item : UiState data class Error val msg: String : UiState object Empty : UiState // NEW } fun render s: UiState = when s { is UiState.Success - showList s.items is UiState.Error - showError s.msg else - showSpinner // written when only Loading remained } Red herring: "the backend returns 200 with an empty body".

title: Records and data classes
text: What do records and data classes give you, and what are their limits? Are they immutable? They generate the constructor, accessors, equals , hashCode and toString from the components, so value semantics are free and consistent. They are only shallowly immutable: a List component can still change. Kotlin adds copy and destructuring; a Kotlin data class with var is mutable.

title: Variance in API design
text: Fix the signatures with variance and justify each choice, including the array proposal. You are designing a public EventBus library used by 40 internal teams. Draft signatures: void publish List<Event events ; List<? extends Event drain ; void subscribe Handler<Event h ; interface Handler<T { void on T e ; } Early users complain: they cannot pass a List<OrderEvent to publish , cannot register a Handler<Object for logging, and callers of drain cannot add to the result. A teammate also proposes returning Event for speed.

title: Coroutine cancellation
text: Explain the leak and the fix. An Android app's profile screen leaks. Leak canary shows ProfileViewModel retained after the user left the screen; ANR rate rose from 0.2% to 0.9% after a release. A diff shows a "make it robust" change: viewModelScope.launch { try { val p = api.loadProfile // suspend, can be cancelled render p } catch e: Exception { log.warn "load failed", e retryLoop // keeps running } } W/Profile: load failed kotlinx.coroutines.JobCancellationException: StandaloneCoroutine was cancelled Red herrings: "network is flaky", "increase timeout".

title: Evolving published APIs
text: You own a widely used library type. How do interface versus abstract class affect your ability to evolve it over five years? An interface lets me add default methods without breaking implementers, but removing or changing is breaking; an abstract class uses up the user's only superclass slot and exposes protected hooks that become frozen contracts. I publish an interface and an optional abstract skeleton, keep the class hierarchy shallow, and use final or sealed where I don't want extension.

title: Erasure at the JSON boundary
text: Why does this compile and break late? How do you fix it? After a refactor, a pricing service reads rules from JSON into a generic helper. It works in unit tests but fails in production 2 minutes after startup. static <T List<T readList String json, Class<T type { return gson.fromJson json, List.class ; // refactored from a typed call } List<Rule rules = readList json, Rule.class ; double d = rules.get 0 .discount; // fails later java.lang.ClassCastException: class com.google.gson.internal.LinkedTreeMap cannot be cast to class Rule at Pricing.apply Pricing.java:88 Red herrings: "Gson version", "JSON field names changed".

title: Exceptions as control flow
text: Redesign error handling to hit the SLO without hiding real failures. A validation endpoint at 50,000 requests/second spends 22% of CPU in Throwable.fillInStackTrace . 35% of requests contain invalid input and the code throws ValidationException for each, from 9 frames deep within a framework stack of about 60 frames. async-profiler: 22.4% java.lang.Throwable.fillInStackTrace 6.1% ValidationException.<init p99 latency 180 ms SLO 100 ms Red herring: "GC pauses".

title: Composition vs inheritance
text: Why do people say "favour composition over inheritance"? When is inheritance still right? Inheritance couples a subclass to the parent's internals fragile base class and is fixed at compile time. Composition holds a collaborator and forwards, so I can swap parts and keep encapsulation. Inheritance is right for a real, stable is-a with a base designed for extension, where Liskov holds.

title: Dependency injection basics
text: What is dependency injection and why does it matter beyond using Spring or Hilt? DI means a class receives its collaborators instead of creating them. It makes dependencies explicit and swappable, so I can test with fakes and change implementations without editing the class. A framework is optional; a composition root with plain constructors is DI.

title: Four composition patterns
text: Distinguish decorator, strategy, adapter and facade with one real example each. Decorator wraps the same interface to add behaviour caching, retry . Strategy swaps an algorithm behind an interface pricing . Adapter converts one interface to another legacy SDK to my port . Facade is one simple entry point over a messy subsystem checkout .

title: Fragile base class
text: Why 6, and how do you restructure it? A metrics wrapper counts how many elements were added to a set. After a JDK upgrade the dashboard shows exactly double the expected count for bulk adds. class CountingSet<E extends HashSet<E { int count; @Override public boolean add E e { count++; return super.add e ; } @Override public boolean addAll Collection<? extends E c { count += c.size ; return super.addAll c ; } } var s = new CountingSet<String ; s.addAll List.of "a", "b", "c" ; System.out.println s.count ; // 6 Red herring: "the JDK introduced a bug".

title: Test doubles
text: What is the difference between stub, fake, mock and spy, and how do you choose? A stub returns canned answers, a fake is a lightweight working implementation in-memory repo , a mock records and verifies interactions, a spy wraps the real object. I use the cheapest that works: fakes for state, stubs for inputs, mocks only for outgoing side effects that matter, like "payment charged once".

title: Field injection and circular dependencies
text: How do you resolve this properly? A Spring service fails to start after a PR adds a notification feature. Staging boot time is also now 14 s was 6 s . The test for OrderService needs a full Spring context 11 s because dependencies are field-injected. @Service class OrderService { @Autowired private NotificationService notifier; @Autowired private InventoryService inventory; } @Service class NotificationService { @Autowired private OrderService orders; } APPLICATION FAILED TO START The dependencies of some of the beans in the application context form a cycle: orderService - notificationService - orderService Red herring: "set spring.main.allow-circular-references=true ".

title: Time as a dependency
text: Why is it flaky and how do you restructure? A coupon test passes locally and fails randomly in CI at midnight UTC and on the 1st of each month. class CouponService { boolean isValid Coupon c { return Instant.now .isBefore c.expiresAt ; } String newCode { return "C" + new Random .nextInt 1 000 000 ; } } @Test void validToday { var c = new Coupon Instant.now .plus 1, ChronoUnit.SECONDS ; assertTrue new CouponService .isValid c ; // flaky on slow CI } Red herring: "the CI machine's clock is skewed".

title: Decorator ordering
text: Explain both symptoms and fix the design. A product-catalog client is wired as a decorator stack. During a 90-second upstream outage, users keep seeing errors for 60 more seconds after the upstream recovers, and upstream sees 3x normal traffic during the outage. Fetcher f = new CachingFetcher new RetryFetcher new HttpFetcher , 3 ; // Caching Retry Http : cache stores whatever Retry returns class RetryFetcher { / returns "" on exhaustion instead of throwing / } 12:01:03 GET /p/42 upstream 503 x3 - RetryFetcher returns "" - cached TTL 60s 12:02:40 upstream healthy; GET /p/42 - cache hit - "" Red herrings: "CDN", "DNS TTL".

title: Code smells and cures
text: Name five code smells you look for in a review, and the refactoring that cures each. Long method extract method , God class extract class, SRP , primitive obsession value object like Money , switch on type polymorphism or strategy , feature envy move method . A smell is a hint to look, not proof of a bug.

title: Over-mocking
text: How do you proceed so the refactoring is safe and the suite survives the next one? A team wants to extract a pricing module from OrderService . The change is behaviour-preserving, but 213 of 480 unit tests fail. Each test has 6 to 9 mocks and verifies call order. Release is in 3 days. verify repo .findCart id ; verify pricing, times 1 .quote any ; verify tax .apply any ; InOrder inOrder = inOrder repo, pricing, tax ; inOrder.verify repo .save captor.capture ; CI shows 31 minutes total; the suite also takes 11 minutes of Spring context startup.

title: DI scopes and leaks
text: Explain the leak in DI terms and fix it without losing the feature. An Android app's crash-free rate dropped from 99.7% to 98.9% after a DI cleanup. LeakCanary shows CheckoutActivity retained after back navigation; native memory grows 40 MB per checkout; OOM crashes on 2 GB devices. @Singleton class AnalyticsTracker @Inject constructor private val activity: Activity { ... } @Module @InstallIn SingletonComponent::class object Providers { @Provides fun provideActivity : Activity = currentActivity!! // static holder } LeakCanary: GC ROOT static Providers.currentActivity - CheckoutActivity destroyed, still referenced Red herrings: "images in the cart", "RecyclerView".

title: Safe refactoring process
text: How do you refactor a 400-line method with no tests in production code that cannot be down for a day? First add characterization tests that record current behaviour, then change in tiny steps extract, rename, move , running tests and committing after each. Never mix refactoring with new behaviour. For big replacements use the strangler pattern behind a flag.

title: Primitive obsession
text: Plan a migration to a safe money model while production keeps running. Invoices use double price throughout 140 files. Finance finds a daily 1-3 paise cent-level drift in totals; for 20k invoices a day reconciliation is off by up to Rs 140. Multi-currency support is next quarter. subtotal = 0.1 + 0.2 - 0.30000000000000004 Math.round price 100 /100 - rounding done differently in 6 places DB column: DECIMAL 10,2 in one table, FLOAT in two Red herring: "just round at the end".

title: Liskov violation
text: What principle is violated, and how do you redesign? A team made ReadOnlyCart extends Cart to reuse display code, throwing from mutators. The checkout page crashes for 0.4% of users those on the shared-link view with UnsupportedOperationException , and a pricing job silently skips carts. class Cart { public void add Item i { items.add i ; } public double total { / sums items / } public void applyCoupon Coupon c { discounts.add c ; } } class ReadOnlyCart extends Cart { @Override public void add Item i { throw new UnsupportedOperationException ; } @Override public void applyCoupon Coupon c { / ignored / } } void checkout Cart c { c.applyCoupon promo ; c.add freeGift ; pay c.total ; } Red herring: "caller should catch the exception".

title: relational model and storage
text: What does "relational" actually mean in a relational database, and how does Postgres store a table differently from MySQL InnoDB? "Relational comes from the math term relation: a set of tuples with the same typed columns. It is not about relationships between tables. You declare what you want in SQL and the planner decides how. Physically, Postgres keeps rows in an unordered heap and every index points to a row location, while InnoDB stores the row inside the primary-key B+tree, so the table is the primary index."

title: keys
text: Explain candidate key, primary key, alternate key and superkey. Can a table have several, and can a primary key be NULL? "A superkey is any column set that uniquely identifies a row. A candidate key is a minimal superkey: remove any column and uniqueness breaks. The primary key is the candidate I pick as the main identifier; the others are alternate keys, enforced with UNIQUE NOT NULL. A table has one PK, many candidate keys, and PK columns can never be NULL."

title: NULL logic
text: What is three-valued logic in SQL, and why does WHERE col < 5 not return rows where col is NULL? "NULL means unknown, so comparisons with it yield UNKNOWN, not true or false. WHERE keeps only rows where the predicate is TRUE, so UNKNOWN rows are dropped. col < 5 with col NULL is UNKNOWN, and the row disappears. To include them I use IS DISTINCT FROM or an explicit OR col IS NULL ."

title: NULL pitfalls
text: Find both bugs, explain them, and fix. A coupon system. Product asks: "show orders that did not use the SUMMER10 coupon" and "make sure a user has at most one active coupon". CREATE TABLE orders id bigint PRIMARY KEY, user id bigint, coupon text, total int ; CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one active ON user coupons user id, redeemed at ; SELECT count FROM orders WHERE coupon < 'SUMMER10'; -- returns 6,100 SELECT count FROM orders; -- returns 10,000 SELECT count FROM orders WHERE coupon IS NULL; -- returns 3,400 Active coupons have redeemed at IS NULL . Support complains some users have 3 active coupons. The first count looks low compared to expectations finance expects 7,000+ .

title: surrogate vs natural keys
text: Surrogate key or natural key as primary key? When would you pick each? "Default to a surrogate key bigint identity as PK because it is small, stable and meaningless, so nothing outside needs to change when business data changes. I still declare the natural key as UNIQUE NOT NULL so the business rule is enforced. I use a natural key only when it is truly immutable and small, like ISO country code, or for join tables where the pair is the identity."

title: foreign key performance
text: Why is the delete so slow and what do you do? Postgres 15, customers 2M rows, orders 80M rows with customer id REFERENCES customers id . Nightly cleanup runs DELETE FROM customers WHERE id IN ... for 5,000 inactive customers. It used to take 3 seconds; last night it ran 40 minutes, holding locks, and the API timed out on signups. orders.customer id has no index someone dropped it to save disk . pg stat activity shows one backend running the delete; auto explain -style output: -- illustrative Trigger for constraint orders customer id fkey: time=2410000.1 calls=5000 CPU is moderate, disk reads high. A red herring: replication lag is also up.

title: referential actions
text: Compare ON DELETE CASCADE, SET NULL, RESTRICT and NO ACTION. Which would you use for orders to customers and why? "RESTRICT and NO ACTION reject deleting a parent with children; the difference is when the check runs RESTRICT immediately, NO ACTION at statement end and deferrable . CASCADE deletes children. SET NULL orphans them explicitly. For orders referencing customers I use RESTRICT: financial records must not vanish, so a customer is anonymised or soft-deleted instead."

title: constraints
text: How do you make double booking impossible at the database level? A meeting-room booking service on Postgres. bookings id, room id, starts at, ends at . The app checks for overlap with a SELECT, then INSERTs. Under load about 300 booking requests/sec at 9 AM support finds double-booked rooms: 23 overlaps last week. Someone proposes a unique index on room id, starts at . Another suggests locking the whole table. Logs show two requests inserting 10:00-11:00 and 10:30-11:30 within 4 ms.

title: ER modelling
text: Walk through your ER model and the DDL. Interview prompt: "Design the schema for a course platform. Students enrol in courses, courses have instructors, and we want to track the grade and enrolment date." The interviewer stops there. Scale hint when asked: 2M students, 20k courses, 40M enrolments, a course can have co-instructors, a student can retake a course.

title: key choice at scale
text: UUID v4, bigint identity or UUID v7 as a primary key: how do they behave at hundreds of millions of rows in Postgres and InnoDB? "Random UUID v4 inserts land on random B-tree leaves, so the whole index must be cached, pages split, and WAL grows from full-page writes. Bigint identity is compact and append-only, but needs coordination across shards and leaks counts. UUID v7 is time-ordered, so it keeps insert locality like a sequence while still being generated anywhere. I default to bigint for single-primary OLTP and v7 when ids must be generated client-side or across shards."

title: constraints on live tables
text: How do you ship it safely? Postgres 14, payments has 600M rows 900 GB , 4,000 writes/sec. Orphan rows exist: about 12k payments reference deleted orders . You need payments.order id NOT NULL REFERENCES orders id . A teammate ran this on staging 1 GB in 200 ms: ALTER TABLE payments ADD CONSTRAINT fk order FOREIGN KEY order id REFERENCES orders id ; ALTER TABLE payments ALTER COLUMN order id SET NOT NULL; Production SLO: no write stall over 2 seconds. Red herring: staging has no concurrent traffic.

title: integer key overflow
text: What is your plan? events.id is serial int4 , 1.9 billion rows, growing 25M/day. Max is 2,147,483,647, so about 10 days of headroom about 247M ids left . Table is 700 GB, 3 secondary indexes, referenced by 4 child tables with int4 FKs. Writes are 400/sec steady, no maintenance window. Alert sample: ERROR: nextval: reached maximum value of sequence "events id seq" 2147483647 -- what you will see on day 10 A teammate suggests ALTER TABLE events ALTER COLUMN id TYPE bigint . Red herring: disk is 40% free.

title: schema smells
text: What would you recommend? A product team stores customer-defined fields in a table attributes entity id, key, value text EAV . 5M entities, 60 attributes each, so 300M rows. Reports like "customers in Pune with plan=pro and seats 10" need three self-joins and are timing out EXPLAIN shows nested loops, 40 s, illustrative : -- illustrative Nested Loop actual time=0.9..40211 rows=812 - Index Scan using attr key value on attributes a1 rows=1.2M - Index Scan using attr pkey on attributes a2 ... loops=1200000 Values are all text so seats 10 is a string comparison and returns wrong rows '9' '10' . PM wants "flexible schema, no migrations".

title: uniqueness and soft delete
text: Run the review: causes, correct design, and how to roll it out. Post-incident: users could not re-register after deleting their account "email already exists" , and separately 300 ghost accounts shared one email because a bug path created rows with deleted at set. The schema: CREATE TABLE users id bigint PRIMARY KEY, email text NOT NULL, deleted at timestamptz, CONSTRAINT users email key UNIQUE email ; Soft-deleted rows stay for 90 days for legal reasons. In the incident someone "fixed" it by dropping the UNIQUE constraint; two live accounts then registered with Ann@x.com and ann@x.com .

title: anomalies
text: What problem does normalization solve? Explain update, insert and delete anomalies with an example. "Normalization removes redundancy so each fact is stored once. Redundant copies cause anomalies. Update: change a customer's city in one row but not the other 40 rows. Insert: you cannot record a new product until someone orders it. Delete: removing the last order erases the only record of the customer."

title: 1NF
text: What does First Normal Form require, and is storing a JSON column or an array a violation? "1NF means each column holds a single atomic value, there are no repeating column groups like phone1, phone2, phone3, and each row is uniquely identifiable. A comma-separated list violates it. A JSON or array column is a grey area: it is fine when the value is treated as an opaque document and never filtered, joined or constrained by its parts."

title: functional dependencies
text: What is a functional dependency, and how do you use it to find the candidate keys of a table? "X - Y means that whenever two rows agree on X they must agree on Y, so X determines Y. To find keys, I compute the attribute closure of a column set: keep adding everything determined by what I already have. A set whose closure covers all columns, and is minimal, is a candidate key."

title: update anomaly
text: Why is the report wrong and how do you fix the design? A support dashboard shows revenue by customer tier. Numbers do not add up: total by tier is 4% higher than total orders. Table: CREATE TABLE order lines order id bigint, line no int, customer id bigint, customer tier text, product id bigint, product name text, unit price int, qty int, PRIMARY KEY order id, line no ; -- illustrative query SELECT customer tier, sum unit price qty FROM order lines GROUP BY 1; SELECT customer id, count DISTINCT customer tier FROM order lines GROUP BY 1 HAVING count DISTINCT customer tier 1; -- 1,812 customers Tier changes via a nightly job that updates only the last 30 days of rows. Red herring: a recent timezone fix.

title: 2NF vs 3NF
text: Explain 2NF and 3NF with one example each, and the difference in what they remove. "2NF applies to composite keys: every non-key column must depend on the whole key, not part of it. 3NF says non-key columns must depend only on the key, not on another non-key column. Partial dependency is a piece of the key determining something; transitive is key - A - B."

title: 1NF violation
text: What do you do and what are the options? An articles table keeps tags text as 'sql,postgres,index' . 4M articles. Queries: "articles tagged postgres" via WHERE tags LIKE '%postgres%' takes 2.4 s seq scan, illustrative : -- illustrative Seq Scan on articles actual time=0.1..2380 rows=18400 Filter: tags '%postgres%'::text Rows Removed by Filter: 3981600 It also returns articles tagged 'postgresql' and 'postgres-xl'. The tag list page needs counts per tag, done by splitting strings in the app. Editors want to rename a tag.

title: BCNF
text: What is BCNF and when is a table in 3NF but not in BCNF? Give an example. "BCNF requires that for every non-trivial FD X - Y, X is a superkey. 3NF is weaker: it also allows Y to be part of a candidate key. A table can be in 3NF but not BCNF when a non-key column determines part of a candidate key, usually with overlapping composite candidate keys."

title: normalizing a flat file
text: How do you design the tables? What do you ask first? Finance exports a monthly CSV that the team must load into Postgres: invoice no, invoice date, customer code, customer name, customer address, line no, sku, sku description, unit price, qty, tax rate . About 2M rows per month. A junior loaded it as one table with PK invoice no, line no . Now product asks for "an invoice screen and a customer page". The interviewer adds nothing else.

title: read-model denormalization
text: What do you do? A social feed page joins 6 tables posts, users, follows, likes, comments, media . p95 is 1.8 s at 3,000 requests/sec peak; the DB CPU is 85%. The feed is read 200x more than written. Plan excerpt illustrative : -- illustrative Hash Join actual time=410..1620 rows=50 loops=1 - Aggregate like counts actual time=300..900 rows=1.2M - Aggregate comment counts actual time=200..700 rows=800k Likes can be 5 seconds stale. A teammate wants to "denormalize everything into one wide table"; another says never denormalize.

title: lossless decomposition
text: When is a decomposition lossless, and how do you show a decomposition that is lossy? Why does it matter in practice? "A decomposition of R into R1 and R2 is lossless if joining them gives exactly R back. The test: the common attributes must be a key of at least one of the parts R1 ∩ R2 - R1 or R2 . If not, the join produces spurious rows. In practice it explains why you split on a determinant, not on arbitrary columns."

title: splitting a wide table
text: Plan the migration to a companies table. accounts has 180M rows and 90 columns, including company name, company tier, company billing country, company vat id repeated per account companies average 40 accounts . Updating a company's tier means updating 40 rows; a bug left 2.3M accounts with the wrong tier. 6,000 writes/sec, 30k reads/sec, many services read accounts directly via SELECT . No downtime allowed.

title: analytics vs OLTP shape
text: What do you recommend? The analytics team runs 40 ad hoc queries a day against the OLTP Postgres primary: 7-way joins over orders, items, products, customers, regions; each takes 2 to 8 minutes and one caused replica lag of 90 s last Tuesday. They ask: "Please denormalize the OLTP tables so our queries are simple." OLTP does 2,500 TPS.

title: deliberate redundancy
text: Who is right? A code reviewer flags: " order items.unit price duplicates products.price , this violates 3NF, remove it." The order system has 50M order items. Marketing changes prices weekly; a refund last month for an order from 2023 computed the amount from products.price and refunded $14 too much per unit. Another reviewer says the column is fine.

title: derived data drift
text: Review the incident and propose the design. users.follower count is maintained by the app: UPDATE users SET follower count = follower count + 1 after inserting into follows . After a deploy, 3% of users show wrong counts some negative . Evidence: retries after timeouts re-ran the increment without the insert the insert was idempotent via ON CONFLICT , and a bulk "remove spam accounts" script deleted follows rows without decrementing. Hot celebrity rows with 4M followers show lock waits of 800 ms.

title: logical query order
text: In what order does SQL logically evaluate a SELECT, and why can't you use a column alias in WHERE? "The written order is not the evaluation order. Logically it is FROM and JOINs, then WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, window functions, SELECT where aliases are born , DISTINCT, ORDER BY, then LIMIT. WHERE runs before SELECT, so an alias defined in SELECT does not exist yet. ORDER BY runs after SELECT, so it can use aliases."

title: join types
text: Explain INNER, LEFT, FULL and CROSS joins. What changes when a filter is in ON versus WHERE for a LEFT JOIN? "INNER keeps only matching pairs. LEFT keeps every left row, filling NULLs when nothing matches. FULL keeps unmatched rows from both sides. CROSS is every combination. For a LEFT JOIN, a condition in ON decides what counts as a match and keeps unmatched left rows; the same condition in WHERE runs after the join and removes NULL-extended rows, turning it into an inner join."

title: aggregation correctness
text: Why is the customers column wrong, and how do you fix it? Task: "for each city, number of customers and number of orders". Query written: SELECT c.city, count AS customers, count o.id AS orders FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer id = c.id GROUP BY c.city; -- result with the sample data: Pune 3 3 Delhi 1 1 NULL 1 0 -- expected: Pune 2 3 Delhi 1 1 NULL 1 0 Sample: Asha Pune, 2 orders , Chitra Pune, 1 order , Ben Delhi, 1 order , Dev no city, 0 orders . A teammate suggests DISTINCT .

title: outer join filter
text: Find the bug and fix it, including an index. A "customers and their May orders" report must show all customers, including those with no May orders. Output has 3,100 rows while the customers table has 5,000. SELECT c.id, c.name, o.id AS order id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer id = c.id WHERE o.created = '2025-05-01' AND o.created < '2025-06-01'; The data team says "the join must be broken, let's use FULL JOIN". Red herring: orders has 90M rows and a recent index rebuild.

title: NOT IN and NULL
text: What happened, and how do you write it safely and fast? A nightly job finds users to email: users who have never placed an order. SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE id NOT IN SELECT user id FROM orders ; For 2 years it returned about 40k rows. Today it returns 0 rows and the campaign did not send. No errors. Yesterday a new import path inserted 120 orders with user id NULL guest checkout . Red herring: the users table was vacuumed at the same time.

title: ranking functions and frames
text: Differentiate ROW NUMBER, RANK and DENSE RANK, and explain why last value often returns the wrong thing. "All three number rows within a partition by ORDER BY. ROW NUMBER gives unique numbers even for ties, RANK gives ties the same number then skips, DENSE RANK gives ties the same number without gaps. last value surprises people because with an ORDER BY the default frame ends at the current row, so it returns the current row's value, not the partition's last."

title: top-N per group
text: Make both uses fast. Product wants "the 3 most recent orders per customer" for a 2M-customer, 60M-order system. Current query: SELECT FROM SELECT o. , row number OVER PARTITION BY customer id ORDER BY created DESC rn FROM orders o t WHERE rn <= 3; It takes 38 s illustrative : -- illustrative WindowAgg actual time=21000..36000 rows=60000000 - Sort Sort Method: external merge Disk: 4800000kB It runs per-request for one customer's page as ... WHERE customer id = 42 , yet someone also uses it for a nightly export of everyone.

title: join fan-out
text: Diagnose and fix, and explain how you would prevent it. Finance reports revenue of $12.4M for May in the dashboard but the ledger says $8.1M. The dashboard query: SELECT date trunc 'month', o.created m, sum o.total AS revenue, count AS orders FROM orders o JOIN order items i ON i.order id = o.id WHERE o.status = 'paid' GROUP BY 1; Orders have on average 1.5 items. The change last week: an item-level "product category" filter was added by joining order items . orders count in the dashboard is also inflated by about 50%. Red herring: refunds are in a separate table.

title: EXISTS, IN and JOIN
text: When would you use EXISTS, IN or a JOIN to filter rows by related data? Are they equivalent? "For 'rows that have a match', EXISTS and IN are semi-joins and return each outer row once. A JOIN returns one row per match, so it can duplicate rows and needs DISTINCT, which hides fan-out. Planners usually give the same plan for IN and EXISTS. NOT EXISTS and NOT IN are not equivalent: NOT IN returns nothing if the list contains a NULL."

title: deep pagination
text: Why is it slow and unstable and how do you redesign? An admin export API paginates GET /orders?page=N with ORDER BY created DESC OFFSET N-1 50 LIMIT 50 . 120M rows. A partner script crawls pages 1 to 2.4M. DB CPU rises to 90%, p99 for the API goes from 40 ms to 6 s, replicas lag. Plan at page 400,000 illustrative : -- illustrative Limit actual time=2100..2100 rows=50 - Index Scan Backward using orders created idx actual time=0.03..2095 rows=20000050 Some rows are also missing or repeated between pages because orders are inserted constantly. Red herring: the connection pool is only 40% used.

title: CTE materialization
text: Is a CTE an optimization fence? How did Postgres change in version 12, and when would you force materialization? "Before Postgres 12 every CTE was materialized, so filters from the outer query were not pushed into it. From 12, a non-recursive, side-effect-free CTE referenced once is inlined like a subquery; one referenced multiple times is materialized by default. I can override with MATERIALIZED or NOT MATERIALIZED. I force MATERIALIZED when the CTE is expensive and used several times, or to stop the planner from picking a bad plan; I use NOT MATERIALIZED to allow predicate pushdown."

title: recursive CTE safety
text: How did one small table consume 40 GB, and how do you fix and prevent it? A category-tree endpoint uses a recursive CTE to list all descendants of a category. After a bulk import, the endpoint hangs; Postgres shows one backend at 100% CPU for 12 minutes, temp files growing to 40 GB, then the disk alarm fires. WITH RECURSIVE t AS SELECT id, parent id FROM categories WHERE id = $1 UNION ALL SELECT c.id, c.parent id FROM categories c JOIN t ON c.parent id = t.id SELECT FROM t; The table has 80k rows. Investigation: category 514 has parent id = 9120 and 9120's ancestor chain loops back to 514. Red herring: a vacuum was running.

title: correlated subqueries at scale
text: Will it hold at 10x? What do you change? A customer listing shows last order date and total spent via correlated subqueries: SELECT c.id, c.name, SELECT max created FROM orders o WHERE o.customer id = c.id AS last order, SELECT sum total FROM orders o WHERE o.customer id = c.id AS spent FROM customers c WHERE c.city = 'Pune'; Today: 20k Pune customers, 5M orders, 120 ms. Growth plan: 10x customers and orders. orders customer id has an index. The query is run for every segment page load. Excerpt for current plan illustrative : -- illustrative SubPlan 1 actual time=0.004..0.004 loops=20000 SubPlan 2 actual time=0.012..0.012 loops=20000 Customers in the biggest segment have 5,000+ orders each.

title: window function execution
text: How does a database execute a window function, what does it cost, and can an index help? "The engine sorts the input by partition keys then order keys, then streams through it computing the function per row with a frame. So cost is dominated by the sort, O n log n , and memory for the frame state. An index whose columns match PARTITION BY then ORDER BY can supply sorted input and skip the sort. Window results cannot be filtered in WHERE; you wrap them in a subquery."

title: What an index buys and costs
text: What does an index actually do, and why not just index every column? An index is a separate sorted structure that maps column values to row locations, so a lookup reads a handful of pages instead of the whole table. The price is paid on every write: each INSERT, DELETE and any UPDATE of an indexed column must also update every index, and each index takes disk and cache. So I index for queries I have measured, not for every column.

title: B+tree structure
text: How does a B+tree index work, and why can it find one row among a billion in a few page reads? A B+tree is a wide, balanced tree where each node is one disk page holding hundreds of keys. With fan-out around 300, three levels cover about 27 million keys and four cover billions. Inner nodes only hold separators; the real entries sit in sorted, linked leaf pages, so a lookup is a few page reads and a range scan walks leaves sideways.

title: Index skipped due to function
text: Why is the index not used, and what do you change? A login endpoint does SELECT id, password hash FROM users WHERE lower email = lower $1 . users has 8M rows and an index users email idx ON users email . The endpoint takes 350 ms and CPU on the primary is climbing. A teammate says "the index is there, so it must be the network". -- illustrative Seq Scan on users cost=0.00..201000.00 rows=40000 width=72 actual time=0.1..340.2 rows=1 loops=1 Filter: lower email = 'a@x.com'::text Rows Removed by Filter: 7999999

title: Composite index column order
text: Explain the leftmost-prefix rule and how you decide column order in a composite index. A composite index on a, b, c is sorted by a, then b within a, then c within a, b . It can seek only on a leftmost prefix. My rule: equality columns first, then the ORDER BY column, then range columns last, because a range on a column stops later columns from narrowing the scan. Among equals I pick the order that serves the most query shapes.

title: Skewed flag and queue table
text: How would you restructure the indexing? A jobs table has 120M rows; 99.9% have done = true , a few thousand are done = false . Workers poll SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE done = false ORDER BY created LIMIT 50 every second from 40 workers. Someone added CREATE INDEX ON jobs done last quarter. Poll latency is 1.5 s, the index is 4 GB, and the index shows heavy write cost. -- illustrative Limit actual time=1480..1480 rows=50 - Sort actual time=1480..1480 rows=50 Sort Method: top-N heapsort - Index Scan using jobs done idx on jobs actual rows=61342 loops=1 Index Cond: done = false Red herring: the team suspects the 40 workers are overloading the connection pool.

title: Choosing composite column order
text: Redesign the index and justify the order. What other query shapes could break your design? events has 300M rows, 40k tenants, 6 event types, and occurred at timestamps. The hot query is: SELECT FROM events WHERE tenant id = $1 AND occurred at = now - interval '1 day' AND type = $2 ORDER BY occurred at DESC LIMIT 100; Existing index: occurred at, tenant id, type . Query takes 900 ms on a 40-core primary and reads 2M index entries per call.

title: Clustered vs heap indexes
text: How do InnoDB's clustered index and Postgres's heap-plus-index layout differ, and how does that change your primary key choice? In InnoDB the primary key B+tree is the table, so rows are stored in PK order and secondary index leaves store the PK value; a secondary lookup is two tree descents. In Postgres the table is an unordered heap and every index leaf stores a TID pointing at the heap, so every lookup is one descent plus one heap jump. Consequently, in InnoDB a wide or random PK hurts the table and every secondary index; in Postgres it mostly hurts the PK index.

title: Index-only scan that still hits the heap
text: Why is the "index-only" scan still reading the heap and what do you do? A wallet service runs SELECT balance FROM wallets WHERE user id = $1 at 6,000 req/s. Last sprint you added CREATE INDEX wallets user inc ON wallets user id INCLUDE balance to get an index-only scan. Load tests looked great; in production p99 is 40 ms and disk read IOPS are 3x higher than expected. The table is updated 2,000 times/s balance changes . -- illustrative Index Only Scan using wallets user inc on wallets actual time=0.02..0.31 rows=1 loops=1 Index Cond: user id = 8123 Heap Fetches: 1 Buffers: shared hit=3 read=1 Red herring: someone points at shared buffers being too small.

title: HOT updates and covering indexes
text: What is a HOT update in Postgres, and how do indexes and INCLUDE columns affect it? Postgres never updates a row in place; it writes a new tuple version. Normally every index needs a new entry pointing at the new TID. A HOT heap-only tuple update skips index maintenance when no indexed column changed and the new version fits on the same heap page. Indexing or INCLUDE-ing a frequently updated column disables HOT for those updates, so write cost, WAL and bloat rise.

title: Building indexes on a live table
text: How do you finish this safely? You must add tenant id, status to invoices 600M rows, 200 GB on the primary of a payments system doing 3,000 writes/s. The first attempt, run by a teammate with plain CREATE INDEX , queued writes for 8 minutes and caused API 500s when the connection pool filled. Second attempt with CONCURRENTLY failed after 2 hours with ERROR: deadlock detected during the second scan. Now pg index shows: -- illustrative indexrelid indisvalid indisready invoices tenant idx f t A replica is also used for reporting. Disk headroom is 90 GB.

title: How the planner picks index vs seq scan
text: Walk me through how Postgres decides between a sequential scan, an index scan and a bitmap scan for a filter, and which knobs shift that decision. The planner estimates the fraction of rows the filter keeps from statistics, then costs each path. A seq scan reads all pages sequentially cheap per page, seq page cost 1.0 . An index scan does random heap reads random page cost , 4.0 by default , so it wins only for a small fraction. A bitmap scan sits between: it sorts matching page numbers and reads each heap page once. Raising the matched fraction, or lowering the random cost, moves the crossover.

title: Write amplification and index pruning
text: How do you prune indexes safely and what is the plan for 10x writes? An ingestion table readings has 14 indexes and sustains 2,000 inserts/s. Product wants 20,000/s next quarter. CPU is 40%, but iowait and WAL volume are high: WAL grows at 160 MB/s; replica lag spikes to minutes. pg stat user indexes on the primary stats reset 9 days ago : -- illustrative indexrelname idx scan size readings dev ts 5.1M 18 GB readings dev 12.0M 9 GB readings ts 0 14 GB readings dev ts val 40 22 GB readings flag 0 3 GB ... 9 more, mixed A BI team uses a replica for month-end reports.

title: Index bloat after churn
text: Lead the post-incident discussion: what failed, what do you fix now and what do you change so it does not recur? Post-incident review. A session store table sessions 40M rows, deletes and inserts constantly, TTL purge nightly saw lookups by token degrade from 0.2 ms to 25 ms over 3 months; no alerts fired. The index sessions token idx was 30 GB where the live data needed 8 GB. During the incident someone ran REINDEX INDEX sessions token idx in business hours; writes blocked for 4 minutes, the API errored, and the incident widened. -- illustrative pgstattuple-style index size: 31 GB avg leaf density: 24% leaf fragmentation: 61%

title: Substring search requirement
text: What do you ask, and what do you build? Product asks: "Make the customer search box fast." The backend runs SELECT FROM customers WHERE name ILIKE '%' $1 '%' OR email ILIKE '%' $1 '%' LIMIT 20 on 25M rows. It takes 6 s. A colleague proposes CREATE INDEX ON customers name and email ; they tested it on 10k rows and it was "instant". -- illustrative Seq Scan on customers actual time=0.1..5900 rows=20 loops=1 Filter: name '%ann%' OR email '%ann%'

title: Query pipeline and cost-based planning
text: What happens between sending a SQL string to Postgres and getting rows back? The server parses the text and resolves names, rewrites views and rules, then the planner enumerates ways to run it scan types, join orders, join algorithms and picks the cheapest by estimated cost. The executor then runs the chosen plan as a tree of nodes, each pulling rows from its children. The plan depends on statistics, so wrong estimates, not the SQL text, are the usual reason a query is slow.

title: Reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE
text: How do you read an EXPLAIN ANALYZE output, and what do you look at first? I read the tree bottom-up, innermost node first. Then I compare estimated rows= with actual rows= on each node: a 10x or larger gap is where the planner went wrong. I multiply actual time and rows by loops , check Rows Removed by Filter , Buffers hit vs read and any Sort Method: external merge or Batches 1 spill. EXPLAIN alone estimates; ANALYZE actually runs the query, so I wrap writes in BEGIN/ROLLBACK.

title: N+1 from the application layer
text: What is wrong, and how do you fix it? An endpoint GET /orders returns 500 orders with items. It takes 1.2 s; the DB CPU is 10% and each query in pg stat statements averages 0.9 ms. The ORM code: orders = db.query "SELECT FROM orders WHERE user id = %s LIMIT 500", uid for o in orders: o.items = db.query "SELECT FROM order items WHERE order id = %s", o.id Network RTT to the DB is 1.5 ms. Red herring: the team wants to upgrade the instance size.

title: Scan types and bitmap scans
text: Compare seq scan, index scan, bitmap scan and index-only scan: when does each win and what is a bitmap scan for? Seq scan reads everything sequentially and wins for large fractions or tiny tables. Index scan follows the index and does a random heap read per match, so it wins for few rows or when it supplies ORDER BY ... LIMIT. Bitmap scan is the middle: it collects matching row locations from the index, sorts them by heap page, and reads each page once, which is cheaper than many random reads and can AND/OR several indexes. Index-only scan skips the heap when the index has all columns and the visibility map allows.

title: Estimate gap and nested loop explosion
text: Diagnose and fix. After a Friday deploy, an API endpoint p99 jumps from 80 ms to 4 s. pg stat statements shows a new query dominating total exec time . Plan excerpt illustrative : Nested Loop cost=0.85..2400.10 rows=20 width=64 actual time=0.1..3890 rows=250000 loops=1 - Index Scan using ads campaign idx on ads a rows=20 actual rows=250000 loops=1 Index Cond: campaign id = 9 Filter: region = 'IN' AND city = 'Pune' - Index Scan using clicks ad idx on clicks c rows=1 actual time=0.01..0.015 rows=3 loops=250000 The table was loaded last week by a backfill; autovacuum says "last analyze: 9 days ago". Red herring: a recent index was added to clicks .

title: Sort spill and deep pagination
text: Fix it without a giant work mem . The admin "recent orders" page uses SELECT FROM orders ORDER BY created DESC OFFSET 100000 LIMIT 50 . orders has 40M rows. It takes 2.1 s and gets slower for deep pages. Plan illustrative : Limit actual time=2080..2080 rows=50 - Sort actual time=1850..2060 rows=100050 Sort Method: external merge Disk: 187000kB - Seq Scan on orders actual rows=40000000 Red herring: the DBA proposes raising work mem to 1 GB globally.

title: Join algorithms
text: Compare nested loop, hash join and merge join. When does the planner choose each? Nested loop probes the inner side for each outer row; it is best with a small outer and an indexed inner, and terrible for two large unindexed inputs. Hash join builds a hash table from the smaller side and probes it with the other: O n+m , equality only, needs work mem or it spills in batches. Merge join walks two sorted inputs together; good for large pre-sorted data and range-style comparisons on sortable keys. The choice flips with row counts, so accurate estimates matter.

title: Hash spill and work_mem sizing
text: What do you do? A reporting join of events 200M to accounts 6M runs in 90 s. Plan excerpt illustrative : Hash Join actual time=21000..88000 rows=6000000 loops=1 - Seq Scan on events ... - Hash actual time=4100..4100 rows=6000000 loops=1 Buckets: 131072 Batches: 64 Memory Usage: 4096kB work mem is 4 MB. The primary also serves 300 OLTP connections. A teammate wants ALTER SYSTEM SET work mem = '1GB' .

title: Statistics and cardinality estimation
text: What statistics does Postgres keep, how are they used for row estimates, and what are their blind spots? ANALYZE samples the table and stores per-column null fraction, n distinct, most common values with frequencies, a histogram of the rest, and physical correlation. The planner multiplies selectivities to estimate rows. It assumes columns are independent, so correlated predicates are underestimated; stale stats after bulk loads, expression filters and skew with a long tail also mislead it. Fixes: ANALYZE, extended statistics, higher per-column statistics target.

title: Stats after bulk load
text: What is going on, how do you recover, and how do you make the next migration safe? You are migrating 40M rows from a legacy table into new ledger entries via INSERT ... SELECT in 500k batches while traffic stays live. After the cutover the dashboard query that took 200 ms now exceeds 40 minutes. Plan illustrative : Nested Loop cost=0.00..8000.00 rows=10 width=48 actual rows=3200000 loops=1 - Seq Scan on ledger entries l rows=1000 actual rows=40000000 - Index Scan on accounts a ... loops=40000000 pg stat user tables : reltuples = 1000 , n mod since analyze = 40000000 , last autoanalyze is empty. Autovacuum is "running" on other big tables.

title: Generic vs custom plans
text: Explain what happened and what you change. Post-incident review. A service uses prepared statements through a driver: SELECT FROM orders WHERE customer id = $1 ORDER BY created DESC LIMIT 20 . One huge customer customer id = 1 has 18M of 60M rows; typical customers have 40. For two days, requests for the huge customer ran 12 s; a restart "fixed" it, then it returned. Observations illustrative : -- 6th execution onward Index Scan Backward using orders created idx on orders rows=20 -- filter customer id = $1 Rows Removed by Filter: 17,100,000 Red herring: a deploy occurred the same day.

title: Join order search and plan stability
text: How does the planner choose join order for a 10-table query, and what goes wrong with many joins? The number of join orders grows factorially, so Postgres does dynamic programming for up to join collapse limit / from collapse limit tables default 8 and switches to the genetic optimiser GEQO at geqo threshold 12, which is randomized and can return worse plans. Errors in each join's cardinality estimate compound multiplicatively, so large joins yield bad plans. Mitigations: simplify queries, split into steps/CTEs or temp tables with ANALYZE, and fix statistics.

title: Slow queries that are not plan problems
text: What do you ask and what do you do? Support says "the app is slow sometimes, mostly around 14:00". The DB team looks: EXPLAIN ANALYZE of the reported query shows Execution Time: 3 ms . Yet the application times out at 5 s. pg stat activity at 14:02 illustrative : state wait event type wait event count active Lock transactionid 112 idle in transaction 38 active IO DataFileRead 7 There are 480 connections to a 16-core server; the app has no pooler. A batch job runs at 14:00 updating 2M rows in one statement.

title: Dashboard counts at 10x scale
text: What do you do for the global count and the tenant count at 10x? A dashboard runs SELECT count FROM events WHERE tenant id = $1 AND created = date trunc 'day', now plus an overall SELECT count FROM events for a header badge. events grew from 20M to 400M rows expected 4B next year . The tenant count takes 80 ms; the global count takes 9 s and is called by every page load 300 req/s . -- illustrative Finalize Aggregate actual time=9100..9100 rows=1 - Gather ... Parallel Seq Scan on events actual rows=133000000 loops=3 Red herring: someone suggests adding an index on id to speed up count.

title: What a transaction is
text: What is a database transaction, and what happens if you never write BEGIN? A transaction groups statements into one all-or-nothing unit: BEGIN, then COMMIT to keep everything or ROLLBACK to discard it. Without BEGIN, Postgres wraps each single statement in its own tiny transaction autocommit , so two statements in a script are not atomic together. In Postgres, once a statement errors inside a transaction, the transaction is aborted and every later statement fails until you ROLLBACK or ROLLBACK TO a savepoint.

title: ACID mechanisms
text: What does each letter of ACID guarantee, and which mechanism in Postgres provides each? Atomicity: all or nothing, done with versioned rows and the commit log, so aborted versions are just ignored. Consistency: committed data obeys declared rules, via constraints, triggers and foreign keys; the database enforces only what you declare. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-done work, via MVCC snapshots and locks. Durability: committed data survives a crash, via the write-ahead log flushed with fsync before COMMIT returns.

title: Invariants in app code
text: Find the bugs and fix them properly. A signup handler checks uniqueness in code, and a wallet service checks balance in code: def signup email : if db.query "SELECT 1 FROM users WHERE email=%s", email : raise Conflict db.execute "INSERT INTO users email VALUES %s ", email def withdraw acc, amt : bal = db.query one "SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id=%s", acc if bal = amt: db.execute "UPDATE accounts SET balance=%s WHERE id=%s", bal-amt, acc Under load, support reports duplicate user rows with the same email and a few accounts with negative balances. Red herring: the team suspects clock skew.

title: Atomicity without undo
text: How does Postgres make a transaction atomic without an undo log, and what are the consequences? Postgres never overwrites a row in place. An UPDATE writes a new tuple version and marks the old one with the updater's xid in xmax . If the transaction aborts, readers consult the commit log pg xact , see it as aborted, and ignore the new version, so rollback is instant, even for a huge transaction. The consequence is dead tuples that VACUUM must reclaim later. InnoDB instead updates in place and keeps undo, so rollback is slow but no vacuum is needed.

title: Savepoints and subtransactions
text: What is happening and how do you fix it? An importer processes 5,000 rows per request. The framework wraps each row in a "nested transaction" a savepoint so one bad row can be skipped. After a traffic increase, throughput collapses: DB CPU 90%, many sessions waiting. pg stat activity illustrative : wait event type wait event count LWLock SubtransSLRU 61 LWLock SubtransBuffer 22 A separate report query runs for several minutes in a repeatable-read snapshot. Red herring: the team suspects the importer's rows are too wide.

title: Adding constraints to a live table
text: Plan the rollout. You must add a foreign key payments.order id - orders.id and CHECK amount 0 to payments 900M rows, 400 GB on a live system doing 1,500 writes/s. Last time someone ran ALTER TABLE payments ADD CONSTRAINT ... FOREIGN KEY ... the table was locked for 11 minutes and the API timed out. Possibly 0.02% of rows violate the rule bad data from an old bug .

title: Durability and synchronous commit
text: What does COMMIT actually guarantee in Postgres, and what do synchronous commit and fsync change? COMMIT returns only after the commit WAL record is flushed fsync to disk; the table pages are written later by checkpoints and are recoverable from WAL. synchronous commit = off returns before the flush: a crash can lose the last few hundred milliseconds of commits but never corrupts data. fsync = off can corrupt the whole cluster. With synchronous replicas, remote write , on or remote apply decide how far the commit must propagate before acknowledgement.

title: Row-by-row commits
text: Speed it up 10x without risking data. A nightly job loads 20M rows with a loop issuing one INSERT per row in autocommit mode. It runs 3 hours at 1,800 rows/s. CPU is 15%, disk write bandwidth is low but pg stat wal shows wal sync count 1,800/s. Storage is a cloud SSD with 0.5 ms fsync. Red herring: the team wants a larger instance.

title: Why long transactions hurt
text: Why are long-running and idle-in-transaction sessions dangerous in Postgres, and what guardrails do you set? A transaction keeps its snapshot, so VACUUM cannot remove dead row versions newer than the oldest open snapshot the xmin horizon . It also holds locks, blocking others. An idle in transaction session does nothing yet keeps both. I keep transactions short, never hold them across HTTP calls or user think time, and set idle in transaction session timeout and statement timeout , plus monitor the oldest xact start .

title: Idle transaction and bloat
text: Run the post-incident review: causes, remediation and prevention. Post-incident review. Over a weekend the orders table grew from 20 GB to 62 GB; p99 for order lookups tripled; autovacuum showed as constantly running but n dead tup kept rising. Evidence illustrative : pid state age query 8812 idle in transaction 41:12:07 SELECT FROM report cache WHERE ... relname n live tup n dead tup last autovacuum orders 52,000,000 38,000,000 3 min ago Red herring: someone raised autovacuum vacuum cost limit and saw no improvement.

title: Outbox and idempotent consumers
text: Why can't you atomically write to Postgres and publish to Kafka, and how do the transactional outbox and idempotency fix it? A database transaction cannot include the broker, so saving then publishing can leave one succeeded and the other failed. With the outbox I write the business row and an outbox row in the same local transaction, and a relay polling or CDC like Debezium publishes outbox rows and marks them sent. Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent, usually with a dedupe key or a unique constraint. End-to-end exactly-once does not exist; at-least-once plus idempotency approximates it.

title: Dual write failure
text: Which do you pick and how do you roll it out? Checkout does: 1 INSERT INTO orders and COMMIT, 2 POST to the Inventory service, 3 publish OrderCreated to Kafka. Every week a few dozen orders exist with no inventory reservation or no email event. The code is: def checkout cart : order id = db.insert order cart commits inventory.reserve order id, cart HTTP, sometimes times out kafka.send "OrderCreated", order id sometimes the pod is killed first The team debates three options: 2PC across services, a saga, or the outbox. Volume is 400 orders/s; the inventory API is owned by another team.

title: Durability requirement vs latency
text: How do you resolve the conflict? A new "audit events" service must have "zero data loss" per the compliance lead, and also "p99 under 5 ms per write" per product. It writes 8,000 events/s, single region, Postgres on cloud NVMe with 1 ms fsync, one synchronous standby in another AZ 2 ms RTT . Initial benchmarks: -- illustrative synchronous commit=on + sync standby, 1 client: p99 6.1 ms, 160 commits/s per connection synchronous commit=off: p99 0.4 ms A developer proposes synchronous commit=off "since Postgres never corrupts". Another proposes fsync=off .

title: Idempotency keys and retries
text: Explain the failure and fix it. A payments API supports an Idempotency-Key header. The implementation: def charge key, req : prior = db.query "SELECT response FROM idem WHERE key=%s", key if prior: return prior resp = psp.charge req external, 2 s latency db.execute "INSERT INTO idem key, response VALUES %s,%s ", key, resp return resp After a mobile client retried aggressively on a slow network, 41 customers were charged twice. Logs show two requests with the same key 1.3 s apart, both finding no prior row. A UNIQUE index exists on idem.key ; the second INSERT failed with a unique violation after the PSP charged, and the API returned 500.

title: Isolation levels overview
text: What are the SQL isolation levels, and does Postgres implement them the way the standard describes? Isolation controls how much of other running transactions I can see. The standard defines four levels, Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read and Serializable, by which anomalies they forbid. Postgres deviates: Read Uncommitted is just Read Committed, Repeatable Read is snapshot isolation so it also blocks phantoms, and only Serializable, which uses SSI, blocks write skew. The default is Read Committed.

title: Dirty read
text: What is a dirty read, and can it happen in Postgres? A dirty read is seeing another transaction's uncommitted write. If that transaction rolls back, I acted on data that never existed. Postgres never allows it, even if I ask for Read Uncommitted, because readers only see committed row versions.

title: Read Committed vs Repeatable Read snapshots
text: Explain a non-repeatable read and how Read Committed and Repeatable Read differ in Postgres. A non-repeatable read is reading the same row twice in a transaction and getting different committed values. In Read Committed every statement gets a fresh snapshot, so it can happen. In Repeatable Read the snapshot is taken at the first statement and held until the end, so both reads return the same value.

title: Lost update
text: Find the bug and fix it. What are your options? A wallet service runs on Postgres at the default isolation. Support reports that when a user taps "redeem 20 points" twice quickly, only one deduction is recorded, but two rewards were issued. Traffic is 300 req/s. The handler: def redeem conn, user id, cost : with conn.transaction : pts = conn.execute "SELECT points FROM wallet WHERE user id=%s", user id, .fetchone 0 if pts < cost: raise Insufficient conn.execute "UPDATE wallet SET points=%s WHERE user id=%s", pts - cost, user id grant reward conn, user id A log excerpt: T1 read 100 , T2 read 100 , T1 write 80 , T2 write 80 . Your colleague blames the connection pool.

title: Phantom reads
text: What is a phantom read, how does it differ from a non-repeatable read, and how do Postgres and MySQL prevent it? A non-repeatable read is a row I already saw changing. A phantom is the set of rows matching a predicate changing, a new row appearing or one vanishing. Row locks cannot stop it because the new row did not exist to lock. Postgres Repeatable Read prevents it with the snapshot; InnoDB uses next-key gap locks for locking reads.

title: Consistent reporting
text: Explain the discrepancy and propose a fix without hurting writers. A nightly finance export runs five queries totals by day, by region, by merchant, refunds, row count on Postgres at the default level while 800 orders/s are inserted. Finance complains the five numbers never reconcile: the row count is higher than the sum of regional counts by 40-300. The export takes 4 minutes. The team proposes locking the orders table.

title: Write skew
text: What is write skew? Show an example and give several ways to prevent it. Two transactions read overlapping data, each concludes an action is safe, and each writes a different row. There is no write-write conflict, so snapshot isolation allows both, but together they break an invariant. Prevent it with Serializable plus retry, with FOR UPDATE on the rows I read, with a shared guard row, or with a constraint.

title: Engine migration
text: Why did the behaviour change and how do you fix it safely during live traffic? A team moves a ticket-allocation service from MySQL InnoDB default Repeatable Read to Postgres default Read Committed . The code does SELECT COUNT FROM tickets WHERE event id=? AND status='sold' , then inserts a sale if below capacity. In MySQL staging they never oversold. After cutover at 1,200 req/s, event 311 capacity 500 shows 507 sold. Nobody changed the SQL. Logs show no errors and no deadlocks.

title: Check-then-act
text: What is wrong, and what is the cheapest correct fix? Product asks: "usernames must be unique, case-insensitive". The signup handler runs SELECT 1 FROM users WHERE lower name =lower $1 , and if no row, INSERT INTO users name, ... . At 40 signups/s it has worked for a year. During a marketing campaign 400 signups/s support finds two accounts, Priya and priya . The table has a plain unique index on name . A teammate says "just use Serializable".

title: Serializable Snapshot Isolation
text: How does Postgres implement Serializable, and what must the application do to use it correctly? Postgres uses Serializable Snapshot Isolation. Transactions run on snapshots without extra blocking, while the engine tracks read-write dependencies with SIREAD predicate locks. When it sees a dangerous structure, two consecutive rw-dependencies, it aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE 40001. The application must retry the whole transaction.

title: Choosing a level
text: What do you change, and what would you tell product about the design trade-off? A flash-sale seat service sells 100,000 seats, launch traffic 5,000 req/s, many people fighting for the same popular seats. The booking transaction today is Serializable with a retry loop: it reads SELECT holder FROM seats WHERE id=$1 , checks null, then updates. At 500 req/s in the last event it worked. In the load test at 5,000 req/s: p50 40 ms, p99 2.8 s pg stat database xact rollback: 38% of transactions app log: ERROR could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies 40001 retries per request avg 3.4, max 5 then 500 CPU on the DB is 55%.

title: Mixed levels
text: Why does Serializable not protect the rule? Fix it. A team protects the "at most 3 active projects per workspace" rule with Serializable in the API path create project . Violations still occur workspace 88 has 5 . Code review shows: api path with conn.transaction isolation="serializable" : n = conn.execute "SELECT count FROM projects WHERE ws=%s AND active", ws, .fetchone 0 if n = 3: raise Limit conn.execute "INSERT INTO projects ws, active VALUES %s, true ", ws, import job batch, default isolation conn.execute "INSERT INTO projects ws, active SELECT %s, true FROM staging WHERE ...", ws, Postgres log shows no 40001 for workspace 88.

title: Serialization failures
text: Triage and fix. After a deploy that set default transaction isolation = 'serializable' for a 6-node API fleet, error rate climbs. Metrics: 5xx: 0.2% - 4.7% in 20 minutes Postgres log: ERROR: could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions HINT: The transaction might succeed if retried. pg locks: 410k rows of mode SIReadLock, 'relation' granularity on orders shared memory warning: out of shared memory max pred locks per transaction Only the orders service has retry logic. A big nightly-style report query is running during business hours.

title: Concurrency testing
text: What do you present? Postmortem: a meeting-room booking service double-booked room R7 for 14:00. Two requests arrived 3 ms apart. Code does SELECT ... WHERE room=? AND tstzrange overlaps then inserts. Unit tests passed; staging never reproduced it. The incident review asks for 1 a root cause, 2 a fix that prevents recurrence in the database, and 3 a test that would have caught it.

title: MVCC
text: How does MVCC work in Postgres, and what does it cost? Postgres never updates a row in place. An UPDATE inserts a new tuple version and stamps the old one's xmax. Each query uses a snapshot of which transactions were committed, so readers see the old version while the writer builds the new one. Readers never block writers and vice versa; only two writers on the same row wait. The cost is dead tuples that VACUUM must reclaim.

title: Lock modes
text: What table-level lock modes does Postgres have, and which statements take the strong ones? Weakest to strongest: ACCESS SHARE plain SELECT , ROW SHARE and ROW EXCLUSIVE FOR UPDATE, DML , SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE VACUUM, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY , SHARE plain CREATE INDEX, blocks writes , and ACCESS EXCLUSIVE most ALTER TABLE, DROP, TRUNCATE, VACUUM FULL , which blocks even SELECT. Row locks are separate and live in the tuple header.

title: SKIP LOCKED queue
text: What is the bug and what is the better query? A team uses a Postgres jobs table as a queue with 10 workers. Duplicate processing is reported: the same job id ran on two workers about 1 in 2,000 times. Each worker runs: BEGIN; SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status='pending' ORDER BY id LIMIT 50; -- app loops over ids UPDATE jobs SET status='running', worker='w3' WHERE id = ANY $ids ; COMMIT; The throughput is only 200 jobs/s. A teammate suggests adding Redis locks.

title: Row locking variants
text: Compare FOR UPDATE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR SHARE, FOR KEY SHARE, NOWAIT and SKIP LOCKED. FOR UPDATE is the strongest: blocks other writers and lockers on the row. FOR NO KEY UPDATE is for updates that do not change key columns and does not block FK checks, which take FOR KEY SHARE; a normal UPDATE takes it automatically. FOR SHARE and FOR KEY SHARE block writers but allow other sharers. NOWAIT errors immediately if locked; SKIP LOCKED ignores locked rows, ideal for queues.

title: DDL lock queue
text: Explain the outage and give the safe procedure. At 14:02 a deploy runs ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN locale text; on a 60M-row table. Within 20 seconds the API returns 503s, the pool is exhausted at 200/200. Monitoring: pg stat activity state / wait : 1 active SELECT ... FROM users ... running 8 min -- analytics export 1 active ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN locale text Lock: relation 187 active SELECT/UPDATE users ... Lock: relation CPU 12%, IOPS normal. The team believes adding a nullable column is instant.

title: Deadlock diagnosis
text: Why does this happen and how do you remove it? A transfer endpoint moves money between two accounts. At 600 transfers/s, about 15 deadlocks per minute appear. Log excerpt: ERROR: deadlock detected DETAIL: Process 4417 waits for ShareLock on transaction 8801923; blocked by process 4421. Process 4421 waits for ShareLock on transaction 8801920; blocked by process 4417. CONTEXT: while updating tuple 21,4 in relation "accounts" STATEMENT: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 10 WHERE id = 2 Code: UPDATE accounts ... id = from; UPDATE accounts ... id = to; . The team wants to raise deadlock timeout .

title: Deadlocks
text: What is a deadlock, how does Postgres handle it, and how is it different from a long lock wait? A deadlock is a cycle of waits, A holds X wanting Y, B holds Y wanting X. After deadlock timeout default 1 s Postgres finds the cycle, aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE 40P01 and the other proceeds. A long wait is a chain with no cycle: someone is just slow, and the timeout never aborts it.

title: Advisory locks and poolers
text: Explain both failures and fix the design. A nightly "close the books" job runs on one of 4 app instances. To avoid double runs it calls SELECT pg try advisory lock 42 at start and pg advisory unlock 42 at the end, over PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode. Two weeks in: some nights the job never runs try lock returns false on every instance , other nights it runs twice. pg locks shows: locktype objid mode granted pid advisory 42 ExclusiveLock t 5523 idle, connection in pool, no client Nobody holds the job now.

title: Optimistic vs pessimistic
text: Compare optimistic and pessimistic concurrency control and say when each is right. Pessimistic locks first FOR UPDATE and prevents conflict; optimistic does no locking, remembers a version, and at write time updates only if the version is unchanged, retrying on zero rows. Use pessimistic for short transactions with frequent conflicts; use optimistic when conflicts are rare or when a human thinks between read and write, so no lock or transaction can stay open.

title: Hot row
text: What do you do now and what do you build for 10x? A video platform keeps videos.view count updated per view: UPDATE videos SET view count = view count + 1 WHERE id=$1 . At 500 views/s total it was fine. A viral video now gets 12,000 views/s on one row. Symptoms: p99 latency of that endpoint 6 s; pool 100/100 busy pg stat activity: 94 sessions wait event Lock:transactionid all updating id=9001 WAL 40 MB/s; table videos has 3x bloat on hot pages Other videos are fine. A teammate proposes optimistic locking with a version column.

title: Safe migrations
text: Give a step-by-step plan for each change with the lock each takes. Orders table: 200 GB, 400M rows, 2,500 writes/s, zero downtime allowed. Required changes: 1 add index on user id , 2 add CHECK total = 0 , 3 add column channel text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'web' , 4 change status from varchar 20 to an enum. The index build takes about 30 minutes in staging.

title: Lock escalation and foreign keys
text: Does Postgres escalate row locks to table locks? Which operations take table-wide locks that surprise people? No. Postgres stores row locks in the tuple header so there is no lock-table memory pressure to escalate from. But several operations take table locks: most ALTER TABLE forms ACCESS EXCLUSIVE , CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY blocks writes , VACUUM FULL, CLUSTER, TRUNCATE, non-concurrent REINDEX. Foreign keys add row locks on parent rows, which can cause contention.

title: Distributed locking
text: What are the design flaws, and how do you make double payment impossible? A payout service uses pg advisory xact lock hashtext 'merchant:' id so only one worker pays a merchant at a time. A worker took the lock, then hit a 70 second GC pause while calling the bank API. Its transaction was killed by idle in transaction session timeout=30s ; another worker took the lock and paid. The first worker woke up and its API call went through too. Merchant 5521 was paid twice INR 4.2 lakh . w1: lock acquired 02:00:01 ... pause ... bank call at 02:01:15 - paid w2: lock acquired 02:00:40 - bank call at 02:00:42 - paid

title: Batch upsert deadlocks
text: What do you present? Two services, pricing-sync and inventory-sync , both bulk upsert into sku stats 6M rows with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT sku DO UPDATE in batches of 5,000, concurrently, every 10 minutes. Since a data-source change, the jobs fail about 30% of the time: ERROR: deadlock detected DETAIL: Process 901 waits for ShareLock on transaction 77120044; blocked by process 877. Process 877 waits for ShareLock on transaction 77120037; blocked by process 901. CONTEXT: while inserting index tuple 88213,5 in relation "sku stats pkey" A previous fix attempt, retrying the whole job, made the job time 4x longer. Incident review asks for the root cause and prevention.

title: Pages and heap
text: How does Postgres physically store a table, and how does an index find a row? A table is a heap: a file of 8 KB pages, with rows packed in arrival order, not sorted by key. Each row has a ctid page number, slot . Indexes store ctids, so an index lookup goes to the page, then the slot via a line pointer. Large values go to TOAST.

title: Buffer pool
text: What are shared buffers and the OS page cache, and how do you tell whether memory is the bottleneck? shared buffers is Postgres's own page cache. A read goes to shared buffers, then the OS page cache, then disk. A common start is about 25% of RAM, leaving the rest for the OS cache, work mem and connections. I check hit ratio, EXPLAIN ANALYZE, BUFFERS showing shared hit vs read, and iowait.

title: Row size estimation
text: Is 56 GB right? Estimate the real heap size and say what you would do about it. A new page views table has columns: id bigint , user id bigint , url id int , ts timestamptz , ua id smallint , about 28 B of data. Expected 2 billion rows in the first year. Finance asks for a disk estimate. Someone computed "28 B x 2B = 56 GB". Also, a query SELECT count on a 10M-row staging copy reads 780 MB.

title: Write-ahead log
text: Why does Postgres write a WAL, and what happens step by step on an UPDATE and COMMIT? The WAL is an append-only log of changes written before the data page reaches disk. An UPDATE modifies the page in shared buffers dirty , appends a WAL record with an LSN, and at COMMIT the WAL is flushed with fsync before I get an acknowledgement. Data pages are written later by the bgwriter or a checkpoint. That turns many random page writes into one sequential log append.

title: Checkpoint I/O spikes
text: Diagnose and fix. Latency on a 4 TB OLTP database spikes every few minutes. p99 goes from 12 ms to 700 ms for about 40 seconds. Log and stats: LOG: checkpoint starting: wal LOG: checkpoint complete: wrote 612000 buffers 46.7% ; write=38.1 s, sync=1.2 s checkpoints timed = 41, checkpoints req = 3,820 since reset settings: max wal size = 1GB, checkpoint timeout = 5min, checkpoint completion target = 0.9 WAL generation about 25 MB/s; disk: iowait 70% during spikes The team proposes lowering the checkpoint timeout "for safety".

title: Checkpoints
text: What is a checkpoint, what triggers it, and what trade-off do the settings control? A checkpoint flushes all pages dirtied before a point in the WAL, then records that point, so crash recovery only replays WAL after it. It triggers on checkpoint timeout default 5 min or when WAL approaches max wal size . Writes are spread over checkpoint completion target of the interval. Frequent checkpoints give faster recovery but more I/O and WAL; rare ones the reverse.

title: WAL disk growth
text: What do you do right now, and how do you prevent it? 03:10 alert: primary disk 96% full. pg wal is 1.4 TB while max wal size is 16 GB. Archiving is healthy. Findings: SELECT slot name, active, restart lsn, pg size pretty pg wal lsn diff pg current wal lsn , restart lsn FROM pg replication slots; slot name active retained debezium 1 f 1.38 TB replica a t 12 MB The CDC consumer was decommissioned 3 days ago. Disk fills in about 40 minutes. A teammate wants to delete old files from pg wal .

title: Crash recovery
text: Walk through what Postgres does after a crash. Why does it not need an undo phase? On startup Postgres reads pg control to find the last checkpoint's redo LSN and replays every WAL record after it, bringing data files to the state at the crash. Transactions that did not commit simply stay invisible because their xids never became committed in pg xact , so there is no undo pass. The cost of that design is that dead versions need VACUUM.

title: Bloat
