text: Why can't vacuum clean up, and what is the plan? The sessions table has a stable 2M live rows but is 38 GB and growing 1 GB/day. Queries slow down. Data: relname n live tup n dead tup last autovacuum sessions 2,010,000 61,000,000 2026-11-08 02:11 pg stat activity: pid 3310 idle in transaction xact start 2026-11-07 17:40 BI tool autovacuum log: "tuples: 0 removed, 61000000 are dead but not yet removable, oldest xmin: 884412001" Autovacuum is running, yet nothing is removed. Ops want to run VACUUM FULL now.

title: VACUUM and wraparound
text: What does VACUUM do, why does Postgres need it, and what is transaction ID wraparound? UPDATE and DELETE leave old tuple versions. VACUUM finds those no snapshot can see, marks the space reusable the file does not shrink , updates the visibility and free-space maps, and freezes old xids. Xids are 32 bit, so after about 2 billion transactions old rows must be frozen or they would appear to be in the future; if autovacuum falls behind, Postgres eventually refuses writes to protect data.

title: Wraparound
text: Recover, then explain how this happened and how to prevent it. Writes start failing on a 6 TB primary: ERROR: database is not accepting commands to avoid wraparound data loss in database "app" HINT: Stop the postmaster and vacuum that database in single-user mode. SELECT datname, age datfrozenxid : app 2,146,100,000 Autovacuum workers: 3 running on 'events' 4.1 TB , each at 8% progress after 6 days autovacuum vacuum cost limit = 200 default , prepared transaction 'tx 77' open for 11 days Reads still work. Business is down for writes.

title: Capacity sizing
text: Produce the sizing and the key settings, with reasoning. Plan infrastructure for an orders table: 200M rows at 1,000 writes/s, 150 B per row, four indexes. Hot data is the last 30 days. Finance wants a disk, RAM and WAL plan for a 32 GB box. Last year's attempt provisioned 40 GB heap only and ran out of space in 5 months.

title: Config review
text: Review this file: what is wrong, what would you set, and why? A new 64 GB primary is configured by a script. After go-live: random OOM kills, slow commits ruled out, and replicas diverge after a power test. The config: shared buffers = 52GB work mem = 512MB max connections = 400 effective cache size = 8GB fsync = off full page writes = off checkpoint timeout = 30s maintenance work mem = 4GB autovacuum = off Logs: Out of memory: Killed process 2210 postgres , and after the power test, invalid page in block 4181 of relation base/16384/20871 .

title: Retention deletes
text: Redesign retention without downtime and explain the migration. An events table holds 1.2 TB, 90 days of data, 15,000 inserts/s. A nightly job runs DELETE FROM events WHERE ts < now - interval '90 days' and now takes 7 hours, generating 400 GB of WAL, spiking replica lag to 40 minutes and leaving the table at 1.6 TB with high dead tuples. Autovacuum runs most of the day. Product wants to keep exactly 90 days.

title: Why replicate
text: We have a Postgres primary. Why would you add replicas, and what will replicas not fix? I add replicas for three reasons: high availability so a copy can take over, read scaling by sending read-only queries to copies, and isolation so reports and backups do not hurt production. They do not raise write throughput, because in Postgres only one primary accepts writes and every replica must replay all of them.

title: Sync vs async replication
text: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous streaming replication in Postgres, and what does each cost you? In async, COMMIT returns after the primary flushes its own WAL; if the primary dies, the last few commits may not have reached a standby, so RPO is above zero. In sync, COMMIT also waits for a standby, so RPO is zero but every commit pays a network round trip, and if the sync standbys are all down, writes block.

title: Physical vs logical replication
text: Physical streaming replication and logical replication both copy data between Postgres servers. When do you use which? Physical replication ships WAL byte for byte, so the standby is an exact binary copy of the whole cluster on the same major version. That is what I use for HA and read replicas. Logical replication ships decoded row changes per table through publish/subscribe, so it can cross major versions, replicate a subset, and feed CDC like Debezium, but it does not copy DDL or sequences.

title: Replica lag and read-your-writes
text: How do you diagnose and fix this? A social app routes all SELECTs to 2 replicas and writes to the primary. After a release, support tickets say "I posted a comment, refreshed, and it vanished, then it came back". Primary: 1,500 writes/s. Replicas look healthy, CPU 40%. A quick check shows: application name state replay lag replica1 streaming 00:00:00.004 replica2 streaming 00:00:02.800 Replica2 runs nightly-style reports during the day too. The release added a "load comments" call fired immediately after POST. A red herring: the CDN also caches the comments API for 5 seconds.

title: PgBouncer transaction mode
text: What is wrong and how would you fix it? A Java service moved behind PgBouncer to cut connections. After the rollout, intermittent errors appear: "prepared statement S 12 does not exist", jobs occasionally run twice, and a SET statement timeout seems ignored. Config and code: ; pgbouncer.ini pgbouncer pool mode = transaction max client conn = 3000 default pool size = 30 // worker startup runs once per connection stmt.execute "SET statement timeout = '5s'" ; // job lock stmt.execute "SELECT pg advisory lock 42 " ; doWork ; stmt.execute "SELECT pg advisory unlock 42 " ; Red herring: CPU on Postgres is at 30%, so "capacity" is not the problem.

title: Logical vs physical backups
text: Compare pg dump and physical base backups. Which would you use for a 1 TB production database and why? pg dump is a logical, portable export that can restore one table or move across versions, but restore replays inserts and rebuilds indexes, so for 1 TB it takes many hours. A physical base backup copies the data files, restores about as fast as the copy, and with WAL archiving gives point-in-time recovery. For production I use physical pgBackRest or similar and keep pg dump only for small targeted or cross-version needs.

title: PITR after a bad DELETE
text: What do you do? At 10:42 UTC an engineer ran DELETE FROM orders; on production no WHERE . It was noticed at 10:50. The database is 1.2 TB, the app takes about 300 writes/s, WAL archiving to object storage with pgBackRest is on, last full backup was at 02:00, and the replica is already identical it replayed the delete . Business wants orders back and as little downtime as possible. Another team suggests failing over to the replica.

title: Replica query conflicts
text: A long report on a hot standby gets "canceling statement due to conflict with recovery". Why does that happen and what are your options? The primary's VACUUM removes dead row versions and writes that to WAL. If the standby's query still needs those versions, replay would break its snapshot. Postgres either delays replay up to max standby streaming delay default 30 s and then cancels the query. I can raise the delay on a dedicated reporting replica, or turn on hot standby feedback so the primary keeps rows, at the cost of bloat.

title: Replication slot disk fill
text: Walk through your response. 3 a.m. page: the primary's data volume is 96% full and growing at about 4 GB/h. Normal database growth is 1 GB/day. df shows the pg wal directory at 380 GB usually 4 GB . slot name active restart lsn wal status replica old f 5/1A000000 extended replica1 t 8/F2000000 reserved Last week a team decommissioned a staging replica replica old but nobody dropped its slot. Red herring: archive command also shows a few failures from the same night.

title: Failover design
text: Design automatic failover for a Postgres primary with two standbys. What stops split brain? I need five pieces: failure detection with a tolerant timeout, leader election in a consensus store like etcd so only one node can win, promotion of the best standby, client routing through HAProxy or a virtual IP, and fencing so the old primary cannot take writes. Patroni implements this: the leader holds a key with a TTL, and if it cannot renew, it demotes itself.

title: False failover and split brain
text: Lead the post-incident review. What failed, how do you recover data, and what changes? A self-managed cluster primary A, standbys B and C, scripted failover with a VIP, no consensus store had a 40-second network blip between the monitor and A. The script promoted B and moved the VIP. A kept running and still had 120 app connections pinned by IP. Over 11 minutes, A accepted 18,000 writes and B accepted 41,000. Detected when two customers saw different balances. monitor: A unreachable x3 30s - promote B A: still accepting connections on 10.0.0.5 timelines diverged at LSN 4/9A000000 Red herring: the engineers first suspected data corruption on B.

title: Connection storm and pooling
text: What do you recommend? A 16-core, 64 GB Postgres runs behind 100 pods, each with a HikariCP pool of 20 2,000 connections . max connections = 2200 . Every deploy, p99 jumps from 40 ms to 4 s for 3 minutes, and logs show: FATAL: sorry, too many clients already vmstat: r=180 cs=420000 us=55 sy=35 pg stat activity: 1,950 rows, 40 active, 1,900 idle Traffic is about to grow 10x and the team proposes max connections = 10000 and a bigger instance.

title: Major upgrade via logical replication
text: Plan the migration. Postgres 12 3 TB, 2,500 writes/s, 200 tables must reach 16 with a cutover window under 60 seconds. Business forbids a 6-hour dump/restore. Known facts: 14 tables have no primary key, the app uses sequences heavily, there is a monthly ALTER TABLE migration, and the primary has 20% IO headroom. A trial subscription copied 2.1 TB but UPDATEs on a keyless table errored on the publisher. ERROR: cannot update table "audit log" because it does not have a replica identity and publishes updates

title: Backup strategy and cost
text: Redesign the backup approach and justify the cost. Current setup: nightly pg dump of a 1.5 TB database to a bucket in the same cloud account, taking 7 hours and using 1 TB of storage per copy at 30 copies retained cost about 30 TB . Last quarter's untested restore attempt ran for 19 hours. The new RPO target is 5 minutes, RTO 2 hours. Budget is flat. An engineer proposes "just add a replica, it is a backup".

title: Partitioning vs sharding
text: What is the difference between partitioning and sharding, and in what order would you reach for scaling options? Partitioning splits a table into pieces inside one database server; sharding splits it across several servers. I climb a ladder: fix queries and indexes, add pooling, scale up, add replicas and caching, partition, split by service, and only then shard. Steps up to partitioning and functional split are mostly reversible; sharding is a one-way door.

title: CAP and PACELC
text: Explain CAP and PACELC without saying "pick two of three". CAP says that during a network partition a replicated system must choose between consistency and availability; since partitions happen, the real choice is CP versus AP when they do. PACELC adds that even with no partition you trade latency against consistency, because synchronous coordination costs time.

title: Choosing a NoSQL family
text: How do you choose between key-value, wide-column, document, graph and search stores? I start from the access pattern. Key lookups at huge throughput point to key-value; massive write streams read by a partition key point to wide-column; aggregate-shaped flexible JSON points to document; relationship traversal to graph; full text and faceting to a search engine. If I need ad-hoc relational queries and transactions I stay on Postgres.

title: Shard key selection
text: Which shard key and strategy do you pick? A B2B SaaS has 4 TB across 6,000 tenants; the top tenant is 9% of rows and the top 10 are 35%. Queries: 85% are per-tenant, 10% are admin-wide reports, 5% are cross-tenant joins for partner features. Writes: 12,000/s. Proposed keys: user id hash, tenant id hash, created at range, and country . Target: no shard above 500 GB.

title: Orphaned prepared transactions
text: What is happening and what do you do? An internal XA-style coordinator performs transfers across two Postgres databases. At 14:05 the coordinator host was OOM-killed mid-run. By 14:40: table bloat alarm, a few updates hang, and autovacuum does not shrink dead tuples. gid prepared owner tx-8841 2026-11-09 14:05:11 app tx-8849 2026-11-09 14:05:12 app SHOW max prepared transactions; - 100 oldest xmin age: 12.4M and growing Red herring: someone blames a recent index migration.

title: Sharded IDs and cross-shard queries
text: List the bugs and the fixes. After sharding orders into 4 Postgres shards by hash customer id % 4 , these bugs reached production within a week. routing def shard for customer id : return hash customer id % 4 Python's built-in hash on str id generation each shard has its own SERIAL starting at 1 INSERT INTO orders customer id, total VALUES %s, %s RETURNING id; admin page for shard in shards: rows += shard.query "SELECT FROM orders ORDER BY created at DESC LIMIT 50" return rows :50 lookup by order id shard = shard for order id Symptoms: customers see someone else's order on /orders/17 ; some customers' data vanished after a deploy; the admin list misses recent rows and order is odd. Red herring: a team member suspects replication lag.

title: Two-phase commit vs sagas
text: How does two-phase commit work, why is it avoided across services, and what do you use instead? In 2PC a coordinator asks every participant to PREPARE, meaning make the transaction durable and promise it can commit; if all say yes it logs the decision and sends COMMIT, otherwise ABORT. The problem is blocking: if the coordinator dies after PREPARE, participants hold locks until it returns. It also adds round trips and requires all participants up. Instead I use sagas with compensating actions, or an outbox with idempotent consumers, or design so a transaction stays within one shard.

title: DynamoDB hot partition
text: Why is it throttling and how do you fix it? A DynamoDB table events partition key date , e.g. "2026-11-09", sort key event id is provisioned at 20,000 WCU. At peak the app receives ProvisionedThroughputExceededException while CloudWatch shows consumed capacity at only 4,000 WCU, about 20% of provisioned. Writes: 5,000/s all stamped with today's date. Red herring: the team suspects the SDK retry config.

title: Raft quorum and cluster sizing
text: How does Raft commit a write, and why do you run 3 or 5 nodes rather than 4? One leader per term appends the write to its log and replicates it to followers; once a majority has it durably, the entry is committed and acknowledged. The group tolerates f failures with 2f+1 nodes, so 3 tolerate one and 5 tolerate two. A fourth node adds cost but still tolerates only one failure, since a majority of 4 is 3.

title: Multi-region CockroachDB latency and retries
text: Diagnose and propose changes. A payments service moved from Postgres to a 9-node CockroachDB cluster across us-east, eu-west and ap-south 3 nodes each , default replica placement, serializable isolation. After the move: p50 write 4 ms became 140 ms; p99 under contention 2.5 s; clients log restart transaction: TransactionRetryWithProtoRefreshError SQLSTATE 40001 about 3% of the time; a hot "balance summary" row is updated by many transactions. EXPLAIN ANALYZE: ... round trips to leaseholder in eu-west for rows owned by US users Red herring: someone says "CPU is only 20%, so the cluster has headroom".

title: LSM trees vs B-trees
text: Explain how an LSM tree handles writes and reads, and when you would choose it over a B-tree. An LSM writes to a WAL and an in-memory memtable, flushes sorted immutable SSTables, and compacts them in the background. Writes are sequential and cheap; reads may touch several files, helped by Bloom filters. A B-tree updates pages in place: better point reads and range scans, but random IO on writes. I choose LSM for write-heavy ingest like time series and messaging, and B-tree for read-heavy general OLTP.

title: Compaction backlog
text: What is going on and what do you do? A 12-node Cassandra cluster ingests 150,000 writes/s of sensor data. After a marketing spike doubled ingestion, read p99 went from 8 ms to 900 ms, and disk usage climbs 4% per hour. nodetool shows: Pending compactions: 1,840 SSTables per read p99 : 38 Write latency: normal 2 ms Disk: 78% used, compaction output needs space Red herring: GC pauses look normal, and CPU is 55%.

title: Live resharding
text: How do you reshard? A 6 TB orders table lives on 4 shards hash customer id % 4, no logical shards . Each shard hits 85% disk and 70% CPU; growth is 12% per month. Business wants no downtime beyond 30 s and no lost writes. Moving to 8 shards by changing the modulus would relocate about half of the data, and the app has the shard count hard-coded in 14 services.

title: Ambiguous scaling request
text: How do you respond? The CTO says: "We keep getting slow and need to scale; let's move to Cassandra or Cockroach." Facts you find: Postgres 15 on one 16-core, 128 GB node, 1.1 TB data, 1,800 writes/s peak, 9,000 reads/s. A top query does a seq scan on a 300M-row table, 2,400 connections open directly from the app, one 4 TB reporting join runs hourly on the primary, and p99 is 1.8 s. Replicas: none. Last quarter's outages were related to connection exhaustion.
